nodes.label: Research booklet
nodes.text: Virtual Validation of a Collision Mitigation System for Heavy Off-Road Machines — pre-project research: thirteen questions answered from the published evidence (October 2026).

nodes.label: Glossary & prerequisites
nodes.text: Glossary and Prerequisites — a plain-language companion to the research booklet: every term, acronym, standard, tool, method and organization explained from zero. The research booklet answers thirteen questions about how to prove that an automatic braking system on a heavy machine is safe, using simulation as much as possible, on a short timeline. It was written for engineers. This companion is for everyone else, and for engineers who are new to one of the fields it touches: mining and construction operations, safety engineering, sensors, simulation, vehicle physics, statistics, standards and regulation, tools, and project planning. It assumes no background. Every technical term, acronym, standard, tool, method and organization in the booklet is explained from zero, in plain English, with an everyday comparison and an example from a mine, quarry or construction site. Entries say how the booklet uses the term and what the booklet concluded about it, with the chapter number in brackets, so that this document can also be used as a map back into the b

nodes.label: Introduction & synthesis
nodes.text: Booklet front matter: introduction, research map and cross-chapter synthesis. This section pulls together what the thirteen chapters say, organized around the five challenge questions and the cross-cutting constraints. It is a map of the evidence, not a plan. Chapter numbers in parentheses point to the detail.

nodes.label: Chapter 1: The full range of options
nodes.text: Chapter 1 of the booklet: The full range of options. What every documented way of shortening the validation of a sensor-based automatic braking function can and cannot deliver, how the approaches are combined in practice, what resists compression, and what a team starting in October 2026 can realistically have working by mid-2027.

nodes.label: Chapter 2: Precedents and realistic timelines
nodes.text: Chapter 2 of the booklet: Precedents and realistic timelines. Who has already validated collision warning or automatic braking with less physical testing, how long it took, where it failed, and what that implies for a four-month validation window in 2027.

nodes.label: Chapter 3: Rules and acceptance criteria
nodes.text: Chapter 3 of the booklet: Rules and acceptance criteria. Which standards and regulations govern collision warning and automatic braking on heavy off-road machines, what counts as passing, and whether simulation is accepted as evidence.

nodes.label: Chapter 4: Real accidents and operator behavior
nodes.text: Chapter 4 of the booklet: Real accidents and operator behavior. What accident records from several countries say about who gets hit by heavy off-road machines and how, how operators really respond to proximity warnings, and which new hazards automatic braking brings with it.

nodes.label: Chapter 5: Creating virtual job sites
nodes.text: Chapter 5 of the booklet: Creating virtual job sites. Every documented way to build virtual 3D job sites for sensor and machine testing, from hand-built models and procedural rules to survey capture, machine-log reconstruction and neural or generative scenes, what each one costs in effort and gives in accuracy, what an environment needs beyond appearance, whether field recordings can be turned into test sites, how teams decide when they have enough sites, and which published off-road examples exist.

nodes.label: Chapter 6: Simulating sensors, weather, and light
nodes.text: Chapter 6 of the booklet: Simulating sensors, weather, and light. How well today's methods can simulate cameras, radar, lidar, ultrasonic and thermal sensors on a heavy machine in rain, snow, fog, dust, mud, glare and darkness, and how that realism is proven.

nodes.label: Chapter 7: Testing the old and the new system
nodes.text: Chapter 7 of the booklet: Testing the old and the new system. How to measure the existing detection and warning system as a baseline without driving the machine, how to compare the new braking system against it fairly when sensors, positions or software differ, and what has to be recorded now for any of this to be possible.

nodes.label: Chapter 8: Machine motion and brake timing
nodes.text: Chapter 8 of the booklet: Machine motion and brake timing. How heavy off-road machines actually stop, which models predict it well enough, and how the moment of automatic braking is decided, tested and tuned.

nodes.label: Chapter 9: Covering the combinations and tuning
nodes.text: Chapter 9 of the booklet: Covering the combinations and tuning. How to test a very large space of site, weather, light, machine and sensor combinations with a limited number of runs, what can honestly be claimed from the results, and how to use them to tune the system without over-fitting.

nodes.label: Chapter 10: When simulation can be trusted
nodes.text: Chapter 10 of the booklet: When simulation can be trusted. What makes simulation results acceptable as evidence for a safety decision on an automatic-braking function for heavy off-road machines, how agreement between simulation and physical tests is measured, and how much physical testing has to remain.

nodes.label: Chapter 11: Tools, vendors, and cost
nodes.text: Chapter 11 of the booklet: Tools, vendors, and cost. A neutral map of the simulation tools, open-source projects and service providers available for virtual testing of driver-assistance and autonomy functions on heavy off-road machines, what each is proven to do, what the market will and will not say about prices, and what it costs in compute, people and risk to build this capability.

nodes.label: Chapter 12: Planning and presenting the plan
nodes.text: Chapter 12 of the booklet: Planning and presenting the plan. How to plan an eleven-month, first-of-a-kind virtual-validation programme under a hard deadline, estimate it honestly, tie every work package to the safety evidence it must produce, and present the result so that skeptical engineers, safety specialists and executives accept it.

nodes.label: Chapter 13: The skeptic's review
nodes.text: Chapter 13 of the booklet: The skeptic's review. What a hostile but fair review panel would say about the plan to replace most physical validation with virtual testing inside a four-month window, and what evidence would answer each objection.

nodes.label: Glossary Part A: Machines & job sites
nodes.text: Glossary Part A: Machines & job sites. This part gives the vocabulary of the workplace: the machines, the places they work, the people around them, the accidents that happen, and the systems that warn or brake. It ends with the project words that the booklet uses on almost every page, such as the validation window and the sensor freeze. Everything else in the glossary builds on this part.

nodes.label: Glossary Part B: Safety engineering
nodes.text: Glossary Part B: Safety engineering. Safety engineering has its own grammar: hazard, risk, requirement, safety function, evidence, acceptance, release. This part explains that grammar and the two families of safety thinking that the booklet relies on, functional safety (what if a component fails) and safety of the intended functionality (what if nothing fails but the system still gets it wrong). It also covers the safety case, the document in which everything is argued, and the way a project is reviewed and released in stages.

nodes.label: Glossary Part C: Sensors & perception
nodes.text: Glossary Part C: Sensors & perception. A braking system can only act on what it detects. This part explains each sensor type, what it measures, how it fails in dust, fog, snow, darkness and glare, and how detections are judged (the four outcomes, precision and recall). It then covers the data side: ground truth, labels, machine-learning detectors, synthetic data, and what must be recorded on a machine so that the recordings can be replayed later.

nodes.label: Glossary Part D: Simulation & X-in-the-loop
nodes.text: Glossary Part D: Simulation & X-in-the-loop. This part is the heart of the glossary. It starts with what a model and a simulation are, how a virtual job site is built, and the file standards that describe scenes and scenarios. It then walks up the ladder of test methods from model-in-the-loop to shadow mode and the proving ground, and explains the two ideas that decide what each method can prove: open loop versus closed loop, and the sim-to-real gap.

nodes.label: Glossary Part E: Motion & braking
nodes.text: Glossary Part E: Motion & braking. Stopping a loaded machine is physics. This part works through mass, speed, grade, surface and brake delays to the stopping distance, then turns the result around to find how far a sensor must see. It also explains how the decision to warn or brake is made, how interventions are staged, and why hard automatic braking is itself a hazard that has to be designed for.

nodes.label: Glossary Part F: Test design & statistics
nodes.text: Glossary Part F: Test design & statistics. No campaign can test every combination of site, machine, weather, speed and object. This part explains how tests are chosen, what a set of results can prove, and how to keep the honest numbers separate from the failure hunting. It also covers tuning: adjusting thresholds and zones for several goals at once without fitting them to the test set, and carrying settings across machine models.

nodes.label: Glossary Part G: Simulation credibility
nodes.text: Glossary Part G: Simulation credibility. A simulation is trusted only within the envelope where it has been checked against reality. This part explains the frameworks that aerospace, medicine, nuclear power, rail and car regulation use to decide when a model is credible, the metrics used to compare simulated and measured results, and the documented cases where simulation gave false confidence. It ends with what a safety board or outside assessor expects to see.

nodes.label: Glossary Part H: Standards & precedents
nodes.text: Glossary Part H: Standards & precedents. This part has three runs of entries. The first explains what standards and regulations are and how they work. The second explains every standard and regulation the booklet names, with its status as of October 2026. The third covers the organizations, industry groups and precedent programs, from the mining round tables to the European research projects and the aviation and space cases that the booklet uses as lessons.

nodes.label: Glossary Part I: Tools, cost & planning
nodes.text: Glossary Part I: Tools, cost & planning. This part covers the practical side: the categories of simulation tools and the products the booklet lists in each, described neutrally; the computing they need and what it costs; and the vocabulary of planning and presenting a program under high uncertainty, from Gantt charts and P80 estimates to evidence gates, red teams and the one-page summary.

nodes.label: Heavy off-road machine
nodes.text: A heavy off-road machine is a very large, very heavy vehicle built to move earth, rock or materials on a job site rather than to travel on public roads.
nodes.synopsis: The manufacturer is developing automatic braking when an operator fails to react to a proximity warning; the principal documented fatal accident pattern is a large machine moving forward over an unseen person or light vehicle [f1, f2977]. Powered haulage accounted for 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal mining injuries (9%) in calendar 2025 [f2979, f2980]. Validation must span different machine sizes and sensor positions, potentially 100 or more sites and applications, while stopping depends heavily on terrain; machine types, brake systems and other essential manufacturer inputs remain unknown [f8256, f11376, f11374, f5863, f8]. The research found neither a complete numeric off-road automatic-braking type-approval test nor a standard accepting simulation instead of physical testing, although ISO 21815-1:2022 covers relevant machinery classes, ISO 3450:2011 specifies earth-moving brake performance tests, and South Africa’s Regulation 8.10 was the strongest explicit off-road automatic-braking mandate found [f2147, f7539, f2149, f10651, f2277]. Major evidence gaps include simulated stopping-distance validation on difficult terrain and public demonstrations combining heavy machines, varied geometries, more than 100 site types, severe weather, soiling and closed-loop braking; highway-to-quarry transfer remains uncertain, and road-vehicle mileage requirements do not transfer numerically [f3743, f4409, f45, f6664]. The roadmap faces a hard deadline and a first-time capability build: past physical testing and tuning took three to four years per model, no quantified off-road reduction in physical testing was found, and expert advice calls for representative sensors and machines before the final validation window [f9400, f9401, f7507, f7563, f4460].

nodes.label: Wheel loader
nodes.text: A wheel loader is a four-wheeled machine with a large bucket at the front that scoops up loose material and tips it into a truck or onto a pile.
nodes.synopsis: Wheel loaders are the booklet’s clearest nuisance-braking challenge because normal work can resemble a collision threat; its recommended starting domain is reverse-only, low-speed operation [f11395, f11397]. Vendor precedents are narrowly scoped: Volvo’s January 2023 system brakes in reverse at 3–15 km/h for 2–3 seconds on named models, while Cat’s May 2025 medium-loader system is reverse-only and can inhibit reverse engagement after at least 15 seconds stationary with an object in the critical zone [f1238, f1380, f356, f10637]. Front-end loaders were involved in 33% of 22 US surface-mine blind-area deaths from 2000 to mid-2006, but internationally comparable, exposure-adjusted rates were not found, so these counts cannot establish a reliable machine-type collision-rate ranking [f2985, f3238]. Virtual validation has some direct evidence—a 2025 radar hall experiment required manual material tuning and exposed missing double reflections, and a 2025 AGX digital twin was calibrated against a physical loader—but a 2024 digging simulation needed a friction coefficient of 2.0, flagged as a sim-to-field warning [f4421, f5049, f8292, f6090, f6376]. Major gaps remain in production-loader brake-delay distributions, peer-reviewed measured response times, production-scale vehicle-in-the-loop testing, and published vendor weather limits, false-intervention rates and validation methods [f252, f6065, f5342, f11394]. Safety planning must also account for abrupt-stop instability and operating exclusions: Komatsu advises disabling stop control on steep slopes, slippery or soft ground, with suspended loads and during trailer loading, while validated braking-related occupant-injury curves were not found [f10549, f10550, f3395].

nodes.label: Haul truck
nodes.text: A haul truck is a very large off-road dump truck that carries rock or ore from where it is dug to where it is dumped or processed.
nodes.synopsis: The fatality evidence points beyond object collisions: of 54 US haul-truck deaths in January 2005–June 2021, 21 involved berms, 12 dump points, 13 collisions with people or vehicles, and eight other causes; 12 of the 13 collision deaths involved forward movement [f2989, f2990]. Unintended braking can itself create serious hazards, including load shift, loss of traction, rollover or instability, and rear-end impacts from following trucks; shadow mode cannot establish whether a false stop causes such a collision [f1129, f8201, f596]. Sensor validation must address substantial blind areas and occlusion: a 50 t truck's front-right blind area extends at least 18 m, while a 2026 mine study reported only 5.0% lidar visible-region recovery for an occluded truck [f11403, f4357]. The evidence base remains limited: the 2022 NIOSH review found detection-reliability testing in only 13 of 99 metric instances, avoidance or intervention systems in only 10% of 97 cases, and only 8% of articles above technology readiness level 7; the booklet still identifies the 2006 radar study as its best hard false-alarm source [f5170, f5171, f5172, f5173]. December 2021 Wabtec tests demonstrated controlled deceleration up to 30 km/h but still required physical detection-zone adjustment, while modern machine-delay distributions and site reconstruction studies at large-machine sensor heights of 3–6 m were not found [f1345, f1247, f5899, f4382]. Validation also needs to cover operational failures rather than perception alone: 2019 autonomous-haulage collisions implicated communications and traction, and a WorkSafe WA report dated 7 March 2025 records trucks resuming movement after communications returned while operators misunderstood their mode; transferring on-road evidence to loaded haul trucks on gravel remains an open question [f1371, f10718, f11349].

nodes.label: Articulated hauler (ADT)
nodes.text: An articulated hauler, also called an articulated dump truck (ADT), is an off-road dump truck whose front and rear halves are joined by a hinge so it bends in the middle to steer.
nodes.synopsis: Articulated haulers steer through a hinge between their front and rear halves; although a straight, level stop can resemble simple-mass braking, a simple braking model cannot represent hinge dynamics, and braking during turns, on side slopes or at large articulation angles can cause rolling or swinging [f11411, f11412, f11419, f11413]. Bell's Pin 3 E-series integration capability dates to late 2020 and supports third-party PDS/CAS up to Level 9 through an ISO 21815-2 gateway, with laptop-based virtual integration testing; coverage depends on the supplier, and the research found no Bell-validated braking performance [f1390, f1687, f1690, f1688, f1689, f1691]. Scale and operating conditions matter: the Volvo A60 is about 44 t empty and 99 t gross, while regulatory worked examples give 30.82 m at 50 km/h for a 25 t ADT on level ground and 42.25 m at 32 km/h for a 60 t ADT tested at 50 t for a 13% site grade [f5961, f5985, f5986]. These examples are not automatic-braking validation: direct quantitative ADT automatic-braking data, modern production brake-delay distributions and published automatic-braking jackknife or roll data were not found, so response times and delay distributions must be measured [f6292, f5899, f11418, f6067, f6429]. Accident evidence also has a scope gap: a mining study analysed 54 fatality reports involving rigid or articulated haul trucks from January 2005 to June 2021, but construction-site ADTs have only aggregate struck-by evidence despite being within the required product coverage [f3070, f3660, f3661].

nodes.label: Excavator
nodes.text: An excavator is a digging machine with a long jointed arm and a bucket, mounted on a body that can rotate a full circle on top of its tracks or wheels.
nodes.synopsis: Excavators can strike people or trucks with their counterweight or working equipment during swing without travelling; swing contact can be fatal, but separate agency statistics quantifying its frequency or share of serious collisions were not found [f3377, f3579, f3380, f11424]. Rotation therefore needs distinct detection zones and interventions: ISO 21815-4 was under publication in October 2026 and addresses motion inhibition before rotation starts, expressly excluding avoidance through automatic braking [f11428, f11422, f15153]. Komatsu KomVision launched on the PC200-11 in Japan in December 2019, followed by the PC200i-12 in December 2024; it stops at travel or swing start rather than during ongoing swing, and must be disabled during trailer loading because a rapid stop can destabilize the machine [f1640, f1642, f11427]. Virtual evidence remains limited: the 2019 excavator safety algorithm used kinematic working-area prediction and time-to-collision-based modes but had no field comparison, and comprehensive production-scale excavator vehicle-in-the-loop testing was not found [f6204, f6366, f5342]. TERA couples excavator and terrain mechanics and compares track deformation and velocity with a real excavator, but is not an ISO 21815 braking study; virtual swing scenarios still need upper-structure kinematics [f3968, f3969, f4131, f4361]. Available tools include MathWorks R2026b excavator examples, but rendered excavator images retain a significant reality gap, and transferring braking settings between loaders and excavators requires justified machine similarity rather than assuming exchangeability [f8285, f10582, f7027, f14451].

nodes.label: Dozer and grader
nodes.text: A dozer pushes earth and rock with a wide blade at the front, and a grader levels and shapes road surfaces with a long angled blade under its body.
nodes.synopsis: Dozers and graders work slowly, reverse frequently and operate close to other machines; at tip heads, dozers and loaded trucks necessarily share tight working spaces [f11432, f3355]. Heavy-machine contacts are described as the most frequently reported collision type but rank seventh by harm, whereas reversing-over incidents involving small vehicles or pedestrians rank second; the 12 August 2019 Snapper fatality involved a reversing dozer whose operator did not know a light vehicle was present [f11440, f3552, f3519, f3116]. Barrick's 2015 trial found high nuisance alarms on blades and dozers working near equipment, and operators preferred a less intrusive awareness layer, supporting the requirement not to treat every nearby truck as an emergency [f10578, f10713, f11442]. Braking validation must account for tracked-machine stopping behavior: the glossary distinguishes track grip from tire grip and identifies ISO 10265 for slow crawler machines, while manufacturer specifications put the D11 dozer at 106,614 kg, approximately 107 t [f11441, f11438, f11439, f5963, f11372]. Important evidence gaps remain: production-scale off-road vehicle-in-the-loop testing, validated automatic-braking occupant-injury curves and safe jerk limits, and exposure-adjusted collision rates by machine type were not found, so the evidence does not establish comparative machine-type risk or safe automatic-stop thresholds [f5342, f3395, f3238].

nodes.label: Load-haul-dump machine (LHD)
nodes.text: A load-haul-dump machine (LHD) is a low, long loader built for underground mines, where it scoops broken rock, carries it along narrow tunnels and dumps it into a truck or a chute.
nodes.synopsis: An LHD, also called a scoop or underground loader, is a low, long machine that carries broken rock through narrow tunnels; its operator sits sideways in a low cab, and its own bucket load can create a blind spot [f11443, f11444, f11445, f11452]. NSW Safety Bulletin SB25-05, issued in July 2025, recorded 30 underground coal LHD and personnel-transport collisions in the previous 12 months, often involving bulky loads such as concrete kibbles that obstructed visibility [f3113, f3114, f11447]. The booklet ranks these collisions eighth by harm, mostly involving damage and injury, and identifies confined roadways as a protection-design concern; however, the glossary says frequency data for this lower-ranked group were not found, creating tension with the reported collision count [f3560, f3563, f11587, f3113]. Underground collision systems can slow and stop machines but depend on every person and machine carrying a tag; Epiroc Titan CAS and CAS Interface launched for underground loaders and trucks in 2021 [f11449, f11450, f1667]. NIOSH's dynamic-model work included LHDs within 145 underground haulage vehicles, but planners should not automatically transfer underground safety evidence to surface haul roads, and scenario-level evidence beyond mining remains limited [f6131, f11451, f3659].

nodes.label: Trackless mobile machinery (TMM)
nodes.text: Trackless mobile machinery (TMM) is the South African legal term for any self-propelled mining machine that does not run on rails, from haul trucks and loaders to light vehicles.
nodes.synopsis: South Africa is the booklet’s main case of mandatory collision-prevention intervention preceding validation standards: its TMM regulations were promulgated on 27 February 2015, and the critical sub-regulations commenced on 21 December 2022 with no transitional period [f11458, f11461, f15555]. The requirements call for diesel-powered machines to detect and warn, slow to a safe speed and automatically brake if no action prevents a potential collision, and fail to safe without human intervention [f15556, f11456]. Although one chapter describes a mandate for all surface and underground TMMs, the detailed legal account specifies diesel-powered machines and stipulated significant collision risks; coverage of battery-electric machines remains unclear [f1087, f2279, f2280, f15559]. Industry developed surface-TMM verification specifications in 2025 and 2026, including one dated 29 August 2025; MOSH requires verification of each type, model and serial number where braking characteristics differ, while mine-specific codes of practice and commissioning add another acceptance layer [f11459, f555, f5613, f2283]. Safe intervention itself needs validation: MOSH warns of unintended consequences from unsafe slowing or stopping, and fixed stopping gaps can obstruct loading unless the collision-prevention system is switched off [f5815, f3344]. South Africa recorded nine TMM-related deaths in 2024 versus six in 2023, but published scenarios do not establish how many automatic braking could have prevented; the reported single TMM collision death in 2022 is unverified and cannot be directly compared with the broader transport-and-mining fatality total [f3140, f3141, f3145, f3144].

nodes.label: Light vehicle
nodes.text: On a mine site, a light vehicle is an ordinary pickup, four-wheel-drive or van used by supervisors, maintenance crews and visitors to move among the heavy machines.
nodes.synopsis: Mine-site light vehicles are pickups, four-wheel-drives and vans used among heavy machines; they share haul roads with trucks weighing roughly a hundred times more, and blind areas plus this size mismatch are central factors in deadly collisions [f11463, f11464, f3588]. The booklet ranks a haul truck crushing a light vehicle in front of it as the highest-harm collision scenario, although berm and dump-edge events rank higher by fatal-event frequency [f3512, f3584]. The detailed US analysis covers 13 haul-truck collisions in January 2005–June 2021, including five light-vehicle cases and one double fatality; other summaries describe five of 13 deaths, leaving an unresolved distinction between incident and death counts [f3073, f3243, f3514, f11467]. All five light-vehicle cases involved forward movement: two trucks started from stationary, two encountered parked light vehicles, and one interaction was head-on; this supports prioritizing detection before moving off, when time-to-collision calculations give no answer [f3516, f3077, f11591, f11473, f11474]. Visibility aids do not eliminate the hazard: two parked pickups had their strobes switched off, one was momentarily hidden by a cab pillar, and another vehicle's flag may have been inadequately illuminated; a reversing dozer also killed a light-vehicle driver at Snapper Mineral Sands Mine on 12 August 2019 [f3080, f3081, f3082, f3116]. Validation therefore calls for sensor-representative light-vehicle surrogates under a haul truck's nose and includes proving-ground controller tests using light vehicles under the MOSH regime dated 11 October 2025; earlier radar work reported 75 m detection in 2005, while the separate on-road FMVSS 127 rule of 9 May 2024 requires AEB on new light vehicles by 1 September 2029 [f13506, f5352, f6368, f1513].

nodes.label: Operator and cab
nodes.text: The operator is the person who drives and controls a machine, and the cab is the enclosed compartment where that person sits.
nodes.synopsis: The system automatically brakes when an operator fails to react to a proximity warning, but ISO 21815 treats collision systems as assistance and retains operator responsibility because the technology cannot cover every situation [f1, f5836, f3647]. Validation therefore requires assumptions about operator behavior and timing, yet the booklet found neither a field-measured distribution of warning-response times nor a validated off-road operator model; it recommends sensitivity testing with uncertain operator response [f11484, f11481, f11829, f11485]. Automatic stops introduce restraint and cab-safety concerns: seven of 12 drivers killed in US haul-truck dump-point cases during 2005–2021 were unbelted, and MSHA engineers estimate that adequate seat belts, provided and worn, could save three to four miners annually [f3628, f3001, f3625]. Workers reported jarring and concerns about forceful stops, while MSHA stated in 2017 that it knew of no resulting on-board operator injuries; this remains unresolved and unmeasured, supporting caution rather than a quantified injury claim [f3392, f3394, f3619]. The booklet recommends jerk-limited deceleration and operator action before braking release, while site acceptance expectations include operator review of false and correct interventions plus training and competence evidence [f13638, f6158, f11137, f11145].

nodes.label: Job site
nodes.text: A job site is any place where heavy machines work, and the booklet is concerned with four main kinds: surface mines, underground mines, quarries and construction sites.
nodes.synopsis: A machine may operate across 100 or more job sites and applications, with different geometry, surfaces, traffic and light; the braking system must work across site types, weather, lighting and machine models [f16, f276, f2956]. Site controls materially affect the same braking algorithm’s safety results, and machinery conformity and functional-safety verification do not guarantee mine authorisation; destination-site legislation and site acceptance therefore remain essential [f804, f2930, f2271, f806]. The accident evidence underscores transport and pedestrian hazards: British quarry guidance attributes 40% of accidents and 60% of deaths to transport, while vehicle or machine strikes were the leading cause of death at US road construction sites during 2005–2016 [f11493, f3549, f11496]. Virtual coverage should include genuinely different captured environments, site-specific human behaviour, traffic rules and geometry, but no standard specifying the number of exact sites needed for broad coverage was found, and road-oriented tools require adaptation [f4106, f4355, f10670, f4320, f8337, f8607]. Confidence remains constrained by missing public off-road exposure data and uncertain transfer of on-road rare-event acceleration; the proposed response to field-engineer objections is field-derived parameter distributions and shadow-mode fleet collection through mid-2027 [f6918, f1114, f7440, f10659, f10669, f10650].

nodes.label: Haul road, berm, bench and pit wall
nodes.text: These are the built features of a surface mine or quarry: the haul road is the internal road the trucks use, a berm is a ridge of material piled along an edge as a barrier, a bench is one horizontal step of the pit, and the pit wall is the steep face between benches.
nodes.synopsis: Terrain-edge hazards dominate the cited US surface-mining fatality analysis: of 54 haul-truck deaths from January 2005 to June 2021, 21 involved berms and 12 dump points, versus 13 involving people or vehicles; 10 of the 12 dump-point cases involved an absent or inadequate berm [f2989, f2998, f3000]. This exposes a mismatch with research focused on vehicle-to-vehicle collisions: object detection alone covers an incomplete risk picture, and berm or dump-edge prevention may also require road-edge, geofence, speed and stability controls [f6577, f11511, f3250]. Berm handling must be context-aware rather than brake for every berm or learn away repeated dump-edge alarms; the glossary's claim that using berms as bump stops is safe is qualified by two fatal cases where repeated bumping pushed the berm toward the edge [f11512, f3353, f3354, f11864, f3351]. Virtual validation needs accurately located edges because errors of tens of centimetres can corrupt stopping-distance tests, while terrain editing in Gaussian scenes and realistic terrain reproduction by the discussed over-the-air devices remain gaps [f3910, f3880, f5327]. Representation should distinguish structured haul roads from unstructured terrain: OpenDRIVE is recommended for structured road elements, but lane-free haul-road suitability remains a gap and dig faces, stockpiles and free terrain require additional representations [f3982, f7158, f7202, f13216].

nodes.label: Stockpile, dump point and tip point
nodes.text: A stockpile is a pile of loose material waiting to be used, a dump point is where a truck tips its load, and a tip point or tip head is the active edge of a dump where trucks and a dozer work together.
nodes.synopsis: Berm and dump-point events, rather than object collisions, accounted for most deaths in the cited analysis of 54 US surface-mining haul-truck fatalities from January 2005 to June 2021: 21 involved berms, 12 dump points, 13 people or vehicle collisions, and eight other causes [f2989, f3246]. Of the 12 dump-point deaths, six involved reverse-overs and six ground failures; ten involved absent or inadequate berms and seven drivers were unbelted, supporting consideration of edge, geofence, speed and stability controls alongside object detection [f2999, f3000, f3001, f3250]. Normal production deliberately brings machines close to piles, dump edges and other machines, yet a change of intention can turn tip-head proximity into a collision; the 12 August 2019 Snapper Mine fatality involved a light vehicle struck by a reversing dozer whose operator did not know it was there [f11375, f3356, f3116]. Validation must distinguish intended pile approaches from intrusions without suppressing genuinely dangerous berm detections; Volvo CE uses slope memory to avoid braking while reversing down stockpiles, but published surface-machine stockpile nuisance-alarm frequency data were not found [f11521, f11522, f11392, f3360]. Braking itself can worsen marginal ground support at dump edges, and stockpiles, trailers and close loading are identified as critical false-stop scenarios for testing [f6299, f11011, f11119]. Virtual coverage also has gaps: forward-facing route logs miss stockpile backs and other unseen surfaces, OpenDRIVE needs supplementary representations for stockpiles and free terrain, and Scenic fits these settings better than road-oriented languages but is not a standard [f3811, f7158, f6694].

nodes.label: Spotter and pedestrian
nodes.text: A pedestrian is any person on foot near a working machine, and a spotter is a person whose job is to stand where the operator can see them and guide a reversing or maneuvering machine by hand signals or radio.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus identifies unseen people and light vehicles being run over by large machines as the deadliest documented collision pattern; smaller trucks and loaders particularly back over people [f2983, f11293, f2995]. The January 2005–June 2021 US evidence covers 13 haul-truck collisions, including three pedestrian collisions, but one summary describes the category counts as victims while another describes incidents and notes a double fatality, requiring care with denominators [f2992, f3073]. Pedestrians can legitimately be close to machines: workers 0.5–5 m behind them occupy a weak range for digital radar simulators, and near-zero relative speed can make time-to-collision misleading even at centimeter separation [f6220, f5328, f6214]. Protection must account for camera limitations involving posture and weather, cooperative systems requiring everyone to carry tags, and reported worker responses including tag removal, riskier positioning and requests for bypasses [f1638, f1670, f3034]. Regulatory acceptance emphasizes timely detection or warning and risk reduction; US 30 CFR 77.410 specifically requires enough sensing coverage for an endangered person to escape [f2397, f2084, f2444]. Virtual validation therefore needs site-specific pedestrian controls and separately validated human models, yet no validated off-road pedestrian-behaviour model was found and transfer of on-road detection and rare-event methods remains unproven or uncertain [f11499, f10350, f4356, f5406, f1114].

nodes.label: Blind spot and operator visibility
nodes.text: A blind spot is any area around a machine that the operator cannot see from the seat, and operator visibility is the overall picture of what the operator can and cannot see with eyes, mirrors and cameras.
nodes.synopsis: Across the accident evidence, blind areas and the size mismatch between heavy machines and people or light vehicles are central to the deadliest collisions; although forward run-overs are identified as the deadliest documented pattern, 67% of the 22 US surface-mine blind-area deaths recorded from 2000 to mid-2006 involved victims behind reversing equipment [f2977, f3588, f2984, f2986]. In that dataset, dump trucks were involved in 38% of deaths and front-end loaders in 33%; a 50 t haul truck's front-right blind area extends 18 m or more and grows with truck size [f2985, f3221]. US construction and metal/non-metal mining rules require reverse warnings, specified alternatives or observers when rear visibility is obstructed, with OSHA interpretations accepting cameras only when they genuinely provide the required clear view [f2228, f2237, f2229]. Validation should map blind zones before hardware arrives and build scenarios around each machine model's blind areas, because geometry and sensor placement limit evidence transfer between models; low-speed work may still require relatively large warning zones measured in stopping distances [f5601, f7038, f11551, f11552, f6226]. The proposed geometric methods have verification gaps: ISO 5006 is listed as not verified, and UNECE R159's reported 50 mm cylinder detail was not confirmed against the regulation text [f15219, f5356, f15220].

nodes.label: Reversing and reverse alarm
nodes.text: Reversing (backing up) is driving a machine backward, and a reverse alarm is the loud beeping a machine makes automatically while it does so.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends starting with a narrow reverse-only, low-speed wheel-loader operating domain: Volvo CE’s January 2023 system operates at 3–15 km/h and brakes for 2–3 seconds, while Caterpillar’s medium-wheel-loader system also targets reverse operation [f11397, f1238, f356]. Reversing risk is population-specific: 67% of 22 US surface-mine blind-area fatalities from 2000 to mid-2006 involved the rear blind area of reversing equipment, but the booklet identifies forward motion or starting from rest as the deadliest haul-truck pattern [f2986, f2993, f11409]. US construction and metal/non-metal mining rules require reverse alarms, observers or specified alternatives when rear visibility is obstructed; ISO 21815-3:2023 covers both forward and reverse warning and avoidance through speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition, not automatic steering [f2228, f2237, f2163]. The 2006 NIOSH study recorded 580 alarms over 618 reversals during seven days of testing: 102 were false alarms (18%), 243 nuisance alarms (42%), and only 235 actionable alarms (41%), highlighting alarm-quality concerns [f5436, f5174, f5175]. Virtual validation has a critical close-range gap because workers 0.5–5 m behind machines occupy the range where digital radar simulators are weakest, although AGX Dynamics for Unity added a lidar-based reverse auto-brake example on 4 April 2025 [f5328, f8573]. Planning should account for reversal requests, transmission delays and opposite-direction collision risks, while treating coverage of reversing trailers under draft ISO 21815 Part 5 as provisional, with publication planned for November 2026 [f6338, f6039, f6747].

nodes.label: Vehicle interaction
nodes.text: Vehicle interaction is the mining industry's term for any situation in which a moving machine comes close to another machine, a person or a fixed feature of the site, whether or not contact happens.
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT PR-5A Rev 3.0, dated September 2024, provides mining surface-interaction scenarios and a nine-layer control model whose Level 9 automatically slows and stops machines; intervention is only one layer, not a silver bullet [f2120, f7744, f390]. Collisions remain a practical problem: New South Wales reported no meaningful year-on-year reduction in vehicle interactions in July 2023 and recorded 30 underground collisions involving load-haul-dump machines and personnel transports in the 12 months to mid-2025 [f3003, f3004, f11446]. Validation coverage is misaligned with fatality evidence: 85% of research cases addressed vehicle–vehicle interactions, but these accounted for only 9% of the 91 fatal haul-truck accidents reviewed for 2005–2018, while vehicle–environment events accounted for the largest share [f5822, f5824]. Virtual tests therefore need multiple actors, site traffic rules and geometry, and recognition that other actors may react to braking; automatic or partial braking can itself create following-machine conflicts [f4358, f10670, f5547, f6267, f11260]. Scenario-based acceptance already covers following, overtaking, head-on encounters, junctions, multiple interactors and congested areas, while representative-mine interaction tests follow laboratory testing and a controlled mixed-traffic pilot is expected by the site operations manager [f2456, f1355, f11142]. Important uncertainties remain: no comparable large off-road naturalistic interaction dataset was found, published descriptions cite 24 PR-5A scenarios versus 17 storyboards, and one planning passage explicitly did not review EMESRT interaction controls [f6859, f7745, f9808].

nodes.label: Collision
nodes.text: A collision is a machine striking a person, a vehicle, another machine or a fixed object, and on job sites a small number of collision types cause most of the deaths.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet distinguishes the deadliest documented collision pattern—a large machine moving over an unseen person or light vehicle—from the most frequently reported type, heavy-machine-to-heavy-machine contact, which usually causes property damage [f11293, f2977, f11440]. In the US haul-truck evidence for January 2005–June 2021, 54 deaths comprised 21 berm events, 13 collisions with people or vehicles, 12 dump-point events and eight other causes; 12 of the 13 collision deaths involved forward motion, and four began with victims within about 15 m [f2989, f2990, f2991]. This exposes a coverage mismatch: collision research emphasizes vehicle-to-vehicle interactions even though most haul-truck fatalities involve the environment [f395, f5935]. Australia's Model WHS regulation 215 requires collision risk control so far as reasonably practicable and a warning device, while the reviewed 2022 draft ISO 21815-3 requires sufficient CxS distance to stop before hitting an intended object [f2783, f2421]. Validation must address grade, non-longitudinal motion and braking timing—not merely detection or peak deceleration—and retain physical closed-loop tests near the collision/no-collision boundary [f6000, f6001, f6218, f7783, f10663, f7888]. Automatic stopping can itself cause rear-end collisions, tipping or load spill, shadow mode cannot establish those consequences, and no separate agency statistics were found for serious excavator swing collisions [f5814, f596, f11424].

nodes.label: Fatality, serious injury and property damage
nodes.text: Accidents are counted in three bands of severity, deaths, serious injuries and damage to equipment or structures, and the records get thinner and less reliable as severity goes down.
nodes.synopsis: Fatality patterns differ from collision frequency: heavy-machine contacts are described as the most frequently reported collision type but usually cause property damage, while powered haulage accounted for 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries (9%) in 2025 [f11440, f2979, f2980]. For haul trucks, berm and dump-point events dominate deaths: of 54 deaths from 2005 to mid-2021, 21 involved berms, 12 dump points and 13 collisions with people or vehicles; a separate NIOSH review classified 54% of 91 fatal accidents from 2005–2018 as vehicle-environment events [f11404, f5821]. Within the haul-truck collision subset, 12 of 13 deaths involved forward motion, and four began with trucks starting while people were within about 15 m; this should not be generalized to all equipment, since 67% of 22 surface-mine blind-area victims were behind reversing equipment [f11405, f11406, f2986]. Testing should retain known fatal-accident patterns, but vehicle-to-vehicle-focused research and object detection leave the dominant vehicle-environment hazard insufficiently addressed, while automatic braking can itself cause operator injury, load spill, rear-end impacts and rollover [f6639, f6577, f5825, f7456]. On-road precedent illustrates both rare-event validation difficulty and uncertainty in incident evidence: RAND estimated 275 million failure-free miles for a specified fatality-rate demonstration and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement, while Honda crash and injury totals differ across outlets [f6662, f6663, f1487]. No specific fatality investigation involving failure of a simulation-validated collision avoidance system was found; separately, Tesla PE22-002 closed on 29 June 2026 with no crashes, injuries or defect finding, despite about 25,900 incident reports covering 695,000 vehicles [f7989, f11171, f1501].

nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.text: Exposure is the amount of opportunity for something to happen, measured in units such as hours of machine operation, kilometers driven, loading cycles or number of close approaches, and it is the denominator that turns a count of events into a rate.
nodes.synopsis: Exposure is the opportunity for an event to occur—measured in operating hours, distance, cycles or close approaches—and supplies the denominator needed to convert counts into rates; the accident sources examined lack these denominators, preventing reliable collision-rate comparisons between countries or machine types [f11606, f11610]. Field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance: RAND's 2016 on-road analysis required hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles and tens to hundreds of fleet-years, while off-road machines accumulate less exposure per unit [f313, f5466, f6924, f11613]. Statistical acceleration can reduce exposure by orders of magnitude, but these reductions are not product safety sign-offs, and their transfer to off-road work is limited by missing exposure distributions and disagreement over how accurately open-ended interactions can be modelled [f1945, f1219, f352, f7439]. The booklet recommends logging the existing warning fleet through winter 2026–2027 to build a real-site exposure model; customer telematics, warning logs and site studies are the identified data routes, although the proposed campaign identifies warning logs alone as its source of real exposure and false-alarm data [f708, f6919, f7368, f11615]. Operator acceptance should be assessed through unwanted warnings or interventions per task-specific hour, cycle, reverse maneuver or legitimate close approach, not merely per detection; the only identified field study with a clean denominator was small, reporting alarms in 94% of 618 reverse movements over seven days [f11608, f11609, f11611]. The field exposure needed to substantiate rare missed detections or unintended braking remains uncertain, and the booklet recommends delaying brake control while retaining validated warnings if the safety case remains incomplete [f8181, f10998].

nodes.label: Near miss
nodes.text: A near miss is an event that could have caused a collision or injury but did not, usually because someone stopped, swerved or was lucky.
nodes.synopsis: A near miss could have caused a collision or injury but did not; the booklet distinguishes these no-contact events from collisions and non-collision accidents, and defines residual safe distance as the deliberate gap preventing contact [f11617, f11578, f14001]. Queensland recorded 48 mobile-equipment collisions and near misses at open-cut coal mines between 1 January and 27 May 2017; a NSW incident summary for the week ending 13 March 2026 describes two haul trucks making emergency stops about 15 m apart after one drove on the wrong side of the centre bund at night [f3106, f3115]. Near misses are valuable for tuning because fatal accidents are too rare, but under-reporting distorts frequency estimates, accident databases capture them poorly, and warning-system logs obscure what would have happened without operator response; ignored-warning events are especially valuable but often lack ground truth [f11623, f3650, f3046, f11625, f7943]. The booklet therefore recommends detailed warning and intervention logging, incident replicas where data exist, and field monitoring that feeds near misses into the scenario taxonomy and targeted regression tests, treating the four-month campaign as the start of a living evidence base [f3652, f4108, f7446, f11628]. Shadow mode alone cannot establish effectiveness in true near misses or closed-loop braking effects, while the aviation precedent also illustrates uncertainty: March 2022 committee minutes reported European findings of more near mid-air collisions with ACAS Xa than TCAS that MIT Lincoln Laboratory did not reproduce [f968, f1436].

nodes.label: Collision Mitigation System (CMS)
nodes.text: A Collision Mitigation System (CMS) detects an object close to a machine, warns the operator, and if the operator does not react, applies the brakes automatically to avoid the collision or make it less severe.
nodes.synopsis: The CMS is being developed as a successor to proximity warning: it automatically brakes when the operator does not react, and adding braking changes the safety-engineering scope rather than merely the performance metric [f1, f2955, f5221]. Prototype hardware and software are due in mid-2027, with validation required in under four months afterward—a substantial compression relative to the three-to-four-year validation history reported for comparable functions [f2, f3, f4, f4391]. Requirements span more than 100 job-site types, more than 10 operating scenarios per machine, multiple machine models, and weather and lighting conditions including rain, snow, fog, dust, dusk, darkness and glare [f5130, f2956, f285]. This broad scope is in tension with the glossary's expected reverse-only, low-speed wheel-loader operating domain and the recommendation to test forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing separately [f11397, f2996]. Evidence remains limited: independent off-road collision-system field data are old and sparse, underground injury figures lack speed and motion detail needed for braking design, and braking depends on sensor detection [f5169, f3256, f11302]. The recommended programme architecture combines systems-engineering V&V and TEMP-style test planning with evidence-based stage gates, reserving TRLs for critical-technology maturity [f9588, f9589, f9590].

nodes.label: Collision Warning System (CWS) and Collision Avoidance System (CAS)
nodes.text: A Collision Warning System (CWS) only alerts the operator to a nearby object, while a Collision Avoidance System (CAS) also acts on the machine, slowing or stopping it.
nodes.synopsis: The existing warning system alerts the operator, whereas adding automatic braking changes machine motion and moves the function across ISO 19014-2’s boundary from excluded awareness systems to motion-control safety functions [f380, f2075, f10521]. ISO 16001:2017 covers warning rather than braking, while ISO 21815 covers collision avoidance through speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibit; ISO 21815-1:2022 does not permit automatic steering [f161, f5061, f5909]. Common detection and warning-stage metrics remain comparable, but braking measures need new safety requirements, and the warning system’s field history does not transfer to the braking function [f5498, f5445, f7938]. Evidence is weighted toward warning and immature systems: the 2022 NIOSH review covered 97 cases, only 10% involving avoidance, while a seven-day 2004 radar study classified 42% of 580 alarms as nuisance alarms and 18% as false alarms [f5933, f5934, f3011]. The research found neither an off-road standard accepting simulation instead of physical collision-avoidance tests nor a documented full validation in about four months for a new machine family; synthetic-only reliability evidence and warning-data-to-braking certification precedents were also absent [f7539, f1255, f6690, f1253]. The MSHA surface-equipment rule does not mandate collision avoidance, while a multi-year Applied Intuition–Komatsu partnership announced on 9 September 2025 includes Level 9 collision avoidance for staffed operations, indicating development activity rather than closing the validation gaps [f1369, f8399, f8400, f10425].

nodes.label: Proximity Detection System (PDS)
nodes.text: A Proximity Detection System (PDS) senses when a person or machine comes within a set distance of a machine and warns or stops it; the term is used mainly in US underground coal mining and in South Africa.
nodes.synopsis: The manufacturer already offers proximity awareness that warns operators, while mining PDS evidence covers systems capable of stopping machines; the glossary characterizes underground PDS as the richest field evidence for that intervention [f9, f11658]. US regulation 30 CFR 75.1732 (2015) requires continuous-miner systems to warn audibly and visually and stop before contacting a miner, but specifies no numeric stop distance; no final rule was found for the separate 2015 proposal covering underground mobile machines [f2240, f2626, f7752]. Retrospective assessments judged 32 of 39 continuous-miner fatalities in 1984–2015 (82%) and 42 underground mobile-haulage fatalities in 1984–2014 potentially preventable by proximity systems, rather than demonstrating those reductions in deployment [f3095, f3098]. Nuisance interventions are the main documented reason systems were disabled: workers at seven mines reported unnecessary shutdowns ranging from once daily to 15 times during one coal cut, while production accounts range from a manufacturer's reported 5–10% loss to two operators reporting recovery to baseline [f116, f11659, f3029, f3030]. Integration readiness does not establish coverage or stopping adequacy: Epiroc requires all machines and persons to carry tags or sensors, Bell's coverage depends on the supplier, and NIOSH identified stopping-distance concerns when transferring slow-crawler systems to faster rubber-tired haulage [f1349, f1688, f1689, f6354]. Validation therefore remains equipment- and environment-specific, with NIOSH recording stop-zone differences averaging 1.4 m and reaching 3.6 m across nine field tests; intelligent PDS selectively disables hazardous motions, but published field-measured operator reaction-time distributions were not found [f5575, f10647, f5929, f6244, f11481].

nodes.label: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) and Advanced Emergency Braking System (AEBS)
nodes.text: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB), called an Advanced Emergency Braking System (AEBS) in United Nations vehicle regulations, is the function on modern cars and trucks that brakes by itself when a crash with the vehicle or person ahead is about to happen.
nodes.synopsis: The next-generation CMS retains proximity warnings but adds automatic braking when the operator does not act; this is a different safety function, so matching the old warning system is not an adequate validation target [f12, f10417]. Automatic braking invalidates recorded replay at the first new brake command, making interactive closed-loop agreement important; a useful virtual environment therefore needs physically connected sensor, ground and object models, not merely a 3D scene [f108, f4813, f3904]. Major evidence gaps remain: no end-to-end heavy off-road vehicle-in-the-loop case, validated simulated braking distances on gravel, mud, ice or slopes, or off-road standard accepting simulation instead of physical braking tests was found [f342, f3970, f7539]. ISO 16001:2017 covers warnings rather than braking, and ISO 21815-4, listed for October 2026, excludes automatic brake application; South Africa was the only jurisdiction found to legally require automatic slowing and braking, while 2025 amendments to UN R152 permit virtual substitution for some car and van AEBS tests [f2070, f7543, f2077, f5162, f7546]. Prototype hardware and software are expected in mid-2027, but the organization has never developed this virtual-testing capability, and the research found no precedent for taking a new automatic-braking function from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about four months; every documented virtualization retained physical referents [f8250, f9401, f58, f10415]. Validation must address long stopping distances and legitimate work that resembles a collision, because false positives become machine-motion commands; available wheel-loader examples are limited to reverse operation, with Volvo CE's January 2023 system operating at 3–15 km/h for 2–3 seconds, and transferring road-vehicle evidence to quarry operations remains uncertain [f11381, f11384, f3024, f356, f11391, f11385].

nodes.label: Forward Collision Warning (FCW)
nodes.text: Forward Collision Warning (FCW) is the car and truck function that warns the driver of an imminent crash ahead but leaves the braking to the driver.
nodes.synopsis: FCW warns car and truck drivers of an imminent crash ahead but leaves braking to them; the booklet uses this on-road research as a counterpart to the manufacturer's existing proximity warning, not as direct evidence about off-road operators [f11678, f11679, f11686]. Regulatory precedents are likewise on-road: FMVSS No. 127 requires FCW alongside AEB for light vehicles up to 4,536 kg GVWR and does not apply to off-road machines, while NHTSA's heavy-vehicle research and 2023 proposal concern road trucks and buses [f2831, f2535, f1816]. On-road FCW plus AEB reduced rear-end striking crashes by 50% in Cicchino's 2017 study, but insurance evidence also showed a 20% increase in being struck from behind, making automatic stopping a potential trade-off rather than an unqualified benefit [f3459, f3409, f14017]. False-alarm evidence is mixed: an 18% rate was associated with drivers ignoring warnings (12%) or abandoning FCW (11%), whereas simulator warnings with 20–33% false alarms still shortened brake reactions, and a 2025 study found no cry-wolf effect at 33% despite unnecessary braking [f11680, f11681, f11682]. Real-driving false alerts varied from 12% when turning to 2% during lane-keeping, drivers reduced sensitivity over time, and alarms with visible causes harmed trust less; no accepted off-road false-alarm rate was found [f11683, f11684, f11685, f11687]. Validation therefore needs to distinguish measured warning performance from modeled benefit: open-loop replay can establish detection, false-alarm rates and warning timing only for recorded configurations and situations, while a virtual cyclist-overtaking FCW assessment estimated 53–96% fatality reductions depending predominantly on its driver-response model [f5234, f3497].

nodes.label: Pedestrian AEB (PAEB)
nodes.text: Pedestrian Automatic Emergency Braking (PAEB) is the version of car AEB that detects people on foot and brakes for them.
nodes.synopsis: PAEB detects people on foot and brakes for them; the corpus identifies pedestrians as the main people heavy off-road CMS must protect, while describing pedestrian detection as especially condition-dependent [f11688, f11696, f11698]. FMVSS 127 requires pedestrian AEB at 10–73 km/h in daylight and darkness, but applies to light on-road vehicles up to 4,536 kg GVWR, not off-road machines; Chapter 3 states UN R152 pedestrian tests use 20–60 km/h while also flagging that range as unverified against primary text [f11691, f2831, f2824, f2528]. A peer-reviewed 2019 retrospective on-road simulation evaluated time-to-collision triggers and latencies against US pedestrian crash data, showing that avoidance depends on both parameters [f6346, f6189]. Independent nighttime tests improved from no avoidance by four vehicles at 25 mph in 2019 to 60% avoidance in the study published 16 October 2025, which tested four recent cars at 40 km/h and still left roughly 40% failures under ideal conditions [f7975, f7976, f7977]. High-visibility clothing caused complete detection loss in some tested systems, and nighttime and clothing conditions were under-represented in consumer protocols, demonstrating that protocol-based evidence can give false confidence outside its tested envelope [f7980, f7981, f7982]. Because job-site pedestrians wear high-visibility clothing and much work occurs at night, the corpus recommends retaining physical night and weather tests where simulation is weakest; Caterpillar also warns of detection limitations for crouching or lying people, low light and inclement weather [f11697, f11699, f11695].

nodes.label: Intervention
nodes.text: An intervention is what a collision system does to the machine itself when the operator has not acted: it reduces speed, stops the machine, or prevents it from starting to move.
nodes.synopsis: The studied Collision Mitigation System automatically brakes when the operator fails to respond to a proximity warning; the mining control model distinguishes warning at Level 8 from automatic intervention at Level 9 [f1, f11295, f11296]. ISO 21815-1 and -3 cover intervention through speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition, not automatic steering; Part 3 places intervention at collision-risk level 4 or above and forbids overriding stronger operator braking, while the MOSH surface specification requires warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention [f316, f5909, f9778, f5912, f5913, f2115]. Nuisance interventions are the main documented reason deployed mining proximity systems were disabled: workers at seven underground coal mines reported unnecessary shutdowns from once daily to 15 times per cut, and nearly 70% expressed concern about when and how systems take control [f116, f3013, f3287]. Validation therefore needs to address both failure to intervene and unsafe or unnecessary intervention, using matched real and simulated closed-loop runs; tuning should treat missed or late interventions as hard constraints while optimizing unnecessary braking, false warnings and productivity loss, because replay cannot establish what happens after braking changes the scene [f2141, f4812, f6671, f336]. Documented off-road intervention launches were deliberately narrow: Volvo CE's January 2023 system brakes for 2–3 seconds, Komatsu's 2019–2020 stop function operates only at slow travel or motion initiation, and Caterpillar's cited loader system inhibits reverse engagement from standstill; Hexagon announced TRL4 verification on 25 March 2026 before integrated site testing, rather than completion of that testing [f10434, f10436, f10439, f10440, f1350].

nodes.label: Staged intervention
nodes.text: Staged intervention means that a collision system acts in steps of increasing force, from a quiet information signal through warnings and gentle slowing to hard braking and a locked stop, rather than jumping straight to an emergency stop.
nodes.synopsis: The CMS retains existing proximity warnings and automatically brakes if the operator does not act; the intervention ladder spans warning, advice, slowing, stopping and motion inhibition from standstill [f12, f150, f5923]. South African mining regulations require slowing diesel-powered trackless mobile machines to a safe speed before automatic braking when no action is taken, while MOSH specifies warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention and slowing below 10 km/h [f1361, f2441, f2608, f5562]. Mine leaders preferred slowing to a crawl before setting the brake rather than abrupt stops, but warnings only buy response time if operators believe them and the interface enables a response [f3393, f11795, f11843]. Validation should set separate tolerances, thresholds, tests and evidence for each intervention stage, with human simulation examining operator responses to warning, waiting and braking [f2634, f11733, f571]. No universal off-road maximum deceleration, tuning data for standardized automatic slowing interfaces, or evidence for off-road partial service braking was found; escalation should therefore consider remaining stopping margin and uncertainty, including conditions that affect risk, rather than distance alone [f11719, f6508, f6514, f11725]. On-road precedents include a minimum 0.8-second warning and brief haptic brake cues above 4 m/s², but the reviewed off-road legal texts did not establish a 2.0-second warning requirement [f2519, f6498, f2472].

nodes.label: Nine levels of control
nodes.text: The nine levels of control are the mining industry's ladder of defenses against vehicle interactions, running from how a site is designed (Level 1) to a machine that brakes by itself (Level 9), with warning technology at Levels 7 and 8.
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT PR-5A Revision 3.0, dated September 2024, supplies the nine-layer vehicle-interaction model: controls run from site requirements through operator awareness at Level 7, advisory controls at Level 8, and automatic slowing and stopping at Level 9 [f2120, f4080, f6229]. Level 9 is a machine-control capability rather than a standalone product, and effective upper-level controls require understanding and maintaining the Level 1–7 baseline; site conditions can make the same braking algorithm safe in one location and troublesome in another [f2585, f11750, f11753]. Regulatory emphasis differs: NSW and NIOSH favor lower-level controls with collision systems as backup, while South Africa mandated Level 9 for surface and underground trackless mobile mining machinery from 21 December 2022 without a transitional period; one earlier trade report instead suggested December 2023 [f3624, f1087, f1088, f1364]. That mandate pushed deployment followed by refinement, whereas Epiroc recommends evaluation before enforcing Level 9, and EMESRT/ICMM warn that unqualified deployment can impair production and accelerate brake wear [f359, f6420, f2892]. Wabtec's December 2021 Komatsu haul-truck tests demonstrated controlled deceleration up to 30 km/h but still relied on physical testing to adjust detection zones, while the reviewed sources yielded no public simulation-validated Level 9 collision-avoidance evidence from mining OEMs [f1345, f1247, f4128]. The ACARP framework separates proving object detection from proving Level 8 or 9 intervention, reinforcing the need to validate both sensing and machine response rather than treating the Level 9 label as sufficient evidence [f559, f11752].

nodes.label: Nuisance braking
nodes.text: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, either because there was no real object (a false intervention) or because the object was real but posed no danger (an unnecessary intervention).
nodes.synopsis: Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented automatic-braking failure mode in the cited on-road evidence, while nuisance interventions, production loss and operator disabling are repeatedly identified as reasons deployed mining proximity systems failed [f115, f1223, f116, f6306]. The on-road evidence includes an April 2024 NHTSA investigation covering 2,997,604 Honda vehicles; mining interviews found unnecessary vehicle shutdowns ranging from once a day to 15 times during a single cut of coal [f10422, f3285]. False braking is itself a safety hazard, potentially causing load shift, rollover, instability near edges or rear-end impacts, so validation must address machine-stability consequences as well as collision avoidance [f8201, f9370]. Acceptance should report nuisance and missed-intervention rates together, but the research found no published off-road hourly acceptance values; MOSH requires no false interventions or false warnings at its TRL4 gate, and conservative fail-to-safe intervention remains in tension with productivity and adoption [f6418, f2121, f2119, f5781]. Under a zero-event Poisson calculation, 300 representative hours without unnecessary braking support a 95% upper bound below one event per 100 hours, and 3,000 hours support below one per 1,000 hours, although the field exposure needed to substantiate rare unintended-braking probabilities remains uncertain [f6658, f6659, f8181]. Shadow mode can measure hypothetical nuisance interventions at scale but cannot establish consequences such as a following-truck collision, while simulators cannot establish long-term operator responses; validation should cover benign clutter and legitimate close approaches, with field monitoring after limited-domain release [f589, f596, f580, f8206, f4362, f3342, f722].

nodes.label: False alarm and alarm accuracy
nodes.text: A false alarm is a warning given when nothing dangerous is there, a nuisance alarm is a warning about something real that is not dangerous in the situation, and alarm accuracy is the share of all alarms that deserved a response.
nodes.synopsis: False and nuisance alarms are repeatedly identified as a leading cause of deployed proximity-system failure, with documented distrust, disabling and operator rejection; achieving an acceptable detection–false-positive balance took the manufacturer years of calibration [f5928, f6494, f10496, f10]. The strongest cited quantitative evidence remains the 2006 NIOSH report of seven days of 2004 Caterpillar 793B testing: 580 alarms over 618 reversals, with 18% false alarms and 42% nuisance alarms; the chapters report the action-worthy share slightly differently, as 40% versus 235/580 (41%) [f5173, f3010, f3011, f5174, f5175, f5176]. Validation should use real operating exposure and fleet logging, including winter 2026–2027, rather than staged targets alone; replay results remain limited to the sensors, mounting positions and scenarios actually recorded [f6656, f11336, f728, f95]. Published off-road hourly acceptance limits and standard statistical sample sizes were not found, so the program must establish separate criteria for advisory warnings, urgent warnings, speed reduction and full braking, despite MOSH's requirement for no false warnings or interventions at TRL4 [f2121, f5160, f2124, f2119]. Tuning should constrain missed or late interventions while optimizing false warnings, unnecessary brakes and productivity loss, without suppressing genuinely dangerous repeated berm alarms; false alarms in automatic braking can cause a brake slam [f136, f11522, f11306].

nodes.label: Alarm fatigue
nodes.text: Alarm fatigue is the state in which a person has heard so many alarms that did not matter that they stop reacting to alarms at all, including the one that does matter.
nodes.synopsis: Across the booklet, nuisance alarms undermine trust and can lead operators to ignore, override or disable proximity-warning systems, making nuisance rate a safety objective rather than merely a comfort issue [f3306, f7000]. In the NIOSH haul-truck study, drivers found continuous audible warnings annoying because most did not signify danger, and researchers found the warning disabled after shifts; however, the Morenci radar trial reported occasional false alarms that were not frequent enough to cause the system to be ignored [f3280, f3281, f7001]. Automatic braking does not remove this human-factors risk: operators may carry warning-ignore habits into their first automatic stops, while overly conservative triggers can introduce unnecessary braking, fatigue and intervention-created hazards [f1169, f6569]. ISO 21815-3 flags false-positive-induced alarm fatigue, but the booklet found no direct mining measurements of the probability of ignoring successive warnings or longitudinal physiological studies [f2427, f3304, f3305]. On-road evidence is mixed and should remain distinguished from mining evidence: one finding linked an 18% false-alarm rate to drivers ignoring FCW (12%) or giving up on it (11%), whereas a 2025 study found no “cry wolf” effect at 33% false alarms, despite unnecessary braking [f11680, f11682]. Validation therefore needs to address habituation, warning meaning, reaction time, predictable escalation and restart, alongside tuning unnecessary warnings and braking as safety goals [f2924, f14430].

nodes.label: Switching off and bypassing
nodes.text: Switching off and bypassing means defeating a safety system on purpose, by turning it off, overriding it, removing the tag it tracks, or redesigning its zones so it no longer protects what it should.
nodes.synopsis: Across the booklet, nuisance interventions are identified as the main documented reason mining proximity systems were disabled; bypasses, overrides, tag removal and altered zones can ultimately remove protection when needed [f116, f6306, f11764]. Direct examples include a Caterpillar 793B audible alarm found switched off after shifts and a June 2017 underground fatality involving a worker with 87 prior emergency-stop override activations; however, the alarm observation was partly anecdotal, and the research separately reports finding no field data on disabling collision mitigation systems [f3012, f3283, f11802, f5840]. ISO 16001:2017 prohibits single-action disablement, while MOSH forbids routine override use and requires monitored, abuse-resistant overrides limited to under five minutes and under 10 km/h [f2068, f2413, f2922, f5839]. Deactivation is nevertheless required in some operating conditions: Komatsu specifies switching off stop control during trailer loading because rapid stops can destabilize the machine, and wheel-loader guidance also lists slopes, slippery or soft ground and suspended loads [f1241, f10420]. On-road findings should not be treated as a uniform predictor of off-road behavior: an 18% false-alarm rate was associated with ignoring or abandoning warnings, whereas simulator studies with 20–33% false alarms still shortened brake reactions, and another finding reports 93% of drivers leaving automatic braking enabled [f3020, f3038]. Validation therefore needs to address override behavior and nuisance-induced disengagement, not just detection and stopping distance, with documented deactivation rules; whether configuration-based disabling is permissible in some markets, and its effect on the EU safety case, remains unresolved [f577, f1986, f10731, f2953].

nodes.label: Operator reaction time
nodes.text: Operator reaction time is the time between a warning (or the appearance of a hazard) and the moment the operator begins to act, for example by pressing the brake.
nodes.synopsis: The manufacturer is developing automatic braking that intervenes if the operator does not react, so validation still requires assumptions about operator actions and intervention waiting time [f2955, f11484, f11821]. No representative field-measured distribution of heavy-machine operators’ responses to proximity warnings, or validated off-road operator model, was found; the booklet recommends uncertain response parameters and sensitivity analysis rather than a validated average [f11814, f3040, f11822]. Borrowed road-research delays are 0.5–1 s, while the broader cited assumptions span approximately 0.5–2.5 s and a Hitachi patent allows a 1–3 s margin; the illustrative combined operator-plus-mechanical delay of 2 s adds 22.2 m of travel at 40 km/h before braking distance [f3017, f6228, f6206, f3220]. ISO 3450:2011 excludes operator reaction from stopping distance, whereas US MSHA Table M-1 includes 1 s of operator time plus 0.5–2.5 s of system response; the corpus also says ISO 21815-3 both excludes operator time from stopping distance and accounts for operator action time, leaving the distinction insufficiently explained [f5976, f6058, f2898, f6241]. Machine simulators can establish responses to warnings, and warning-fleet history may anchor response timing, but behaviour under automatic braking may differ from warning-only behaviour [f960, f7931, f7479]. Human-machine interface timing and warning-zone extent must provide response opportunity, and driver-model choice materially affects predicted benefit: cited road research estimates warning-system benefits of 53–96% [f11843, f13901, f3045].

nodes.label: Human factors
nodes.text: Human factors is the field that studies how people perceive, decide and act when working with machines, and designs the machine so that real people, tired or busy or distracted, can use it safely.
nodes.synopsis: As of October 2026, the booklet treats human factors as essential to heavy off-road collision-mitigation validation: coverage must include warning meaning, habituation, reaction time, predictable escalation and restart, while operator and pedestrian models require their own validation [f2957, f2924, f10350]. Acceptance is a material operational risk: 2024 mining research links false-positive interventions to production losses, wear and operator resistance; workers at seven coal mines reported unnecessary shutdowns from once daily to 15 times per cut, and nearly 70% worried about how and when proximity systems take control [f1530, f3013, f11660]. The booklet recommends measuring unwanted warnings and interventions by operating hour and task rather than per detection, because an excellent aggregate false-positive rate can conceal an intervention during nearly every loading cycle; no published operator-accepted false-alarm rate was found [f11608, f11609, f248]. Evidence remains incomplete: searches found no validated off-road operator model, reaction distributions or study quantifying the change from warning-only to automatic braking, so current fleet behavior may not predict future reliance, reactions or overrides [f250, f3042, f7482, f7479, f7480]. Human-in-the-loop evidence may be needed for operator-response claims, but simulator studies cannot establish long-term trust, complacency or production-pressure effects, and independently validated perception and braking components do not establish closed-loop safety [f8208, f961, f8196].

nodes.label: Human-machine interface (HMI)
nodes.text: The human-machine interface (HMI) is everything through which the system and the operator communicate: the screens, lights, sounds, vibrations and buttons in the cab.
nodes.synopsis: HMI is a safety-critical part of collision mitigation: warnings can fail if operators do not notice, understand or trust them, and the interface determines whether staged intervention leaves real time to respond [f11824, f11843]. The University of Queensland’s ACARP C24028 project ran in 2017 with follow-on work to 2019; its modified haul-truck simulator provided the strongest haul-truck-specific human-interface evidence found, with a richer proximity display reducing collision risk, braking force and travel time, but the project addressed advisory interfaces rather than automatic braking [f3314, f3315, f3468, f3466, f573].
