ISO 16001:2017 requires audible warnings at least 3 dB above ambient under specified operating conditions, visual warnings within a forward 120° arc, a flashing red light for the most severe warning, and no haptic-only warnings; ISO 21815-3 requires distinguishable warning levels [f2406, f2408, f2410, f6240]. Nuisance and ambiguous indications remain material risks: continuous haul-truck audible warnings were annoying enough to be switched off, an 18% false-alarm result does not establish an acceptable lower rate, and WorkSafe SIR 286 links recovery problems to mode misunderstanding and desensitization [f11840, f3331, f10719, f10839]. Operator studies should precede expensive prototype safety tests, VIL can exercise the real interface alongside braking dynamics without exposing people or targets, and recordings must capture operator inputs and warning states to assess usefulness [f13415, f13393, f5636, f5637]. Haptic effectiveness remains an explicit research gap, despite on-road provisions allowing very brief brake-jerk cues above 4 m/s²; degraded modes, annunciation, recovery procedures and human understanding therefore need explicit validation [f5837, f6498, f11035].

nodes.label: Operator behavior change
nodes.text: Operator behavior change is the way people start to work differently once a protective system exists, including risk compensation (taking more risk because they feel protected) and over-reliance (letting the system do the watching).
nodes.synopsis: Operator behavior can change positively or negatively after protective technology is introduced; automatic braking may prompt reliance, resistance, overrides or disabling after nuisance interventions [f791, f1982]. Mining evidence strongly establishes that operators override or disable functions that interfere with production, although frequency across sites is unknown; the June 2017 fatal continuous-miner investigation found emergency-stop override had become common practice [f3449, f3294]. Off-road risk compensation remains a credible but unmeasured hypothesis: worker reports describe riskier positioning and a false sense of security, but representative surface-mining evidence of faster driving, closer following or greater risk-taking was not found [f3424, f3034, f3455]. Warning-only fleet data cannot reliably characterize future automatic-braking behavior because operator reactions censor logs and behavior changes when warnings become interventions; shadow mode also cannot establish whether operators counteract actual braking [f7940, f7480, f8205, f598]. Long-term adaptation cannot be established through simulators or the four-month validation window, so the booklet recommends explicit behavioral validation, staged release with field monitoring, and collection of missing quantitative data during pilot deployment [f580, f378, f1105, f11859, f11860].

nodes.label: Tasks that look like a collision risk to a sensor
nodes.text: Many normal, intended parts of the job, such as loading a truck, bumping a dump berm or working beside ground crew, put a large object close to the machine in exactly the way a sensor is designed to flag.
nodes.synopsis: Normal loading, stockpiling, dump-berm approaches and authorized ground-crew proximity can look dangerous to sensors; the booklet identifies wheel loaders as the clearest and hardest case for avoiding nuisance braking [f124, f3022, f11395]. A nuisance warning detects a real object without collision risk, unlike a false warning with no object present; in the NIOSH Caterpillar 793B study, 243 of 478 technically true alarms were nuisance alarms, accounting for 42% of all alarms, demonstrating the need for context rather than sensor precision alone [f5434, f3276, f3279]. Protection must distinguish intended approaches from intruding people or vehicles without simply ignoring loading zones, and legitimate ground-crew proximity requires a controlled task-and-mode concept [f11521, f11863, f3367]. Fixed stop gaps can prevent truck loading, Komatsu requires its stop function to be off during trailer loading, and Volvo uses slope memory to permit reversing down stockpiles; unnecessary automatic stops can themselves be hazardous [f3344, f1538, f10631, f7457]. Validation should use separate production-task scenarios, per-task metrics and shadow-mode reviews before brake actuation, rather than copying road-practice thresholds [f11874, f11876, f10729, f6196]. Evidence gaps remain for stockpile/wall nuisance-alarm frequency and intentional loading/spotting accident rates, while berm terminology is in tension: some facts classify berms as nuisance-warning objects, but another says their protective edge-reference detections should not be treated as nuisance [f3360, f3568, f5434, f11864].

nodes.label: New risks created by automatic braking
nodes.text: An automatic stop can itself cause harm, through the jolt to the operator, a shifting or spilled load, loss of stability on a slope, a following machine running into the stopped one, or the machine rolling back once the brake is released.
nodes.synopsis: Automatic braking introduces hazards of its own: sudden operator jolts, load spill, rollover or articulation instability, sliding, secondary collisions and rollaway; allowable interventions depend on the machine and operating situation [f114, f5941, f7456, f1539]. Moving from warning to intervention turns a false classification into a machine-motion command, while nuisance stops can encourage disabling or bypass and ultimately remove protection when needed [f3024, f11706, f11764]. The booklet recommends separately analyzing missed interventions and unsafe or unnecessary interventions, assigning each its own acceptance thresholds and including both in the simulation matrix [f2642, f8203]. ISO 19014-2:2022 brings brake-command integrity, faults, degraded modes and unintended activation into validation, but no off-road standard prescribing the balance between the two intervention categories was found [f5223, f8204]. On-road evidence identifies unnecessary braking as the dominant documented failure mode and reports a 20% increase in being struck from behind, whereas off-road intervention-created risks remain unmeasured: workers report jolting stops, the regulator knows of no resulting injuries, and evidence of braking-caused load spills, slope instability or rear-end strikes was not found [f115, f11674, f3025, f3026, f3027, f3031]. Important validation gaps remain: no safe maximum automatic deceleration for articulated machines was found, warning-product field evidence does not establish braking consequences, and passive shadow recording cannot prove them [f6555, f7945, f5737].

nodes.label: Warning-system fleet
nodes.text: The warning-system fleet is the set of machines the manufacturer has already sold with the proximity warning system, and its field history is the record of what those machines have detected, warned about and got wrong in real use.
nodes.synopsis: The existing warning-system fleet is identified as the best available early asset for off-road braking validation, providing recorded-data replay, shadow-mode evaluation and the only identified route to field-representative false-positive evidence before prototype arrival [f1252, f333, f1604]. Logging should begin immediately in October 2026 and capture winter 2026–2027, which is the last chance to obtain fleet snow and cold data before validation; the indicative plan instead specifies a November 1, 2026 start lasting 300 days, while a functioning recording and replay pipeline by mid-2027 is considered realistic but conditional [f1600, f11944, f897, f64, f834]. Fleet history can anchor exposure distributions, environmental conditions, nuisance warnings and operator responses, and its false-alarm history is the best available basis for setting braking intervention thresholds [f7931, f11897, f1168]. However, useful raw sensor data, machine signals, synchronized timestamps and labels are not established, replay requires an independent record of what was actually present, and validation use depends on ground truth, consent and data rights that the research did not fully examine [f519, f11899, f8246, f8247]. Warning-fleet history can validate simulation inputs and components but not the new closed-loop braking chain; no public off-road shadow-mode precedent or earth-moving authority accepting this history as the principal simulation-validation basis was found [f11901, f1602, f7949]. Operator responses censor the logs, learned disregard of frequent warnings creates transition risk, and how existing warning-system tuning should carry over to automatic braking remains unexamined [f11903, f1169, f1170].

nodes.label: Sensor and prototype freeze
nodes.text: The sensor freeze is the project milestone at which the sensor types, numbers and mounting positions are fixed, and the prototype freeze is the milestone at which the first representative hardware and software are fixed; the booklet uses "before freeze" and "after freeze" to divide the work.
nodes.synopsis: Prototype hardware and software are expected in mid-2027, leaving under four months for validation; the plan depends on that arrival date [f1173, f10375, f11636]. The proposed capability-building period runs from October 2026 through June 2027, and the booklet recommends completing the credibility envelope and preparatory infrastructure before prototype arrival rather than treating arrival as the start of preparation [f1478, f71, f11340, f11341]. Sensor selection remains unconfirmed and is described as the largest schedule risk: the recommendation is to lock it by early 2027, while keeping the architecture sensor-agnostic and freezing supplier-independent interfaces early [f287, f1618, f1616, f485, f5577]. Most infrastructure can be developed without the final sensor or ECU if interfaces are established early, but sensor-model validation requires representative hardware, and a validated sensor digital twin should not be claimed before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated [f5568, f5115, f508]. Freeze is also a change-control boundary: a later sensor-modality change requires re-deriving affected statistical strata and re-drawing samples, consuming the short validation window, while software, calibration and simulator versions should be frozen or subject to impact analysis [f7491, f7492, f8229].

nodes.label: Validation window
nodes.text: The validation window is the period of less than four months after the prototype arrives in mid-2027 in which the Collision Mitigation System must be validated.
nodes.synopsis: Across the corpus, prototype hardware and software are expected in mid-2027, with validation required in less than four months; Chapter 12 describes about seven months, October 2026–April 2027, for preparing virtual-testing capability [f3, f1173, f9402, f11338]. Comparable functions previously required three to four years of mostly physical testing and per-model tuning, and the research found no documented case proving full validation of a new machine family in about four months [f2030, f4391, f1255, f7350]. Expert opinion makes feasibility conditional on completing simulation credibility and sensor-model validation before prototype arrival, so the final window should confirm preparations, correlate models and resolve discrepancies rather than establish the methodology [f7591, f4458, f5614, f7593, f11342]. The proposed route combines an analytical safety case, credibility-framed simulation and targeted physical tests, but this evidence plan is a research-derived recommendation, not a requirement imposed by the sources; completing the indicative physical matrix also depends on shared instrumentation across machine families [f2137, f2637, f6178]. Important constraints remain: the window excludes northern cold-season conditions, finite simulation capacity forces selective high-fidelity testing, and the research does not establish that testing volume caused the historical three-to-four-year duration [f4403, f10460, f8871, f10394].

nodes.label: Site type and the "100+ site types" claim
nodes.text: A site type is a class of job site with a characteristic layout, surface and traffic (an open pit, a quarry face, a stockpile yard, a road works), and the "100+ site types" claim is the challenge statement that one machine may work across 100 or more job sites and applications.
nodes.synopsis: The challenge is that one machine may work across 100 or more job sites and applications; chapters repeatedly frame this as a requirement for braking coverage across more than 100 site types, with more than 10 operating scenarios per machine [f16, f283, f5130, f11497]. Combining sites, scenarios, roughly seven weather/light conditions and machine variants exceeds 7,000 validation cells, while finer combinations can reach millions [f5206, f5468, f11331]. Site counts alone are not evidence of coverage: the booklet recommends an auditable taxonomy of sensing- and stopping-relevant attributes, parameterised representative environments anchored to surveyed real sites, and testing of equivalence classes and interactions [f8213, f8214, f3705, f6729]. No single environment-creation method or tool has demonstrated the required breadth in the available time; expert judgment rejects a newcomer’s fully credible all-site, all-weather, all-sensor toolchain by mid-2027, and a four-month simulation window forces low-fidelity sweeps with high fidelity reserved for critical cases [f3699, f8281, f1590, f8871]. Statistical generalisation remains unresolved, with no known exposure distribution for the 100-plus site population; fielded warning-system logs and leave-one-site-type-out validation are proposed ways to improve evidence, not proofs of unrestricted coverage [f2879, f352, f6611, f6995].

nodes.label: Season and weather coverage
nodes.text: Season and weather coverage means making sure the system has been tested in all the conditions it will meet, including rain, snow, fog, dust, mud, glare, dusk and darkness, and the problem is that the validation window falls in a season that contains few of them.
nodes.synopsis: The braking system must work across rain, snow, fog, dust, dusk, darkness and glare, but coverage cannot be assumed to transfer between different sites, machines and weather combinations [f285, f3599, f614]. The planned mid-2027-plus-four-month validation window falls in northern summer and autumn, excluding natural snow, freezing fog and low winter sun; winter 2026–2027 is the last cold-season collection opportunity before that window [f11943, f10461]. Start existing warning-fleet sensor recording in October 2026 and continue through winter, capturing raw sensors, machine buses and environmental metadata; preferentially selecting good-weather, daytime recordings would bias coverage [f97, f728, f5661]. Weather chambers, generated dust, fog and rain, southern-hemisphere sites and winter fleet recordings can partly mitigate the seasonal shortfall, but proving grounds cannot control weather or establish natural exposure, dust remains the biggest off-road sensor-simulation gap, and no accepted simulated-weather realism score exists [f777, f5729, f11949, f11950]. The proposed coverage strata already exceed 7,000 cells, statistical demonstration of off-road weather generalisation remains unresolved, and expert judgment rejects a newcomer delivering a fully credible all-weather toolchain by mid-2027 [f5468, f2879, f1590].

nodes.label: Hazard, harm and risk
nodes.text: A hazard is something that could hurt someone, harm is the injury or damage that actually happens, and risk is how likely the harm is, combined with how bad it would be.
nodes.synopsis: Hazard means a potential source of harm, harm is actual injury or damage, and risk combines probability with severity; the booklet ranks a haul truck crushing a light vehicle in front of it as its number-one harm scenario [f11961, f11472]. The fatal-risk picture extends beyond people and vehicles: NIOSH's 2022 review found 85% of research cases focused on vehicle–vehicle interactions even though vehicle–environment events accounted for the largest share of reviewed fatal haul-truck accidents [f3002, f5824, f5825]. Automatic braking can introduce hazards as well as reduce them, with safe interventions depending on the machine and operation; validation must separately address failure to brake and unsafe or unnecessary braking [f1539, f808, f11966, f5816]. Regulatory duties emphasize risk reduction and evidence rather than a universal braking mandate: Australia's model WHS regulation 215 requires reasonably practicable collision-risk control and a warning device, while Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 requires risk reduction, reliable controls and technical conformity evidence [f2125, f2783, f2202]. Simulation cannot establish zero risk or cover unconceived hazards, and staged release does not establish safety beyond its operating domain; sensor models need real-measurement calibration, and highest-risk cases need physical confirmation [f995, f789, f976, f5598, f11124]. The plan should trace every requirement, test and acceptance criterion to a named hazard and explicitly state its safety boundaries; unresolved coverage includes attachment hazards outside the cited draft ISO 21815-4 scope, while software-related braking risks lack quantified collision-incident evidence [f11969, f10155, f6589, f3665].

nodes.label: Hazard analysis and risk assessment
nodes.text: Hazard analysis is the organized search for everything about a machine and its use that could cause harm, and risk assessment is the judgment of how likely and how severe each of those harms would be.
nodes.synopsis: Automatic braking requires a new, machine-specific hazard analysis: missed braking and unsafe or unnecessary intervention must be assessed separately, and neither stopping sooner nor matching the old warning system establishes safety [f1977, f118, f11891, f10529]. Its scope must include pedestrian strikes, shifted loads, downhill and loss-of-control cases, and post-brake hazards such as rollaway, brake latching and second collisions during restart; downhill and loss-of-control cases were omitted from the booklet's eight questions [f3102, f3400, f6599, f3630]. ISO 19014-1 requires safety analysis to determine risk reduction and machine performance level, while Part 5 tables can avoid a full analysis for every new model; ISO 13849-1:2023 alone does not specify the collision function's required performance level [f10516, f2076, f2350]. Validation should trace requirements, scenarios, tests and acceptance criteria to named hazards and justify coverage of the operating population; statistical methods cannot repair missing hazard classes or an unvalidated simulator [f11969, f8030, f9730, f650]. The indicative plan starts hazard-analysis and scenario work on 1 October 2026 for 90 days, calls for a machine-readable hierarchy during October 2026 to mid-2027, and requires approved intervention analysis before prototype arrival to avoid consuming the four-month validation window in debate [f893, f7361, f11970]. Risk prioritization should not be driven by a 5-by-5 heat map, because the corpus reports ranking defects and range compression in such matrices [f9894, f9442, f9895].

nodes.label: Safety function and safety-related control system
nodes.text: A safety function is one specific job that a machine's control system must do to keep people safe, and the safety-related control system is the chain of parts (sensor, computer, actuator) that performs that job.
nodes.synopsis: Adding automatic braking changes an awareness-only system into a motion-controlling safety function within ISO 19014-2; matching the old warning system is therefore the wrong acceptance target, and braking targets must come from hazard analysis [f2075, f11986, f11989]. The safety case should separately analyze failure to intervene when required and intervention when unsafe or unnecessary, with separate acceptance thresholds [f2141, f11987]. Validation needs evidence for control hardware, software and environmental qualification beyond perception testing, and even perfect sensor simulation cannot compensate for incorrect braking or machine-dynamics models [f1098, f7735, f5089]. Cybersecurity, configuration and updates become safety-relevant when software commands brakes, while ISO 19014-4 excludes cybersecurity and therefore requires separate coverage [f3664, f7488]. Field exposure alone cannot prove a rare-event safety function, and the corpus found no published quantified reductions in physical testing for off-road safety functions [f312, f7563, f7865]. Planning remains qualified by standards described as draft, under revision or under publication in October 2026, unresolved machine-specific applicability, and disagreement over excluding machine learning versus assuring it within the safety function [f6547, f10419, f9786, f1125].

nodes.label: Functional safety
nodes.text: Functional safety is the part of safety that depends on a control system doing the right thing at the right time, including when its own parts fail.
nodes.synopsis: For brake-commanding functions on earth-moving machines, the corpus identifies ISO 19014, using MPLr, rather than ISO 26262 as the functional-safety framework; awareness-only systems are excluded from ISO 19014-2, but issuing brake commands crosses that scope boundary [f2071, f2196, f11985, f11986]. Adding automatic braking therefore changes the safety-engineering scope: targets should come from hazard analysis rather than matching the warning system, and validation must address faults, degraded modes, missed braking and unintended braking beyond perception performance [f5221, f11989, f5223, f5810, f11089]. Required evidence spans control hardware, software and environmental qualification, including documented safety-function performance under expected environmental conditions [f1098, f7735]. Planning should confirm standards applicability early with a qualified functional-safety specialist and map the minimum evidence package to the October 2026 editions; all five ISO 19014 parts were due for reissue that month, shortly before design verification freezes, while several cited sources remain marked draft or under revision [f9787, f11099, f12000, f6548, f1098]. Cybersecurity, configuration control and software updates become safety-relevant when software commands brakes, but ISO 19014-4 excludes cybersecurity, and no incident statistics quantify these risks, so separate safety and cybersecurity processes are needed rather than unsupported accident frequencies [f3664, f10820, f3665, f3666]. The corpus also flags a planning gap: the eight machine-motion and brake-timing questions omitted functional safety and integrity level, while the skeptic's review objects to treating the new safety-control function as an incremental feature [f6579, f10515].

nodes.label: Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF)
nodes.text: SOTIF is the part of safety concerned with a system that has no broken parts yet still behaves unsafely, because its sensing or decision-making is not good enough for the situation it meets.
nodes.synopsis: SOTIF concerns unsafe sensing or decision-making despite no broken parts, including both missed people and nuisance braking for harmless objects [f12007, f12013]. ISO 21448:2022 is a road-vehicle standard outside the scope of heavy off-road machines; the booklet nevertheless borrows its triggering-condition logic for scenarios, requirements and the perception safety case [f2355, f12008, f12015, f15295]. The booklet pairs ISO 19014 for the intervention chain with SOTIF-related perception concepts, but functional safety and fault injection alone cannot establish healthy-system perception performance [f12018, f12021, f1009]. Visibility in dust, snow, fog, glare and darkness remains the hardest uncertainty and the least suited to simulation, so perception robustness must rest on physical and recorded-sensor evidence [f12019, f12020]. The research did not verify the on-road ISO 21448 approach, and Chapter 8's evidence linking braking safety and perception limits is draft, limiting the assurance planners can draw from these references [f5812, f6580].

nodes.label: Performance Level (PL) and Category
nodes.text: A Performance Level is a five-step grade, written a to e, that says how reliably a safety function on a machine must work, and the Category describes the circuit architecture used to reach that grade.
nodes.synopsis: Performance Level (PL) grades safety-function reliability from a (lowest) to e (highest), while Categories B, 1, 2, 3 and 4 describe circuit architectures; achieved PL also depends on component MTTFd, diagnostic coverage and common-cause-failure protection [f12022, f12023, f12026, f12025]. ISO 13849-1:2023 supplies the generic machinery method, including software, but does not assign the collision-mitigation function's required PL: that comes from application-specific risk assessment or a type-C standard, with severity, exposure and avoidability informing the assessment [f15263, f2350, f12024, f11972]. ISO 19014 provides the earth-moving-machine framework, using required and achieved Machine Performance Levels (MPLr and MPLa); ISO 13849 remains relevant for generic subsystems and machines outside that sector's scope [f12034, f15264]. The intervention path needs a PL or integrity assignment plus fault testing, and the required level drives architecture and validation effort as much as threshold tuning; however, the Chapter 8 evidence is draft, its motion-and-braking questions omitted functional integrity, and Chapter 9 did not verify standard editions [f7455, f6581, f6579, f12033]. PL a spans approximately one dangerous failure per 10,000–100,000 hours; the glossary gives PL e a band of 10^-8–10^-7 per hour and compares it roughly with SIL 3, although its accompanying 'fewer than one per 10 million hours' wording is stricter than the band's upper endpoint [f12027, f12028, f12052]. Leaving hazard analysis, level allocation, acceptance metrics or applicable editions undecided in 2027 threatens to consume the validation window, described in the glossary as four months [f10766, f11022, f12458].

nodes.label: Machine Performance Level (MPL)
nodes.text: The Machine Performance Level is the earth-moving-machinery version of the Performance Level, defined in the ISO 19014 series, with a required level (MPLr) set by hazard analysis and an achieved level (MPLa) demonstrated by the design.
nodes.synopsis: For brake-commanding heavy off-road functions, the corpus uses ISO 19014 Machine Performance Levels rather than ISO 26262/ASIL; MPL uses levels a–e and is tailored to earth-moving machinery [f2071, f12035, f12066]. Hazard analysis through the Part 1 Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA) assigns MPLr, and design evaluation must demonstrate MPLa at least as high, with Part 2 addressing architecture, reliability and fault behavior [f15169, f2337]. Part 5 tables can replace a full MCSSA for each new model when their use-case assumptions hold, but the booklet neither reviewed a collision-avoidance/automatic-braking table entry nor found a published MPLr for that function [f2332, f2334, f2335]. The standards baseline needs confirmation: Chapter 8 marks its Part 5 evidence as draft, while other passages describe normative tables and report second editions of Parts 1–4 and the first full edition of Part 5 under publication for October 2026 [f6284, f10523, f12041]. The planning recommendation is an approved MCSSA before prototype arrival, covering failure to intervene and incorrect intervention, allocated performance levels and requirements-to-test traceability; postponing these decisions risks consuming the four-month validation window in debate rather than evidence gathering [f10530, f10540]. MPLr determines the redundancy, diagnostics and evidence needed for the braking chain, and the functional safety engineer expects both required and achieved levels to be allocated [f12046, f11088].

nodes.label: Safety Integrity Level (SIL)
nodes.text: A Safety Integrity Level is a grade from 1 to 4 used in the IEC 61508 family of standards to say how much risk reduction a safety function must deliver, and the same three letters are used in this booklet for software-in-the-loop, a completely different thing.
nodes.synopsis: Safety Integrity Level denotes the IEC 61508 safety-function grades SIL 1–4, not software-in-the-loop; context distinguishes reliability requirements from test methods, where the booklet recommends software-in-the-loop for volume and hardware-in-the-loop for timing, interfaces and faults [f12048, f12050, f12058, f12057, f13341]. For frequently acting functions, SIL specifies dangerous-failure probability bands: SIL 1 spans one failure in 100,000 to one million hours, each higher grade is ten times stricter, and SIL 3 spans 10^-8–10^-7 per hour and is roughly as demanding as PL e [f12051, f12052]. The grade also governs hardware-analysis and software-development rigor, while FMEDA supplies failure classifications for diagnostic coverage and PL, MPL and SIL probability calculations [f12053, f12098]. Chapter 9 requires the collision-mitigation intervention path to receive a performance-level or integrity assignment plus fault testing, consistent with the glossary requirement and mining customers’ safety-integrity specifications [f7455, f15273, f12059]. Standards selection remains unresolved: IEC 61508, IEC 62061 and ISO 25119 are listed as alternatives whose fit was not verified, Chapter 9’s editions were not verified, and IEC 62061:2021 is listed as current but not reviewed [f12054, f7455, f15267].

nodes.label: Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL)
nodes.text: ASIL is the road-vehicle grading of how demanding a safety requirement is, from A (lowest) to D (highest), defined in ISO 26262, and it does not apply by scope to off-road machines.
nodes.synopsis: ASIL is ISO 26262’s road-vehicle safety-requirement grading scale, ranging from A (lowest) to D (highest); it does not apply by scope to the heavy off-road collision mitigation system considered here [f12060, f12065]. Its hazard assessment combines severity S0–S3, exposure E0–E4 and controllability C0–C3 to yield ASIL A–D or QM, meaning ordinary quality management with no safety requirement [f12062, f12063]. Chapter 3 and the glossary consistently distinguish ISO 19014’s Machine Performance Level (MPL) scale from ASIL, so the program plan must translate ASIL terminology to MPL rather than adopt ASIL targets or passenger-car braking values and scenarios for a loaded haul truck on gravel [f2356, f12066, f15294, f12044, f12071]. Automotive terminology remains common among suppliers and engineers, while ISO 26262 Parts 2 and 8 and ISO/PAS 8800 are retained only as reference material explicitly marked as on-road evidence [f12070, f12067, f12068, f12069]. The facts establish the scope boundary and translation requirement but provide no specific ASIL-to-MPL mapping [f12060, f2356, f12071].

nodes.label: Fail-safe, safe state, controlled stop and emergency stop
nodes.text: A fail-safe system moves itself to a safe state when something goes wrong, and for a moving machine that safe state is usually reached by a controlled stop or, when time is short, an emergency stop.
nodes.synopsis: South African mining regulations require collision-prevention systems to fail to safe without human intervention; Regulation 8.10 describes warning, retardation toward a safe speed if the operator does not act, and then automatic braking [f1362, f2441]. MOSH specifies fail-to-safe within 500 ms of detecting a critical failure and lost-connection detection within 500 ms, although one HIL comparison lists both 500 ms and 50 ms fail-to-safe limits without explaining their respective scope [f2359, f12076, f5698]. MOSH specifies emergency-stop deceleration of 1.9 m/s² for machines exceeding 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for others, versus controlled-stop values of 1.0 or 0.5 m/s²; abrupt or false braking can itself create hazards and reduce acceptance [f5560, f5561, f1536, f3622]. Post-stop safety requires attention to brake hold and release: ISO 21815-3 recommends operator action before release where needed to prevent rollaway, but off-road implementation data was not found [f6305, f6525, f6526]. Human overrides and recovery are material risks: a June 2017 fatal-accident investigation recorded 87 prior emergency-stop overrides, while WorkSafe WA Report 286, dated 7 March 2025, describes autonomous trucks resuming movement after communications restoration while operators approached them [f3295, f10718]. HIL data injection can test timing, diagnostics and fail-to-safe behaviour, but functional safety does not establish perception capability; validation should explicitly cover degraded modes, recovery and post-stop hazards rather than nominal driving alone [f5697, f12021, f10778, f11035, f6600].

nodes.label: Fault, failure, failure mode and fault injection
nodes.text: A fault is a defect inside a system, a failure is the moment the system stops doing its job because of a fault, a failure mode is the particular way it fails, and fault injection is deliberately introducing faults to see how the system responds.
nodes.synopsis: Fault evidence is required alongside intended-function validation: the braking architecture must address sensor, computation, communication and actuator faults, while fault injection alone cannot establish perception performance when hardware works normally [f384, f10528, f659]. MOSH requires supplier FMECA identification of critical faults, fail-to-safe within 500 ms of critical-failure detection, and lost-connection detection within 500 ms [f2358, f2359, f12076]. The recommended allocation is SIL for test volume and HIL for timing, interfaces and faults; ISO 13849-2:2012 includes software simulation of faults, but SIL cannot prove final-ECU timing, processor or I/O faults [f12057, f9767, f5269]. Nominal simulation fidelity does not demonstrate fault tolerance: corrupted messages, dropouts, timing faults, bus congestion, frozen values and actuator faults need explicit testing, and replay cannot establish performance for failures absent from its logs [f8199, f8200, f5241]. Degraded braking, thermal limits and brake-system state belong in the safety case; sensor unavailability differs from confidently incorrect sensing, and recovery or degraded modes can remain unsafe despite successful nominal collision avoidance [f3634, f7464, f10777]. Unnecessary braking dominates the cited on-road failure evidence, although complaints do not always indicate defects; the booklet also identifies omitted brake-degradation questions and warns that postponing fault-response decisions until prototype delivery can consume the four-month validation window [f1223, f1229, f6593, f10540].

nodes.label: FMEA, FMECA and FMEDA
nodes.text: These are three related table-based methods that go through a system part by part and ask, for each part, how it could fail, what would happen, how serious that would be and, in the FMEDA, whether the system would notice.
nodes.synopsis: FMEA, FMECA and FMEDA examine component failures, effects and severity; FMEDA additionally assesses detection and classifies failures as safe or dangerous and detected or undetected, feeding diagnostic coverage and PL, MPL and SIL probability calculations [f12097, f12098]. MOSH requires a supplier FMECA to define critical faults for collision prevention products, treats degraded sensing as a fault, and requires fail-to-safe within 500 milliseconds of detecting a critical fault [f2358, f2905, f12102, f15643]. FMEA or FMEDA are inputs to fault injection and robustness testing, alongside injectable interfaces, SIL/HIL benches and diagnostic requirements; FMEDA tells testers which faults to inject and which diagnostics must catch, and can be completed before a prototype arrives [f1010, f12103, f12104, f12105]. The illustrative radar power-connector open circuit is dangerous because it prevents detections and braking commands; heartbeat loss detects it within 500 milliseconds, followed by fail-to-safe, but the example does not separately quantify the post-detection transition time [f12099, f12100, f12102]. In the illustrative automatic-braking safety case, FMEDA combines with fault-injection results and software verification to support the required Machine Performance Level claim, rather than establishing that claim alone [f12244].

nodes.label: Fault tree analysis (FTA)
nodes.text: A fault tree starts from one unwanted top event and works downward, drawing the combinations of smaller failures that could cause it, joined by AND and OR logic.

nodes.label: Common-cause failure and independence of channels
nodes.text: A common-cause failure is one event that knocks out two or more parts that were supposed to back each other up, so redundancy only counts when the channels are truly independent.
nodes.synopsis: Redundancy earns safety credit only when a single cause cannot disable both channels; shared power, software bugs, environmental stresses, assumptions or calibration errors can defeat apparent independence [f12112, f12113, f12114]. Achieved Performance Level depends partly on common-cause protection, and ISO 13849 scores defenses including separation, diverse technologies and environmental protection; the glossary identifies diversity as the strongest defense discussed [f12025, f12115, f12116]. Sensor fusion therefore requires evidence addressing correlated degradation and disagreement between modalities, including physical evidence for environmental contrast, contamination and calibration [f505, f506, f12117]. Across planning and skeptical review, the booklet warns that shared assumptions in the product, virtual sensors, collision logic and test oracle can yield consistent but misleading results; independent real-world referents and validation sources that do not share simulator assumptions are the proposed defenses [f10344, f10606, f11245, f11247, f12123]. This virtual-testing risk is an inference from standard verification and validation practice: no documented off-road collision-system case producing misleading virtual results, or off-road accident attributed to a product–test-environment common-mode error, was found [f10607, f11246].

nodes.label: Diagnostic coverage and dead time of a safety function
nodes.text: Diagnostic coverage is the share of dangerous faults that the system can detect by itself, and dead time is any period during which the safety function is not actually protecting anyone, because a fault has not yet been noticed or because the function is degraded or switched off.
nodes.synopsis: Diagnostic coverage is the proportion of dangerous failures detected by the system itself; dead time includes undetected faults, start-up before self-tests finish, sensor blindness and degraded or switched-off operation [f12124, f12125, f12128]. Achieved Performance Level depends partly on diagnostic coverage, with ISO 13849 bands of none below 60%, low from 60–90%, medium from 90–99%, and high at 99% or above [f12025, f12126]. ISO 16001:2017 requires start-up self-checking and continuous fault monitoring, while off-road contamination makes sensor self-diagnosis and degradation detection particularly important [f2411, f2412, f2002]. MOSH requires disconnection detection within 500 ms, but the booklet's critical-fault wording differs between reaching safety within 500 ms after detection and detecting the failure and reaching safety within 500 ms; planners should resolve that timing distinction [f5284, f12102, f12132]. No published off-road acceptance value for availability or diagnostic coverage was found, so the booklet recommends measuring availability, time in degraded mode and fault-detection coverage rather than relying on detection rates measured only while available [f12133, f2633, f5441, f12129]. HIL data injection can test diagnostics and fail-to-safe behaviour, but treating degraded sensing as a fault can increase stops, and excessive stops or alarms risk operators switching systems off [f5697, f12134, f12135].

nodes.label: Residual risk and as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP)
nodes.text: Residual risk is the risk that remains after all the protective measures are in place, and ALARP is the principle that risk must be reduced until the cost of reducing it further would be grossly out of proportion to the benefit gained.
aliases: Residual risk and as low as reasonably practicable
nodes.synopsis: Residual risk remains after protective measures; ALARP requires further reduction unless its cost in money, time or trouble is grossly disproportionate to the benefit, with proportionality judged rather than calculated by a formula [f12138, f12143, f12144]. Australia's model WHS regulation 215 requires powered mobile plant collision risk to be controlled so far as reasonably practicable and requires a warning device [f2783]. Collision warning or avoidance technology cannot cover every situation, and failure-free testing does not prove zero risk; the program also faces risks from unnecessary stops and uncertainty from relying on simulation [f3646, f12150, f12149]. Which residual risks cannot credibly be represented virtually remains unresolved, so assessor-quality evidence should explicitly state residual risks and what simulation does not establish [f1973, f8054]. The proposed evidence chain ends in a residual-risk decision, with a single “golden thread” tracing one requirement from a real test through the model and virtual result to that decision [f10795, f10919]. Acceptance needs a named person or board and a documented disposition of unresolved risks; although deadline pressure can encourage acceptance, launch should depend on unresolved safety evidence rather than the calendar [f12139, f11136, f12151, f12152].

nodes.label: Acceptance criteria and pass or fail criteria
nodes.text: Acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions, agreed before testing starts, that decide whether a result is good enough, and pass or fail criteria are the same idea applied to one test.
nodes.synopsis: Published off-road acceptance targets remain sparse: ISO 16001:2017 is the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers, including 300 ms detection time; South Africa's braking regulation supplies no detection percentage, false-alarm limit or stopping test, while the MOSH surface specification requires at least 200 m detection range [f160, f165, f174, f2063, f2081]. No accepted off-road false-alarm rate was found, although ISO 21815-1:2022 requires physical performance tests with pass/fail criteria and a false-positive test; South African mine acceptance rests with the operator against the regulation, using industry guidelines as reference [f3605, f7726, f1367]. Automatic braking must be validated as a new safety-control function rather than against warning-system equivalence, with nuisance interventions weighted equally to missed interventions and stopping distance assessed against ISO 3450 or MOSH requirements [f10417, f10476, f5931, f5443]. Acceptance thresholds, statistical tests, confidence levels and stopping rules should be fixed before testing or hardware arrival, and the program should define criteria approved by technical authority [f644, f6956, f10600]. Test sufficiency should follow the claim and safety-relevant error bounds at declared operating boundaries—not fixed test or virtual-site counts—and public literature alone cannot establish whether the proposed architecture meets company release criteria [f5201, f6169, f4113, f4975]. Expert recommendations call for mature acceptance metrics and assessor agreement, plus a statistical acceptance plan and supporting validation infrastructure, by mid-2027; the manufacturer should retain ownership of acceptance criteria even when implementation is outsourced or hybrid [f7592, f5616, f8765, f8771, f8797].

nodes.label: Requirements and requirements-based testing
nodes.text: A requirement is a written statement of what the system must do, precise enough to be tested, and requirements-based testing means that every test exists to check a named requirement and every requirement has at least one test.
nodes.synopsis: Requirements engineering is the organizing backbone of validation: hazard analysis grounds requirements and acceptance criteria, and the traceability chain runs from hazard through safety and functional requirements, scenarios, tests, runs and results to safety-case evidence [f11978, f7105, f11969]. Starting in October 2026, planning should establish hazards, standards mappings and acceptance metrics before sensor and prototype freeze; the requirement–hazard–scenario hierarchy should be frozen during October 2026 to mid-2027, and an approved machine control system safety analysis should precede prototype arrival to avoid consuming the four-month validation window in requirements debate [f725, f7361, f12006, f10540]. SIL can establish requirements tests and large-scale closed-loop regression, but each safety requirement should be allocated to a test level containing its failure mechanisms; the new braking stage must be assessed against its own requirements rather than against a warning-only predecessor [f5266, f5780, f5500]. Requirements must address incorrect intervention as well as failure to intervene, with a remaining gap around unnecessary-braking rates and machine-stability consequences; object-class braking semantics also need safety requirements before threshold tuning [f10530, f9370, f6591]. South African mining provides performance requirements and a verification regime dated 11 October 2025, including TRL4 and TRL7 gates, while the program must baseline actually published ISO 19014 editions rather than assume planned October 2026 reissues are available, because standards transitions can force rework [f556, f2590, f12001, f8927].

nodes.label: Traceability
nodes.text: Traceability is an unbroken written chain of links from each safety claim to the requirement it rests on, to the scenarios and tests that check that requirement, to the recorded evidence, so that anyone can follow the chain in either direction.
nodes.synopsis: Traceability is a bidirectional written chain from safety claims through requirements, scenarios and tests to recorded evidence; the programme should establish this mapping before hardware is available and challenge disconnected work or unsupported claims [f12190, f1001, f727, f9818]. The operational test chain adds functional performance requirements, individual runs, results and safety-case evidence, while the credibility chain adds real-world referents, model credibility, uncertainty and residual-risk decisions [f7105, f10795]. Reproducibility requires detailed run manifests, archived tool and configuration versions, and traceable calibration inputs; missing binary or configuration provenance prevents results from being tied to an exact product state [f7108, f9386, f7043, f5664]. Before prototype arrival, the recommended safety analysis should derive requirements for failure to intervene and incorrect intervention, allocate performance levels, and map each safety requirement to simulation, hardware-in-the-loop or machine testing [f10530, f10542, f11095]. The decisive early demonstration is a single “golden thread” from a real test through a model and virtual result to a residual-risk decision: failure to demonstrate it by the first half of 2027 is an early warning, and simply multiplying scenarios would increase questionable evidence rather than assurance [f10919, f12195, f12196, f10796]. Traceability alone does not establish credibility: simulation traceability remains a validation item omitted from the machine-motion questions, and updates without regression and revalidation could leave 2027 evidence certifying an obsolete configuration [f6608, f11252].

nodes.label: Verification versus validation (V&V)
nodes.text: Verification asks "did we build the thing correctly, according to its specification?", validation asks "did we build the right thing, one that works in the real world for its intended use?", and V&V is the pair.
nodes.synopsis: Validation must finish in less than four months after prototype hardware and software arrive in mid-2027, against a historical baseline of three to four years of physical testing and tuning per machine model [f3, f281, f2029, f1174, f5858]. The research found no case in any industry of a new automatic braking function reaching accepted validation about four months after first representative hardware; vendor claims of sub-day validation concern incremental on-road builds on an existing platform, not that milestone [f58, f1201, f1209, f1211]. The manufacturer has not previously used simulation for this kind of validation, and expert opinion considers a working evidence factory—not completed off-road collision mitigation validation—realistic by mid-2027 [f7512, f10387, f372]. Standards recognize simulation among verification methods and, in ISO 13849-2:2012, among validation methods, but neither passing ISO 3450 nor using example stopping-distance calculations establishes that the complete braking function works [f9456, f9457, f9458, f2361, f7729]. Credible validation requires independently established ground truth with controlled measurement uncertainty, validation of sensor stimulation equipment, and evidence matched to the sensor interface actually consumed by the function; credibility communities have not agreed on validation metrics [f5196, f7473, f4864, f4869, f9357]. Planning must also account for uncertain ISO 19014 revisions expected in October 2026 and baseline the editions actually published at design-verification freeze, while public evidence remains incomplete for manufacturer validation methods, ultrasonic material fidelity, and realistic operator responses [f2330, f2331, f11394, f3944, f3469].

nodes.label: The V-model of development
nodes.text: The V-model is a picture of a development process shaped like the letter V: the left arm breaks the need down into requirements and designs, the bottom is where the parts are built, and the right arm climbs back up through tests that check each level against the level opposite it.
nodes.synopsis: The V-model links decomposition of needs into requirements and designs to matching tests; planning each test when its requirement or design is written establishes requirements-based testing and traceability [f12221, f12222]. IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 explicitly depict it, machinery software standards such as ISO 19014-4 follow its shape, and machine-learning extensions treat training data as a development artifact and SIL as the first closed-loop stage; the Chapter 1 evidence is labelled on-road [f12223, f12224, f532, f404]. The booklet assigns SIL to logic, HIL to timing and interfaces, and whole-machine testing to stopping, within a program of domain and scenario definition, large-scale virtual verification, smaller-scale physical confirmation, and staged release with field monitoring [f12225, f12226]. A generic toolchain can be built before hardware exists, but correlation requires the real sensor and machine, so the validation program must start before prototype arrival even though integrated product validation starts at arrival [f12227, f12228]. The planning conclusion is that four months covers only the top of the testing arm: the entire requirements-and-design arm and most test preparation must be completed before mid-2027 [f12229].

nodes.label: Safety case and safety argument
nodes.text: A safety case is a structured written argument, supported by evidence, that a system is acceptably safe for a stated use in a stated environment, and the safety argument is the reasoning that connects the evidence to the claim.
nodes.synopsis: The safety case organizes claims, arguments and evidence; the plan should be built backwards from the top-level claim to required evidence, methods, credibility levels, work packages and gates, rather than treating a complete scenario spreadsheet as physical evidence [f11298, f9453, f656]. For a four-month validation, the recommended route is an analytical safety case plus targeted physical tests and credibility-qualified simulation; the four months after hardware arrival should include sensor and braking correlation, discrepancy investigation, high-risk physical spot-checks and evidence assembly [f2137, f1596]. The claim spans the full chain from environment and sensing to machine motion and collision outcome, must address both missed and unsafe or unnecessary braking, and should derive its assurance target from the new hazard analysis rather than comparison with the old warning system [f383, f2141, f5816, f10529]. Simulation acceptance requires physical correlation and demonstrated credibility, but model accuracy is not system safety, no mature rule establishes sufficient sim-to-real agreement, and public literature cannot establish whether the proposed plan meets company release criteria [f8341, f7756, f7814, f5071, f4975]. Evidence reuse across machine variants is safety-case-specific and requires explicit transfer justification, configuration-controlled differences and bridging tests where changes affect safety; quantified production precedents for reducing physical validation were not found in the cited forklift, automated guided vehicle and military ground-vehicle cases [f7394, f7045, f7908, f7910, f1413, f1426, f1894]. Safety-case efficacy evidence is mainly case studies and cases can become paperwork, so the argument should disclose validity limits, address operator-dependent protection and be checked against final 2026 standards publications; the general machinery-safety obligation and functional-safety case already exist in 2027 for ML elements [f9451, f9452, f10683, f11807, f11833, f8930, f2380].

nodes.label: Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) and Structured Assurance Case Metamodel (SACM)
nodes.text: GSN is a standard set of diagram shapes for drawing a safety argument, and SACM is a formal data model that lets software tools store and exchange such arguments.
nodes.synopsis: GSN structures a safety argument as contextualized goals decomposed through strategies into subclaims and evidence; the booklet identifies GSN Community Standard version 3 (2021) as its current definition [f9705, f12251]. SACM instead defines the underlying assurance-case data model, enabling exchange across tools and links to requirements and test databases rather than prescribing a drawing style [f12253]. Across Chapters 10 and 12, the booklet recommends a structured simulation-credibility argument, a GSN or CAE sketch in the plan’s safety-scope section, and a preliminary argument in Appendix A; the scope section is allocated 1.5–3 pages [f8021, f10155, f10156, f10182]. The intended value is organizing what evidence must demonstrate and making the argument accessible to different stakeholders, not strengthening the evidence merely by drawing it [f12241, f12258, f12259]. The booklet found neither direct comparative evidence that notation improves heavy-machinery safety outcomes nor controlled studies of readers’ understanding, and warns that diagrams can make unsupported premises look persuasive [f9722, f9888, f9721].

nodes.label: Assurance case for autonomous products (UL 4600)
nodes.text: UL 4600 is a standard that explains how to build and judge a safety case for a product that makes decisions on its own, by setting out a long list of topics and questions the case must answer.
nodes.synopsis: UL 4600, third edition dated 17 March 2023, structures an autonomous-product safety case around questions and claims answered with evidence, rather than prescribed designs, tests or performance numbers [f12261, f15375, f12262, f15377]. Its coverage includes hazards, operating domain, perception, machine learning, metrics and field feedback, with conformance judged by the completeness of the responses [f12263]. The booklet recommends borrowing those question lists for the heavy off-road collision-mitigation validation plan and suggests 1.5–3 pages for the safety scope and top-level claim, using GSN v3 and UL 4600 as sources [f9984, f10156]. However, an automatic brake on an operator-driven machine is not an autonomous product, no off-road body has adopted UL 4600, and the plan should borrow its thoroughness without claiming compliance [f12267, f12269, f12270]. These recommendations do not establish simulation acceptance: the research did not examine UL 4600's simulation-credibility content or verify its simulation-acceptance provisions, and it also records both proponents and critics of safety cases [f7706, f15383, f10319].

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.text: Evidence is any recorded fact (a test result, a measurement, a field record, an analysis, a document) that supports or weakens a claim, and its strength depends on who produced it, how independently, and how directly it bears on the claim.
nodes.synopsis: The research used documented cases to judge what a team starting from zero in October 2026 could achieve by mid-2027, without internal machine recordings, site video, sensor specifications or documents; missing evidence had to be reported as “not found,” not replaced with estimates [f296, f7, f302]. Important claims were to distinguish independent evidence, vendor claims and expert opinion, report failures as well as successes, and explicitly mark on-road evidence because its transfer to off-road machines is an inference [f1191, f1193, f10402]. The off-road evidence base remains thin: a 2022 NIOSH review covered 64 articles from 2000–2020 and 97 haul-truck collision-system cases, yet mining intervention evidence is low-maturity, independent field data are old and sparse, and no peer-reviewed synthetic-only demonstration of heavy-machine collision-avoidance reliability was found [f5933, f5932, f5169, f6690]. Accident statistics establish the importance of mobile-machine risk rather than the fraction automatic braking could address, while near-miss under-reporting and unmeasured braking-created risks limit conclusions [f2982, f3007, f3025, f3046]. No reviewed excerpts of ISO 21815 or ISO 17757:2019, confirmed in 2024, set simulation-evidence rules, and no regulator acceptance of off-road virtual evidence was found; the FAA provides a published compliance example, while FDA credibility guidance makes evidence adequacy risk- and context-dependent rather than prescribing a universal physical-test minimum [f3908, f5215, f7619, f7642, f7646]. Programme work packages should therefore specify the safety evidence they must produce, organized into a safety case, with simulation directing scarce physical-test time and multiplying evidence rather than replacing physical tests [f9398, f11298, f11311].

nodes.label: Independent assessment, independent test body and safety board
nodes.text: Independent assessment is a review of the safety evidence by people who did not produce it; an independent test body is an outside organization that runs or witnesses tests; and a safety board is the internal group with the authority to accept or reject the safety case.
nodes.synopsis: Independent assessment is distinct from engineering confidence: in most markets, the manufacturer's internal safety board and customers accept the evidence, while a four-month evidence decision concerns externally acceptable simulation credibility rather than engineering speed alone [f12288, f1455, f12290]. South African mining published its independent verification specification on 29 August 2025, and MOSH requires supplier verification plus independent physical verification at TRL4 and TRL7, including separate coverage where machine braking characteristics differ [f348, f2478, f2459, f5613]. This regime creates substantial scheduling risk: as of October 2025, laboratory lead time was 18 weeks and growing, throughput was 1.6 tests per week, and first-pass rates were 42%–83%, supporting immediate booking and provision for at least one retest [f5787, f5788, f5789, f5790]. A program starting in October 2026 could realistically have an assessor-seen credibility dossier by mid-2027; the proposed March–April 2027 readiness gate requires assessor feedback and an independent decision on readiness, restricted scope or fallback [f69, f10198]. Credible review requires claim-to-evidence traceability, a declared validity envelope, independent physical evidence and assessor-selected confirmation tests, with decisions constrained to demonstrated validity [f12200, f12291, f7887, f7603]. External acceptance precedents exist in road applications, but no independent performance test was found for the listed off-road automatic-braking vendors, no explicit acceptance of legacy field history as a simulator reference was found, and the EU Machinery Regulation assessor and competence requirements remain unidentified [f1260, f7566, f1242, f7948, f12294].

nodes.label: Evidence gate and decision gate
nodes.text: A decision gate is a planned point at which management must decide whether a program continues, changes course or stops, and an evidence gate is a decision gate whose pass criterion is a piece of evidence obtained, not a date reached.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends four or five evidence gates whose pass criteria are demonstrated knowledge—such as model correlation and scenario coverage—not dates reached; legitimate outcomes include proceeding, restricting release, changing course or stopping [f9509, f9510, f12301, f16369]. Initial release should cover a narrow operating domain, with expansion to new sites, machine models, speeds and conditions allowed only as evidence arrives, preventing narrow-domain results from being silently generalised [f379, f723, f756]. Gate criteria should be signed in advance with a named decision-maker, safety specialists should co-own them, and an independent acceptance authority must be able to reject insufficient evidence [f12300, f10361, f1586]. The proposed G0–G4 milestones run from November 2026 to August–September 2027, but an alternative layered roadmap places credibility in February–March and evidence release in May–August, so the example calendars are not identical [f12304, f12305, f12306, f12307, f12308, f9875]. Market-access validation is not the only acceptance hurdle: site-specific requirements form a second gate, South African MOSH requirements include no false interventions at TRL4 and no false interventions or warnings at the laboratory gate, and standards applicability remains unresolved pending specialist confirmation [f2931, f178, f12164, f9786, f9787]. Launch and physical-test savings must remain contingent on accepted safety evidence and specific approved simulation substitutions; inadequate evidence must remain a legitimate programme conclusion rather than being overridden by calendar pressure [f10708, f10753, f10909, f10332].

nodes.label: Staged release and limited operating domain
nodes.text: Staged release means switching the automatic brake on first only for a narrow, well-understood set of machines, movements, speeds and conditions (the limited operating domain), and widening that set step by step as evidence from the field arrives.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends a restricted first release that widens only through evidence gates; all off-road collision-intervention products found in the research launched with narrow operating domains [f73, f379, f608, f11941]. The proposed initial envelope is reverse-only, low-speed braking on selected machine models, subject to a closed safety case; expert judgment additionally recommends a brief brake pulse returning control to the operator and exclusions for stockpiles, trailer loading and slopes [f721, f10972, f1597]. Volvo CE’s January 2023 precedent operated only in reverse at 3–15 km/h, and industry scope limits reflect hazards discovered through field experience [f420, f10640]. Narrowing the envelope reduces validation burden and can shorten time to a bounded release, but it does not validate excluded conditions; staged release requires runtime domain monitoring, a field-data loop and regulatory acceptance [f1599, f615, f616]. Field operation should begin without brake authority, warning-only behavior should remain outside the released envelope, and operator behavior change requires staged release with field monitoring [f752, f10975, f11859]. The proposed G4 release gate is August–September 2027, with release, restricted release or withholding determined by evidence supporting explicitly bounded claims; a funded restricted-scope fallback is recommended alongside virtual-validation development [f12308, f10747].

nodes.label: Field monitoring and operational monitoring
nodes.text: Field monitoring, also called operational or in-service monitoring, is the planned collection and review of data from machines in real use after release, to check that the system behaves as the safety case predicted and to catch the problems the tests missed.
nodes.synopsis: Field monitoring is planned collection and review of real-use data after release to check safety-case predictions and catch missed problems; the proposed programme therefore ends in staged, limited-domain release with runtime domain monitoring, a field-data loop and regulatory acceptance [f12336, f701, f616]. The four-month campaign should start a living evidence base: record warnings and interventions with machine, environmental and operator context, map near-misses and false brakes into scenarios, and use results for regression testing, model updates and operating-domain changes [f7447, f2934, f3652, f7446, f12339]. Production-readiness monitoring should extend over periods such as 3 months or 2000 hours, but no published MOSH TRL9 statistics were found; monitoring also addresses evolving site conditions, service errors and dust/glare model gaps [f5797, f5798, f7445, f5829, f8053]. Operator-behavior evidence remains incomplete: mining-specific post-deployment validation of calibrated trust and field data on disabling systems were not found, missing quantitative behavior data should be collected in pilots, and fatal accidents are too rare for post-release tuning [f3428, f5840, f11860, f3651]. On-road precedent shows that field performance can change quickly—Tesla's February and March 2022 updates were followed by unexpected-braking reports falling to 45 in 2024, 19 in 2025 and three by early 2026—but investigations can take years, so every post-release software change should be reassessed against accumulated safety evidence [f1502, f1505, f2017, f1156].

nodes.label: Proven in use and reuse of evidence
nodes.text: "Proven in use" is a formal route in the functional-safety standards for trusting a component because it has already worked reliably for a long time in the same conditions, and reuse of evidence is the broader idea of carrying test results and analyses from one machine model or product to another instead of repeating them.
nodes.synopsis: Evidence reuse across machine models is described as the biggest validation lever and the least documented: it must be designed in early, using common-core evidence plus explicit variant deltas rather than blanket family qualification [f366, f617, f12359]. No published case quantified cross-model time savings or demonstrated a heavy-machine family's validation shrinking from years to months; an under-four-month window therefore requires a narrower release claim or substantial evidence already in place [f261, f12361, f889]. Aerospace provides a qualified precedent: Lockheed Martin attributes F-35 Auto-GCAS integration in 2019, seven years earlier than planned, to agile development and reuse of F-16 work, while the booklet emphasizes decades of foundational development behind that acceleration [f1443, f1569]. Formal proven-in-use credit concerns a reused element with identical or highly similar definition and operating conditions, supported by sufficient service history; the booklet reports a 70% confidence basis for ISO 26262 and higher confidence under IEC 61508, but did not verify either route comprehensively [f12351, f7935, f7936, f7704, f15271]. Warning-system history can anchor encounter frequencies, detections, environmental distributions and operator behavior, but cannot validate the simulator or new closed-loop braking chain: adding braking changes the item, and warning-era records do not establish post-intervention outcomes [f12355, f12357, f7938, f11710]. Aviation guidance likewise permits relevant service history only with justified similarity and differences, while machine-family reuse requires explicit applicability arguments and configuration control covering sensors, tyres, brakes, payloads and software versions [f7925, f7045, f1141].

nodes.label: Equivalence argument between machine variants
nodes.text: An equivalence argument, also called a similarity argument, is the reasoned and evidenced claim that evidence gathered on one machine variant also holds for another, because the differences between them do not affect the safety-relevant behavior.
nodes.synopsis: Equivalence is a reasoned, evidenced claim that variant differences do not affect safety-relevant behavior; transferring validation to another machine model or sensor position is therefore a validation-domain extension requiring similarity and bridging evidence, not automatic inheritance [f12362, f189, f7569]. Evidence reuse is described as the biggest validation lever but the least documented, and neither quantified time savings nor a demonstrated reduction of large-family validation from years to months was found [f366, f261, f12361]. The recommended approach is common-core evidence plus explicit variant deltas, a parameterized family model validated at envelope corners, sensitivity analysis, and targeted bridge tests; whether the product range can actually be reduced to a few such families remains an experiment [f12359, f7573, f12365, f10887]. Machine-specific braking, dynamics, integration and sensing geometry limit transfer, while the reported MOSH regime requires independent verification of every type, model and serial number where braking characteristics differ [f3437, f11552, f5613]. As of the October 2026 basis described in the booklet, similarity arguments draw on ISO 19014-5, machine-specific ISO 21815-3 calculations and sampled physical verification, but no formal off-road regulatory acceptance, universal representative-machine rule, accepted transferred-brake-model test count or published off-road variant-transfer example was found [f2942, f2943, f6683, f6557, f7574]. Planning must also account for a 2027 sensor change invalidating parts of the reuse argument and for the unexamined requalification process following brake-component or control-software changes [f11912, f6612].

nodes.label: Safety of machinery (ISO 12100)
nodes.text: ISO 12100 is the foundation standard for machine safety: it defines the basic words (hazard, risk, protective measure) and sets out the general method for reducing machine risk in a fixed order.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 12100 is the foundational Type-A machinery-safety standard, defining safety terminology and the general method for assessing and reducing risk [f12374, f11962, f12375, f15261]. Its method starts by defining machine and use limits, identifying hazards, and estimating and evaluating risk, then requires reduction in strict order: inherently safe design, safeguarding and complementary protective measures, and information for use [f12378, f12379, f15261]. Automatic braking belongs to the second step rather than replacing safe design or site controls; consequently, identical braking algorithms can yield different safety results under different traffic rules and pedestrian controls [f12380, f12381, f12387]. Chapter 3 and the glossary consistently place ISO 21815-3:2023 beneath this framework as a machine-specific Type-C standard; the glossary says Type-C standards take precedence and distinguishes them from generic control-system standards such as ISO 13849 [f2165, f2664, f12377, f15007]. The mining nine-layer model reflects the same sequencing: understand site design and operating controls at Levels 1–7 before adding advisory technology at Level 8 and intervention technology at Level 9, while residual risk remains the risk left after protective measures [f12386, f12140].

nodes.label: Electro-sensitive protective equipment (ESPE) and safety-related sensors
nodes.text: ESPE is the family of certified safety sensors (light curtains, laser scanners and, recently, radar) that detect a person without touching them and trigger a protective stop, and IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 are the standards that define how such sensors are shown to be reliable.
nodes.synopsis: ESPE comprises certified non-contact person-detection sensors—light curtains, laser scanners and radar—that trigger protective stops; IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 provide their reliability framework [f12388]. Certification covers detection capability, response time and fault behavior, but assumes a stationary machine in a controlled space; IEC TS 61496-5:2023 establishes a radar certification basis while explicitly excluding aspects of moving radar protective-device applications [f12390, f672, f673]. Certified sensors can shorten the component-level safety argument and bound what learned perception must prove, but cannot establish whole-system performance on moving outdoor machines in dust, rain and glare [f12399, f12400, f1039]. IEC TS 62998-1 addresses safety-related sensors outside classic ESPE categories, including mobile and outdoor applications, but Inxpect’s reported use for its radar remains a vendor claim [f12391, f674, f1045]. The safety-rated sensor approach requires certified sensors and a certification body, with Low setup effort through buy-in, Medium relative cost and Low to Medium heavy-off-road maturity [f1041, f1042, f1043, f1044]. Separately, ISO 16001 specifies a 300-millisecond detection time and continuous self-checking for object detection systems, but has no lidar technology annex [f12396, f12397].

nodes.label: Machine learning in safety functions
nodes.text: Machine learning (ML) is software whose behavior is learned from examples rather than written as explicit rules, and when such software helps decide whether to brake, safety engineers treat it differently because its rules cannot be read, its failures are hard to predict, and the standards for it are still being written.
nodes.synopsis: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027 and places self-evolving ML safety components on a notified-body route, but whether trained-then-frozen perception qualifies is disputed; notified-body positions were not found, and Chapter 12 acknowledges reliance on secondary rather than verified primary wording [f12407, f2091, f11187, f10308]. The corpus repeatedly gives 2 August 2028 for machinery-related high-risk AI obligations, while also reporting removal from direct AI Act high-risk classification and a shift to Machinery Regulation delegated acts, which had not been adopted by 1 October 2026 [f53, f10453, f2095, f2096, f2098]. Notified-body lead time could exceed the four-month validation window, but published lead-time evidence was not found; an early opinion on frozen-model classification is recommended, with absent pre-consultation by early 2027 identified as a warning sign [f364, f259, f7436, f10786]. Deterministic radar or cooperative channels can limit what ML perception must prove, but the glossary makes differing failure modes a condition; a non-ML safety-channel option is recommended to reduce regulatory rejection risk [f676, f12122, f11058]. ML perception needs separate assurance because physics-based FDA/V&V 40 methods exclude it, and formal or static verification alone cannot establish recognition of arbitrary real scenes [f8220, f1025]. The standards landscape remains incomplete: ML safety standards are mostly draft, ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 is guidance rather than a requirement, and ISO/PAS 8800:2024 is road-vehicle-only; UL 4600 instead requires a safety case to address or explicitly argue away ML and other assurance prompts [f2099, f2100, f2101, f2102, f12263].

nodes.label: Product liability and the EU Product Liability Directive (PLD)
nodes.text: Product liability is the legal duty of a manufacturer to compensate people harmed by a defective product, and the European Union's new Product Liability Directive extends that duty explicitly to software and makes it easier for claimants to obtain the manufacturer's internal evidence.
aliases: Product liability and the EU Product Liability Directive
nodes.synopsis: Across the synthesis, planning chapter, skeptic’s review and glossary, Directive (EU) 2024/2853 is stated to apply to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026; the skeptic’s review also includes products put into service and explicitly includes software updates as products [f51, f9802, f10676, f10678, f12422]. Courts may order disclosure of evidence, and defectiveness may be presumed when evidence is withheld or technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult, making simulation records, assumptions and gaps potential claimant evidence [f10679, f10680, f12201, f12434]. The proposed braking function’s regulatory route remains unconfirmed, no universal rule on virtual testing’s sufficiency for this off-road product was found, and machinery-specific simulation-admissibility case law was not found; the reviewer therefore identifies no legal safe harbor for simulation [f10499, f10672, f10674, f12426]. Planning should identify records retained for disclosure, assess liability if virtual evidence is challenged, obtain counsel’s opinion, and document credible, reproducible simulation and its validity limits rather than justify reduced physical testing by schedule pressure [f10237, f10278, f10675, f10683, f12426]. The on-road Benavides v. Tesla verdict of 1 August 2025 assigned Tesla 33 percent responsibility and awarded about $243 million, including $200 million punitive damages; the cited design theories concerned operating-domain restrictions and driver attention, informing recommendations to enforce and log the domain and retain event data rather than establishing an off-road ruling [f10685, f10687, f12429, f10690]. A 2015 warning about machine-function integration without OEM approval supports obtaining written brake-interface approvals, while the reviewer warns that final-stage legal sign-off is too late and liability review may reject the safety case [f10692, f12430, f12432, f10787].

nodes.label: Red team and hostile review
nodes.text: A red team is a group given the explicit job of attacking a plan to find its weaknesses before real reviewers, customers or accidents do, and a hostile review is the same stance applied to a document.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends structured elicitation and genuine skeptics, giving an independent red team an adversarial charter to show that the plan cannot support its safety claim by the deadline—not a proofreading assignment—and scheduling it in preparation month 4 [f9486, f9967, f9961, f9973]. Governance should identify who may disagree with the accountable technical owner, while the final plan should record dissent and red-team findings with dispositions [f10265, f10189]. Chapter 13 applies a hostile but fair review through seven professional perspectives, requiring documented evidence or explicit opinion labels and ranking objections by centrality, evidence strength, off-road relevance and late-recovery difficulty [f10391, f10399, f10400, f10472].
