Its central finding is that credibility, rather than test volume, is the plan's weakness; the strongest objection is that the simulator has not earned the right to replace physical evidence [f12449, f14525]. Coverage remains incomplete: cybersecurity, human factors and the customer's safety regulator are omitted as reviewers, their objections are addressed only indirectly, and several incident and programme references remain unverified leads [f11277, f11278, f11273, f11275, f11276]. Red teaming is documented practice, including the UK Ministry of Defence's 2021 handbook, but no controlled engineering-outcome evidence was found, leaving the claim that it improves safety-board review survival unproven [f9954, f9963, f9964, f12450].

nodes.label: Failure mode of a project and early warning sign
nodes.text: Borrowing the engineering word, a failure mode of a project is one specific way the project could fail to deliver what it promised, and an early warning sign is an observable symptom that appears while there is still time to act.
nodes.synopsis: Immature technology at commitment is the corpus’s most consistently documented cause of schedule failure; late integration, unstable requirements and supplier lead times compound the risk, and independent review cannot rescue incomplete engineering late in a project [f204, f9643, f9644, f9647, f1056]. Barrick’s experience illustrates the consequences: systems were abandoned after supplier claims failed in field use and costs escalated, while its multi-year program encountered detection failures, nuisance alarms, installation problems and operator-acceptance difficulties [f10736, f10858]. For this program’s four-month validation window, unresolved hazard analysis, performance-level allocation or pass/fail metrics in 2027 signal that requirements debate may consume the available time [f12458]. Toolchain credibility requires agreed correlation metrics by the first quarter of 2027; the overriding warning is inability, by the first half of 2027, to demonstrate an auditable chain from a real test through the model and virtual result to a residual-risk decision for one representative requirement [f10756, f12196, f12462]. Planning should expose vulnerable assumptions, assign warning signs and contingencies, and exercise integration early, especially because documented escalation of commitment can keep failing projects alive [f9558, f9674, f9646, f9447, f9681]. Important uncertainties remain: compute and defect triage are proposed bottlenecks without program-specific evidence, and the claim that test volume explains a three-to-four-year off-road development duration is unproven; requirements definition is only a suspected alternative bottleneck [f10789, f10790, f10853, f12186].

nodes.label: Fallback option
nodes.text: A fallback option is a pre-planned, less ambitious but still responsible outcome that the program switches to when the main plan cannot be delivered on time, chosen so that safety is preserved rather than the headline schedule.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats a fallback as a pre-planned, less ambitious but responsible outcome that preserves safety when the main plan cannot be delivered on time; it should be designed before optimism pressure peaks and costed and funded alongside the main plan [f12465, f9691, f12469]. Every decision gate should permit at least four outcomes—go, go with restrictions, pivot or fallback, and stop—with an illustrative independent readiness gate in April 2027 [f9687, f9655]. The preferred release fallback restricts automatic braking to an operating envelope where the safety case is closed, potentially split by machine family, while retaining warning-only behavior outside that envelope; incomplete safety evidence warrants delaying brake control rather than exposing operators to unresolved uncertainty [f14865, f12326, f10998]. The descoping ladder reduces scenario classes, then narrows the operating envelope, then substitutes decision-support evidence for safety-case evidence; off-ramps include physical tests for highest-integrity claims, simulation limited to screening, and engineering-learning rather than safety-credit results [f9693, f12468]. Planning should identify scope-reduction dates and report P50/P80 dates and deadline probability for August or September 2027 deliverables, but the four-month target remains a business objective rather than a pass criterion: full scope should be delayed rather than supported by indefensible virtual equivalence [f10250, f10151, f12478].

nodes.label: Sensor
nodes.text: A sensor is a device that measures something about the world, such as distance, light or speed, and turns the measurement into an electrical signal a computer can read.
nodes.synopsis: The research had no internal sensor specifications or recordings, and sensor selection remained unconfirmed across chapters; the October 2026 plan therefore recommends a sensor-agnostic architecture, with sensor simulation selected only after a shortlist is known [f7, f8, f287, f8257, f485, f507, f8796]. A programme starting in October 2026 could realistically have software-in-the-loop simulation with partly validated sensor models working by mid-2027, but each sensor type needs its own credibility argument and simulation can replace only part—not most—of physical sensor testing [f65, f1577, f4407]. Sensor/environment fidelity is identified as a leading uncertainty precisely where risk lies: no accepted off-road qualification method was found for dust, snow or fog, glare-related effects are poorly validated, and physical characterization is recommended at mounting-geometry extremes and in degraded visibility [f10424, f212, f331, f4406, f7885]. Existing recordings cannot establish performance for unrecorded sensor types or positions, and rare-event methods cannot substantiate failure modes whose sensor physics the simulation omits [f3729, f5240, f6853]. Detection is necessary for braking but insufficient for safe overall performance: normal production tasks can appear dangerous to sensors, and improving sensors alone does not resolve task-dependent nuisance braking [f11302, f124, f3487, f11766].

nodes.label: Perception
nodes.text: Perception is the chain of steps by which a machine turns raw sensor signals into a short list of the things around it, with positions and speeds, that the braking logic can act on.
nodes.synopsis: Perception is the hardest technical gap in virtual validation, especially for camera, radar and lidar under dust, rain, mud and occlusion; simulation alone cannot certify it, and no published method was found for transferring evidence across sensor mounting positions [f10338, f326, f260, f370]. Evidence shows substantial simulation-to-real mismatch: a 2023 MAVS/RELLIS-3D comparison found large domain shifts, while a November 2025 on-road study reported average DCD of 0.63 and segmentation mIoU of 21%; whether such similarity metrics predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain [f4741, f4816, f5067]. Recorded raw sensor logs can test perception and trigger timing but not stopping, while object-list replay cannot prove perception; validation should compare real and simulated sensor outputs and downstream perception distributions for each sensor technology and mounting family using withheld real data [f109, f11320, f5258, f10558, f11105]. The safety claim extends beyond detection accuracy to decision logic, machine control, braking and final separation, so perception-error distributions should feed separate braking simulations and detector operating points require closed-loop assessment of stopping margins and unnecessary interventions [f383, f6410, f6982]. On-road precedents leave major off-road gaps: Euro NCAP virtual testing permits perfect perception, Michigan acceleration studies do not establish equivalent acceleration for off-road perception failures, and combinatorial-testing evidence has not established transfer to physical perception [f2111, f1452, f6826, f7238]. Planning remains uncertain: no off-road OEM case validating a new perception-based braking function in under four months was found, machine-learning assessment lead time could alone exceed that window, and the regulatory classification of fixed non-learning networks remains unresolved; systems detecting only people and vehicles also cover an incomplete portion of fatal risks [f376, f364, f2369, f11592].

nodes.label: Detection, classification and tracking
nodes.text: Detection says "something is there", classification says "it is a person" or "it is a truck", and tracking follows the object over time so the system knows where it is going; the result is written down as an object list.
nodes.synopsis: The strategy must establish a virtual performance baseline for the existing detector, but raw sensor-log replay measures only recorded sensors, mounting positions and scenarios; changes to sensor modality, mounting or processing prevent fair direct comparison of raw detections and per-sensor statistics [f25, f95, f107]. Detection is necessary for braking but insufficient for complete safety: vehicle-and-person detection leaves environmental interactions unaddressed, and passing detection or ISO 3450 brake tests does not establish overall human-machine or perception-system performance [f11302, f11575, f3487, f2361]. ISO 16001:2017 requires unambiguous, uninterrupted detection signals and detection within 300 ms, while detection, confirmation, risk computation and intervention initiation consume distance before deceleration builds; nevertheless, reviewed standards supply no detection or false-alarm sample sizes, and South Africa's Regulation 8.10 supplies no numerical detection or false-alarm thresholds [f2403, f2405, f6052, f5160, f2281]. Environmental robustness remains uncertain: 2023–2026 construction and mining studies report lidar degradation in real dust, and on-road evidence includes complete pedestrian-detection loss with high-visibility clothing in tests reported on 16 October 2025; these findings should not be treated as quantified off-road performance [f6688, f7980]. Credible validation therefore needs explicit object-class and exclusion records, real-versus-simulated dust correlation, and real-data results by condition bin with confidence intervals; ideal sensor models and object-list replay can conceal raw-sensor deficiencies or assume perception has already succeeded [f8008, f10562, f10566, f4480, f5259].

nodes.label: Field of view (FOV), range, resolution and frame rate (FPS)
nodes.text: These four numbers describe how much a sensor can see: how wide (field of view), how far (range), in how much detail (resolution) and how often (frame rate).
nodes.synopsis: Sensor requirements vary by acceptance regime: MOSH specifies a minimum 200 m surface machine-to-machine detection range and range accuracy of 1.5 m or 10%, while the cited US construction rules prescribe neither a numeric range nor automatic braking [f2605, f2114, f2765]. The booklet derives required detection range backwards from stopping distance and treats sensing cadence as part of braking delay: at 15 km/h and 10 FPS, each extra confirmation frame adds about 0.4 m of travel before braking [f12545, f13921]. Coverage depends on mounting geometry and self-occlusion, so moving a sensor can invalidate correlation; variants inside the validated parameter hull should receive reduced physical checks covering brake calibration, field of view and detection at the new mount [f5601, f1997, f7917]. Weather-dependent range needs physical evidence: 2023 on-road measurements found aluminium and steel targets unobserved at 20–30 m in specified rain and fog conditions, while fog chambers limited to, for example, 30 m require extrapolation of long-range behaviour [f6382, f4652]. Simulation and stimulation have important limitations: hardware-in-the-loop constrains distance and field of view, reported radar minimum ranges differ between a 2021 review's 20–30 m and vendor claims of 0.6 m partly because architectures differ, and actual sensor workloads require benchmarking rather than an assumed real-time factor [f4437, f5777, f8874]. Comparisons should use a common stopping-distance or risk-based evaluation zone rather than native sensor fields of view, because coverage outside their overlap is not directly comparable; KomVision's numerical travel speeds and detection ranges remain unreported in the supplied findings [f5479, f5484, f1643].

nodes.label: Latency
nodes.text: Latency is the delay between the moment something happens in front of the machine and the moment the machine reacts, measured in a braking system from sensing to the brake command and on to actual deceleration.
nodes.synopsis: Latency is a system-level braking concern: sensing, networking, fusion, decisions and actuation all affect the stopping point, so settings should scale with measured latency and machine physics rather than copied constants [f4346, f138, f3437]. The corpus repeatedly reports ISO 16001:2017's maximum detection time as 300 ms, but Chapter 9 says this was not verified against the purchased standard and must be confirmed before safety-case use; separately, MOSH requires a machine reply within 50 ms, and ISO 21815-3 requires manufacturers to declare delays [f2064, f7494, f7495, f5285, f2666]. SIL cannot establish unexpected CAN/J1939 timing behavior; HIL is recommended for timing and interface tests, VIL can establish real braking and controller delays, and physical anchor tests should measure latency to 10% g [f530, f712, f5333, f6415]. Independent validation of perception and brakes does not establish closed-loop safety, while object-list replay can hide sensor latency; neutral real-sensor OTA/HIL latency benchmarks were not found [f8196, f5259, f4956]. On-road evidence shows that avoidance depends jointly on trigger timing and latency, and secondary accounts of the Uber crash report emergency recognition 1.2 seconds before impact but braking only 0.2 seconds before impact; the program therefore recommends explicit intervention-latency constraints and early latency/jitter benchmarking [f6189, f10698, f6961, f8924].

nodes.label: Camera (RGB camera, CMOS sensor, lens, image signal processor ISP, HDR, rolling shutter)
nodes.text: A camera collects visible light through a lens onto a grid of light-sensitive cells and produces a color image that a computer can search for people and objects.
nodes.synopsis: The camera remains a candidate rather than a confirmed sensor for the heavy off-road braking system; the research therefore covers multiple sensing modalities, whose weather-related failures differ [f2035, f6625, f11303]. Camera and lidar logs with accurate poses support replay and near-path novel-view simulation, but camera logs cannot recover radar or ultrasonic responses, and injected video bypasses physical camera components rather than revalidating them [f80, f84, f5286]. Validation still needs physical correlation for optics, processing, contamination, vibration, glare, darkness and precipitation: visually convincing RGB output and simulator input specifications do not establish detector-level accuracy [f490, f1737, f4558, f3940]. Caterpillar warns of missed crouching or lying people and impaired detection in low light or snow, rain and fog; NIOSH's 2022 review also reported snow and grime degradation in off-road work [f1638, f10557]. UniSim (2023) and S2R-Bench (December 2025) show camera sim-to-real gaps, especially in adverse weather; no published validated camera dust model with a reported error metric was found, and fidelity for the exact units remains uncertain [f329, f254, f8174]. A December 2024 RGB–lidar excavation de-dusting study scored 65.58% in one far-dense-dust case versus 94.85–96.73% in other cases of that scenario, while evidence that pairwise or three-way coverage suffices for coupled sensor failures remains unproven [f10564, f6827].

nodes.label: Image quality terms: modulation transfer function (MTF), point spread function (PSF), noise, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)
nodes.text: These measures say how sharp and how clean a sensor's picture is, so that a simulated camera can be checked against a real one.
nodes.synopsis: MTF, PSF, noise and SNR describe image sharpness and cleanliness; the booklet recommends matching virtual and real camera component responses before simulating scenes or trusting virtual detections [f12588, f12589, f12594]. Higher-fidelity camera simulation includes calibrated optical blur, shot and read noise, exposure, saturation and image processing, while thermal-camera validation uses MTF and noise equivalent temperature difference [f4554, f12590]. Darkness modelling requires calibrated noise, exposure and image processing, and signal-level validation should check SNR against rain rate or visibility [f4691, f12591]. Visual realism alone is insufficient: generated images can violate sensor-verification quantities, synthetic scenes can lack real sensor noise, and detectors trained on clean images can fail on noisy or blurred ones [f4904, f3756, f12593]. The evidence includes both a precedent gap—sensor noise was not assessed in the encounter-model comparison discussed at the March 2022 RTCA SC-147 meeting—and a concrete validation example, TaCOS (2024), which checked a simulator noise model against a FLIR camera [f1437, f4755].

nodes.label: Stereo camera and depth camera (RGB-D)
nodes.text: A stereo camera uses two cameras a known distance apart to work out how far away things are, and a depth camera (RGB-D) delivers a color image plus a distance for every pixel.
nodes.synopsis: Stereo cameras estimate distance using two cameras with a known separation, while RGB-D cameras provide color and per-pixel distance; a wider stereo baseline improves long-range accuracy [f12595, f12596]. Fielded examples include Toyota SEnS+ (August 2021), which distinguishes people from objects using a rear stereo camera and slows a forklift by cutting power rather than braking, and John Deere SmartDetect Assist, which combines cameras, stereo and radar [f15785, f12598, f1654]. Simulation tools offer depth-camera capabilities through CARLA and NVIDIA Isaac Sim, but simulating flash or indirect time-of-flight cameras requires multipath and sensor-specific depth-noise models [f8468, f8478, f4603]. Camera depth is described as cheap, but stereo matching struggles on textureless surfaces, active depth-camera types have short range, and both retain general camera weaknesses [f12601, f12597]. No validation of camera-depth sensors for heavy-machine braking in dust or darkness was found, and Chapter 6 separately reports no public heavy-construction or mining automatic-braking validation evidence for flash or indirect time-of-flight depth cameras [f12602, f4604].

nodes.label: Lidar (light detection and ranging)
nodes.text: A lidar sends out very short laser pulses, times how long each takes to bounce back, and so builds a precise three-dimensional map of distances around the machine.
nodes.synopsis: Lidar remains an option rather than a confirmed sensor for the heavy off-road automatic braking system, and ISO 16001:2017 has no dedicated lidar annex; lidar also should not be described as approved under MSHA 30 CFR 77.410, although it could qualify as “another effective device” [f2035, f6625, f2069, f2235]. Rain and fog are the best-validated lidar simulation cases, but the evidence is on-road: model agreement depends on rain distributions, signal processing and sensor imperfections, and mismatch increases as fog visibility falls [f4412, f7557, f4417, f7821]. Target properties strongly affect performance: 2023 field measurements found aluminium and steel targets unobserved at 20–30 m in rain of 30–40 mm/h and fog visibility below 50 m, while retroreflective targets retained at least 74% of clear-weather point count [f6382, f6383]. Dust is identified as the biggest off-road lidar gap: field evidence shows returns from cloud leading edges, effects beginning around 71–74% atmospheric transmittance with substantial variability, and published de-dusting results limited to single datasets [f12498, f10559, f10560, f10427]. Planning therefore still requires physical correlation for weather, reflectivity, contamination, ghost returns and scanner timing, supported by surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS, and human-audited auto-labels; lidar stimulation, especially for solid-state devices, remains a gap [f1741, f5197, f5192].

nodes.label: Point cloud
nodes.text: A point cloud is a large set of measured points in three-dimensional space, each with an x, y and z position and often a brightness value, that together outline the shapes around a sensor.
nodes.synopsis: Point clouds represent measured 3D geometry, often with intensity; machine lidar produces tens of thousands of points ten or more times per second, and perception groups these raw points into objects and tracks [f12617, f12618, f12619]. Synthetic point clouds and replay offer broad lidar-validation coverage, particularly for geometry, occlusion and object placement, but recordings should preserve the rawest useful data and validation must address the interface perception actually consumes rather than only final object lists [f494, f1740, f4029, f5231, f4869]. Realism remains a major limitation: a May 2025 on-road study found measurable real–synthetic gaps, while Sim2Radar produced only about 12% of real radar point density—251 versus 2,057 points per frame—in five indoor scenes [f7073, f3932]. No single accepted point-cloud realism score exists: metrics disagree, and although density-aware Chamfer distance correlated best with perception in a November 2025 study, scans averaged DCD 0.63 with only 21% segmentation mIoU; whether these metrics predict safety-relevant errors remains uncertain [f12630, f4440, f4441, f4442, f5067]. Weather validation includes an August 2023 published lidar rain-and-fog model validated against on-road time-domain and point-cloud evidence, but the booklet recommends a dedicated real-dust correlation campaign and could not confirm direct real–simulated point-cloud comparisons in the 2026 CARLA mining-dust framework [f7819, f10562, f4743]. Site reconstruction also requires caution: lidar surveys provide direct metric samples and derived meshes are easier to edit, but AutoDRIVE's reported twin accuracy appears to reflect self-consistency against its own point cloud rather than independent ground truth [f3801, f4211, f3861].

nodes.label: Radar (radio detection and ranging)
nodes.text: A radar sends out radio waves and listens for their echoes, measuring both the distance to objects and, from a shift in the returned frequency, how fast they approach or recede.
nodes.synopsis: The braking system’s sensor set remains unconfirmed, so radar is one option requiring investigation rather than a settled design choice [f2035, f6625]. Radar simulation requires wavelength-specific material data, often measured at 77 GHz, and a modeled processing chain; physical correlation remains necessary for signatures, multipath, mounting, clutter and interference [f3715, f4420, f1739, f493]. Evidence shows substantial fidelity limitations: a 2025 wheel-loader simulation required manual material tuning yet missed double reflections, one 2026 ray-tracing study produced about 12% of real point density, and no validated radar or camera dust model with a reported error metric was found [f4421, f4422, f3716, f254]. Historical haul-truck testing in 2004 recorded alarms during 94% of 618 reversals over seven days; the study reported in 2006 classified 18% of 580 alarms as false, 42% as nuisance and 40% as warranting action, with nuisance alarms associated with ignoring or disabling behavior [f3010, f3011, f5174, f5175, f3480]. Detection evidence does not establish braking performance: the 2005 Griffith study detected light vehicles at 75 m but did not study brake thresholds, and a single rear radar missed people near haul-truck rear tyres [f6368, f6369, f7039]. Radar-equipped commercial systems do not independently prove adverse-environment validation is solved, while site interoperability and radar interference remain Medium to High risks for which interface and radio-frequency coexistence tests are recommended [f1749, f11076, f11078].

nodes.label: Ultrasonic sensor
nodes.text: An ultrasonic sensor sends out a short burst of sound too high for people to hear and measures the echo to find the distance to the nearest object within a few meters.
nodes.synopsis: Ultrasonic remains a possible sensing option, not a confirmed component of the heavy off-road automatic braking system; the research therefore covers it alongside camera, radar, lidar and other options [f2035, f3678, f6625, f8257]. Expert opinion identifies low-speed near-field geometry and control logic as useful virtual-testing applications, but acoustic reflections, installation effects, weather and contamination still require physical correlation [f1742, f1743, f499]. The booklet rates ultrasonic simulation among its weakest-evidenced cases: it found no published simulation-versus-reality validation in rain, snow, wind, dust or mud, and the accessible 2024 road-sensor study did not establish performance across the requested heavy-off-road weather and soiling matrix [f4432, f4581, f4577, f12659]. Commercial acoustic stimulation is evidenced for automotive parking, but independent heavy-off-road HIL/VIL evidence was not found; Isaac Sim's ultrasonic implementation is a ray-cast range model rather than an acoustic model [f5321, f5322, f8548]. Planning should therefore treat ultrasonic simulation as low credibility until correlated with company measurements, obtain ultrasonic-specific range or echo recordings rather than rely on camera logs, and ensure test surrogates reproduce the relevant ultrasonic response [f7086, f7099, f5626, f84, f2556].

nodes.label: Thermal camera (long-wave infrared, LWIR, NETD)
nodes.text: A thermal camera makes an image from the heat that objects give off, so it can show a warm person against cold ground in complete darkness.
nodes.synopsis: Thermal cameras image emitted heat in the LWIR band, roughly 8–14 micrometers, and can detect warm people without lighting, but useful contrast depends on temperature differences and NETD [f12509, f12665, f12512, f12667]. Simulation requires scene emissivity, temperatures and thermal history as well as camera spectral response, optics, NETD and processing; the booklet recommends matching the virtual and real camera in MTF and NETD before scene simulation [f3945, f12668, f12669, f12590]. Thermal and ultrasonic simulation have the weakest evidence reviewed: no public 2023–2026 automotive or off-road thermal-camera study was found covering the listed environmental conditions, and the cited 2026 model had only indoor quantitative validation and a qualitative real-camera comparison limited by unknown spectral response [f91, f4591, f12670, f12671]. Job-site thermal material and emissivity datasets were not found; the glossary's stronger claim that no emissivity dataset exists goes beyond the chapter's search finding, while missing validation is explicitly an evidence gap rather than proof that the physics cannot be modeled [f3717, f3946, f12673, f4592]. Although Cognata and dSPACE advertise thermal or infrared simulation capabilities, the corpus found no adverse-weather or off-road validation for thermal simulation [f8413, f8539, f4435]. Planning should therefore retain physical evidence for environmental contrast, contamination, calibration and correlated sensor failures, include modality disagreement in the fusion safety argument, and ensure test targets reproduce realistic thermal signatures [f506, f505, f569, f5389].

nodes.label: Tag-based proximity systems (UWB, RFID, magnetic field)
nodes.text: A tag-based proximity system does not look for people and objects; it listens for a small electronic tag that each person or vehicle carries, and warns or stops when a tag comes too close.
nodes.synopsis: Tag-based systems are common in mining collision avoidance and can narrow what perception must prove, but their protection depends on people and machines being equipped; Epiroc Titan CAS and CAS Interface explicitly require everyone and every machine to be tagged [f4593, f12692, f1670]. Untagged people and objects fall outside cooperative sensing, so mixed fleets containing non-equipped objects need validation arguments for both tag-based and perception-based detection [f503, f2005]. Tag removal is a documented operational weakness: MSHA’s January 2017 notice recorded mechanics removing wearable tags to diagnose leaks in the red zone, while broader reports describe bypass requests and a false sense of security [f3297, f3034]. Position and message paths are comparatively easy to emulate and fault-inject, but validation still requires physical evidence for coverage, radio propagation, synchronisation and tag failure; the corpus found neither simulation-fidelity studies for these proximity technologies nor validated simulation of propagation around large metal machines [f500, f502, f4598, f4599]. Testing must distinguish physical radio/interface stimulation from downstream measurement injection, and deployment planning must address interoperability: mines may mix systems, while the glossary reports that devices from different suppliers did not interoperate [f5323, f7484, f12690].

nodes.label: Satellite positioning (GNSS, GPS, RTK) and inertial sensing (IMU, INS)
nodes.text: Satellite positioning tells a machine where it is on the earth, inertial sensing tells it how it is moving and turning from moment to moment, and together they give the position and motion to which every other measurement is referred.
nodes.synopsis: Satellite positioning and inertial sensing provide the position and motion reference for other measurements, so reference accuracy sets the floor for warning-distance and stopping-distance accuracy [f12695, f12707]. The recommended ground truth combines surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS for continuous distance and timing, and human-audited auto-labels; lidar’s blindness in dust requires a “truth unavailable” state [f100, f5197, f12613]. Reconstruction needs synchronised, calibrated sensor logs, and Para-Lane found RTK/INS trajectories alone insufficient for frame alignment, adding lidar mapping and camera-to-lidar registration [f3852, f4020]. Underground and GNSS-denied sites undermine RTK/INS-dependent reconstruction, so the booklet recommends retaining state-estimation inputs and solutions; Pretoria’s methodology uses GPS truth on the surface and lidar, cameras and radar underground [f4365, f4019, f1726]. Position and message paths are comparatively easy to emulate, but physical coverage, propagation, synchronisation and failure evidence remain necessary; NIOSH observed a brief 15 m GPS position shift during 2007 field work [f500, f502, f689]. Several tools offer GPS/GNSS and IMU models, but the research found no fidelity studies for GNSS/V2X proximity systems and no current public heavy off-road standard prescribing their laboratory-injection architecture, leaving model availability distinct from demonstrated validation adequacy [f8381, f8468, f8495, f8511, f4598, f5325].

nodes.label: Sensor fusion
nodes.text: Sensor fusion is the combining of measurements from several different sensors into one picture of the surroundings that is more reliable than any single sensor could give.
nodes.synopsis: Sensor fusion combines measurements into a more reliable scene, aligning outputs in space and time; multi-technology systems are the norm in mining collision avoidance, but both raw-data and object-list fusion require accurate calibration and a shared clock [f12708, f12709, f12710, f680]. Complementary sensing does not eliminate perception validation: the safety argument must cover disagreement and common-cause degradation, supported by physical evidence for environmental contrast, contamination, calibration and correlated failures [f504, f681, f505, f506]. Synthetic scenes must provide consistent geometry and timing across modalities; separately validating sensors does not prove the fused stack correct, and the booklet identifies both cross-sensor consistency and function-level validation as gaps, recommending outcomes such as false and missed brakes [f5101, f5086]. Replay of object lists tests downstream fusion and decisions, not perception, while reliable ground truth should combine complementary sensors, accurate pose estimation and an explicit “truth unavailable” state when all sensors degrade [f5628, f5391, f12715]. A construction RGB–lidar de-dusting study published in December 2024 scored 65.58% in one far, dense-dust case versus 94.85–96.73% in other cases of the same scenario, demonstrating a substantial condition-specific performance gap [f10564]. Bosch's camera–radar tram system and a Daimler presentation dated 29 July 2025 provide relevant precedents, but industry signals do not establish sensor diversity's effectiveness, and the Daimler example concerns on-road rather than heavy-off-road validation [f1417, f1748, f1334, f1822].

nodes.label: Calibration (intrinsic and extrinsic) and sensor mounting
nodes.text: Calibration is the measurement of how a sensor sees (its internal, intrinsic properties) and where it sits on the machine (its external, extrinsic position and angle), so that its readings can be placed correctly in the real world.
nodes.synopsis: The braking system must work across machine models with different sizes and sensor positions, but mounting-dependent blind areas prevent evidence from transferring freely; the existing proximity-awareness system took years of calibration to balance detection and false positives [f286, f11552, f10]. Physics-based sensor models can respond causally to changed sensor pose, but no published perception-evidence transfer approach or universally acceptable off-road transfer distance or angle was found; new mounting heights should be expected to require retraining or adaptation, not just threshold changes [f4466, f370, f7905, f7037]. Raw-log replay is limited to recorded sensors, mounts and scenarios, and raw detections and per-sensor statistics are not comparable when modality, mounting or processing changes [f5166, f5211]. Mounting geometry has demonstrated practical consequences: NIOSH found that one rear radar missed people near haul-truck rear tyres, while two antennas approximately 1.8 m apart with beams crossed inward approximately 20 degrees improved detection there [f7039, f7040]. Planning should retain physical characterization at mounting-geometry extremes, document calibration and measurement uncertainty, and validate each sensor technology and mounting family against withheld real raw data; a sensor change in 2027 would invalidate multiple evidence streams, and a validated sensor digital twin should not be claimed before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated [f7885, f9729, f10558, f11912, f11917].

nodes.label: Time synchronization and time stamps
nodes.text: A time stamp is the exact time written next to each measurement, and time synchronization is making sure every sensor and computer on the machine writes those times from the same clock.
nodes.synopsis: Synchronization is a prerequisite for reconstructing scenes, replaying recordings and assessing braking performance, but the existing warning system's retention of synchronized raw data and useful labels is not established [f3852, f5232, f1139, f519]. Recordings should preserve hardware timestamps on a common clock, calibration, clock offsets, synchronization status, dropped-data counters and resynchronization events; per-frame timestamps may be insufficient for moving machines with rolling or scanning sensors [f5629, f4016, f4018]. Unsynchronized clocks can create an entirely artificial algorithm latency of 100–300 ms, while smaller errors can reorder approach events; at 15 km/h, a 100 ms timing error shifts measured object position by 42 cm [f5654, f5655, f12738]. The booklet identifies timing and cross-sensor consistency as gaps in its seven sensor questions: realistic individual sensor values do not establish correct fused perception or braking when acquisition, network, controller or actuator timing is wrong [f5092, f5101]. Recommended validation includes known-event tests timestamping every stage from detection to measurable deceleration, independently calibrated and synchronized ground truth, and a dedicated data-pedigree workstream [f6159, f5642, f11244, f10346]. Tool integration must align clocks, time bases, dynamics and rendered sensor poses while preserving deterministic ECU replay; ASAM MDF 4.3.0, dated September 2025, provides a standardized recording format that includes synchronization metadata [f8718, f8721, f7115].

nodes.label: Sensor degradation: dust, mud, rain, snow, fog, spray, glare, darkness, artificial lighting, vibration
nodes.text: Sensor degradation is the loss of a sensor's performance when the environment interferes with it, by blocking its view, dirtying its window, flooding it with light or shaking it.
nodes.synopsis: The braking system must work in rain, snow, fog, dust, dusk, darkness and glare, but the mid-2027 validation window will not include snow and cold conditions [f285, f2033, f3676, f8255, f4403]. Dust is identified as the biggest off-road sensor-simulation gap, and perception models for dust, rain, mud and occlusion are the hardest technical gap in virtual validation; construction and mining studies from 2023–2026 report lidar degradation in real dust [f89, f10338, f6688]. Lidar rain-and-fog simulation is the best-validated case, based on on-road evidence, but agreement depends on matching real conditions and deteriorates as fog visibility falls [f4412, f7556, f7557, f7558]. A fog-chamber test found that at 10 m visibility all lidars but one failed to detect a target at 10.5 m; if dust prevents person detection at the required stopping range, speed must decrease or stopping cannot be promised [f7559, f11330]. Snow, glare and darkness validation remains weak or absent, while raw sensor-log replay does not retest contamination, vibration or glare upstream of the re-injection point and cannot establish performance in environmental conditions absent from the logs [f6488, f96, f5241]. Incident evidence does not establish adverse weather's share of collisions, and published complete-system off-road false-positive and false-negative rates were not found; planning therefore must allocate environmental variability to simulation, uncertainty bounds or residual physical testing, with adverse-environment sensor models experimentally correlated [f3234, f3235, f6385, f10348, f5219].

nodes.label: Occlusion (hidden objects) and sensor obstruction (blocked sensor)
nodes.text: Occlusion is when an object is hidden behind something else so the sensor cannot see it, and obstruction is when the sensor itself is blocked, for example by mud on its window.
nodes.synopsis: Occlusion and sensor obstruction are central validation risks: perception in dust, rain, mud and occlusion is identified as the hardest technical gap, and brakes cannot recover safety margin when reliable detection range falls below required stopping distance [f10338, f6585]. Virtual testing is useful for camera and lidar geometry and occlusion, but simplified sensor models require explicit encoding of partial occlusion, while lens and cover soiling and its accumulation, drying and cleaning remain poorly reproduced [f1736, f1740, f4479, f4772]. Acceptance requirements address both hidden targets and blocked sensors: MOSH Rev 1 requires detection without line-of-sight, while on-road FMVSS 127 requires detection and communication of obstruction-related degradation; the program still needs explicit blockage, maintenance and calibration requirements [f2458, f2000, f2929, f7463]. Variant validation may need several physical representatives because worst stopping distance and worst occlusion need not coincide, and mounting changes and non-monotonic geometry effects undermine unproven transfer across a fleet of 100+ models [f626, f7919, f7921, f10589]. Physical correlation and trustworthy reference labels remain essential: high-value occlusion phenomena need physical reference tests, ground truth needs an unavailable-or-ambiguous state, and published reference-stack validation across the full mining-condition set was not found [f7374, f5394, f5399].

nodes.label: Cluttered and reflective surroundings
nodes.text: Cluttered and reflective surroundings are environments full of metal, water, walls and piles that bounce sensor signals in confusing ways, producing echoes from nowhere and hiding real objects.
nodes.synopsis: Cluttered off-road environments create both missed-detection and unnecessary-braking risks: idealized perception cannot establish that radar resolves a worker beside a large metal structure, while operational triggers include rock piles, berms, adjacent machines and the truck’s own tyres [f2578, f3022, f4362]. Radar is considered most likely to remain useful in dust and darkness, but radar and ultrasonic simulation of off-road clutter remains low credibility until correlated with the company’s own measurements [f12650, f12774]. The strongest direct off-road radar evidence is the 2025 wheel-loader study, whose synthetic results required hand-built geometry and tuned materials yet still missed real double reflections; validated simulation of piles, highwalls, large steel structures and machine self-reflection was not found for any sensor [f4714, f4422, f12768, f4718]. Real site captures preserve geometry, clutter and unexpected correlations, although photogrammetry itself can fail on textureless soil, glare, reflections and moving objects [f3701, f3753, f4203]. Planning should therefore pair high-value simulated phenomena with physical reference tests before prototype arrival and retain physical testing for unresolved effects within the four-month validation window, rather than treating bench stimulation as realistic reproduction of terrain clutter or steel-structure multipath [f7374, f12751, f5327].

nodes.label: Ground truth
nodes.text: Ground truth is the trusted, independent record of what was really in front of the machine, where and when, against which the system's detections and warnings are scored.
nodes.synopsis: Ground truth must independently describe the physical scene and machine state; using the production detector’s output as truth is circular and can conceal missed objects [f99, f5358, f5359]. Replay against this reference is an established way to baseline an existing warning system without driving the machine, but usable logs need synchronized raw sensors, machine signals, calibration and labels; valuable ignored-warning near misses often lack ground truth [f94, f520, f11899, f7943]. The recommended reference combines surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS, and human-audited auto-labels, with complementary sensors and an explicit “truth unavailable” state when reference sensing degrades [f5197, f12715]. Ground truth itself requires calibration, synchronization and uncertainty budgets, with measurement uncertainty substantially below acceptance margins or measured discrepancies; otherwise reference errors can dominate system differences [f7473, f8222, f7474, f11243]. Weather facilities provide important validation references, but a 2019 survey says chambers cannot fully replace real weather, while a 2026 paper proposes rainfall corrections; reconstructed or generated environments likewise do not automatically supply trustworthy geometric truth [f5056, f5085, f5104, f4046]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, preparing a ground-truth specification alongside physical-test procedures, a soft-target kit and independent-test-body engagement is considered realistic by mid-2027, although labeling and ground truth are identified as likely replay bottlenecks [f851, f1144].

nodes.label: Labeling and annotation (human labels, auto-labeling, offboard detectors)
nodes.text: Labeling, or annotation, is the work of marking what is in recorded sensor data, such as drawing a box around each person and naming it, so that detectors can be trained and their results scored.
nodes.synopsis: Labels are a distinct simulation layer, not a by-product of visual realism: their ontology must follow safety requirements, and useful truth channels extend to geometry, trajectories, visibility, machine state and braking-related quantities [f86, f3979, f3978]. The recommended ground-truth approach combines surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS and audited automatic labels, with an explicit “truth unavailable or ambiguous” state for dust, occlusion and reference-sensor failure [f5197, f5394]. Automatic labeling offers scale, but on-road successes do not establish validity near heavy off-road equipment; one 2026 labeler achieved recall of 0.88–0.98 but precision of only 0.52 in crowded indoor scenes, supporting pre-labeling with stratified human audits rather than an unaudited safety oracle [f5199, f5200, f5382, f5383]. Procedural simulation can supply automatically generated, nominally perfect labels, but this does not resolve whether those labels represent the safety-relevant categories and states [f3975, f4295, f3979]. For a team starting in October 2026, a labeled replay pipeline is considered realistic by mid-2027 only if suitable data exist; the indicative plan starts 180 days of labeling and replay work on January 1, 2027, while current retention of suitable logs and labels remains unestablished [f837, f898, f519]. Labeling is expected to dominate replay costs and may be its real bottleneck, yet project cost figures were not found, so a small representative annotation trial is recommended before budgeting at scale [f522, f1144, f10828, f10829].

nodes.label: Datasets and benchmarks (what MOCS, SODA, RELLIS-3D, RUGD and similar names are)
nodes.text: A dataset is a large collection of recorded and labeled sensor data that researchers share, and a benchmark is a dataset plus an agreed scoring rule, so that different methods can be compared on the same test.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus identifies substantial research datasets, including SODA with 19,846 construction images, MOCS with 41,668 images reported in a September 2026 preprint, and LiDARDustX with 30,000 mining-truck lidar frames, more than 80% dusty [f10825, f10826, f7065, f7066]. Their availability does not establish collision-warning validity: the discussed construction datasets are image-only with fixed or aerial viewpoints, and no off-road collision-warning validation was found for RELLIS-3D, RUGD, GOOSE or TartanDrive [f5845, f5851]. Simulation benchmarks also require real-data checks: simulated versus real RELLIS-3D data showed large domain shifts, while S2R-Bench highlights failures to predict real weather robustness [f4741, f776]. Major gaps include job-site ultrasonic and thermal material data and large off-road naturalistic interaction datasets; these limit sensor modeling and the defensibility of rare-event evaluation claims [f3717, f6859, f7277]. The adverse-weather gap is stated more categorically in the glossary than in Chapter 6, which acknowledges MINE4DRAD and real-dust lidar exceptions; planning should therefore assess the manufacturer's existing fleet recordings and their machine, site and weather coverage before deciding what additional data can be collected [f12822, f5102, f12823, f272].

nodes.label: True positive, false positive, false negative, miss (the four outcomes)
nodes.text: Every time a detector looks for something, one of four things happens: it finds something real (true positive), it reports something that is not there (false positive), it misses something real (false negative, or miss), or it correctly stays quiet (true negative).
aliases: True positive, false positive, false negative, miss
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats missed hazards and false positives as a coupled calibration problem: reducing misses increases false alarms, and achieving an acceptable balance in the manufacturer's proximity-awareness system took years [f11305, f10]. Automatic braking makes false positives machine-motion hazards, with potential loss of control or conflict with following plant, while mining reports associate nuisance interventions with production losses, wear and resistance to adoption [f3024, f6303, f5567]. Acceptance planning should measure scenario-conditioned detection and intervention, dangerous misses, false warnings and unnecessary interventions per operating hour, and collision avoidance; however, no acceptance value for detection probability or miss rate was found, nor a source-attributable consensus on the acceptable miss–nuisance trade-off [f2632, f2620, f2884]. With zero misses, demonstrating miss rates of at most 1%, 0.1% and 0.01% at 95% one-sided confidence requires respectively 299, 2,995 and 29,956 independent trials per claimed population; at 99% confidence, the corresponding counts are 459, 4,603 and 46,050 [f6650, f6651, f6652, f6653]. Validation must avoid circular detector-derived ground truth and replay that assumes perception succeeded, and should retain physical ISO 21815-1 clause 6 performance and false-positive tests [f5359, f5259, f7884]. Evidence remains incomplete: NIOSH's 2022 review identified false-positive testing and other validation gaps, and published complete off-road automatic-braking false-positive and false-negative rates under adverse environmental conditions were not found [f10425, f6385].

nodes.label: True positive rate, precision, recall, F1 score
nodes.text: These single numbers summarize the four outcomes: recall (the true positive rate) is the share of real objects that were found, precision is the share of reports that were real, and the F1 score blends the two.
nodes.synopsis: Recall (true positive rate) measures the share of real objects found, precision measures the share of reports that are real, and F1 combines them using their harmonic mean; both precision and recall matter, as a 2026 labeler achieved recall of 0.88–0.98 but precision of only 0.52 in crowded indoor scenes [f12841, f5382]. The recommended baseline measures detection per independent encounter by object class, distance, bearing and condition, reports curves or bins rather than a fleet average, and includes real-data confidence intervals and audited-label precision and recall [f14339, f11102, f5422]. Demonstrating at least 95% or 99% detection with 95% confidence requires respectively 59 or 299 consecutive successful encounters per stratum, but no acceptance value for detection probability or miss rate was found [f5202, f5203, f2620]. Replay establishes detection, false-alarm rates and warning timing only for recorded configurations and situations; probability-based sampling supports unbiased estimates for the assumed scenario distribution, while poor field telemetry leaves aggregate real-world weighting uncertain [f13444, f6830, f7423]. Detector-threshold tuning using ROC, DET or precision-recall operating points is recommended, but specific off-road evidence was not identified, and detection-only validation can overlook nuisance braking that prompts operators to disable the system [f6980, f7306, f1986]. The 2022 off-road lidar de-dusting result of F1 = 97.55% measures filter performance on its own dataset, not sensor-model fidelity, while synthetic coverage can make mAP misleading despite real–simulation differences [f10563, f7832, f12842].

nodes.label: ROC curve and DET curve
nodes.text: A ROC curve and a DET curve are graphs that show how a detector's misses and false alarms trade against each other as its sensitivity setting is turned up or down.
nodes.synopsis: ROC and DET curves show the trade-off between detector misses and false alarms as sensitivity changes; Chapter 9 and the glossary describe operating-point selection as a simple, transparent, standard detector-tuning method [f12849, f7303, f12850]. Its appropriate scope is the perception-layer detector threshold alone: it ignores closed-loop timing and braking and serves a single objective, rather than validating the automatic brake as a whole [f6980, f7302, f7304, f12851]. The recommended procedure is to select the operating point on a validation split and then perform closed-loop evaluation, with Chapter 9 identifying moderate over-fitting risk [f7305, f12852, f14426]. For automatic braking, misses and false alarms have very different costs, the appropriate operating point depends on speed, zone and task, and constant alarms can cause operator rejection; false alarms should therefore be measured per hour or per maneuver [f12855, f12854, f12853]. The booklet consequently treats detector curves as one input to multi-objective tuning under hard safety constraints, while noting that the evidence for operating-point tuning is generic machine learning evidence, with no specific off-road evidence identified [f12856, f7306].

nodes.label: Time to collision (TTC) and trigger distance (as perception outputs that matter for braking)
nodes.text: Time to collision is how many seconds remain before the machine and an object meet if neither changes speed, and trigger distance is how far away an object must be when the system decides to warn or brake; both are only as good as the distance and speed that perception delivers.
nodes.synopsis: TTC estimates the seconds until machine and object meet if neither changes speed, while trigger distance marks the decision to warn or brake; both depend on perceived range and relative speed [f12857, f12859]. Trigger distance includes travel during detection and decision, brake response, physical stopping, and a residual safe distance; a one-meter range error or speed estimate lag of a few tenths of a second changes TTC and the trigger point [f12858, f12860]. TTC alone is weak at work-site speeds, so the referenced standard and consensus favor stopping-distance and risk-zone logic with TTC as one input; an unnamed mining specification requests warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention, limiting traceability of that requirement [f12864, f12865, f12863]. Sensor-model validation should compare matched real and simulated TTC and trigger distance, with calibrated 3D reference labels when distance or TTC matters [f12867, f5402]. Across system comparison and campaign evaluation, the corpus recommends common ground truth and hazard zones, warning TTC, and verdicts extending beyond collisions to detection, intervention, stopping margin, nuisance effects and operator-warning sequence; scenario search can deliberately worsen TTC or other robustness measures to expose failures [f106, f7373, f6835].

nodes.label: Machine learning detector (neural network, convolutional neural network CNN, training data, inference)
nodes.text: A machine learning detector is software that has learned to find people and objects in sensor data by being shown many labeled examples, instead of being programmed with hand-written rules.
nodes.synopsis: Across construction, mining and on-road studies, synthetic data is supported as training augmentation rather than a replacement for real data: studies from 2023–2026 report benefits from mixing, but persistent gaps with synthetic-only training and benefits that depend on detector family [f6685, f6686, f6689, f7047, f7057]. Reported examples include 50% fewer real images and a 16% detector improvement in a 2023 construction study, cited through a 2025 secondary summary, and a 2025 study whose best result used 1,500 real plus 1,500 synthetic images [f7049, f7050, f7051]. Visual realism does not establish detector validity: real-trained radar detectors failed on most simulated vehicles despite improved image similarity, while mining evidence shows degradation in dust in a dataset of 30,000 lidar frames, over 80% dusty [f4423, f4826, f12610]. The recommended training loop anchors simulation in real off-road logs, tests on untouched real data and collects targeted real data for residual gaps; shared training/testing generators or assets can contaminate validation, and new mounting heights require retraining or adaptation rather than threshold changes alone [f7102, f7097, f7037]. Formal or static verification cannot prove recognition of arbitrary real scenes, the cited FDA guidance does not cover a neural-network detector, and manufacturers must address machine-learning vision gaps in test standards with evidence [f668, f7645, f2911]. Retraining can invalidate prior validation, and whether a trained-then-frozen detector is “self-evolving” under EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 remains disputed; the booklet notes deterministic safety channels as a way to avoid placing the entire proof burden on learned perception [f2940, f6700, f12877].

nodes.label: Training data, validation data, test data, and the independence rule (data lineage)
nodes.text: Machine-learning data are split into three parts, one to teach the detector, one to choose its settings and one to score it honestly, and the independence rule says the scoring data must never have touched the teaching.
aliases: Training data, validation data, test data, and the independence rule
nodes.synopsis: The corpus distinguishes training data for teaching the detector, validation data for choosing settings, and test data for honest scoring; judging data must have played no part in building or tuning the system [f12882, f14471]. For this program, validation and estimation data must be real or physically independent of the training-data generator, with different assets, sites, people and generator documented in a data-lineage record [f7100, f14472]. Studies from 2023–2026 generally support mixing synthetic and real training data in data-poor construction settings, but synthetic data has not been shown to replace real validation, and no peer-reviewed study was found establishing synthetic-only field-level collision-avoidance reliability across the stated heavy-machine conditions [f7412, f6684, f7103]. Practical safeguards include holding out entire sites or scenario families, maintaining separate tuning, validation and audit sets, preallocating physical datasets before prototype testing, and never tuning against final validation data [f6675, f6676, f8226, f11032]. Learned models and automatic labelers inherit training-domain limitations and biases; improving virtual metrics while held-out real performance stalls signals simulator overfitting [f4487, f12785, f12892]. Warning-fleet logs could supply independent replay evidence, but their validation use depends on ground truth, consent and data rights, and customer-site recording permissions were not examined [f7932, f8246, f8247].

nodes.label: Synthetic and generated training data (domain gap, data augmentation)
nodes.text: Synthetic training data are sensor data made by a simulator or a generative model rather than recorded in the field, and the domain gap is the difference between that artificial data and real data that makes a detector trained on one do worse on the other.
nodes.synopsis: Across construction, mining and road studies, synthetic data supports training augmentation rather than substitution: mixed real-and-synthetic training generally performs better in data-poor settings, while synthetic-only training leaves a domain gap [f7047, f12900]. A 2023 construction-worker study, reported through a secondary summary, reduced real-image needs by 50% and improved detector performance by 16%; a 2025 construction-object study achieved its best result with 1,500 real plus 1,500 synthetic images [f7049, f7050, f7051]. Benefits are context-dependent: on-road synthetic-fog pre-training followed by real-fog fine-tuning added at most 0.0117 mAP, and broader synthetic coverage can inflate mAP despite domain differences [f4896, f4818]. Generative models can create new views, rare scenarios and weather variations, but whether weather editing preserves sensor physics remains uncertain, and hybrid models’ maturity for safety credit is unresolved [f3819, f3824, f4308, f5078]. Reported reality gaps include rendered excavators and Unity construction scenes, although the cited 2025 review and 2026 Unity study are preprints; no peer-reviewed demonstration was found that synthetic-only training or validation establishes heavy off-road collision-avoidance reliability [f10582, f10584, f10585, f6690]. Planning should therefore use generated data to target training gaps, test detectors on untouched real data, and document validation-data independence; validation and estimation data must be real or physically independent of the training-data generator [f12890, f12885].

nodes.label: Generative models (GAN, diffusion models) and what "generated weather" means
nodes.text: Generative models are machine-learning systems that create new, realistic-looking images or sensor data, and "generated weather" means using them to add rain, fog, snow, dust or night to a recording made in clear weather.
nodes.synopsis: Generative models create realistic-looking images or sensor data; generated weather adds rain, fog, snow, dust or night to clear-weather recordings, potentially converting thousands of recorded hours into bad-weather data without waiting for winter [f12910, f12911]. Across chapters, the recommended role is training, failure discovery and wider test coverage—not stand-alone pass/fail evidence or a replacement for physically traceable sensor simulation [f93, f4871, f12922]. A 2026 on-road benchmark reported 94.8% realism acceptance for the best generative editor versus 26.3% for the best rule-based library, but this commercial, non-peer-reviewed preprint used a vision-language-model jury, and night-edit acceptance remained only 12.5–17.6% [f4447, f4878, f4894]. Visual plausibility does not establish sensor fidelity: generated images can violate radiance, geometry and cross-sensor consistency, while 2026 Waymo novel-view results of 13.19–20.82 dB PSNR were judged low fidelity for safety testing [f4904, f3758, f3822]. Experts disagree about generative world models as validation tools, quantitative off-road re-weathering validation was not found, and no standard or regulator treats generated weather as physically equivalent to real sensor measurements [f7442, f3825, f12919]. The recommended hybrid uses generation to propose tests while anchoring physics to models and measured weather-affected sensor behavior; labels such as “20 mm/h rain” or “50 m visibility” require calibration against real sensor data, otherwise their physical meaning remains unknown [f12923, f10888, f12921].

nodes.label: Neural rendering: NeRF and Gaussian splatting (3DGS) as ways to rebuild a scene from photos
nodes.text: Neural rendering takes many photographs or scans of a real place and learns a model of it that can then produce new views from positions where no camera ever stood.
nodes.synopsis: NeRF and 3D Gaussian splatting are strongest near recorded viewpoints: accurately posed camera and lidar logs support replay and near-path novel views, but neural reconstruction degrades at offsets of 1–4 m [f3703, f80, f5213]. On-road benchmarks quantify substantial losses: Para-Lane (2025) reports 22.99 to 17.05 dB PSNR between recorded and adjacent lanes, while MV² (August 2026) reports 29.13 dB at drone height versus 10.36 dB from a car, reinforcing the risk of transferring scenes between machine sensor heights [f3707, f3709, f82]. NeuroNCAP (2024) found nearly identical real and rendered performance in open loop across 14 on-road sequences, but this does not settle off-trajectory credibility; re-rendering for new sensor mounts is recommended as a development aid rather than validation evidence [f4566, f4567, f5785, f5517]. Off-road maturity remains very low, with 2026 preprints reporting terrain, calibration-drift and moving-vegetation degradation; harsh-weather limitations and the need for underlying collision geometry mean neural rendering should be one toolchain layer, not the simulator itself [f5725, f3710, f4517, f12933, f12938]. NuRec is integrated into Isaac Sim and CARLA 0.9.16, which added neural reconstruction in September 2025, but its admissibility as test evidence remains uncertain, and reported compute evidence is insufficient for program-level hardware sizing [f8609, f8298, f9355, f4948]. Collect reconstruction-quality logs now using synchronized, calibrated sensors, multiple passes and clear weather, while keeping visually inferred surfaces separate from geometric truth; only 50 of 200 MV² sequences passed pose-quality checks [f12937, f12936, f12757, f3727].

nodes.label: Physically based rendering (PBR), BRDF and BSDF (how materials reflect light and radar)
nodes.text: Physically based rendering computes what a sensor sees from the real physics of light and materials, and a BRDF or BSDF is the mathematical description of how a given surface sends incoming energy back out in each direction.
nodes.synopsis: Physically based rendering uses light and material physics to compute sensor observations, but non-visual material behaviour cannot be inferred from RGB appearance and must be specified by wavelength or sensor band [f12939, f3713, f3926, f4298]. Lidar needs wavelength-specific reflectance and BRDF, radar needs permittivity, conductivity, roughness and multipath, thermal sensing needs emissivity, and cameras need physically based materials and spectral response; modelling darkness additionally requires calibrated noise, exposure and image processing [f12940, f12941, f12942, f12943, f4691]. Material-aware radar interaction and multipath improve sim-to-real behaviour over simple one-hit ray casting, while wet-ground lidar effects and difficult wet or dirty BRDFs show why surface realism matters [f5054, f4719, f4723]. ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D version 1.0.0, dated April 2025, lets assets carry camera-, lidar- and radar-relevant properties, but excludes weather and lighting; planned version 1.1.0 adds better conductivity modelling and measured-reflectance-to-BRDF conversion [f12945, f12946, f3924]. No job-site measurement campaign in an OpenMATERIAL-type format was found for the listed materials, so the validation programme must measure or estimate properties itself—a larger schedule item than computing power, despite some camera and basic lidar simulations running in real time or faster [f4383, f12951, f4926]. The corpus retains a methodological tension between measured physics-first realism and learned models that reproduce observed output distributions, while warning that erroneous simulated reflectance and radar cross-section can compromise machine-learning training data [f4327, f7092].

nodes.label: Ray tracing and shooting-and-bouncing rays (SBR) for sensor simulation
nodes.text: Ray tracing simulates a sensor by following imaginary rays of light, radio or sound from the sensor into the virtual scene, bouncing them off surfaces and recording what comes back; shooting-and-bouncing rays is the radar version that launches very many rays and adds up their reflections.
nodes.synopsis: Ray tracing follows light, radio or sound rays through a scene; radar shooting-and-bouncing rays (SBR) sums multiple reflections, enabling multipath ghosts and Doppler effects rather than treating every surface hit as a detection [f12952, f12953, f12956]. The corpus identifies ray-traced lidar using the actual scan pattern and full signal chain as the best-validated sensor-model type, reporting errors of 1.7% for amplitude, 8.5% for point count and 9.3% for mean intensity only when processing and sensor imperfections were included [f12955, f4417]. Radar material models improve agreement with real images, but Sim2Radar (February 2026), using standard 77 GHz material values in five indoor scenes, produced only about 12% of real point density—251 versus 2,057 points per frame—so ray tracing alone does not guarantee fidelity [f4531, f3931, f4305, f13191]. Transfer to untested machines or mounting positions depends on known materials and sensor internals; reliable 77 GHz material values were lacking in one on-road study, heavy precipitation increases errors, and the booklet's most directly relevant heavy-machine result was RadaRays tested on a wheel loader in a hall [f12964, f12958, f4530, f12959, f15952]. Whole-quarry full-wave simulation is considered impractical, motivating combinations of ray tracing, approximations and statistical electronics models, but no published scene-scale benchmark comparing full-wave simulation with modern real-time radar ray tracers was found [f4536, f4537]. Available tools include dSPACE AURELION and Chrono::Sensor; runtime examples range from 14 hours for a 12-second CPU scenario to about 12 ms per GPU frame and 7.8–18.8 ms per independent ray-traced image, and the corpus explicitly warns against using these as planning constants [f8446, f8495, f12960, f12961, f12962, f12963].

nodes.label: Electronic control unit (ECU)
nodes.text: An electronic control unit is one of the small, rugged computers built into a machine, each running one job such as controlling the engine, the brakes or, here, the collision system.
nodes.synopsis: Across the booklet, HIL places a real or representative ECU and its I/O against a real-time simulated plant to establish timing, communications, diagnostics, fault response and fail-to-safe behavior; SIL cannot prove the final ECU’s timing, processor or I/O faults [f533, f5279, f13350, f5269]. Expanding the real test boundary from software to ECU, sensor and machine captures more failure modes but reduces speed, scalability and controllability, while ECU-level injection still leaves the sensor front end unproven [f5227, f12970]. HIL requires hard real time, and realistic sensor values alone are insufficient: synchronization, network delays, ECU scheduling and actuator latency can defeat braking, while an offline-accurate renderer may fail deterministic ECU timing [f13418, f5092, f8923]. Most infrastructure can be developed before final hardware arrives using established interfaces and surrogate controllers, but a production-relevant ISO/TS 21815-2 HIL bench is only a possible mid-2027 target and should not become critical-path work unless ECU, bus and actuator interfaces stabilize early [f5568, f5587, f5588, f857]. Sensor stimulation is recommended for final sensor/ECU regression, timing tests and supplier-independent characterization, but injection remains sensor- and ECU-specific and bidirectional sensor–ECU behavior remains an open interface issue [f4500, f8641, f5093]. Brake-request timing and fault behavior require evidence separate from sensor realism; one mining-regime example specifies disconnection detection within 500 ms and a machine reply within 50 ms, rather than establishing universal thresholds [f12975, f12969].

nodes.label: Vehicle network: CAN bus, SAE J1939, DBC file
nodes.text: The vehicle network is the wiring and message system through which a machine's computers talk to one another, and J1939 is the standard dialect heavy machines use on it, including for the message that asks the machine to slow or stop.
nodes.synopsis: ISO/TS 21815-2:2021, edition 1, was published on 14 July 2021 and confirmed in December 2024; it defines the on-board J1939 collision-avoidance interface, including slow-down, controlled-stop, emergency-stop and motion-inhibit commands, capability discovery and keep-alive messaging [f2156, f2057, f3638, f12979]. The interface anchors the booklet’s brake-request contract and offers a precedent for reusing evidence across machine models, but is explicitly not plug-and-play: machine and collision-system manufacturers must agree integration details and demonstrate interoperability [f13229, f367, f2159, f10726]. SIL cannot establish unexpected CAN/J1939 timing behaviour, whereas HIL can test real controller, bus and I/O timing; validation through a third-party J1939 interface must include end-to-end integration latency [f530, f931, f8198]. A production-relevant HIL bench could target mid-2027, but should not become critical-path work unless ECU, bus and actuator interfaces stabilise early; unanalysed interface or controller changes in 2027 may invalidate the pre-built simulator [f857, f11028]. Record machine-network state, brake requests and measured responses with adequate rate and precision, preserving DBC/message-schema versions and exact hardware/software provenance so behaviour can be reconstructed [f5634, f12982, f5646, f12992]. Spoofed or stale messages, bus faults and incompatible implementations must not cause unsafe brake commands, and explicit fault testing is required; nevertheless, J1939 cybersecurity was omitted from the machine-motion questions and needs separate treatment because ISO 19014-4 excludes it [f2936, f8200, f6607, f5832].

nodes.label: Data logging (what to record on the machine, raw versus processed data, common mistakes)
nodes.text: Data logging is recording what the machine's sensors saw, what the machine did and what the system decided, in enough detail that the whole event can be replayed and judged later.
aliases: what to record on the machine
nodes.synopsis: The existing warning fleet offers an immediate data source: vendors already log warning events and locations, and the booklet recommends starting sensor and shadow-mode logging in October 2026, continuing through winter toward a recording-and-replay pipeline by mid-2027 [f1254, f97, f7365, f64]. However, the research used no internal recordings or sensor specifications, and neither retention of replay-quality raw data nor use of existing field data to characterize sensors and site conditions was established [f7, f519, f5121]. Useful records need synchronized sensor streams, machine and braking state, calibration, environmental context and defensible ground truth; every warning and intervention should also capture operator response, task phase and whether braking was necessary [f520, f3652]. These logs can support exposure modeling and candidate-braking replay, but operator reactions censor the data, ignored-warning near misses often lack ground truth, and validation use depends on ground truth, consent and data rights [f11615, f1601, f7578, f7943, f8246]. MOSH requires 10 Hz intervention logging, seven days of onboard retention and three months on a server, with operator ID, firmware version and tamper resistance; no universal off-road event logging format was found [f2592, f2932, f2933]. Preserve raw data and model versions, verify platform compatibility with eventual sensors, and do not assume earlier recordings can replace final-hardware data: radar and ultrasonic responses cannot be recovered from camera logs [f10684, f8659, f7870, f84].

nodes.label: Data formats and versioning (MDF, CSV, YAML, XML, JSON, Robot Operating System ROS bags)
nodes.text: A data format is the agreed way a file is laid out so that software can read it, and versioning is the practice of giving every file, setting and program a unique identifier so that any result can be traced back to exactly what produced it.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats stable, machine-readable data models and immutable identifiers as more important than tool brands: each run should identify every result-changing component, preferably through content hashes, because results without an exact product state are unusable as safety evidence [f7124, f13015, f13019, f16255]. ASAM MDF 4.3.0, dated September 2025, is a neutral binary option for signals, bus traffic and sensor data with metadata and synchronization; alternative structured or in-house formats are acceptable if provenance and long-term readability are controlled, but no universal off-road event logging format was found [f7115, f7116, f2933]. OpenODD 1.0.0, dated 3 April 2025, represents operating-domain taxonomies in YAML and CSV, while JSON, YAML and XML suit settings and scenarios rather than gigabytes of sensor data; ROS bags retain messages with timestamps [f13208, f13009, f13013]. Replay can be built before new software if recording formats and interfaces are fixed, but discovering late that recordings cannot be injected at the required interface or data rate is a recognized risk; guidance recommends retaining original bytes or packets and adding decoding and injection plugins afterward [f921, f5669, f5606]. Traceability also requires versioned coordinate transforms, interface and message schemas, and checksums; lossy compression can change detector outputs, and evolving sensor-interface standards remain a versioning risk [f5411, f13016, f13017, f13020]. Open standards support heterogeneous simulation tool chains, although the cited road-ADAS integration and ROS/Autoware replay examples are on-road evidence rather than direct off-road validation [f9331, f5607].

nodes.label: Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC)
nodes.text: Electromagnetic compatibility is the ability of a piece of electronics to work correctly amid electrical noise from other equipment and to avoid producing noise that disturbs others.
nodes.synopsis: EMC means electronics must operate amid electrical noise without disturbing other equipment; ISO 16001:2017 requires EMC to ISO 13766 for object detection systems on earth-moving machines [f13021, f2414, f15254]. Field evidence includes variable-frequency-drive nuisance shutdowns documented in 2010, cross-zone interference reported in 2017, and interference involving dust monitors, computers, survey lasers and steel-braided water lines [f3371, f3372, f3373]. The booklet identifies EMC and multi-radar/lidar interference as simulation blind spots, so complete-machine EMC remains a physical-test requirement; MOSH includes EMC in its TRL4 laboratory phase [f5100, f13030, f13031, f493, f5595]. Acceptance criteria must address electromagnetic false triggers, and simultaneous sensor-suite mounting must be tested when it changes electromagnetic or optical behaviour [f13032, f5511]. The skeptic's review rates site-system interoperability and radar interference Medium to High risk and recommends ISO/TS 21815-2 interface tests and radio-frequency coexistence tests; an on-road example illustrates the concern but is reported through a secondary summary [f11076, f11078, f11255].

nodes.label: Over-the-air (OTA) sensor stimulation (as a sensor concept)
nodes.text: Over-the-air sensor stimulation means presenting an artificial signal, a radio echo, a projected image, a laser return or a sound, to a real sensor's own antenna or lens so that the sensor believes it is seeing a real scene.

nodes.label: Model and model fidelity
nodes.text: A model is a simplified description of a real thing, written in mathematics or computer code, that behaves like the real thing closely enough to answer one particular question, and its fidelity is how closely it does so.
nodes.synopsis: A program starting in October 2026 can realistically reach software-in-the-loop simulation with partly validated sensor models by mid-2027, but credibility belongs to the model, configuration, intended use and evidence—not to a platform intrinsically [f65, f7755]. Sensor and environment fidelity remain the hardest uncertainty: no accepted qualification method was found for off-road dust, snow or fog, no off-road fidelity thresholds were found, and degraded-visibility conditions are least validated [f10424, f331, f5220, f7886]. Clear-weather sensor accuracy can be high when the complete signal chain is modeled: one ray-traced lidar study reported errors of 1.7% for amplitude, 8.5% for point count and 9.3% for mean intensity, but field dust behavior is not captured by simple attenuation models [f4416, f4417, f4426].
