No validated off-road operator model was found; on-road warning-benefit estimates ranged from 53% to 96% depending on the driver model, illustrating the importance of behavioral assumptions [f250, f3040, f3045]. Greater vehicle-model complexity does not imply greater accuracy, yet articulated maneuvers and hydrostatic braking require appropriate physical detail rather than universally simplified representations [f5908, f6028, f6049, f6050]. Planning should identify the physical measurements validating each model, experimentally correlate adverse-environment sensors, and retain physical testing where models are weak; rare-event methods cannot establish claims about sensor physics outside simulation scope [f10229, f5219, f10470, f6853].

nodes.label: Simulation and simulator
nodes.text: A simulation is a computer run in which models of the machine, the site, the sensors and the people act together over time, and a simulator is the software that runs it.
nodes.synopsis: Exhaustive field coverage of more than 7,000 testing strata is infeasible; a 1% miss-rate claim in each of 20 critical strata at 95% one-sided confidence requires about 6,000 zero-miss trials, making simulation or hardware-in-the-loop essential for volume, alongside a credibility argument [f132, f6654, f6925]. Simulation can establish logic, timing and braking-envelope correctness across large parameter sweeps, but behavioural, sensor and closed-loop simulation must not be treated as interchangeable, and semantic object injection assumes perception has succeeded [f909, f462, f5779]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, abstract closed-loop machine-and-site simulation is considered realistic by mid-2027; documented reductions in physical testing relied on years of prior investment or narrow operating envelopes, and no published manufacturer statement confirming shortened off-road validation time was found [f844, f1256, f257]. Credibility remains limited by poorly validated glare and reflective-clothing effects, missing evidence for mud or dirt on radar, and uncertainty about predicting combined environmental and machine effects; calibration in fog and rain chambers and field validation are recommended [f4406, f4678, f9343, f10574]. Vehicle-and-environment simulation does not represent operator adaptation and related behavioural changes, so human delay should be explored through uncertain parameters or distributions, while behaviour change requires months of field time [f8206, f3478, f11858]. ISO 18497-4:2024 explicitly includes simulation as a verification method for agricultural machinery, but simulator errors can mask defects when results become safety evidence; recommended safeguards include upgrade regression testing and, as a fallback, using simulation for screening while retaining physical verification for acceptance [f5275, f10543, f8897, f9697].

nodes.label: Virtual validation (virtual testing)
nodes.text: Virtual validation means collecting evidence that a system meets its safety requirements by testing it in simulation and on laboratory benches instead of, or before, testing the complete real machine.
nodes.synopsis: The manufacturer wants to validate most Collision Mitigation System behavior virtually, including establishing an existing-system baseline and comparing the new system in the same environments, but it has no current virtual-testing capability or prior experience with this validation [f6, f25, f26, f8258, f7512]. The programme has an eleven-month hard deadline, while the examined proposal allows four months to validate the new braking system; documented capability-building cases took years, and no single approach is documented as compressing validation from years to months [f9396, f10389, f1203, f308]. Simulation can multiply evidence and prioritize scarce prototype tests, but cannot certify perception alone; how much physical testing can safely be replaced remains uncertain, and sensor simulation can replace only part, not most, of physical sensor testing [f11311, f326, f5757, f4407]. No identified off-road document accepts simulation as compliance evidence or permits replacing prescribed physical tests, although ISO 18497-4:2024 was the closest off-road support found for simulation as a verification method; in contrast, 2025 supplements to UN Regulation No. 152 permit some virtual substitution for car and van AEBS [f2103, f5277, f7546]. Credibility rather than test volume is the central weakness: physical correlation is needed, dust remains the biggest off-road sensor-simulation gap, and no independent evidence supports purely virtual or HIL validation across 100+ site types and all relevant machines and environmental conditions without substantial real-world correlation [f10409, f8341, f4424, f5760]. For four-month validation, the recommended defensible route is an analytical safety case, targeted physical tests and simulation under a credibility framework, with closed-loop simulation required to capture braking-induced trajectory changes [f2137, f11322].

nodes.label: Physics-based versus data-driven models
nodes.text: A physics-based model computes what happens from the laws of nature, while a data-driven model learns what usually happens from recorded examples.
nodes.synopsis: Physics-based and data-driven sensor models form a continuum rather than mutually exclusive alternatives: physics models compute causal responses, while learned models reproduce recorded distributions, and neither has an unconditional advantage [f13087, f4463, f4328, f13096]. Physics-based models can respond to changed machines, materials and sensor positions, making them attractive for a program covering different sensor heights, but transfer of validity across mounting positions was not demonstrated; measured job-site material data are also missing, and heavy precipitation or simplified physics can undermine accuracy [f4466, f13097, f5118, f13098, f4470, f4473]. The recommended division of labor is physics-based testing of important sensor effects and selected corner cases, with learned models supporting training, replay editing, scenario variation and robustness testing; hybrids should anchor important physical dimensions in physics and real measurements, but their maturity for safety credit remains unresolved [f4474, f4491, f4919, f5078]. Reduced-order motion and braking surrogates fitted to high-fidelity simulation and tests are common and very fast, suitable for millions of threshold and uncertainty evaluations, but unsafe extrapolation is a risk and no earth-moving transfer benchmark was found [f6105, f6481, f6482, f6479]. ASME V&V 40-2018 and the November 2023 FDA guidance are rated the most transferable credibility framework, but their stated scope is physics-based models, leaving machine-learned perception needing separate assurance [f8077, f8220]. Practical maturity remains uneven: calibrated construction-vehicle twins existed in 2025 but focused on dynamics and digging rather than perception, physics-based lidar is the most mature sensor family, and physics-based ultrasonic simulation was not found in Isaac Sim, Chrono::Sensor or CARLA [f468, f4501, f8547].

nodes.label: Digital twin
nodes.text: A digital twin is a detailed computer model of one specific real machine or site, kept matched to the real thing by measurements.
nodes.synopsis: A digital twin represents one specific real machine or site and promises agreement checked against measurements; neither the label nor a simulation package establishes credibility, which depends on the model, configuration, intended use and evidence [f13099, f13100, f7755]. The booklet recommends parameterised machine states and layered models per machine family rather than one ultimate twin, while machine geometry, self-occlusion and braking models can support coverage and blind-zone calculations before final hardware arrives [f1981, f6406, f13840, f5600, f5601]. This early modelling must not be presented as a validated sensor twin before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated, and a team starting in October 2026 should not promise full multisensor, all-weather correlation by mid-2027 [f508, f871, f870]. For sites, exact copies and parameterised digital cousins serve complementary purposes, but no head-to-head perception or collision-avoidance comparison was found, reconstruction does not automatically yield simulation-ready truth, and no job-site twin price or person-day figures were found [f3751, f3752, f5104, f3903]. Evidence includes a physically calibrated AGX wheel-loader twin in 2025 and SynFog’s 2024 fog-chamber twin with matching simulated sensor trends, although SynFog is on-road evidence and existing construction-vehicle twins focused on dynamics and digging rather than perception [f8292, f4563, f468]. The only vendor off-road speed-up claim found was Robotec.ai/Boliden’s 30% faster validation cycles, but it concerns autonomous fleet behaviour rather than collision-intervention perception and lacks independent verification [f481, f482, f483].

nodes.label: Virtual job site (virtual environment, scene, 3D asset)
nodes.text: A virtual job site is a three-dimensional computer model of a mine, quarry or construction site in which simulated machines, sensors and people can be tested.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus concludes that no single method can deliver valid camera, radar, lidar and ultrasonic environments across 100+ site types in the available time; it recommends parameterized representative sites, procedural rules and asset libraries anchored to surveyed real sites [f75, f76, f3705]. A proposed starting point is 15–30 site archetypes anchored by 3–5 surveyed sites, explicitly planning assumptions rather than evidence; no published method or standard setting the required number was found [f11937, f255]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, abstract closed-loop machine and site simulation is considered realistic by mid-2027, with sensor-independent geometry, scenario and evaluation foundations recommended now [f844, f1592]. Photorealism alone does not establish sensor validity: separate sensor and physical layers need material data, cross-sensor geometry and timing must remain consistent, and sensor/environment fidelity remains the hardest uncertainty [f85, f86, f5101, f10424]. Road-oriented formats fit lane-free sites poorly; custom off-road representations are often needed, while OpenMATERIAL 3D version 1.0.0, dated April 2025, standardizes assets and material properties for sensor-perception simulation [f7157, f8724, f7083]. Building meaningful site/material assets took more effort than rendering in the one heavy-machine study found, and published environment-building effort, cost, team-size or timeline figures were not found [f4457, f256].

nodes.label: Terrain model, digital elevation model (DEM), mesh and collision proxy
nodes.text: A terrain model describes the shape of the ground, a digital elevation model (DEM) is its simplest form, a mesh is the surface of small triangles that a computer draws, and a collision proxy is the invisible simplified shape used to detect contact.
nodes.synopsis: A terrain model describes ground shape, a digital elevation model is a grid of ground heights, a mesh represents surfaces with triangles, and simplified invisible collision proxies provide contact detection; the booklet also uses DEM for the unrelated discrete element method in soil physics [f13123, f13124, f13127, f13126]. Visual fidelity alone is insufficient for braking: neural scenes lack native collision surfaces, field-recording environments need explicit geometry and other simulation components, and a berm-edge error of tens of centimetres can corrupt stopping-distance tests [f3913, f3726, f3910]. Hybrid scenes can combine Gaussian appearance with invisible collision meshes, fill reconstruction holes with explicit geometry and enable terrain editing, whereas terrain edits in neural reconstructions were not demonstrated [f3818, f4284, f4283, f4231]. Practical evidence includes a 2025 quarry mesh optimized to 50,000 polygons, but reconstructed RadaRays meshes produced empty sensor frames and were too large to clean manually; the booklet found no validation of heavy-machine simulated braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes [f3796, f5103, f13132]. Scenario standards remain incomplete for off-road terrain: OpenDRIVE covers haul roads but needs additional representations for dig faces, stockpiles and free terrain, OpenCRG fits haul-road surfaces rather than open terrain and had unverified status, and ASAM identified missing deformable-terrain and related concepts [f7158, f7159, f7160, f7195].

nodes.label: Photogrammetry, laser scanning and SLAM
nodes.text: These are three ways of measuring a real site in three dimensions: from overlapping photographs, from laser distance measurements, or from a moving machine's own sensors as it drives.
nodes.synopsis: Photogrammetry, laser scanning and SLAM measure real sites from photographs, laser distances and machine recordings respectively; reality capture is strongest for preserving real geometry and clutter, but does not automatically yield simulation-ready truth [f13133, f3701, f5104]. The booklet recommends parameterised representative site types anchored to surveyed real sites; a possible starting portfolio of 15–30 archetypes and 3–5 lidar-plus-photogrammetry anchors is explicitly a planning assumption, not an evidence-based target [f3705, f4112]. Accuracy claims need reconciliation: survey capture is described as assessable against standards, while some passages restrict that distinction to laser scanning, despite ASPRS 2024 covering photogrammetry and a separate finding reporting controlled photogrammetric centimetre-level accuracy; the cited lidar result of 1.3 cm mean absolute error concerns road scenes [f78, f13136, f3719, f4198, f3721]. Photogrammetry is vulnerable to textureless soil, glare, motion and baked lighting, while forward-facing machine logs leave unseen surfaces that a taller future sensor may expose [f3722, f3873, f3811, f3812]. For the 2027 schedule, reconstruction-quality logs should be collected before sensor selection, with synchronised timestamps and retained calibration; adverse-weather replay should be separated from clean static-site mapping, although no off-road study was found quantifying weather contamination of reconstructed geometry [f4059, f4016, f4043, f4044]. Closed-loop braking requires substantial conversion beyond reconstruction, and captured moving objects need replacement with controllable agents; reusable site representation remains a bottleneck before scenario volume matters [f4000, f3885, f9364].

nodes.label: Structure from motion (COLMAP) and scene reconstruction
nodes.text: Structure from motion is the mathematical method that recovers camera positions and a three-dimensional point cloud from ordinary photographs, COLMAP is a widely used free program that does it, and scene reconstruction is the whole process of turning recordings into a usable virtual site.
nodes.synopsis: Structure from motion recovers camera positions and 3D points from photographs; COLMAP implements this method, while scene reconstruction extends it into a usable virtual site through registration, cleanup, classification, collision proxies, sensor materials and qualification against held-out measurements [f13144, f13145, f13151]. The booklet calls existing machine recordings the cheapest route to real site geometry, but reconstruction requires synchronized, calibrated logs and accurate poses; in one dataset, only 50 of 200 sequences passed the pose check [f13153, f4216, f4290, f13152]. Camera-only reconstruction depends on texture, similar illumination, overlap, at least three observations per object and genuinely different viewpoints; textureless terrain, glare, reflective surfaces and insufficient parallax can cause failure [f3799, f4034, f4035, f4040]. One benchmark required more than 800 hours of COLMAP compute and more than 300 hours of manual selection, but the compute figure is on-road evidence, not a direct job-site digital-twin cost estimate [f13150, f3898]. The conclusion is that reconstruction can make recordings replay-ready or near-path simulation-ready, but not braking-validation-ready or radar/ultrasonic-ready: reconstructed mesh artifacts actually occluded simulated radar and produced empty frames, so sensor-mounting comparisons require validated reconstruction and position-specific sensor models [f13154, f5103, f5492].

nodes.label: Procedural generation
nodes.text: Procedural generation builds many different virtual sites automatically from rules and parameter ranges instead of modeling each site by hand.
nodes.synopsis: Procedural generation automatically creates virtual sites from rules and parameter ranges; once rules exist, hundreds of variants are inexpensive, and parameterized archetypes enable rapid sensor-pose changes and deliberate edge cases [f13155, f13158, f3754]. The booklet judges it to have the strongest off-road track record, citing agriculture, forestry, construction and off-road autonomy: CropCraft reported a 9.9% average segmentation sim-to-real gap, while Boreal3D produced 1,000 synthetic plots across four laser-scanning platforms [f77, f13161, f3731, f3732]. CropCraft is identified as an open-source Blender/Python tool dated November 2025; separately, a 2023 construction study found that real lighting by date improved realism [f3787, f7059]. However, internally exact procedural geometry is not site-true unless calibrated, and broad parameter ranges do not ensure meaningful coverage when rules omit failure-generating structures, rare correlations or unencoded hazard categories [f4188, f3736, f3793, f13308]. The recommended approach is therefore a hybrid factory of parameterized site families, asset libraries and a few surveyed real anchors, with evidence that adding small amounts of real data improves transfer in agriculture and construction [f76, f13168, f4296]. Reproducible testing requires freezing random seeds, generator versions, assets and material libraries, plus model weights for generative tests; otherwise failures may not be replayable months later [f13167, f4377, f4378].

nodes.label: Game engine (Unreal Engine, Unity)
nodes.text: A game engine is the software core of a video game, which draws three-dimensional worlds, moves objects with simple physics and runs in real time, and many sensor simulators are built on one.
nodes.synopsis: Game engines provide reusable real-time visual worlds, making virtual job sites affordable and fast enough for the program’s four-month window, but machine and sensor models must be added separately [f13172, f13181]. Reported Unreal Engine 5 terrain-rendering results range from 60 FPS for a single building to 17 FPS for a 23-million-Gaussian scene, so demonstrated performance depends on scene scale [f3893, f3894]. CARLA 0.10.0 moved to Unreal Engine 5.5 with Chaos physics on 19 December 2024 and includes a mining earth-mover asset; the separate UE4 release 0.9.16 followed on 16 September 2025, making a frozen, qualified build advisable [f8464, f8297, f8466, f15938]. CARLA’s UE5 hardware requirements include an RTX 3000-series GPU or better, at least 16 GB VRAM and 130 GB disk space [f8850]. Visual realism is not validated sensor or braking physics: specialized machine behavior requires coupled physics tools, wavelength-specific sensor materials are absent from ordinary visual textures, and a 2026 study found photometric divergence in Unity construction scenes despite extensive domain randomization [f13178, f13179, f13182, f10584].

nodes.label: Material and sensor material (ASAM OpenMATERIAL)
nodes.text: In simulation, a material is the description of how a surface responds to light, radio waves or sound, and ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D is a standard format for storing those properties for camera, lidar and radar.
nodes.synopsis: A useful virtual job site needs coordinated geometry, collision surfaces, ground mechanics and sensor-specific materials, not just convincing visuals; non-visual responses cannot be inferred from RGB textures, and camera, lidar and radar require wavelength-specific material data [f13113, f3713, f3715]. ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D standardises assets and material properties for sensor-perception simulation: version 1.0.0 was released on 3 April 2025, while version 1.1.0 was planned for October 2026 but was not listed on the main page accessed that month [f7083, f3714, f3923, f3925]. Its coverage does not remove the need for separate environmental and contamination models, because weather and lighting are outside its stated scope and sensor soiling is explicitly excluded [f3919, f9372]. Radar credibility depends on material properties and the signal chain, with 77 GHz properties often requiring measurement; a 2025 wheel-loader study needed manual material tuning and reported detector failures partly attributable to guessed materials [f4418, f4420, f4421, f4423]. The booklet found no published job-site ultrasonic datasets, also reported missing thermal datasets, and recommends that the program measure or estimate material properties itself—a larger schedule item than computing power [f3943, f3717, f12951]. Site geometry and material libraries are proposed as work that can be completed before mid-2027, but acquiring and maintaining physically meaningful assets may consume more engineering effort than rendering them, and adapting road-centric material libraries to mines and quarries is non-trivial [f4973, f4966, f8462].

nodes.label: Scene description standards: OpenUSD, OpenDRIVE, OpenCRG, OpenSCENARIO, OpenLABEL, OpenODD, OpenXOntology
nodes.text: These are agreed file formats that let different simulation tools exchange the same description of a world, a road, a road surface, a sequence of events, a set of labels, an operating domain or a shared vocabulary.
nodes.synopsis: These formats enable simulation tools to exchange scene, road, surface, scenario, label and operating-domain descriptions; alongside OSI and FMI, they serve as integration glue, but compatibility does not establish physical fidelity [f13196, f8335, f13214]. OpenUSD is domain-neutral and can represent mines and construction sites, whereas OpenDRIVE assumes road networks and fits sites without lanes poorly; stockpiles, berms, ruts and other off-road features often need additional representations [f8610, f3982, f8724]. The cited releases include OpenODD 1.0.0 on 3 April 2025, OpenSCENARIO DSL 2.2.0 on 19 March 2026, OpenDRIVE 1.9.0 in May 2026, and OpenSCENARIO XML 1.4.0 in 2026, with June reported by a secondary listing [f6707, f7152, f7156, f7149]. OpenODD and related ISO structures are useful architectural templates, but their road-oriented scope and attributes require a manufacturer- or industry-governed off-road taxonomy [f6642, f6709, f7163]. Off-road scenario standardisation remains incomplete, with missing concepts including deformable terrain, particles, vegetation, heavy-machine manipulation and sensor degradation; the booklet anticipates extensions being unlikely before mid-2027, rather than treating OpenX as unusable [f7432, f7195, f7172, f7196]. The recommended approach is a manufacturer-owned, domain-neutral, version-controlled scenario catalogue, OpenDRIVE for structured haul roads, OpenUSD and OpenMATERIAL for scenes, and OpenSCENARIO exports where required, with open-format exports and exit clauses protecting against supplier dependence [f13215, f13216, f8887].

nodes.label: Open Simulation Interface (ASAM OSI) and the ASAM organization
nodes.text: ASAM OSI is a standard set of messages that lets an environment model, a sensor model and the function under test talk to each other during a simulation, and ASAM is the industry association that publishes it.
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OSI is the message standard published by ASAM for connecting environment, sensor, fusion and function models, including time-stamped ground truth, sensor views, sensor data and detected objects [f13218, f5260, f13219]. The booklet rates OSI as domain-neutral and transferable to off-road work, but stresses that its road-vehicle heritage and cited on-road evidence do not constitute proof for quarry machines [f13224, f5507]. OSI supports portable, sealed sensor-model delivery; recommendations include requesting an OSI/OSMP-packaged FMI 2.0 FMU when suppliers withhold internals and fixing supplier-independent object, warning and brake-request semantics before hardware [f13220, f13221, f4857, f13228]. Existing abstractions leave gaps in camera spectral irradiance, radar raw waveforms and bidirectional sensor–ECU behaviour; ASAM's high-fidelity extension runs from April 2025 to March 2027, overlapping planned first-tool-chain integration and creating versioning risk [f7081, f5093, f13227, f15870, f8619]. ASAM also reports no standardized sensor-simulation quality metrics, with the metrics project still at proposal stage in September 2025; separately, the research did not verify OSI's status [f13225, f13226, f7165].

nodes.label: Co-simulation, Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI), Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU) and SSP
nodes.text: Co-simulation runs several separate simulation programs together in step, FMI is the standard that lets them plug into each other, an FMU is one model packaged to that standard, and SSP describes how a set of FMUs is wired together.
nodes.synopsis: Co-simulation combines separate simulation programs in step: FMI standardizes their connections, FMUs package individual models, and SSP records connections and parameters so arrangements can be shared and reproduced [f13230, f13234]. The booklet treats FMI/SSP as domain-neutral and suitable for off-road work, with about 250 FMI-supporting tools reported by mid-2025, although Chapter 9 says the research did not verify FMI/SSP's status [f7167, f8336, f7165]. Practical applications include connecting reduced-order machine models to high-fidelity components and coupling Mevea with Simulink through FMI or TCP/IP [f6395, f8562, f8699]. When sensor internals are unavailable, the recommendation is to request a black-box OSI/OSMP FMU using FMI 2.0; secure black-box exchange approaches existed in 2024, but cited independent lidar-model examples are on-road evidence [f4857, f4858, f4504, f6381]. Standards do not eliminate integration risk: coordinate systems, clocks, synchronized machine pose and material semantics still need alignment, specialist integration requires co-simulation expertise, and the lowest-cost Chrono-to-Isaac heavy-machine chain is not turnkey or qualification-ready without major work [f13237, f8729, f8758, f9280].

nodes.label: Operational design domain (ODD) and operating-domain taxonomy
nodes.text: The operational design domain is the written description of the conditions under which a system is designed to work, and an operating-domain taxonomy is the organized list of attributes used to write it.
nodes.synopsis: The framework aims to provide confidence across conditions, configurations and environments, including more than 100 job-site types, but the corpus warns that a collision system cannot be assumed to handle every site–machine–weather combination [f31, f7508, f3599]. Published off-road intervention launches have deliberately narrow scopes, so the recommended strategy is restricted release followed by widening through evidence gates; Volvo CE's January 2023 example is reverse-only at 3–15 km/h with braking lasting 2–3 seconds [f10434, f379, f1238]. Validation coverage should be organized around an operating-domain taxonomy, a scenario catalog and parameterized scenario families, rather than site counts or one Cartesian matrix; relevant dimensions include surface, slope, objects, weather, light, machine model and sensor pose [f119, f4063, f11498]. On-road standards offer transferable structures, not off-road content, and no heavy-machinery equivalent of ISO 34502:2022 was found for operating-envelope and scenario coverage, leaving the programme to define its own taxonomy [f6642, f10334, f10335]. A programme starting in October 2026 could realistically have an operating-domain definition and scenario catalog working by mid-2027, with ownership retained in-house and the final plan explicitly documenting coverage, exclusions and the envelope of its safety claim [f63, f8797, f10155, f10184]. Simulation also needs its own credibility and applicability envelope: the cited on-road approach permits virtual ODD coverage only inside the validated envelope, while validation across mine conditions remains an outstanding need [f7998, f7841, f3601].

nodes.label: Scenario (functional, logical, concrete)
nodes.text: A scenario is a description of a situation that unfolds over time, written at one of three levels of detail: in words (functional), with parameter ranges (logical), or with every value fixed (concrete).
nodes.synopsis: Across the chapters, the braking system is required to work across more than 10 operating scenarios per machine; Chapter 7 also specifies more than 100 job-site types [f284, f1176, f2032, f3675, f4393, f5130, f5860, f6622, f7509, f8254, f10384]. Scenario-based testing is the validation backbone, with parameterised families at functional, logical and concrete levels and probability distributions feeding sampling, search and estimation [f315, f6640]. Coverage must distinguish forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing: four of 13 fatal US haul-truck collisions in January 2005–June 2021 began as trucks started moving with victims within 50 ft (15 m), while parking, workshops and maintenance also need separate scenarios [f2991, f2996, f3369]. Off-road collision kinematics differ from road tests, and realistic scenarios need multiple actors, machine-specific blind areas and explicit sensor-degradation conditions rather than generic proximity or weather representations [f2567, f4358, f11551, f9371]. Simulation volume alone does not establish safety: encounters rather than frames are the analysis unit, success percentages require a defined scenario population and selection mechanism, and even a validated simulator can miss important hazards; the roadmap therefore calls for hazard-to-scenario traceability and a coverage rationale [f130, f5425, f6933, f8211, f9730]. Scenario definitions are among the deliverables considered achievable before mid-2027, but field sample sizes remain claim-dependent, and acceptance thresholds should be measured by scenario [f4973, f5782, f10967].

nodes.label: Scenario catalog, scenario family and scenario parameter
nodes.text: A scenario catalog is the complete, traceable list of situations a system must be tested against, a scenario family is one logical scenario with its parameter ranges and probability distribution, and a scenario parameter is one of the variables in that family.
nodes.synopsis: The recommended test space combines an operating-domain taxonomy, a traceable catalog ensuring known fatal-accident patterns are tested, and parameterized scenario families with probability distributions; ISO 21815 and EMESRT PR-5A provide off-road anchors rather than a passenger-car library copied directly into mining or construction [f119, f6641, f1527]. Most platforms have at least 10 critical operating scenarios, but EMESRT counts remain inconsistent: a 2019 trade article reports 24 scenarios, while the 2024 Activity Report counts 17 surface storyboards published in 2019 [f17, f4079]. Scenario count is not coverage, and coverage is separate from model credibility: the plan should prioritize accident-informed cases, expose uncovered cells, and make direct statistical claims for safety-critical classes rather than rely on a full Cartesian matrix or an aggregate coverage score [f10506, f8210, f10622, f9880, f5470]. A programme starting in October 2026 can realistically have its operating-domain definition and scenario catalog working by mid-2027, with scenario development and model preparation undertaken before prototype arrival [f63, f5615]. The manufacturer should retain ownership of the catalog, operating domain, acceptance criteria and correlation data, and provide an assessor-quality catalog traced to hazards, EMESRT and ISO 21815 [f8797, f8030]. A complete scenario spreadsheet is not physical safety evidence: physical performance and false-positive tests should remain for each scenario class, alongside assessor-selected end-to-end confirmation including at least one run per EMESRT family [f656, f7884, f7887].

nodes.label: Test case, test matrix and scenario grid
nodes.text: A test case is one fully specified test with an expected result, a test matrix is a table of test cases arranged by the factors they vary, and a scenario grid is a matrix whose cells are concrete scenarios.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet requires the operating design domain to be written first, in October 2026, before scenarios, sites or sample sizes are planned, and recommends coverage through domain attributes, equivalence classes and interactions rather than repeated site names [f13253, f13251]. The proposed combinations exceed 7,000 cells, making 59–299 physical trials in every cell impractical; the indicative physical anchor matrix instead comprises roughly 60–100 instrumented runs per machine family [f5206, f5469, f6177]. Coverage must distinguish forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing, include degraded and recovery cases, and report safety-critical detection performance per cell rather than as one aggregate [f2996, f10778, f5454]. Correlated models should support large-matrix virtual regression, but simulation is not sole evidence; Euro NCAP's on-road precedent verifies randomly selected prediction-grid cells physically [f881, f1607, f1755]. No universal off-road coverage prescription or standardised national matrix in the reviewed India DGMS guidance was found, and neither scenario counts nor perfect sensor models establish adequate coverage [f5475, f2453, f10506, f5108]. Plans should leave uncovered cells visibly blank and predeclare primary statistical claims because checking hundreds of cells at 95% confidence produces chance passes or failures [f9479, f12172].

nodes.label: Corner case, edge case and rare event
nodes.text: An edge case sits at the limit of one parameter, a corner case sits at the limits of several at once, and a rare event is a situation that happens so seldom in normal operation that waiting for it is not a practical way to test it.
nodes.synopsis: Field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event safety, including for off-road machines; the proposed alternative combines stratified testing, simulation and safety analysis, while the required field exposure for rare misses or unintended braking remains uncertain [f312, f6924, f5467, f8181]. The sampling burden is substantial: zero observed misses requires 299 independent trials to demonstrate a miss rate of at most 1%, or 29,956 for at most 0.01%, and RAND’s on-road estimate reaches hundreds of millions of miles [f13303, f13304, f13305]. In 2016, Michigan researchers reported importance-sampling acceleration factors of roughly 300–100,000 for car-following crashes and 2,000–20,000 for lane-change conflicts, but credible rare-event estimates require valid input distributions and tail models, and the glossary identifies no known exposure distribution for 100 or more site types [f1220, f1221, f8183, f11614]. Simulation can deliberately generate rare events and corner cases, but only for conceived and parameterised hazards; procedural scenes can miss real correlations and rare structures, while design-of-experiments methods cannot establish global corner-case coverage or exclude narrow nonlinear failures [f13307, f3793, f7215, f7222]. Selected difficult cases therefore warrant qualification-quality sensor models and higher-fidelity machine models where simpler models fail, followed by controlled whole-machine confirmation of worst cases [f4474, f6409, f719]. The recommended pilot is a difficult end-to-end slice with physical or bench comparators and predeclared decision criteria, using 3–5 scenario classes including at least one edge case; a four-month window cannot cover all seasons, rare events or operator adaptation [f9914, f9916, f12348].

nodes.label: The X-in-the-loop family (MIL, SIL, HIL, PIL, VIL, DIL)
nodes.text: "X-in-the-loop" names a family of test setups in which one real part of the system (the X) is connected to a simulation of everything else, and the family forms a ladder from all-virtual to all-real.
nodes.synopsis: X-in-the-loop is a ladder from all-virtual toward all-real testing: expanding the real-system boundary from software to ECU, sensor and complete machine exposes additional failure modes but increases complexity and sacrifices speed, scalability, controllability and test volume [f13311, f5227, f13321]. The recommended allocation is MIL/SIL for high-volume early testing, HIL for real-controller timing, interfaces and faults, selective VIL where added fidelity warrants investment, and real machines for stopping, terrain and environmental effects; these methods complement rather than replace one another [f13313, f13314, f13315, f5743]. The pipeline should operate under continuous integration with automatic pass criteria and proving-ground anchors, with a versioned scenario library, SIL/HIL suite, statistical acceptance plan and correlated machine-dynamics models ideally ready by mid-2027 [f7142, f7141, f5616]. Engineering simulation can find defects and tune thresholds before machines exist, but the cited Daimler Truck India and HCLTech examples demonstrate engineering development rather than external safety acceptance; ISO 19014-4's 2020 edition contains normative Annex B on software validation test environments [f1447, f1449, f10532]. Commercial IPG offerings have direct off-highway MIL/SIL/HIL/VIL relevance, but documented sensor-stimulated VIL is limited to road vehicles, a 2024 road-vehicle survey reports high cost and varying accuracy, and no end-to-end heavy off-road automatic-braking VIL case was found [f8807, f13318, f13319, f13320].

nodes.label: Model-in-the-loop (MIL)
nodes.text: Model-in-the-loop testing runs a model of the control logic against a model of the machine and its surroundings, with no real software or hardware yet.
nodes.synopsis: MIL tests a model of control logic against modeled machinery and surroundings, without real software or hardware, so rules can be checked before controller code is written [f13324, f13325]. It is the cheapest and earliest testing rung and can catch logical errors, such as warnings failing during articulation, while fixes still take minutes [f13326, f13330]. The recommended pipeline uses MIL and SIL for high-volume validation, targeting thousands of runs per night on cloud or on-premise compute [f7138, f13314, f13327]. Much of the relatively simple warn-then-brake logic can be designed and checked in late 2026 before sensor selection, but MIL provides no knowledge about sensors or real timing [f13332, f13329]. Tool options include a middle-cost chain reusing models across MIL, SIL and HIL, while IPG Automotive is reported to support off-highway testing through vehicle-in-the-loop with real tractors [f13328, f8652, f8807].

nodes.label: Software-in-the-loop (SIL)
nodes.text: Software-in-the-loop testing runs the real braking software, compiled for an ordinary computer, inside a simulated machine on a simulated site, so that thousands of scenarios can be tried without any hardware.
nodes.synopsis: For a program starting in October 2026, an executable SIL regression framework with machine-dynamics and braking models is realistic by mid-2027 if interfaces can be defined; how much work starts earlier depends on when the manufacturer's software can run on a computer, and sensor models may still be only partly validated [f840, f270, f65]. SIL is the economical volume-testing stage for software correctness, requirements regression and closed-loop behavior, supporting sweeps of 100+ site types and 10+ scenarios and thousands of nightly runs [f527, f925, f5266, f5267, f13327]. Its credibility depends on correlated models: it cannot independently prove production ECU timing, actual brake hardware or sensor physics in dust, snow and glare, so the recommended allocation combines SIL with HIL and whole-machine tests [f5271, f711, f5269, f5270, f5268, f13323]. HCLTech's on-road Level 3 example reports up to 75 percent less test-design effort and incremental-release validation in under a day, but discloses neither platform build time, staffing nor retained physical testing, limiting its usefulness as a planning benchmark [f1791, f1306, f1307, f1308]. Compressing validation from three or four years to under four months is credible only if the scenario library, replay adapters, SIL/HIL suites and correlated models are ready before the prototype arrives, making that period a confirmation campaign [f13085].

nodes.label: Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) with data injection
nodes.text: Hardware-in-the-loop testing connects the real electronic control unit, with its real wiring and network messages, to a simulator that runs in real time and feeds it the data a real machine would produce.
nodes.synopsis: HIL with data injection connects a production ECU and its real interfaces to deterministic real-time simulation, proving timing, communications, diagnostics, faults and fail-to-safe behaviour; the booklet allocates SIL to volume and HIL to timing, interfaces and faults [f533, f5283, f12057]. Injection cannot prove the sensor front end or true machine and brake behaviour when those components are bypassed or modeled, and post-intervention evidence depends on model validation [f5286, f5287, f5553]. Physical sensor stimulation tests real sensors and firmware, but has limits on targets, field of view, weather and soiling; raw-signal HIL also carries the highest relative integration effort [f4436, f4437, f8731]. A program starting in October 2026 could realistically commission one HIL bench by mid-2027, using the ISO/TS 21815-2 J1939 intervention interface, with deterministic real time prioritized over throughput [f66, f538, f8848]. About 6,000 zero-miss trials are required for a 1% miss-rate claim across 20 critical strata at 95% one-sided confidence, judged feasible only in simulation or HIL, but the required compute or HIL throughput remains unquantified [f6654, f7449]. Published on-road work provides a physical-track benchmarking precedent, but neither an off-road perception-AEB end-to-end HIL case nor an off-road OEM statement demonstrating reduced validation time was found [f10416, f535, f257].

nodes.label: Direct digital or raw signal injection
nodes.text: Raw signal injection feeds simulated or recorded sensor data into the sensor's electronics at a defined electrical point, so that everything downstream of that point is tested and everything upstream is not.
nodes.synopsis: Raw signal injection feeds simulated or recorded data into sensor electronics at a defined electrical interface; its evidential scope is determined by that boundary, with real downstream hardware tested but upstream components excluded [f13361, f5291, f5247]. Across the synthesis, sensor-testing chapter and glossary, the booklet consistently warns that injection cannot establish lens, imager, antenna or environmental performance, including contamination, vibration and glare; over-the-air stimulation exercises more of the real sensor front end [f96, f4498, f5296, f13037]. Camera injection can test downstream processing, bandwidth, timing, corrupted-frame handling and interface faults, and one vendor argues it avoids camera-box synchronization and field-of-view problems, although that argument is on-road vendor evidence [f13364, f5289]. Integration is sensor- and ECU-specific and ranked highest-effort: it requires the exact electrical/protocol interface, a realistic stream, synchronization and an adapter, making early confirmation of recording-format and data-rate compatibility important [f8641, f8731, f5292, f5669]. Every injection result should state its boundary, production injection ports must not remain open, and no current public heavy off-road standard prescribing an injection architecture for the listed positioning and infrastructure-aided systems was found [f13371, f5834, f5325].

nodes.label: Over-the-air sensor stimulation (sensor-in-the-loop)
nodes.text: Over-the-air stimulation presents a real, complete sensor with artificial light, radio waves or sound generated from the virtual scene, so that the whole sensor, including its optics or antenna and its firmware, is in the loop.
nodes.synopsis: Over-the-air stimulation exposes a complete real sensor and its downstream system to controlled optical, RF or acoustic stimuli from a virtual scene, testing the front end and firmware; ordinary HIL or injected objects alone cannot establish optical or RF perception [f5299, f5302, f932, f13394]. Its suitability depends on the manufacturer's sensor types, and the booklet reserves it for sensor/ECU regression, timing tests and supplier-independent characterization rather than strong close-range off-road validation [f267, f13387, f13386]. Radar processing latency adds 1 m of apparent range per 6.67 ns: a review published on 19 May 2021 reported typical minimum ranges of 20–30 m, whereas vendors claim minima of 0.6–1.5 m and capacities from five to several hundred objects; workers 0.5–5 m behind a machine are consequently a critical weak point [f5305, f5306, f13381, f13386]. Stimulation does not reproduce the described off-road terrain clutter, dust plumes or steel-structure reflections, weather and soiling are mostly not reproducible, and physical lidar stimulation—especially solid-state lidar—remains a gap [f13385, f4497, f13383]. Documented sensor-stimulated VIL evidence is limited to road vehicles, a 2024 survey describes it as costly with varying accuracy, and neither a neutral cross-technology benchmark nor exemption from validating the stimulation equipment is available [f340, f341, f4605, f4864].

nodes.label: Vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL) and mixed reality
nodes.text: Vehicle-in-the-loop testing drives the complete real machine on a safe, empty test area while virtual hazards are fed to its sensors or controller, so that it brakes for a worker who exists only in the simulation.
nodes.synopsis: VIL drives a complete real machine in a safe test area with virtual hazards, allowing real braking dynamics, controller and actuator delays, latency and operator-interface behaviour to be tested without endangering people or targets [f13388, f5333]. It does not establish perception of injected objects unless sensors are stimulated over the air, and fidelity remains constrained by stimulation, testbench dynamics and simulated versus real ground interaction [f5335, f940]. The 2024 on-road survey reports costly, variably accurate systems and no full-scale platform ready for comprehensive industrial testing; no complete heavy-off-road automatic-braking VIL case was found, although vendor material describes real-tractor VIL [f341, f5340, f342, f8652]. The recommended hierarchy uses SIL for volume, HIL for timing, interfaces and faults, VIL only where added physical fidelity justifies investment, and real machines for stopping, terrain and environmental evidence [f13313]. Accordingly, a team starting from zero in October 2026 should not promise a complete multi-sensor heavy-off-road VIL facility by mid-2027, and the programme's economic justification remains uncertain [f866, f1119].

nodes.label: Driver-in-the-loop (DIL), operator-in-the-loop and the machine simulator
nodes.text: Driver-in-the-loop or operator-in-the-loop testing puts a real person in a simulator cab, with screens, controls and sometimes motion, to study how operators react when the machine warns, waits and then brakes.
nodes.synopsis: Driver-/operator-in-the-loop testing puts a real person in a simulator to study reactions to warnings, delays and braking; it assesses the human response rather than sensor detection or real braking hardware [f13402, f571, f578]. The booklet’s strongest off-road human-interface evidence is ACARP’s modified haul-truck simulator research in Australian open-cut coal operations during 2017–2019: a richer schematic proximity display reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time, although benefits were smaller in an experiment with fewer experienced drivers [f3465, f3468, f3466, f3467]. That research addressed proximity advisory rather than automatic braking, and no off-road study of operators experiencing automatic braking in a simulator was found [f573, f576]. Simulator-to-field transfer remains unestablished for demanding operating conditions, and simulator studies cannot establish months-long complacency, risk compensation or production-pressure effects; operational monitoring and field time remain necessary [f3469, f580, f792, f767]. On-road findings also resist simple assumptions: a 2025 simulator study reported no cry-wolf effect at 33% false alarms but did report unnecessary braking, while other on-road truck warning data showed a strong cry-wolf effect [f3335, f3336, f3623]. The program therefore recommends operator studies before prototype safety testing and potentially requires human-in-the-loop evidence for operator-dependent safety claims, but the setup duration for operator-simulator capability is undocumented [f13415, f11833, f849].

nodes.label: Real time (hard real time)
nodes.text: A simulation runs in real time when one simulated second takes exactly one real second, and in hard real time when every computing step is guaranteed to finish within its deadline, every time.
nodes.synopsis: HIL tests production-controller timing, communications, interfaces and fault responses against a simulated plant; SIL cannot show whether the production processor misses deadlines [f5283, f529]. HIL requires deterministic hard real time because the real ECU cannot wait: missing even an expected 50-millisecond sensor-message deadline can produce a false test result, so throughput alone is insufficient [f13418, f16179, f13420]. Reported performance varies substantially: ISPRS 2024 terrain examples achieved 60 FPS for a single building and 17 FPS for a 23-million-Gaussian scene, while higher-fidelity Chrono CRM terrain reportedly runs 50–200 times slower than real time [f3893, f3894, f8499]. Sensor acceleration is promising but configuration-specific: 2020 vendor radar figures report about 12 ms per frame against a 30 FPS target, and a 2021 publication with vendor authors reports above 160 FPS for one single-channel radar [f4932, f4933]. Planning should therefore benchmark actual geometry, sensors, latency and jitter early, retaining separate offline high-fidelity and real-time models where necessary rather than assuming a generic real-time factor [f13425, f8924].

nodes.label: Open loop versus closed loop
nodes.text: In an open-loop test the system's output does not change what happens next, while in a closed-loop test the system's actions feed back and alter the situation it then sees.
nodes.synopsis: Recorded-data replay is open loop: it remains useful for perception and brake-trigger timing, but its recorded future ceases to represent the machine’s counterfactual future at the first brake command absent from the original run [f11321, f109, f108]. Braking consequences therefore require new closed-loop evidence from simulation, bench or hardware-in-the-loop testing, and physical tests; warning-system fleet history can validate inputs and submodels, not the new braking chain [f11711, f110, f7575]. Converting recordings into closed-loop environments requires explicit geometry, sensor properties, controllable actors and machine dynamics, with substantial conversion and calibration beyond ordinary reconstruction [f3726, f4000]. MineSim demonstrated mining-specific closed-loop feasibility in April 2025, and abstract machine-and-site simulation is considered realistic by mid-2027 for a team starting in October 2026, but scenario infrastructure is not validated sensor physics and no public demonstration was found combining heavy machines, severe weather and closed-loop braking [f330, f844, f845, f12532]. Detector-threshold tuning must be followed by closed-loop evaluation of stopping margin and unnecessary interventions; independently validating perception and the brake plant cannot exclude emergent failures in their combination, so physical tests at the collision/no-collision boundary remain recommended [f6982, f8196, f7888].

nodes.label: Replay and re-simulation of recorded data (open-loop replay)
nodes.text: Replay feeds sensor data recorded on real machines back into the software, exactly as recorded, to see what the software would have detected and decided.
aliases: Replay and re-simulation of recorded data
nodes.synopsis: Recorded-data replay is an established, low-cost way to baseline the warning system and evaluate candidate perception, warning timing and braking triggers, but it cannot validate stopping because the recorded world does not react to a brake command [f94, f332, f10925, f11320, f11321]. Recording should start in October 2026 rather than wait for a prototype; the existing fleet is suitable, and a recording-and-replay pipeline could realistically be running by mid-2027 [f5168, f333, f64]. Evidence covers only the recorded sensors, mounting positions and scenarios, excludes effects upstream of the re-injection point, and ceases to represent the machine's counterfactual future at the first brake command absent from the original run [f95, f96, f108]. Reliable replay requires raw sensor inputs, synchronized timestamps, machine signals, geometry, calibration and independent ground truth; insufficient fidelity, missing metadata or large unexplained discrepancies should trigger stopping or escalation [f11899, f12991, f10928]. Camera and lidar recordings can support reconstruction and near-path novel views, but quality is restrictive—only 50 of 200 MV² sequences passed pose checks—and no validated evidence supports re-simulating an unrecorded sensor type [f3985, f3727, f3729]. Replay therefore belongs within a broader validation programme combining simulation, benches, physical tests and staged field operation, while published sources yielded no off-road OEM statement demonstrating that simulation, replay or HIL shortened validation time [f309, f257].

nodes.label: Semantic or object-list replay
nodes.text: Semantic replay feeds the decision software not with raw sensor data but with a list of objects (type, position, speed), either recorded or taken from ground truth, so that only the warning and braking logic is tested.
nodes.synopsis: Semantic replay bypasses perception and feeds real decision, warning and braking logic with recorded or ground-truth object lists in common coordinates plus machine state; it can operate open loop or closed loop, with lists regenerated as the virtual machine slows [f5253, f5254, f13457, f13459]. It tests thresholds, threat assessment, warning stages and brake-request rules independently of sensor modality, but cannot prove perception and can hide latency, occlusion, false detections and range or classification errors; reported off-road maturity is medium for logic and absent for perception [f5256, f13463, f5686]. It is described as the cheapest way to sweep large scenario sets, supporting millions of braking-logic combinations through highly parallel CPU workloads on commodity servers without rendering or ray tracing [f13460, f9322, f16181]. Recording only object lists limits future replay to downstream software and prevents testing new perception algorithms, sensor models or mounting positions; where suppliers expose only object lists, validating a phenomenological model at that interface is considered more defensible than inventing a raw-signal model [f5628, f12990, f4868]. The recommended progression starts SIL with semantic inputs before adding realistic sensor errors, and pairs semantic replay with end-to-end replay when warning logic changes but perception remains unchanged: semantic coverage and expensive raw-sensor testing are complementary, rather than one approach dominating [f13466, f5497, f5779].

nodes.label: Shadow mode (silent testing)
nodes.text: In shadow mode the new braking software runs live on working machines, sees everything the sensors see and decides when it would brake, but its brake commands are disconnected, so it only records what it would have done.
nodes.synopsis: Shadow mode runs candidate braking software live on working machines with brake commands disconnected, recording hypothetical interventions; replay and shadow mode are the cheapest large-volume validation methods, and the company already has a suitable fleet [f13467, f332, f333]. The booklet recommends starting warning-fleet logging immediately during October 2026–mid-2027 to obtain field-representative false-positive evidence before the prototype arrives, then using the four-month physical campaign to confirm predictions rather than tune the system [f1600, f1604, f1611]. Nuisance-rate evidence must use representative real operating hours, with warnings, sensor data and context logged and results broken down by site type and weather; simultaneous old/new recording supports paired comparisons, ideally against independent common ground truth [f6912, f1601, f5480, f5495]. Before enabling braking, hypothetical interventions should be reviewed with operators and safety engineers, and frequent operationally unacceptable events should trigger stopping or escalation; acceptance thresholds must come from the organization's own shadow data and vendors' documented switch-off conditions [f10729, f10951, f10952, f11281]. Shadow mode remains open-loop and cannot establish actual braking consequences, including loaded wet-decline stability, following-truck collisions, load shifts, operator resistance or actuator faults [f335, f336, f13471]. No publicly documented heavy-off-road shadow-mode validation programme or warning-data-to-braking certification case was found, and sensor-specific evidence makes the sensor decision a gate for much pre-prototype work [f588, f1253, f2006].

nodes.label: Proving ground, track test and whole-machine test
nodes.text: A proving ground is a closed, controlled area where the complete real machine, with its real sensors, is tested against physical targets; a track test is one such test, and a whole-machine test is any test in which nothing is simulated.
nodes.synopsis: Comparable heavy off-road braking functions historically took three to four years to validate, largely through physical testing and tuning for each machine model; off-road validation remains more physical than automotive practice, with immature test infrastructure [f282, f11919, f1243, f344]. The recommended approach retains physical testing but reserves proving-ground and field work for calibration, simulator qualification, coupled behavior and final high-risk cases, using real machines to confirm stopping, terrain and environmental effects [f4110, f7669, f551]. Physical targets provide an end-to-end reality anchor, but level-track success can conceal grade-related trigger errors, and staged-target track tests cannot measure nuisance braking, which requires real operations [f5345, f6350, f11767]. Physical tests also remain part of acceptance frameworks: ISO 17757:2019 uses physical braking and steering tests, while Euro NCAP’s 2026 virtual-testing protocol requires random physical verification and rejects a cluster dossier below a 75% verification-test pass threshold [f7734, f1216, f2513]. A program starting in October 2026 could realistically have a proving-ground kit working by mid-2027, but unexamined booking lead times, capacity and machine suitability create a planning gap; post-prototype work should correlate models, rerun trusted scenarios, confirm worst cases on track and run shadow mode [f68, f5120, f11342].

nodes.label: Soft target, robotic target and target platform (ISO 19206)
nodes.text: A soft target is a dummy of a person or vehicle that a machine can hit without damage, a robotic target or target platform is a low, self-driving carrier that moves the dummy along a programmed path, and ISO 19206 is the standard series that specifies such targets for road-vehicle testing.
aliases: Soft target, robotic target and target platform
nodes.synopsis: Robotic soft-target platforms are established in road AEB testing but are built for passenger-car speeds; Euro NCAP 2026–2028 uses ISO 19206 pedestrian and bicyclist targets, while UN R131 specifies an ISO 19206-2 child target crossing at 5 km/h [f345, f2546, f2547, f2522]. For heavy off-road validation, the recommendation is to transfer ISO 19206’s standardized-surrogate design principle rather than reuse road targets: surrogates must cover PPE-clad people, light vehicles beneath a haul truck’s nose, machines and fixed obstacles, with responses matched to each sensing modality [f2554, f2555, f2556]. Proving-ground tests provide strong complete-chain confirmation and accurate, repeatable geometry and timing references, but staged targets cannot establish statistical rates or broad coverage of weather, site objects and natural behaviour [f552, f5386, f5388, f953]. The booklet found neither an off-road ISO 19206-equivalent target standard nor publicly documented high-throughput robotic-target validation for heavy machines, and did not identify a site, chamber or target supplier handling 50–400 t machines at representative speeds; automation is therefore a candidate investment, not a proven shortcut [f15329, f566, f1166, f568]. Sensor selection should not be delayed because target realism depends on the selected sensors, and a visually convincing dummy can still have incorrect radar, lidar, ultrasonic or thermal characteristics [f570, f2912, f2913, f2914, f5389]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, physical-test procedures, a procured or adapted soft-target kit, ground-truth specifications and independent-test-body engagement are considered realistic by mid-2027, using an ACARP Tier 1 and Tier 2 style protocol [f851].

nodes.label: Correlation test
nodes.text: A correlation test is a physical test run specifically to check whether the models predicted what the real machine did, and by how much they were wrong.
nodes.synopsis: Physical correlation is the prerequisite for trusting virtual collision-mitigation results: models need stated validity domains, representative real-versus-simulated comparisons, correlation bounds and an approved virtual-test envelope before the full scenario matrix is rerun [f4339, f746, f747, f757]. On-road precedents exist, but the corpus reports no published quantitative off-road comparison of simulation-tuned braking thresholds with field results and no independent evidence that virtual or hardware-in-the-loop testing alone covers 100+ off-road site types and all relevant machines and environmental conditions [f153, f154, f5760]. Euro NCAP’s 2026 protocol, version 1.00 dated March 2025, requires physical correlation before prediction submission and random physical verification; at least 75% of verification tests per cluster must meet qualification criteria, although these are on-road requirements [f1215, f1454, f2627]. Planning recommendations distinguish early measurement campaigns on existing machines in 2026–2027 from prototype correlation after arrival in mid-2027, when tests should measure latency, detection range, brake timing, stopping dynamics, repeatability and model error for representative variants [f9375, f744]. Environmental correlation should cover adverse sensor conditions, including measured dust events and dynamic approaches at representative speeds; hardware and mounting must be frozen and correlated before claiming a validated sensor digital twin, and a 2027 sensor change invalidates substantial existing evidence [f5219, f10562, f10658, f11917, f11912]. Expensive integrated tools do not eliminate manufacturer-owned physical correlation, and the programme initially bears both simulation and physical-validation costs; its evidence should explicitly link virtual claims to paired physical tests and pre-declared acceptance bounds [f9318, f10511, f7472, f10207].

nodes.label: Regression testing and continuous integration (CI/CD) for simulation
nodes.text: Regression testing re-runs old tests after every software change to make sure that nothing which used to work now fails, and continuous integration is the automated factory that does this on every change.
nodes.synopsis: Continuous automated regression turns captured or synthesised scenarios into permanent tests that catch software-change failures, but neither automation nor millions of runs establishes that the test set represents the real operating domain [f1031, f1032, f671]. Regression must remain separate from failure-seeking discovery and frozen, pre-registered performance estimation; discovered failures should become permanent regression tests rather than estimation data [f133, f6665, f6946, f6949, f7137]. Simulation is intended to select informative physical tests and provide broad regression around physical anchors, with SIL supporting high-volume closed-loop testing, recorded-data replay supporting perception regression, and sensor stimulation supporting final sensor/ECU regression and timing tests [f484, f5266, f918, f4500]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, an executable SIL framework with dynamics and braking models, continuous regression and fault injection is considered realistic by mid-2027 if software interfaces can be defined; the reported under-a-day incremental validation precedent is a vendor claim for on-road Level 3 assistance [f840, f1307]. Reproducibility and change control require configuration/version traceability, frozen generation inputs, regression testing of simulator upgrades, and physical re-correlation after prototype changes [f5106, f13167, f8897, f11029]. Post-launch perception or braking updates need defined regression and revalidation rules, otherwise 2027 evidence could certify an obsolete configuration; an off-road case addressing post-release software and model updates was not found [f11251, f11252, f11254].

nodes.label: Test management, versioning and the traceability chain
nodes.text: Test management is the record-keeping that lets thousands of runs be planned, reproduced and traced from the hazard they address to the evidence they produce, and versioning gives every ingredient of a run a fixed identifier.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats traceability as essential to usable safety evidence: each run must connect hazard, safety and performance requirements, scenario, test case, result and safety-case evidence, with the exact software and models identifiable [f7105, f12202]. Run manifests should retain immutable identifiers, configuration and calibration versions, seeds, assets, metrics, verdicts and data checksums; configuration control extends to physical machine variants and the current site, not just software [f7108, f7109, f1141, f3831, f11072]. Credible models alone are insufficient: the toolchain must be qualified, controlled and reproducible, and changes must trigger impact analysis or revalidation rather than silently inherit obsolete evidence [f8227, f8048, f8229, f10232]. The G1 gate at the end of January 2027 requires one reproducible end-to-end scenario under configuration control and an unresolved-assumption report, while the plan must define sustainment and revalidation responsibilities after September 2027 [f10197, f10179]. Implementation remains a planning risk: ASAM TestSpecification was still developing infrastructure in October 2026, tool qualification and configuration management can become late blockers, and version drift is rated High risk despite no off-road case being found [f7119, f10351, f11066, f11067].

nodes.label: Cloud execution and compute budget
nodes.text: Cloud execution means renting computers by the hour from a data-center provider to run many simulations in parallel, and the compute budget is the money and machine-hours set aside for that.
nodes.synopsis: High-volume model-in-the-loop and software-in-the-loop testing targets thousands of runs per night on cloud or on-premises compute, with logic tests suited to commodity servers or containers and sensor tests assigned to GPU workers [f7138, f16220]. The illustrative budget buys ten single-GPU cloud instances running continuously for 122 days: about USD 54,490 for at most roughly 29,000 GPU-hours, limiting full-sensor-fidelity coverage and motivating tiered testing [f8869, f13548]. Cost per simulated hour depends on the measured real-time factor, so the example is not a quantified workload budget; the required compute remains unquantified and should be budgeted before mid-2027 [f13549, f14511]. Although compute is described as comparatively cheap relative to specialist labor, the skeptic's review flags compute and defect triage as potential bottlenecks, and recommends benchmarking preparation, correlation and triage before scaling infrastructure [f13550, f10789, f16235]. Parallel-execution licensing and intellectual-property rights also require explicit procurement attention: vendor cloud terms were not reviewed, export control and data residency were not researched, and technical access does not necessarily authorize cloud use [f8901, f8907, f8912, f8913, f10813].

nodes.label: Headless simulation versus rendered simulation
nodes.text: A headless simulation runs without drawing any picture, computing only the numbers a test needs, while a rendered simulation produces images or sensor views, which costs far more computing.
nodes.synopsis: Across Chapter 5 and the glossary, the four-month validation window makes tests per wall-clock hour more important than real-time rendering [f4350, f13559]. Headless simulation computes only required test quantities without pictures; object-list braking tests can represent the machine and worker as points and calculate stopping distance [f13555, f13556]. These runs use ordinary processors, run far faster than real time, and can scale across thousands of cheap processor cores, supporting the recommendation to run most of the millions of braking-logic combinations headless [f13557, f13561]. Rendering is needed when camera, lidar or radar models require scene views, but GPU ray tracing slows simulation toward real time or below [f13558]. The recommended allocation is therefore broad screening with lower-fidelity models and scarce high-fidelity rendered runs for perception-sensitive cases selected through correlation and sensitivity work; the facts provide no numerical split between these workloads [f13560, f13562].

nodes.label: Sim-to-real gap
nodes.text: The sim-to-real gap is the difference between what a system does in simulation and what it does in reality, caused by everything the models leave out or get wrong.
nodes.synopsis: Simulation shortens validation, but cannot certify perception alone: the cited on-road evidence documents gaps across sensor types, including radar at CVPR 2024, lidar studies from 2023–2025, and camera studies from 2023 and December 2025 [f326, f471, f327, f328, f329]. Transferring road-based braking validation to quarry terrain and articulated machines is a larger change than transferring passenger-car tests to heavy trucks; no standards-body or industry-group study of that transfer was found, and sim-to-field transfer of machine motion and tuned thresholds remains unproven [f1236, f1248, f6421, f6558]. Sensor and environment fidelity is judged the hardest uncertainty, with dust the biggest off-road gap; idealized sensors can look realistic at tracking level while having the highest raw-data gap, and lidar mismatch increases at high rain rates [f10424, f11949, f4480, f4610]. Recorded-scene reconstruction is also constrained: on-road neural re-simulation degrades at viewpoint offsets of 1–4 m, while quantitative off-road validation of generative re-weathering was not found [f5213, f3825]. Construction and mining evidence from 2023–2026 supports synthetic data as augmentation rather than replacement for real data, including synthetic-only detection gaps and photometric divergence despite extensive domain randomization [f6686, f10580, f10581, f10584]. Planning should retain critical physical camera correlation and ongoing in-service feedback: the booklet calls monitoring the only route to close dust and glare model gaps over time, and warns that good virtual metrics can conceal field failures clustered by rain, dust, night or glare [f1737, f8053, f12455].

nodes.label: Domain randomization
nodes.text: Domain randomization deliberately varies the appearance and conditions of simulated scenes at random (lighting, colors, textures, object positions) so that software trained or tested on them does not depend on details that will differ in reality.
nodes.synopsis: Domain randomization varies simulated appearance and scene conditions to reduce dependence on details that differ in reality; the booklet presents it as a way to improve machine-learning perception robustness, not as functional safety evidence [f13585, f13586, f13594]. A vendor-labelled 2026 overview describes Isaac Sim Replicator randomizing pose, scale, lighting and materials, while a 2022 construction study provides an excavator-pose estimation example [f3791, f4135, f13588]. Its benefits have limits: a 2026 study found that Unity-rendered construction scenes still diverged from real photometric distributions despite extensive randomization, and the glossary reports a persistent synthetic-only training gap while noting that mixing real and synthetic images helps [f10584, f13590, f13589]. Randomized appearance does not establish correct radar physics or braking distance, and no peer-reviewed demonstration was found that synthetic-only training or validation establishes collision-avoidance reliability for heavy off-road machines [f13592, f13591]. Randomized simulation runs must freeze their random seeds for reproducibility [f13593].

nodes.label: "Do not make one simulator carry every test" (multi-simulator architecture)
nodes.text: This is the booklet's recommendation to spread the test program across several levels of simulation fidelity and several tools, each used for the questions it answers well, instead of running every case in one maximum-fidelity simulator.
aliases: "Do not make one simulator carry every test"
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends a multi-fidelity, multi-tool architecture at every cost level rather than one universal simulator, because the market survey found no single tool with public evidence covering earth-moving automatic braking across many sites and all-weather sensing [f4968, f9321, f13071]. A four-month window, GPU-hour limits and coverage spanning 100-plus sites, 10-plus scenarios, weather and machine variants constrain full-fidelity testing; high-fidelity soil simulation runs 50–200 times slower than real time [f13548, f13606, f13605]. The proposed ladder combines millions of fast functional tests, medium-fidelity closed-loop regression, selected high-fidelity perception and soil cases, HIL for timing and interfaces, and targeted physical tests for correlation and final evidence [f9322, f9323, f9324, f9325, f9326, f9327]. Perception simulation should remain separate from braking simulation while supplying detection-delay, range and error distributions; machine-family braking models should likewise range from fast threshold models to selected high-fidelity edge cases [f6410, f13840]. Fidelity allocation must follow sensitivity and correlation work, with learned models used where held-out real-data evidence exists [f9328, f4971]. Modular tool chains require substantial integration work, which open standards reduce but do not eliminate; integrated suites reduce interfaces and support burden, and no independent evidence establishes a universal winner between integrated and modular architectures [f13240, f13609, f9359].

nodes.label: Mass, payload and gross vehicle weight (GVWR)
nodes.text: Mass is how much matter a machine contains, payload is the load it carries, and the gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) is the maximum total of machine plus load that the manufacturer allows.
aliases: Mass, payload and gross vehicle weight
nodes.synopsis: Mass and payload are central to off-road braking validation: grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to the deceleration itself, while real machines face finite brake torque, thermal limits, load-induced balance changes and deformable ground—even though mass cancels in a friction-limited point-mass model [f145, f5900, f5887, f5888]. The recommended control policy limits commanded deceleration by stability, brake capacity and payload, with a jerk limit; validation must cover laden and unladen stopping, grade stability and behavior after stopping [f152, f11890]. Existing published MOSH closed-loop tests require unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, leaving loaded and slope cases uncovered, whereas Queensland stopping assumptions require fully laden vehicles and the worst relevant road, grade, tyre and brake-delay combination [f5564, f5565, f3403]. Physical validation should therefore test maximum payload and slopes, but the research identified no suitable facility or supplier for representative-speed testing of 50–400 t machines, and facility availability may independently constrain scheduling [f1610, f1166, f1167]. Transfer across machine families should use model-specific stopping curves by grade, load and surface, with validity records documenting mass and payload coverage; US FMVSS No. 127, limited to vehicles up to 4,536 kg GVWR, is an on-road reference rather than an applicable off-road requirement [f7017, f8005, f2831].

nodes.label: Speed, acceleration and deceleration
nodes.text: Speed is how fast something moves, acceleration is how quickly its speed increases, and deceleration is how quickly its speed decreases.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus recommends transferring collision-mitigation settings across machines through physics-based zones using speed, latency, braking deceleration, sensor pose and machine envelope, rather than copying constants [f138, f6681]. At 5–15 km/h, latency can account for half or more of stopping distance; an engineering example adds 22.2 m before braking for a two-second combined operator and mechanical delay at 40 km/h, but this is not a measured reaction time or collision-speed distribution [f144, f5898, f3220]. Grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to deceleration itself, so validation must include machine-state factors and cannot establish avoidance with incorrect simulated terrain-dependent deceleration and pitch [f145, f5900, f5819, f3972]. Vendor operating envelopes are narrow: Volvo CE's January 2023 system operates only in reverse at 3–15 km/h and brakes for 2–3 seconds, while Komatsu's stop function acts only at slow travel speeds or the start of motion; the cited Freightliner tests also show that higher-speed success does not imply lower-speed success [f1238, f10439, f1330]. Detection range must support stopping at the operating speed: dust may require slower driving, lidar positioning error increased by up to 27% with speed in one study, and fidelity for real mining dust remains uncertain [f11330, f4705, f5064].
