Planning gaps include the absence of an identified collision-speed distribution and an identified test facility or target supplier capable of handling 50–400 t machines at representative speeds; validity records should explicitly bound speed, acceleration, deceleration, brake timing and friction [f3216, f1166, f8010].

nodes.label: Stopping distance
nodes.text: Stopping distance is how far a machine travels from the moment a stop becomes necessary until it stands still.
nodes.synopsis: Latency is a first-order stopping-distance contributor: at 5–15 km/h it can account for half or more of the distance, motivating a calibrated point-mass model with measured latency, brake build-up lag and worst-case deceleration dependent on grade, payload and surface [f144, f146]. ISO 21815-3:2023 frames collision-avoidance distance around detection, decision and action time, machine stopping distance and a safety distance; inadequate detection range in dust requires slower driving or prevents a promise to stop [f6680, f11330]. Real-machine and proving-ground tests are recommended as anchors for actual stopping behaviour, while validation should cover the full causal timing chain rather than minimum stopping distance alone [f551, f5345, f7786]. Published validation of simulated heavy-machine braking on gravel, mud, ice or slopes was not found, nor was an off-road automatic-braking stopping-distance tolerance; the broader terramechanics review also found no adequate validation across 100+ site types, but did not review Project Chrono validation literature [f253, f7808, f10611]. Coverage and acceptance remain limited: the reported mining stopping tests covered only unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, South Africa's Regulation 8.10 specifies no fixed stopping-distance test, and ISO's example stopping calculations are not a validation method [f5182, f2281, f7729].

nodes.label: Brake dead time and brake build-up time
nodes.text: Brake dead time is the pause between the brake command and the first braking effect, and build-up time is the further period until the brakes reach their full force.
nodes.synopsis: Brake dead time runs from brake command to the first braking effect, while build-up time continues until full braking force; ISO 3450 stopping distance includes both but excludes operator reaction time [f13664, f13674, f5976]. At 5–15 km/h, latency can account for half or more of stopping distance, and a half-second error in assumed dead time causes about 2 m of stopping-distance error at 15 km/h [f5898, f13682]. Published architecture-specific examples include under 0.3 s for a 2026 tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake, 0.41 s for a 2025 mining electric vehicle brake-by-wire system, and historic retarder lags of 1–2 s; MSHA instead prescribes weight-class response assumptions of 0.5–2.5 s plus one second of operator time [f5893, f5894, f5897, f6053, f6058]. Queensland's two-second, 22.2 m delay example at 40 km/h combines operator reaction and mechanical delay, so it is not a measured automatic-brake response [f3220]. Modern production-loader, articulated-hauler and haul-truck delay distributions were not found, so prototype testing should measure the automated braking path before large scenario sweeps and characterize timing variability as well as average delay [f13683, f13684, f12573, f13678, f13680]. The recommended core is a calibrated point-mass stopping model with measured latency, build-up lag and worst-case deceleration by grade, payload and surface, validated against the full detection-to-position timing chain rather than minimum stopping distance alone [f146, f7786].

nodes.label: End-to-end latency budget
nodes.text: The end-to-end latency budget is the list of every delay between an object appearing and the machine standing still, with a time allowance for each.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats latency as a first-order stopping-distance contributor: at 5–15 km/h it can account for half or more of stopping distance, and milliseconds in sensing, networking, decision and actuation change the stopping point [f144, f13659, f4346]. The reviewed 2022 DIS and ISO 21815-3:2023 distance structures include detection, determination and action, physical stopping and residual safety distance; a practical engineering model adds speed multiplied by detection, decision and actuation times to braking distance, machine-envelope offset and margin, but is not a verbatim ISO equation [f2419, f7007, f7010]. In the worked 40 t example at 15 km/h on a 10% downgrade with 1.0 s delay, stopping takes about 8.5 m and 1 m clearance raises minimum detection range to 9.5 m before sensor-error allowance; the US mining rule's assumed 2.0 s delay alone contributes 8.3 m at that speed [f13656, f13658]. Validation should timestamp a known object event through detection, confirmation, risk decision, brake request, interface receipt, actuator response and measurable deceleration, test the automated rather than merely pedal brake path, and include end-to-end integration latency when using the specified third-party J1939 interface [f6159, f6142, f8198]. When the prototype arrives in mid-2027, correlation measurements on representative variants should precede the full scenario matrix, establishing latency, detection range, brake-command timing, stopping dynamics, repeatability and model error [f744, f13512]. A coverage gap remains because the seven sensor questions omitted synchronization and latency, so realistic individual sensor values do not guarantee a working braking function; detector operating-point metrics also omit downstream braking logic and timing, while combined mining-document delays must not be interpreted as measured human reaction-time distributions [f5092, f6981, f3327].

nodes.label: Grade (slope) and its effect on braking
nodes.text: Grade is the steepness of the ground; going downhill reduces how hard a machine can slow down, and going uphill helps it.
nodes.synopsis: Grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to deceleration itself; in the New South Wales example, a 100 t rigid truck designed for a 20% grade and tested on 9% requires 1.79 m/s² deceleration, with about 1.04 m/s² attributable to grade correction alone [f145, f5900, f5901, f5902]. NIOSH reports retarder disadvantage at excessive speed on descents steeper than 9%, and a stopping model found combinations where downhill grade exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop [f3085, f5903]. Automatic braking can itself create instability and other secondary hazards on grades, supporting context-dependent intervention rather than a universal brake command; Komatsu documentation accessed in 2026 tells wheel-loader users to disable stop control on steep slopes and in several other hazardous operating conditions [f1129, f1975, f10550]. Published validation of simulated heavy-machine stopping distances on slopes and difficult surfaces was not found, while the cited MOSH closed-loop testing is restricted to unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less and does not cover slope and loaded cases [f253, f3743, f3970, f5564, f5565]. The booklet therefore recommends retaining physical stopping tests across machine classes, load, slope and surface extremes, and documenting the grades and environmental ranges for which validation is valid rather than assuming a model conservative on dry soil remains conservative on an icy grade [f7881, f8009, f7965].

nodes.label: Surface and traction
nodes.text: Traction is the grip between a tire or track and the ground, and on loose, wet or soft surfaces there is less of it, so braking is limited by the ground rather than by the brakes.
nodes.synopsis: Heavy off-road stopping depends on ground conditions as much as brakes, with grade, payload, tyre or track condition, brake temperature, hydraulic response and articulation changing stopping distance and the safe intervention point [f11374, f7452, f5818]. Transfer from road AEB remains unresolved: dry-asphalt assumptions and road-oriented standards do not establish validity for deformable surfaces or heavy machinery, and published validation of simulated heavy-machine braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes was not found [f2571, f7696, f11349, f253, f3970]. The 2019 Jimblebar collision involved an unloaded autonomous truck losing traction in bad weather; unintended full braking can also be hazardous, and Komatsu documentation accessed in 2026 advises disabling loader stop control on steep slopes and slippery or soft ground [f1375, f2342, f10550]. Queensland guidance requires stopping assumptions to cover worst relevant combinations of wet or slippery roads, downhill grade, maximum speed, full load, poor tyres and brake delay, rather than a single proving-ground surface [f3403, f2901]. The recommended validation approach retains physical stopping tests across machine, load, slope and surface extremes, bounds dynamics models with those results, and reserves high-fidelity soil simulation for traction-sensitive cases; a proposed stopping-distance matrix covers two machine families across three surfaces and grades [f7881, f10612, f9325, f10940].

nodes.label: Wheels versus tracks
nodes.text: Wheeled machines roll on rubber tires, tracked or crawler machines run on steel or rubber belts, and the two grip, steer and stop differently.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet uses wheeled versus crawler as the first discriminator for machine families with separate braking models, because their physics, brake standards and test methods differ; machine types and brake systems were not yet confirmed during the research [f13733, f5864]. ISO 3450:2011, confirmed in 2022, covers wheeled earth-moving machines and rubber-tracked machines with top speeds of at least 20 km/h, while ISO 10265:2008 covers crawlers at 20 km/h or less; the stated scopes therefore meet at exactly 20 km/h [f15190, f5979]. Tracks retain more shear force than tires in soft soil, and crawler modeling must account for distributed ground contact, sinkage, differential track speed, skid steering and counter-rotation; collisions can occur without longitudinal closing speed [f6007, f6023, f6024, f6218]. No universal safe deceleration was found across machine types, loads and slopes, so the proposed operating-domain taxonomy includes surface conditions, grade, cross-slope, tire or track state and payload [f6310, f6724]. A published 2026 tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake response is under 0.3 seconds, and a single-machine hydraulic model reported pressure accuracy above 96% and response-time accuracy above 95%; these results are architecture-specific and do not establish temperature or wear effects [f5893, f13668, f6438, f13816]. Virtual validation has supporting tools and calibration examples: Chrono models wheeled and tracked vehicles on deformable terrain, while TERA compared track deformation and terrain-dependent velocity against a real excavator, with a December 2024 preprint and SIMPAR 2025 publication [f9333, f4130].

nodes.label: Articulated steering
nodes.text: Articulated steering turns a machine by bending it at a hinge between its front and rear halves, which suits rough ground but makes the machine swing and pitch when it brakes.
nodes.synopsis: Articulated machines cannot always be represented as straight point masses: braking while turning, on cross-slopes or at large articulation angles introduces yaw, roll, load-transfer and hinge dynamics that limit usable deceleration and warrant multibody modelling [f6028, f6030, f6077]. Automatic braking can itself create instability and secondary hazards, so commanded deceleration should be capped by articulation and roll state, with safe limits derived per machine family and physically tested across steering, cross-slope and payload conditions [f5941, f13742, f13770]. Validation should include load, slope and articulation in closed-loop SIL/HIL models, and express detection range relative to machine swept envelopes rather than sensor origins; changes in articulation or sensor placement can invalidate prior correlation [f5557, f5501, f1997]. Draft ISO/PRF 21815-5 covers articulation and other non-longitudinal motions; it was at proof stage in September 2026, with publication planned for November 2026 [f1136, f2176, f6747]. Tools offer articulated-machine capabilities, but accurate prediction of combined environmental and machine-motion effects remains uncertain, articulated-braking evidence is mostly academic and scaled, and published automatic-braking jackknife or roll-event data were not found [f8301, f8599, f9343, f6031, f6037].

nodes.label: Hydrostatic drive, retarder and service brake
nodes.text: Heavy machines slow down in three ways: with friction brakes (the service brake), with a retarder that uses the drivetrain to hold speed on long descents, and on many machines with a hydrostatic drive that brakes by itself when the operator eases off.
nodes.synopsis: Heavy machines combine service brakes, drivetrain retarders and, on many machines, hydrostatic slowing; deployed intervention approaches differ, ranging from Toyota SEnS+ power shutoff to Liebherr hydrostatic stopping and Hexagon retarder/service-brake intervention [f13744, f1407, f1648, f1663]. Retarder deceleration is power-limited, declining with speed and mass and further reduced downhill; historic haul-truck studies reported 1–2 seconds of lag, but these are not valid design constants for a 2027 system [f5994, f5897, f6063]. Braking models should represent state-dependent actuator blending and hydrostatic capacity rather than a constant or single pedal-to-torque gain, because ignoring hydrostatic slowing can trigger collision intervention too early or too late [f6048, f6049, f6050, f6145]. ISO 3450 separates service, secondary and parking functions, and hydrostatic slowing cannot substitute for parking braking; meanwhile, no US federal construction or mining rule requiring automatic service-brake intervention after an ignored warning was found [f13746, f6544, f2247]. Higher-fidelity modeling is targeted at hydraulics and latency, articulated/high-center-of-gravity stability, hydrostatic capacity and deformable ground, but modern production brake-delay distributions and recent hydrostatic modeling evidence remain gaps [f5906, f6551, f6446].

nodes.label: Load shift and stability
nodes.text: Stability is a machine's resistance to tipping, sliding or losing control, and hard braking is itself a hazard because it throws the load forward and can push the machine past its limits.
nodes.synopsis: Automatic braking can itself destabilize heavy off-road machines through load shift, rollover, sliding, articulation effects and secondary collisions, particularly on slopes, with elevated or suspended loads, or during manoeuvres [f117, f5814, f5941]. Komatsu requires KomVision to be off during trailer loading; its wheel-loader guidance also calls for disabling stop control on slopes, slippery or soft ground and with suspended loads, on an undated page accessed in 2026 [f1646, f10550]. The booklet’s published position is to cap commanded deceleration at the minimum of collision-avoidance need, traction, stability, machine braking capability and load limits, while limiting jerk to reduce operator jolts and load shift [f11888, f13638]. Validation therefore needs loading and implement-position coverage, controllability outcomes beyond stopping distance, and richer models where articulation, high centres of gravity or deformable terrain matter [f3400, f6149, f6075, f6077]. These hazards are mechanically credible, but quantified off-road load-shift incidents and direct evidence of automatic-braking-induced rollover or slope instability were not found; shadow mode cannot establish actual stopping stability or load movement [f3397, f3405, f595, f597].

nodes.label: Vehicle dynamics model
nodes.text: A vehicle dynamics model is a set of equations that predicts how a machine moves, slows, turns, leans and pitches in response to brake, drive and steering inputs.
nodes.synopsis: A program starting in October 2026 can realistically have a parameterized machine-and-brake model working by mid-2027; an executable SIL regression framework on that schedule is conditional on defining software interfaces [f67, f840]. Off-road braking follows the same underlying physics as road braking, but machine dynamics, ground interaction and brake response do not transfer automatically from road vehicles or between machine families [f5886, f1731, f10430]. Models must account for payload, articulation, terrain interaction, brake capability and latency, while ground-induced changes in machine attitude also change sensor pose; even perfect sensor simulation cannot compensate for incorrect braking dynamics [f3971, f3959, f5089]. SIL and modeled-machine HIL cannot establish true machine behavior, while VIL can demonstrate real braking and delays but may omit soft soil, grades and other important conditions; physical stopping tests should therefore bound models for each machine family and surface class [f926, f5287, f5333, f5336, f10612]. The recommended approach layers fast threshold, stability and selective high-fidelity models, with separate validation and uncertainty reporting: greater complexity is not automatically greater credibility, as a 2026 on-road round robin reported spreads of 0.033 s and 0.314 m for more complex models, and NIOSH's 2018 stopping model still required validation [f13060, f10617, f5907, f5949].

nodes.label: Tire model and tire-soil interaction
nodes.text: A tire model is a formula or table that gives the forward, braking and sideways force a tire produces for a given load, slip and surface; tire-soil interaction is the harder case where the ground deforms under the tire.
nodes.synopsis: Tire–ground behavior is a critical limit on virtual braking validation: simulation alone cannot establish real behavior without correlation, and nonlinear ground shear invalidates the simple assumption that heavy and light machines stop in the same distance [f911, f5954, f5957]. Full-vehicle models require tire parameters fitted for unpaved ground, with the glossary recommending real-machine tests rather than road-car values and a low-speed friction matrix covering hard, loose and wet conditions for each machine family [f6452, f13787, f13789]. Evidence remains narrow: MAVS has validated tire–soil models for sand and clay, and some single-wheel studies report force errors under 10%, but tuning varies with slip angle and the skeptic’s review found no evidence establishing terramechanics fidelity for braking prediction [f3965, f6098, f6099, f11189]. A 2024 AGX wheel-loader digging model needed a friction coefficient of 2.0 to match measurements, characterized as physically implausible in the glossary, with remaining errors attributed to tire-pressure modeling and a flat-ground assumption [f6090, f13775, f6091]. Tool compatibility and computational cost constrain higher-detail modeling: Chrono developers say Pacejka, TMeasy and Fiala handling models do not work with deformable terrain, while one 2024 study adopted rigid tires because deformable tires combined with deformable soil produced unrealistic training times [f8498, f3964]. The recommended role for high-detail DEM or deformable-terrain simulation is to investigate stopping-distance sensitivity to soil, slope, payload and tire or track interaction, not to assume that tool coupling establishes valid physics [f8602, f8725].

nodes.label: Terramechanics (SCM, DEM, SPH, CRM, FEM)
nodes.text: Terramechanics is the science of how wheels and tracks interact with soil, and SCM, DEM, SPH, CRM and FEM are five ways of computing that interaction, from a fast approximate formula to very slow grain-by-grain simulation.
nodes.synopsis: Off-road braking depends on soil-mediated shear, sinkage, rolling resistance, slip and directional response; a ground model may therefore need friction, cohesion, compaction, rutting, moisture and roughness rather than merely visual terrain [f6005, f3960, f4300]. Some single-wheel semi-empirical studies report force errors below 10%, but the cited 2023 tuning varies with slip angle, and the validation evidence is limited to single-wheel rigs and sand rather than full machines [f6462, f6466, f6012]. The booklet found no published terramechanics validation adequate for braking-distance prediction across 100+ site types, but explicitly notes that Project Chrono validation literature was not reviewed; documented simulator capabilities do not establish machine-specific emergency-stopping accuracy [f10611, f6016]. Higher-fidelity CRM terrain reportedly runs 50–200 times slower than real time and requires an NVIDIA GPU, while uncertain soil inputs can overwhelm model fidelity; no evidence was found that DEM, SPH or FEM is required for automatic-braking threshold prediction across production machines [f8499, f8500, f6104, f6102]. The recommended approach is physical low-speed testing across hard, loose and wet surfaces for each machine family, conservative deceleration envelopes where transferable, and richer offline or detailed soil models only where necessary, retaining physical brake tests to address machine-ground uncertainty [f13724, f6151, f6075, f10613].

nodes.label: Brake model and powertrain model
nodes.text: A brake model predicts how much braking force arrives, and how quickly, after a command; a powertrain model predicts how the engine, transmission and drive add to or fight that braking.
nodes.synopsis: A program starting in October 2026 can realistically have a parameterized machine-and-brake model and executable SIL regression framework by mid-2027, provided software interfaces can be defined; the under-four-month product-validation window is distinct from brake-model validation [f67, f840, f12208]. Off-road braking follows the same underlying physics as road braking but differs in magnitude and dominant influences, including payload, grades, deformable ground, thermal limits and drivetrain braking; published brake-response latencies span 0.3–2.5 seconds [f5886, f5888, f239]. Machine types and brake systems remain unconfirmed, and models do not transfer automatically across machine families; articulated steering, moving payloads and deformable surfaces require more than a simple braking model [f5863, f10430, f5885]. SIL and data-injection HIL cannot establish actual brake-chain behavior when that chain is modeled, so safety evidence requires real-machine anchoring, with VIL or proving-ground stops for each machine braking class and measurement of both brake requests and physical responses [f531, f5287, f770, f5558, f5640]. Brake-plant capability remains subject to ISO 3450 where applicable, but no published off-road automatic-braking stopping-distance model tolerance was found; small simulated clearance margins are not robust when comparable to geometry, friction, timing and brake-model uncertainties [f2340, f7808, f4343].

nodes.label: Model fidelity levels for braking
nodes.text: Model fidelity is how much physical detail a model includes; for braking, the levels run from a lookup table or single formula, through a point-mass model with measured delays, to a full multibody simulation with soil.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends layered braking models per machine family: a calibrated point-mass core with measured latency, brake build-up lag and conservative deceleration by grade, payload and surface, supplemented by stability challenges and selected high-fidelity edge cases rather than one ultimate digital twin [f146, f13840]. Higher fidelity is justified for brake hydraulics and latency spread, articulated or high-center-of-gravity stability, state-dependent hydrostatic braking, and soft or deformable ground [f5906]. The runtime trigger should remain small, identifiable and conservative, while richer offline models challenge its safety assumptions; the selection rule is the lowest fidelity that predicts every safety-relevant output within a validated uncertainty envelope [f6074, f6075, f13837]. Complexity is not an accuracy guarantee: in a 2026 on-road round robin, point-mass implementations reproduced the prescribed profile exactly, while more complex models produced spreads of 0.033 s and 0.314 m [f5907, f5908]. No universal off-road prediction error is supplied for any fidelity level, and evidence of heavy-machine braking-distance fidelity on loose and wet surfaces was not found, so each level must be checked against the program’s own physical tests [f13842, f4307, f13843]. Detailed terrain simulations are too costly for exhaustive sweeps and can be dominated by uncertain soil inputs; the proposed alternative is to learn soil effects with richer models, fit simpler models for regression testing, confirm their envelope physically, and avoid surrogate extrapolation outside the trained domain [f6103, f6104, f15994, f6106].

nodes.label: Physical tests needed to build and check a braking model
nodes.text: These are the measurements on a real machine that give a braking model its numbers (calibration) and then show whether its predictions hold on cases it has not seen (validation).
nodes.synopsis: Virtual stopping models need real-machine anchors before carrying safety evidence: SIL and operator simulators cannot prove actual brake hardware, and ISO 3450 requires physical brake-performance testing [f770, f5270, f13412, f10431]. Testing should cover machine-specific dynamics, adverse braking configurations, maximum payload where required, slopes and surface extremes, with physical anchors for materially different dynamics architectures [f5559, f5967, f5968, f1610, f7881, f11019]. The booklet recommends measuring braking and sensor behavior on existing machines in 2026–2027 before prototype arrival, then using prototype tests for correlation, parameter identification and independent falsification rather than repeating every virtual scenario; a proposed pilot pre-specifies 10–30 physical test points [f9375, f774, f6137, f9917]. Brake identification must exercise the automated rather than merely pedal-operated path, characterize response dynamics, and measure the end-to-end latency chain; the recommended early latency sweep includes at least 10 repetitions across oil temperatures per machine family [f6142, f13679, f13697, f13699, f13685]. Published modern brake-response figures and full-machine stopping distances on wet clay or loose gravel were not found, while cited terrain findings came from single-wheel rigs and sand, leaving machine-ground behavior to be bounded through physical testing [f12565, f6018, f6012, f10612]. Simulation can narrow physical cases, but family models still need envelope-corner validation, and new variants require a reduced physical check after demonstrating that they lie inside the validated parameter hull [f772, f7916, f7917].

nodes.label: Decision logic (when to warn, when to brake)
nodes.text: Decision logic is the set of rules inside the system that turns "there is an object over there" into "do nothing", "warn the operator" or "apply the brakes".
nodes.synopsis: Decision-logic validation must establish when automatic braking should occur and cover the full chain from environment and sensing through warnings, operator opportunity, intervention, machine dynamics and collision outcome; the existing warning product's field history has never exercised that complete braking chain [f28, f11638, f7946]. The corpus favors stopping-distance and risk-zone intervention over a fixed time-to-collision threshold, which is weak at work-site speeds and gives no answer for a stationary machine starting up; ISO 21815-3:2023 places intervention at collision-risk level 4 or above [f149, f5917, f5921, f5912]. Intervention must reflect machine physics: a 2015 on-road simulation's grade-blind trigger worked at 0% grade but produced collisions at 11% and 17%, while the published earth-moving-machine position limits deceleration by avoidance need, stability, brake capacity and payload, with a jerk limit [f5904, f152]. Context matters: logic must avoid emergency braking for every nearby object during loading without suppressing the entire loading zone, and the same algorithm can produce different safety results under different site traffic and pedestrian controls [f3346, f3347, f804]. Semantic replay can isolate decision thresholds and brake-request logic, and hardware-in-the-loop can test production timing and control behavior, but replay alone cannot establish changed braking decisions' closed-loop consequences; detector tuning therefore requires closed-loop stopping-margin and unnecessary-intervention evaluation [f5256, f5283, f919, f6982]. Human-automation interaction remains safety-critical: the NTSB's 2019 report on the 18 March 2018 Uber crash found that the design precluded emergency braking in the relevant condition and relied on operator intervention, and found that one-second action suppression delayed planned braking [f10870, f10695, f10871].

nodes.label: Time to collision (TTC), time headway and trigger distance
nodes.text: Time to collision is how many seconds remain before two things meet if nothing changes, time headway is how many seconds the machine needs to reach the spot an object occupies now, and trigger distance is the range at which the system must act.
nodes.synopsis: Across the synthesis, machine-motion chapter and glossary, a fixed TTC threshold is judged a weak primary brake trigger at work-site speeds; ISO 21815-3:2023 instead uses stopping-distance and risk-zone logic, retaining TTC as an input or secondary layer for faster haul traffic [f148, f6202, f13894]. TTC becomes huge or unstable near zero closing speed, is undefined for a stationary machine starting up, and can miss articulation or track counter-rotation hazards; however, no head-to-head off-road comparison of distance-and-zone logic against TTC alone was found [f6214, f6219, f6218, f6224]. The proposed trigger distance combines detection/confirmation distance, travel during machine-action delay, stopping distance and safety clearance; braking zones must cover that distance, warning zones must add operator-reaction travel, and cited reaction assumptions range from 0.5–2.5 s [f13891, f13901, f13895]. Road benchmarks include the 2024 NHTSA NCAP setup with 12–40 m headways and 0.3–0.5 g target deceleration, while a 2026 simulation round robin used a 1.0 s TTC trigger explicitly as a research definition, not an earth-moving threshold [f2630, f6194]. No standard or peer-reviewed study supplies tuned off-road TTC or deceleration values, so program-specific models and tests must establish them; validation also needs recorded machine and actuator state to reconstruct TTC, zone entry and braking [f13885, f5663].

nodes.label: Zones (warning zone, braking zone, detection zone)
nodes.text: Zones are areas drawn around the machine in which the system reacts in a particular way: it must see objects anywhere in the detection zone, it warns when one enters the warning zone, and it brakes when one enters the braking zone.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21815-3:2023 defines forward and reverse risk areas using a stopping-distance framework, incorporating detection, determination, action, stopping and residual safe distance rather than time to collision alone [f2058, f5911, f6202]. The corpus recommends scaling zones with machine physics and geometry—not copied distance constants—and validating forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing separately; the cross-model transfer method is explicitly identified as expert opinion with independent supporting studies [f6681, f2996, f6770]. Field evidence reinforces the need for calibration: nine NIOSH underground tests found average between-site stop-zone differences of 4.7 ft (1.4 m), reaching 11.7 ft (3.6 m), while Wabtec's December 2021 integration still used physical testing to adjust detection zones [f5929, f1247]. Old-versus-new comparisons should use common ground truth and a common physical hazard zone, while the reviewed 2022 ISO draft recommends detection coverage at least as large as the collision-risk area and requires smaller coverage to be disclosed as a limitation [f5210, f5479, f2423, f2424]. Operational acceptance remains a design tension: proposed 3 ft stopping and 5 ft warning distances were not adopted in the US rule, fixed gaps can prevent loading, and nuisance interventions can encourage bypass or tag removal, yet suppressing an entire loading zone can leave unexpected entrants unprotected [f2241, f3344, f11764, f3347].

nodes.label: Thresholds and filters
nodes.text: Thresholds are the numbers at which the system changes its behavior, and filters are the rules that stop it from reacting to a single noisy measurement.
nodes.synopsis: Virtual validation must support tuning automatic-braking thresholds before field tests; SIL can exercise decision logic at scale, and object-list replay can test thresholds and brake requests independently of sensor modality [f29, f925, f528, f5256]. Simulation-tuned thresholds have been checked against field results on-road, but no published quantitative off-road comparison was found, leaving transfer to off-road operation unknown [f153, f6374, f6558]. A fixed time-to-collision threshold is considered a weak primary trigger at work-site speeds: the booklet favors distance and risk zones, while ISO 21815-3:2023 leaves machine-specific numbers to manufacturers and integrators, and neither generally tuned off-road TTC/deceleration values nor a reliable cross-product terrain-friction table was found [f13894, f6203, f5916, f6017]. Threshold selection must balance misses against nuisance interventions and task constraints; existing fleet false-alarm history is identified as the best available calibration evidence, but how warning-system tuning should carry over to automatic braking was not examined [f11305, f6569, f11519, f1168, f1170]. Tuning variables include confidence, speed-dependent zones, N-of-M track confirmation, persistence, debounce and filter constants; DOE with response surfaces suits a handful of continuous settings, whereas ROC/DET/precision-recall selection addresses only the detector threshold, not closed-loop timing and braking [f6957, f7297, f12851]. Validation must cover configurable parameters and integrator changes: modifying a threshold after inspecting audit failures contaminates the audit set, safety-relevant late threshold changes require fresh independent statistical confirmation, and ISO 16001 allows at most 300 ms detection time with an uninterrupted signal sequence [f2927, f6952, f7389, f13914].

nodes.label: Staged interventions in the decision logic
nodes.text: Staged intervention means the system escalates step by step, from information to warning to slowing to partial braking to maximum safe braking and, for a stationary machine, to refusing to move, rather than jumping straight to a full stop.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet proposes staged intervention rather than an immediate full stop: information and warning progress to slowing, partial braking and maximum safe braking, with motion inhibit for a stationary machine whose projected path is obstructed [f13925, f6255]. Escalation gives the operator a chance to respond: sufficient operator deceleration stops the escalation, while shrinking stopping margin drives further intervention; transition to maximum braking should use remaining stopping margin and its uncertainty, not range alone [f13926, f13880, f11713, f6280]. Maximum safe braking is reserved for otherwise unavoidable collisions and remains constrained by stability and control limits; automatic slowing can be inadequate downhill, drivetrain response varies, and partial braking can conflict with following machines [f6268, f6262, f6263, f6267]. ISO 21815-3:2023 places intervention at collision-risk level 4 or above and permits prior warning, while South African law specifies detect, warn, retard to safe speed, then brake; ISO 21815-1 excludes automatic steering [f6201, f13939, f13936]. Mine leaders preferred slowing to a crawl before setting the brake, but accident data alone cannot establish whether full braking, staging, speed reduction or propulsion inhibit is appropriate for a particular machine and conditions [f3028, f3406]. Much of the relatively simple warn-then-brake logic can be designed and checked at model-in-the-loop level in late 2026 before sensor selection, with stage-specific acceptance tolerances and virtual tuning informed by measured brake delays and deceleration maps [f13332, f13942, f14054].

nodes.label: Deceleration limits and how regulators specify them
nodes.text: A deceleration limit is a rule about how hard a machine must, or may, slow down, and regulators write such rules in several different and not directly comparable ways.
nodes.synopsis: The regulatory values are not directly comparable: UN R152 specifies commanded braking demand, ISO 3450 derives mean deceleration from stopping distance, MSHA assumes constant deceleration with separate response times, and New South Wales uses net deceleration on grade; pooled values therefore require conversion to a common definition [f13640, f13641]. NSW guidance proposes service/secondary-brake minima of 0.60/0.30 m/s² in service and 0.75/0.40 m/s² in type testing, with grade and mass corrections—not an adopted rule—whereas MSHA Table M-1 uses approximately 2.94 m/s² and MOSH emergency-stop targets are 1.9 m/s² above 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² otherwise [f13946, f5989, f5560]. On-road requirements include braking demands of at least 5.0 m/s² under UN R152 and 4 m/s² under UN R131; the November 2024 FMVSS 127 amendment instead addresses false activation relative to manual braking, using a 0.25 g peak-deceleration threshold [f5993, f2520, f2617]. Although the synthesis says no universal maximum automatic deceleration exists, the more qualified finding is that no published universal safe maximum or tuned off-road deceleration values were found; South Africa Regulation 8.10 also prescribes no deceleration curve [f151, f13769, f5916, f2442]. The recommended approach is machine-family-specific limits: command the minimum of collision-avoidance need, traction, stability, brake capability and load limits, with a jerk limit, and derive stability caps through layered models and physical tests involving steering or articulation, cross-slope and relevant payloads [f11888, f152, f13840, f13770].

nodes.label: Operator-already-reacting detection
nodes.text: This is the part of the logic that notices the operator is already braking or steering away, so the machine does not brake on top of a person who is handling the situation.
nodes.synopsis: Operator-already-reacting detection avoids adding automatic braking when the operator is already stopping or steering safely away; unnecessary braking can jolt a loaded machine and shift its load [f13960, f13961]. ISO 21815-3:2023 forbids overriding stronger operator braking, while UN R131 and R152 allow conscious driver actions to interrupt automatic braking; these override provisions do not establish validated off-road reaction-detection logic [f5913, f5943, f13971]. The recommended production approach fuses operator commands with machine response, crediting sufficient achieved deceleration or a demonstrably safer evasive trajectory rather than control movement alone [f13967, f13968, f6336, f6342]. Throttle release is particularly weak evidence because a downhill machine can still accelerate, and standing down after a startled operator briefly touches a control can collapse the stopping margin [f13970, f13969]. No off-road validation was found, so the program should define the reaction state machine before hardware arrives and test it in operator-in-the-loop and physical trials [f6332, f13972]. The architecture guidance is not fully aligned: Chapter 8 calls suppression a secondary layer at a_measured ≥ a_required, whereas the glossary calls it a third layer and recommends an additional deceleration margin [f6402, f13884, f13968].

nodes.label: Nuisance braking from the decision side
nodes.text: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, and "from the decision side" means the cases where the sensors saw something real but the logic should have known not to brake.
nodes.synopsis: Decision-side nuisance braking occurs when sensors detect a real object but the logic incorrectly treats it as a collision; relevant operating situations include loading near piles, berm contact, spotters, and tight-clearance maneuvers [f13973, f13974, f13975]. The booklet identifies nuisance interventions as the main documented field failure of deployed proximity systems and the main reason operators disable them, but suppressing all interventions in loading zones or repeated berm alarms would also conceal genuine hazards [f13982, f13980, f13981]. Context-aware approaches include Volvo’s remembered-slope logic and University of Pretoria’s 2024 steering-trajectory research, although the latter’s initial results are simulation-only [f1384, f6331]. Validation should include dedicated benign-but-dangerous-looking scenarios, drawing on road false-activation tests; millions of benign interactions may occur per imminent collision, making absence of hazardous braking harder to establish than a few successful stops [f1992, f15415, f1994, f1993]. Tuning should minimize nuisance subject to hard safety constraints rather than pursue zero false brakes: evidence for the optimum off-road trade-off is thin, no off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found, and the program must derive its acceptance threshold from shadow-mode data before enabling braking [f7312, f7460, f6570, f13984, f13985, f14058].

nodes.label: Required detection range
nodes.text: The required detection range is how far the sensors must reliably see, worked out backwards from how far the machine needs to stop plus a safety margin.
nodes.synopsis: Required detection range is reliable sensing distance calculated backwards from stopping distance, all detection/decision/actuation delays, clearance and sensor error; it varies with speed, grade, load, surface and delay and must be achieved in every approved operating condition [f13987, f13993]. ISO 21815-3:2023 structures avoidance distance around detection, determination and action, stopping and a safety distance, while the booklet's engineering equation adds a machine-envelope offset and is explicitly not a verbatim ISO equation [f7007, f7010]. MOSH specifies a minimum 200 m surface-machine detection range, whereas US surface-coal rules require enough sensing range for an endangered person to escape without specifying metres; a separate 40 t example at 15 km/h on a 10% downgrade requires at least 9.5 m before sensor-error allowance, not a replacement for those regulatory requirements [f13995, f2622, f13656]. If degraded sensing falls below the required stopping range, braking models cannot restore the lost margin, so speed may need limiting; weather-aware sensor models should therefore feed detection delay, range and error into braking simulation [f6585, f11330, f6487]. Prototype correlation tests should precede the scenario matrix when the prototype arrives in mid-2027, and a sensor change in 2027 would invalidate detection-range evidence and sensor correlation; the claimed coverage of “100+ job-site types” remains unsupported without a taxonomy connecting sites to sensing and stopping variables [f744, f11912, f8214].

nodes.label: Residual safe distance
nodes.text: Residual safe distance is the gap deliberately left between the stopped machine and the object, so that a stop is a near miss and not a light touch.
nodes.synopsis: Residual safe distance is an explicit part of the stopping budget: ISO 21815-3:2023 includes detection, determination, action, machine stopping and final safe clearance; the reviewed 2022 draft defines safe distance as an authorised person's safe offset plus measurement error [f5911, f6198, f2420]. MOSH specifies stop gaps of 1.0–4.0 m at speeds of 10 km/h or less and 15 m ± 5 m above 10 km/h, whereas South Africa Regulation 8.10 and US 30 CFR 75.1732 provide no numeric stopping-margin value; the proposed US 3 ft distance was not adopted [f2610, f2611, f2626]. The booklet calculates remaining margin by subtracting perception, decision, action, predicted stopping distance and safe clearance from predicted path distance; its 40 t example at 15 km/h on a 10% downgrade with 1.0 s delay requires detection at least 9.5 m away for 1 m clearance, before sensor-error allowance [f6208, f13656]. Validation should measure stopping margin and minimum clearance in closed-loop runs, and tuning should impose a hard minimum-margin constraint rather than relying only on detector performance or collision/no-collision verdicts [f4812, f6961, f6982, f7373]. Intervention escalation should depend on remaining margin and its uncertainty rather than range alone, and operator-reaction detection must avoid standing down merely because controls move while the actual stopping margin continues collapsing [f6280, f6343, f13968].

nodes.label: Secondary hazards of an automatic stop
nodes.text: Secondary hazards are the new dangers an automatic stop creates by itself: being struck from behind, blocking an escape route, stalling or rolling back on a grade, spilling the load, or hurting the operator.
nodes.synopsis: Automatic braking can create hazards of its own—operator jolts, shifted or spilled loads, slope instability, rear-end impacts and rollback—and stopping before an object is therefore not a complete safety result [f11877, f2896]. Risk varies by machine and operation, requiring machine-specific hazard analysis and potentially context-dependent braking rather than a universal fastest-stop command; Komatsu specifically requires KomVision to be off during trailer loading because rapid stopping can destabilize the machine [f808, f1977, f1975, f1646]. Validation must address both failure to brake and unsafe or unnecessary braking: shadow mode cannot establish closed-loop secondary effects, whereas branched closed-loop SIL or HIL evaluates stopping distance, clearance and secondary hazards [f5816, f968, f5529]. Most secondary hazards are reported rather than measured: off-road event frequencies and deceleration injury thresholds were not found, worker reports of jolting remain unresolved against MSHA's lack of known injuries, and on-road evidence varies—a reported 20% increase in rear-end strikes contrasts with no collision-producing loss of following distance in the cited Tesla investigation [f11878, f3613, f3612, f3619, f3032, f1503]. Post-stop safety also matters: ISO 21815-3 warns against rollaway when intervention ends and recommends operator action, such as applying the parking brake, before braking is released [f6157, f6158].

nodes.label: Mixed motion and prediction of movement
nodes.text: Mixed motion is the case where both the machine and the person or vehicle are moving, so the system must predict where each will be, not just where they are now.
nodes.synopsis: Mixed motion requires predicting both participants’ future positions, with collision decisions based on the machine’s predicted swept volume and the other actor’s trajectory rather than proximity or object labels alone [f14031, f14034, f7021, f7476]. Straight-line time to collision is insufficient for sideways, rotating or initially stationary motion, and turning, articulation or skid steering can create collisions without longitudinal closing speed [f14039, f5920, f13731]. Motion scope must be defined machine by machine: ISO 21815-3:2023 covers forward/reverse intervention, Part 4 excludes automatic braking during rotation, and draft Part 5 reached proof stage on 9 September 2026 for other motion forms [f10906, f10900, f10902, f10904]. Pretoria’s October 2024 steering-rate collision-prediction results were simulation-only; production recommendations treat steering as an avoidance cue, not proof of safety, and require demonstrably safer predicted trajectories before suppressing intervention [f6331, f6367, f6336, f6342]. Recorded replay cannot establish other actors’ reactions after counterfactual braking, so closed-loop simulation needs regenerated observations and reactive agents, while mixed motion also requires controlled whole-machine tests because validated off-road behavioral models were not found [f5525, f14043, f5539, f14041, f14042]. Planning remains constrained by missing accident speed/motion detail and worldwide motion-type collision shares, and the proposed single swept-volume collision logic must be reconciled with concerns about treating swing and rotation as one function [f3256, f3610, f7021, f10899].

nodes.label: Tuning thresholds in simulation before field tests
nodes.text: Tuning in simulation means adjusting the decision thresholds, zone sizes and filters on a computer model of machine, sensors and site, so that field tests confirm settings rather than discover them.
nodes.synopsis: The strategy requires virtual testing to improve the new collision-mitigation system to meet or beat the current system and to tune thresholds and calibration before field testing; previous physical testing and tuning took three to four years per machine model [f27, f29, f8252]. On-road precedents demonstrate threshold evaluation, including a 2019 sweep of time-to-collision triggers and latencies, but no published quantitative off-road comparison with field results was found, leaving transferability unknown and constituting the programme’s main technical risk [f6346, f6558, f155]. Tuning should pursue multiple objectives under hard safety constraints rather than start with one weighted cost, and should prefer broad stable operating regions over fragile optima; detector operating-point tuning alone misses closed-loop timing and braking [f6959, f6963, f6989, f7304]. Settings include confidence thresholds, speed-dependent zones, confirmation filters and timing constants, while intervention staging should use remaining stopping margin and uncertainty rather than range alone [f6957, f6280]. Virtual tuning can explore trigger structure, grade and payload dependence and initial zone sizes, but production brake characteristics, real-site friction, adverse-condition sensor behaviour and nuisance rates require measurements and shadow-mode logs; a 2026 on-road round robin also found simulator disagreements of 0.033 seconds and 0.314 metres [f14054, f14055, f14048]. The proposed sequence is to freeze the decision architecture and sweep scenarios before hardware arrives, reserve the first six weeks after delivery for physical anchoring, then rerun calibrated sweeps and measure nuisance rates in shadow mode before enabling braking; requirements definition and field tuning may remain the real bottleneck [f14056, f14057, f14058, f10859].

nodes.label: Test space and the combinatorial explosion
nodes.text: The test space is the set of every situation the braking system could meet, and the combinatorial explosion is the way that set grows so fast, when conditions are multiplied together, that nobody can test it all.
nodes.synopsis: Across 100-plus site types, 10-plus scenarios, weather/light conditions and machine variants, the booklet estimates more than 7,000 validation strata; adding finer parameters produces millions of combinations, making exhaustive field coverage infeasible [f131, f11331, f132]. It recommends structuring testing through an operating-domain taxonomy, a scenario catalog and parameterized scenario families, with site dimensions represented as attributes and impossible combinations explicitly excluded [f119, f6727, f6762]. Scenario counts alone do not establish coverage: nearly identical sites can contribute little diversity, expert catalogs miss unanticipated scenarios, and no source quantifies how environmental diversity relates to failures found [f4064, f6775, f4379]. A four-month simulation window forces tiered fidelity, while simulation can cover the otherwise infeasible interior only after physical boundary testing and independent validation establish predictive credibility [f13548, f8061]. Combinatorial testing can shrink test suites but does not establish that low-order interactions suffice for collision avoidance; the booklet also recommends separating coverage, failure discovery and statistical estimation streams [f4332, f11334].

nodes.label: Parameter, parameter range and parameterized scenario family
nodes.text: A parameter is one adjustable quantity in a test (such as machine speed), its range is the span of values it may take, and a parameterized scenario family is one scenario description with those quantities left open so that thousands of concrete tests can be generated from it.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends structuring validation around an operating-domain taxonomy, a catalog that retains known fatal-accident patterns, and parameterized scenario families with probability distributions—not one exhaustive Cartesian matrix; impossible combinations and conditional factors should be encoded explicitly [f119, f6762]. A parameterized machine and brake model could realistically be working by mid-2027 for a program starting in October 2026, with SIL recommended for sweeping 100+ site types and 10+ scenarios [f67, f5267]. For virtual environments, the proposed route is representative parameterized archetypes anchored to surveyed sites; 15–30 archetypes and 3–5 surveyed sites are explicitly planning assumptions, not evidence of sufficiency [f11501, f11937]. Coverage should be judged against operating-domain parameters rather than site or scenario counts, and broad ranges cannot compensate for omitted failure-generating structures or hazard classes nobody has conceived [f4063, f10781, f3792, f789]. Probability distributions derived from field data or expert estimates enable later field-success estimates, but ignoring dependencies such as dust occurring with dry, windy, high-traffic conditions misweights the test strata [f6761, f13284, f6771]. Simulation is strongest for sweeps inside physically anchored, validated domains: validity is parameter-space specific, and even NIOSH’s 2018 stopping model with six variables at five values each still required validation [f7851, f5072, f5949].

nodes.label: Test selection method
nodes.text: A test selection method is a rule for choosing which of the countless possible tests to actually run, and each rule can honestly answer only certain kinds of question.
nodes.synopsis: Test selection is a safety decision, not simply a way to shrink a giant matrix: the booklet recommends predefined coverage models, hazard-driven scenario classes, equivalence classes, boundary analysis and uncertainty sampling rather than an exhaustive Cartesian product [f14074, f5470, f11042, f13297]. No single method provides discrete-configuration coverage, continuous-parameter coverage, failure discovery and field-rate estimation; coverage designs, failure-seeking searches and a separate frozen statistical sample must serve different purposes [f6798, f14098]. Reported success across 20,000 scenarios is not statistically meaningful without a defined population and selection mechanism, and failure-hunting searches cannot report a failure rate [f6933, f14096]. Prioritization should use accident data, especially fatality patterns, while frequency and damage estimates are weaker evidence; safety-critical interactions still require hazard analysis, field failures and engineering knowledge [f10622, f11605, f4076]. Reported efficiencies include NIST test-set reductions of 20–700 times and on-road dense-reinforcement-learning acceleration of 10^3–10^5 times, but the latter is not proven off-road and requires a large naturalistic dataset for legitimate evaluation claims [f6820, f7078, f7079, f7277]. An initial statistical plan and coverage metrics are considered realistic by mid-2027 for a team starting in October 2026, but no universal off-road coverage prescription was found; within a four-month window, the recommended hybrid approach uses simulation for screening and informative physical-test selection rather than proof by itself [f846, f5475, f13496, f9697, f14059].

nodes.label: Design of experiments (DOE)
nodes.text: Design of experiments (DOE) is the branch of statistics that plans which combinations of settings to test so that the effect of each factor, and of factors acting together, can be measured with the fewest runs.
aliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology
nodes.synopsis: DOE is strongest for estimating how factors and low-order interactions affect detection distance, stopping margin and false alarms; screening identifies influential factors, while response-surface designs support fine tuning of a few smooth parameters [f6799, f6805, f6801, f6673]. The booklet places modest DOE or D-optimal tests in post-prototype calibration, and recommends sequential braking-model experiments whose stopping criterion is sufficiently small safety-relevant error bounds at every declared operating boundary—not a fixed test count [f14109, f14504, f6166, f6169]. DOE points are not weighted by operational frequency, so they cannot establish field failure probability; fractional designs also alias higher-order effects and cannot rule out narrow, nonlinear failures between test points [f6807, f6800, f6808, f6809]. NIST software research reports equivalent fault detection with test sets reduced by factors of 20–700, but this does not demonstrate that pairwise or other low-order coverage suffices for off-road collision avoidance or coupled perception failures [f6820, f4075, f7425]. No off-road collision-avoidance study using DOE was found, and NIOSH's 2022 review identifies DOE and standard simulation-method gaps that additional synthetic runs do not close [f6812, f10508].

nodes.label: Combinatorial testing (t-way testing, pairwise testing, covering arrays)
nodes.text: Combinatorial testing chooses a small set of tests that still guarantees every combination of values of any t factors (for pairwise testing, any two) appears at least once.
nodes.synopsis: Combinatorial testing uses smaller test sets to guarantee that every combination of values of any t discrete factors appears at least once; pairwise testing covers any two factors [f4074, f6817, f14111]. NIST reports fault detection equal to exhaustive testing with 20–700 times fewer tests in software research, where most bugs involve one or two parameters and progressively fewer involve three or more, up to about six [f14113, f6819]. This evidence does not establish that pairwise or 3-way coverage suffices for off-road camera, radar or lidar perception failures, and transfer of the software interaction rule remains unproven [f4075, f6827, f14122]. The booklet therefore recommends covering arrays for machine-by-sensor-by-weather-by-scenario configuration coverage, with safety-critical interactions identified through hazard analysis, field failures and engineering knowledge, and perception tests supplemented by physics-guided hypotheses and failure-seeking search [f7233, f4076, f14123]. Covering arrays cannot establish coverage of continuous regions, interactions above t, or operational failure rates; they belong in the coverage and discovery streams rather than serving as the basis for a release claim [f7235, f14283, f14143].

nodes.label: Random sampling, stratified sampling and probability-weighted sampling
nodes.text: Random sampling picks tests by chance according to how often each situation occurs in real operation, stratified sampling first divides the situations into groups (strata) and samples each group deliberately, and probability-weighted sampling keeps track of each test's real-world frequency so that results can be scaled back to the field.
nodes.synopsis: Exhaustive field coverage of more than 7,000 testing strata is infeasible; the booklet therefore calls for stratified sampling plus simulation, with important machine, site and weather strata deliberately sampled and weighted back to operational prevalence [f132, f6829]. Coverage, failure discovery and performance estimation must remain separate: release-rate claims require a frozen, stratified random sample drawn from the declared operating-domain distribution before tuning and never used for tuning [f11334, f14131]. Random and probability-weighted sampling can support unbiased detection and false-alarm estimates with classical confidence intervals, but those claims fail if the assumed scenario distribution does not match real operation; defensible parameter distributions are an identified weak point, and the required field distribution is unavailable in public sources [f6830, f6833, f14086, f14132]. The booklet consequently urges shadow-mode logging on the existing warning fleet now, and requires acceptance criteria, strata, confidence levels and stopping rules to be fixed before hardware arrives [f14133, f14292]. A claim of at most 1% misses in each of 20 critical strata needs about 6,000 independent zero-miss trials; encounters, runs, shifts or sites—not individual frames—must determine the effective sampling units [f6887, f5462].

nodes.label: Space-filling designs (Latin hypercube)
nodes.text: A space-filling design spreads test points as evenly as possible across the ranges of several continuous parameters at once, so that no region of the space is left unexplored.
nodes.synopsis: Space-filling designs, including Latin hypercube, Sobol and other quasi-random methods, spread continuous-parameter tests more evenly than naive random draws and are recommended for coverage, exploration and surrogate-model training [f6813, f7227, f14138]. Latin hypercube divides each parameter range into n equal slices and places n points so that every slice of every parameter is used exactly once; applications include exploring detection range under dust, glare and speed and feeding surrogate-guided search [f14136, f14144]. This geometric coverage is not probability sampling and does not represent quarry operating frequencies, where most approaches are slow and most weather is clear; it cannot establish unweighted rates or worst cases [f6815, f14140, f7229]. Unrealistic regions receive equal treatment unless constraints and distributions are added, so the booklet assigns these designs to the coverage stream alongside combinatorial designs, not as a basis for the release claim [f6816, f14143, f7353]. The stated evidence for these methods is generic expert opinion from statistical synthesis, rather than application-specific validation evidence [f7232].

nodes.label: Falsification (failure-seeking search)
nodes.text: Falsification is a test method that treats "find a case where the system fails" as a search problem and uses optimization to steer the simulator toward the most dangerous combinations of conditions.
nodes.synopsis: Falsification optimizes scenario parameters to worsen measures such as time-to-collision, stopping margin or detection confidence, seeking reproducible failures and weak boundaries within the simulated space [f6835, f14146, f6841]. The recommended discovery campaign targets stopping boundaries, partial visibility, high closing speed, field-of-view edges and sensor degradation; weather tests should reproduce measured degradation rather than merely realistic appearance [f14155, f10937]. Discovery must remain separate from frozen estimation samples and regression testing: its failure fraction is biased by design, cannot represent an operational failure rate, and found failures should become logical scenarios or permanent regression tests [f133, f6842, f14157, f6949]. Failure-free searches do not prove failures absent, objectives can miss different failure types, and searches can exploit simulator artefacts [f6843, f6845, f6844]. Evidence includes on-road and aerospace work, but no off-road demonstration was found; VerifAI with Scenic reported up to a fivefold speed-up from parallel multi-objective falsification in 2021 [f14158, f6839]. The planning recommendation is to run inexpensive early falsification experiments before building major infrastructure [f10912].

nodes.label: Rare-event methods (importance sampling)
nodes.text: Rare-event methods deliberately make dangerous situations happen more often in simulation, then mathematically correct the results so that the estimated rate still refers to normal operation.
nodes.synopsis: Rare-event methods deliberately oversample dangerous simulated situations and reweight results to estimate normal-operation failure rates; unbiased estimation requires known likelihood ratios and sampling that reaches the failure region [f14159, f14160, f6851]. On-road Michigan studies in 2016 reported acceleration factors of roughly 300–100,000 for car-following and 2,000–20,000 for lane-change conflicts, while D2RL, reported on 22 March 2023, achieved 10^3–10^5-fold acceleration while remaining unbiased [f1220, f1221, f6848]. These are statistical exposure reductions, not product safety sign-offs: the Michigan evaluations did not eliminate model, sensor or vehicle testing, and no regulator accepted production AEB on their basis [f1219, f1299, f1300]. Transfer to heavy off-road machines remains unproven: the known exposure distribution needed across 100+ site types is absent, and no comparable large off-road naturalistic interaction dataset was found [f352, f6858, f6859]. High-dimensional or unknown distributions can produce unstable, high-variance weights, and acceleration cannot establish failure modes omitted from the simulation, including unrepresented sensor physics [f6852, f6853]. Although naive Monte Carlo cannot reach low failure rates in four months, the planning recommendation is to use importance sampling for estimation only where a defensible field distribution exists and otherwise classify it as discovery; experts disagree about how far acceleration can replace real exposure [f10337, f6866, f14170].

nodes.label: Adaptive and Bayesian test selection
nodes.text: Adaptive test selection chooses each new test based on the results of the tests so far, often using a Bayesian model that keeps track of what is still uncertain.
nodes.synopsis: Adaptive and Bayesian selection uses previous results, a surrogate model and an acquisition rule to choose subsequent tests, distinguishing boundary learning from optimisation for best or worst settings [f14171, f14173, f14174, f14175]. The booklet recommends these methods for efficiently characterising collision-mitigation decision boundaries and places adaptive search in the proposed campaign’s discovery stream [f7280, f7281, f7354]. Multi-objective and safe Bayesian optimisation can reduce expensive HIL or physical evaluations and constrain exploration, but the cited evidence is general engineering methodology rather than off-road braking research [f6974, f6976]. Its efficiency claims depend on the assumed surrogate and acquisition model; surrogate uncertainty can be wrong, and discontinuities and adaptive bias are additional limitations [f7281, f6862, f6978]. Because adaptive sampling deliberately favours interesting regions, its results cannot support naive binomial confidence intervals or population-rate claims: discovery and boundary characterisation must not be treated as rate estimation [f14177, f7282, f14179, f7401].

nodes.label: Monte Carlo methods
nodes.text: A Monte Carlo method answers a question by running the same experiment many times with randomly chosen inputs and counting what happens.
nodes.synopsis: Monte Carlo estimates miss rates by repeatedly drawing scenario parameters from probability distributions and counting outcomes; the booklet recommends it as the honest default for rate estimation and uses a frozen sample for its estimation campaign [f14181, f14182, f14188, f14183]. For large simulation sweeps, it selects the point-mass transient braking model and recommends preparing the Monte Carlo engine, parameter database, metrics and traceability before prototype testing [f6435, f6404]. However, pure Monte Carlo is extremely inefficient for rare dangerous events: a true miss rate of one in 10,000 yields about one miss per 10,000 runs, requiring tens of thousands of runs for a precise estimate, and naive Monte Carlo cannot reach low failure rates within four months [f6834, f14185, f10337]. Precedents include ACAS X validation representing billions of flight hours and a 2005 Griffith University study combining Monte Carlo with a Doppler-radar field demonstration that reported light-vehicle detection at 75 m [f1908, f6368]. For planning, Monte Carlo samples task durations and should communicate milestone uncertainty through P50/P80 S-curves or fan charts; reference class forecasting outperformed Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting in a 2016 test only when reference-class similarity was high [f16335, f9889, f9606].

nodes.label: Sample size, confidence level and confidence interval
nodes.text: The sample size is how many independent trials you run, the confidence level is how sure you want to be, and the confidence interval is the range of values for the true rate that the data support at that level of sureness.
nodes.synopsis: Statistics are the binding constraint on demonstrating collision-mitigation performance: the reviewed off-road standards specify what to test but supply neither statistical acceptance targets nor detection and false-alarm sample sizes [f125, f324, f5154, f5160]. Sample size follows the claim: with zero misses, 95% one-sided confidence requires 299 independent trials for a miss rate of at most 1%, 2,995 for 0.1%, and 29,956 for 0.01% per claimed population; at 99% confidence these rise to 459, 4,603 and 46,050 [f5201, f6650, f6651, f6652, f6653]. Trials must be independent encounters rather than correlated sensor frames, and release-rate claims require a frozen stratified random sample; checking hundreds of cells separately at 95% confidence also creates chance outcomes, so primary claims should be named beforehand [f130, f12833, f6648, f12172]. Rare-event field proof is difficult: RAND's 2016 road-vehicle analysis required hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles, while the synthesis calls for 300 representative hours without unnecessary braking to show fewer than one unnecessary brake per 100 hours [f313, f129, f1993]. Virtual testing can address exposure volume, but large simulated samples do not remove model-form uncertainty, and the real exposure needed for rare false negatives or unintended braking, as well as statistical weather/site generalisation off-road, remains uncertain [f9755, f8182, f8181, f2879]. Real-data detection and false-positive rates with confidence intervals are expected for each environmental condition bin, while no study was found establishing that generatively edited data predict real detection rates at the confidence needed for a braking safety argument [f11102, f4909].

nodes.label: Binomial claims and the rule of three
nodes.text: A binomial claim is a statement about the probability of a yes-or-no outcome (detected or missed) based on a count of trials, and the rule of three is the shortcut that says: with zero failures in n trials, you can be about 95 percent confident that the true failure probability is below 3 divided by n.
nodes.synopsis: The rule of three approximates the 95% upper failure-probability bound as 3/n after zero failures; exact one-sided binomial inference uses (1 − q)^n ≤ alpha [f14202, f6875]. At 95% confidence, miss-rate limits of 5%, 1%, 0.1% and 0.01% require respectively 59, 299, 2,995 and 29,956 independent zero-miss trials; at 99% confidence these rise to 90, 459, 4,603 and 46,050 [f14193, f14194]. These counts apply per claimed population, not across an entire product family: separate claims need their own evidence or justified pooling, and 20 critical strata with 1% miss-rate claims require about 6,000 zero-miss trials, described as feasible only in simulation or HIL [f6885, f6886, f14199]. Independence and sampling validity are essential: correlated sensor frames cannot count as separate encounters, and naive binomial intervals from adaptively selected tests are invalid [f5205, f6874, f6861]. When misses occur, exact binomial or another pre-declared interval is needed; the cited examples require about 474 trials with one allowed failure and 630 with two for a 1% miss-rate claim at 95% confidence, but provide no corresponding 99% counts [f14196, f6879, f6880]. False-alarm claims instead use exposure-based rates: zero events over T representative hours gives an approximately 3/T upper rate bound at 95% confidence, so 300 event-free hours supports fewer than one event per 100 hours [f5448, f6657, f224].

nodes.label: Bayesian methods and sequential testing
nodes.text: Bayesian methods combine what you believed before the test (the prior) with the test results to produce an updated belief, and sequential testing lets you stop testing early once the evidence is clearly good or clearly bad.
aliases: In a sequential probability ratio test
nodes.synopsis: Bayesian analysis can formally combine simulation-derived prior evidence with physical tests, potentially reducing physical testing, but the corpus gives no fixed virtual-to-physical exchange rate: this depends on assessor acceptance of prior strength and documented simulation/toolchain credibility [f6898, f14218, f14227, f14275]. Prior sensitivity is substantial: the cited independent, on-road ISSRE 2019 analysis reduced RAND’s 275 million fatality-free miles to 69 million with a strong prior carrying 90% prior confidence, but increased it to 476 million with a weak prior; proponents and critics therefore disagree about simulation-derived priors’ benefits [f6900, f6901, f6902, f7437]. The recommendations are to use conservative Bayesian methods because assessors will challenge priors, and to learn machine-response distributions from existing machines before 2027, even where brake hardware differs [f6899, f14222, f6405]. Bayesian or hierarchical pooling can share evidence across genuinely similar machine families while retaining variant uncertainty, but requires a justified similarity model to avoid hiding a bad variant [f645, f646]. Sequential testing permits early stopping when evidence is clearly good or bad, provided acceptance thresholds, statistical tests and stopping rules are fixed in advance—not chosen when results look favorable [f643, f644, f6903, f6905, f14225]. Its use in the four-month validation window is attractive, although the chapter labels that application expert opinion while the glossary presents trial savings and program attractiveness as a finding [f6904, f14224].

nodes.label: Hypothesis testing basics (null hypothesis, significance, McNemar test)
nodes.text: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is too large to be a coincidence, by assuming at first that there is no real difference (the null hypothesis) and computing how surprising the data would then be.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet defines hypothesis testing as assessing an observed difference against a null hypothesis of no real difference; validation sample sizes must match the claim, with binomial detection tests sized by significance, power and the separation between acceptable and unacceptable probabilities [f14228, f5448, f5453]. For old-versus-new warning systems, it recommends paired recording on the same machine and hazards: McNemar's test uses only discordant outcomes, illustrated by 12 hazards caught only by the new system versus 3 caught only by the old, while separate deployments confound site, operator and weather [f14237, f14233, f14234, f14235, f14236]. Sequential tests can stop early on clearly good or bad evidence, but acceptance thresholds and statistical tests must be fixed in advance [f6903, f644]. Checking hundreds of scenario cells individually at 95% confidence risks chance-driven passes or failures, so primary claims should be predefined and multiplicity or simultaneous-confidence methods used where claims must hold together [f7485, f7486]. As an on-road scale illustration, RAND's April 2016 analysis estimated about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% fatality-rate improvement with 95% confidence and 80% power; that estimate concerns autonomous road vehicles, not a supplied off-road validation sample size [f6663, f6923, f14263].

nodes.label: Base rate and exposure-based rates (events per 1,000 hours)
nodes.text: A base rate is how often something happens in normal operation, and an exposure-based rate expresses it per unit of exposure, such as false alarms per 1,000 operating hours, rather than per staged test.
nodes.synopsis: False alarms and unnecessary interventions should be measured against representative operational exposure, such as operating hours, loading cycles or close approaches, rather than staged tests or discovery-campaign failure fractions [f11336, f3342, f134]. No published authoritative off-road acceptance rates were found, so programs must set their own criteria separately for advisory warnings, urgent warnings, speed reduction and full braking, with nuisance-stop thresholds agreed with site operations [f2121, f2880, f2124, f10716]. Under a homogeneous Poisson model, zero events in T hours gives a one-sided 95% upper rate bound of approximately 3/T: 300 representative event-free hours supports fewer than one unnecessary brake per 100 hours, and 3,000 supports fewer than one per 1,000 hours; clustered alarms require different statistical models [f5456, f6658, f6659, f6660]. Shadow-mode logging and replay can estimate unnecessary braking per operating hour by site type and weather, while field testing should use continuous, untriggered recording in representative site classes [f1601, f5472]. Accident counts cannot establish comparable collision rates without exposure denominators and compatible categories, and even ten million operating hours with few recorded incidents says little about detector performance without encounter counts and recording completeness [f11610, f3047, f7939].

nodes.label: Weighting strata to a field rate
nodes.text: Weighting strata means combining the measured rate in each group of conditions (each stratum) into one overall rate by multiplying each by the share of real operating time that group represents.
nodes.synopsis: The overall field rate is calculated as Σ w_i p_i: each stratum’s measured detection or false-alarm rate is multiplied by its share of real exposure, and uncertainty in those shares must accompany the result [f6916, f14253, f14254]. The booklet prefers stratified sampling that adequately covers critical conditions and then restores operational weights; DOE and uniform parameter-space coverage do not establish field probabilities without those weights [f6829, f14127, f6807, f6815]. Importance sampling likewise requires a sufficiently known field distribution, including dependencies such as dust occurring with dry, windy, high-traffic conditions [f642, f7264, f6771]. Off-road exposure distributions were not found publicly, so the booklet recommends starting fleet logging and classifying years of existing warning-system records now; it identifies telematics, warning logs and site studies as acquisition routes, although another glossary statement calls the warning baseline the program’s only exposure source [f6918, f14133, f7366, f6919, f14350]. Weighting does not remove the need to substantiate individual population claims: the example requires 299 zero-miss trials for one defined population, or about 6,000 for separate 1 percent miss-rate claims across 20 critical strata unless justified pooling is used [f14212, f14213].
