nodes.label: The RAND argument
nodes.text: The RAND argument is the finding, from a 2016 report by the RAND Corporation (a research organization), that proving a self-driving car is as safe as a human driver by simply driving it would take hundreds of millions to billions of miles, far more than any fleet can drive.
nodes.synopsis: Kalra and Paddock’s RAND report, dated 12 April 2016, provides the booklet’s statistical rationale for virtual testing: driving-only safety demonstrations require hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles, taking existing fleets tens or hundreds of years [f5464, f313, f5466, f9755]. Its benchmarks include 275 million fatality-free miles to demonstrate a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles at 95% confidence, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement at 95% confidence and 80% power [f6922, f6923]. A 2019 conservative Bayesian analysis illustrates sensitivity to assumptions: a strong prior with 90% prior confidence reduces the 275-million-mile requirement to 69 million, while a weak prior raises it to 476 million [f6900, f6901, f6902]. The booklet says RAND’s statistical logic transfers to off-road machines, whose lower exposure makes field-only demonstration harder, but its numerical mileage requirements do not transfer because off-road claims concern detection and intervention per encounter [f314, f6664]. Staged encounters and thousands of simulation runs make the four-month plan conceivable, with rare-event claims requiring stratified testing, simulation volume and a credibility argument rather than customer-site hours alone [f14267, f14265, f14268]. There is an evidence-status tension: multiple chapters treat RAND’s conclusion as established, but the skeptic’s review says the report was identified as relevant without being verified in the research [f7400, f14268, f11203].

nodes.label: Combining simulation and physical evidence
nodes.text: Combining simulation and physical evidence means using a large number of virtual runs to supply the statistical volume and a smaller number of physical tests to prove that the simulation can be trusted, so that the two together support a claim neither could support alone.
nodes.synopsis: Across the corpus, simulation complements rather than eliminates physical testing: it selects tests deserving scarce prototype time and expands evidence around physical anchors, while documented validation programmes retain physical tests and staged field operation [f11311, f484, f309]. Exhaustive field coverage of more than 7,000 validation cells is infeasible, so simulation or HIL should supply large stratified trial counts, with physical validation in each stratum and smaller-sample independent confirmation [f5207, f6889]. Substitution is defensible only inside a measured, independently reviewed credibility envelope; physical confirmation remains necessary at boundaries, after influential changes, and where models are weak [f10467, f7536, f10470]. On-road precedents retain physical checks: Euro NCAP's 2026 Virtual Testing protocol, version 1.00 dated March 2025, requires randomly selected physical verification after simulation predictions, but no prescribed simulation share or off-road regulatory acceptance of simulation-based rate claims was found [f1216, f4316, f6931]. For a four-month off-road validation programme, the recommended approach is an analytical safety case with targeted physical tests and credible simulation, organized as an integrated strategy; the principal calendar saving comes from moving work before prototype availability, not removing physical validation [f2137, f9555, f311].

nodes.label: Keeping failure-seeking tests separate from performance estimates
nodes.text: Tests designed to find failures and tests designed to measure how often failures happen must be kept in separate pools with separate data and separate rules, because mixing them makes the measured rate wrong in one direction or the other.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus requires separate purposes, data and governance for failure discovery, performance estimation, and requirement/regression testing; coverage designs support understanding but must not supply the release-rate claim [f133, f6935, f11334, f14143]. Discovery deliberately concentrates on failures, so its failure fraction is not an operational rate; conversely, tuning against estimation cases can understate failures by turning the audit into a measure of fit to those cases [f6842, f14287, f14288]. Performance estimation uses a frozen, pre-registered, stratified random sample from the declared operating-domain distribution, with weighting and estimators fixed before inspecting results; correctly weighted rare-event campaigns require defensible distributions and known likelihood weights [f6939, f6941, f7288, f6951]. Search-found failures should become scenarios or regression tests, with their frequency estimated separately, while the estimation set is reserved for release candidates rather than continuous tuning [f6949, f6950, f13527]. The proposed release claim uses the frozen estimation sample plus physical anchors, and a four-month deadline makes stream separation a governance priority; the glossary's statement that a frozen random sample is the “only basis” needs qualification alongside the allowance for correctly weighted rare-event estimation [f7358, f14295, f14095, f7288].

nodes.label: Pre-registration
nodes.text: Pre-registration means writing down, before the data exist, exactly what will be claimed, how it will be measured, which samples will be used and when testing will stop, so that the analysis cannot be bent to fit the results.
nodes.synopsis: Pre-registration is a core control against result-driven analysis: before hardware arrives, the program should fix acceptance criteria, strata, confidence levels and stopping rules, with the statistical plan scheduled for October 2026 to mid-2027 [f6956, f7363]. Release-rate claims must use a frozen stratified random sample drawn from the declared operating-domain distribution before tuning and never used for tuning; discovery, estimation and regression tests must remain separate [f14131, f133]. Statistical safeguards include pre-declared binomial intervals when misses occur, fixed sequential stopping rules, and predefined primary claims with multiplicity methods where many claims must hold together [f6891, f14225, f7486]. The recommended pilot is a difficult thin vertical slice predicted blind against pre-registered criteria, with a proposed 10–30 physical test points and metrics such as detection-range error, stopping-distance error and false-negative agreement [f9485, f9917, f9919]. Evidence supporting pre-declared progression criteria and locked metrics comes from health and social research, so its transfer to engineering remains an analogy rather than direct proof; few sensor-realism studies define acceptance thresholds before testing [f9903, f9904, f4839]. A late change in sensor modalities can invalidate the frozen plan, requiring sensor-dependent strata to be re-derived and the sample redrawn, consuming validation time [f7490, f7491, f14303].

nodes.label: Over-fitting
nodes.text: Over-fitting is what happens when a system's settings are adjusted so closely to the particular tests it was tuned on that it performs well on those tests and worse on anything new.
nodes.synopsis: Over-fitting means settings fit the tuning tests well but perform worse on new tests; for braking-system release claims, the booklet requires a frozen, stratified random sample from the declared operating-domain distribution, drawn before tuning and never used for tuning [f14306, f14131]. The main controls are grouped holdouts of whole sites, weather episodes, machines or scenario families, separate tuning/validation/untouched audit datasets, and limited frozen-set use at release candidates rather than continuous optimisation against failures [f137, f6990, f6992, f12889, f7135]. Simulator over-fitting is identified as a critical risk, with improving virtual metrics alongside stalled or worsening held-out real performance as its warning sign, but the skeptic’s review found no off-road case and explicitly treats the risk as an inference [f11030, f10784]. Independent withheld physical datasets and blind correlation tests are recommended safeguards; failed tests and discrepancy dispositions should remain visible rather than mismatches being tuned away or scenarios removed from reporting [f11032, f8047, f8024]. Separately, Chapter 5 reports severe over-fitting and poor novel-path generalisation in single-traversal 3DGS, a problem addressed by VEGS in July 2024; this evidence is labelled on-road, not an established off-road braking-function case [f4010, f4011, f10783].

nodes.label: Hold-out set, tuning split and cross-validation
nodes.text: A hold-out set is a portion of the test data kept back and never used for tuning, a tuning split is the division of data into parts for tuning, confirming and auditing, and cross-validation is the practice of rotating which part is held out so that every part is used for checking once.
nodes.synopsis: Across the synthesis, simulation-credibility chapter and glossary, the central rule is to separate tuning, validation or confirmation, and untouched audit data; data used to judge the system must not have helped build or tune it [f135, f7589, f6992, f14471]. Splits should hold out whole sites, weather episodes, machine identities or scenario families rather than random frames, because adjacent frames shared between tuning and validation create severe leakage [f137, f6990, f6991, f14327]. The release-rate claim must rest on a frozen, stratified random sample from the declared operating-domain distribution, drawn before tuning; fixed seeds and content hashes protect its identity, and full-set evaluation is reserved for release candidates [f14131, f14298, f7134]. Audit governance limits the tuning team to aggregate pass/fail results, prohibits optimizing against audit failures, and requires contaminated cases to be retired and replaced; tuned-versus-frozen performance should be reported because a large gap signals over-fitting [f6954, f7135, f6953, f14313]. Physical-model credibility requires frozen calibration challenged on independent boundary conditions, while using every physical case for tuning leaves no untouched predictive evidence; the cited 2017 expert-weighting cross-validation study likewise found strong in-sample performance with an out-of-sample penalty [f6167, f8225, f9946].

nodes.label: Performance baseline
nodes.text: A performance baseline is a careful measurement of how well the existing warning-only system performs, made before the new braking system is judged, so that "better" has something to be better than.
nodes.synopsis: The strategy requires measuring the existing warning system in virtual environments, comparing the new system in the same environments, and using simulation to improve it against that baseline [f25, f26, f27]. The established off-field method is replaying raw sensor logs against independent ground truth; baseline quality depends on recording coverage, and using the production detector's own outputs as truth makes missed objects disappear from the assessment [f94, f271, f5359]. Measurement should be encounter-based and stratified by object class, distance and condition, with warning rates, timing and operational availability reported rather than hidden in fleet averages; glossary sample-size guidance specifies 59 consecutive successful encounters per stratum for a 95% detection claim and 299 for a 99% claim [f14339, f14340, f14342, f14347]. Recording should start in October 2026, with the old-system baseline and supporting validation infrastructure ideally ready by mid-2027, before prototype-dependent work becomes the bottleneck [f5168, f5615, f5616]. A central tension is that matching or beating the warning system is not an adequate braking acceptance target: common stages can be compared, but braking must be assessed in closed loop against new hazard-derived requirements [f27, f111, f5500, f12188].

nodes.label: Fair comparison of old and new systems
nodes.text: A fair comparison judges the old warning system and the new braking system on the same hazards, in the same conditions, using the same yardstick, so that any difference is due to the systems and not to the circumstances.
nodes.synopsis: The strategy requires testing the new collision-mitigation system in the same virtual environments as the baseline, but fair comparison rests on common system outputs in world or risk coordinates—not raw sensor statistics when sensors, mounting or processing differ [f26, f105, f107, f5211]. The strongest experiment records both sensor suites simultaneously on one machine against an independent reference trajectory; separate deployments confound site, operator and weather, and mounting interference must itself be tested [f5509, f5482, f5511, f14364]. Common measures include warnings and interventions per hazard, missed hazards, false and nuisance alarms per hour under equal exposure, and warning timing against common ground truth and a shared hazard zone; calibrated ground truth is essential because verdict errors can dominate system differences [f106, f5478, f7474]. The old fleet supplies the warning-performance baseline, including false and nuisance alarm rates to beat, but this is not the assurance target for automatic braking: only common warning stages are directly comparable, while braking must meet new hazard-derived requirements and be assessed in closed loop [f11783, f11906, f10529, f14363]. Replay supports comparison only with genuinely equivalent inputs, and the corpus reports unresolved evidence gaps, including missing exposure denominators for accident comparisons and no apples-to-apples stopping-distance accuracy benchmark across tools on the same production machines [f5238, f5512, f3658, f6397].

nodes.label: Regression (a new version performing worse)
nodes.text: A regression is a case that used to pass and now fails after a change to the software or the settings, and regression testing is the habit of rerunning a fixed set of cases after every change to catch exactly that.
nodes.synopsis: Regression testing reruns previously passing cases after software or settings changes to detect newly broken required behaviour; the proposed campaign requires automatic regression on every change and makes captured, synthesised and search-discovered cases permanent tests [f14365, f6944, f7359, f1031, f14368]. Updates have materially changed field behaviour in on-road precedents, while changes to perception, sensors, mounting, braking or calibration can invalidate prior validation; every post-release software change therefore requires reassessment against accumulated safety evidence [f2013, f2940, f1156]. The proposed execution strategy combines smoke tests on every code change, mandatory safety tests on eligible builds, larger overnight or release-gate campaigns, and risk-selected hardware-in-the-loop and physical confirmation [f14369, f14370, f14371, f14372]. Within the four-month validation window, an existing automated pipeline is described as the only affordable way to check late tuning changes against earlier results, although demonstrating unchanged expected output remains a difficult simulation-tool integration task [f13531, f8723]. Regression volume does not establish operating-domain representativeness: the frozen estimation set must remain separate from continuous tuning, and late safety-relevant threshold changes require new independent statistical confirmation for affected claims [f14377, f14374, f14375].

nodes.label: Key performance indicator (KPI) and metric
nodes.text: A metric is any quantity you measure, and a key performance indicator (KPI) is a metric that has been chosen, with a target value, to judge whether the system or the project is succeeding.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus recommends judging off-road automatic braking through multiple metrics, including detection and missed hazards, nuisance interventions, timing and stopping outcomes, rather than one aggregate score; comparisons require common ground truth and hazard zones [f188, f7818, f5210]. No fleet-statistical acceptance KPIs were found in off-road standards or regulations, and there is no accepted sensor-simulation realism score or agreed simulation-quality metric framework; recommended metrics therefore should not be mistaken for published thresholds [f2603, f92, f8952, f9357, f7818]. Operator acceptance requires task-specific unnecessary-warning and intervention rates, with nuisance interventions weighted equally to missed interventions; these rates require real operations, preferably shadow mode before braking is enabled, because an excellent overall false-positive rate can conceal an unwanted intervention in nearly every loading or dump cycle [f3342, f5931, f11767, f759, f3655]. Coverage and agreement claims need visible gaps, frozen-set comparisons, pre-agreed tolerances and explicit failures: a vendor reports coverage rising from 12% to 87% in six months, but the booklet warns against hiding uncovered cells inside an overall coverage score [f1558, f9880, f6678, f9934]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, an initial statistical test plan and coverage metrics are considered realistic by mid-2027; the business case should track cost per credible campaign, wall-clock throughput and analyst hours, not merely raw simulated runs [f846, f10748, f10749].

nodes.label: Constrained multi-objective optimization
nodes.text: Constrained multi-objective optimization is the task of choosing settings that do well on several goals at once (few misses, few false alarms, few unnecessary brakes, little lost production) while never violating certain hard limits.
nodes.synopsis: The introduction, Chapter 9 and glossary consistently frame collision-mitigation tuning as constrained multi-objective optimization: impose hard safety limits first, then optimize nuisance warnings, unnecessary braking and productivity while keeping the Pareto frontier visible [f136, f6671, f14395]. Hard limits cover stopping margin, miss probability, intervention latency and hazardous-scenario coverage; zero misses in critical scenarios is an example, not a universal numerical requirement [f6961, f6962, f14393]. Safety and productivity criteria must be set jointly: detection-only optimization can repeatedly stop production, while a “no false brakes” target pushes toward late or missed braking; pricing these competing outcomes is a documented safety-policy decision, with weight sensitivity analysis required if weighted costs are used [f12171, f7461, f6985, f14846]. Robust optimization should protect the worst stratum or a high percentile, and final settings should favor stable regions and be confirmed independently to limit over-fitting [f6988, f14400, f14403]. Evolutionary and Bayesian multi-objective methods suit expensive evaluations but weaken beyond about 20 parameters or with discontinuous responses; a 2021 on-road example reported up to fivefold speed-up, while no off-road evidence was identified for constraint-based tuning or desirability aggregation [f6674, f6839, f7316, f7311].

nodes.label: Pareto front and trade-off
nodes.text: A trade-off is a situation where improving one goal worsens another, and the Pareto front is the set of settings where no goal can be improved any further without making some other goal worse.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus frames collision-mitigation tuning as constrained multi-objective optimization: missed or late interventions are hard constraints, while nuisance warnings, unnecessary braking and productivity loss remain visible on a Pareto front for accountable safety-policy selection [f136, f6672, f14442]. Excessive conservatism can create alarm fatigue, productivity loss and intervention-created hazards, and operators switching off nuisance-heavy systems gives unnecessary braking a safety significance rather than merely an economic cost [f6569, f14416, f14441]. Evolutionary methods including NSGA-II, attributed to Deb and colleagues in 2002, expose the frontier and support parallel simulation, while multi-objective Bayesian variants cited in 2024 seek the frontier with sample-efficient selection; the identified evidence is generic engineering rather than specific off-road braking evidence [f6970, f14420, f6975, f7324, f7322]. Evolutionary tuning requires many evaluations and carries over-fitting risk, so the booklet recommends nested validation, pre-declared safety constraints for final-point selection and independent confirmation; operational evidence establishing optimum braking conservatism remains thin [f7319, f7320, f7321, f6570]. In the illustrative zero-miss example, A has 2 unnecessary brakes per 100 hours and a generous stopping margin, whereas B has 0.5 per 100 hours and a thinner margin; selecting between them is a safety-policy decision [f14406, f14407, f14408, f14411]. The example also declares C dominated, but its stated comparisons—less margin than A and more nuisance braking than B—do not alone establish that one alternative is at least as good on every objective, leaving the dominance explanation incomplete [f14404, f14409, f14410].

nodes.label: Optimization methods named in the booklet (genetic algorithms, NSGA-II, Bayesian optimization, gradient-free search)
nodes.text: These are the search procedures the booklet names for finding good settings when the only way to judge a setting is to run it through a slow simulation and see what happens.
aliases: Optimization methods named in the booklet
nodes.synopsis: The booklet presents genetic algorithms, NSGA-II, Bayesian optimization and gradient-free search as ways to tune settings through slow simulations; it matches evolutionary methods to braking trade-offs, Bayesian optimization to expensive HIL or physical evaluations, and response surfaces to a few smooth parameters [f14417, f14427, f14428, f14425]. Evolutionary methods, including NSGA-II attributed to Deb and colleagues in 2002, expose the Pareto frontier and parallelise readily, but require many evaluations and leave the acceptable trade-off to policy [f14420, f6970, f7319]. Bayesian optimization uses surrogate predictions and uncertainty for sample-efficient trial selection, but weakens beyond roughly 20 parameters or around discontinuities and can wrongly extrapolate safety [f6974, f7325, f6979]. Although gradient-free search suits threshold-like braking outcomes, this does not remove Bayesian methods’ discontinuity limitations; evolutionary tuning also needs nested validation and independent confirmation to control over-fitting [f14418, f7325, f7320, f7321]. Transfer methods reuse a tuned machine model and search residual settings, but risk negative transfer, while safe multi-task optimization remains research rather than established heavy-machinery practice [f7031, f7341, f7034]. The evidence is predominantly generic engineering: the booklet identifies no specific off-road evidence for evolutionary or Bayesian tuning and no off-road collision-avoidance application of the discussed transfer methods [f7322, f7328, f7035].

nodes.label: Human factors as a tuning objective
nodes.text: Treating human factors as a tuning objective means counting the rate of unnecessary warnings and brakes as a safety goal in its own right, because operators who are interrupted too often stop trusting the system and start disabling it.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats nuisance warnings and unnecessary braking as safety objectives: frequent interruptions can undermine trust and lead operators to ignore or disable the system [f7000, f14430, f14437]. After hard safety constraints are satisfied, tuning should balance nuisance rates, comfort, productivity loss and braking timing through constrained multi-objective optimisation, rather than pursue zero misses or zero nuisance alone [f6963, f14441, f14442]. In a seven-day NIOSH radar trial on a Caterpillar 793B, 580 alarms occurred in 618 reversals; 18% were false, 42% concerned objects already known to the driver, and 41% warranted action, with researchers finding the audible warning disabled after shifts [f14431, f14432, f14433]. Another trial reported false alarms infrequent enough that the system was not ignored, but no study defines an acceptable false-alarm rate for off-road operators [f14434, f14439]. The proposed way to establish practical limits is an operator clinic measuring acceptance thresholds by scenario, with escalation or stopping if the design cannot meet those thresholds; useful tuning measures include unnecessary warnings or interventions per operating hour, loading cycle and reverse maneuver [f10966, f10967, f10968, f14440].

nodes.label: Transferring settings across machine models (physics-based parameterization, archetypes, partial pooling, transfer optimization)
nodes.text: Transferring settings means getting a braking system tuned on one machine model to work on another, with a different size, mass and sensor layout, by expressing the settings in physical terms that can be measured on each machine instead of re-tuning each one by hand.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends transferring collision-mitigation settings through measured physics—not copied thresholds—using speed, latency, braking deceleration, sensor pose and machine envelope; this aims to replace per-model tuning with per-model measurement [f138, f6681, f13909]. It proposes parameterized machine-family models rather than twenty unrelated models, covering dynamics, payload, articulation, sensor installation and environmental effects, with families identified before the 2027 hardware arrives [f7906, f7907, f6124]. This approach addresses a historical three-to-four-year physical-testing and per-model-tuning burden, but whether the product range actually reduces to a few validated families remains an experiment on which the schedule and business case depend [f2030, f6620, f12373]. NIOSH's work used 145 underground haulage machines in five categories to select representative parameter sets, but neither that precedent nor any published ISO rule found establishes how many representative machines validate a manufacturer's family; a published earth-moving benchmark proving model transfer across a machine range was also not found [f6131, f6362, f6132, f6683, f6107]. Partial pooling and transfer optimization are proposed for residual differences, but similarity must be justified, negative transfer is possible, safe multi-task optimization remains research, and no off-road collision-avoidance application of the discussed transfer optimization and meta-learning methods was found [f6682, f646, f7033, f7034, f7035]. Transfer should therefore be checked with envelope-corner validation, bridge tests, a six-week physical anchor campaign after hardware delivery and a substantially different second-machine portability test; extensive bespoke tuning and low reuse should trigger stopping or escalation [f190, f13494, f10946, f10948].

nodes.label: Variant management
nodes.text: Variant management is the discipline of keeping track of every version of the machine, its sensors and its settings, so that the right evidence is attached to the right variant and a change to one does not silently invalidate another.
nodes.synopsis: Variant management must support confidence across machine configurations and operating conditions; historically, comparable braking-function validation took three to four years, largely through physical testing and tuning per machine model [f31, f282, f1174]. The proposed reuse strategy is a parameterized machine-family model validated at envelope corners, with configuration-controlled deltas and targeted bridge tests for each new variant; physics-based families should be identified before the 2027 hardware arrives [f190, f7573, f7908, f6124]. Reuse cannot rest on sensor validation alone, because braking architecture, latency, mass, payload, implements and software integration change outcomes, and the reported mining regime requires separate verification of machines with different braking characteristics [f3437, f5181]. Evidence reuse is potentially a major lever, but no published quantified time-saving case, safe number of removable physical tests, or ISO rule validating a family through N representative machines was found [f617, f261, f1960, f6683]. Even 2,995 independent zero-miss opportunities support only an aggregate detection-at-least-99.9% claim at 95% confidence for a defined population, not sufficient evidence for an entire product family [f6885]. Planning should explicitly delimit covered variants and exclusions, consider an initial release split by machine family with a restricted operating envelope, and establish which subsequent changes trigger partial or full revalidation [f10155, f12326, f10365].

nodes.label: Data lineage and the independence rule
nodes.text: Data lineage is the recorded history of where every piece of data came from and what was done to it, and the independence rule says that the data used to judge a system must have had no part in building or tuning it.
nodes.synopsis: Data lineage records data origins and transformations, while the independence rule requires that evidence used to judge a system played no part in building or tuning it; production-detector outputs cannot serve as independent ground truth [f14471, f99]. Across braking-model calibration, simulation credibility and collision-mitigation tuning, the corpus requires separate development, validation and withheld confirmation or audit data, with whole sites, weather episodes, machine identities or scenario families held together rather than randomly splitting adjacent frames [f6170, f7589, f6992, f6990, f6991]. Audit failures must not feed back into tuning: examined cases used to change thresholds are contaminated, and a late safety-relevant threshold change requires new independent statistical confirmation for the affected claim [f6952, f6953, f14375]. For machine-learning validation and estimation, the stated rule requires real or physically independent data, different assets, sites, people and generators, and documented lineage; its cited ISO/PAS 8800:2024 connection is explicitly on-road evidence and expert opinion from a third-party summary, not direct off-road proof [f7100, f7101]. Reproducible evidence also needs immutable run manifests, versioned assets, checksums and controlled archival, alongside a dedicated data-pedigree workstream; privacy obligations remain unquantified, and technical access to supplier data does not necessarily confer simulation, sharing, retention or derivative-model rights [f11069, f10346, f1145, f10813].

nodes.label: Scenario description languages (OpenSCENARIO, DSL)
nodes.text: A scenario description language is a formal written format for describing a test situation (who is where, moving how, under what conditions) so that a computer can generate and run it, and a domain-specific language (DSL) is a small programming language built for one subject area.
nodes.synopsis: Scenario-language choice determines whether thousands of concrete tests can be generated, varied and traced automatically; the booklet recommends an open, manufacturer-owned, domain-neutral, version-controlled catalogue using Scenic or an in-house YAML schema with an OpenODD-style taxonomy, exporting to OpenSCENARIO where required [f14493, f1606, f14491]. OpenSCENARIO XML 1.4.0 (2026) supports precise synchronized maneuvers, while DSL 2.2.0 (March 2026) supports abstract scenarios, parameter variation and performance indicators, but both retain road-traffic domain models [f13204, f13205, f13206]. OpenSCENARIO XML and OpenDRIVE have broad tool support, yet identified off-road gaps include deformable terrain, airborne particles, vegetation, heavy-machine manipulation and sensor degradation; extensions or a manufacturer domain model are therefore needed rather than abandoning OpenX [f8616, f14488, f7434]. Scenic 3 offers 3D geometry, occlusion-aware visibility and probabilistic placement without lanes, but is not an ISO or ASAM standard, leaving adopters responsible for requirements, rig and exchange-format mappings [f7174, f7177]. No single off-road scenario language covers the problem, and planning should not depend on an off-road standard arriving before mid-2027; existing EMESRT storyboards provide useful mining-hazard content but are not machine-readable [f7147, f7205, f7184].

nodes.label: Campaign (test campaign) and campaign architecture
nodes.text: A test campaign is a planned set of test runs executed together for one purpose, and the campaign architecture is the overall arrangement of campaigns, in time and by purpose, that turns a limited window into a defensible safety claim.
nodes.synopsis: The central recommendation is to complete scenario architecture, fleet-data pipelines, tools and credibility work before prototype arrival in mid-2027, so the roughly 16-week window becomes confirmation, calibration and discrepancy resolution rather than initial method development [f11643, f7379, f7593]. Campaign governance should separate failure-seeking discovery, frozen pre-registered performance estimation, and requirement/regression testing; discovery failure fractions must not be presented as field failure rates [f133, f6935, f6669]. The proposed architecture combines inexpensive high-volume testing with selected high-fidelity and physical checks, including a physical anchor campaign during the first six weeks after hardware delivery [f693, f8871, f13494]. Credibility requires safety-derived acceptance criteria agreed before the main campaign and advance reviewer agreement on evidence taxonomy and substitution rules, because internal engineering confidence does not guarantee an externally acceptable dossier [f11085, f11039, f1988]. Planning remains conditional: no published off-road precedent was found for compressing three or four years of validation into under four months, a working evidence factory rather than completed validation is judged realistic by mid-2027, and compute and result triage remain unbudgeted despite an illustrative four-month, ten-GPU cost of about USD 54,000 [f7350, f372, f10507, f8312]. The campaign should therefore initiate a living evidence base, with field near misses and newly encountered scenarios feeding subsequent validation [f11628, f724].

nodes.label: Credibility of a simulation
nodes.text: The credibility of a simulation is the degree to which a decision maker can trust its results enough to act on them, and it is earned with evidence, not with realistic-looking pictures.
nodes.synopsis: Simulation credibility is an evidence-building process, not a tool feature: the checked frameworks require a defined use, risk-scaled effort, verification, physical-data validation, quantified uncertainty, independent review and a documented validity envelope [f5214, f7525]. On-road acceptance requires documented toolchain credibility and physical spot checks, but ISO 21815 does not explain how to establish credibility, and a 2026 preprint characterizes virtual-testing frameworks as “largely declarative” [f1214, f6928, f4411, f9455]. The ambition to provide confidence across all conditions and configurations faces substantial off-road gaps: no accepted sensor-model qualification method was found for dust, snow or fog, vendor sensor physics lacks independent weather validation, and photorealism alone does not establish validity [f31, f331, f8291, f3711]. Greater model complexity is not necessarily more accurate: a 2026 on-road round robin reported spreads of 0.033 seconds and 0.314 metres for more complex vehicle models, while point-mass models reproduced the prescribed profile exactly [f5907, f5908]. Credible capability took 42 months and 17 partners in PEGASUS and years in every other documented case; documented reductions in physical testing depended on earlier investment, a narrow operating envelope, or both, rather than a universal physical-test percentage [f60, f61, f59, f7534]. For a four-month heavy off-road validation, the recommended route is an analytical safety case, targeted physical tests and simulation under a credibility framework, with credibility evidence built before prototype arrival and no validated sensor-digital-twin claim before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated [f2137, f11643, f11917].

nodes.label: Verification, validation and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ)
nodes.text: VVUQ is the three-part discipline of checking that a simulation program is built correctly (verification), that it matches the real world (validation), and how much its answers could still be wrong (uncertainty quantification).
nodes.synopsis: Across the compared credibility frameworks, VVUQ is part of a risk-scaled process requiring a defined context of use, physical-data validation, quantified uncertainty, independent review and a documented validity envelope [f186, f7525, f7595]. Verification checks implementation against the mathematics, validation checks representation of the real application, and neither replaces uncertainty quantification; calibration to a test is not validation [f10601, f14532, f14535]. For heavy off-road collision mitigation, the booklet recommends separate results for sensors, machine dynamics, brake actuation, environment and system timing, with remaining uncertainty smaller than the decision’s safety margin; otherwise, improve the model, narrow its envelope or add physical tests [f14539, f14537]. The illustrative roadmap places correlation, V&V and uncertainty quantification in February–March 2027, producing a pilot evidence package and model-credibility assessment before an April credibility gate [f9654, f9871]. NASA-STD-7009B, dated 5 March 2024, is a cited foundation, but the research did not verify AIAA G-077, ASME V&V 10 or ASME V&V 20, despite discussing ASME V&V 10 elsewhere [f10599, f7632, f9748]. Evidence gaps remain: few sensor-realism studies report uncertainty bands, and NIOSH identifies continuing gaps in simulation procedures and environmental validation [f4838, f10883].

nodes.label: Code verification versus solution verification
nodes.text: Code verification checks that the simulation software has no errors in how it solves its equations; solution verification estimates how much numerical error remains in one particular run.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet distinguishes code verification, which checks software implementation, from solution verification, which estimates numerical error in a particular run; verification is also distinct from validation against the real application [f14540, f10601]. Code verification uses problems with known exact answers once per software version, while solution verification refines time steps or spatial grids for each kind of run; a stopping-distance change from 41.9 m to 41.2 m after halving the time step illustrates numerical error that belongs in the uncertainty budget [f14541, f14542, f14543]. The credibility frameworks place code and solution verification before comparison with physical data, because unknown numerical artifacts can be mistaken for physics or tuned away [f14545, f14546]. A 2026 on-road round robin reported tool disagreements of 0.033 seconds and 0.314 metres despite prescribed triggering and braking, supporting the warning that a common scenario does not ensure equivalent simulator implementations [f14048, f6352]. Planning should therefore generate code and tool verification evidence, regression tests, solver checks and a verification report, supported by toolchain configuration management; model-verification exercises can begin before prototype arrival [f9727, f11107, f8034, f8238].

nodes.label: Model validation versus model calibration
nodes.text: Calibration adjusts a model's parameters until it matches a set of measurements; validation tests whether the adjusted model then predicts measurements it has never seen, and doing both on the same data is cheating.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats model credibility as a separate task requiring comparison with reality, independent validation evidence, and distinct calibration, validation and withheld-confirmation datasets; failed validation cases must remain recorded [f11310, f12123, f7589, f7590]. Physical tests anchor the validated domain, simulation fills its interior, and physical confirmation remains necessary at boundaries and after influential changes; existing warning-system history cannot validate the new closed-loop braking chain [f7536, f7575]. Important evidence gaps persist: no published validation of heavy-machine braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes was found, sensor studies mostly address individual effects on road vehicles or in laboratories, and the organization currently lacks the described simulation-credibility foundations [f253, f4408, f10414]. A program starting in October 2026 could realistically achieve SIL with partly validated sensor models by mid-2027, but sensor calibration requires real sensors; the final four-month campaign is variously framed as confirmation plus calibration, calibration and testing, or confirmation rather than tuning [f65, f914, f70, f3772, f1611]. The recommended stopping-distance core is a calibrated point-mass model with measured latency, brake build-up lag and condition-dependent worst-case deceleration, while machine-class VIL or proving-ground stops should validate the brake model; the 2025 AGX wheel-loader example demonstrates calibration against a physical machine, not a stated independent-validation result [f5905, f5558, f8292].

nodes.label: Context of use and question of interest
nodes.text: The question of interest is the exact decision a simulation is meant to inform, and the context of use is the precise role the simulation's output plays in making that decision.
nodes.synopsis: The question of interest is the exact decision a simulation informs, while the context of use specifies how its output contributes to that decision; the compared credibility frameworks tie trust to that use, wrong-decision risk, verification, physical-data validation, uncertainty, independent review and a bounded validity domain [f14558, f186, f7595]. For heavy off-road automatic braking, “simulation validates automatic braking” is too broad: detection, classification, decision timing, brake response, stopping distance, impact-speed reduction, nuisance interventions and residual collision risk should be separate claims with claim-specific physical evidence and validity limits [f7648, f7649, f7650]. Fidelity is therefore purpose-specific rather than a global simulator rating: a model suitable for perception may be unsuitable for collision assertions, while an imperfect simulator may still be conservative enough for a particular decision [f4118, f4319, f7815]. The illustrative programme assigns October–November 2026 to establishing signed scope and context of use, and recommends mature context-of-use definitions, acceptance metrics, uncertainty budgets, physical-test design and assessor agreement by mid-2027 [f9652, f7592]. Acceptance remains a planning gap: no off-road authority has committed to accept virtual evidence, and technical excellence alone is insufficient if the relevant reviewer or authority will not accept it for the intended decision [f12177, f10326].

nodes.label: Model risk: influence times consequence
nodes.text: Model risk is how much a simulation's output drives a decision (its influence) combined with how severe a wrong decision would be (the consequence), and it sets how much credibility evidence the simulation must have.
nodes.synopsis: Model risk combines a simulation’s influence on a decision with the consequence of getting that decision wrong, and determines the credibility evidence required; although described as influence multiplied by consequence, it is operationalized as a low/medium/high grid rather than a formula with units [f14567, f7597, f14570]. Across the frameworks reviewed, credibility is conditional on a defined use and operating envelope, with risk-scaled verification, physical-data validation, uncertainty assessment and independent review; the comparisons include ASME V&V 40 (2018), FDA guidance from November 2023, NASA-STD-7009B (2024) and its February 2026 handbook, while NATM evidence is explicitly on-road [f186, f8073, f9454, f9760]. Credibility goals must be agreed before evidence collection, and neither a universal agreement tolerance nor a universal minimum or percentage of physical testing is prescribed [f7642, f7538, f7646, f14577]. For this collision-mitigation program, the physical brake model is judged probably the highest-risk model because of wear, temperature and braking consequences, while sensor models in dust, darkness and glare also carry high risk because validation is weakest there [f14574, f14575]. The resulting planning recommendation is to rate each claim’s risk and retain physical confirmation for high-consequence or weak-model claims; broad procedural scene coverage alone is not adequate if generation rules omit the structures that cause real failures [f14579, f10552, f10990, f3736].

nodes.label: Credibility factors and credibility levels
nodes.text: Credibility factors are the separate aspects of a simulation that are each rated, and credibility levels are the 0 to 4 scale on which the NASA standard scores each factor, without adding the scores into one total.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends NASA-STD-7009B credibility assessment for the collision-mitigation simulation toolchain, reserving technology readiness levels for genuinely novel elements rather than evidence quality [f9433, f14590, f14614]. Credibility is multidimensional and decision-specific: factors are rated separately from 0 to 4, without combining them into a total that could hide weak validation behind stronger areas [f14580, f8018, f14521]. Required factor thresholds should be declared before evidence collection according to decision criticality; validation Level 4 requires all outputs to compare favorably with real-system data across the full operating range in the real environment [f14588, f8065, f14632, f7608]. Reporting should preserve best estimates, uncertainty, factor-level assessments, supporting evidence, limitations and assessor independence, while the planning ledger connects sub-claims to methods, required credibility levels, acceptance criteria, owners and gates [f7587, f8001, f9811]. The original 2008 scale had eight factors in three groups; secondary-source descriptions of an overall lowest-factor score sit in tension with the current standard's rejection of a scalar and the 2026 handbook's warning against totals [f7611, f7612, f14586]. Although the surveyed industries share core credibility principles, a 2026 preprint challenges frameworks as largely declarative and reliant on self-reporting, leaving a tension over their practical adequacy [f7524, f9756, f10324].

nodes.label: Credible Simulation Process and simulation quality (ASAM QSQ)
nodes.text: The Credible Simulation Process is a German industry method for building credibility evidence into every step of a simulation project, and ASAM QSQ is a standardization project trying to define measurable simulation-quality metrics, still unfinished in 2026.
aliases: Credible Simulation Process and simulation quality
nodes.synopsis: Simulation credibility is a documented development process, not a tool feature: SET Level's Credible Simulation Process, published in August 2021, embeds evidence planning, assumptions, verification, validation and credibility documentation throughout product development, with credibility tied to task criticality [f5214, f14592, f14594, f15703]. Related references include M&S SPICE (2023) and prostep ivip's Simulation Credibility technical paper, version 8.1 (2024), but the process frameworks do not specify what physical evidence remains necessary and are not proven for off-road automatic braking [f14595, f14593, f8128, f8130]. ASAM QSQ project P_2025_04 seeks machine-readable simulation-quality metrics with use-case-specific weighting; its proposal workshop took place on 11 September 2025, and it remained under way in 2026 [f14597, f14599]. ASAM reports that standardized simulation-quality metrics, particularly for sensors, do not yet exist, while credibility communities agree validation is required without agreeing on metrics [f14598, f9357]. The planning implication is to use documented credibility discipline for software-in-the-loop development now, while agreeing correlation metrics with the assessor rather than waiting for a standard [f5582, f14602].

nodes.label: NASA-STD-7009 and NASA-HDBK-7009
nodes.text: NASA-STD-7009 is the US space agency's standard for models and simulations, written after the Columbia accident, and NASA-HDBK-7009 is its implementation handbook.
nodes.synopsis: NASA-STD-7009B was approved on 5 March 2024, and its companion NASA-HDBK-7009B was finalized on 3 February 2026; the booklet recommends a simulation credibility scale such as NASA's for the toolchain, reserving technology readiness levels for genuinely novel elements [f7604, f7613, f9433]. The framework requires verification, validation and uncertainty quantification, with validation against the real application rather than merely internal consistency [f7605, f10755]. Required credibility is set by decision criticality: acceptance criteria must be program-defined and approved by technical authority, and each credibility factor is rated from 0 to 4 rather than collapsed into a single total [f8065, f10600, f14609, f7614]. Reports to decision makers must include the best estimate, uncertainty, credibility assessment, limitations and risk of accepting the result, while dissenting technical opinions must also be disclosed [f14610, f9741]. For off-road collision mitigation, the booklet treats NASA's framework as a governance template, not a regulation, and found no direct equivalent for automatic braking on earth-moving machines [f7617, f7740]. A cross-chapter verification gap remains: Chapter 5 says NASA-STD-7009 was not verified and its edition, application dates and simulation clauses need checking, despite later chapters giving specific versions, dates and requirements [f4336, f7604, f7613, f7605].

nodes.label: ASME V&V 10, V&V 20 and V&V 40
nodes.text: These are three standards from the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) on verification and validation: V&V 10 for structural models, V&V 20 for fluid-flow and heat-transfer models, and V&V 40 for judging model credibility by risk, written for medical devices.
nodes.synopsis: ASME V&V 10 covers structural models, V&V 20 fluid-flow and heat-transfer models, and V&V 40 risk-based credibility for medical-device models; the booklet relies most on V&V 40 (2018), interpreted through FDA guidance dated November 2023 [f14616, f14620, f14624, f8072]. V&V 40 ties credibility to a stated context of use and model risk—model influence combined with decision consequence—with credibility goals set prospectively; it prescribes neither a universal acceptance error nor a universal minimum amount of physical evidence [f14621, f14622, f8075, f7790, f8076]. Across the planning and review chapters, ASME and NASA support validation against the real application, rather than internal consistency or simulation run count alone [f9454, f10755, f10884]. The booklet rates V&V 40 and FDA guidance as the most transferable reasoning framework for off-road automatic braking, but they are not proven for that application, and no direct equivalent framework was found for earth-moving-machine automatic braking [f8077, f8078, f7740]. Their scope is physics-based models: vehicle dynamics and brakes can use this framework, while machine-learned perception needs separate assurance; V&V 10 and V&V 20 were named but not verified in the research [f14627, f14623].

nodes.label: FDA guidance on computational modeling for medical devices
nodes.text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published final guidance in November 2023 on assessing the credibility of computer models in medical-device submissions, and the booklet cites it as the clearest regulator-level statement of how to start from the decision rather than from the simulator.
nodes.synopsis: The FDA’s final guidance on computational-model credibility in medical-device submissions was published in November 2023, with a Federal Register notice dated 17 November 2023; it builds on ASME V&V 40-2018 and is identified as the booklet’s clearest regulator-level statement of decision-first credibility assessment [f14628, f7638, f7639, f14629]. Its approach starts with the question of interest and context of use—including the decision, model output and permitted role of that output—then scales credibility by model risk, defined as model influence multiplied by decision consequence [f7640, f8002, f8073]. The framework uses a nine-step process and eight evidence categories, with credibility goals set prospectively and evidence adequacy assessed afterward; neither acceptance error nor the minimum amount of physical evidence is universal [f7643, f7642, f14637, f7646]. Credibility is limited to the stated context of use, so new uses require new or stronger evidence, and a new medical-device variant requires an applicability argument [f7647, f8075, f7903]. The booklet rates FDA/V&V 40 reasoning as highly transferable to off-road automatic braking but not proven there: its physics-based scope can cover vehicle dynamics and brakes, while machine-learned perception needs separate assurance [f8077, f8078, f7645, f8220]. For planning, this supports splitting “simulation validates automatic braking” into separate testable claims and stating credibility relative to intended use, operating envelope and consequences of error [f14638, f10293].

nodes.label: Nuclear practice: EMDAP, PIRT and BEPU
nodes.text: EMDAP is the US nuclear regulator's 20-step process for building and judging a safety-analysis model, PIRT is its ranked list of the physical phenomena that matter most, and BEPU is the nuclear practice of reporting a best-estimate result with its uncertainty rather than a single worst-case number.
aliases: Evaluation Model Development and Assessment Process
nodes.synopsis: NRC Regulatory Guide 1.203, issued in December 2005, defines EMDAP as four elements comprising 20 steps; PIRT ranks important physical phenomena, while BEPU reports a best-estimate result with quantified uncertainty rather than stacked conservative assumptions [f7651, f7652, f14640, f14647]. EMDAP grounds model assessment in physical experiments, emphasizes highly ranked phenomena, and requires scaling, applicability justification and uncertainty treatment when extending predictions beyond the assessment matrix or physical scale [f14644, f7836, f7661, f7663]. For automatic braking, the proposed adaptation separates component-level tests from coupled full-machine tests and uses PIRT-ranked phenomena to decide which physical tests to retain; this is expert guidance, not a nuclear requirement or a framework proven for off-road braking [f7669, f14651, f7670, f8094]. Within the validated parameter hull, changes not affecting ranked phenomena may use documented simulation-only evaluation, changes affecting them should trigger targeted physical tests, and departures from the hull or new phenomena warrant full re-validation [f7912, f7913, f7918]. The safety board should distinguish aleatory from epistemic uncertainty, but the booklet did not individually verify BEPU or CSAU, and its descriptions disagree over whether the criticism of subjective PIRT ranking was peer-reviewed [f8219, f7665, f14652, f7667]. No clean case was found in which simulation accepted under the cited nuclear framework directly produced false confidence; nevertheless, nuclear assumptions and models have been revised following operating experience and accidents [f7994, f7993].

nodes.label: Aerospace practice: FAA similarity rules, DO-178C, DO-330 and MIL-STD-3022
nodes.text: Aviation accepts simulation and prior evidence under strict rules: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lets a validated model cover similar designs and accepts service history for similar systems, DO-178C and DO-330 govern software and the tools that produce evidence, and MIL-STD-3022 is the US defense template for documenting model verification, validation and accreditation.
nodes.synopsis: FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A, dated June 2018, is the booklet’s clearest simulation-as-compliance precedent: a baseline seat undergoes physical dynamic testing and model validation, after which eligible variants within the same family may use simulation; changes to load paths, failure mechanisms, materials or interfaces require new physical evidence [f14654, f14655, f14656, f14657]. Aerospace also accepts satisfactory service history for sufficiently similar systems when differences are identified and justified, but simulation extrapolation remains limited to conditions similar to those physically validated [f14659, f14658]. The transferable rules are that calibration is not validation and agreement with another validated model is insufficient; the seat guidance’s 10% agreement criteria are application-specific and must not become generic off-road braking tolerances [f7625, f7626, f7779]. Validation must address decision-relevant quantities and uncertainty: one FAA example had only 0.3% peak error but 60.4% time-history error, while another required about 1,430 lb to provide 95% confidence below a 1,500 lb limit [f7622, f7555, f7794]. DO-178C concerns airborne software, DO-330 qualifies tools whose outputs are relied upon without further checking but does not establish physics-model validity, and MIL-STD-3022 documents model verification, validation and accreditation; the booklet did not verify these three standards [f14660, f14661, f14662, f14663, f14664]. For the collision-mitigation program, simulator errors can mask defects, so tool qualification should be budgeted separately from establishing model validity [f14669, f14670, f14662].

nodes.label: Rail practice: EN 14363 and DynoTRAIN
nodes.text: EN 14363 is the European rail standard for approving how a vehicle runs on track, and it is the one standard in the booklet that formally lets a validated simulation extend acceptance to new conditions and modified vehicles; DynoTRAIN is the research project that built its validation method.
nodes.synopsis: EN 14363:2016+A2:2022 is the booklet’s only identified standard formally allowing validated simulation to extend acceptance to new conditions and modified vehicles; informative Annex T addresses simulated on-track tests, while Annex U addresses acceptance extension for vehicles of the same basic design [f14672, f15362]. Physical running tests remain the reference anchor: they validate the model before simulation extends conditions, assesses vehicle modifications or compares against an approved reference vehicle [f8136, f14675]. DynoTRAIN developed the validation method, with results published in 2014–2015, drawing on multiple models, tools, vehicles and countries and more than 1,000 simulations; unscalable engineering-judgment review motivated objective metrics [f14677, f7711, f7712]. Agreement is assessed using at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons per quantity from at least 12 track sections, with limits on means and standard deviations across the comparison set [f14680]. The booklet rates rail as its strongest family-transfer and test-reduction precedent for off-road automatic braking, advocating similarity arguments, documented changes and targeted bridging tests, but transfers the acceptance mechanism rather than the much more deterministic wheel-rail physics [f8137, f15373, f14682]. No percentage of physical tests actually removed across rail certifications was published, and no documented accident in which an EN 14363-validated simulation itself created false confidence was found [f7856, f7990].

nodes.label: Technology readiness level (TRL)
nodes.text: A technology readiness level is a 1 to 9 score of how mature a technology is, from a basic idea (TRL 1) to a system proven in real operation (TRL 9), defined for space systems in ISO 16290:2013.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats TRLs as useful vocabulary but weak measurement: component maturity does not establish integration, data, model credibility, scenario coverage or safety-argument maturity, so it recommends TRLs only for genuinely novel elements and NASA-STD-7009B credibility assessment for the simulation toolchain [f9430, f9432, f9433, f14691]. Heavy-off-road maturity must not be inferred from automotive maturity; NIOSH's 2022 review found predominantly component/prototype evidence, only 8% of articles above TRL7, and little operational evidence for complete systems despite commercial availability [f458, f393, f5172, f6378]. MOSH requires independent verification at TRL4 and TRL7, no false interventions or false warnings at TRL4, and extended production monitoring at TRL9—for example, three months or 2,000 hours; its surface CPS TRL7 specification is dated 20 January 2026 [f2459, f2119, f5797, f557]. Hexagon announced on 25 March 2026 that its current-generation Vehicle Intervention System had passed Pretoria TRL4 verification before integrated site testing, but capability-building and verification durations were not found [f1350, f1846]. Immaturity at commitment is identified as the most consistently documented schedule-failure cause, while South African regulation illustrates readiness-policy tension: Regulation 8.10 was suspended in 2015 for unavailable technology, and collision-prevention clauses entered force in December 2022 despite a 2019 finding of immaturity [f9424, f10457, f2891]. Full-scale heavy-machine VIL maturity remains uncertain, and the booklet treats it as emerging and capital-intensive rather than a proven shortcut; the cited 2024 finding of no industrial-ready full-scale platform is specifically on-road evidence [f5765, f13401, f5340].

nodes.label: Sim-to-real gap, measured
nodes.text: The measured sim-to-real gap is the difference between what a simulation produces and what the real sensor, machine or function produces in the same situation, expressed as a number with a stated metric and condition rather than as a general worry.
nodes.synopsis: The recommended programme is a hybrid environment factory: parameterised representative sites anchored to surveyed real sites, with prototype tests measuring latency, detection-range correlation, brake timing, stopping dynamics, repeatability and model error [f76, f3705, f879]. Credibility should be quantified separately for each phenomenon using several metrics, not one universal score; the corpus reports no consensus on quantifying the domain gap and no accepted weather-realism score [f7468, f7552, f476, f11950]. Reported gaps are substantial but condition-specific: Sim2Radar produced 251 simulated versus 2,057 real points per frame across five indoor scenes, CropCraft reported a 9.9% average mIoU gap, and a November 2025 scan comparison reported DCD of 0.63 and segmentation mIoU of 21% [f3932, f3731, f4442]. Weather agreement depends on matching conditions: lidar rain mismatch increased with rain rate and depended on drop-size assumptions, while fog mismatch increased as visibility fell; realistic tracking outputs can also conceal large raw-data errors [f4414, f7556, f7557, f7821, f4540]. The main technical risk is the absence of a published quantitative off-road comparison of simulation-tuned brake thresholds against field results, alongside missing generic stopping-error benchmarks and validation gaps for dust, ultrasonic weather effects and thermal-camera conditions [f155, f251, f6094, f7561, f4581, f4591]. Physical confirmations should update discrepancy models rather than silently tune away errors, with comparisons at both sensor and perception-output levels; warning signs include no agreed correlation metrics by the first quarter of 2027, per-scene tuning, unreported residuals and uncertainty, and stalled or worsening held-out real performance [f7385, f11105, f10756, f10784].

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.text: In this field, correlation means the demonstrated agreement between a simulation and a physical test of the same situation, measured with agreed metrics; it is the act of anchoring the virtual world to the real one.
nodes.synopsis: Correlation is a prerequisite for credible simulation, not a substitute for physical testing: credibility applies only to dimensions with adequate paired simulation-to-real agreement, and Euro NCAP’s 2026 protocol, version 1.00 dated March 2025, requires correlation before predictions plus random physical verification [f7375, f1215, f1719]. Agreement must be assessed with multiple metrics and bounded by operating regimes, configuration and pre-agreed tolerances; a camera model may agree in daylight but fail under glare [f188, f7552, f9934, f7469]. Physical evidence shows both achievable agreement and important limits: underground stop-zone repeats agreed within about ±13 cm, while an on-road 2026 round robin still showed tool disagreements of 0.033 s and 0.314 m in a prescribed brake-only test [f5930, f6351]. The proposed programme should own correlation data in-house, use real sensors and machines for correlation, and gate progress on evidence rather than calendar dates; the four-month window cannot accommodate all correlation and other validation needs, and missing agreed metrics by the first quarter of 2027 is an early warning [f201, f10894, f9509, f378, f10756]. Remaining evidence gaps include unconfirmed simulated-to-real point-cloud comparison for the 2026 CARLA mining-dust framework and missing independent correlation results for Cognata and heavy-machine evidence for BeamNG.tech; large simulation counts cannot compensate for an uncorrelated model [f4743, f8415, f8509, f12203].

nodes.label: Scalar-output agreement
nodes.text: Scalar-output agreement compares one number from the simulation with the same number from the physical test, for example stopping distance or the time at which braking was triggered, usually as a percentage error with an agreed error band.
nodes.synopsis: Scalar-output agreement compares a simulation result with its physical-test counterpart using absolute difference divided by the measured value, usually against a pre-agreed percentage band; an illustrative stopping-distance comparison of 38.0 m measured versus 39.5 m simulated gives 3.9% error [f14727, f14728, f14731]. For heavy off-road automatic braking, the booklet recommends stopping-distance, intervention-time, residual impact-speed, range and relative-speed errors, but requires scalar checks to be combined with timing, waveform, distribution and outcome evidence [f14737, f8042]. Scalar agreement alone can be misleading: one aviation comparison had only 0.3% peak error but 60.4% time-history error, and equal peak decelerations can still produce different collision outcomes if their timing differs [f7555, f14736]. Aviation guidance uses application-specific 10% criteria, and one example achieved 3.42% peak error and 7.2% time-history error; the booklet explicitly warns against adopting 10% as a generic off-road braking tolerance [f7777, f7782, f7779]. Acceptance bands must also account for uncertainty: in the aircraft-seat example, a 1,500 lb limit and approximately 42 lb standard deviation require a prediction below about 1,431 lb for 95% confidence, so a nominal prediction of 1,490 lb is insufficient [f14732, f14733, f14734, f14735].

nodes.label: Time-history agreement
nodes.text: Time-history agreement compares a whole curve over time from the simulation with the same curve from the physical test, so that differences in timing and shape are caught, not only differences in the peak value.
nodes.synopsis: Time-history agreement compares complete simulated and measured curves to expose timing and shape differences that peak-only checks miss; for automatic braking, identical peak deceleration can still produce different collision outcomes [f14739, f7783]. The booklet’s FAA example shows 0.3% peak error but 60.4% time-history error, whereas another example has 3.42% peak error and 7.2% time-history error, both within that example’s 10% guideline; these are aviation examples, not stated heavy-machine acceptance thresholds [f7785, f7782, f7764]. The proposed heavy-machine program should validate the entire chain from detection through brake-pressure build-up to deceleration, speed and position, including distance-to-object and relative-speed histories near the collision boundary, using multiple agreement metrics rather than one score [f7786, f7787, f8042]. Available methods include Sprague-Geers magnitude-and-phase comparison and ISO 18571’s corridor, phase, magnitude and slope rating; the glossary identifies ISO 18571 use in a 2026 automatic-braking/proving-ground demonstration [f7763, f15332, f14745]. Cross-chapter sensor evidence also includes Haider et al.’s time-domain and point-cloud validation, dated October 2022 in Chapter 6 and associated with an August 2023 publication in Chapter 10, but both accounts identify the evidence as on-road [f4505, f7819].

nodes.label: Distributional agreement
nodes.text: Distributional agreement compares the whole spread of many simulated results with the whole spread of many measured results, which is needed when repeated runs of the same situation legitimately differ.
nodes.synopsis: Distributional agreement compares the spreads of repeated simulated and measured results, rather than matching individual runs or points, because perception trials and sensor returns legitimately vary [f14749, f14750, f4801, f12621, f7802]. The booklet recommends multi-level, multi-metric validation, including distributions and downstream perception or closed-loop outcomes; sensor-family reports should use withheld real raw data rather than rely on visual realism [f14716, f14797, f10558]. In a November 2025 on-road study, density-aware Chamfer distance correlated best with perception among the metrics compared, but real-versus-simulated scans averaged DCD 0.63 with only 21% segmentation mIoU, and prediction of safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain [f4815, f4816, f5067]. The area validation metric measures the area between simulated and measured cumulative distributions in the output quantity’s units; the booklet treats it as model-form uncertainty and describes extrapolating it to untested conditions as an additional prediction margin [f7796, f7797, f7798]. Its acceptance role is disputed because greater experimental scatter can make a model appear better, and mixing epistemic and aleatory uncertainty can produce over- or under-compensation [f7799, f7800, f8191]. Rail validation supplies an established distribution-based analogue, using at least 24 comparisons per quantity across at least 12 track sections, with statistics and limits applied to the deviations [f7803, f7804, f7805, f7807].

nodes.label: Image and field similarity metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, FID, mutual information)
nodes.text: These metrics score how much a simulated image, radar map or other field of values resembles a real one; they are useful for rendering quality but can disagree with whether a detector behaves the same on both.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats image and field similarity as measures of appearance and structure, not proof of perception or safety equivalence: PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS require pixel-matched pairs, whereas FID compares image collections [f14791, f14773, f14771]. Chapter 5 documents substantial viewpoint sensitivity: Para-Lane (2025) falls from 22.99 dB PSNR in the recorded lane to 17.05 dB in the adjacent lane, while MV² (August 2026) falls from 29.13 dB at drone height to 10.36 dB from a car; these results are on-road evidence [f3707, f3709]. Generative novel-view methods achieved 13.19–20.82 dB PSNR on Waymo in a 2026 preprint, which the booklet interprets as low fidelity for safety testing rather than metric-faithful validation [f3821, f3822, f4330]. Across Chapters 6 and 9, improved visual or radar-map similarity does not reliably imply equivalent system behavior: RadaRays improved mutual-information and structural-similarity scores, yet a detector trained on real radar images still failed on simulated images [f4824, f14776, f7071]. Whether FID and certain geometric distances predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain, and FID does not target a specific perception algorithm [f5067, f4819]. Planning should therefore pair image similarity with task-level and closed-loop validation, checking higher assessment layers rather than inferring them from lower-layer agreement [f4827, f14778, f14797].

nodes.label: Error metrics (MAE, MAPE, RMSE)
nodes.text: MAE, MAPE and RMSE are three standard ways to turn many individual simulation-versus-measurement differences into one average error figure.
nodes.synopsis: MAE, MAPE and RMSE summarize simulation-versus-measurement differences as average error figures, but they hide the error distribution and are insufficient on their own for complete validation [f14779, f14785, f14789]. On-road lidar mapping with pose refinement reduced map thickness error from 4.5 cm to 1.3 cm MAE; a separate 2022 physical-lidar study reported 14.65 cm mean depth error at 33 m against an Ouster sensor, using indoor and outdoor objects rather than a job site [f3804, f3929]. A ray-traced lidar model achieved MAPE values of 1.7% for amplitude, 8.5% for point count and 9.3% for mean intensity only when the full processing chain and sensor imperfections were modeled; the cited evidence is on-road [f4417, f12605]. Published lidar applications report MAPE rather than use it as a thresholded acceptance criterion, and MAPE misbehaves near zero measured values [f7766, f14783]. Low average error can coexist with dangerous optimism near the collision boundary, while conventional mean and RMSE errors cannot accommodate both aleatory and epistemic uncertainty in stochastic radar detections [f7816, f4821]. The corpus reports that a validated radar or camera dust model with a published error metric was searched for but not found [f254].

nodes.label: Task-level gap versus pixel-level similarity
nodes.text: Pixel-level similarity asks whether a simulated sensor output looks like the real one; task-level gap asks whether the software that uses it (detector, tracker, braking logic) behaves the same on both, and a pretty image can still fail the second test.
nodes.synopsis: Across the booklet, visually convincing scenes and improved image-quality scores do not establish sensor fidelity or equivalent detector, tracker and braking behaviour; photorealism is insufficient as validation evidence [f3711, f7071, f10554, f14790]. Radar studies illustrate the gap: RadaRays improved image similarity and produced realistic odometry, yet a detector trained on real data failed to transfer, while the 2025 wheel-loader study reported failure on most simulated cars, partly because material properties were guessed [f4826, f4423]. In a November 2025 point-cloud study, density-aware Chamfer distance correlated best with perception among the metrics compared, but real-versus-simulated scans still averaged 0.63 DCD with only 21% segmentation mIoU; whether these distributional metrics predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain [f4441, f4442, f5067]. Appearance metrics are not universally uninformative: a 2024 study found correlations with visual-odometry behaviour as gamma varied, and camera photorealism may matter, but fidelity must be selected for the sensor and tested requirement rather than ranked by screenshots [f4758, f4331]. Validation should compare withheld real raw data with simulation at sensor-output, perception, task and closed-loop levels, including TTC, trigger distance, false brakes and missed brakes; the booklet identifies function-level perception and fusion validity as a gap in its seven-question scope [f10558, f4444, f12867, f5086]. Practical checks include a pre-registered one-sensor correlation pilot and weather falsification tests against measured degradation, with good virtual metrics but rain-, dust-, night- or glare-clustered field failures treated as warning signs [f10934, f10937, f12455].

nodes.label: Closed-loop agreement
nodes.text: Closed-loop agreement checks that, when the simulated braking system is allowed to act and the simulated machine responds, the outcome (when the brake fired, where the machine stopped, and whether it braked when it should not have) matches the real machine doing the same.
nodes.synopsis: Closed-loop agreement is the ultimately relevant validation layer for automatic braking: matched real and simulated runs must agree on brake timing, stopping trajectory or location, clearance, and false or missed interventions—not merely image similarity [f14803, f14804, f14805, f4444]. Existing warning-system history can validate inputs and submodels, but replay cannot establish the consequences of a changed machine trajectory; after the first new brake command, evidence depends on the machine, environment and sensor models [f191, f1102, f14807, f14808]. Separately validated perception and brake models do not establish combined safety, because timing, communications, saturation and operator interactions can produce emergent failures; physical full-system stopping tests should therefore remain at the collision/no-collision boundary [f8196, f8197, f14812]. An on-road IDIADA–MathWorks demonstration recorded on 14 April 2026 correlated a closed-loop AEB simulation with production-vehicle proving-ground tests using ISO 18571 metrics, but no public demonstration was found jointly covering heavy machines, many geometries, more than 100 site types, severe weather and soiling, and closed-loop braking [f1269, f4409].

nodes.label: Tolerance and acceptance band
nodes.text: A tolerance, or acceptance band, is the amount of disagreement between simulation and physical test that is allowed before the model is judged not good enough for the decision it supports.
nodes.synopsis: Across the corpus, no credibility framework supplies a universal simulation-to-test tolerance or physical-test percentage; acceptance must reflect model influence, decision consequence, applicability and uncertainty [f187, f7535, f14577]. Sector-specific numbers are precedents, not off-road defaults: FAA seat guidance uses 10% tolerances that must not be copied to braking, while Euro NCAP VT v1.00 (2025) requires at least 75% qualification per verification-test cluster but leaves several ISO-score and KPI tolerances provisional [f7537, f14668, f2627, f2628, f2503]. The off-road evidence gap remains material: no sensor-simulation fidelity thresholds were found, few realism studies predefine acceptance thresholds, and documented terrain-model capabilities do not establish machine-specific stopping-distance accuracy [f5220, f5764, f4839, f6016]. The programme should pre-agree tolerances and metrics, distinguish advisory, urgent-warning, speed-reduction and full-braking interventions, and bound its conclusions by operating regime and configuration [f9930, f2634, f9934]. A narrow simulated clearance is not a robust pass when uncertainty is comparable to the safety margin; reference measurements must be substantially more precise than acceptance margins, and reports should carry tolerances alongside results [f4343, f14013, f7473, f4344].
