The example roadmap places initial checks in December–January, a correlation campaign in February–March and a threshold decision at an April gate; failed calibration criteria, excessive stopping-distance residuals or tolerances beyond production capability should trigger recalibration, stopping or escalation [f9872, f6422, f10942, f10945].

nodes.label: Uncertainty: aleatory versus epistemic
nodes.text: Aleatory uncertainty is natural randomness that no amount of study removes; epistemic uncertainty is lack of knowledge that more data or a better model could reduce, and the two must be tracked separately.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus explicitly identifies both aleatory and epistemic uncertainty in stochastic radar detections, for which mean and RMSE errors alone are inadequate; it recommends distribution-level validation when individual sensor returns cannot meaningfully be matched one-to-one [f4821, f4801]. Across the safety case, sensor, operator-response and machine-response uncertainties should remain separate, and the illustrative two-second operator/mechanical delay must not be treated as a validated population distribution or percentile [f3504, f11830, f3475]. Stopping predictions and braking escalation should use uncertainty-bounded stopping margins, while ground-truth measurements need independent uncertainty budgets and an explicit unavailable or ambiguous state [f6210, f6280, f5394, f7473]. Credibility requires physical anchors, a stated validity envelope and explicit uncertainty, rather than simulation run count; the proposed programme claim is therefore bounded by machine configuration, operating envelope, safety-function scope and residual uncertainty [f11325, f10884, f9724]. Important gaps remain: few sensor-realism studies report uncertainty bands, unknown exposure distributions can destabilize rare-event reweighting, and active-learning uncertainty estimates can themselves be wrong [f4838, f6852, f6862]. Planning should communicate numeric ranges rather than blanket contingency or verbal hedges, while treating absent correlation metrics by the first quarter of 2027 as an early credibility warning; uncertainty graphics are not guaranteed to improve trust [f9641, f9863, f9474, f11006, f9892].

nodes.label: Sensitivity analysis
nodes.text: Sensitivity analysis changes a model's inputs, one or several at a time, to learn which of them most affect the output, so that effort, physical tests and worry go where they matter.
nodes.synopsis: Sensitivity analysis identifies which inputs most affect safety outputs, directing careful measurement and physical validation toward influential inputs while allowing weakly influential inputs to remain nominal; preliminary studies can start before prototype arrival [f14840, f14841, f8239, f14849]. NIOSH’s 2018 stopping tool varied six inputs at five values each, producing 30 simulation rows, and its transient modeling found strong sensitivity to brake force, grade, initial speed, lag and rolling resistance [f6179, f6081]. Operator response should be treated as uncertain rather than represented by one supposedly validated average, and cost-weighted tuning should test weight sensitivity, impose safety constraints before aggregation and favor stable operating regions over knife-edge optima; these are booklet recommendations, not a universal standards requirement [f3478, f7310, f6989, f6986]. Sensitivity analysis should guide machine-variant transfers and validation-envelope corners, but whether a small set of extremes bounds all intermediate machines remains uncertain because geometry, articulation, occlusion and braking can behave non-monotonically [f7909, f7916, f7919, f8178, f8179]. Credibility packages should combine sensitivity and uncertainty analysis with a documented validity envelope, while test allocation across fidelity levels should follow sensitivity and correlation evidence rather than assumptions or sheer simulation counts [f8043, f9328, f8953]. The corpus cites sensitivity analysis within UNECE’s on-road NATM credibility requirements under UN R152 and NASA-STD-7009B, dated 5 March 2024, while recommending tornado charts for presenting the validation plan and identifying schedule-sensitive tasks [f4830, f10599, f9483, f16328].

nodes.label: Validity envelope (domain of validity) and extrapolation
nodes.text: The validity envelope is the documented range of machines, sensors, conditions and scenarios within which a simulation has been validated against physical data; extrapolation is using the simulation outside that range, and it is where credibility fails fastest.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus recommends building a measured, independently reviewed credibility envelope before the prototype arrives, and substituting virtual for physical evidence only within that envelope [f71, f10466, f72, f10467]. Across credibility frameworks, this requires a defined use, risk-scaled effort, verification, physical validation, quantified uncertainty and independent review; physical tests anchor the model and confirm boundaries and influential changes [f186, f7536]. Validation does not automatically transfer across sites, weather, machine models or sensor positions: extensions require similarity arguments plus bridging evidence, while replay proves only conditions actually recorded [f614, f7569, f95, f5241]. Neural reconstruction illustrates the extrapolation risk: Para-Lane (2025) reports PSNR falling from 22.99 to 17.05 dB between recorded and adjacent lanes, while MV² (August 2026) reports 29.13 dB at drone height versus 10.36 dB from a car [f3707, f3709]. The planning gap is substantial: the organization reviewed lacks a documented credibility assessment, defined use envelope and validation against reality, and published operating limits were not found for several commercial precedents [f10414, f1656, f1660, f1666].

nodes.label: Validated parameter ranges and known model limits
nodes.text: Validated parameter ranges are the specific values of each input (speed, mass, mount height, visibility) between which a model has been checked against physical data, and known model limits are the documented places where it is known to be wrong, approximate or silent.
nodes.synopsis: Model credibility is specific to validated parameter space and configuration; the roadmap should define an applicability envelope and extrapolation rules, and label every simulation result as interpolated or extrapolated [f5072, f10488, f9733, f8016]. Sensor pose needs an explicit validated range, relocation outside it should trigger bridge testing, and repaired machines need a field diagnostic confirming return to the validated state [f7922, f10810]. Important sensor and scene limits remain: neural reconstruction degrades sharply beyond a 1–4 m viewpoint shift, degraded-visibility sensor models are least validated, and on-road nighttime pedestrian avoidance was 0% in 2019 and 60% in 2025 despite shortcomings not revealed by daytime protocols [f241, f7886, f7585]. Mechanical evidence also has narrow scope: published mining stopping tests cover unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, cited terramechanics findings come from single-wheel rigs and sand rather than full machines, and common Chrono handling tire models do not work on deformable terrain [f5182, f6012, f8498]. Machine-family claims should identify invariant parameters and bounds confirmed physically, while the physical anchor campaign should test family membership, conservatism and failure regions [f5784, f6416]. Simulation should replace only defined repetitive tests within specified machine, sensor, configuration and environment envelopes, retaining physical boundary tests; weak-model regions must be established empirically, and the brief does not justify a fixed fraction of physical testing to retain [f10910, f10991].

nodes.label: Held-out measurements and independent physical data
nodes.text: Held-out measurements are physical test results deliberately kept away from the people and processes that build and tune the model, so that they can later prove, rather than suggest, that the model predicts reality.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats independent physical measurements as essential to simulation credibility: calibration, validation and withheld confirmation data must remain separate, and synthetic data can augment training but cannot replace real validation data [f7589, f12212, f139]. The preferred safety argument uses physical tests to establish anchors and boundaries, independent validation to demonstrate prediction with known uncertainty, simulation to cover the interior, and targeted physical confirmation at high-risk boundaries and after influential changes [f12238]. In practice, braking models should be fitted on designated calibration data, frozen and challenged on unused boundary conditions; sensor validation should use withheld raw measurements to assess sensor-output distributions and downstream perception, not merely visual resemblance [f6167, f10558]. Blind prediction is a central safeguard: Sandia challenge predictions often diverged from experiment, while improving virtual metrics alongside stalled or worsening held-out real performance signals simulator overfitting [f9752, f9753, f10784]. Planning should secure seasonal reference data during winter 2026–2027 and agree correlation metrics by the first quarter of 2027; evidence generated only during the four-month period after the mid-2027 prototype arrives warrants particular skepticism if that period also includes parameter discovery and tuning [f10953, f10756, f8055]. Important gaps remain: weather-simulator reference data is thin, and off-road radar-clutter simulation is considered low credibility until validated against company measurements; conditions without credible referent data should trigger escalation or exclusion from the operating envelope [f10480, f12650, f10956, f11016].

nodes.label: Deciding which physical tests to keep and which to replace
nodes.text: The decision follows information value and extrapolation risk, not a fixed percentage: physical tests stay where they anchor new physics, boundaries and high-consequence outcomes, and simulation fills the repetitive interior between those anchors.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus recommends using simulation to select scarce physical tests and expand evidence around physical anchors, rather than promising wholesale replacement; no checked credibility framework prescribes a universal physical-test percentage [f484, f11311, f7534]. Physical tests should identify parameters, validate model fidelity, confirm boundaries and high-risk outcomes, and satisfy deterministic requirements, while simulation fills the validated domain’s interior [f6137, f7396, f7536, f4110]. Substitution should remain inside a measured, independently reviewed credibility envelope, with physical testing retained for weakly modelled conditions such as dust, soiling, vibration and heavy rain [f10467, f4972, f74]. Every documented reduction depended on years of prior investment, a narrow operating envelope, or both; Volvo CE’s reverse-only wheel-loader example covers 3–15 km/h, making the proposal to replace most physical testing within four months a substantial credibility challenge [f59, f1258, f10389]. No off-road acceptance of simulation replacing prescribed physical tests was found, and ISO 3450 requires physical brake-performance testing, but incomplete access to full standards prevents treating non-discovery as a blanket prohibition [f2103, f10431, f7544].

nodes.label: Extending a validated model to another machine model or sensor position
nodes.text: A model validated on one machine is extended to another by showing what changed, whether the change can affect a validated phenomenon, and what targeted bridging tests close the gap; it is never inherited automatically.
nodes.synopsis: Evidence reuse across machine models is described as the biggest validation lever but the least documented; extension requires similarity arguments and bridging evidence, not automatic inheritance [f366, f189, f7569]. The proposed method uses a parameterized family model validated at envelope corners, a documented change assessment, and targeted bridge tests; a variant inside the validated family hull receives reduced physical tests, typically brake calibration and sensor field-of-view and detection checks [f7573, f12368]. Sensor relocation can invalidate the envelope even with unchanged software: blind-area geometry changes, height shifts degrade neural reconstruction more than sideways shifts, and learned sensor models extrapolate weakly to new viewpoints [f12370, f11552, f82, f4489]. Explicit geometry and physics-based sensor models offer useful transfer capabilities, but viewpoint-valid geometry alone does not validate appearance or sensor response [f4181, f4466, f4174]. Rail, aerospace and nuclear practice provide formal extension precedents, yet no published off-road variant-transfer example or formally accepting off-road regulator was found; neither the removable physical-test count for dozens of variants nor an accepted transferred-brake-model test count was established [f7570, f7571, f7572, f7574, f2943, f1960, f6557].

nodes.label: Using the existing warning system's field history as a reference
nodes.text: The years of recorded operation of the current warning system can validate the simulation's inputs and some of its submodels, but not the new closed-loop braking chain, and only if three traps are respected.
nodes.synopsis: The existing warning fleet is the best available source of real off-road exposure, sensor recordings and false-alarm history: its logs can validate simulation inputs and submodels, but not the new closed-loop braking chain [f1252, f5122, f6611, f7575]. Collection should begin immediately, with fleet logging through winter 2026–2027, a searchable event corpus and exposure model; several early experiments can start in October 2026 [f708, f730, f10914]. Open-loop replay against independent ground truth establishes the warning-system baseline, while direct sensor-model reuse requires equivalent sensors and mounting, usable ground truth and coverage of relevant conditions; prototype sensor equivalence remains unknown [f94, f7930, f10891]. Three central traps limit inference: relevant-encounter exposure may be unknown, operator braking censors counterfactual outcomes, and warning history never exercised the detection-to-command-to-stopping chain; automatic braking also changes future human-system interaction [f12357, f7480]. Independent alarm evidence remains old and sparse: the cited 2006 NIOSH Caterpillar 793B study reported 18% false alarms and 42% nuisance alarms, and found the audible alarm switched off after shifts [f101, f102, f103, f104]. Despite its value, Chapter 6 did not consider this field-data source, no standard or assessor acceptance of legacy history as a simulator-validation reference was found, and the new braking target must come from its own hazard analysis rather than matching warning performance [f5121, f7580, f11989].

nodes.label: False confidence from simulation
nodes.text: False confidence is trusting a result more than its evidence justifies, and the booklet documents three ways it happens: using a model outside its data, choosing a metric that hides the error, and relying on a test protocol that never sampled the dangerous condition.
nodes.synopsis: Across chapters, false confidence arises when plausible or repeatable simulation results exceed their evidence: millions of tests cannot establish operating-domain coverage, and statistical methods cannot repair missing hazards or an unvalidated simulator [f671, f650, f8916]. Extrapolation is a central warning: Columbia was lost in 2003 partly because a model was used outside its validity envelope, with debris estimated at about 400 times the size represented in its test database (640 times in an early briefing); even a well-calibrated braking model may fail on downhill or different-load conditions [f11326, f7582, f6171]. Metrics can conceal error: a 2021 radar study found deceptively realistic tracking despite the largest raw-point-cloud gap, while CVPR 2024 on-road research showed that open-loop planning metrics could be matched using vehicle state alone [f4540, f5518]. Test design also matters: incorrect scenario distributions invalidate sampling-based performance claims, correlated frames artificially narrow confidence intervals, and shared assumptions across sensors, collision logic and the pass/fail oracle can produce consistent but misleading results [f6833, f5461, f12118]. These risks extend beyond sensors to site generation, terrain physics and human response: generators may omit failure-generating structure, common handling tire models do not work on deformable terrain, and on-road warning-system benefit estimates ranged from 53% to 96% with the chosen driver model [f3736, f8339, f3045]. Planning should therefore avoid blanket validation claims, review oracle independence, and separate replay, post-intervention simulation and real-machine stopping evidence; the proposing organization has not yet validated its simulator against reality, leaving replacement of physical evidence unjustified [f9762, f10233, f5551, f10475].

nodes.label: Simulation specialist's objections
nodes.text: In the booklet's hostile review, the simulation specialist's objections reduce to three: the model is unvalidated, the simulator architecture is being frozen against assumed hardware, and metrics risk being chosen for convenience after the fact.
nodes.synopsis: The simulation specialist’s three core objections are an unvalidated model, simulator architecture frozen against assumed hardware, and metrics chosen for convenience after results are known; the hostile review ranks the simulator’s unearned right to replace physical evidence as its strongest objection [f14949, f14525]. Credibility requires a defined validity envelope and evidence beyond internal consistency, because shared simplifying assumptions across the virtual sensor, collision logic and test oracle can produce consistent but misleading results [f10593, f14952, f10606]. The toolchain is built against assumed hardware until mid-2027, while changes to sensors, mounting, controller timing or the brake controller in 2027 can invalidate it without impact analysis; the specialist therefore recommends resolving supplier dependencies before architecture freeze and reserving physical re-correlation tests [f14954, f14955, f14956]. Metrics and thresholds should be declared prospectively, absence of agreed correlation metrics by early 2027 is a warning sign, and physical confirmatory tests should be selected by the assessor or risk analysis rather than convenience [f14957, f14959, f14958]. Before committing to the plan, the specialist recommends a credibility-framework pilot and an evidence package covering independent held-out physical validation, uncertainty and sensitivity analysis, configuration control, revalidation rules and explicitly unsupported claims [f10602, f14961]. The cited European automated-vehicle credibility requirements are explicitly on-road, while the planning guidance calls for recording dissenting technical opinions rather than leaving objections undocumented [f14951, f10234].

nodes.label: The credibility package (what a safety board or outside assessor expects to see)
nodes.text: The credibility package is the full set of documents an internal safety board or external assessor needs before relying on simulation evidence, and it contains far more than simulator results.
nodes.synopsis: The credibility package is broader than simulation results: it must establish context of use, requirements traceability, criteria declared in advance, independent physical evidence, a validity envelope, failed-test disposition and residual risk; internal engineering confidence alone does not guarantee an acceptable dossier [f12291, f1988]. Decision makers expect best estimates, uncertainty statements, factor-by-factor credibility assessments and explicit limitations, with calibration, validation and withheld confirmation data separated and failed validation cases retained [f193, f7587, f7590]. For heavy off-road work, the recommended file records sensor and machine configurations, reference-instrument uncertainty, environmental conditions, acceptance thresholds, invalid regions and validation-data tuning, while the validity record distinguishes physically validated, interpolated and extrapolated regions [f4840, f8012, f8019]. Acceptance precedents requiring dossiers, physical-to-virtual correlation and verification are on-road evidence, and sensor-realism publications lack a common reporting format, leaving a need to identify the accepting authority and agree the evidence approach early [f1564, f6928, f4836, f1987, f7592]. A program starting in October 2026 can realistically have an assessor-seen dossier by mid-2027; the proposed August–September 2027 release gate requires an envelope, limitations and residual uncertainty, and permits release, restricted release or withholding [f69, f10201]. All seven reviewers should receive a one-page credibility map linking claims, evidence types, validating real-world data and responsibility for remaining uncertainty; late exposure of the credibility argument risks rejection, and reproducibility and traceable evidence retention are expected [f10907, f11038, f9997, f10706].

nodes.label: Independent review of the test plan
nodes.text: Independent review of the test plan is having people who did not write the plan, and who do not need it to succeed, examine what will be tested, how, with which metrics and thresholds, before the tests begin.
nodes.synopsis: Independent test-plan review means reviewers who neither wrote the plan nor need it to succeed examine its scope, methods, metrics and thresholds before testing; thresholds must be fixed before results are seen [f14988, f14992]. Across Chapters 1, 12 and 13, the recommendation is to embed independence early, review the plan before prototype safety testing, and build a measured, independently reviewed credibility envelope before the prototype arrives [f741, f10356, f10466]. Review should cover data separation, physical confirmation, scenario coverage and the validity envelope, while skeptical reviewers challenge assumptions, acceptance thresholds, integration dependencies and evidence independence [f14991, f9962]. Scheduling requires early agreement on the assessment counterpart and review criteria, and a safety/legal dry run should produce written comments on a representative evidence package months before launch; review queues can become the critical path [f8245, f10964, f14998]. The corpus presents independent review as a practice- and standards-supported safeguard, not a proven cure: it cannot rescue incomplete engineering late, and the booklet found no evidence that red teams improve engineering outcomes [f15001, f1056, f15000].

nodes.label: Standard
nodes.text: A standard is a written agreement, produced by a committee of experts, that says how something should be made, tested or described so that everyone means the same thing.
nodes.synopsis: Existing standards cover collision avoidance, automatic intervention, control-system hardware and software, and environmental qualification, and provide scenario vocabulary, but they become binding only through legal incorporation or other applicable conformity and contractual routes; South Africa's braking mandate preceded a validation standard [f830, f315, f2062, f2144, f11458]. Heavy-machinery standards accept simulation as one verification method, but no off-road clause accepting it as a replacement for the physical tests discussed was found; the full paid texts were unavailable, so this is not evidence that replacement is prohibited [f9456, f7739]. The reviewed standards do not define simulation-credibility acceptance or prescribe testing quantities: gaps include detection and false-alarm sample sizes, required virtual job-site counts, and a published ISO rule validating a machine family from N representative machines [f5110, f5154, f5160, f11933, f6683]. Survey capture is the only environment-creation method identified whose geometric accuracy can be measured against a published standard, whereas no standard or regulator-endorsed method was found by October 2026 treating ordinary generative weather or lighting edits as physically equivalent safety-critical sensor evidence [f78, f3719, f4910]. The booklet labels standards unissued by October 2026 as draft, under publication or under revision, and several ISO parts were due to change in late 2026; a 2027 programme should therefore use actual published editions and maintain an agreed baseline with change control rather than freeze the October snapshot [f46, f11913, f1161, f11914, f11222]. Applicability to the specific machine, jurisdiction and safety function remains unresolved and should be an early specialist-confirmed gate; no standard guarantees that a first-time simulation organization can meet a four-month validation schedule [f9786, f9787, f7594].

nodes.label: Standards bodies (ISO, IEC, CEN, CENELEC, ASAM, SAE, IEEE, UL and national bodies)
nodes.text: Standards bodies are the organizations that run the committees, hold the votes and publish the standards.
aliases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
nodes.synopsis: Standards bodies run committees, hold votes and publish standards; ISO and IEC provide an international baseline, while EN texts can carry legal weight in Europe through the harmonization process [f15016, f15031, f15077]. For heavy off-road validation, program-level collision-mitigation acceptance values should not be described as ISO mandates without a normative clause, and national adoptions may differ from their originals [f2636, f15032]. The booklet reports no standards-body or industry-group study establishing whether on-road simulation methods transfer to off-road machines; ASAM's 2023 off-road workshop led to a concept project, but its evidence is expert opinion rather than normative evidence, and standardized simulation-quality metrics remain absent [f1248, f7191, f7197, f15024]. European adoption of ISO 19014-1 was in CEN approval alongside the 2026 series changes, while the glossary's assertion that Standards Australia publishes AS 21815.1:2023 sits in tension with Chapter 3's failure to locate its catalogue entry [f2211, f15179, f15027, f2873]. Aviation offers an acceptance precedent through standards bodies and authorities, with DO-385 and ED-256 published in October 2018, but confidence in credibility frameworks remains contested by a 2026 preprint calling them “largely declarative” [f1470, f15747, f10324].

nodes.label: Technical committee ISO/TC 127 and how a standard is numbered
nodes.text: ISO/TC 127 is the ISO committee for earth-moving machinery, and the numbers, parts and years in a standard's name tell you exactly which document and which edition is meant.
nodes.synopsis: ISO/TC 127 is the technical committee for earth-moving machinery and produces nearly every off-road standard covered by the booklet, including collision systems, detection, brakes, functional safety, autonomous machines and machine definitions [f15033, f15034]. Standard numbers, parts and years identify specific documents and editions; each part has its own scope and date, while prefixes distinguish document types and national or regional adoptions [f15033, f15036, f15040, f15041]. ISO 21815 covers earth-moving machines defined in ISO 6165, underground mining machines under ISO 19296, and road-construction machines [f15140]. An older edition year does not itself imply obsolescence: ISO 16001’s current edition is 2017, and ISO 3450:2011 was reviewed and confirmed in 2022 [f15037, f15038]. All five ISO 19014 parts change in October 2026, so the program should baseline the editions actually published rather than mix clauses from different years; ISO 21815-4 should not be cited as published until its text appears [f15039, f15042, f15043]. The booklet found no ISO/TC 127 study applying road-vehicle simulation methods to off-road machines, with the chapter-level search also reporting no such study across several other organizations [f1698, f15035].

nodes.label: Stage codes (TS, PAS, TR, DIS, FDIS, PRF, under revision, under publication)
nodes.text: Stage codes are the labels that tell you how far a standard has traveled from first draft to published text, and whether the published text is about to change.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet uses “draft,” “under publication” and “under revision” to flag standards not issued by October 2026; these labels distinguish pending text from published requirements [f46, f1200, f9419]. ISO 21815-4, covering swing and rotation, is listed at stage 60.00 (“Under publication”) for October 2026, but one chapter explicitly leaves its final publication status uncertain; its scope excludes avoidance by automatic brake application [f1708, f2059, f5074, f7543]. ISO/PRF 21815-5 reached proof stage in September 2026, remained at proof stage in October, and was expected to publish in November 2026, covering motions including articulation and reversing trailers [f323, f6025, f6026, f6747]. All five ISO 19014 parts were reported under publication for October 2026, shortly before design verification would freeze, but another chapter lists revised ISO 19014-1 for 22 November 2026, leaving a scheduling discrepancy [f48, f12000, f7738]. For virtual-validation planning, ISO/PAS 34506 remained unfinished and road-vehicle-specific, and no developing off-road scenario standard was found that could arrive before mid-2027 [f3746, f7695, f7206].

nodes.label: Regulation, directive, law and guidance note
nodes.text: A law is a rule the state can enforce, a regulation and a directive are two forms that European Union law takes, and a guidance note is official advice that explains how to comply without itself being law.
nodes.synopsis: South Africa is the only jurisdiction found to legally require automatic slow-down and braking, effective since 21 December 2022; the remaining regions are characterized as having risk-based duties without an automatic-braking mandate [f164, f2125]. MSHA's surface mobile equipment rule took effect on 19 January 2024 and was enforced from 17 July 2024, requiring written safety programmes and consideration of technology rather than mandatory collision avoidance [f5842, f5843]. The EU Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, before the prototype arrives; the Digital Omnibus on AI entered into force on 27 July 2026, but its machinery provisions rely on secondary summaries with conflicting Annex I application dates of 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 [f6696, f6698, f10309, f10310]. ISO 21815 standards are not inherently law, and the most concrete mining acceptance numbers come from industry specifications rather than legislation [f2062, f173, f2112]. No universal legal acceptance rule for virtual evidence or published off-road regulator commitment to accept it was found, and the glossary states that simulation cannot replace a prescribed physical test [f11037, f258, f12004]. Planning therefore calls for jurisdiction-specific applicability sign-off, explicit checks on simulation acceptance and assessor engagement, while unresolved issues include the final status of the proposed heavy-vehicle AEB rule, data-governance requirements, and unverified EU Data Act and Cyber Resilience Act application dates [f10165, f10235, f11126, f1333, f5800, f10817].

nodes.label: Harmonized standard, presumption of conformity and state of the art
nodes.text: A harmonized standard is one that European law officially lists, so that a product built to it is presumed to meet the law, and "state of the art" is the legal phrase for the level of safety that current good practice makes possible.
nodes.synopsis: Harmonized standards are officially listed under European law and give a presumption of conformity only within their scope; EN 474 offers such a route where cited, but is not an automatic-braking performance matrix [f15075, f15080, f2719]. In 2026, the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 list was still being prepared, no standards had yet been cited according to the skeptic’s review, and future harmonization of EN 474 or EN ISO 21815 remained unverified, so a status checkpoint is recommended immediately before the 2027 declaration [f2208, f10501, f11217, f2209, f15084]. FprEN ISO 19014-1 was linked to the Regulation through M/605, adopted on 20 January 2025, with publication planned for 22 November 2026; this does not establish that it had been cited, while the possible interim use of AI Act standards until delegated acts expected by 2 August 2028 remained unverified commentary [f10538, f11218, f11219, f7431]. Great Britain designated the EN 474:2022 family on 8 August 2026 under its separate machinery regime, providing a presumption-of-conformity route and a parallel declaration calendar, although the claimed notice number 0139/26 was not confirmed [f15244, f15496, f2875]. Where no harmonized standard fits automatic braking, the manufacturer’s own safety case must demonstrate safety using the state of the art, with standards providing evidence even when not harmonized and a lawyer expecting comparison against Volvo, Caterpillar and Komatsu systems [f15082, f15085, f11133]. Standards are generally voluntary but acquire legal significance through legislation, harmonization or designation, contracts, procurement requirements, or the manufacturer’s chosen state-of-the-art route [f2144, f15083].

nodes.label: Type approval, self-certification and conformity assessment
nodes.text: Conformity assessment is the process of checking that a product meets the rules; type approval and self-certification are two ways of doing it, an authority checking a sample and issuing an approval, or the manufacturer checking and declaring for itself.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus found no off-road document accepting simulation as compliance evidence, no precedent for regulatory or notified-body acceptance of off-road collision-avoidance simulation, and no published criteria resolving how much virtual evidence would be accepted [f167, f7417, f10307]. On-road acceptance provides a limited precedent under strict credibility rules: UNECE NATM uses virtual testing within a wider assessment, and even the most simulation-friendly EU automated-driving regime does not allow simulation to substitute for physical tests [f168, f7679, f10410]. For an EU machine introduced in mid-2027, Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027 and requires risk reduction, safe and reliable controls, and technical conformity evidence; every Annex I Part A conformity route involves a notified body, including the listed category of self-evolving machine-learning safety components [f2201, f2202, f363, f794]. Standards compliance is not equivalent to legal compliance, and UL 4600, ISO 34502 and NASA guidance provide safety-case or methodological help rather than off-road conformity routes [f2146, f12267, f449, f8070]. Formal approval is a hard calendar constraint, the proposed braking function's regulatory route remains unconfirmed, and the booklet recommends jurisdiction-specific legal and conformity planning now rather than legal review at the end of validation [f360, f10499, f10702, f10848].

nodes.label: CE marking and notified body
nodes.text: CE marking is the label a manufacturer puts on a product to declare that it meets European Union law, and a notified body is an independent organization appointed by the authorities to check high-risk products before that label may be applied.
nodes.synopsis: The EU Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027; Annex I Part A covers self-evolving machine-learning safety components and machinery embedding them, and every Part A conformity route involves a notified body [f12407, f15106]. Whether a trained perception model frozen before delivery qualifies as “self-evolving” remained disputed and unsettled in 2026, so the booklet recommends planning for notified-body involvement for EU products using machine learning in safety functions unless legal advice concludes otherwise [f15107, f2643]. No published commitment or precedent accepting off-road simulation evidence was found, and the competence needed to assess a simulation-based collision-mitigation argument was not identified [f258, f7417, f8243]. Notified-body lead times were also not found; the warning that assessment alone could exceed the four-month validation window is therefore a planning risk, not a documented duration [f259, f364]. The booklet recommends early notified-body and counsel consultation on both legal scope and simulation acceptance, escalating if physical confirmation is required but unscheduled [f10960, f10962]. Its timing advice is in tension: contact is described as realistic by mid-2027 for a team starting in October 2026, while absence of pre-consultation by early 2027 is already treated as a warning sign of regulatory rejection [f855, f11056].

nodes.label: Test method (test object, distance, speed, condition, pass criterion)
nodes.text: A test method, as a standard or regulation defines it, is the exact recipe for one test: what object to use, where to place it, how fast to drive, under what conditions, and what result counts as a pass.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21815-1:2022 provides off-road collision-warning and avoidance test procedures; clause 6 specifies physical test environments, surfaces, machine conditions, objects, pass/fail performance tests and false-positive tests [f5156, f5353, f7726]. Complementary methods include ISO 16001:2017 for detection bodies, zones and times, ISO 3450:2011 for braking, and ISO 17757:2019 for testing in manual and autonomous modes; ISO 3450 prescribes adverse braking configurations and maximum payload for dumpers [f5155, f10651, f8938, f13623]. The review found neither a complete numeric regulatory type-approval test for off-road automatic braking nor an off-road Euro NCAP equivalent, and it did not establish universal target dimensions, test counts or acceptance of simulation evidence [f2147, f346, f5410, f11192]. South African mining published independent verification specifications on 29 August 2025, with industry specifications written in 2025 and 2026; the published closed-loop specification uses unloaded machines and gradients of 1 percent or less, while the regulation itself supplies no detection percentage, false-alarm limit or stopping test [f348, f11459, f13715, f165]. Heavy-truck precedents show why passenger-car tests should not be copied directly: stopping distances and towing equipment required adaptations, and Daimler disputed the real-world relevance of a steel-trench-plate reproduction scenario [f1232, f1233, f1314]. Reproducible product tests also leave operational limitations: static tests miss speed-dependent detection effects, and ISO tests cannot predict a fatigued operator's response to repeated nuisance warnings [f10656, f3494].

nodes.label: ISO 21815 series (collision warning and avoidance)
nodes.text: ISO 21815 is the family of international standards that says what a collision warning or collision avoidance system on an earth-moving machine must do, how it talks to the machine, and how to work out the distance at which it must act.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21815 is the core off-road collision-warning and avoidance family: Part 1:2022 covers detection, warnings, automatic intervention and tests for earth-moving, mobile underground-mining and road-construction machinery; intervention is limited to speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition, not automatic steering [f2055, f5156, f5909]. Part 2:2021 supplies the J1939 intervention interface, confirmed in December 2024, while Part 3:2023 covers forward/reverse risk areas, builds avoidance distance from detection, decision, action, stopping and safety-distance components, and places intervention at risk level 4 or above [f2057, f5158, f6680, f5912]. As of 1 October 2026, Part 4 was under publication for October and Part 5 was at proof stage for November; Part 4 addresses swing/rotation mainly by preventing motion from starting and expressly excludes avoidance by automatic brake application, so later users should re-check catalogue status [f49, f50, f11423, f7543, f55]. The family supplies physical test procedures, including performance pass/fail and false-positive tests, but the corpus found no rules establishing acceptable simulation evidence or virtual-only validation, and the listed standards do not supply a statistical acceptance target [f7726, f8321, f9459, f324]. Standardized intervention does not establish quantified field effectiveness or second-order hazards, public previews supplied no human reaction model, and safe-operation responsibility remains with the operator [f3443, f3493, f10874]. For planning, ISO 21815 and EMESRT scenarios anchor the validation test space; a program starting in October 2026 could realistically have an operating-domain definition and scenario catalogue working by mid-2027, with interoperability demonstrated through the Part 2 interface and common site products [f6641, f63, f10726].

nodes.label: ISO 19014 series (functional safety for earth-moving machinery)
nodes.text: ISO 19014 is the family of standards that tells a maker of earth-moving machines how to make sure the electronic control system behind a safety function, such as an automatic brake, is designed, built, tested and programmed so that its faults do not cause harm.
nodes.synopsis: For brake-commanding earth-moving functions, the corpus identifies ISO 19014—not ISO 26262—as the functional-safety framework using MPLr; adding braking crosses the boundary from excluded awareness-only systems into motion-affecting safety control [f2071, f2075, f11993]. Validation therefore needs to address brake-command integrity, faults, degraded modes and unintended activation, with machine-control safety analysis determining required risk reduction and performance level; Part 5 supplies tabulated MPLr intended to avoid a full safety analysis for every new model [f5223, f10516, f2076]. The series covers hardware, software and environmental testing, including documented performance under expected environmental conditions, while ISO 19014-4 leaves cybersecurity to separate coverage [f322, f7735, f7488]. The review found no simulation-credibility acceptance criteria, statistical acceptance target or wording permitting virtual-only validation, but incomplete access to paid texts means these findings do not establish that replacing physical tests is prohibited [f5110, f324, f9459, f7544]. Parts 1–4 edition 2 and Part 5 edition 1 reached publication stage 60.00 in August 2026 with October publication scheduled, but a separate chapter lists 22 November 2026 for revised Part 1, so final status should be rechecked before design freeze and the plan should allow re-baselining [f2073, f7738, f6286, f10369]. For most markets, the internal safety board and customers accept validation evidence, but applicability to the particular machine, function and jurisdiction remains unresolved; an assessor-quality package should trace simulation claims to requirements or hazards and the final pass/fail argument [f1613, f10316, f8029].

nodes.label: ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 (brake performance)
nodes.text: ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 are the standards that say how well the brakes of an earth-moving machine must work and how to test them, ISO 3450 for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines and ISO 10265 for slow crawler machines.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 3450:2011, reconfirmed in September 2022, specifies service, secondary and parking-brake performance and tests for wheeled and high-speed rubber-tracked earth-moving machines; ISO 10265:2008 covers crawlers at 20 km/h or less [f10651, f15190, f5979]. ISO 3450 measures stopping distance from brake-control actuation to standstill, including brake-system response but excluding operator reaction, and requires the most adverse braking configuration, including maximum specified payload for dumpers and certain other machines [f5976, f5967, f5968]. Stopping distance is not the sole acceptance outcome because controllability also matters, and passing ISO 3450 does not establish that perception, classification, threat assessment or trigger logic work [f6149, f2361]. The proposed four-month validation plan uses ISO 21815-3 CxS distances calculated for each machine model from ISO 3450 brake data and declared delays; physical brake testing remains necessary, with no identified off-road document accepting simulation as a replacement for prescribed physical tests [f2638, f10431, f2103]. These standards do not establish a calibration-stop count that guarantees prediction across 100-plus site types, multiple brake architectures and all stated weather conditions, supporting separate machine-family braking models rather than assuming universal transfer [f6162, f6163, f13733]. Verification is uneven across chapters: some report scope and edition details, while others say ISO 10265 or ISO 3450 details were not verified; the reported 32 km/h or 80%-of-maximum test speed and stopping-distance formulas come from secondary material requiring confirmation against the standard [f8946, f8947, f2197, f7013, f11197, f15193, f2436].

nodes.label: ISO 16001 and ISO 5006 (object detection, visibility aids and operator visibility)
nodes.text: ISO 16001 sets performance requirements and tests for the systems that detect objects and help the operator see around an earth-moving machine, and ISO 5006 defines how the operator's own field of view is measured.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 16001:2017, dated November 2017 and confirmed in 2023, sets performance and test requirements for object-detection systems and visibility aids; its scope is warning and visibility, not braking [f6744, f2181]. The booklet identifies it as the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers, reporting a maximum detection time of 300 ms, audible warnings at least 3 dB above ambient, and a flashing red light for the most severe warning [f160, f2065, f2066]. It also reports continuous self-checking and no single-action disablement, while noting that the 2017 edition has no dedicated lidar annex [f2067, f2068, f12614]. ISO 5006 and ISO 16001 visibility-type methods support geometric computation of coverage and blind zones for each machine model before hardware arrives, although ISO 5006 was not verified in the research [f5602, f11549, f2197]. ISO 16001 defines a test body, detection zone and detection time, and specifies physical-test-body procedures; evidence that it accepts simulation was not found, and it does not set statistical sample sizes or simulation-credibility rules [f5354, f11232, f11192, f6749]. Although the 300 ms limit is attributed to public-preview clause 4.5 and used in physics parameterisation, it was not verified against the purchased standard and should be confirmed before safety-case reliance [f7493, f7494, f7495].

nodes.label: ISO 17757 and ISO 19296 (autonomous machine safety and underground mining machines)
nodes.text: ISO 17757 is the safety standard for autonomous and semi-autonomous earth-moving and mining machine systems, and ISO 19296 is the general safety standard for mobile machines that work underground.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 17757:2019 is edition 2, published in July 2019 and confirmed in 2024; it covers autonomous and semi-autonomous earth-moving and mining systems, including infrastructure, hardware and software, while ISO 19296 addresses mobile underground machines and is not a stand-alone collision-avoidance performance protocol [f2182, f9781, f2183, f15223, f2193]. ISO 17757’s “defined functional environment” provides a precedent for staged, limited-domain release, and the 2022 ODD-UM paper adapts it to underground mining [f606, f422, f6711]. Applicability to operator-driven automatic braking remains unresolved because function-specific automation is excluded unless part of an autonomous or semi-autonomous system; this conflicts with Chapter 10’s claim of direct applicability to off-road automatic braking, so the glossary recommends settling standards early with a qualified functional-safety specialist [f2184, f2186, f8153, f15236]. The corpus describes functional-safety requirements for control parts and physical braking and steering tests in both manual and autonomous modes under ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 [f2346, f7734]. Reviewed excerpts and public previews did not establish simulation acceptance, substitution rules or a validity envelope, and physical evidence remains necessary; this is an evidence gap rather than an established prohibition, since paid-text provisions remain uncertain and Chapter 7 did not verify ISO 17757 [f3908, f8940, f8151, f8152, f8186, f5811].

nodes.label: ISO 6165 and ISO 20474 / EN 474 (classification and general safety of earth-moving machinery)
nodes.text: ISO 6165 defines which machines count as earth-moving machinery, and ISO 20474 and its European twin EN 474 set the general safety requirements that every such machine must meet.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 6165 names and classifies earth-moving machines, including loaders, excavators, dozers, dumpers and graders; ISO 20474-1:2017 and Parts 2–15 provide their baseline general and machine-specific safety requirements, with EN 474 serving as the European counterpart [f15239, f2189, f15243]. These baseline standards are not automatic-braking acceptance standards or performance matrices: braking evidence must instead come from ISO 21815, ISO 19014 and the safety case [f2190, f2720, f15248]. ISO 19014 is the sector-specific functional-safety framework for ISO 6165 machines, but projects spanning surface and underground machines must check applicability machine by machine rather than assume it for mining machines outside that classification [f2196, f2351, f15249]. There is a scope tension: one glossary entry makes ISO 6165 inclusion determinative for ISO 21815-1 applicability, while another says ISO 21815 also covers underground mining machines under ISO 19296 and road-construction machines [f15240, f15140]. Great Britain designated the EN 474:2022 family on 8 August 2026, providing a presumption-of-conformity route under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, but the attributed notice number 0139/26 was not confirmed [f15244, f2875]. Presumption of conformity is limited to the standard's scope, and harmonisation of EN 474 or EN ISO 21815 under Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 remained unverified while the list was being prepared in 2026 [f15080, f2209, f15081].

nodes.label: ISO 15998 and ISO 13766 (withdrawn control-system standard and EMC)
nodes.text: ISO 15998 was the former functional-safety standard for electronic machine-control systems on earth-moving machinery, withdrawn in 2022 and replaced by ISO 19014, and ISO 13766 is the standard for electromagnetic compatibility of such machines.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 15998 formerly covered functional safety of electronic machine-control systems on earth-moving machinery; ISO 15998:2008 and ISO/TS 15998-2:2012 were withdrawn on 14 June 2022 and replaced by ISO 19014 [f15250, f2344, f15251]. A legacy-reference tension remains: ISO 16001:2017 still cites ISO 15998 for environmental conditions, while allowing ISO 19014-3 as an alternative; readers encountering supplier references to ISO 15998 should request the ISO 19014 equivalent [f2345, f15252, f15253, f15257]. ISO 16001 requires electromagnetic compatibility to ISO 13766, meaning electronics must neither disrupt other equipment through radio interference nor be disrupted by external interference [f2414, f15254, f15255]. EMC matters for automatic braking because brake requests travel over an electronic network and radar shares radio space; MOSH includes EMC testing in its TRL4 laboratory phase, and an on-road example identifies radio-frequency coexistence as one reason a factory emergency brake was disabled [f15258, f15256, f15259].

nodes.label: ISO 12100, ISO 13849, IEC 62061 and IEC 61508 (the machinery and functional-safety family)
nodes.text: These four standards form the general toolkit for making any machine safe: ISO 12100 for assessing and reducing risk, ISO 13849 and IEC 62061 for the safety of control systems on machinery, and IEC 61508 as the parent standard for electronic safety systems in every industry.
nodes.synopsis: The family provides a layered machine-safety toolkit: ISO 12100 governs risk assessment and reduction, ISO 13849 and IEC 62061 address machinery control-system safety, and IEC 61508 supplies the cross-industry electronic-safety framework; ISO 12100 prioritizes design measures, then safeguards, then information for use [f15260, f15261]. ISO 13849-1:2023 is the generic machinery method, including software, but does not prescribe the collision-braking function's required Performance Level: that assignment must come from application-specific risk analysis or a type-C standard, with ISO 19014 providing the earth-moving sector framework [f2194, f2350, f12029]. The intervention path needs a Performance Level or integrity assignment and fault testing; for a team starting in October 2026, a safety-case skeleton using ISO 13849 or IEC 62061 alongside ISO 19014 is considered realistic by mid-2027 [f7455, f829]. ISO 13849-2:2012 permits simulation, including software simulation of faults, but only among several validation methods; its validation-plan structure is recommended for this project [f9767, f10294, f9986]. The booklet says the 2012 edition remains current, with an Edition 3 draft issued in 2026, but neither that draft nor ISO 13849-1:2023 and IEC 62061:2021 were reviewed, limiting confidence in detailed compliance claims [f9766, f9768, f9769]. IEC 61508-3 tool classes T1–T3 are used as a simulator-qualification reference, yet their provisions and the proven-in-use route were not verified in detail; the fit of IEC 61508 and IEC 62061 as alternatives also remains unverified [f15269, f15271, f12054].

nodes.label: IEC 61496, IEC TS 62998, ISO 3691-4 and ISO 18497 (safety sensors, driverless industrial trucks and agricultural automation)
nodes.text: These are neighboring standards from other sectors: IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 certify safety sensors in factories, ISO 3691-4 covers driverless warehouse trucks, and ISO 18497 covers automated farm machines, including how to test their obstacle detection.
aliases: IEC 61496, IEC TS 62998, ISO 3691-4 and ISO 18497
nodes.synopsis: The ISO 18497:2024 agricultural series, published in July 2024, is identified as the closest published cousin of heavy off-road collision mitigation, covering obstacle protection and verification/validation, including braking, steering and person or obstacle detection tests [f7187, f15283, f7188, f1711]. ISO 18497-4 explicitly lists simulation among several verification methods and supplies simulation test objects, but the research found neither a defined virtual-evidence share nor authorization to replace field tests with simulation [f9764, f5276, f1954, f15288]. Its premise that detection is imperfect yields four failure categories—failure to detect, late detection, incorrect classification and localization error—which the booklet recommends using with ISO 21815-3 risk areas to structure the scenario catalogue [f15285, f15289]. IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 offer a component-level sensor certification basis, but IEC TS 61496-5:2023 excludes aspects of moving radar protective-device applications; certification therefore does not establish whole-machine performance in dust and rain, and mobile outdoor use of IEC TS 62998-1 is presented as a vendor claim [f1038, f12393, f15280, f1045]. No simulation wording was found in ISO 3691-4:2023, which is described as current and under revision with an Edition 3 DIS in progress [f9784, f9783]. These positive findings coexist with chapters saying that ISO 18497 details or simulation provisions, and ISO 3691-4 provisions, were not verified, so editions and clauses require checking before reliance [f4335, f7741, f11198].

nodes.label: ISO 21448, ISO 26262 and the AI safety standards (ISO/PAS 8800, ISO/IEC TR 5469, ISO/IEC 42001, 23894, 24029)
nodes.text: ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 are the road-vehicle standards for functional safety and for safety when sensors and software misjudge a situation without failing, and the ISO/PAS 8800 and ISO/IEC documents are the first, mostly unfinished, attempts to write standards for machine learning in safety functions.
aliases: ISO 21448, ISO 26262 and the AI safety standards
nodes.synopsis: For the heavy off-road braking function, the booklet identifies ISO 19014—not ISO 26262—as the governing functional-safety framework; ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 are road-vehicle standards outside this program's scope [f162, f2355, f12065]. Nevertheless, it recommends borrowing ISO 21448 and ISO/PAS 8800 perception-assurance concepts, with a safety-case skeleton realistically achievable by mid-2027 for a team starting in October 2026 [f12018, f829]. ISO/PAS 8800:2024, published in December 2024, addresses AI safety for road vehicles only, while ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024, published in January 2024, provides guidance rather than testing requirements [f2730, f2731, f2726, f2727]. Experts disagree over whether to exclude machine learning from safety functions or accept it through ISO/PAS 8800-style assurance, and the booklet found neither off-road/mining standards with ML clauses nor a separate ISO 19014 acceptance process for ML perception [f1125, f15303, f15304]. ISO 26262-8 tool-confidence provisions offer a reference regime, but clause 11 was confirmed only through contents and secondary sources; proven-in-use concerns element reuse, not simulator validation [f9758, f7703, f7579]. Important verification gaps remain: ISO 21448 and several other standards were not verified, ISO/IEC 42001, 23894 and 24029 were not verified in the ML-rules review, and the corpus characterizes ML safety standards as mostly draft [f4336, f2392, f2099].

nodes.label: ISO 34501 to 34505, ISO/PAS 34506, ISO/TS 5083 and ISO 19206 (scenario-based evaluation and test targets)
nodes.text: The ISO 3450x series and ISO/TS 5083 are road-vehicle standards for describing, sorting and choosing the test scenarios of an automated driving system, and ISO 19206 defines the dummies and foam cars that stand in for people and vehicles in crash-avoidance tests.
aliases: ISO 34501 to 34505, ISO/PAS 34506, ISO/TS 5083 and ISO 19206
nodes.synopsis: ISO 34501–34505 provide road-vehicle scenario vocabulary, ODD specification, categorisation and test-case methods; their structure can inform off-road validation, but their road-specific content is not off-road compliance evidence and acceptance for earth-moving collision avoidance remains uncertain [f7692, f6642, f449, f4315]. No heavy-machinery equivalent of ISO 34502 was found, so the programme must define its own scenario or hazard taxonomy; the booklet adopts functional, logical and concrete scenarios, using ISO 21815 and EMESRT storyboards for off-road content [f9881, f9882, f15323]. ISO 34505:2025, dated June 2025, specifies test-case identifiers, objectives, inputs, steps, platform and expected results, while ISO 34503 provides a hierarchical ODD structure whose road-oriented attributes require adaptation [f6732, f6706, f6709]. These standards primarily address coverage rather than model credibility, establish no physical-to-virtual testing ratio, and do not address risk scaling; ISO/PAS 34506 concerns virtual-environment qualification but remained a draft in October 2026 [f7693, f7694, f8119, f4072]. TÜV SÜD nevertheless summarizes ISO 34502 and European automated-driving regulation as requiring the virtual platform itself to be demonstrated fit for purpose, so scenario coverage alone should not be confused with platform qualification [f1283, f7693]. No off-road equivalent of ISO 19206 standardized targets exists in the corpus: its transferable value is target-design principles, with surrogates representing off-road people, vehicles, machines and obstacles and matching each sensor’s relevant response [f15329, f15325, f15326].

nodes.label: ISO 18571, ISO 16290 and ISO 25119
nodes.text: ISO 18571 defines a score for how closely two curves agree, ISO 16290 defines the technology readiness levels, and ISO 25119 is the functional-safety standard for control systems on farm machines.
nodes.synopsis: ISO 18571 compares measured and simulated time histories using corridor, phase, magnitude and slope sub-scores; the booklet warns that peak-only comparisons can mislead, citing a 0.3% peak difference alongside a 60.4% time-history error [f15331, f15332, f15335]. An IDIADA–MathWorks demonstration recorded on 14 April 2026 correlated closed-loop virtual AEB against production-vehicle proving-ground tests using ISO 18571, providing an on-road precedent rather than direct heavy off-road validation [f1269]. The glossary reports that Euro NCAP virtual testing requires qualification against physical tests using an ISO score and defined KPIs, and recommends this kind of metric for correlation testing [f15333, f15341]. ISO 16290:2013 standardizes the one-to-nine TRL scale and assessment criteria for space systems; the booklet uses TRLs only for critical-technology maturity, while South African mining's MOSH regime uses TRL4 and TRL7 gates [f9512, f14684, f14686, f15338, f15337]. ISO 25119 covers functional safety for agricultural control systems and may apply to a heavy off-road program by contract, but its fit, editions, application dates and simulation provisions were not verified, so its inclusion is not evidence of an established acceptance route [f15339, f15343, f12054, f4335, f7741].

nodes.label: Systems and software engineering standards (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, 29119, 42010, 15026-2, IEEE 1012, ISO 31000, IEC 31010)
nodes.text: These are the general standards for how to run an engineering project: how to organize a system's life cycle, document tests, describe an architecture, write an assurance case, verify and validate, and manage risk.
nodes.synopsis: These standards provide general engineering discipline rather than collision- or brake-specific requirements: they structure an evidence plan linking claims to evidence, methods, acceptance criteria, owners and gates, but do not determine what to test [f15344, f15345, f15357]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, INCOSE’s 2023 handbook, NASA’s handbook and IEEE 1012 underpin verification and validation planning; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3:2021 and Part 4:2021 supply test-documentation structures and test-design techniques without collision-avoidance content [f9537, f15347, f7112, f7113, f7114]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 supports architecture views tailored to their audience, with a recommended 2–3-page capability and architecture section and a toolchain description distinguishing real, modeled, emulated and substituted elements [f9886, f10160, f15352]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2:2022 structures assurance arguments from claims through evidence, addressing the program’s ultimate question of whether a safety board can trust a virtual result enough to support a safety decision [f15353, f15356]. ISO 31000:2018 and IEC 31010:2019 underpin risk-register practice, but the booklet identifies thin outcome evidence for risk registers [f15354, f15355].

nodes.label: Rail and aviation standards (EN 50126 to EN 50129, EN 50716, EN 14363, DO-178C, DO-330, DO-385, ED-256)
nodes.text: These are the safety and simulation standards of two industries, railways and aviation, that have accepted simulation as evidence for longer than road or off-road vehicles have.
nodes.synopsis: Rail and aviation offer precedents from industries that have accepted simulation as evidence longer than road or off-road vehicles, with railway practice providing the booklet’s clearest template for extending validation across heavy off-road machine models and sensor positions [f15358, f15373]. EN 14363:2016+A2:2022 covers railway running-behavior acceptance, including simulated on-track tests and extension to similar vehicles; related validation practice uses at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons from at least 12 track sections and limits deviations across the whole comparison set [f15362, f15363, f15364]. The proposed transfer is to validate a family model at its envelope corners, document vehicle changes and add targeted bridging tests, consistent with railway guidance on using modified validated models as evidence [f15373, f15365]. EN 50716:2023 is identified as the current railway software standard and successor to EN 50128, but EN 50126, EN 50128, EN 50129 and EN 50716 were not verified in this research [f7717, f7718, f7716]. Aviation contributes tool qualification through DO-330, which does not establish physics-model validity; both DO-178C and DO-330 are listed as not verified [f15367, f15368, f15369, f15374]. ACAS X provides a statistical-simulation precedent involving encounters equivalent to billions of flight hours, with its DO-385 and ED-256 minimum operational performance standards published in October 2018; the booklet emphasizes that aviation acceptance followed years of underlying model development [f15372, f1429, f15374].

nodes.label: UL 4600 (autonomous products safety case)
nodes.text: UL 4600 is a standard that tells a developer what a complete safety case for an autonomous product must cover, in the form of long lists of questions and claims to be answered with evidence.
nodes.synopsis: Published by Underwriters Laboratories, UL 4600 specifies evidence-backed coverage for an autonomous-product safety case; its third edition is dated 17 March 2023 [f15026, f15375, f15376]. It structures an intended-use safety claim into supported subclaims and uses question lists to check completeness, but sets no performance numbers and prescribes no tests [f15378, f15379, f15377]. The booklet recommends those lists for structuring the heavy off-road collision-mitigation validation plan, including a 1.5–3-page safety-scope and top-level-claim section [f9984, f10156]. This addresses an acceptance gap: the booklet says no regulation spells out off-road automatic-braking acceptance, so a structured safety case connects simulation, physical tests and analysis to assessable claims [f15386, f15387]. However, UL 4600's applicability and simulation-acceptance provisions were not verified, and the booklet records both proponents and critics of safety cases [f15384, f15383, f10319].

nodes.label: UN regulations (UN R152, R131, R159, R171) and UNECE WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM
nodes.text: The UN regulations are the shared road-vehicle approval rules written at the United Nations in Geneva, R131 and R152 for emergency braking on trucks and cars, R159 for moving-off information and R171 for driver assistance, and WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM are the forum, working party, expert group and method that produce them.
aliases: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats UNECE virtual-testing rules as on-road precedents, not direct off-road approval routes: NATM and DCAS require adaptation, and off-road simulation should provide coverage and design evidence qualified against physical tests [f7545, f5112, f2143]. R171 permits virtual testing for hard-to-reproduce scenarios only after rigorous toolchain credibility evaluation, with the Annex 5 assessment supplied to the Type Approval Authority; dSPACE reports that WP.29 added virtual testing at the end of 2024 [f1217, f2488, f1276]. NATM combines simulation with scenario catalogues, track and real-world tests, audit and in-service monitoring; credibility assessment defines the tool's usable envelope, while physical testing remains necessary [f9743, f9745, f10330]. WP.29 adopted R152 virtual-testing supplements in 2025, but the text dated 28 August 2025 leaves physical confirmation-test numbers to manufacturer–authority agreement, unlike the 30% minimum reported in a working document; January 2024 criticism had identified unresolved credibility issues [f7546, f7549, f7547, f7144]. R152's 5.0 m/s² threshold is a minimum braking demand, not measured deceleration, creating tension with glossary wording that calls it deceleration; R131 and R152 also permit conscious driver interruption of emergency braking [f5993, f6307, f13632, f6323]. The booklet proposes transferring R159-style small-cylinder geometry into machine digital twins for coverage and blind-zone analysis, but the reported 50 mm cylinder dimension was not confirmed against the regulation text [f15220, f5603, f5356].

nodes.label: FMVSS 127, NHTSA, NTSB and IIHS
nodes.text: FMVSS 127 is the United States rule requiring automatic emergency braking on new cars, NHTSA is the agency that writes such rules and investigates defects, NTSB is the independent board that investigates accidents, and IIHS is the insurer-funded institute that tests and rates vehicles.
nodes.synopsis: FMVSS 127 was finalized on 9 May 2024 and requires AEB on new US light vehicles by 1 September 2029; its scope ends at 4,536 kg GVWR, so it is an on-road reference rather than a rule applicable to off-road machines [f1513, f2831]. It requires lead-vehicle avoidance up to 62 mph, forward-collision warning, and pedestrian AEB at 10–73 km/h in daylight and darkness; specified false-activation tests fail when peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by at least 0.25 g, while the braking algorithm remains the manufacturer's choice [f15420, f11691, f15421, f15422, f6185]. The timetable remains contested: manufacturers challenged the rule over false-activation risk, and in March 2026 the Department of Transportation proposed preparing a two-year lead-time extension, which the booklet explicitly says was not adopted [f1228, f2537]. Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented on-road AEB failure mode, but investigation outcomes require care: Tesla's probe closed on 29 June 2026 with 695,000 vehicles and about 25,900 incident reports yet no crashes, injuries or defect finding, while the Detroit Assurance investigation escalated in October 2025 and reproduced braking on a steel trench plate [f115, f11170, f11171, f1317, f1812]. For heavy-machine validation, the corpus points to necessary adaptations for stopping distance and equipment, alongside NHTSA heavy-vehicle stationary-target false-positive tests and a −0.05 g braking-onset threshold [f1732, f6192, f6193]. Other evidence highlights both benefits and safety-management failures: IIHS reported a 78% reduction in backing-crash involvement with rear automatic braking, camera and sensors, while NTSB's Uber fatality investigation found disabled factory emergency braking, a one-second action suppression despite emergency recognition 1.2 seconds before impact, and deficient safety risk management and culture [f15436, f15432, f15433, f15434].

nodes.label: Euro NCAP and its virtual-testing protocol
nodes.text: Euro NCAP is the European consumer program that crash-tests cars and awards star ratings, and its virtual-testing protocol is the first published procedure under which an outside assessor accepts a manufacturer's simulation results for crash avoidance, subject to correlation and random physical checks.
nodes.synopsis: Euro NCAP is an independent consumer-assessment body, not a regulator; its virtual-testing protocol version 1.00 was dated March 2025 and entered into force in January 2026, and its ratings do not constitute legal approval or regulatory evidence for machines [f1272, f15443, f2107]. The corpus identifies it as the clearest collision-avoidance precedent for external acceptance of simulation: manufacturers qualify models against physical tests using ISO scores and defined KPIs, submit a model dossier and full-grid predictions, and Euro NCAP physically verifies randomly selected cells [f1260, f15447, f15448]. Acceptance requires at least 75% of verification tests in each scenario cluster to meet qualification criteria; otherwise that cluster's dossier is rejected, with re-simulation or physical testing available [f15449]. Its permission to assume perfect perception limits its usefulness for sensor robustness, while unconfirmed ISO-score and KPI tolerances should not be copied as final off-road acceptance thresholds [f15451, f2502, f2503]. No off-road equivalent was found or adopted, so the booklet recommends using simulation as coverage and design evidence qualified against physical tests, rather than treating this consumer protocol as off-road approval [f346, f2507, f2143, f15443]. Planning must include credibility work beyond simulation runtime, but manufacturer-specific build and validation durations were not found; the research also reports that Euro NCAP virtual testing was not verified, qualifying confidence in its detailed account [f1565, f1273, f7702].

nodes.label: EU Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, the AI Act, the Product Liability Directive and the Data Act
nodes.text: These four European Union laws set the legal ground for a machine sold in Europe from 2027: the Machinery Regulation governs its safety and conformity, the AI Act and its 2026 amendment govern artificial intelligence in it, the Product Liability Directive governs who pays when it causes harm, and the Data Act governs access to the data it produces.
nodes.synopsis: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, before the braking prototype arrives, and EU acceptance of collision-mitigation systems runs through machinery conformity rather than a separate route [f361, f6696, f7754, f2009]. Annex I Part A covers self-evolving machine-learning safety components and machinery embedding them, with notified-body involvement required; whether a trained-then-frozen detector qualifies remains disputed, and notified-body lead time alone could exceed the four-month validation window [f2090, f363, f2091, f11928]. The corpus reports that Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was adopted on 8 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, shifting machinery high-risk AI obligations to 2 August 2028 and leaving machinery-specific AI requirements to a delegated act [f2093, f2094, f6699]. The Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026, treats software as a product, and allows court-ordered disclosure for those products [f51, f9462, f10451]. Acceptance of simulation evidence remains uncertain, with neither guidance nor the outside assessor identified; some chapters relied on secondary legal summaries or did not verify the regulation, so users after October 2026 are advised to re-check regulatory dates [f8184, f8185, f8242, f9463, f4335, f55]. The supplied facts provide no substantive Data Act requirements, leaving that part of the four-law hub uncovered.

nodes.label: United Kingdom rules (HSE, Supply of Machinery Regulations, UKCA)
nodes.text: In Great Britain the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) enforces workplace safety, the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 govern what machines may be sold, and UKCA is the British conformity mark that replaced CE marking after the United Kingdom left the European Union.
nodes.synopsis: Great Britain’s Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, as amended, impose general machinery safety and conformity obligations; SI 2026/867 amendments take effect on 20 January 2027 [f2218, f2758, f15490]. The EN 474:2022 earth-moving machinery family was designated by a notice dated 8 August 2026, providing a presumption-of-conformity route, but the attributed notice number 0139/26 was not confirmed [f15244, f2875]. This designation is not an automatic-braking performance matrix: the booklet found neither a dedicated Great Britain off-road automatic-braking test regime nor a UK collision-avoidance mandate, with the latter explicitly framed as an expert-opinion planning caution [f2222, f2219, f2227]. The program needs a parallel British declaration path and standards-designation calendar; Great Britain has UKCA and approved bodies, whereas Northern Ireland remains under EU product law, so one declaration route should not be assumed to cover both [f15496, f15110, f15494]. HSE figures report 126 worker deaths in Great Britain in 2025/26, including 24 deaths from moving vehicles, the second most common cause; guidance attributes nearly a quarter of workplace-transport deaths to reversing and 40% of quarry accidents and 60% of quarry deaths to transport [f15498, f15499, f15500, f15501]. These figures support the system’s harm-prevention rationale, but the booklet did not verify the Quarries Regulations 1999 or relevant HSE and industry guidance in its UK regulatory review [f15503, f2225, f2226, f15502].

nodes.label: United States rules (OSHA 29 CFR 1926.601, MSHA 30 CFR, NIOSH)
nodes.text: In the United States, OSHA writes and enforces construction safety rules, MSHA does the same for mines, and NIOSH is the research institute whose studies and tests inform both; none of their rules requires automatic braking.
nodes.synopsis: For the off-road scope discussed, US requirements emphasize warnings and written risk programs rather than mandatory automatic braking; OSHA/MSHA require reverse alarms or an observer, and the surface-mobile-equipment rule requires technology evaluation and at least annual program updates [f166, f2083, f7750, f9806]. That rule was finalized on 20 December 2023, became effective on 19 January 2024, and had a compliance date of 17 July 2024; one expert-opinion fact reports 863 citations through April 2026, although the skeptic’s review says post-2024 status was not verified [f11229, f5844, f11231]. The non-mandate conclusion needs a scope qualification: the 2015 continuous-miner rule requires proximity detection that stops the machine before miner contact, while no final rule was found for the separate underground mobile-machine proposal [f2085, f7752]. MSHA Table M-1 uses approximately 2.94 m/s² deceleration, weight-dependent brake-system delays of 0.5–2.5 seconds, and one second of operator response; the glossary’s assumption of a 2.0-second total delay for very heavy equipment is in tension with those detailed inputs [f5989, f5990, f13658]. MSHA’s extension-of-approval route offers a precedent for evidence reuse, but the surface-equipment rule does not mention simulation and NIOSH identifies validation across mine conditions as an outstanding need [f621, f9807, f3601]. Mobile-equipment feasibility remains uncertain: commenters called proximity detection unproven, and Barrick warned in 2015 that automatic slowing and stopping would need cooperation and approval from multiple OEMs [f11227, f10691].

nodes.label: Canada and Australia rules (CSA M424, WHS laws, NSW Resources Regulator, RSHQ QGN 27 and QGN 33, DMIRS)
nodes.text: Canada regulates mining province by province with CSA M424 as the relevant national standard, and Australia uses model Work Health and Safety laws plus state mining regulators in New South Wales, Queensland and Western Australia, none of which mandates automatic braking.
nodes.synopsis: Australia’s model WHS regulation 215 requires reasonably practicable control of collision risks and a warning device where collision is possible, but prescribes no automatic braking, test speed or distance; the model regulations operate only when adopted by a state or territory [f2254, f2255, f2257, f2256].
