Canada is described as regulating mining province by province, with CSA M424 as the relevant national standard, but the booklet did not verify that standard or provincial regulations, found no federal collision-avoidance or automatic-braking rule, and recommends a province-by-province compliance matrix [f15525, f15528, f15526, f15529]. NSW braking guidance proposes service/secondary minimum mean net decelerations of 0.60/0.30 m/s² in service and 0.75/0.40 m/s² in type testing, with grade and mass corrections; these are proposed values, not an adopted rule, qualifying passages that describe 0.60 m/s² as a requirement [f13946, f236, f5889]. Incident evidence shows continuing risk: NSW reported no meaningful year-on-year reduction in vehicle interactions in July 2023 and 30 underground-coal LHD/personnel-transport collisions over the 12 months to mid-2025, while Queensland ranked mobile-plant collisions highest among high-potential incidents in 2024 and warned of under-reporting [f3111, f3196, f3006, f3049]. Queensland guidance calls for foreseeable-scenario assessments and testing across objects and environmental conditions, warns that idealised detection zones can create false protection, and identifies QGN 33 as guidance rather than a Recognised Standard [f3603, f3600, f5753, f2268]. Australian state-specific collision-avoidance requirements were not found and should be checked before reliance; likewise, the Australian modifications to AS 21815.1:2023 were not accessible, and the listed standards are not law unless incorporated by a regulator or contract [f7501, f7502, f2260, f2263].

nodes.label: South Africa rules (MHSA, DMRE, Chapter 8 regulations, MOSH, CPS verification specifications)
nodes.text: South Africa is the only country the booklet found that legally requires automatic slow-down and braking on mining machines, through regulations under the Mine Health and Safety Act, with the industry's MOSH specifications and independent test regime filling in the numbers the law leaves out.
nodes.synopsis: South Africa is the only jurisdiction the booklet found with a legal mandate for automatic slow-down and braking on heavy mining machines; the relevant regulations were published on 27 February 2015 and commenced on 21 December 2022 without a transitional period, after suspension because suitable technology was unavailable [f164, f1363, f10724, f11457]. For diesel-powered trackless mobile machinery, the rules require detection and warning, slowing to a safe speed and automatic braking if the operator does not act, plus failure to a safe state without human intervention [f2079, f2080]. The law preceded validation standards and specifies no detection percentage, distance, false-alarm limit or stopping-distance test; subsequent industry specifications supply quantitative criteria, including a 200 m minimum detection range and emergency-stop deceleration of 1.9 m/s² above 20 km/h or 1.0 m/s² for other machines [f1360, f2081, f11458, f2113, f5560]. Independent verification milestones include the surface TMM test specification dated 29 August 2025, the verification regime dated 11 October 2025 and the TRL7 stage-gate specification dated 20 January 2026, but the corpus identifies no prescribed allowance for virtual testing [f555, f556, f557, f1249]. The immediate Level 9 mandate pushed deployment before refinement, while a trade report suggesting December 2023 conflicts with the documented December 2022 commencement [f358, f359, f11461, f1364, f1363]. Safety outcomes remain a concern rather than proof of mandate effectiveness: total mining fatalities fell from 55 in 2023 to 42 in 2024, but trackless-mobile-machinery fatalities rose from six to nine [f3138, f3140].

nodes.label: South America and Asia rules (NR-22, NR-12, DS 132, SERNAGEOMIN, DS 024-2016-EM, DGMS, GB standards, JARI)
nodes.text: Brazil, Chile, Peru, India, China and Japan each have general mining or machinery safety rules, and in none of them did the booklet find a dedicated rule with numeric tests for automatic braking on off-road machines.
nodes.synopsis: Across Brazil, Chile, Peru, India, China and Japan, the booklet found general mining or machinery safety obligations but no dedicated rule with numeric tests for off-road automatic braking; for the South American findings, “not found” explicitly does not mean “not required” [f15576, f15586]. South America has no continent-wide machinery regime: Brazil uses NR-22 and NR-12, Chile DS 132, and Peru DS 024-2016-EM; Brazil's NR-22 was last modified on 29 January 2026, while Chile's DS 132 was promulgated in 2002, published in 2004 and consolidated to 2024 [f2285, f2130, f2131, f2132, f2286, f15581]. India's DGMS circular dated 21 August 2024 calls for proximity-warning or anti-collision devices on wheeled trackless machinery in opencast coal mines, a 2025 circular addresses fail-safe braking before tipper deployment, and a cited circular sets 30 km/h; these details have low confidence because only secondary summaries were reviewed, and no standardised national interaction-test matrix was found [f2302, f2303, f2304, f2307, f2453]. China's reported underground requirement is at least 50 m between rubber-tyred vehicles travelling in the same direction, but the regulation itself was not reviewed, and relevant GB/GB/T adoptions were not established [f2298, f2299, f2198]. No dedicated Japanese off-road automatic-braking rule was found, general safety provisions should not be interpreted as such a mandate, and JARI is a weather-test facility rather than a regulator [f2308, f2309, f15594]. Planning should therefore retain project acceptance criteria grounded in general obligations and configurable site-specific expectations, while recognising unresolved Chilean regulator guidance and uncertainty in the Indian and Chinese evidence [f15596, f15597, f2293, f2307, f2299].

nodes.label: EMESRT and PR-5A (Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table, vehicle interaction performance requirement)
nodes.text: EMESRT is a group of mining companies that writes shared safety requirements for the makers of mining machines, and PR-5A is its requirement for controlling collisions between vehicles and people, which gives the industry its nine-layer model of controls and its catalog of collision scenarios.
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT PR-5A supplies mining vehicle-interaction scenarios and a nine-layer control model: Level 7 is operator awareness, Level 8 advisory controls, and Level 9 automatic slowing and stopping; several chapters identify Revision 3.0 dated September 2024, although another chapter leaves the current edition uncertain [f2120, f5924, f6231, f4321]. Level 8–9 implementation depends on understanding the Level 1–7 baseline and integrating existing site controls; EMESRT guidance is not itself law or proof of product acceptance, while South African intervention requirements were gazetted on 21 December 2022 [f702, f704, f2586, f2587, f3624]. Scenario counts remain unresolved: a 2019 trade article reports 24 scenarios, whereas EMESRT's 2024 Activity Report reports 17 surface storyboards published in 2019 [f4079]. The storyboards provide useful mining hazard content, but are not machine-readable, cover only expert-envisaged situations, and provide no occurrence frequencies; no equivalent practical general-construction taxonomy was found [f7184, f6755, f6756, f4082]. For a programme starting from zero in October 2026, an ISO 21815-3/EMESRT-mapped operating domain and scenario catalogue is considered realistic by mid-2027, with physical confirmation recommended for at least one run per scenario family [f831, f7887]. These positive findings coexist with planning and skeptic-review passages saying EMESRT controls or leads were not reviewed or verified, so source verification remains an explicit gap [f9808, f11206, f11274].

nodes.label: ICMM, the nine-layer control model and the ICSV program (International Council on Mining and Metals, Innovation for Cleaner Safer Vehicles)
nodes.text: ICMM is the international association of the largest mining companies, and its Innovation for Cleaner, Safer Vehicles program set the industry goal of making collision avoidance technology available by 2025, using EMESRT's nine-layer model of controls.
aliases: ICMM, the nine-layer control model and the ICSV program
nodes.synopsis: ICMM is an international association of major mining companies and associations; its ICSV program brought mining companies and equipment makers together to target collision-avoidance technology availability by 2025, using EMESRT requirements and adopting EMESRT’s nine-layer model [f15612, f15613, f15614, f15615]. The ICMM–EMESRT Vehicle Interaction Leading Sites Program, published in April 2024, treats intervention as one control layer rather than a complete solution and requires understanding the effectiveness of Levels 1–7 before adding advisory Level 8 and intervention Level 9 controls [f15616, f15617, f11750, f12386]. For validation planning, the corpus calls for integration with existing site controls and scenario-based functional-performance requirements, rather than validating an automatic brake in isolation [f704, f703, f15622]. It also warns that technology can change human performance positively or negatively, and unqualified Level 9 deployment can harm production and accelerate brake wear; the booklet therefore recommends measuring nuisance braking as carefully as missed interventions [f581, f15620, f15623]. These positions are useful planning guidance, but the booklet did not review ICSV in depth and explicitly identifies verification gaps in Chapters 10, 12 and 13; the 2025 date is a stated availability goal, not evidence here that it was achieved [f15621, f2588].

nodes.label: ACARP and its two-tier test approach (Australian Coal Association Research Program)
nodes.text: ACARP is the research fund of the Australian coal industry, and its project C26028 proposed a two-tier framework for testing proximity detection systems: first prove that the system detects objects, then prove that its advisory or intervention action works.
aliases: ACARP and its two-tier test approach
nodes.synopsis: ACARP is the Australian coal industry's levy-funded research fund; Mining3 delivered its C26028 proximity-detection testing framework in January 2021 as a shared physical-test protocol, not a simulator [f15625, f15626, f15627, f16088]. The framework proves object detection in Tier 1 before testing Level 8 or Level 9 advisory or intervention in Tier 2, providing comparability and credible independent evidence alongside other industry frameworks [f15628, f15630]. Its baseline covers only limited choreographed scenarios and excludes pre-existing site controls and complex, multi-variable vehicle interactions, so independent review cannot alone establish site-specific performance [f15629, f1055]. The booklet recommends this structure for physical testing after high-throughput regression, covering stopping performance, grades, loads, nuisance braking and other adverse conditions; for a team starting in October 2026, procedures, soft targets, ground-truth specifications and independent-body engagement are considered realistic by mid-2027 [f15634, f749, f851]. Separately, the University of Queensland's C24028 advisory-interface study ran in 2017 with follow-on work to 2019, using a modified haul-truck simulator; richer schematic displays reduced collision risk, braking force and travel time, but this was advisory-warning research rather than automatic-braking validation [f15631, f15632, f13405]. The booklet treats that study as its main off-road evidence for operator-in-the-loop testing, while an acceptable false-alarm rate remains an explicit unresolved research question [f15635, f15633, f3605].

nodes.label: MOSH and its TRL stage gates (Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health learning hub)
nodes.text: MOSH is the learning hub of the Minerals Council South Africa that turned the country's automatic-braking law into engineering specifications and a staged, independently verified test regime organized by technology readiness level.
aliases: Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health
MOSH and its TRL stage gates
nodes.synopsis: MOSH supplies industry functional and technical performance requirements and a verification regime used alongside Regulation 8.10; mines check evidence against these requirements, including independent verification at two readiness gates [f1366, f1614, f12289]. Its TRL gates support staged release into an operating domain that widens over time, and a surface CPS TRL7 Stage Gate specification is dated 20 January 2026 [f423, f557]. Surface requirements include 200 m detection, range accuracy of 1.5 m or 10%, warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention, and stop gaps of 1–4 m at speeds up to 10 km/h or 15 m ±5 m above that speed [f2113, f2114, f2115, f2116, f2117]. Critical-failure fail-to-safe and disconnection detection have 500 ms limits, while machine reply has a distinct 50 ms limit; the HIL comparison's description of both as fail-to-safe limits therefore needs clarification [f2359, f5284, f5285, f5698]. University of Pretoria testing reported pass rates of 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces across 189 tests, with 79% verification tests and 21% development tests; throughput was 1.6 tests per week with an 18-week lead time as of October 2025 [f5178, f5179, f5180]. Planning must account for independent verification across machinery variants with differing braking characteristics and the TRL4 requirement for no false interventions or false warnings, because MOSH warns that nuisance slowing and stopping can disrupt production enough to prompt systems being switched off [f5613, f2119, f3300].

nodes.label: NIOSH, MSHA, BLS and CPWR (US bodies that publish accident data)
nodes.text: These four United States bodies produce the accident statistics the booklet relies on: NIOSH researches workplace safety, MSHA regulates mines and records their accidents, BLS counts all workplace deaths and injuries, and CPWR analyzes the construction figures.
aliases: US bodies that publish accident data
nodes.synopsis: The booklet draws on NIOSH for workplace-safety research, MSHA for mine accident records, and BLS data analyzed by CPWR for construction statistics; NIOSH has no enforcement power [f15654, f15655]. MSHA's calendar-2025 figures attribute 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries (9%) to powered haulage [f3051, f3052]. Construction evidence includes 7,681 vehicle/mobile-equipment deaths during 1992–2010, about 404 annually, and 170 struck-by deaths in 2019, 47.1% involving transport vehicles [f3188, f3190, f3191]. NIOSH evidence exposes a research-coverage imbalance: vehicle-environment events represented 54% of 91 fatal haul-truck accidents reviewed for 2005–2018, while 85% of research cases addressed vehicle-vehicle interactions [f5821, f5824]. Alarm evidence needs reconciliation: the synthesis reports 18% false alarms and 42% nuisance alarms in a 2006 Caterpillar 793B study, whereas Chapter 7 reports 59% false or nuisance alarms in 2006–2007 [f102, f103, f5751]. Planning should account for databases' stronger coverage of fatalities than property damage or near misses, and must not combine different agencies' figures into one rate [f15671, f15672].

nodes.label: WorkSafe New Zealand, WorkSafe Western Australia (SIR 286), HSE and EU-OSHA
nodes.text: These are workplace-safety regulators and agencies whose incident reports and statistics the booklet uses: WorkSafe New Zealand for mines and quarries, WorkSafe Western Australia for the Significant Incident Reports on autonomous haul trucks, Britain's HSE for national figures, and EU-OSHA, the European agency, mainly as a source of legislation summaries.
aliases: WorkSafe New Zealand, WorkSafe Western Australia
nodes.synopsis: The booklet uses WorkSafe New Zealand for mines and quarries, WorkSafe Western Australia for autonomous-haulage incident reports, and HSE for Great Britain statistics; EU-OSHA is an information agency, not a regulator, used mainly for legislation summaries [f15673, f15674, f15681, f15685, f15686]. New Zealand's August 2017 alert documented heavy-plant interactions during ordinary operations, while its October–December 2019 event distribution was 46% overturning, 27% unintended movement or brake failure, 11% collision with other plant, 4% berm breach and 12% burst tyre; this single-quarter, incompletely reported distribution must not be treated as a long-term national profile [f3122, f15676, f15677, f15678, f3198, f3131]. WorkSafe WA's SIR 286 describes trucks resuming movement during recovery when communications returned, illustrating risks from misunderstood modes, overridden controls and desensitization; the booklet therefore calls for communications-loss, blocked-sensor, restart and recovery tests, although the original issue dates of SIR 226 and 286 remain uncertain despite March 2025 webpage dates [f15682, f15683, f15689, f15690, f11207]. HSE's cross-industry 2025/26 figures report 126 worker deaths, including 24 from moving vehicles, second to 31 falls-from-height deaths; its undated quarry guidance attributes 40% of accidents and 60% of deaths to transport, while cross-industry reversing guidance attributes nearly a quarter of workplace-transport deaths to reversing [f3146, f3147, f3155, f3156, f3153]. The 2024/25 figures require reconciliation: an HSE release attributes about 16% of fatal injuries to moving vehicles, whereas a vendor summary reports 14 of 124 deaths, a materially lower proportion [f3149, f3152]. The booklet found no EU-OSHA collision breakdown by movement type, and says non-EU target markets can make MSHA, WorkSafe WA and South African Regulation 8.10 the primary legal context [f15687, f11285].

nodes.label: PEGASUS, VVM, SET Level, VaViM and EVIDENT (German and European research programs on scenario-based validation)
nodes.text: These are the publicly funded research programs, mostly German and Swedish, that worked out how to validate automated driving with scenarios and simulation, and whose durations show how long building such a capability takes.
aliases: PEGASUS, VVM, SET Level, VaViM and EVIDENT
nodes.synopsis: These mostly German and Swedish research programmes provide on-road reference-class evidence for planning virtual validation, rather than proof of an accepted off-road capability [f15692, f9614, f15704]. PEGASUS ran from January 2016 to June 2019 for 42 months, involving 17 partners, about 1,791 person-months and EUR 34.5 million; it produced a validation method for one highway function, not a certified product or approval [f1204, f1290, f1546]. Its functional, logical and concrete scenario levels subsequently entered ISO 34501–34505, while SET Level's Credible Simulation Process, published in August 2021, offers a development-process template with credibility levels [f6735, f7697, f8949, f15704]. VVM ran from July 2019 to June 2023 with EUR 47 million project volume, and EVIDENT ran from April 2022 to December 2024, about 33 months, developing simulation credibility methods [f15700, f1206, f1459, f15710]. VaViM's February–August 2022 effort was only a pre-study, but is identified as the nearest off-road precedent: validated models and real tests must operate side by side, without assuming automotive sensor and environment models are valid off-road [f1250, f1552, f1251, f15716]. The planning conclusion is to use a four-month window for validation, not capability construction; however, despite detailed programme descriptions elsewhere, multiple chapters flag PEGASUS, VVM and SET Level as unverified leads requiring checks before reliance [f15713, f15714, f4336, f7701, f11276].

nodes.label: Waymo and Motional collision-avoidance validation methods (on-road precedents)
nodes.text: Waymo and Motional are developers of self-driving road vehicles whose published safety methods show how simulation, replay, closed-course tests, public roads and shadow mode are layered, and whose material the booklet treats as vendor evidence from on-road.
aliases: Waymo and Motional collision-avoidance validation methods
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats Waymo and Motional as on-road vendor precedents for layered validation: simulation, replay and shadow mode filter candidates before scarce physical testing, rather than replace it [f15718, f15729]. Waymo published its collision avoidance testing methodology in 2022 and documented city-by-city expansion as evidence accumulates; the booklet cites these programs as evidence for staged release within a limited operating domain [f604, f15720, f15730]. Motional’s 2026 material describes progression from simulation and recorded-data re-simulation through closed-course and public-road testing to deployment, including daily shadow-mode evaluation before broader roll-out [f15725, f15726]. The booklet recommends shadow mode on the existing warning-only fleet as the most valuable lever for collecting false-positive evidence before the prototype arrives; Motional’s example runs new software without executing its actuator decisions [f15731, f15727]. Waymo’s material also distinguishes replay from closed-loop simulation and highlights reproducible dataset requirements and inconsistent human labeling, but neither developer discloses validation durations or physical-test shares sufficient for verified sign-off, and Waymo’s 2026 scene-generation world model has no off-road qualification [f15721, f15722, f15723, f15728, f15724].

nodes.label: Auto-GCAS (Automatic Ground Collision Avoidance System for fighter aircraft)
nodes.text: Auto-GCAS is the system on F-16 and F-35 fighter aircraft that takes control and pulls the aircraft up when it is about to fly into the ground, a precedent for an automatic intervention that had to be proven both effective and free of nuisance activations.
nodes.synopsis: Auto-GCAS takes control of F-16 and F-35 aircraft to avert imminent ground collision; it is a precedent for automatic intervention, not object-triggered machine braking [f15732, f1446]. Research began in the early 1980s, F-16 Block 40/50 retrofits began in September 2014, and capability development took about three decades [f1439, f1440, f1461]. F-35 integration followed in 2019, with the manufacturer attributing delivery seven years ahead of plan to agile development and reuse; this illustrates fast reuse after slow foundational construction, not elimination of flight testing [f1443, f15742, f1445]. A 2007 NASA release reported 98 percent effectiveness, and Lockheed Martin credited the system with saving eight F-16 pilots by 2019, although the booklet identifies save counts as secondary-press evidence [f1442, f1444, f2023]. Nuisance-free operation and avoiding harm were explicit priorities, motivating the recommendation to prove a machine brake does no harm and does not annoy before proving protection [f1441, f15743]. Validation combined simulation and flight tests with nuisance criteria, and acceptance came from military bodies—the US Air Force and Joint Program Office—rather than a civil regulator [f1915, f1919, f15741].

nodes.label: ACAS X and TCAS (aircraft collision avoidance, encounter models)
nodes.text: TCAS is the long-standing system that warns airline pilots of a possible mid-air collision and tells them to climb or descend, ACAS X is its successor, and the encounter model is the statistical description of near-collisions that let ACAS X be validated largely by simulation.
nodes.synopsis: ACAS X succeeds TCAS but remains an advisory, pilot-in-the-loop system, making it a precedent for collision-warning logic rather than automatic braking [f1428, f15748]. Its threat-resolution validation relied primarily on encounter-model Monte Carlo simulations covering millions of encounters equivalent to billions of flight hours, alongside pilot assessment and retained flight evaluation [f1907, f1571, f1908, f1911]. This capability took years to build from radar-derived encounter models: European CREME drew on twelve million flights, while the MIT Lincoln Laboratory model used nine months of radar recordings; the booklet did not establish validation duration once that capability existed [f1909, f1430, f1433, f1910]. Acceptance came through RTCA, EUROCAE and aviation authorities, with minimum operational performance standards DO-385 and ED-256 published in October 2018 [f1434, f1429]. March 2022 committee minutes recorded European results suggesting ACAS Xa induced more near mid-air collisions than TCAS, a disparity MIT Lincoln Laboratory did not observe; sensor noise had not been assessed, leaving model representativeness in question and warning against reliance on one simulation toolchain [f1436, f1437, f1968, f1969]. For heavy off-road collision mitigation, the precedent supports statistical simulation as primary safety evidence only with substantial real-data foundations, motivating field-interaction logging on the existing warning fleet [f15756, f15757].

nodes.label: Honda CMBS investigations (NHTSA PE22-003, EA24-002, EA25-002) as a precedent for unnecessary braking
nodes.text: The Honda investigations are the United States regulator's inquiries into cars whose Collision Mitigation Braking System braked hard with nothing in the way, the largest documented case of unnecessary automatic braking reaching a production fleet.
nodes.synopsis: Honda’s CMBS investigations document unnecessary automatic braking reaching large production fleets: PE22-003 opened on 21 February 2022 with 278 complaints, including six alleging collisions and reports of large speed changes with no obstruction [f15758, f15760]. In April 2024, EA24-002 covered 2,997,604 Accord and CR-V vehicles and 1,294 complaints; January 2025 analysis EA25-002 added 295,125 Insight and Passport vehicles, with about 412 reports cited by Honda versus 475 reviewed by NHTSA [f15761, f15763, f15764]. Crash and injury totals conflict across outlets, and secondary sources reported that the investigation remained open without a recall as of 2026, leaving its outcome uncertain [f1487, f1801, f1961]. Honda’s explanation that some customers misunderstood the system competes with the complaint record, while dealers unable to reproduce faults reportedly called the behavior “normal AEB operation” [f1970, f15765]. Published evidence does not establish what validation was performed, its methods or timing, or remaining physical testing, and does not demonstrate that weak pre-production validation caused the field problem [f1799, f1800, f15768]. For planning, the booklet recommends extensive non-triggering scenarios, treating unreproducible pilot complaints as early warnings, and assessing unnecessary braking rather than measuring success only through collisions avoided [f1992, f15772, f15771].

nodes.label: Rail, port, forklift and agriculture precedents (Wabtec and others)
nodes.text: These are the neighboring industries the booklet searched for cases of automatic braking validated with less physical testing, and in each it found products on the market but no published validation method, duration or share of physical testing.
aliases: Rail, port, forklift and agriculture precedents
nodes.synopsis: The cross-sector search found marketed products but no published validation method, duration or physical-testing share demonstrating substantially reduced physical validation; this is a research gap, not proof that relevant cases are absent [f15773, f1413, f2019]. Bosch’s tram system combines camera and radar with warnings and automatic braking, with public-transport approval reported by 2016, but its development duration, validation split and approval evidence package remain undisclosed in the research; other rail systems were not investigated deeply [f1417, f1420, f1421, f1422, f1423, f1424]. Wabtec’s December 2021 Komatsu haul-truck tests demonstrated controlled deceleration up to 30 km/h, followed by further physical testing to adjust detection zones for speed, payload, braking distance and road grade [f15781, f15782]. The neighboring-sector analogues require care: Kalmar’s June 2024 port case demonstrates warnings rather than stated automatic braking, Toyota SEnS+ slows through power cut-off rather than braking to a stop, and no currently sold agricultural or forestry system with documented object-triggered emergency braking and a public operating envelope was found [f1415, f15785, f15786, f1693]. The glossary concludes that the search supports no roughly four-month precedent from first representative hardware to accepted validation, but its categorical wording is stronger than the research’s explicit distinction between cases not found and cases confirmed absent [f15792, f2019].

nodes.label: The Pretoria process and MineSim (mining research precedents)
nodes.text: The Pretoria process is the University of Pretoria's step-by-step method for independently verifying mining collision-avoidance systems, and MineSim is an open-source simulation test system for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines.
nodes.synopsis: Pretoria independently verifies mining collision-avoidance systems under South Africa’s MOSH regime through staged laboratory tests followed by representative-mine trials, with brake robots and high-precision GPS used in the protocol [f15795, f1244, f6372]. Across 189 tests, reported pass rates were 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces; testing ran at 1.6 tests per week with an 18-week lead time as of October 2025, creating a constraint on a four-month schedule [f5178, f5180, f15809]. Hexagon’s Vehicle Intervention System reportedly passed Pretoria TRL4 verification in March 2026 before integrated site testing, but the cited vendor release provides no numbers [f1665, f6373]. Pretoria’s 2024 research links conservative collision-avoidance systems and false interventions to production losses, wear and resistance to adoption; steering-rate sampling aims to reduce those interventions, but its initial results are simulation-only [f15803, f6331]. MineSim, published in April 2025, is an open-source, peer-reviewed simulation system for autonomous open-pit trucks, incorporating scenarios from two real mines and mining-specific features such as unstructured roads and heavy-truck response lag [f464, f465, f466]. It demonstrates that mining-specific closed-loop scenario and planning simulation is feasible, not that sensor physics is validated; the booklet identifies sensor models in dust, snow and fog as an unresolved gap [f15808, f15810].

nodes.label: RAND Corporation and GAO (the Driving to Safety report and the US Government Accountability Office cost and schedule guides)
nodes.text: RAND is an independent American research institute whose 2016 report showed that road miles alone cannot prove a self-driving car is safe, and GAO is the audit arm of the United States Congress whose guides and program reviews show what makes cost and schedule estimates credible.
nodes.synopsis: RAND’s April 2016 Driving to Safety analysis estimated that demonstrating a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles requires 275 million failure-free miles at 95% confidence; demonstrating a 20% improvement requires about 11 billion miles at 80% power [f6662, f6663]. The booklet treats this as a statistical reason for virtual testing: the rare-event logic transfers to off-road machines, but the numerical road-mile estimates do not, and the proposed approach combines simulation, statistics and targeted tests rather than relying on field hours [f15817, f15815, f15826]. However, Chapter 13 calls RAND 2016 an unverified research lead, creating a verification gap against the detailed claims elsewhere [f11203, f11275, f6662, f6663]. GAO’s reviews support knowledge before commitment: in its 2006 evidence, most of 23 major defense programmes began development with immature technologies, and 10 already expected more than 30% cost growth or at least a year’s delay [f9683, f9425, f9426]. A July 2026 GAO report covered 104 programmes; the chapter reports that almost half of middle-tier programmes entered with immature technologies, time frames were overly optimistic, and average capability delivery exceeded 12 years [f9523, f9427, f9428, f9429]. The booklet uses GAO’s principle for gate-based planning and ranges instead of dates, while explicitly warning that the supporting audit evidence is correlational and sometimes small-sample rather than causal [f15827, f9423, f16427].

nodes.label: DARPA RACER program (off-road autonomy research)
nodes.text: RACER is a program of the United States defense research agency DARPA to make military ground vehicles drive themselves fast across rough off-road terrain, and its simulation arm built a very large virtual off-road environment.
nodes.synopsis: RACER pursues high-speed autonomous military ground-vehicle driving over unstructured off-road terrain; its relevance here is off-road simulation, not demonstrated construction or mining use [f15829, f15889]. RACER-Sim was announced in January 2022 with Duality Robotics and Intel-Federal as primes, a reported Phase 1 budget of about USD 6 million, and a task for Duality with Neya Systems to build an 80 km² environment measuring 20 km by 4 km [f8419, f8420, f8421]. NASA JPL contracted Duality for RACER Phase II in September 2024, documenting government use and supporting the feasibility of large virtual job sites [f8422, f15839]. This does not establish acceptance of simulation as braking safety evidence: Chapter 2 found no documented RACER precedent with quantified simulation substitution, while Chapter 13 retained RACER as an unverified lead worth checking [f15840, f1427, f11274]. Separately, the booklet uses DARPA's Heilmeier questions and phase go/no-go metrics as planning and review analogues, rather than as braking-validation evidence [f16460, f9909, f15840].

nodes.label: Columbia Accident Investigation Board (why a space shuttle accident appears in a mining booklet)
nodes.text: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board was the body that investigated the loss of the space shuttle Columbia in 2003, and its findings about a computer model used far outside the range it had been tested on are the textbook case of false confidence from simulation.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet uses Columbia as a warning for heavy off-road collision mitigation: simulation should not be trusted for machines, sensors or weather outside physically tested conditions, and every simulation claim needs an explicit validity envelope and margin [f15856, f15854]. Following a January 2003 foam strike, engineers assessed damage using Crater; Columbia was lost on re-entry on 1 February 2003, and the investigation board reported in August 2003 [f7950, f7958, f15848]. The debris was about 400 times the size represented in Crater's test database, versus 640 times in an early briefing; engineers extrapolated the model's small-impact conservative bias and overrode its prediction of penetration deeper than the tile [f7582, f7956, f7953]. The interpretation remains contested: the booklet presents both a model-validity failure and Wayne Hale's 2011 argument that the model warned correctly but management overrode it [f8192, f7960]. Across the trust and planning chapters, the board's criticism of slides that buried key information supports presenting validity limits and caveats in plain charts and words rather than dense slide decks [f7959, f8020, f9856].

nodes.label: Tool chain
nodes.text: A tool chain is the set of separate software programs and hardware boxes that are connected together so that one virtual test can run from start to finish.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies credibility—not tool choice—as the decisive toolchain risk; cited on-road frameworks require documented credibility assessments, but these are not presented as off-road acceptance rules [f200, f6928, f7673, f10411]. The market is modular, combining strong on-road sensor/scenario tooling with heavy-machine terrain/hydraulics tools, yet no single tool has public evidence covering heavy-machine automatic braking across many job-site types and all-weather sensing, and public pricing is largely absent [f195, f8281, f197]. Expert judgment rejects a newcomer achieving coverage of more than 100 site types, all weather and every sensor type by mid-2027, but considers a narrow first-release toolchain feasible if work starts in October 2026 and reuses existing simulators [f1590, f1591]. Most infrastructure can be built before hardware arrives if interfaces are established early, but the architecture must accommodate sensor physics and final correlation requires the real sensor and machine; assumed hardware remains a risk until mid-2027 [f5568, f11916, f12227, f10492]. The four-month validation window cannot be compressed, so scenario catalogs, fleet-data pipelines, tools and credibility evidence should be prepared beforehand [f11923]. Planning should assign explicit ownership of qualification and model credibility, use credibility maturity measures rather than toolchain TRLs, and provide verification and configuration-management evidence; component-level physical testing remains a point of debate in the cited on-road material [f5792, f9536, f8034, f7690].

nodes.label: Complete and near-complete simulation platforms
nodes.text: A complete simulation platform is a commercial or open-source product that tries to cover several layers of the tool chain at once: scenarios, environments, sensors, vehicle motion and test execution.
nodes.synopsis: Complete platforms aim to cover scenarios, environments, sensors, vehicle motion and test execution, but usually still require separate machine models, controllers, asset pipelines or hardware benches; “complete” is relative [f15871, f8344, f15872]. The market is modular: road-vehicle tools are strong in sensors and scenarios, heavy-machine tools in terrain and hydraulics, and no single tool has public evidence of validating earth-moving-machine automatic braking across many site types and all-weather sensing [f13604, f194, f13071]. Off-road evidence includes MathWorks’ shipped excavator, backhoe and haul-truck examples in R2026b, the September 2025 Applied Intuition–Komatsu partnership, and Duality Falcon’s military applications, but independent heavy-machine automatic-braking validation was not found [f15878, f15882, f15889, f15921]. Integrated commercial stacks are considered faster for on-road-like elements but still need heavy-machine content; no time-to-first-useful-result benchmark or independent evidence of a universal integrated-versus-modular winner was found [f8750, f8749, f9359]. Nearly every commercial platform requires vendor quotations for budgeting; Falcon’s USD 20/month education license is a limited public-price exception, with its commercial price unavailable [f15922, f15888]. AURELION 26.2 was released on 15 July 2026, but listed AURELION/SIMPHERA evidence remains on-road only, and frame rates were not found for AURELION, CarMaker, DRIVE Sim/Omniverse, CARLA or MAVS [f8451, f8997, f4957].

nodes.label: Open-source simulators
nodes.text: An open-source simulator is a simulation program whose source code anyone may read, change and use without paying a license fee, under conditions set by its license.
nodes.synopsis: Open-source simulators are viable low-license-cost cores for heavy off-road automatic-braking validation, but not the lowest-total-cost option: coupling, assets, scenarios and validation evidence still require specialist labor, potentially producing a seven-figure annual program [f196, f8303, f8318]. Expert judgment supports a narrow first-release toolchain if work starts in October 2026 and existing simulators are reused; precedents include MineSim, published in April 2025 for autonomous mining trucks, and AutoDRIVE-based vision-guided AEB testing across 128 simulated off-road cases [f1591, f464, f467]. Capabilities differ materially: Chrono offers deformable-soil models, MAVS has validated tire-soil and lidar-vegetation models, while CARLA has a mining earth-mover asset but no soil physics [f3739, f3740, f15901, f15902]. These capabilities do not establish safety-case credibility: CARLA, Gazebo and Isaac Sim were not verified in this research, none was found validated for off-road collision warning, and open-source availability alone does not establish verification, validation or applicability [f5850, f5851, f7758]. Planning should account for separate asset-license terms, freeze a qualified build as projects change, and investigate maintenance and security-patch arrangements, which the research did not examine [f8908, f15936, f15938, f9392, f9393].

nodes.label: Sensor simulation tools
nodes.text: A sensor simulation tool produces artificial camera images, radar returns, lidar point clouds or ultrasonic echoes from a virtual scene, so the braking software can be tested without a real sensor.
nodes.synopsis: Sensor simulation adds a model that must itself be validated; photorealistic appearance alone is insufficient, and camera, lidar, radar and ultrasonic responses require separate simulation layers and material data [f470, f13068, f85, f86]. Across chapters, no validated off-road sensor models or fidelity thresholds were found, standardized quality metrics are lacking, and dust is identified as the biggest gap; evidence for snow, glare and darkness remains weak or absent [f5763, f5764, f5217, f89, f6488]. Lidar is described as the best-validated sensor type, but weather evidence is mostly on-road, and the 2021 lidar dust-cloud model compared with experiments was vendor-coauthored rather than independent evidence of broad off-road qualification [f12604, f7087, f6380]. Planning should start the environment and sensor-model pipeline in October 2026, with calibrated models for one or two sensor types in clear and dusty conditions only conditional mid-2027 targets; production-intent validation depends on sensor selection, mounting and calibration data [f3771, f860, f861]. The recommended use is qualification-quality testing of selected sensor effects and corner cases, feeding detection delay, range and error into braking simulation; compute costs span more than three orders of magnitude, and ten continuously running GPUs over four months provide at most about 29,000 GPU-hours [f4474, f6487, f4451, f8313].

nodes.label: Vehicle and machine dynamics tools
nodes.text: A vehicle and machine dynamics tool calculates how a machine moves: how it accelerates, steers, tips, sinks into soft ground and stops when the brakes act.
nodes.synopsis: The market is modular: road-oriented tool chains are strong in sensors and scenarios but weak in soil physics, while heavy-machine physics tools are mature in dynamics, terrain and hydraulics but have thin sensor and scenario tooling [f195, f15860, f8290]. Braking-test quality depends on the machine model, which must include friction, slope, mass, payload, attachment position, tire or track state, and brake and hydraulic delay; implementation options range from point-mass models with lumped hydraulics to full multibody models with detailed plant [f15960, f15978, f6437, f6454]. Documented off-road options include Altair tracked-machine soft-soil workflows and Project Chrono 10.0.0, released on 27 March 2026, with wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles on deformable terrain; however, common handling tire models do not work on Chrono's deformable terrain [f6388, f8301, f8496, f15970]. A coupled renderer, dynamics, soil and HIL chain requires high integration effort, and heavy-machine vendors' sensor physics is not independently validated in weather [f13240, f15980]. No public apples-to-apples stopping-distance benchmark or evidence of toolchain superiority was found, and the skeptic's review describes Project Chrono as an unverified lead despite documented capabilities and research use elsewhere in the booklet [f6397, f6561, f6396, f11206, f15908].

nodes.label: Terrain and soil tools
nodes.text: Terrain and soil tools calculate how the ground deforms under a machine, how a bucket digs into a pile and how loose material flows, because soft ground changes how a machine stops.
nodes.synopsis: Terrain and soil tools model ground deformation, digging and loose-material flow because soft ground changes machine stopping; semi-empirical terramechanics can predict braking force and sinkage [f15981, f6461]. Across the booklet, the market is modular: heavy-machine tools offer strong terrain and hydraulics but thin sensor and scenario tooling, and combining separate renderer, dynamics, soil and HIL tools requires high integration effort [f195, f8283, f15860, f13240]. Available methods range from fast Bekker-Wong SCM to grain-based DEM and continuum SPH/CRM; Project Chrono 10.0.0, dated 27 March 2026, supports wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles on deformable terrain [f15982, f15983, f15984, f8301]. High fidelity is not suitable for broad scenario sweeps: Chrono continuum soil simulation runs 50–200 times slower than real time, while uncertain soil inputs can overwhelm the benefit of model fidelity [f15992, f16233, f15993]. The recommended approach is to use detailed terrain simulation to characterize stopping-distance sensitivity to soil, slope and payload, fit simpler models for regression testing, and confirm the parameter envelope through targeted physical tests [f15994].

nodes.label: Environment creation and reconstruction tools
nodes.text: Environment creation and reconstruction tools build the three-dimensional virtual job site, either by designing it by hand and by rules or by rebuilding a real site from photographs, laser scans and machine recordings.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus recommends a hybrid “environment factory”: combining methods matters more than selecting one authoring package, and a quarry model can mix plans, surveys, hand-built gaps, asset libraries and hundreds of procedural variants [f3700, f3775, f3774, f15998]. It identifies eleven method families; existing plans and asset libraries are the fastest resources for a broad portfolio, while hybrid multi-source twins have the highest initial integration effort but lower effort per subsequent variant [f3773, f3704, f4279]. Planning estimates remain uncertain: no numeric effort or cost per site was found for any of the eleven families, no independent cost-normalisation study was found, and comparison ratings are relative judgements unless numbers are supplied [f4170, f4171, f4172, f4169]. RoadRunner supports imports, reconstruction and simulator exports, with R2026b the latest release found, but its road-oriented editor needs custom work-site semantics; OpenUSD and Omniverse can represent sites but do not constitute a validation method [f8605, f8606, f9156, f8607, f9168]. Reconstruction is a bottleneck rather than a solved prerequisite: reusable site representations are needed before scenario volume matters, reconstructed RadaRays meshes were too large to clean manually, log-based appearance reconstruction struggles with viewpoint changes, and every captured environment needs a capture date and revision history [f16011, f4964, f16004, f16013].

nodes.label: Scenario generation and test management tools
nodes.text: Scenario generation tools describe and vary the test situations; test management tools decide which runs to execute, run them, and keep track of the results.
nodes.synopsis: Scenario generation tools describe and vary test situations, while test management tools select, execute and record runs and report coverage; scenario count alone is not coverage [f16014, f16015, f16016, f16030]. The market is modular: road-vehicle chains offer strong sensor and scenario tooling but weak soil physics, while heavy-machine tools offer strong terrain and hydraulics but thin sensor and scenario tooling, so a specialist physics engine is not a substitute for validation management [f15860, f8345]. Foretellix Foretify combines constrained-random, coverage-driven generation with large-scale validation management and external-simulator integration; its off-road relevance is documented by a March 2021 Volvo Autonomous Solutions partnership targeting mines and quarries, but it is not a machine or soil physics engine [f8621, f8622, f8625, f8627]. Evidence listed for VTD ScenarioEngine and dSPACE SIMPHERA is on-road only, off-road deployments of AVL SCENIUS and Scenic were not found, and esmini was not assessed—these are evidence gaps rather than proof that tools lack capabilities [f9199, f9204, f9189, f9209, f8836]. Before prototype arrival, the program should build a simulator-independent scenario library, campaign generator and automated verdict functions, backed by traceability, version control, continuous integration and result storage; the middle-cost stack does not supply large-scale coverage-driven scenario management [f7372, f16028, f9300].

nodes.label: Data replay and HIL hardware
nodes.text: Data replay feeds recorded real sensor data back into the braking software, and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) hardware is the real-time computer and signal equipment that lets the real control unit run against a simulated machine.
aliases: CPU with a field-programmable gate array
nodes.synopsis: Data replay feeds recorded sensor data into braking software, while HIL runs a real control unit against a simulated machine; the glossary identifies HIL as the only way to test ECU timing and interfaces before the machine exists [f16032, f16042]. The booklet recommends an ISO/TS 21815-2-interface HIL bench for mid-2027, but keeping it off the critical path unless interfaces stabilize early; sensor injection is sensor- and ECU-specific, with raw-signal benches requiring the most integration effort [f16044, f16043]. Commercial alternatives span dSPACE, NI, Speedgoat and OPAL-RT, but the cited on-road replay/HIL evidence establishes architectural feasibility rather than suitability for this off-road manufacturer; OPAL-RT separately names off-highway and defense users [f8363, f8364, f5610, f9235]. An NI PXIe-8842 controller is listed at about USD 5,200, not a complete bench price; the NI system requires a quote, and no full-system dSPACE price was found [f8644, f9227, f8642].

nodes.label: Operator-in-the-loop simulators
nodes.text: An operator-in-the-loop simulator is a cab, screens and controls where a real person drives a simulated machine, so that human reactions to warnings and automatic braking can be measured.
nodes.synopsis: Operator-in-the-loop simulators let a person drive a simulated machine using a cab, screens and controls, enabling studies of warning reaction time, surprise at automatic stops and tolerance of nuisance stops [f16045, f16046]. Because warning-then-brake intervention depends on operator reaction and nuisance interventions are documented as the primary reason deployed proximity systems fail, the booklet recommends an early operator clinic and makes operator acceptance a release criterion [f16053, f16054, f16052, f16056]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, operator-simulator experiment capability is realistic by mid-2027, conditional on a simulator existing or being procurable [f848]. Named resources include Fraunhofer ITWM RODOS, CM Labs Vortex, Mevea mining simulators, Volvo CE's Simulink/Simscape excavator simulator and an academic haul-truck proximity-interface simulator; Mevea claims over 100 simulator models for more than 50 customers [f16047, f16048, f16049, f16050, f16051, f15964]. The booklet identifies these simulators as a likely need for validation, but the need for warning-then-brake human-factors work remains qualified, and CM Labs' documented use is mainly training rather than collision-mitigation validation [f16055, f9379, f8579, f15968].

nodes.label: Cloud execution services
nodes.text: Cloud execution means renting computers, including graphics processors, by the hour over the internet instead of buying them, so that thousands of simulations can run in parallel.
nodes.synopsis: Cloud execution rents computing capacity by the hour for parallel simulations, matching bursty demand that could otherwise leave purchased machines idle; vendor clouds run particular simulators, while generic clouds rent raw machines [f16057, f16058, f16059, f16061]. Quoted 2026 public rates include AWS g6e.xlarge with one L40S at about USD 1.861/hour, eight-L40S capacity at USD 30.131/hour, and Google g2-standard-32 with one L4 at USD 1.734/hour; a one-year AWS commitment lowers the single-L40S rate to about USD 1.17/hour [f8855, f8858, f8861, f8859]. Spot capacity suits checkpointable regression rather than deterministic HIL or irreplaceable long jobs, and its quoted AWS prices vary widely between trackers [f8864, f8860]. Compute is described as cheap relative to engineering labor, but the four-month window limits throughput: ten single-processor instances running continuously for 122 days cost roughly USD 54,000 and provide at most about 29,000 processor-hours [f16070, f16071]. Public prices were not found for the named simulator-vendor clouds, and vendor terms, export controls and data residency were not researched; sensitive site scans, mine layouts and machine CAD motivate an on-premises or private-cloud option [f9256, f16068, f16069]. Procurement should price concurrent workers and cloud rights rather than desktop seats alone, recheck regional prices, and address capacity constraints with multi-region planning, justified reservations and a local fallback [f16486, f8865, f8925, f8926].

nodes.label: Mining, construction, agriculture and forestry specific tools
nodes.text: These are the few simulation tools, datasets and frameworks that were built for, or deliberately adapted to, off-road working machines rather than road cars.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus distinguishes tools built for or deliberately adapted to off-road working machines from predominantly road-origin simulation platforms, noting that quarry environments lack lanes, curbs and traffic lights [f16072, f16073]. Relevant options include mobile-machinery physics tools, road-validation platforms with explicit off-road packages, and procedural scene generators with examples across agriculture, forestry and construction [f16074, f16075, f4194]. Concrete milestones include Foretellix’s 2021 mines-and-quarries partnership, MineSim’s April 2025 open-pit truck benchmark, Applied Intuition–Komatsu’s 9 September 2025 partnership covering staffed-site collision avoidance, and MathWorks R2026b excavator, backhoe and haul-truck examples [f9184, f16083, f8399, f8379]. Scene-creation examples include Agri-Sim reported in August 2026 and AgriGen on Isaac Sim reported in September 2026; MineSim draws on two real mines and models unstructured roads and truck response lag, but is treated as evidence of closed-loop scenario feasibility rather than validated sensor physics [f4147, f4142, f16084, f16092]. For planning, off-road relevance should not be equated with braking validation: only a few suppliers publicly position for construction or mining sensing, most capabilities remain claims rather than independently demonstrated results, and independent automatic-braking validation for any listed tool, dataset or framework was not found [f8284, f16091].

nodes.label: Engineering service companies and research institutes
nodes.text: Engineering service companies sell engineering work by the hour or by the project, and research institutes sell applied research, test facilities and independent assessment; both can do parts of virtual validation for a manufacturer.
nodes.synopsis: Engineering service companies can supply contracted integration, modeling and testing, while research institutes contribute methods, facilities and experienced personnel; independent assessment checks results without having built them [f16093, f16094, f16095, f16096]. Relevant off-road offerings include AVL's sector-specific validation work and tractor demonstration, Mevea's modeling and simulators, and Fraunhofer ITWM's directly relevant heavy-machinery research [f8800, f8804, f8810, f8823]. Quantitative and dated examples include AVL's claimed vehicle-model correlation of up to 97% and IDIADA's 2026 demonstration of simulated versus proving-ground automatic-braking correlation, but heavy off-road proof was not found for several other providers [f16098, f16109, f8813, f8816, f8818]. The booklet favors a hybrid arrangement: a partner accelerates the first correlated sensor model while the manufacturer retains the operating-domain definition, scenarios, acceptance criteria and correlation data [f16125]. Although the highest-cost integrated commercial tool chain can provide partner capacity for the four-month window, no public provider contract values or delivery timelines were found, and named environmental-test facilities' availability and machine-size suitability were not examined [f9313, f16126, f16124].

nodes.label: Build, buy or partner
nodes.text: Build, buy or partner is the decision between writing the simulation capability in-house on open-source parts, buying commercial products, or paying an outside company to deliver it.
nodes.synopsis: The research treats build, buy and partner as vendor-neutral alternatives, but identifies credibility—not tool choice—as the decisive risk in selecting an off-road automatic-braking validation toolchain [f297, f200]. For a manufacturer with no virtual-testing capability and nine months before hardware, it recommends a hybrid: retain the operating-domain definition, scenario catalog and correlation data internally, license or co-develop machine physics, and engage a partner for the first correlated sensor model [f8258, f8342]. Expert judgment says a newcomer starting in October 2026 can build a narrow toolchain for the first-release envelope by reusing commercial or open-source simulators rather than writing them from scratch; quick prototypes should not be confused with safety-credible capability [f1591, f8742]. Open-source development offers low license costs but high internal labor and responsibility for credibility evidence, while an integrated commercial stack reduces integration burden without eliminating substantial domain-modeling and correlation work [f16128, f16129, f8748]. Partner-led delivery may be fastest and address the 2027 deadline, but lasting control depends on contracts and knowledge transfer; the booklet recommends clear ownership clauses, editable technical deliverables and open-format export to limit dependency [f16133, f16139, f8764, f16134, f16137, f13217]. No independent 2024–2026 benchmark establishes total cost, headcount or time to a first useful result, and the available vendor cases are qualitative rather than controlled measurements, so the preferred hybrid is a judgment rather than a quantitatively demonstrated winner [f8734, f8315, f16136, f8342].

nodes.label: License types and pricing models
nodes.text: A software license is the permission to use a program under stated conditions, and the pricing model is how the vendor charges for it: per computer, per shared pool, per year, per person, or not at all.
nodes.synopsis: Open-source tools are viable as a low-license-cost simulation core, but do not provide the lowest total cost; even free software can underpin a program costing seven figures annually because of engineering labor [f196, f8296, f13551]. Public tool prices are almost entirely absent and nearly every commercial tool is quote-only, so budgets should use vendor quotations; the few dated price points found include an unofficial January 2024 MathWorks list, a Falcon education license, an NI controller and cloud GPU rates [f8304, f8305, f16441]. License permissions vary by component and use: Isaac Sim's core is Apache 2.0 and free for internal R&D, but some assets have additional terms and redistribution with Omniverse Kit requires NVIDIA AI Enterprise, whose price was not found [f8483, f8484, f8486]. Procurement should price peak concurrent workers, continuous-integration and cloud rights, subcontractor access, HIL nodes and disaster recovery rather than desktop seats alone; marketplace asset terms may also prohibit redistribution or training use [f16486, f4373]. The plan needs ownership, budget, licences and revalidation rules after September 2027, an identified sustainment blind spot; supplier rights still under negotiation near prototype delivery and unbudgeted license invoices are warning signs [f10179, f10367, f11025, f11083].

nodes.label: The three example tool chains at different cost levels
nodes.text: The booklet sketches three ways to assemble a tool chain, from an open-source core to a fully commercial chain with a partner, and labels them lowest, middle and highest by relative cost and integration posture, not by dollar figures.
aliases: Speedgoat or NI for later hardware-in-the-loop
three example tool chains at different cost levels
nodes.synopsis: The three chains are expert assessments: an open-source core with in-house integration, a model-based engineering stack with heavy-machine physics, and an integrated commercial chain with a partner; “lowest”, “middle” and “highest” indicate relative cost and integration posture, not dollar budgets, because almost every commercial vendor is quote-only [f16155, f16156, f16157]. The lowest-cost chain supports camera/lidar testing, deformable-terrain machine dynamics and scripted scenarios, but validated radar, physics-based ultrasonic, correlated weather effects and qualification evidence require major work; scarce skills and manufacturer-owned integration mean low license cost need not mean low total cost [f16160, f16161, f9281, f9284]. The middle-cost chain couples machine physics to controls through FMI and supports MIL, SIL and HIL, but lacks broad validated multi-sensor weather physics and large-scale coverage-driven scenario management, with module prices unpublished [f13239, f13328, f16164, f16165]. The highest-cost chain offers physics-based simulation of all four sensor types, large-scale regression and partner capacity for a four-month window, yet cannot guarantee off-road realism or eliminate manufacturer correlation tests, and no public evidence establishes end-to-end off-road automatic-braking validation [f16169, f16170, f16171]. At every cost level, the recommended “fourth architecture” allocates tests across fast functional testing, medium-fidelity dynamics, selective high-fidelity simulation, HIL and targeted physical correlation, with allocation determined by sensitivity and correlation work rather than assumption [f16172, f16173].

nodes.label: CPU, GPU, FPGA, VRAM and real-time computers
nodes.text: These are the kinds of computing hardware a simulation program needs: the central processor for general work, the graphics processor for massively parallel work, the programmable chip for exact timing, the graphics memory that holds the scene, and computers built to answer on a fixed schedule.
nodes.synopsis: The corpus rejects a single simulation hardware specification: logic and object-list tests suit commodity CPUs or cloud containers, sensor rendering suits GPU workers, soil simulation suits dedicated GPU/HPC workers, and HIL needs a local deterministic real-time system [f8839, f16220]. Radar figures illustrate workload-dependent performance: a vendor CPU solver took 14 hours for a 12-second scenario, a vendor GPU solver reported about 12 ms per frame, and independent RadaRays measurements ranged from 7.8–18.8 ms per image on an RTX 2070 Super, only for the tested radar, model and scene [f4931, f12961, f4936]. CARLA UE5 requires at least an RTX 3000-series GPU with 16 GB VRAM and 130 GB disk, while Chrono CRM requires an NVIDIA GPU and reportedly runs 50–200 times slower than real time; consumer hardware can also struggle with fields containing thousands of vegetation assets [f8469, f8851, f15989, f3895]. For HIL, timing matters more than throughput: missing a required sensor-message deadline of 50 milliseconds can produce a false test result [f16187, f16179]. The cloud-budget example buys about 29,000 GPU-hours for USD 54,490 using ten single-GPU instances continuously for 122 days, but actual geometry, sensors and achieved real-time factors must be benchmarked before infrastructure commitments [f16226, f16190, f10832]. Remaining sizing gaps include insufficient mostly on-road neural-rendering evidence and unestablished data rates, storage sizes and ruggedized logger requirements for continuous raw recording on working machines [f4948, f5801].

nodes.label: Graphics cards named in the booklet
nodes.text: A graphics card is a circuit board carrying a graphics processing unit (GPU) and its memory, and the booklet names specific models because the speed of sensor simulation depends heavily on which one is used.
nodes.synopsis: Graphics-card choice strongly affects sensor-simulation speed and scene capacity: ray-tracing cores accelerate camera, lidar and radar calculations, while VRAM limits scene size; most named cards are NVIDIA models because the reviewed simulators depend on NVIDIA ray-tracing libraries [f16191, f16205, f16206, f16192]. CARLA UE5 requires at least an NVIDIA RTX 3000-series GPU with 16 GB VRAM, alongside Ubuntu 22.04 or Windows 11 and 130 GB of disk; the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell offers 96 GB of memory, but its server prices were not found [f8469, f8852, f16198]. The booklet's 2026 cloud prices include AWS G6e with L40S GPUs at USD 1.861–30.131 per hour on demand in us-east-1, and Google g2-standard-32 with one L4 at about USD 1.734 per hour; these are generic pay-per-use options, not evidence of off-road suitability [f9258, f9260, f9257, f9259]. Illustrative performance figures include RadaRays at 7.8–18.8 milliseconds per radar image on an RTX 2070 Super versus 25.8–78.5 milliseconds on a desktop CPU, SplatAD scene training in about one hour on an A100, and weather editing at 20.52 seconds per image on an A40 [f16196, f16200, f16201]. No neutral, controlled cross-vendor benchmark was found, and reported multi-sensor frame-rate losses mean every candidate must be timed with the program's own machine geometry and sensors; Chrono's NVIDIA requirement is explicitly a dependency risk rather than a recommendation [f16208, f16207, f16209, f16193].

nodes.label: High-performance computing (HPC) and cluster, versus workstation
nodes.text: A workstation is one powerful desktop computer; a cluster is many computers wired together and managed as one; high-performance computing (HPC) is the largest class of cluster, built for scientific calculation.
nodes.synopsis: A workstation serves an engineer running one simulation at a time, whereas a managed cluster is recommended for thousands of scenarios within four months; HPC is the largest cluster class, intended for scientific calculation [f16210, f16211, f16213]. Samak et al.'s August 2024 GVSETS work used HPC clusters for 128 simulated off-road braking cases because sequential sweeps could not explore the variability space within time constraints, but the booklet treats this as evidence for scaling methodology rather than a prescribed scenario count [f467, f4104, f4105]. The recommended architecture separates commodity-server logic tests, GPU sensor tests, dedicated GPU or HPC soil tests, and local real-time HIL, while accounting for orchestration, database and storage loads [f16220, f16221]. Within the four-month window, throughput matters more than real-time rendering: inexpensive models should screen broadly, reserving expensive models for selected cases, especially compute-intensive terrain simulation [f16219, f6471, f8846]. Illustrative workloads include an aircraft radar calculation taking about 616 ms per angular position on eight nodes with four AMD MI250X GPUs each, and a European virtual-testing study requiring over 800 compute hours plus over 300 hours of manual case selection; these are not compute estimates for the proposed braking system [f4940, f16217, f16218, f10739]. Actual compute expense, cloud or cluster capacity, licensing and labor costs remain unavailable, and on-premises GPU server prices were not found, leaving the architecture recommendation without a substantiated budget [f10739, f8853].

nodes.label: Compute cost and run time
nodes.text: Compute cost is what it costs to run the simulations, and it is set by three numbers: the price per hour of the computer, how many hours it runs, and how much simulated time each hour produces.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet concludes that compute is cheap relative to engineering labor, but its value depends on simulated time delivered per wall-clock hour; real-time factors must be benchmarked on the actual machine geometry and sensor set [f198, f8309, f13424, f13425]. Recorded-data replay, semantic/object-list replay and SIL are economical routes to large test volumes, whereas coupled high-fidelity terrain models are unsuitable for exhaustive sweeps and excessive fidelity threatens the four-month validation window [f332, f5257, f527, f6103, f13063]. Sensor and weather compute costs span more than three orders of magnitude: examples include 14 hours for a 12-second CPU radar scenario, approximately 12 ms per GPU radar frame, and 20 seconds per diffusion-weather image, but these are examples rather than planning constants [f4451, f4453, f4454, f4456, f12963]. Listed GPU rates are about USD 1.734–1.861 per hour; the booklet estimates ten continuously running GPUs over four months at roughly USD 54,000 and at most about 29,000 GPU-hours, limiting full-sensor-fidelity scenario coverage [f8310, f8311, f8312, f8313]. The assumed thousands of nightly runs and throughput for about 6,000 zero-miss trials across 20 strata plus hundreds of exposure hours remain unquantified, with a recommendation to fix the run and physical-correlation budget before mid-2027 [f7450, f7449, f7451]. Actual program compute, capacity and triage costs are absent from the brief, independent published off-road safety-validation compute costs and ROI were not found, and the proposed compute/triage bottleneck lacks program-specific evidence [f10739, f10615, f10789, f10790].

nodes.label: Software terms a planner meets
nodes.text: These are the everyday words of software work that appear throughout the booklet: how programs talk to each other, which programming tools the simulators use, and how teams package, track and automatically test their code.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet presents software interfaces and programming environments as practical integration choices: CARLA offers Python, Prescan offers Python and MATLAB, RoadRunner uses gRPC, and ROS 2 is integrated across several simulators [f16237, f16240]. Version instability is a central planning risk: CARLA changed from UE4 to UE5 with some APIs unsupported, while Isaac Sim 5.0 deprecated camera-prim RTX workflows and removed annotators; evidence may therefore need re-qualification after updates [f8892, f8487, f16247]. Recommended controls are to freeze and containerize the tool chain, archive containers for the safety case, regression-test upgrades, and record the software build or commit in every run [f16241, f16248, f16243]. Open-source delivery avoids license lock-in but brings GPU, library and version dependencies, requiring reproducible builds, internal competence, upstream and security-patch tracking, and DevOps labor [f8898, f8900, f16244]. Acquisition planning should include cloud and continuous-integration skills, partner handover of continuous-integration scripts, and a software bill of materials with asset and license review for mixed licensing [f16245, f16246, f8909].

nodes.label: Data storage, data lineage and record keeping for thousands of runs
nodes.text: Record keeping for simulation means storing, for every one of thousands of runs, exactly what was run, with which versions and inputs, and where every input came from, so that any result can be reproduced and defended later.
nodes.synopsis: Every executed virtual test should be reproducible from an immutable provenance manifest identifying requirements and hazards, scenario versions and parameters, machine and sensor configurations, software and model versions, random seeds, raw-data checksums, metrics and verdicts; failed validation cases must also remain in the record [f7104, f7108, f7109, f7590]. Reproducibility extends to captured-site dates, coordinates and revision histories, and to archiving toolchain versions, binaries or containers, drivers and assets; neutral formats and canonical data outside vendor formats help avoid costly supplier dependence [f4376, f9386, f7116, f8876, f8886]. Large synchronized camera, lidar and radar programmes create storage, retention, privacy, access-control and provenance obligations, but the research did not establish recording data rates, storage sizes, logger requirements or jurisdiction-specific governance requirements, so these questions need early resolution [f5799, f5800, f5801, f5803]. Evidence may be disclosed in litigation, and the booklet identifies record-keeping and liability from 9 December 2026 as planning blind spots; early legal review, explicit retention policies and preservation of raw evidence, model versions and sign-offs are recommended [f9804, f10362, f10848, f11061, f10706]. Storage and retention also affect throughput and recurring cost: cost figures were not found, and an end-to-end benchmark should measure cost, wall time, storage and analyst hours to identify whether compute, storage or human triage becomes the bottleneck [f10745, f10791, f10957, f10958].

nodes.label: Project plan, work package and deliverable
nodes.text: A project plan says what will be done, by whom and by when; a work package is one bounded chunk of that work; a deliverable is the concrete thing a work package hands over.
nodes.synopsis: The manufacturer needs a strategy and roadmap for predominantly virtual collision-mitigation validation, planned as an eleven-month first-of-a-kind programme under a hard deadline, with about seven months from October 2026 to April 2027 to prepare the capability [f6, f9396, f9400, f9402]. The four-month validation window cannot be compressed: integrated product validation starts at prototype arrival, but earlier work must establish a proven method so that the window becomes a confirmation and calibration campaign [f62, f10895, f11929]. Before mid-2027, the proposed preparation scope includes site geometry, material libraries, scenarios, machine kinematics, reference measurements, metrics, HIL interfaces and generic effect models; each work package should produce safety evidence, with traceable claim-to-requirement-to-scenario-to-test mapping as the first deliverable [f4973, f9398, f12193]. Schedule confidence remains limited: no published case proves the four-month schedule, reliable heavy-off-road setup durations and build-versus-buy staffing, timeline and cost figures are unavailable, and the October 2026 plan is an assessment rather than a documented case [f6398, f811, f8314, f892]. Modeling effort varies substantially—from hours for an energy or constant-deceleration model to months for detailed multibody modeling—while the on-road PEGASUS precedent lasted 42 months and produced a method, not an approval [f6427, f6457, f1543, f1546]. Planning should therefore include standards re-baselining before design freeze, owned supplier dependencies before architecture freeze, budgeted simulation-tool qualification, early independent-test booking with at least one re-test, and a restricted-scope alternative with stage gates [f2948, f10802, f10547, f5790, f11075].

nodes.label: Gantt chart, milestone and dependency
nodes.text: A Gantt chart is a calendar drawing in which each task is a horizontal bar from its start to its finish, a milestone is a single dated event with no duration, and a dependency is the rule that one task cannot start until another has finished.
nodes.synopsis: The proposed first-of-a-kind programme has an eleven-month hard deadline, starting preparation in October 2026 ahead of prototype arrival in mid-2027; the indicative plan represents arrival as a July 1, 2027 milestone [f9396, f706, f2, f903]. Preparation is described as about seven months through April 2027 in the planning chapter, but about eight months before mid-2027 in the trust chapter, so these preparation endpoints need reconciliation [f9402, f8237]. The post-arrival campaign is an approximately 16-week iterative funnel, credible within four months only if the requirements-and-design work and most preparation are already complete; environment construction and pipeline correlation should therefore begin before the prototype exists [f7379, f7351, f12229, f3771, f709]. Schedule dependencies include software availability for early software-in-the-loop work and prior agreement on the assessor and review criteria; the proposed end-November 2026 G0 gate records agreed claims, evidence plans, orders, criteria and a named decision-maker [f270, f8245, f12304]. Confidence remains limited: documented capability-building precedents took years, the finance executive calls the schedule optimistic, independent review and retesting can become critical-path activities, and tool implementation and provider delivery timelines were not found [f1203, f10742, f683, f9352, f8838]. The plan should expose dependencies and gaps, report P50/P80 dates and deadline probabilities, and monitor toolchain milestone slips and failure to demonstrate an end-to-end evidence chain for one safety requirement by the first half of 2027 [f9476, f205, f11074, f12196].

nodes.label: Critical path and buffer
nodes.text: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks in a plan, so any delay on it delays the end date; a buffer is spare time deliberately placed in the plan to absorb such delays.
nodes.synopsis: The four-month validation window is feasible only if preparatory work, including simulation credibility, finishes before the prototype arrives in mid-2027; no standard guarantees that a first-time simulation organization can achieve it [f11340, f14526, f7594]. Sensor and prototype freeze dates set the critical path: the sensor choice should be locked by early 2027 because it gates sensor-specific models and data collection, while a later modality change costs time through reworking strata and samples [f11915, f1616, f2006, f7492]. Independent review can become another critical path: University of Pretoria verification reported 1.6 tests per week and an 18-week lead time in October 2025, supporting immediate booking and provision for at least one retest [f683, f5180, f5790]. Immature technology is the most consistently documented cause of schedule failure, but the prior three-to-four-year effort lacks a root-cause time breakdown, leaving requirements definition and field tuning as possible bottlenecks rather than test count [f204, f273, f10854, f10859]. Planning should locate integration and pre-correlation buffers, distinguish uncertainty from contingency rather than add 20% everywhere, and expose long-lead external dependencies; notified-body and heavy-machine facility access times remain unresolved [f10244, f9650, f9641, f10245, f801, f5120].

nodes.label: Planning fallacy, reference class forecasting and P50 / P80 estimates
nodes.text: The planning fallacy is the proven human habit of underestimating how long one's own work will take; reference class forecasting corrects it by looking at how long similar past projects actually took; and P50 and P80 dates state the finish date with a 50% and an 80% chance of being met.
