nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends replacing single completion dates with program-model-derived P50 and P80 dates—50% and 80% chances of completion—and the probability of meeting the fixed deadline; its empirical warning includes a 1994 study in which only 29.7% finished by their best-estimate date [f205, f16310, f16320, f9599]. Reference class forecasting uses actual outcomes of comparable projects, but reported superiority over other methods depends on genuine similarity; Chapter 13 also says the Flyvbjerg literature was not verified, creating an internal evidence-status tension [f9604, f9606, f9609, f10743]. Documented validation-capability programs took years, including PEGASUS's 42 months and EVIDENT's approximately 33 months, while VaViM's six months delivered only a pre-study; the booklet therefore treats four months as a validation window, not a capability-construction window, and as a target rather than a forecast [f15713, f15694, f15710, f15709, f15714, f10464]. No reference class of first-time programs meeting that four-month window was found, and the manufacturer's internal three-to-four-year history was unavailable; reconstructing that history is recommended before claiming a tenfold schedule reduction, because the actual bottleneck remains unknown [f10465, f11287, f273, f10860, f11288]. For first-of-a-kind work, the recommendation is component-level historical reference classes, openly stated uplifts where data are thin, and schedule-risk analysis, although this decomposition is not a separately validated forecasting method [f9439, f9613, f9615, f9616, f16318]. The proposed March–April 2027 G2 gate requires a blind pilot meeting pre-set metrics, assessor feedback, and a P80 date inside the deadline; the executive brief should show preparation and delivery P50/P80 dates and descoping measures that preserve deadline confidence [f12306, f16323].

nodes.label: Schedule risk analysis and Monte Carlo schedule simulation
nodes.text: Schedule risk analysis gives every task a range of possible durations instead of one number, and a Monte Carlo schedule simulation runs the whole plan thousands of times with random draws from those ranges to find how likely each finish date is.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends reference class forecasting plus schedule-risk analysis as the primary schedule approach, but the outside view is credible only with genuinely similar historical work; the cited 2016 comparison found reference class forecasting superior to Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting only under high similarity [f10070, f9606]. Schedule-risk analysis assigns task-duration ranges and risk events, then Monte Carlo simulation follows the dependency network thousands of times to estimate completion-date probabilities; single-date plans are optimistic where parallel paths converge because of merge bias [f16324, f16326, f16327, f9633]. Plans should report P50 and P80 dates and the probability of meeting the fixed deadline, supported by an auditable integrated schedule, range assumptions, critical path, buffers and an S-curve; these confidence figures must come from the program's own model and cannot be inferred from this research [f205, f10171, f9640]. The illustrative cadence calls for a schedule model as exit evidence from October–November 2026 scoping, but prototype-delivery slippage was not treated as a planned branch in the research and should be modeled explicitly with a signpost and hedge [f9652, f10376, f10377]. GAO treats schedule-risk analysis as best practice and NASA requires joint confidence levels, but evidence that NASA's requirement improves program outcomes was not found; the skeptic's review also demands cost and schedule evidence under pessimistic correlation results [f9628, f9630, f9631, f11155].

nodes.label: Risk register, assumption log and unknowns (known unknowns)
nodes.text: A risk register lists the uncertain events that could hurt the plan, an assumption log lists the propositions the plan currently depends on, and the unknowns list records the questions the team knows it cannot yet answer.
aliases: Risk register, assumption log and unknowns
nodes.synopsis: The programme is a first-time capability build under high technical uncertainty: sensor types, machine types, software maturity and existing recordings were unavailable, supplier cooperation remains unknown, and an unconfirmed sensor choice is identified as the largest schedule risk [f9401, f8, f10801, f1618]. Its main technical risk is the absence of a published quantitative off-road comparison between simulation-tuned braking thresholds and field results; statistical methods cannot compensate for omitted hazards, incorrect exposure models or an unvalidated simulator [f155, f5952, f650, f994]. The recommended approach combines evidence-based stage gates with assumption-based and discovery-driven planning, tracking vulnerable assumptions, failure signposts and hedges while keeping verified facts, expert judgment and management assumptions separate [f203, f9591, f9558, f12277]. This recommendation is not proof of effectiveness: evidence for risk-management outcomes is thin, a 2010 meta-analysis found positive impacts in only two of 29 publications, and rigorous comparative evidence for assumption-based planning was not found [f9440, f9441, f9562]. Supplier-data availability and legal usability, evolving interfaces, facility access and standards changes require explicit treatment; planning should not depend on an off-road scenario standard arriving before mid-2027, and outsourcing needs editable models and validation assets to avoid long-term dependency [f11024, f8619, f1167, f11222, f7205, f8799]. Important unresolved questions include the causes of prior three-to-four-year development timelines, market-dependent EU applicability, security and privacy obligations, and cloud/export/data-residency terms; these gaps should prompt manufacturer questions, supplier requests or early experiments rather than invented estimates [f11185, f10854, f10701, f10823, f16068, f263, f6631].

nodes.label: Pre-mortem, red team and expert review (Delphi method, expert elicitation)
nodes.text: A pre-mortem imagines the project has already failed and asks why; a red team is a group charged with attacking the plan; expert review, including the Delphi method and structured elicitation, is a disciplined way of collecting and weighing what specialists believe.
aliases: Pre-mortem, red team and expert review
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends disciplined expert review and adversarial challenge so a heavy off-road validation plan can withstand scrutiny of fog, low contrast and operation at the edge of its envelope; the red team's task is to attack whether the safety claim can be supported by the deadline, not proofread the plan [f9395, f9961, f16358]. Its proposed sequence is 8–12 interviews in months 1–2, elicitation in month 2, a pre-mortem in month 3, an independent red team in month 4 and a gate review with recorded dissent in months 5–6; it also recommends a second pre-mortem before delivery readiness [f16367, f9666]. Pre-mortems draw on 1989 prospective-hindsight experiments, and the one direct test found involved 178 students in 2010 and reduced confidence more than four alternatives, but evidence of improved real engineering-programme outcomes was not found [f9660, f9661, f9662, f9664]. Across 33 structured-elicitation applications, fewer than one third of experts met the statistical-accuracy criterion, so numerical judgments should be calibrated where practical and otherwise expressed as ranges with disagreement preserved; Delphi consensus does not establish correctness [f9488, f9952, f9953, f16366]. Review evidence favors seeking genuine skeptics and identifying rejection-critical weaknesses, but controlled evidence that red teams improve engineering outcomes—and causal evidence for these planning methods in safety-critical virtual validation—was not found [f16361, f9845, f9848, f9964, f10298].

nodes.label: Stage gate, evidence gate and go or no-go decision
nodes.text: A stage gate is a formal decision point between phases of a project, an evidence gate is one whose pass criterion is demonstrated knowledge rather than a date, and a go or no-go decision is the choice made there to continue, restrict, change course or stop.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends evidence-based stage gates for governance within a layered planning architecture, not as a complete planning method; four or five evidence gates are suggested, while causal evidence for Stage-Gate in highly uncertain, safety-critical virtual validation was not found [f203, f9492, f9510, f9507, f9589]. South African mining provides a staged-verification precedent: the MOSH regime dated 11 October 2025 establishes TRL4 and TRL7 gates, a surface CPS TRL7 specification is dated 20 January 2026, and independent verification is required at both gates [f15563, f557, f2459]. Gate decisions should permit go, restricted continuation, pivot and stop under pre-committed criteria signed by the sponsor and a named decider; launch should depend on unresolved safety evidence rather than calendar pressure [f9449, f10708]. Funding should be tied to early experiments, with explicit stop or escalation triggers for unusable supplier data, missing evidence ownership, and physical-versus-virtual discrepancies that undermine the safety conclusion [f10746, f10918, f10924, f10933]. The eleven-month planning window motivates small parallel options selected at the first gate, and the illustrative cadence ends April 2027 with an independent delivery-readiness decision of ready, restricted scope or fallback [f9594, f9655]. Important limitations remain: public literature cannot establish whether the architecture meets company safety-release criteria, rigid gates can become date-driven ceremonies, and pilot-methodology support for pre-declared progression criteria is analogical rather than direct proof [f4975, f9506, f9487].

nodes.label: Pilot, proof of concept and minimum viable product (MVP)
nodes.text: A proof of concept shows that something can work at all, a pilot tests whether the approach is feasible on a small but real slice, and a minimum viable product (MVP) is the smallest deliverable that is still useful.
aliases: Pilot, proof of concept and minimum viable product
nodes.synopsis: The corpus distinguishes a quick prototype or pre-study from a safety-credible capability: VaViM’s six months in 2022 produced a pre-study, not an accepted virtual-validation capability, and no in-house open-source time-to-first-useful-result benchmark was found [f1207, f1551, f1552, f8741, f8742]. The recommended trust-earning pilot is a deliberately difficult, end-to-end thin slice covering one safety function and one or two machine variants, with physical or bench comparators, blind predictions, pre-registered metrics and explicit go, restricted-go, pivot and stop criteria—not a polished nominal-cycle demonstration [f9914, f9918, f9919, f9921]. The example pilot runs in months 3–5, uses 3–5 scenario classes including an edge case, and pre-specifies 10–30 physical test points; the evidence package is due by March 2027, followed by a proposed March–April 2027 credibility gate requiring acceptable blind-pilot results, assessor feedback and a P80 delivery date inside the deadline [f9915, f9916, f9917, f16270, f12306]. Pilot methodology supports feasibility testing and advance progression criteria, but its transfer from health and social research is an analogy rather than direct evidence for heavy-machine virtual testing [f9899, f9901, f9904, f9905]. Site pilots should follow controlled whole-machine confirmation near safety limits, use trained staff and explicit operational controls, and measure nuisance stops and missing operator-response data rather than assume passenger-car values [f884, f10988, f11138, f3617]. Planning should use pilots to inform bottom-up cost estimates and predefine useful fallback deliverables, including physical-test-backed claims, simulation-only scenario screening or engineering-learning results rather than safety credit [f10752, f11084, f12468].

nodes.label: Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) and integrated test planning
nodes.text: A Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) is the single overarching document that ties every planned test, virtual or physical, to the decision it informs, the data it needs, its resources, its schedule and its pass criteria.
nodes.synopsis: TEMP provides an overarching integrated test plan linking virtual and physical tests to decisions, objectives, data, resources, schedules and acceptance criteria; its IDSK logic runs from decision to evaluation question to required data [f16406, f9549, f16409]. The booklet recommends systems-engineering V&V plus a scaled TEMP-style strategy as the programme’s evidence backbone, with one line per claim recording the decision, evidence, method, comparator, acceptance rule, data, owner and date [f9588, f16413]. Although TEMP is required for major US DoD programmes under November 2020 instruction and January 2017 guidance, a literal defence TEMP would be excessive for this eleven-month programme [f9546, f16412]. This recommendation rests on documented practice rather than demonstrated superiority: comparative outcome studies were not found, and the booklet recommends layering planning methods rather than treating any one as complete [f9556, f9552, f9492, f9420]. Operationally, the plan should reserve four months after prototype arrival for physical measurements and model correlation, then use virtual regression for the large scenario matrix while physical testing targets boundaries and worst cases; it must distinguish reducing physical testing from replacing it for safety credit [f16414, f16415, f16417].

nodes.label: PMBOK, PMI, PRINCE2 and agile
nodes.text: PMBOK, PRINCE2 and agile are general frameworks for how to run projects: two are published bodies of project-management method, and agile is a family of practices that delivers work in short, repeated cycles.
nodes.synopsis: PMBOK and PRINCE2 are general project-management methods, while agile comprises practices for delivering work in short, repeated cycles; relevant editions are PMI’s PMBOK Guide 7 (2021) and PeopleCert’s PRINCE2 7 (2023) [f16418, f16420, f16421]. The booklet recommends borrowing their document structure for the validation plan, but labels these sources expert opinion and stresses that neither establishes whether a simulation is trustworthy [f9982, f16424, f16430]. Agile precedents include Cooper’s 2016 Agile-Stage-Gate hybrid and Lockheed Martin’s claim that agile development plus reuse enabled F-35 Auto-GCAS integration in 2019, seven years earlier than planned [f9501, f16422, f1443]. These precedents do not resolve the evidence gap: the booklet found no consistent outcome evidence for any planning method in programs like this one, and none for rolling-wave planning specifically [f16426, f16425]. Its preferred approach layers methods around systems-engineering verification and validation, with knowledge before commitment as the best-supported principle, although its cost and schedule evidence is correlational rather than causal [f16428, f16427].

nodes.label: Cost estimating and schedule guides (GAO guides, AACE)
nodes.text: These are published handbooks on how to build a cost estimate and a project schedule that can withstand audit, written by the United States Government Accountability Office (GAO) and by AACE International, a professional association for cost engineering.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats GAO and AACE guides as recognized yardsticks for auditable budgets and deadline claims, and recommends GAO cost and schedule checklists as structures for the validation plan [f16431, f16443, f9983]. GAO's Schedule Assessment Guide (GAO-16-89G, December 2015) provides ten best-practice areas, including schedule-risk analysis; the booklet calls for an integrated schedule with reference classes, range assumptions, an S-curve, a critical path, buffers and long-lead items [f9627, f16433, f16438]. The recommended schedule and basis-of-estimate section is 1–3 pages, with detailed schedules, reference-class data and elicitation records in Appendix F [f10172, f10187]. GAO's Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide (GAO-20-195G, March 2020) is the recommended companion template for capability costs, while AACE 57R-09 describes integrated cost and schedule risk analysis using risk drivers and Monte Carlo simulation of a critical-path model [f16434, f10374, f16436]. Cost estimation was omitted from the research questions; the booklet nevertheless recommends bottom-up estimates after pilots and vendor quotations for tool budgets because public prices are almost entirely absent [f16439, f11084, f16441]. GAO audits spanning 2005–2026 associate immature technology and optimistic commitment timelines with failure, and knowledge-based practices with better outcomes, but these findings are correlational rather than causal [f10288, f10289].

nodes.label: Bottom line up front (BLUF) and the one-page summary
nodes.text: Bottom line up front (BLUF) is the writing rule that the conclusion and the decision requested come first, and the one-page summary is the document that applies it so an executive can grasp the decision, the confidence and the risks in a page or two.
nodes.synopsis: BLUF puts the conclusion and requested decision first; the booklet recommends a one-to-two-page executive brief so leaders can grasp the decision, confidence and risks quickly [f16444, f10152, f9995]. For this validation plan, the brief should specify what will and will not exist by August or September 2027, P50 and P80 dates, deadline probability, top risks, stop conditions, fallback and required executive actions; the glossary additionally asks for separate preparation and delivery dates and descoping to keep P80 within the deadline [f10151, f16323]. The first page should expose the hardest uncertainty and fallback rather than lead with promised savings, while all seven skeptical reviewers need a credibility map linking safety claims to evidence, model-validation data, uncertainty and acceptance authority [f16454, f11158, f16451]. Technical readers need the underlying reasoning, assumptions, coverage, acceptance thresholds and disputes, with progressive disclosure supporting either a 12–15-page main body or a two-page brief plus roughly 25–35 core pages [f16448, f9994, f16466]. These formats and lengths remain opinion-based rather than proven routes to programme approval or success, although experiments found numeric ranges preserved trust better than verbal hedges [f9853, f10315, f9474].

nodes.label: PR/FAQ (working backwards) and other presentation formats
nodes.text: PR/FAQ is a planning document written as the press release and the questions-and-answers that would accompany a finished product, and it is one of several named formats for presenting a plan to decision makers and expert reviewers.
nodes.synopsis: PR/FAQ presents a proposed finished product through a press release and accompanying questions-and-answers; working backwards means writing these before building, to clarify who benefits and what must be true [f16455, f16456, f16457]. Chapter 12 places it among practitioner communication formats, including the Pyramid Principle, BLUF, six-page narratives, the Five Case Model and Decision Quality, but no controlled evidence was found that these presentation formats improve technical-program approval or success [f9851, f9853, f16467]. The six-page narrative is recommended as a suitable template for the heavy off-road collision mitigation validation plan, with a documented six-page limit and silent reading at the start of meetings rather than slides [f9980, f9989, f16458]. Planning guidance also recommends a 1–2-page executive decision brief and a fifteen-section plan with appendices; alternative overall lengths—12–15 main-body pages or a two-page brief plus roughly 25–35 core pages—are explicitly opinion rather than demonstrated optima [f10152, f16465, f16466]. The claimed practical value is answering reviewers' actual questions, especially what would show the authors are wrong; assertion-evidence slides have limited evidence for improved comprehension, which is distinct from evidence of improved approval or programme success [f16468, f9859, f16464, f16467].

nodes.label: Visuals that work
nodes.text: Visuals that work are the drawings in a plan that expose dependencies and gaps, rather than decorate; the booklet found no format proven to increase reviewer trust and recommends a division of labor among six kinds.
nodes.synopsis: The booklet defines useful visuals as drawings that expose dependencies and gaps, not decoration; it found no credible basis for claiming that any one format universally earns engineering reviewers’ trust [f16469, f9476, f9864, f16470]. It recommends dividing the work among six kinds: layered roadmaps with gates, claim-to-evidence maps, coverage maps, architecture views, probabilistic schedules and risk views [f16473, f16474, f16475, f16476, f16478, f16479, f16480]. Coverage gaps should remain visibly blank rather than disappear into an “85% coverage” score, and simulation credibility should be mapped into supported and unsupported regions with physical evidence rather than reduced to “95% accurate” or a green dashboard [f9880, f8019]. Schedule communication should show distributions or confidence windows, P50, P80 and deadline probability; risk heat maps may serve familiarity but must not drive prioritization because of documented ranking defects [f9889, f9863, f9894, f9895]. Evidence is narrower than a general trust claim: individual experiments found decision or comprehension benefits, decorative-graph persuasion failed to replicate, and uncertainty-display effects depend on context; plain charts and words should expose caveats, while a pilot traffic light should show both the trusted envelope and failures [f9482, f9858, f9484, f9892, f8020, f9920].

nodes.label: Request for proposal (RFP), non-disclosure agreement (NDA), statement of work, and supplier information
nodes.text: A request for proposal (RFP) asks vendors to propose a solution and a price, a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) lets two companies share secrets safely, a statement of work spells out exactly what a supplier will deliver, and supplier information is the technical data a sensor or tool vendor must hand over for a simulation to represent its product.
aliases: OSI as a Functional Mock-up Unit
nodes.synopsis: Supplier data, models and usage rights are a major schedule risk: they can block validation before testing, and late or legally unusable deliveries are a critical failure mode, especially when brake maps, interfaces or licences remain under negotiation near prototype delivery [f214, f10446, f12459, f10770]. Supplier information determines whether simulation represents the production sensor rather than a generic device; physics-based, signal-level models require supplier internals and material data, and missing spectral information explicitly limited the 2026 LWIR validation [f4842, f4469, f4848]. Access remains uncertain: NIOSH's 2022 review found manufacturer documentation proprietary and mostly undisclosed, while this research did not investigate suppliers' willingness or contract terms for exposing pre-processing data needed to re-test perception from logs [f10448, f5805, f5806]. Contracts should therefore secure model delivery, validation data, recording rights and editable simulation assets; an IP-protecting FMU using FMI 2.0 is recommended when sensor internals cannot be shared, and outsourcing without asset delivery risks meeting the 2027 deadline at the cost of long-term dependency [f4866, f4371, f8798, f4857, f8799]. Budgets must use vendor quotations because public tool prices are largely absent; public provider contract values and delivery timelines were also not found, and RFP pricing should cover concurrent workers, CI/cloud rights, subcontractors and disaster recovery rather than desktop seats alone [f8304, f8308, f16126, f16154].

nodes.label: Total cost of ownership, capital versus operating cost, full-time equivalent (FTE)
nodes.text: Total cost of ownership is everything a capability costs over its life, not just the purchase price; capital cost is money spent once on things that last, operating cost is money spent every month to keep running; and a full-time equivalent (FTE) is the work of one person for one full year.
aliases: Total cost of ownership, capital versus operating cost, full-time equivalent
nodes.synopsis: Open-source simulation is viable as a low-license-cost core, but not the lowest-total-cost option: coupling, assets, scenario databases and validation evidence still require engineering and maintenance [f196, f8296, f8303]. The booklet judges compute cheap relative to engineering labor, estimates a labor floor of roughly USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist per year, and warns that even free-software programs can cost seven figures annually [f198, f13550, f13551]. On-road precedents demonstrate substantial resource commitments—PEGASUS ran January 2016–June 2019 with about EUR 34.5 million and 1,791 person-months, while VVM ran July 2019–June 2023 with EUR 47 million—but no public study supplies team size, timeline or total cost for an off-highway build-versus-buy decision [f1204, f1205, f8314]. Direct job-site creation costs, off-road labeling costs, and independently published off-road compute costs and return on investment remain missing; tool budgets therefore need vendor quotations rather than published benchmarks [f3847, f5424, f10615, f8308]. Vehicle-in-the-loop is emerging and capital-intensive, its economic justification for this program remains uncertain, and it is recommended only where extra physical fidelity warrants the investment [f338, f1119, f550]. Planning should quantify money and scarce engineering capacity, address ownership, budgets and licences after September 2027, and avoid counting physical-test substitution savings before they are earned; until simulator trust is established, dual simulator-and-physical-test costs are an explicit inference [f10273, f10179, f10510, f10511].

nodes.label: Team and skills needed
nodes.text: The team and skills needed are the distinct specialist disciplines a manufacturer must have in place at the same time to build and defend a virtual validation capability.
nodes.synopsis: Building off-road virtual validation requires simultaneous specialist coverage across simulation architecture, machine and soil dynamics, sensor modeling, 3D assets, test automation, data and cloud infrastructure, ECU/HIL, statistics, and safety; the corpus identifies these disciplines but finds no defensible mapping to a specific headcount [f8773, f8774]. No independent 2024–2026 benchmark establishes cost, staffing or time to first useful result from zero; the on-road PEGASUS precedent involved 17 partners, about 1,791 person-months and EUR 34.5 million, rather than establishing a single manufacturer's staffing prescription [f8734, f1287, f1544, f1575]. Engineering labor dominates compute costs, with an estimated floor of USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist annually, so even free software can yield a seven-figure annual programme [f16234, f8318]. With no internal capability and nine months before hardware, the booklet favors hybrid implementation, while partner-led work still needs an internal core owning requirements and acceptance [f16138, f8765]. Governance should establish an accountable technical owner, explicit ownership of tool qualification and model credibility, and independent review; the organization currently lacks documented credibility foundations, and on-road EU requirements explicitly demand competence evidence for both toolchain validators and users [f10265, f5792, f8049, f10414, f10596]. Planning must quantify scarce engineering capacity and address sustainment after September 2027, which remains a blind spot [f10273, f10367].

nodes.label: Cheapest early experiments
nodes.text: The cheapest early experiments are small tests that can start immediately, with existing data and one machine, and are designed to prove the proposal wrong before expensive infrastructure is built.
nodes.synopsis: The cheapest early experiments are intended to falsify the collision-mitigation proposal before expensive infrastructure is built; Chapter 13 identifies sixteen experiments, each producing an artifact and a stopping or escalation signal [f10912, f16532, f16533]. Several can begin in October 2026 using existing warning-system data, historical tests, supplier discussions and one representative machine; parallel recording on current machines is identified as the single most valuable pre-hardware action, and winter 2026–2027 reference data should be captured before the season passes [f10914, f5574, f14351, f10953]. The proposed tests include checking supplier data and legal rights, replaying logs to estimate false activations, correlating one machine and scenario with simulation, and carrying one safety requirement through a real test, model, virtual result and residual-risk decision—the “golden thread,” described as the cheapest decisive experiment [f10915, f10925, f10930, f12195]. These tests must establish credible evidence rather than superficial similarity: weather simulation should reproduce measured sensor degradation, correlation should include residual plots and an uncertainty budget, and hand-made object-list tests provide no evidence that perception works [f10937, f16538, f12536]. Funding should be stage-gated around data availability, correlation, transfer to a materially different configuration and reviewer acceptance; unresolved supplier access, inadequate reference data or excessive bespoke tuning are explicit reasons to stop or escalate, while a published off-road shadow-mode protocol remains missing [f10746, f16550, f10918, f10956, f10948, f10929].

nodes.label: Executive reviewer, finance reviewer, product liability reviewer
nodes.text: These are three of the skeptical readers the plan must satisfy, each needing a different view of the same evidence: the executive decides, the finance reviewer checks the money, and the product liability reviewer checks what would survive in court.
nodes.synopsis: The plan must satisfy skeptical executive, finance and product-liability readers by closing weaknesses rather than adding upside; research on 3,667 Marie Curie applications supports that approach, while 43 reviewers assessing the same 25 NIH applications showed essentially no agreement, cautioning against assuming reviewer consensus [f9404, f207, f9845, f9846]. Executive-facing material should state the decision, deliverables and exclusions, deadline confidence, risks, fallback and resources, with auditable deadline probabilities rather than merely a planned date [f9854, f16337, f16443]. Finance wants cheap early experiments and bottom-up post-pilot estimates before larger commitments: savings may be counted before physical-test substitution is earned, reuse across machine families remains unproven, and independent off-road return-on-investment evidence and recurring-cost information were not found [f16553, f16442, f16560, f16562, f16561, f16563]. Reviewers should approve specific virtual substitutions within validated envelopes, supported by a one-page credibility map, and see a representative safety/legal evidence package months before launch to reduce the critical risk of late rejection [f16557, f16556, f14996, f11036]. Legal involvement at the end is too late: the liability reviewer needs jurisdiction-specific compliance analysis, authorizations, defensible substitutions, auditable provenance and retention, enforced operating limits, and reviewed claims and warnings [f10848, f16565, f16566]. Legal sign-off must address Product Liability Directive disclosure, its application to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026 and treatment of software as a product, Machinery Regulation conformity from 20 January 2027, and the AI Act if applicable [f10849, f16568, f16569, f10850, f10851].

nodes.label: ISO 19014-1
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19014-1 provides Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA) to identify safety-related control-system parts and determine the required Machine Performance Level (MPLr); it requires hazard and risk analysis and MPLr assignment [f2314, f2690]. For brake-commanding collision avoidance, this includes analysing erroneous or missing braking, with MPLr assigned using Part 1 or Part 5 tables; those tables derive from the Part 1 method [f2336, f2333]. Edition 2's FDIS was registered on 5 February 2026, voting closed on 22 August, and it remained under publication as of 1 October, scheduled for October 2026; the published catalogue edition was still the 2018 edition, marked “to be revised” [f2316, f2315]. Publication dates need reconciliation: Chapter 10 lists 22 November 2026 for revised ISO 19014-1, while Chapter 13 attaches that date specifically to FprEN ISO 19014-1, suggesting a possible ISO-versus-European-adoption distinction [f7738, f11219, f15179]. The booklet recommends an immediate gap analysis against revised Parts 1 and 4, but acknowledges that the final series texts were unavailable for review, leaving their final content uncertain [f10541, f2862].

nodes.label: ISO 19014-2
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19014-2 covers safety-control systems that control machine motion or mitigate hazards, but excludes awareness-only systems; adding a brake command therefore moves collision mitigation into its scope [f2311, f2075, f15175]. The booklet treats automatic braking as a new safety-control function rather than a warning function with a brake added, requiring validation of brake-command integrity, faults, degraded modes, unintended activation and failure to activate—not just perception statistics [f10476, f5223, f5810]. Part 2 addresses hardware, architecture and achieved Machine Performance Level (MPLa), including architecture evaluation, component reliability, fault behaviour and diagnostics; safety-function performance under expected environmental conditions must also be demonstrated and documented [f2318, f2693, f7735]. As of 1 October 2026, the published edition was still 2022, while Edition 2 had been at stage 60.00, “under publication,” since 22 August 2026 and was scheduled for October; Chapter 12 instead describes the revision as being at FDIS, creating a status discrepancy [f2319, f2320, f9771]. The forthcoming editions’ final texts were unavailable for review, so their final content remained uncertain and publication status should be rechecked before design freeze [f2862, f6286].

nodes.label: ISO 19014-3
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19014-3 addresses environmental qualification and minimum environmental tests for safety-related electrical/electronic components, including vibration, temperature and electrical robustness [f662, f2470]. The booklet treats component laboratory testing as highly mature for heavy off-road applications and includes Part 3 qualification in the lifecycle of a brake-commanding collision-avoidance function [f1022, f2338]. However, component environmental qualification does not establish camera, lidar or radar perception-chain performance across visibility and weather combinations, leaving the perception-performance question open [f2471, f2907]. ISO 16001:2017 references ISO 15998 for environmental conditions but permits ISO 19014-3 as an alternative [f2345]. As of 1 October 2026, the published edition remained 2018; Edition 2 had its FDIS registered on 5 February 2026, reached stage 60.00 on 22 August 2026, and was scheduled for October publication [f2322, f2323]. The forthcoming ISO 19014 Parts 1–5 texts were unavailable for review, so their final content remained uncertain despite the reported publication schedule [f2862].

nodes.label: ISO 19014-4
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19014-4 supplies the off-road safety-related software and data/signal-transmission basis, requiring systematic development and verification for a brake-commanding collision-avoidance function [f2700, f2339, f12180]. As of 1 October 2026, the published edition remained 2020, while Edition 2 had reached stage 60.00 on 22 August 2026 and was scheduled for October 2026 publication; Chapter 10's DIS-stage description is therefore in tension with the later status reported elsewhere [f2325, f2326, f7737]. The final revised texts were unavailable for review, so the booklet recommends an immediate gap analysis against the second editions of Parts 1 and 4 rather than assuming their requirements are settled [f2862, f10541]. The 2020 edition contains normative Annex B on software validation test environments, supporting the recommendation to map each requirement to simulation, hardware-in-the-loop or machine testing [f10532, f12181, f10542]. Although simulation tool confidence is associated with ISO 19014-4 software verification and validation, the research did not establish whether the standard itself requires tool qualification [f8035, f10545, f11191]. Cybersecurity is explicitly outside both the cited 2020 scope and the second-edition abstract, so brake-command networks and sensor/data interfaces need separate security treatment; functional safety must not be assumed to cover it [f10354, f10534, f5832, f11268].

nodes.label: ISO 19014-5
nodes.synopsis: As of 1 October 2026, ISO 19014-5 edition 1 was under publication for October 2026, replacing ISO/TS 19014-5:2021; its final text was received on 5 February and stage 60.00 began on 22 August, but the catalogue still listed the Technical Specification as the published edition [f2329, f2328]. Part 5 provides normative tables of required Machine Performance Levels (MPLr) for common functions, derived from the Part 1 method with derivation logic and assumptions [f10523, f2327, f2333]. Manufacturers can use these tabulated values instead of a full MCSSA for every new model only when the relevant use cases and assumptions hold [f2332, f12040]. The booklet recommends building the four-month validation plan around Part 5 tables and identifies them as the only sourced route to reducing per-model analysis burden, but it did not review whether collision avoidance or automatic braking has a table entry and found no published MPLr for that function [f2640, f15188, f2334, f2335]. Final contents remained uncertain because the texts were unavailable for review, and publication status should be rechecked before design freeze [f2862, f6286].

nodes.label: ISO 21815-4
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21815-4 passed its FDIS ballot on 28 May 2026 and reached stage 60.00, “Under publication,” on 4 September 2026, with edition 1 scheduled for October 2026; the corpus recommends not citing it as published until its text appears [f2668, f2170, f1708, f2172]. It addresses swing-and-rotation risk areas and levels for earth-moving, underground-mining and road-construction machinery, with coverage described as objects between ground level and cabin top and explicit limitations concerning height and working tools [f1707, f1709, f11239]. Across chapters, it is described as covering motion inhibition before rotation starts while excluding collision avoidance through automatic braking, although two quoted scope statements also exclude “inhibit,” creating an unresolved wording tension [f2171, f3379, f15153, f1710, f7731]. Planning recommendations are to parameterize swing-risk geometry by machine model, track the forthcoming standard during validation, and include standards watching and re-baselining before design freeze [f6770, f2641, f15058]. The corpus reports no statistical sample-size or simulation-credibility rules in the listed standards and no located acceptance of simulation evidence; physical tests remain necessary under the ISO 21815 framework, but unavailable paid texts mean that failure to find simulation-replacement acceptance is not proof of prohibition [f6749, f11237, f8145, f7544]. Whether the final October text matches the quoted catalogue summary remains uncertain because the published text was not reviewed [f1965].

nodes.label: ISO 21815-5
nodes.synopsis: ISO/PRF 21815-5 addresses collision risk from motions beyond ordinary forward/reverse travel and rotation: articulation, four-wheel steering, reversing towed trailers, skid or differential turning, counter-rotation, telescopic movement, and vertical movement, with interventions including speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition [f2176, f1136, f2177]. It specifically distinguishes stationary articulation, where the rear swings without machine travel, from steering during travel [f6038, f13740]. The first-edition project was approved on 27 September 2024; a BSI comment draft was dated 6 June 2025, the DIS ballot closed on 30 August 2025, and the FDIS was approved on 25 June 2026 [f2173, f2174, f2175]. As reported in October 2026, it had been at proof stage 50.20 since 9 September, with publication scheduled or expected for November 2026 rather than confirmed [f10904, f15154, f10905, f5075]. The corpus reports no statistical acceptance target, sample-size rules or simulation-credibility rules from Part 5; its testing requirements were not reviewed, acceptance of simulation evidence was not found, and final content remained uncertain [f324, f6749, f2673, f11237, f2863]. Planning recommendations therefore include tracking the draft, maintaining a standards watch and re-baselining before design freeze, while encoding its motion risk areas as machine-scaled scenario geometry [f6748, f15058, f6770].

nodes.label: EU Product Liability Directive
nodes.text: EU Product Liability Directive
nodes.synopsis: The corpus repeatedly states that the EU Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026; planning should preserve that market-placement qualification rather than rely solely on shorthand references to application “from” that date [f51, f9461, f16261, f16568, f10296]. Software is treated as a product, and updates within the manufacturer's control remain within liability [f10450, f9462, f10503, f16569, f10985]. Courts may order evidence disclosure, and defectiveness may be presumed if the defendant fails to disclose, making the validation program's evidence records potentially consequential in litigation [f10451, f10504, f16262, f16570]. Record-keeping and liability are identified as planning blind spots: retention policies, auditable provenance, forensic logging and legal sign-off on disclosure should therefore be addressed, even without a universal legal logging requirement [f10362, f16263, f11266, f10849]. Users working after October 2026 should re-check regulatory dates, while programs targeting mainly non-EU markets should treat this analysis as background rather than their primary legal context [f55, f11284].

nodes.label: EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230
nodes.text: EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230
nodes.synopsis: The corpus consistently dates application of EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 to 20 January 2027, before the prototype and mid-2027 validation campaign; the glossary says it applies directly across EU member states [f52, f6696, f10700, f15062]. Annex I Part A covers self-evolving machine-learning safety components and machinery embedding them, with notified-body involvement on every conformity route, but whether a trained-then-frozen detector falls within that scope remains disputed and unsettled [f2090, f363, f2091, f7435]. Software ensuring safety functions is described as a safety component, while other chapters identify protection against corruption and, through a secondary summary, recording of safety decisions and software versions [f9789, f5833, f5649]. Simulation acceptance remains uncertain: no relevant acceptance guidance or outside assessor was identified, no simulation-credibility acceptance criteria are defined by the cited regulation and standards, and published notified-body lead times were not found despite a warning that they could exceed the four-month validation window [f8184, f8185, f8242, f5110, f259, f11928]. The harmonised-standards list was still being prepared in 2026 and no standards had yet been cited; machinery AI requirements are reported to come through delegated acts, with an unverified commentary discussing an interim role for AI Act standards until acts expected by 2 August 2028 [f2092, f10501, f2096, f7431]. Planning should therefore include primary-source verification: several chapters explicitly did not verify regulatory dates or implications, Chapter 12 relied on secondary summaries rather than the Official Journal, and the synthesis recommends re-checking regulatory dates after October 2026 [f4335, f5111, f2012, f9463, f55].

nodes.label: Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
nodes.text: Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
nodes.synopsis: The corpus reports that the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was adopted on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026; it amends the AI Act, aviation regulation and Machinery Regulation [f9796, f2374]. Across chapters, Annex III high-risk obligations are dated to 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded high-risk obligations to 2 August 2028, although one secondary summary instead gives 2 December 2027 for Annex I [f11181, f9797, f2375, f9798, f10310]. Machinery is described as removed from direct AI Act high-risk classification and routed to AI health and safety requirements through Machinery Regulation delegated acts, with the transition tied to 2 August 2028 [f2095, f2377, f15475]. No machinery testing delegated acts had been adopted by October 2026, leaving detailed requirements pending [f2757]. The regulation defines a safety function as preventing or mitigating risks to health, safety or property, and merely integrating AI into a product is insufficient [f2378, f15476]. Source confidence is uneven: Chapter 12 says detailed machinery provisions were not read in the Official Journal, whereas Chapter 3 attributes machinery claims to regulation text and commentary; planners using the booklet after October 2026 are advised to re-check regulatory dates and standards statuses [f10309, f2376, f55].

nodes.label: PEGASUS
nodes.text: PEGASUS
nodes.synopsis: PEGASUS was a German on-road research project for validating one Level 3 highway automation function; it ran from 1 January 2016 to 30 June 2019 (42 months), with 17 partners, about 1,791 person-months (149 person-years), and approximately EUR 34.5 million including EUR 16.3 million in public subsidy [f15693, f15694, f15695]. Its output was a validation method rather than a certified product or approval, combining a scenario database from field recordings with simulation, proving-ground testing and field tests [f1290, f1546, f1778]. Its functional, logical and concrete scenario levels subsequently entered ISO 34501–34505 and underpin the booklet's scenario catalog [f6735, f13258]. The booklet uses PEGASUS and related programs as schedule-forecasting precedents: capability building took years, and follow-on VVM added another four-year cycle, July 2019–June 2023, with EUR 47 million volume [f15713, f15717, f1205, f1549]. These are on-road reference cases for planning first-of-a-kind virtual safety testing, not a measured duration for validation after capability becomes available [f9614, f1776]. Evidence quality remains a material caveat: the accounts rely on consortium self-reporting despite being labeled independent, and later chapters say PEGASUS and VVM were not individually verified and should be checked before review [f1294, f7701, f11276].

nodes.label: Germany
nodes.text: Germany
nodes.synopsis: Germany’s PEGASUS project is a substantial but narrowly scoped precedent: it ran from January 2016 to June 2019 for 42 months, involving 17 partners, about 1,791 person-months and EUR 34.5 million to define validation methods for a Level 3 highway chauffeur [f1204, f1285, f15693]. PEGASUS and VVM are cited as examples where reduced physical testing rested on years of prior simulation and statistical-tooling investment, although VVM and SET Level were not verified in the research and require checks before reliance [f1257, f4336]. BMW stated on 6 February 2026 that German authorities recognize virtual crash tests following a TÜV SÜD audit, but supplied no physical-test reduction percentage [f7566]. Germany also supplies relevant institutional and testing infrastructure through ASAM, DIN and CARISSMA, although the booklet does not cite DIN directly [f13222, f15030, f16122]. Important gaps and risks remain: German collision breakdowns by machine movement type were not found, and January 2026 Freshfields commentary says Germany’s draft implementing law presumes defect on non-disclosure regardless of fault [f3170, f10681].

nodes.label: EMESRT
nodes.text: EMESRT
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT (Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table), a mining-company group, supplies the PR-5A nine-level vehicle-interaction control model and mining scenario content; Level 7 covers operator awareness, Level 8 advisory controls, and Level 9 automatic slowing and stopping [f11736, f6229, f6750]. Effective Level 8–9 implementation depends on understanding the Level 1–7 baseline and integrating existing site controls: EMESRT guidance is not law or proof of mine acceptance, although South African requirements are framed at Level 9 and the relevant regulation was gazetted on 21 December 2022 [f11750, f704, f2586, f2587, f8233, f3624]. The corpus cites PR-5A Rev 3.0 dated September 2024, but other passages leave the current edition uncertain or say EMESRT was not reviewed or verified, so source verification remains a planning task [f6231, f4321, f9808, f11206]. EMESRT reports 17 surface storyboards published in 2019, while a trade article reports 24 scenarios; one chapter explains these as different measures, and the storyboards neither establish scenario frequencies nor cover hazards beyond those experts envisaged [f320, f7745, f6234, f6755, f6756]. A programme starting in October 2026 could realistically establish an operating-domain definition and scenario catalogue mapped to ISO 21815 and EMESRT by mid-2027, but no study applying OpenSCENARIO, ISO 34502 or the UNECE assessment method to off-road machines was found among the organizations searched [f831, f1698]. For mining acceptance, the booklet recommends combining EMESRT scenarios with MOSH numerical requirements, tracing the catalogue to hazards, and retaining assessor-selected physical confirmation runs covering every EMESRT scenario family rather than relying solely on simulation [f2645, f8030, f7887, f1122].

nodes.label: Volvo CE
nodes.text: Volvo CE
nodes.synopsis: Volvo CE’s wheel-loader Collision Mitigation System was announced on 11 January 2023, developed in-house and patent-pending; its documented scope was reverse-only operation at 3–15 km/h, with braking lasting 2–3 seconds [f10625, f1379, f1238]. The corpus treats this restricted scope on selected models as a precedent for staged release, while noting that Volvo reports these loaders spend 40–50% of their time reversing and documents conditions for switching intervention off [f10973, f73, f10630, f11167]. The system remembers the last slope climbed to avoid braking when reversing down a stockpile, but no independent performance test was found, and published weather limits, false-intervention rates and validation methods were absent [f11392, f1242, f11394]. An April 2025 announcement covered new-generation L150, L180, L200 High Lift, L220 and L260 wheel loaders [f1385]. For virtual development, an undated MathWorks story describes Volvo CE’s real-time human-in-the-loop excavator simulator built with Simulink and Simscape; such simulators may be needed for warning-then-brake human factors [f8391, f9379]. Volvo reports fewer prototypes and shorter lead time, describing physical prototypes as costing millions of dollars and months, but this evidence is qualitative rather than controlled cross-vendor benchmarking [f8737, f8738, f8315].

nodes.label: Komatsu
nodes.text: Komatsu
nodes.synopsis: Komatsu provides a precedent for restricted-domain releases rather than broad site coverage: documented interventions were limited by direction, speed, model or trigger, and KomVision began on Japan’s PC200-11 excavator, going on sale in December 2019 before its 30 March 2020 announcement [f11166, f10897, f10633]. KomVision detects people with cameras and stops excavators when travel or swing starts, but not during an ongoing swing; Komatsu also requires disabling excavator stop control during trailer loading because rapid stops can destabilize the machine, while wheel-loader cautions extend to slopes, slippery or soft ground and suspended loads [f11425, f11426, f11427, f10550]. Wabtec’s December 2021 Level 9 validation covered Komatsu 730E and 860E trucks at up to 30 km/h and still used physical tests to adjust detection zones; the booklet found neither independent performance tests nor published validation methods, durations or physical-testing shares for the cited Komatsu products [f817, f1247, f1242, f1389]. The multi-year Applied Intuition–Komatsu partnership announced on 9 September 2025 covers Vehicle OS, autonomous haulage and collision avoidance for staffed sites, including planned EMESRT control level 9 development; Applied Intuition is both a tool and autonomy-stack supplier, but its productivity case studies are not controlled cross-vendor measurements [f8399, f8400, f8332, f8735]. Komatsu also describes terrain-and-environment digital twins, while a 2024 wheel-loader digging model co-funded by Komatsu and Algoryx required a tire-ground friction coefficient of 2.0 to match measurements, highlighting a concrete simulation-calibration issue [f4125, f6090].

nodes.label: Caterpillar
nodes.text: Caterpillar
nodes.synopsis: Caterpillar provides a precedent for restricted-domain release: Cat Detect automatic braking launched on medium wheel loaders in May 2025 with reverse-only operation, although Chapter 2 separately reports that no wheel-loader AEB launch date was found [f1067, f1068, f1632, f73]. The loader system inhibits reverse engagement after at least 15 seconds stationary when an object is in the critical zone, and adjusts warning levels with ground speed to reduce nuisance alarms [f10637, f10636]. Asphalt-compactor collision mitigation extends coverage to forward and reverse; it was shown in March 2026 and reported on 29 May 2026 as slated for launch by midyear, rather than confirmed launched [f1070, f1071]. Caterpillar warns that camera-based detection may miss crouching or lying people and can be impaired by low light, snow, rain or fog [f1638]. Warning-event and GPS logging offers a data path for shadow-mode validation, but no independent performance test was found, published validation methods and timelines remain unavailable, and the case's evidence acceptance was internal [f1603, f1242, f1389, f1867].

nodes.label: NIOSH
nodes.text: NIOSH
nodes.synopsis: NIOSH’s 2022 rapid review covered 64 articles from 2000–2020 and 97 haul-truck collision-system cases; evidence largely concerned components or prototypes, only 8% of articles exceeded technology readiness level 7, and only 10% of cases involved avoidance or intervention systems [f5933, f393, f5172, f5171]. The strongest cited hard false-alarm evidence remains the 2006 Caterpillar 793B radar study: among 580 alarms over 618 reversals, 102 (18%) were false and 243 (42%) were nuisance alarms, while the audible alarm was found switched off after shifts [f102, f5174, f5175, f104]. Historical NIOSH evidence counted 22 blind-area fatalities from 2000 to mid-2006, with 67% of victims behind reversing equipment, but these data must not be treated as a 2026 fatality rate [f3060, f11546, f3068]. Research emphasis on vehicle-to-vehicle interactions does not match accident coverage: a later analysis of 54 fatality reports identified 21 berm-related and 12 dump-point-related deaths, versus 13 involving pedestrians or vehicles [f395, f3070, f3072]. Practical findings show that radar placement matters, stopping can fail when downhill grade exceeds brake capacity, and underground stop zones varied across sites by an average 1.4 m and up to 3.6 m [f7039, f7040, f5903, f5929]. Planning still faces gaps in false-positive testing, simulation procedures, environmental effects and real-world validation, alongside mostly undisclosed manufacturer validation documentation and the warning that new technology can introduce new hazards [f10425, f10448, f1370].

nodes.label: Caterpillar 793B
nodes.text: Caterpillar 793B
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats the seven-day Caterpillar 793B radar-warning field test at a US copper mine in 2004, published by NIOSH in 2006, as its strongest available quantitative alarm-performance evidence [f11774, f5173]. Testing covered normal loading, hauling, dumping, parking and maintenance manoeuvres; 580 alarms sounded over 618 reversals, approximately 94% of reverse movements [f3269, f14431, f3010]. Of those alarms, 102 (18%) were false and 243 (42%) were nuisance alarms, leaving 235 warranting action or extra caution; the corpus reports that last share as either 40% or 41%, explicitly attributing the difference to rounding [f5174, f5175, f3277]. No missed detections were reported, but the audible warning was found disabled after shifts, so detection performance did not ensure continued use of the audible warning [f3278, f11780]. False alarms arose from ruts, rocks, foliage and the truck’s own rear tires, while nuisance alarms included real objects already known to the driver [f11779, f7002]. Chapter 9 also describes a Preco Preview trial at Phelps Dodge Morenci whose occasional false alarms were reportedly insufficient to cause the system to be ignored; the glossary calls this another trial, so its more favorable account should not automatically be merged with the disabled-alarm finding [f7001, f14434, f104].

nodes.label: ISO 21815-3
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21815-3:2023 is published and provides a directly relevant framework for forward/reverse collision warning and avoidance through speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition—not steering—for earth-moving, mobile underground-mining and road-construction machinery [f2058, f3905, f2163]. Its collision-risk area accounts for detection, decision and action time, machine stopping distance and a residual safety distance; the booklet therefore favors stopping-distance/risk-zone intervention, with time to collision as one input, and machine-scaled scenario geometry [f5911, f6680, f5922, f6770]. Automatic intervention is placed at collision-risk level 4 or above, warning levels must be distinguishable, stronger operator braking must not be overridden, and safe-operation responsibility remains with the operator [f5912, f11723, f5913, f2164]. Old-versus-new comparisons should use common ground truth and a common risk zone, measuring warnings and interventions per hazard, missed hazards, false/nuisance alarms per hour and warning time to collision [f5210, f5479]. The standard does not establish quantified field effectiveness or second-order hazards, and the reviewed standards supply neither statistical acceptance targets nor simulation-credibility rules; Annex D stopping-distance examples are not a validation method, and physical tests remain necessary [f3443, f324, f6749, f7729, f8145]. Important limitations remain: simulation provisions or acceptance of simulation evidence were not found, universal target dimensions and test counts were not found in public abstracts, and only the 2022 draft was reviewed in full, so the published text may differ [f9780, f11237, f5410, f2167].

nodes.label: NHTSA
nodes.text: NHTSA
nodes.synopsis: NHTSA investigations covering millions of on-road vehicles underpin the corpus's conclusion that unnecessary braking is the dominant documented automatic-braking failure mode, but Tesla's PE22-002 closed on 29 June 2026 after about 25,900 reports across 695,000 vehicles with no crashes, injuries or defect finding [f115, f1230, f11171]. Honda's investigation grew from 278 complaints in February 2022 to 1,294 across 2,997,604 vehicles in April 2024, while secondary evidence says its CMBS investigation remained open without a recall as of 2026 [f1224, f1801]. Heavy-truck evidence includes reproduced false braking on a steel trench plate and a 2021 Cascadia that avoided a stopped target at 40–85 km/h but not below 40 km/h; adaptations for stopping distance and equipment argue against directly copying passenger-car scenarios into construction or mining validation [f1812, f1329, f1233, f1527]. NHTSA documents robotic and soft-target track testing, stationary-vehicle false-positive scenarios and a −0.05 g braking-onset threshold, with track testing remaining central to its multi-year heavy-vehicle research [f562, f6192, f6193, f1331]. Its 2024 NCAP decision is an on-road consumer reference, not applicable to off-road machines, and specifies no-contact AEB tests at 40–80 km/h; FMVSS 127 cost estimates are sharply disputed at US$354.06 million annually versus an industry estimate of US$63 billion [f2838, f2629, f2886]. Regulatory certainty remains incomplete: FMVSS 127's effective date was delayed in January 2025, the final heavy-vehicle AEB rule status was not found, and the Nissan investigation status was also not found [f10866, f1333, f1806].

nodes.label: Pareto front

nodes.synopsis: The booklet frames collision-mitigation tuning as constrained multi-objective optimization: missed or late interventions are a hard constraint, while false warnings, unnecessary braking and productivity loss are optimized with the Pareto front visible [f136]. The glossary further recommends putting the human-factors rate on one axis of that front [f14442]. Chapter 9 recommends preserving visibility so trade-offs become documented safety-policy decisions rather than hidden weights; evolutionary methods make trade-offs explicit but do not determine which Pareto point is acceptable [f6672, f6971, f6973]. Pareto-front, NSGA-II and other evolutionary methods, referenced to Deb et al. (2002), are described as robust and simple to parallelise over simulation, but they require many evaluations [f6970, f6972].

nodes.label: New South Wales
nodes.text: New South Wales
nodes.synopsis: New South Wales guidance addresses mining vehicle-interaction controls, favoring site design, segregation and procedures, with collision systems at Levels 7–9 as backup; the glossary states that NSW does not mandate automatic braking [f2786, f3624, f15525]. Regulator evidence reported no meaningful year-on-year reduction in vehicle interactions in 2023 and 30 underground coal LHD/personnel-transport collisions in the 12 months to mid-2025; bulky loads sometimes obstructed LHD operators’ views [f3004, f3196, f11447]. The 2023 regulator paper also reported that NSW mining had not yet implemented proximity/detection technology reliably able to distinguish hazardous from spurious conditions, supporting the corpus’s concern about unresolved false alarms [f3112, f15540, f15551]. Although several chapters describe 0.60 m/s² as the in-service minimum off-road deceleration, the glossary clarifies that the thresholds are proposals, not adopted rules: service/secondary brakes require 0.60/0.30 m/s² in service and 0.75/0.40 m/s² for type testing, with grade and mass corrections [f141, f5889, f13946]. NSW formulas use net deceleration on grade and assume no skidding; in the 100 t truck example, a 20% design grade and 9% test grade yield a 1.04 m/s² grade correction and 1.79 m/s² required test deceleration, underscoring why definitions and test conditions must be reconciled across standards [f13640, f6295, f5902, f5901, f6614].

nodes.label: MSHA
nodes.text: MSHA
nodes.synopsis: MSHA rules are law rather than standards; its surface mobile equipment rule was published on 20 December 2023, took effect on 19 January 2024, and required compliance from 17 July 2024 [f15010, f2777]. The rule requires written safety programs and evaluation of technologies, but does not mandate collision avoidance; the corpus reports 863 citations from July 2024 to April 2026, identified as expert-opinion evidence [f1369, f2778, f5844]. MSHA reported powered haulage accounted for 13 of 33 US mining fatalities (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries (9%) in 2025 [f3051, f3052]. For braking calculations, Table M-1 specifies approximately 2.94 m/s² constant deceleration and assumes 0.5–2.5 seconds of system response by weight class plus one second of operator time [f5890, f6058]. MSHA's extension-of-approval or RAMP route provides a precedent for evidence reuse, but the research found no MSHA provision allowing simulation to replace prescribed physical performance tests, and no final rule for the underground mobile-machine proximity proposal from 2015 [f621, f2475, f7752]. Practical validation remains a concern: Barrick's 2015 submission reported little mine-site validation data, systems failing to meet supplier claims, and a need for multiple OEMs' cooperation and approval for automatic slowing and stopping [f10644, f10645, f10691].

nodes.label: United States
nodes.text: United States
nodes.synopsis: For the off-road scope discussed, US rules require warnings, detection and written safety programs that evaluate technologies, but not automatic braking; the MSHA surface-mobile-equipment rule was finalised on 20 December 2023, became effective on 19 January 2024, and had a compliance date of 17 July 2024, with 863 citations reported by April 2026 [f2861, f2087, f2777, f2088]. Powered haulage caused 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries (9%) in 2025, supporting its continued importance as a safety priority [f2978, f2979, f2980]. Historical evidence distinguishes collision hazards from other haul-truck hazards: among 54 deaths in January 2005–June 2021, 13 were collisions with people or vehicles, 21 involved berms and 12 occurred at dump points; 12 of the 13 collisions involved forward movement, while a separate blind-area dataset found 67% of victims behind reversing equipment [f2989, f2990, f2986]. MSHA Table M-1 uses approximately 2.94 m/s² constant deceleration, weight-dependent system response of 0.5–2.5 seconds and one second of operator response, whereas a historic mining report gives approximately two seconds of nominal operator reaction and another 1–2 seconds of dynamic-retarder lag [f5989, f6058, f6059, f6060]. US on-road evidence offers threshold-and-latency evaluation methods and cautions about false or unexpected braking, but FMVSS No. 127 is not applicable to off-road machines and the final status of the July 2023 heavy-vehicle AEB proposal remains uncertain [f6346, f6189, f6304, f2831, f1964]. Regulatory compliance should not be treated as proof of proximity-detection feasibility, and the corpus found no dedicated US off-road requirement for an ML collision-avoidance function to meet a specified ML validation standard by 2028 [f11228, f2393].

nodes.label: ISO 21815-1
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21815-1:2022, dated January 2022, covers detection, operator warning, automatic intervention and testing for earth-moving, mobile underground mining and road-construction machinery; the booklet identifies it as the clearest scope match for an OEM-fitted warning-plus-automatic-braking system, but excludes systems installed before publication [f6741, f381, f2154, f2153]. Its permitted interventions are speed reduction, stopping and motion inhibition—not automatic steering—and responsibility remains with the operator because the technology cannot cover every situation [f11701, f11702, f3647]. Clause 6 specifies physical performance tests with pass/fail criteria and false-positive tests, which the project is advised to retain for each scenario class [f7726, f7884]. The review found neither provisions accepting simulation evidence nor statistical acceptance targets, sample sizes or simulation-credibility rules; however, the full paid texts could not be checked, so failure to find simulation substitution does not establish that it is prohibited [f9780, f11237, f324, f6749, f7544]. Functional standardization does not establish quantified field effectiveness or second-order hazards, and the research evidence is concentrated in surface mining and construction despite the standard's underground-machinery coverage [f3443, f1164].

nodes.label: ISO/TS 21815-2
nodes.synopsis: ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 was published in July 2021 and confirmed in December 2024; it defines the on-board SAE J1939 interface through which a collision-avoidance device requests slowing, stopping or prevention of machine motion [f10725, f2057, f2158]. Its commands distinguish controlled stops from emergency stops, include motion inhibit and prevention of movement from standstill, and exclude automatic steering; the interface also includes capability discovery and a keep-alive signal [f3638, f6237, f3639, f12979]. The interface is explicitly not plug-and-play: manufacturers must agree integration details, machines may report that actions can be overridden, and validation must include end-to-end integration latency [f2159, f6238, f8198]. Vendor precedents include Epiroc's 2021 implementation using a draft interface and Bell's August 2023 statement that Pin 3 E-series ADTs support third-party PDS or CAS integration up to Level 9 through a gateway [f1348, f1839, f1391]. Across chapters, the interface anchors brake requests, evidence reuse and HIL testing; a production-relevant HIL bench could target mid-2027, but should stay off the critical path unless ECU, bus and actuator interfaces stabilise early [f5579, f367, f538, f857]. Planning should include interoperability demonstrations and interface tests, while acknowledging that the review found no simulation provisions, did not review interface-conformance testing content, and reports the specification's warning that collision-avoidance algorithms are not yet mature and well understood [f10726, f11078, f9780, f2661, f8934].

nodes.label: ISO 16001
nodes.synopsis: ISO 16001:2017 sets performance and test requirements for object-detection systems and visibility aids; the booklet dates it to November 2017, reports confirmation in 2023, and emphasizes that it covers warning and visibility, not braking [f6744, f2181]. It is the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers: detection within 300 ms, audible warnings at least 3 dB above ambient, and a flashing red light for the most severe warning, alongside continuous self-checking and no single-action disablement [f160, f2064, f2065, f2066, f2067, f2068]. Its framework defines a test body, detection zone and detection time, with physical-test procedures and technology annexes that lack a dedicated lidar annex [f5354, f11232, f2069]. For virtual validation, the corpus uses its detection limit in physics parameterisation and its visibility-type methods for geometric blind-zone analysis, but reports no simulation-credibility acceptance rules and no evidence establishing acceptance of simulation evidence [f7493, f11549, f5110, f11237]. Planners should confirm the 300 ms limit against the purchased standard before safety-case use: it was sourced from a public preview rather than verified against the full standard, while other chapters also flag unverified editions, dates and simulation clauses [f7493, f7494, f7495, f4335, f5111].

nodes.label: ISO 26262
nodes.synopsis: The booklet consistently identifies ISO 19014, using MPLr, rather than ISO 26262 as the functional-safety framework for the brake-commanding earth-moving-machine function; ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 do not apply by scope to this heavy off-road program [f162, f2071, f11993, f2355, f15293]. ISO 26262 governs road-vehicle electronic functional safety and derives ASIL A–D or QM from severity, exposure and controllability ratings, so ASIL should not be treated as the off-road machine's applicable risk scale [f15291, f12062, f12063, f12060]. The booklet recommends borrowing road-vehicle standards' structure as a method, with machine-learning issues explicit in the safety case; ISO/PAS 8800:2024, dated December 2024, tailors ISO 26262 for AI but remains road-vehicle-only reference material [f15309, f15298, f12069]. It reports a 70% confidence level for ISO 26262 proven-in-use calculations and a higher confidence requirement in IEC 61508 practice [f7935, f7936, f12352, f12353]. These statements have an important verification limitation: the research did not verify ISO 26262 and related on-road frameworks, did not review the listed safety standards in full text, and did not verify explicit simulation-evidence acceptance or tool-qualification rules [f7702, f8942].

nodes.label: South Africa
nodes.text: South Africa
nodes.synopsis: South Africa is the only jurisdiction the booklet found with a legal automatic slow-down and braking mandate for heavy mining machines: regulations published on 27 February 2015, suspended because technology was unavailable, commenced on 21 December 2022 with no transitional period [f164, f1363, f10724, f11457]. The rules require diesel-powered trackless mobile machines to detect and warn of collision risk, slow to a safe speed and brake automatically if the operator does not act, and fail to safe without human intervention; acceptance is by the mine operator against the regulation, using industry guidelines as reference [f2079, f2080, f1367]. The mandate preceded validation standards and specifies no detection percentage, distance, false-alarm limit or stopping-distance test; subsequent industry documents include independent verification specifications dated 29 August 2025, a verification regime dated 11 October 2025 and a TRL7 stage-gate specification dated 20 January 2026 [f1360, f2081, f555, f556, f557]. The MOSH surface specification adds a 200 m minimum detection range, warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention, fail-to-safe within 500 ms, defined stop gaps and no false interventions at TRL4, while Pretoria testing reported pass rates of 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces across 189 tests [f174, f175, f177, f176, f178, f5178]. Safety concerns persist: total mining fatalities fell from 55 in 2023 to 42 in 2024, but trackless-mobile-machine deaths rose from six to nine in 2024; guidance also warns that a fixed stop gap would make truck loading impossible [f3138, f3008, f3023]. Planning should distinguish mandatory Level 9 deployment from vendor advice to evaluate without immediately enforcing intervention, recognize conflicting trade reporting about commencement, and not assume simulation can replace prescribed physical tests [f358, f6575, f1364, f2103].

nodes.label: Euro NCAP
nodes.text: Euro NCAP
nodes.synopsis: Euro NCAP is an independent on-road consumer-assessment body, not a type-approval regulator; its 2026–2028 protocols are not applicable to heavy off-road machines, and its score is not regulatory evidence for a machine [f1272, f2843, f2551]. Virtual Testing v1.00, dated March 2025 and effective January 2026, is identified as the clearest collision-avoidance example of simulation evidence accepted by an external assessor [f2107, f1260]. Its workflow requires manufacturer qualification against physical tests using ISO scores and defined KPIs, scenario-grid predictions, and independently selected random physical verification; at least 75% of verification tests in each scenario cluster must meet qualification criteria [f2496, f2497, f1216, f2500]. The 2026 protocols contain more than 1,200 scenarios, but per-manufacturer build and validation times were not found, and several numeric tolerances remain unconfirmed [f2545, f1273, f14821]. No off-road equivalent was found, so the booklet recommends borrowing physical qualification and independent spot-checking as evidence-governance methods rather than treating simulation or robotic-target automation as a proven off-road shortcut [f346, f2143, f1587, f13505]. There is an unresolved research-status tension: detailed protocol requirements are reported elsewhere, while Chapter 10 says Euro NCAP virtual testing was not verified in this research [f2496, f2500, f7702].

nodes.label: UN R171
nodes.text: UN R171
nodes.synopsis: UN R171 covers on-road Driver Control Assistance Systems, including Level 2 assistance in cars, and does not apply to off-road machines [f1766, f2826, f8111]. Physical testing remains the default; virtual testing is permitted for hard-to-reproduce scenarios after a rigorous toolchain credibility evaluation, rather than as a simulation-only regime [f1769, f1217, f8110]. When virtual testing is used, an Annex 5 credibility assessment must be submitted to the Type Approval Authority, demonstrating tool scope, scenario validity and toolchain validation [f15406, f2488, f2489]. The corpus dates the regulatory text to 2024–2025 and the original series publication to 2025; a vendor attributes the addition of virtual testing to late 2024, while the 02 series was still under discussion in January 2026 [f7681, f2827, f1276, f2490]. For off-road validation, the booklet recommends borrowing R171-style credibility packages and qualifying simulation against physical tests, but reports no identified capability-building or validation-duration estimates for the R171 precedent [f2143, f2648, f1768].
