nodes.label: UNECE
nodes.text: UNECE
nodes.synopsis: UNECE’s VMAD-developed NATM treats simulation as one evidence pillar alongside track testing, real-world testing and audit; physical tests remain the default, virtual results are spot-checked, and the number of R152 physical confirmation tests is left to manufacturer–authority agreement [f1281, f1282, f1284, f172]. Its credibility framework defines the envelope of permitted virtual-tool use and covers accuracy, robustness, documentation, verification and validation, calibration, sensitivity analysis, management and team expertise [f6929, f4830, f7143]. A January 2024 working-group paper nevertheless found that the R152 virtual-testing proposal did not yet address every aspect of a credible capability [f1218]. The corpus identifies 2022 NATM guidelines and a March 2023 master document, while another chapter attributes the master document to 2022, leaving a document-date ambiguity [f7143, f8101, f6929]. UNECE and ISO scenario methods can help establish representative virtual-test coverage, but no direct equivalent of UNECE toolchain credibility principles was found for automatic braking on earth-moving machines, so these on-road precedents do not establish an off-road-specific framework [f8031, f7740, f4831].

nodes.label: UN R152
nodes.text: UN R152
nodes.synopsis: UN R152 covers on-road car and van AEBS, not off-road machines; the identified edition is Revision 2 / 02 series (2024), published as EU OJ L 2024/2497 [f2821, f2526, f15400]. It requires a minimum commanded braking demand of 5.0 m/s², not measured deceleration, so the glossary's description of this as demanded deceleration needs qualification [f5993, f6307, f13632, f13951]. The corpus reports car-to-car testing at 10–60 km/h, pedestrian testing at 20–60 km/h and false-reaction scenarios, although one chapter passage explicitly says these reported details were not verified against the primary text [f2823, f2824, f2825, f2527, f2528, f2529]. January 2024 GRVA criticism identified incomplete virtual-testing credibility coverage, including insufficient physical evidence for individual toolchain components; the described method validates the toolchain against physical tests before use within its assessed envelope [f1279, f7690, f9746]. WP.29 adopted supplements in 2025 allowing virtual testing instead of some physical tests, while the text dated 28 August 2025 retains physical confirmation tests with their number agreed between manufacturer and authority [f7546, f7684]. The vendor-reported 30% physical-test minimum is not confirmed for the adopted text and should not be transferred to off-road machines without justification; a November 2025 Russian proposal for mandatory physical model verification also records continuing regulator-level debate [f7685, f7687, f7688, f7691].

nodes.label: MOSH
nodes.text: MOSH
nodes.synopsis: MOSH supplies an engineering compliance route for South African mining collision prevention, combining industry performance requirements with supplier and independent physical verification at TRL gates, rather than treating regulatory wording as a complete specification [f1855, f2478, f2593]. Its surface requirements include 200 m detection, warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention, fail-to-safe within 500 ms of detecting a critical failure, disconnection detection within 500 ms, and machine replies within 50 ms [f174, f175, f2359, f5284, f5285]. Emergency-stop deceleration is specified as 1.9 m/s² for machines with top speeds above 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² otherwise; stopping performance also depends on gradient, side slope and braking response [f5560, f3401]. University of Pretoria testing reported pass rates of 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces across 189 tests, with throughput of 1.6 tests per week and an 18-week lead time as of October 2025 [f5178, f5180]. Verification must separately cover machines with different braking characteristics, yet published stopping tests cover only unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, limiting the demonstrated operating envelope [f5181, f5182]. MOSH requires no false interventions at TRL4, while its 2022 guidance warns that nuisance interventions and fixed stop gaps can disrupt production or loading enough to prompt switching systems off; the glossary also leaves a timing ambiguity by describing both failure detection and reaching a safe state within 500 ms, versus the specification's interval after critical-failure detection [f178, f3300, f3344, f12132, f2359].

nodes.label: University of Pretoria
nodes.text: University of Pretoria
nodes.synopsis: The University of Pretoria independently verifies mining collision-avoidance systems under South Africa’s MOSH regime, progressing from laboratory TRL4 testing to representative-mine trials, with the protocol extending underground [f15570, f14690, f6372]. Results reported in October 2025 covered 189 tests—79% verification and 21% development—with pass rates of 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces; throughput was 1.6 tests per week with an 18-week lead time [f15647, f5179, f5180]. Verification must separately cover machine types, models and serial numbers with different braking characteristics, while published stopping tests cover only unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, limiting the demonstrated operating envelope [f5181, f5182]. Hexagon announced on 25 March 2026 that its current-generation Vehicle Intervention System had passed Pretoria’s TRL4 verification before integrated site testing, but the press release supplied no numbers and capability-building and verification durations were not found [f1350, f6373, f1846]. Pretoria’s 2024 research investigated steering-rate-based collision prediction to reduce false interventions, but its initial results were simulation-only and validation time once available was not found [f6331, f1851]. This research addresses production losses, wear and resistance to adoption from false interventions, exposing a tension between conservative, fail-to-safe intervention and operational acceptability [f5567, f5781].

nodes.label: Space shuttle Columbia
nodes.text: Space shuttle Columbia
nodes.synopsis: Following a foam strike during launch in January 2003, engineers assessed Columbia’s tile damage using the empirical Crater model; the in-flight assessment reported no safety-of-flight issue, and Columbia was lost on re-entry on 1 February 2003 [f7950, f7957, f7958]. The assessed debris was about 400 times the size represented in Crater’s test database, although an early briefing cited 640 times; the model’s conservative bias for small impacts was assumed to persist at this much larger scale [f7582, f14936]. Across the introduction, Chapter 10 and glossary, Columbia is presented as a canonical false-confidence case involving extrapolation beyond a validated domain and human reinterpretation of the result [f192, f7581, f14939]. The interpretation is contested: the investigation board emphasized model validity, while Hale argued that Crater gave a correct warning that management overrode; the booklet records both views [f8192, f15853]. For the heavy off-road program, the lessons are to specify validity envelopes and margins, avoid relying on simulations of physically untested machines, sensors and weather, and communicate caveats plainly; the case also directly drove NASA-STD-7009 [f15854, f15856, f15855, f7962].

nodes.label: RAND Corporation
nodes.text: RAND Corporation
nodes.synopsis: RAND's Driving to Safety report by Kalra and Paddock, published in April 2016, argues that road-driving demonstrations of autonomous-vehicle reliability require hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles—taking existing fleets tens or hundreds of years [f6920, f6921, f5466]. Its benchmarks include 275 million failure-free miles to demonstrate, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement with 95% confidence and 80% power [f6922, f6923]. A separate 2019 conservative Bayesian analysis illustrates sensitivity to prior assumptions: a strong prior with 90% prior confidence reduces the 275-million-mile requirement to 69 million, while a weak prior increases it to 476 million [f6901, f6902]. The booklet transfers RAND's statistical logic, but not its road-mile numbers, to off-road per-encounter detection and intervention claims, recommending simulation, statistics and targeted tests rather than reliance on field hours [f6664, f15826]. RAND also developed assumption-based planning, documented in 1993 and 2002, which the booklet adopts to track load-bearing assumptions, failure signposts and hedges [f9557, f15818, f16345]. Despite repeated use of RAND as an established statistical foundation, the skeptic's review says RAND 2016 was a relevant lead that was not verified in the research, leaving a source-verification tension [f7400, f11203].

nodes.label: Volvo CE Collision Mitigation System
nodes.text: Volvo CE Collision Mitigation System
nodes.synopsis: Volvo CE's Collision Mitigation System launched in January 2023, with a press release dated 11 January; the original wheel-loader system operated only in reverse at 3–15 km/h [f1065, f10625, f1382]. It requires Radar Detect and applies the service brakes for 2–3 seconds before the operator takes over; it is explicitly not intended to replace safe operator behaviour [f1383, f1625, f1630]. The original factory-fit offering covered specified loader models, including L110H and L120H with OptiShift, rather than an unrestricted machine family; Volvo says these loaders spend 40–50% of their time reversing [f10629, f10438, f10630]. Slope memory avoids activation when reversing down stockpiles, and the system can be temporarily deactivated for particular site conditions [f1384, f10631, f10632]. A new generation was announced in April 2025, with reverse obstacle alerts from 0.5 km/h and additional named loader models, but the announcement does not establish whether the automatic-braking speed band changed [f1623, f1386, f1624, f1387]. Development and validation were in-house with internal evidence acceptance, but published validation methods, development and validation durations, remaining physical testing, environmental limits, false-positive rates and minimum object size were unavailable, limiting its usefulness as a validation-planning benchmark [f1379, f1860, f1862, f1066, f1388, f1861, f1631].

nodes.label: EU Machinery Regulation
nodes.text: EU Machinery Regulation
nodes.synopsis: The EU Machinery Regulation applies from January 2027, with the synthesis identifying 20 January 2027 as the precise date [f11301, f244]. The booklet reports requirements for risk reduction, safe and reliable control systems, technical evidence of conformity, and protection against corruption; the regulation also specifies when safety evidence must exist [f12383, f1153, f11300]. How a notified body will assess machine-learning perception and how long that assessment will take remain uncertain, while the booklet does not identify the assessor or required competence for a simulation-based safety argument [f1112, f12294]. Agreement on that assessor and assessment criteria is therefore a prerequisite for the program schedule [f12295]. EN 474 harmonization under the new regulation was not verified because the list was still being prepared in 2026, and the product liability reviewer needs a notified-body or legal opinion on the regulation and AI Act, independent safety sign-off, and a documented launch decision [f15247, f16567].

nodes.synopsis: Chile relies on national workplace and mining regulation rather than a continent-wide South American machinery regime; its Decreto Supremo 132 provides broad mining safety and equipment controls [f2285, f2291]. DS 132 was promulgated in 2002, published on 7 February 2004, and reviewed in a consolidated version incorporating amendments through 2024 [f2290]. The booklet found no dedicated automatic-braking performance or test standard in the reviewed DS 132 material, while SERNAGEOMIN guidance and Codelco standards were not verified [f2292, f2293]. These findings mean numeric acceptance items were “not found,” not that they are “not required”; the booklet also found no dedicated Chilean off-road rule requiring an ML-based collision-avoidance function to meet a specified ML validation standard by 2028 [f15586, f2393].

nodes.label: EMESRT PR-5A
nodes.text: EMESRT PR-5A
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT PR-5A provides mining-specific surface vehicle-interaction scenarios and storyboards that can seed a validation scenario catalogue and supply functional performance requirements in the test traceability chain [f4078, f7747, f7106]. Its nine-level control model culminates in Level 9 intervention, where the system takes control from the operator to automatically slow and stop the machine [f4080, f4081, f7744]. The September 2024 update is confirmed, but its revision number remains uncertain: secondary and vendor sources cite Revision 3.0, while EMESRT’s activity report specifies no revision number [f6566, f6565, f7743, f6564]. Reported counts of 24 scenarios and 17 published surface storyboards appear in tension, although Chapter 8 says they count different things [f4079, f6567]. For mining customers, the booklet recommends mapping validation requirements to PR-5A scenarios and MOSH F&TPR numbers, but PR-5A supplies no statistical acceptance target; its scenario content is not machine-readable, covers only expert-envisaged situations and gives no occurrence frequencies [f2645, f324, f13265, f13266, f13267].

nodes.label: Wabtec
nodes.text: Wabtec
nodes.synopsis: The booklet cites Wabtec for mining applications and describes Level 9 intervention as a machine-control capability rather than a standalone product [f15780, f2585]. Its December 2021 validation on Komatsu 730E and 860E haul trucks demonstrated controlled deceleration at speeds up to 30 km/h, with internal and customer acceptance reported [f817, f1345, f1837]. Physical testing remained primary at integration, including detection-zone adjustments for braking distance, speed, payload and haul-road grade; in 2023, Wabtec described its third-generation system as the result of multiple years of field and production testing [f1347, f15782, f818]. The cited EMESRT PR-5A requirement was reviewed and updated in September 2024 and identified in Wabtec material as Rev 3.0 [f318, f6231]. These examples do not establish a validation timetable: capability-building and subsequent validation durations were not found, and a surface-quarry comparison with Wabtec and Hexagon systems was unavailable [f1835, f2024].

nodes.label: ISO 18497-4
nodes.synopsis: ISO 18497-4:2024 covers verification methods and validation principles for partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous agricultural machinery, including braking, steering, and person or obstacle detection tests; the agricultural family is a close analogue to the heavy off-road collision-mitigation function studied [f1711, f7190]. The 2024 Parts 1–4 were published in July 2024, with Parts 1, 2 and 4 reported as replacing ISO 18497:2018 [f7187, f9763]. Part 4 explicitly lists simulation alongside inspection, measurement, test and analysis, and Annex C provides test objects for simulation, making it the closest off-road standard support for simulation found in the review [f9764, f5276, f5277]. This supports simulation as one method among several, not an established field-test replacement: the research found neither authorization to replace any share of field tests nor an agricultural simulation-based acceptance case [f10294, f15288, f1881]. For planning, important gaps remain: the standard supplies no statistical acceptance target, and the review did not identify a minimum-method table [f324, f9765].

nodes.label: ISO 34502
nodes.synopsis: ISO 34502:2022 supplies a scenario-based safety evaluation framework scoped to road vehicles and limited-access highways; it is methodological precedent, not off-road compliance evidence [f448, f449]. Across chapters, the ISO 34501–34505 process and structure are considered transferable to off-road validation, but their content targets Level 3 and higher road automated driving; useful elements include functional, logical and concrete scenarios originating in PEGASUS [f6642, f7182, f6735]. No heavy-machinery equivalent or study by the listed industry bodies applying ISO 34502 to off-road machines was found, so the programme must define its own scenario or hazard taxonomy for the coverage map [f9881, f1698, f9882]. The standards principally support coverage rather than model credibility: they do not address validation against physical data or risk scaling, establish no physical-to-virtual testing ratio, and do not demonstrate validity for the listed off-road environments and machine conditions [f7693, f8120, f8119, f7694, f7696]. TÜV SÜD nevertheless summarizes European automated-driving regulation and ISO 34502 as requiring the virtual platform itself to be shown fit for purpose, making scenario coverage alone insufficient [f1283, f8120].

nodes.label: RadSimReal
nodes.text: RadSimReal
nodes.synopsis: RadSimReal is a peer-reviewed radar sim-to-real study presented at CVPR 2024 [f327]. It provides on-road evidence that physical radar simulation can narrow the simulation-to-real gap for detection training, with the reported gap reduction limited to urban datasets [f3933, f472]. Nevertheless, the study shows a measurable domain gap, especially in adverse weather, so narrowing the gap does not mean eliminating it [f327, f472]. The glossary groups RadSimReal with Sim2Radar as research tools addressing the radar simulation-to-reality gap; the supplied evidence does not establish performance for heavy off-road machines [f15953, f3933, f472].

nodes.label: CVPR 2024
nodes.text: CVPR 2024
nodes.synopsis: The corpus cites two strands of CVPR 2024 on-road research: RadSimReal on radar simulation-to-real transfer and Li et al. on misleading open-loop evaluation [f327, f5244]. RadSimReal provides evidence that physical radar simulation can narrow detection-training gaps, but the reported results are limited to urban datasets and a measurable domain gap remains, especially in adverse weather [f3933, f472, f327]. Li et al. showed that open-loop planning metrics on nuScenes could be matched using the vehicle's own state alone, creating a misleading impression and potentially biased benchmark conclusions [f5518, f5184]. Chapter 7 consequently flags open-loop replay of raw logs as subject to open-loop bias; the supplied evidence is on-road rather than direct validation for heavy off-road machines [f5679, f3933, f5184].

nodes.label: MineSim
nodes.text: MineSim
nodes.synopsis: MineSim is an open-source, peer-reviewed scenario-based simulation test system and benchmark for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines, published in Accident Analysis & Prevention in April 2025; the cited precedent is academic simulation work only [f464, f15805, f1728]. It incorporates scenarios from two real mines and represents unstructured roads, irregular intersections and heavy-truck response lag, addressing a coverage gap identified in urban simulators [f465, f466, f3983]. Across chapters, the booklet treats MineSim as evidence that mine-specific closed-loop scenario infrastructure is feasible now and useful for scenario and planning validation [f330, f845, f1100, f15810]. This does not establish validated sensor physics: sensor models in dust, snow and fog remain unsolved, and the broader scene, dynamics and sensor simulation category is rated Low to Medium in heavy-off-road maturity [f15808, f15810, f916]. MineSim also demonstrates structured scenario methodology alongside ISO 34502, although the latter is road-specific [f833].

nodes.label: ACARP C26028
nodes.text: ACARP C26028
nodes.synopsis: Mining3 delivered ACARP project C26028 in January 2021 as a proximity-detection testing framework; it is a shared physical test protocol, not a simulator [f15627, f16088]. Its two-tier structure proves object detection in Tier 1 before testing Level 8 or Level 9 advisory or intervention action in Tier 2 [f15625, f15628, f559]. The booklet recommends this sequence for the collision mitigation project's physical test campaign, while warning that choreographed tests cannot replace site-specific, multi-variable dynamics [f15634]. The baseline is explicitly limited to choreographed scenarios and excludes pre-existing site controls and complex, multi-variate dynamic vehicle interactions [f347, f560, f561, f15629]. Despite these limitations, the booklet groups C26028 with the Mining3 toolkit, NIOSH evaluations and MOSH verification as sources of comparability and credible independent evidence [f682, f15630].

nodes.label: Dense deep reinforcement learning
nodes.text: Dense deep reinforcement learning
nodes.synopsis: Dense deep reinforcement learning (D2RL), reported by Feng et al. in Nature on 22 March 2023, achieved unbiased automated-road-vehicle evaluation reported as 10^3–10^5 times faster on highway and urban test tracks using an augmented-reality environment [f6848, f14163]. The method trains background agents and is presented among statistical approaches to shortening validation, with academic open-source code identified as typical tooling [f633, f425, f7279]. Chapter 9 recommends D2RL and naturalistic-adversarial environments for accelerated unbiased evaluation in the collision-mitigation test program, but the demonstrated evidence is only on-road, not off-road [f7275, f7079]. Legitimate evaluation claims require a large naturalistic dataset and a learned naturalistic behaviour model; Chapter 1 additionally identifies a known exposure distribution as necessary and unavailable for the 100+ job-site types [f7277, f7278, f352]. A 2026 Nature Communications paper in the same research line applies dense learning to overcome safety-performance stagnation, but the supplied fact does not establish off-road validation [f6849].

The method trained dense-reinforcement-learning background agents; Chapter 9 also describes the acceleration in terms of naturalistic-adversarial environments and dense RL [f633, f7276]. These results support accelerated automated-road-vehicle validation, but the corpus explicitly identifies a transfer gap: D2RL is proven only on-road, not for off-road testing [f351, f7079].

nodes.text: curse of rarity
nodes.synopsis: The corpus identifies Liu and Feng’s “Curse of rarity,” published in Nature Communications in 2024, as an on-road statistical validation precedent [f635, f426]. Its central explanation is that safety-critical events are rare and embedded in a very high-dimensional environment, making the distribution tail difficult to learn and validate [f635]. The glossary emphasizes that this testing difficulty increases as the number of variables grows [f13306]. Chapter 1 indicates that the tail remains difficult even in accelerated and rare-event statistical validation; the supplied facts do not quantify that difficulty or establish its applicability to heavy off-road machines [f353, f635, f426].

nodes.text: Epiroc
nodes.synopsis: Epiroc (Mernok) fourth-generation collision avoidance and Titan serve mining fleets with Level 9 intervention; Titan claims full Levels 7, 8 and 9 capability using EMESRT PR-5A as a guideline [f1078, f6575]. Epiroc also describes on-site evaluation and traffic management without immediately enforcing Level 9, presented as an off-road analogue to shadow testing and an example of staged release [f587, f11754]. This staged approach contrasts with South African practice pushing Level 9 mandates [f6575]. Mernok and Epiroc reported more than ten years of development behind their fourth-generation system in May 2024 [f823, f1080]. nodes.label: SAE J1939
nodes.text: SAE J1939
nodes.synopsis: SAE J1939 is the heavy-machine network language used by ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 for collision-device intervention; the technical specification was published in July 2021 and confirmed in December 2024 [f12976, f15025, f15146]. Its interface supports slow-down, controlled-stop, emergency-stop and motion-inhibit requests, plus capability discovery and keep-alive, but is explicitly not plug-and-play [f5910, f12979, f12980]. Across chapters, this standardized interface is presented as an off-road anchor for brake requests, a precedent for reusing evidence across machine models, and a natural HIL test interface that a bench can emulate [f5579, f367, f538, f8661]. Validation must cover end-to-end integration latency, adequate machine-state recording with message-schema versions, and protection against spoofing, stale messages, bus faults and incompatible implementations; SIL cannot demonstrate unexpected CAN/J1939 timing behavior [f8198, f12982, f2936, f530]. The booklet nevertheless identifies an omission of J1939 cybersecurity and integrity from its eight brake-timing questions, and warns that interface or controller changes in 2027 without impact analysis may invalidate the pre-built simulator [f6607, f11028].

nodes.label: ICMM
nodes.text: ICMM
nodes.synopsis: ICMM (International Council on Mining and Metals) is identified as a user of the nine-level control model; its joint April 2024 Leading Sites work with EMESRT treats intervention as one layer of controls, not a silver bullet [f11737, f390, f6550]. Effective Level 8–9 implementation requires understanding the Level 1–7 baseline during normal operations and integrating intervention technology with existing site controls rather than replacing them [f702, f2589, f11750, f704]. ICMM and EMESRT call for scenario-based functional-performance requirements, while mining requirements often exceed legal minima through demands for heterogeneous-fleet and third-party interoperability [f703, f2580]. ICMM's ICSV goal was to make collision avoidance technology available to mining companies by 2025 using EMESRT requirements, but the facts do not establish whether that goal was achieved [f2588]. The corpus flags implementation risks: human performance can improve or deteriorate after technology introduction, and unqualified Level 9 deployment can harm production and accelerate brake wear, against the backdrop of South African clauses brought into force in December 2022 despite readiness concerns [f581, f2892]. Research coverage remains uneven: no ICMM study applying the named road-derived scenario/testing frameworks to off-road machines was found, Chapter 12 did not review ICSV, and Chapter 13 treated ICMM as an unverified lead [f1698, f9809, f11206].

nodes.label: Vehicle Interaction Leading Sites Program
nodes.text: Vehicle Interaction Leading Sites Program
nodes.synopsis: ICMM and EMESRT published the Vehicle Interaction Leading Sites Program in April 2024 [f15616, f390]. Across Chapter 1 and the glossary, the programme treats intervention as one layer alongside design, operating and advisory controls, not as a complete solution, and states that there are no silver bullets for vehicle interaction controls [f390, f15617, f15619]. Chapter 3 and the glossary both place a Level 1–7 control baseline before Levels 8 and 9, although Chapter 3 describes this as an emphasis while the glossary frames it as a requirement [f2589, f15618]. Taken together, these findings favour a layered control strategy with a baseline established before higher-level intervention, rather than reliance on intervention alone [f390, f2589, f15617, f15618].

nodes.label: Mining3
nodes.text: Mining3
nodes.synopsis: Mining3 identifies a verification gap in mining collision avoidance: end users cannot easily verify suppliers’ reliability and functionality claims [f396, f687]. Mining3 and EMESRT emphasize field verification and site-specific baselines, in tension with automotive simulation advocates who argue that simulation can carry most of the statistical burden [f1122]. Mining3 delivered ACARP project C26028 in January 2021; the proximity-detection testing framework is a shared physical test protocol, not a simulator [f15627, f16088, f16119]. Access to ACARP and Mining3 methods, alongside MOSH specifications, test sites, a qualified independent body, and traceability, is identified as critical to shared frameworks and independent review [f1057].

nodes.label: CARLA
nodes.text: CARLA
nodes.synopsis: CARLA is a free, MIT-licensed, Unreal-based driving simulator used for scene, sensor and closed-loop simulation; mining-interaction research has explored CARLA and ROS as a route from simulation to small-scale and physical testing [f15900, f15928, f397, f3488]. It has two release lines: 0.10.0, released on 19 December 2024, moved to Unreal Engine 5.5 and added native ROS 2 support and a mining earth-mover asset, while 0.9.16, released on 16 September 2025, remained on Unreal Engine 4 and added neural reconstruction capabilities [f8463, f8464, f8465, f8466, f8298]. Its off-road suitability remains unqualified: it lacks native deformable terrain or soil physics, was not found validated for off-road collision warning, and a 2026 mining-dust framework tuned to real lidar data did not have a confirmed simulated-versus-real point-cloud comparison [f8476, f5851, f4742, f4743]. The chapter 11 statement that no off-road sensor evidence was found is in tension with chapter 6's mining-lidar framework, although tuning alone does not establish validation [f9083, f4655, f4743]. The UE5 build requires Ubuntu 22.04 or Windows 11, at least an RTX 3000-series GPU with 16 GB VRAM, and 130 GB of disk; a frozen, qualified build is recommended because of release changes and installation, content and version friction [f8469, f15938, f8474]. An open-source chain can minimize license costs but demands substantial internal labor, with Chrono proposed for machine dynamics and terrain; frame rates and physics-based ultrasonic simulation were not found for CARLA, and project maintenance funding and security-patch cadence were not examined [f16128, f16158, f4957, f8547, f9392, f9393].

nodes.text: Samak et al.
nodes.synopsis: Samak et al.’s GVSETS 2024 work is cited as an off-road digital-twin example alongside a separate construction-vehicle twin from 2025 [f399]. The cluster-based approach addresses the inability of sequential parameter sweeps to explore large variability spaces under time constraints [f4104]. For virtual-job-site planning, the work supports a scaling methodology rather than prescribing a particular scenario count; the reported 128 cases should therefore not be treated as a required validation target [f4105, f467].

nodes.label: Applied Intuition
nodes.text: Applied Intuition
nodes.synopsis: Applied Intuition is a commercial, road-derived simulation platform adapted for mining, construction and agriculture; its advertised toolchain spans scenario, sensor and vehicle-dynamics simulation, HIL and large-scale cloud execution, while its data platforms ingest logs and manage regression testing [f8964, f8683, f8396, f8658]. It acquired CarSim and TruckSim through Mechanical Simulation in March 2022 and launched an off-road autonomy stack on 17 June 2024 [f8402, f8397]. A multi-year Komatsu partnership announced on 9 September 2025 covers Vehicle OS, autonomous haulage and collision avoidance for staffed sites, including planned EMESRT control level 9 systems; this provides independent evidence of off-road relevance, but independent validation of automatic braking on heavy machines was not found [f8399, f8400, f8684, f8289]. Applied Intuition's R171 blog describes physical tests as expected, with virtual testing permitted for certain difficult-to-reproduce scenarios subject to rigorous toolchain credibility evaluation [f1277, f1278]. Planning gaps include unavailable public pricing, an unverified interface/standards picture, no detailed public sensor matrix and no sensor-model validation evidence for dust, snow or soil; raw-data compatibility must therefore be checked against the eventual sensors [f8405, f8968, f8403, f8407, f8659]. Reported acceleration and productivity gains are marketing rather than independent or controlled cross-vendor benchmarks, and supplying both validation tools and autonomy stacks creates a potential competitive conflict for manufacturers developing their own perception and braking functions [f8406, f8735, f8409].

nodes.label: Waymo
nodes.text: Waymo
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats Waymo as an on-road vendor precedent: its safety methods layer simulation, replay, closed-course and public-road tests, and shadow mode, using virtual methods as filters rather than substitutes for physical testing [f15718, f15729]. Waymo published collision-avoidance testing methods and documented city-by-city release in 2022, widening operating areas as evidence accumulates, but disclosed validation durations and physical-test shares do not establish verified sign-off [f604, f15720, f15728]. Its material distinguishes open-loop replay from closed-loop simulation; its dataset also illustrates the synchronized sensor data, calibration, poses and tracked labels needed for reproducible references, while its labeling study cautions that human labels can be inconsistent [f15721, f15722, f15723]. Waymo's world model announcement of 6 February 2026 remains an on-road vendor claim without off-road qualification; separate generative novel-view research reported 13.19–20.82 dB PSNR on Waymo data, which the booklet judges low fidelity for safety testing [f3759, f15724, f3821, f3822]. Waymo data also supported evaluation of December 2023 CARLA rain-lidar intensity prediction and the August 2026 Clear2Fog study using 270,000 images [f4739, f4897].

nodes.label: Motional
nodes.text: Motional
nodes.synopsis: Motional is an on-road autonomy vendor whose published methods provide evidence for layered validation, not verified sign-off for heavy off-road machines [f15718, f15728]. Its documented progression moves from complementary synthetic simulation and re-simulation of recorded data through closed-course and public-road testing to deployment [f517, f695, f15725]. Its 2026 safety material describes daily testing and shadow-mode feature deployment before broader roll-out; in shadow mode, software produces decisions that vehicle actuators do not execute [f586, f15726, f15727]. The booklet uses Motional and Waymo to support simulation, replay and shadow mode as filters before scarce physical testing—not substitutes for it—and staged release within a limited operating domain [f15729, f15730]. Neither company discloses validation durations or physical-test shares that would count as verified sign-off, leaving those planning quantities unresolved [f15728].

nodes.text: IDIADA
nodes.synopsis: IDIADA provides vehicle-in-the-loop services, including injecting virtual hazards into a real vehicle’s ECU on a track through sensor stimulation [f16108, f406, f540]. With MathWorks, it demonstrated virtual-to-physical correlation of frontal automatic emergency braking for on-road cars on 14 April 2026, using closed-loop virtual sensors, vehicle dynamics and an AEB controller, with production-vehicle proving-ground tests and ISO 18571 correlation metrics [f1761, f1269, f1762]. The demonstration included far more scenario variants than earlier protocol generations but retained proving-ground correlation [f1270, f1764]. This establishes a demonstrated capability, not evidence that a specific vehicle received a rating: the acceptance evidence involved a test house and tool vendor, and no vehicle rating was shown [f1271, f1765]. Capability-building time was not found, and validation time was reported only as a demonstration, leaving the implementation timeline unresolved [f1763].

nodes.label: dSPACE
nodes.text: dSPACE
nodes.synopsis: dSPACE’s cited vehicle-in-the-loop evidence is vendor-supplied and on-road: its intended testing chain stimulates camera, radar and ultrasound and observes responses through brakes and steering, while automotive documentation also describes camera-box limitations and downstream raw-image injection [f408, f545, f5252]. Its DARTS blog of 11 September 2019 claims radar simulation from 0.6 to 3,600 meters, 6 cm range resolution and up to five real objects in the radar test bench [f5310, f5311]. dSPACE advertises mining-truck environments with vehicle dynamics and physics-based sensor simulation, but the glossary characterizes AURELION with SIMPHERA specifically as commercial, supported by on-road-only evidence, with no public price found—leaving a gap between advertised off-road capability and the evidence identified for that package [f4126, f15895]. The booklet identifies a supported ASM–AURELION–VEOS–ModelDesk chain, OpenSCENARIO XML and OpenDRIVE support, SIMPHERA’s reliance on dSPACE ecosystem interfaces, bench integration and RoadRunner exports to dSPACE; some legacy integration technology has announced end-of-life schedules [f8704, f8616, f9205, f15897, f15999, f8894]. dSPACE benches feature in the highest-cost example chain and its real-time products are identified as computing hardware; separately, dSPACE reports that UNECE WP.29 added virtual testing to R171 at the end of 2024 [f9306, f16167, f16180, f1276].

nodes.label: University of Queensland
nodes.text: University of Queensland
nodes.synopsis: The University of Queensland’s ACARP C24028 project studied haul-truck proximity-advisory interface design in 2017, with follow-on work to 2019 [f3314, f15631]. It tested real operators in a machine simulator and used a 5DT haul-truck simulator to evaluate visual and auditory proximity interfaces aimed at reducing collision probability [f414, f572]. Its scope was advisory warnings and human–machine interfaces, not automatic braking, so it should not be treated as evidence of automatic-braking validation [f573, f13405]. The corpus uses this example when rating heavy-off-road operator-in-simulator testing maturity as Medium to High for human factors [f965]. Although the project chronology is given, the accessible project page does not state a clear publication date; Chapter 1 therefore describes the work as approximately 2017-era [f574, f3314].

nodes.label: ACARP
nodes.text: ACARP
nodes.synopsis: ACARP appears in two distinct validation strands: the Mining3-associated C26028 framework, dated January 2021, is a shared physical-test protocol that checks object detection before Level 8 or 9 intervention, whereas the UQ/ACARP simulator work studied proximity advisory and human interfaces rather than automatic braking [f16088, f11752, f573]. The physical framework uses limited choreographed Tier 2 scenarios and omits pre-existing site controls and complex dynamic vehicle interactions; for a team starting in October 2026, preparing an ACARP-style physical-test package is considered realistic by mid-2027 [f958, f803, f851]. The simulator research concerned Australian open-cut coal operations during 2017–2019, although the accessible project page lacks a clear publication date [f3465, f574]. A richer schematic interface reduced collision risk, braking force and travel time, but benefits were smaller with fewer experienced drivers, warning against a single generic operator model [f3466, f3467, f3470]. This is the strongest haul-truck-specific human-interface-loop evidence found, yet public material does not establish real-world operator-response fidelity, and an acceptable false-alarm rate remains unresolved [f3468, f3469, f3605].

nodes.label: ISO 17757
nodes.synopsis: ISO 17757:2019 is edition 2, published in July 2019 and confirmed in 2024; it covers autonomous and semi-autonomous earth-moving and mining machine systems, including infrastructure, hardware and software [f2182, f9781, f2183]. Its “defined functional environment” provides a precedent for staged release within a limited operating domain [f606, f422]. Function-specific automation is excluded unless part of an autonomous or semi-autonomous machine system, leaving coverage of operator-driven automatic braking uncertain; Chapter 10’s assertion of direct applicability is in tension with that qualification [f2184, f2186, f8153]. The standard requires appropriate functional-safety performance for safety-related control parts and physical braking and steering tests in manual and autonomous modes under ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 [f2346, f7734]. Across chapters, the review found no established simulation-acceptance provisions or permission to substitute simulation for physical tests, but incomplete access to paid texts means this is not proof of prohibition [f3908, f8321, f8940, f7544]. Planning should therefore retain physical evidence and settle applicability early with a qualified functional-safety specialist [f8152, f15236].

nodes.label: adaptive stress testing
nodes.text: adaptive stress testing
nodes.synopsis: The booklet presents adaptive stress testing (AST) as both an option for shortening validation and a failure-discovery method within the broader falsification and adversarial-search family [f425, f6936, f14148]. AST treats test selection as optimisation toward failures; the cited Stanford work uses dynamic programming and scene decomposition, and automated-driving simulations have demonstrated searches for the most likely failure trajectories [f6835, f634, f6838]. For this program, AST and reinforcement-learning adversaries are recommended primarily for sequential multi-agent failures, with academic toolkits and in-house tools identified as typical tooling [f7255, f7259]. Their results cannot establish failure rates unless re-weighted, and their effectiveness depends on the agent and environment model [f7257, f7258]. The cited independent evidence includes on-road and aviation applications; the supplied facts do not establish heavy off-road performance or quantify validation savings [f425, f634, f7260].

nodes.label: ISO 21448
nodes.synopsis: ISO 21448:2022 (SOTIF) addresses harm from perception or performance insufficiencies without component failure, but it is a road-vehicle standard and does not apply by scope to the booklet’s heavy off-road collision-mitigation system [f15292, f2355, f12065]. The booklet nevertheless recommends borrowing its triggering-condition logic and assurance structure for perception, scenario engineering and the safety case, rather than presenting it as automatically governing the machine [f654, f12264, f15309, f8945]. Phase 0 should use these concepts when defining the ODD, hazards, scenarios and acceptance metrics; for a team starting in October 2026, a safety-case skeleton using perception concepts from ISO 21448 is considered realistic by mid-2027 [f707, f829]. The glossary explains functional insufficiencies, triggering conditions such as glare and dust, and four situation areas: known safe, known unsafe, unknown unsafe and unknown safe [f12009, f12010, f12011]. Reliance remains qualified: several chapters report that the standard, its simulation provisions and tool-acceptance rules were not verified, while the brake/perception allocation cites draft evidence and Chapter 12 labels its perception-gap reference as on-road evidence [f4336, f8942, f8155, f6580, f10339].

nodes.label: ISO/PAS 8800
nodes.text: ISO/PAS 8800
nodes.synopsis: ISO/PAS 8800:2024 was published in December 2024 and tailors ISO 26262 for AI safety in road vehicles; its stated scope is road vehicles only, with several descriptions explicitly classified as vendor or on-road evidence [f2730, f2388, f2731, f15298]. For heavy off-road validation, the booklet uses its perception and assurance concepts as reference material: a team starting in October 2026 could realistically prepare a safety-case skeleton by mid-2027 alongside ISO 21815 and ISO 19014 mappings [f12069, f829]. It also identifies ISO/PAS 8800 as a source of assurance structures and as consistent with requiring validation and estimation data to be real or physically independent of the training-data generator, although that consistency claim is labelled independent on-road evidence and expert opinion [f655, f7101, f12264]. Acceptance of machine learning in safety functions remains disputed: one view excludes it in favour of certified deterministic sensors, while another accepts ISO/PAS 8800-style assurance [f1125, f12416]. There is also a terminology tension: one table calls the publication an international standard, whereas the glossary explicitly classifies it as a Publicly Available Specification, not a full standard, and describes the wider ML standardization effort as early and mostly unfinished [f2730, f15052, f15290].

nodes.label: IEC 61496
nodes.synopsis: IEC 61496 is the IEC series for electro-sensitive protective equipment (ESPE), including light curtains and laser scanners; IEC TS 61496-5:2023 covers radar protective devices that stop a factory machine when someone enters a zone [f15018, f15277]. Together with IEC TS 62998, it provides an established certification basis for non-contact safety sensors and component-level detection capability [f1038, f12388, f15276]. Chapter 1 presents qualification under these standards as a way to shorten validation of perception-dependent safety functions [f437]. However, these are neighboring-sector factory-sensor standards, and the radar part explicitly does not consider aspects of a moving radar protective device application, limiting what certification alone establishes for mobile-machine use [f15276, f15278]. The corpus also records an unresolved choice between keeping machine learning outside the safety function and using certified deterministic sensors, or accepting machine learning through ISO/PAS 8800-style assurance [f1125].

nodes.label: IEC TS 62998
nodes.text: IEC TS 62998
nodes.synopsis: IEC TS 62998, alongside IEC 61496, provides an established certification basis for component-level detection capability in safety-rated sensors [f1038]. The glossary places these standards in the neighboring factory-safety sector and links them to demonstrating the reliability of contactless protective sensors, including light curtains, laser scanners and recently radar [f15276, f12388]. Qualifying sensors under these standards is presented as an approach to shortening validation of perception-dependent safety functions [f437]. The corpus nevertheless records a disagreement between keeping machine learning outside the safety function through certified deterministic sensing and accepting machine learning under ISO/PAS 8800-style assurance; sensor certification therefore represents one contested assurance approach, not a settled choice [f1125].

nodes.label: IEC TS 61496-5
nodes.text: IEC TS 61496-5
nodes.synopsis: IEC TS 61496-5:2023 addresses radar protective devices and gives them an established certification basis [f438, f672, f12393]. The glossary places it within the IEC 61496 series for electro-sensitive protective equipment, alongside general requirements, light curtains and laser scanners, and describes radar devices that stop a factory machine when someone enters a zone [f12389, f15277]. Both Chapter 1 and the glossary explicitly state that the radar specification does not consider aspects of a moving radar protective device application [f673, f1040, f12393, f15278]. Thus, the established certification basis should not be read as resolving the moving-application gap relevant to this validation work [f672, f673, f12393].

nodes.label: Epiroc Titan CAS
nodes.text: Epiroc Titan CAS
nodes.synopsis: Epiroc Titan CAS and CAS Interface launched in 2021 for underground loaders and trucks, providing EMESRT Level 9 slow-and-stop intervention [f1667, f1668]. Titan uses multi-technology fusion, with detection of tagged people and machines using low frequency, time-of-flight, GPS and AI cameras; everyone and every machine must be tagged [f442, f678, f1669, f1670]. The corpus presents this fusion architecture as relevant to limiting what perception alone must prove [f442]. Epiroc offers evaluation without enforcing intervention, and its Titan page recommends evaluation before enforcing Level 9, despite claiming full Level 7, 8 and 9 capability; this contrasts with South African practice pushing Level 9 mandates [f1079, f6420, f6575]. Speed, direction and operating-condition information were not found for Titan CAS and CAS Interface, leaving important evidence gaps for planning validation [f1671].

nodes.label: ISO 18497-2
nodes.synopsis: ISO 18497-2:2024 covers agricultural obstacle-protection systems, and the booklet treats the ISO 18497 family as a close cousin of heavy off-road collision mitigation and the nearest published off-road precedent for standardized perception test objects [f7188, f7190, f451]. Parts 1–4 were published in July 2024; the planning chapter reports that Parts 1, 2 and 4 replaced ISO 18497:2018 [f7187, f9763]. Part 2 starts from the premise that detection cannot work perfectly under all conditions and identifies four failure categories: failure to detect, late detection, incorrect classification and localization error [f1396, f1712]. The booklet recommends structuring the scenario catalogue around these categories alongside ISO 21815-3 risk areas, and considers the categories relevant to architectures that limit what perception must prove [f1605, f15289, f443]. Although the family includes verification methods and test objects, the review did not find a minimum-method table in Parts 1, 2 and 4; the EN adoption of Part 2 also includes an Annex ZA linking it to the Machinery Directive [f450, f9765, f1397].

nodes.label: Accident Analysis & Prevention
nodes.text: Accident Analysis & Prevention
nodes.synopsis: Accident Analysis & Prevention connects historical mining accident evidence, on-road driver behavior research, and simulation tools across the corpus. Ruff’s 2006 paper reported an average of five blind-area fatalities annually at US surface mines and quarries during 1999–2003, accounting for 12% of all fatalities; dump trucks represented 58% of equipment involved in blind-area fatal accidents [f3064, f3065, f3066]. Markkula et al.’s 2016 naturalistic rear-end emergency study found that braking responses depend on situational kinematics, arguing against a single fixed reaction time [f3495]. Road-truck FCW studies summarized in 2023 linked an 18% false alarm rate to underuse, with drivers ignoring warnings (12%) or stopping system use (11%); these findings concern on-road trucks rather than mining machines [f3332, f3333]. MineSim, published in April 2025, provides an open-source, peer-reviewed, scenario-based simulation test system and benchmark specifically for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines [f464, f15805].

nodes.synopsis: AutoDRIVE is a digital-twin framework used in an off-road braking study; Samak et al. reported at GVSETS 2024 that its open-source framework supported vision-guided AEB across 128 simulated off-road test cases on high-performance computing clusters [f15934, f467]. In 2024, the AutoDRIVE team built an off-road greensward twin from a single lidar run, presented alongside forest MLS as an example of off-road lidar surveying [f3802, f4215]. The team claims a “sub-millimeter-level accurate” twin with a reported mean of 2.28e-4 m [f3860]. That accuracy figure requires caution because it appears to measure self-consistency against the team's own point cloud rather than independent ground truth [f3861].

nodes.text: Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.1.2(b) and 8.10.2.1(b)
nodes.synopsis: South Africa's Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.1.2(b) and 8.10.2.1(b) were published on 27 February 2015 and commenced on 21 December 2022 under Notice 2908, Government Gazette 47790, with no transitional period [f1363, f2078, f612]. Their scope includes surface and underground trackless mobile machinery; for diesel-powered trackless mobile machines, they require retardation to a safe speed followed by automatic brake application if no action is taken to prevent a potential collision [f4337, f1361, f5162]. The collision-intervention system must also “fail to safe” without human intervention [f1362, f5163]. A vendor finding attributes suppliers' deployment and subsequent on-site refinement of collision-intervention systems to commencement without a transitional period, highlighting an implementation pressure rather than disagreement over the commencement date or requirements [f613, f612].

nodes.label: University of Michigan
nodes.text: University of Michigan
nodes.synopsis: University of Michigan researchers learned naturalistic driving distributions, generated more critical interactions in simulation, and used importance sampling to recover unbiased estimates for the modelled event class [f631, f1295]. The corpus reports orders-of-magnitude acceleration in on-road lane-change and car-following evaluations during 2016–2017, with 2016 factors of roughly 300–100,000 for car-following crashes and 2,000–20,000 for lane-change conflicts [f632, f1220, f1221]. These are proofs of principle for on-road automated-driving behavior, not evidence about sensor performance in adverse conditions or off-road perception failures such as quarry-wall radar multipath, occlusion and sensor-position variation [f1298, f1222, f1301]. For planning, the accelerated evaluations do not eliminate model validation or sensor and vehicle tests, and no regulator accepted a production AEB on their basis [f1299, f1300].

nodes.synopsis: The Komatsu 730E appears alongside the 860E in Wabtec’s first Level 9 validation with Komatsu, conducted in December 2021 at speeds up to 30 km/h [f817]. Chapter 2 and the glossary report that these tests demonstrated controlled deceleration; the mining case is also described as using Level 9 slow-and-stop functionality [f1345, f15781, f1832, f1833]. Chapter 1 states that Wabtec’s Level 9 Collision Awareness System covers both truck models up to 30 km/h [f1073]. For virtual-validation planning, the important limitation is that physical testing still dominated the integration stage in this case; the supplied facts do not establish a virtual-only validation precedent [f1347].

nodes.synopsis: SAE appears as a source for autonomous-tractor training data, off-road digital twins, and on-road AEB validation; its reported 50 million images conflicts with Vision Systems Design's 200 million image pairs for Deere obstacle detection [f821]. A 2026 SAE paper describes a Unity-based multimodal off-road digital twin with procedural terrain, cameras, lidar, GPS, IMU, dynamic weather and lighting, and failure annotations [f3790, f4165]. The booklet includes this simulator alongside MAVS and other examples in its assessment that procedural site generation has a strong off-road record [f3734, f4194]. In a separate SAE paper dated 27 September 2016, Salaani and colleagues used an instrumented Volvo tractor-trailer with Bendix radar and AEB for hardware-in-the-loop simulation, benchmarking physical track tests before comparing equivalent simulated scenarios [f10603, f10604]. That validation example is explicitly on-road, so the supplied facts do not establish equivalent validation results for heavy off-road machines [f10603, f10604].

nodes.label: ISO 13849
nodes.synopsis: ISO 13849 is presented as a generic machinery control-system safety standard, while ISO 19014 is the appropriate sector framework for earth-moving machines; the safety-case skeleton uses ISO 13849 or IEC 62061 where ISO 19014 does not reach [f15007, f15168, f15272]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, preparing that skeleton by mid-2027 is considered realistic; the intervention path needs a performance-level or integrity assignment and fault testing, although the relevant editions were not verified [f829, f7455]. The glossary describes risk-based Performance Level selection, common-cause-failure defenses, and four diagnostic-coverage bands: below 60%, 60–90%, 90–99%, and at least 99%; it also cautions that ISO 13849 does not itself assign the required level for the collision function [f11972, f12115, f12126, f15264]. For most markets, the booklet identifies the manufacturer's internal safety board working under ISO 19014 and ISO 13849, together with customers, as accepting the evidence [f1613, f12288]. These recommendations remain qualified: ISO 13849 was not reviewed in full text, simulation-evidence acceptance and tool-qualification rules were not verified, and the automatic-brake safety-function claim relies on draft evidence [f8942, f11198, f6580].

nodes.label: IEC 62061
nodes.synopsis: IEC 62061 is presented as a machinery control-system safety standard using the Safety Integrity Level (SIL) scale, within a general machine-safety toolkit and linked to the parent standard IEC 61508 [f15260, f15267, f15268]. The booklet recommends ISO 13849 or IEC 62061 for the intervention chain in a safety-case skeleton, specifically where ISO 19014 does not reach [f12031, f15272]. That intervention path needs a performance-level or integrity assignment and fault testing; for a team starting from zero in October 2026, the broader safety-case skeleton is considered realistic by mid-2027 [f7455, f829]. Chapter 12 and the glossary identify IEC 62061:2021 as current but not reviewed, while other chapters leave its status or edition unverified and the glossary leaves its fit as an alternative to ISO 19014 unverified [f9769, f15267, f2354, f7455, f12054].

nodes.label: PR-5A
nodes.text: PR-5A
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT’s PR-5A turns vehicle interactions into standard scenarios and provides a nine-level control model originating from a group of mining companies [f11571, f11572, f11736]. A 2019 trade article reports 24 surface vehicle-interaction scenarios; the corpus distinguishes these from 17 published surface storyboards, so the counts measure different things [f6232, f6234]. Chapter 8 identifies PR-5A as Rev 3.0, dated September 2024, citing a Wabtec white paper; EMESRT’s 2024 activity report confirms the September update but does not independently state the revision number [f5925, f6231, f6235]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, an operating-domain definition and scenario catalogue mapped to PR-5A and ISO 21815-3 risk areas is considered realistic by mid-2027, including a machine-by-scenario-by-environment-by-sensor-condition taxonomy [f831].

nodes.label: OpenSCENARIO
nodes.text: OpenSCENARIO
nodes.synopsis: OpenSCENARIO is part of the booklet’s recommended scenario catalogue and integration infrastructure, alongside OpenDRIVE and OSI; usable simulation also requires validated sensor, dynamics and friction models, site models and calibration datasets [f913, f8335, f15862]. It describes actor movement over time: XML version 1.4.0, dated 2026, supports precise synchronized maneuvers, while DSL version 2.2.0, dated March 2026, explicitly represents abstract scenarios, parameter ranges and performance indicators [f13204, f13205]. Both forms retain a road-traffic domain model, and no study was found from the listed industry and standards organizations on applying OpenSCENARIO, ISO 34502 or the UNECE New Assessment/Test Method to off-road machines [f13206, f1698]. The booklet therefore recommends OpenDRIVE only for structured haul roads, OpenUSD and OpenMATERIAL for scenes, and OpenSCENARIO export where tools require it [f13216]. Vendor support includes MathWorks, Prescan and MORAI—the latter listing OpenSCENARIO 1.x—and VTD 2025.2 added a native ScenarioEngine on 1 October 2025; compatibility establishes data exchange, not physical fidelity [f8383, f8458, f8512, f8429, f8921]. Procurement should require OpenSCENARIO, OSI, FMI and OpenUSD exports, with ownership-change exit clauses to mitigate supplier dependence [f16487, f8887].

nodes.label: OpenDRIVE
nodes.text: OpenDRIVE
nodes.synopsis: OpenDRIVE is part of the booklet’s proposed simulation integration stack, alongside OpenSCENARIO, OSI, FMI, OpenUSD and ROS 2; it also appears among the critical inputs for scene, dynamics and sensor simulation [f913, f8335, f15862]. OpenDRIVE version 1.9.0, dated May 2026, describes road networks, including lanes, lane geometry, road marks and junctions [f13201]. Its road assumptions suit structured haul roads but fit lane-free job sites poorly: dig faces, stockpiles and free terrain need additional representations, and the program needs its own job-site operating-domain taxonomy [f8337, f13202, f9361]. Accordingly, the booklet recommends OpenDRIVE only for structured haul roads, OpenUSD and OpenMATERIAL for scenes, and OpenSCENARIO exports where required; OpenUSD and general 3D asset pipelines are at least as strategically important as OpenDRIVE [f13216, f9363]. Listed implementations include MathWorks, Cadence VTD/VTDx and CARLA, but OpenDRIVE or OpenSCENARIO compatibility demonstrates data exchange rather than physical fidelity [f8383, f8986, f9011, f8921].

nodes.label: ASAM OSI
nodes.text: ASAM OSI
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OSI is an open, free messaging standard connecting environment, sensor, fusion and function models; its messages include timestamped ground truth, sensor views, sensor data and detected objects [f9214, f9217, f5260, f13219]. Across the booklet, OSI supports tool-chain integration, semantic replay and branching into closed-loop simulation, while providing a pattern for defining detected objects, warnings and brake requests before hardware selection [f8714, f13464, f5540, f13228]. OSI-compatible sensor models can transfer between simulators and be supplied as sealed intellectual-property-protecting packages; the booklet recommends OSI/OSMP FMUs using FMI 2.0 when suppliers withhold internals [f13220, f13221, f4857]. Although the glossary rates OSI and FMI as domain-neutral and transferable to off-road work, the cited OSI evidence has road-vehicle origins, so quarry deployment remains an engineering adaptation rather than off-road proof [f13224, f5507, f5262]. High-fidelity sensor extensions run from April 2025 to March 2027, leaving interface-versioning risk while the validation program integrates its first tool chain; export capabilities and ownership-change exit clauses are recommended to limit supplier dependence [f8618, f13227, f8619, f8733, f8887].

nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies South African MOSH numbers, alongside PR-5A storyboards, as the most concrete available acceptance targets for mapping the project's requirements and scenario catalog [f15610]. The MOSH regime progresses from laboratory tests to a proving ground and then to a cordoned-off area of a working mine [f13486]. Chapter 1 identifies access to MOSH specifications, ACARP and Mining3 methods, test sites, a qualified independent body, and traceability as critical inputs for shared frameworks and independent review [f1057]. Together, these facts identify acceptance references and a staged testing route, but provide no specific MOSH thresholds or evidence that the required access and review arrangements have been secured [f1057, f15610, f13486].

nodes.label: VVM
nodes.text: VVM
nodes.synopsis: VVM, the follow-on to PEGASUS, ran from July 2019 to June 2023 with a reported EUR 47 million project volume, representing a second four-year capability-building cycle in that programme family [f1205, f1292, f1549]. The booklet uses VVM and related programmes as a reference class for schedule forecasting and concludes that validation capability took years to build in every documented case; these are on-road precedents, not direct off-road evidence [f15717, f15713, f9614]. VVM developed verification and validation methods for urban Level 4 and 5 automation and sought a significant shift from real tests to simulation, but retained proving-ground and field testing [f1548, f1777]. Another account groups PEGASUS and VVM as validating methods rather than products for Level 3 and 4 cars, creating a scope tension; consortium acceptance was reported, but no approval or post-capability validation duration was reported [f1772, f1778, f1776]. Confidence is limited by consortium self-reporting despite “Independent” labels, and later chapters explicitly treat VVM as unverified and recommend checking it before reliance or review [f1294, f4336, f7701, f11276].

nodes.label: EVIDENT
nodes.text: EVIDENT
nodes.synopsis: Sweden’s EVIDENT program, associated with SAFER and Vinnova, ran from April 2022 to December 2024—about 33 months—to develop simulation credibility methods [f1206, f1553, f15710, f1459]. It researched credible virtual driver-assistance and automated-driving verification, correlation, and replacing or complementing real recordings; the VaViM/EVIDENT comparison describes literature studies, feasibility models, comparative physical tests, and validated models used alongside real tests [f1554, f15711, f1926, f1931]. The booklet uses EVIDENT and other publicly funded programs as a schedule-forecasting reference class, concluding that building validation capability, including rigorous credibility methodology, takes years [f15692, f15717, f15713, f1555]. The comparison lists a six-month pre-study capability-building period and a 33-month EVIDENT capability-building period, but marks validation time after capability became available as not applicable, leaving no separate operational validation-duration benchmark [f1927, f1928, f1930]. Funders accepted the VaViM/EVIDENT evidence, but there was no approval, so this precedent demonstrates research credibility rather than an approval outcome [f1932].

nodes.label: Sweden
nodes.text: Sweden
nodes.synopsis: Sweden’s EVIDENT program ran from April 2022 to December 2024 and focused on simulation credibility methods [f1206]. The glossary describes this as about 33 months and names SAFER and Vinnova [f15710]. Chapter 2 cites EVIDENT alongside aviation’s ACAS X and Germany’s PEGASUS and VVM as examples where reduced physical testing rested on years of prior investment in simulation and statistical tooling [f1257]. A separate Swedish program, VaViM, ran from February to August 2022 with Volvo Autonomous Solutions and Blekinge Institute of Technology, funded through Vinnova and Drive Sweden; the supplied facts do not establish its relationship to EVIDENT [f15705, f1206].

nodes.label: VaViM
nodes.text: VaViM
nodes.synopsis: VaViM was a Swedish six-month pre-study running from February to August 2022, involving Volvo Autonomous Solutions and Blekinge Institute of Technology and funded through Vinnova and Drive Sweden [f15705, f1552]. It studied virtual-model validation for autonomous vehicles in fenced areas, produced a feasibility model, and is identified as the nearest precedent for transferring on-road simulation methods to off-road machines [f15706, f1250, f15715]. The booklet describes comparative physical tests as both produced and planned, while describing side-by-side use of validated models and real tests as a conclusion, a long-term goal, and an implemented method; those differences leave the extent of implementation unclear [f1551, f1722, f1251, f1723, f1931]. Its transferable lesson is to adopt automotive-style credibility concepts without assuming automotive sensor and environment models are valid off-road [f1724, f15716]. Six months did not establish an accepted virtual-validation capability: the VaViM/EVIDENT comparison reports funder acceptance but no approval, and marks validation time after capability establishment as not applicable; the broader reference class supports planning capability development in years [f1552, f1932, f1930, f15713, f15717].

nodes.label: Honda
nodes.text: Honda
nodes.synopsis: Honda's Collision Mitigation Braking System (CMBS) is its AEB system; the booklet describes investigations of hard braking with nothing in the way as the largest documented production-fleet case of unnecessary automatic braking [f15759, f15758]. NHTSA opened PE22-003 on 21 February 2022 with 278 complaints, including six alleging collisions, and upgraded the case in April 2024 to EA24-002 with 1,294 complaints covering 2,997,604 Accord and CR-V vehicles and their hybrid variants [f1483, f1484, f1485, f1486]. In January 2025, EA25-002 added 295,125 Insight and Passport vehicles; Honda cited about 412 reports, while NHTSA reviewed 475 in total [f1488, f15764]. Honda attributed some complaints to customers misunderstanding the system or its limits, while technicians unable to reproduce faults called the behavior “normal AEB operation”—accounts the booklet places in tension with the complaint record [f1489, f10775, f1970]. The investigation remained unresolved in the booklet, secondary sources reported no recall ordered as of 2026, and crash and injury totals varied substantially between outlets, leaving both outcome and harm counts uncertain [f2015, f1490, f1487, f1961, f2023]. For off-road validation planning, the corpus recommends large sets of apparently dangerous situations that should not trigger braking and treating workshop-unreproducible complaints as early warnings during field pilots [f1992, f15772].

nodes.label: Daimler
nodes.text: Daimler
nodes.synopsis: The glossary identifies Daimler heavy trucks as one of four manufacturers represented in the booklet’s NHTSA unnecessary-braking investigation record; the detailed Daimler precedent concerns Detroit Assurance AEB in on-road trucks [f15428, f1811]. The investigation opened as PE23-010 in May 2023 after NHTSA reproduced hard braking on a steel trench plate [f1226, f1508, f1812]. NHTSA upgraded it to engineering analysis EA25-006 in October 2025, with reports of 24 crashes, 13 injuries and one fatality [f1510]. Daimler disputed whether the reproduction represented real-world risk, but NHTSA upgraded the case anyway [f1511, f1967]. The engineering analysis remained open in October 2025 and its outcome was uncertain; although the case draws on independent regulator and press evidence, what had been validated was not published, limiting its use as a validation precedent [f1814, f1962, f1815, f1811].

nodes.label: FMVSS 127
nodes.text: FMVSS 127
nodes.synopsis: FMVSS 127 is a US on-road reference for light-vehicle AEB, pedestrian AEB and forward-collision warning up to 4,536 kg GVWR; it does not apply to off-road machines [f2831]. Finalized on 9 May 2024 and amended on 26 November 2024, it identifies 1 September 2029 as the compliance date, but that date is uncertain: DOT announced amendment preparation on 23 March 2026, with a reported two-year extension not established here as enacted [f2832, f2833, f2834, f2877, f10867, f10868]. Requirements include lead-vehicle no-contact avoidance up to 62 mph, pedestrian AEB at 10–73 km/h in daylight and darkness, and detection and communication of sensor-obstruction degradation [f15420, f11691, f2000]. False-activation tests cover a steel trench plate at 80 km/h and passage between parked vehicles, failing when peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more; the booklet calls this the clearest published definition of unacceptable unnecessary braking and identifies no off-road equivalent [f15421, f15422, f15438, f15439]. Manufacturers challenged high-speed feasibility and false-activation risk through petitions and a January 2025 lawsuit, while NHTSA called the risk speculative and rejected judging compliance over multiple trials; judicial review has been held in abeyance since February 2025 [f1966, f15425, f1520]. Cost estimates also remain sharply disputed: NHTSA estimates US$354.06 million annually in 2020 dollars versus an industry estimate of US$63 billion reported through a VBOX white paper, whose characterization of both as internally consistent was seen only in a search snippet [f2886, f2888].

nodes.label: Tesla
nodes.text: Tesla
nodes.synopsis: Tesla’s on-road false-braking investigation PE22-002 opened on 16 February 2022 with 354 complaints and about 416,000 vehicles, and closed on 29 June 2026 covering 695,000 vehicles and about 25,900 reports across all sources [f11169, f1501]. Complaints described repeated rapid deceleration, typically 10–20 mph over one to three seconds at highway speed, but NHTSA identified no crashes, injuries or fatalities and made no defect finding; it concluded the events did not create lane-position changes or following-distance losses sufficient to cause a collision [f1498, f1501, f1503, f11171]. Reports declined steeply after February–March 2022 firmware updates, reaching 45 in 2024, 19 in 2025 and three by early 2026, supporting the booklet’s conclusions that software can quickly change field behavior and complaint volume alone does not establish a safety defect [f1502, f1505, f1504]. Separately, Benavides v. Tesla provides an on-road liability precedent concerning operational-design-domain and driver-monitoring choices: on 1 August 2025, a jury found Tesla 33 percent responsible and awarded about $243 million, including $200 million in punitive damages [f10505, f10685]. Source titles give either $242 million or $243 million for that award, which the booklet attributes to rounding rather than different totals [f11209].

nodes.label: Liebherr
nodes.text: Liebherr
nodes.synopsis: Liebherr’s wheel-loader automatic braking is described as reverse-only, within a broader off-road market offering reverse-only, low-speed or tag-dependent systems [f11393, f1239]. Its product descriptions focus on constrained rear and reverse interactions, not arbitrary forward and reverse movement across more than 100 site configurations [f1695]. Liebherr already logs warning events and GPS locations, providing a data path for proposed warning-fleet shadow-mode evaluation and braking validation [f1254, f1603]. However, no independent performance test or published validation method, validation duration or share of physical testing was found for the described Liebherr products; the glossary also reports no published weather limits or false-intervention rates [f1242, f1389, f11394].

nodes.label: Hexagon
nodes.text: Hexagon
nodes.synopsis: Hexagon supplies the Vehicle Intervention System for surface-mining haulage rather than acting as a machine OEM; the corpus groups its off-road braking offerings with systems limited by reverse-only operation, low speed or tag dependence [f1661, f1239]. Hexagon announced on 25 March 2026 that its current-generation system had passed University of Pretoria TRL4 verification before integrated site testing, but the release supplied no performance numbers; an earlier generation reportedly accumulated more than 10,000 working-mine test hours [f1350, f6373, f1353]. No independent performance test was found, and the vendor-reported move to 4D radar in 2024 does not independently establish radar-only adverse-environment validation or prove sensor diversity's effectiveness [f1242, f1747, f1748, f1749]. A 2026 review identifies Hexagon digital-twin platforms as operational in some tier-1 mines, but updating at operational rather than perception timescales [f3827, f3828]. Cadence acquired Hexagon's Design & Engineering business, including VTD, on 23 February 2026 for about USD 3.1 billion; the glossary records both VTD and VTDx moving to Cadence, while their documented evidence remains on-road-only and public prices were not found [f8330, f15891, f15890]. Hexagon separately spun off Octave in May 2026 [f8331, f8884].

nodes.text: Hexagon Vehicle Intervention System
nodes.synopsis: Hexagon supplies the Vehicle Intervention System for surface-mining haulage rather than acting as a machine OEM; its functions include propulsion inhibition, retarder and service braking, following-distance control and overspeed intervention [f1661, f1663]. On 25 March 2026, Hexagon announced that its current-generation system had passed the University of Pretoria’s TRL4 verification before integrated site testing, describing it as the first open-pit Level 9 system to pass that gate [f1350, f1351]. The case validated detection, tracking, warnings, diagnostics and intervention, with evidence acceptance involving an independent university gate and customers [f1843, f1848]. Its 2024 product evolution added 4D radar, with people and vehicles listed as targets; an earlier generation accumulated more than 10,000 working-mine test hours, which should not be attributed to the current generation [f1664, f1353]. Build time, TRL4 test duration, speed and direction, speed range, weather envelope and object-size specifications were not found, and the March 2026 press release provided no numbers, limiting its usefulness for quantitative timing and operating-envelope planning [f1359, f1666, f6373].

nodes.label: ISO 18497
nodes.synopsis: ISO 18497 covers automated agricultural machinery, including obstacle-detection testing, and the glossary identifies ISO 18497:2024 as the closest published cousin of the heavy off-road collision mitigation project's function [f15276, f15283]. The standard was revised in July 2024 into four parts covering design principles, obstacle protection systems, autonomous operating zones, and verification and validation; Chapter 12 specifically records publication of Parts 1, 2 and 4, replacing ISO 18497:2018 [f1393, f15284, f9763]. The corpus says ISO 18497 defines risk zones and physical test procedures but does not define how much testing may be virtual or prescribe virtual-evidence shares [f1953, f1249, f1954]. The glossary describes four detection failure categories—failure to detect, late detection, incorrect classification and localization error—reflecting the premise that no detection technology works perfectly in all conditions [f15285]. These substantive descriptions must be treated cautiously: Chapters 5, 10 and 13 say ISO 18497 details were not verified, and Chapter 5 recommends checking editions, application dates and simulation clauses before reliance [f4335, f7741, f11198].

nodes.label: ACAS X
nodes.text: ACAS X
nodes.synopsis: ACAS X is the successor to TCAS and an aviation advisory function with the pilot remaining in the loop, so it is a precedent for collision-warning logic rather than automatic braking [f1428, f1435, f15748]. Validation focused on threat-resolution logic, using simulation as primary evidence: millions of simulated encounters represented billions of flight hours, while pilot assessment and flight evaluation remained part of validation [f1907, f1432, f1571, f1911]. This capability took years to build from real radar data; the European CREME encounter model drew on twelve million flights, and a MIT Lincoln Laboratory model used nine months of radar data [f1909, f1430, f1433]. RTCA, EUROCAE and aviation authorities accepted ACAS X evidence, and its DO-385 and ED-256 minimum operational performance standards were published in October 2018 [f1912, f1429]. The booklet treats this as evidence that statistical simulation can be accepted for a safety-critical collision function, but emphasizes the prerequisite investment in encounter models and unresolved sensor-noise disagreements; the validation duration after capability became available was not found [f15756, f1257, f1910].
