nodes.label: ISO
nodes.text: ISO
nodes.synopsis: ISO publishes international standards central to heavy off-road validation, including the collision-warning and avoidance framework of ISO 21815-1, ISO 21815-3, ISO 16001 and the ISO 19014 functional-safety series; standards acquire legal significance through incorporation, harmonisation or designation, contracts, procurement, or a chosen state-of-the-art demonstration route [f15017, f7403, f2144]. As of 1 October 2026, published ISO 19014 Parts 1–4 were respectively dated 2018, 2022, 2018 and 2020, and Part 5 was ISO/TS 19014-5:2021; second editions of Parts 2 and 5 and ISO 21815-4 on swing and rotation were under publication in October 2026, so the program should re-baseline on editions actually published [f2315, f2319, f2322, f2325, f2328, f6285, f7730, f11914]. ISO permits speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition rather than prescribing one response, and its distance budget begins at detection, making reduced reliable detection range a margin that no brake model can recover [f3622, f6584, f13999]. No universal target dimensions, test counts, sufficient hours or encounters, or rule validating an entire machine family from N representative machines was found; acceptance values need a normative clause before being called ISO-mandated, and safety-relevant variants need confirmation evidence [f5410, f5447, f6683, f2636, f14457]. ISO scenario methods help establish representative virtual-test coverage, while the on-road Euro NCAP 2026 protocol requires physical-test correlation using ISO-based scores before virtual results count [f8031, f14718]. Passing conformity assessment, ISO tests and functional-safety verification nevertheless does not guarantee mine operating authorisation [f2930].

nodes.label: AVL
nodes.text: AVL
nodes.synopsis: AVL is classified as an engineering service company with vehicle models and scenario tooling, rather than a complete simulation platform; its offerings include SCENIUS, scenario-based validation and tool-chain integration [f15919, f8802, f8803]. Its off-road engineering spans agriculture, forestry, construction and mining, with GOAS demonstrated on a retrofitted tractor using lidar, radar, camera, GPS and IMU [f8687, f8800, f8805]. In April 2023, AVL coupled CARLA, VSM vehicle dynamics and a soft-soil tire model for autonomous-tractor testing, but the corpus treats this only as an integration precedent; dedicated off-road evidence for SCENIUS was not found [f8475, f9189]. AVL claims VSM model correlation of up to 97%, and appears as an integration and correlation partner in the highest-cost example tool chain [f8801, f9308]. Its regulatory-facing evidence includes a description of Euro NCAP's 2026 simulation regime requiring dossiers and spot checks, and an ASAM presentation on UNECE WP.29 NATM credibility assessment; the cited TNO collaboration evidence is mostly road automotive [f1268, f8951, f8830].

nodes.label: MathWorks
nodes.text: MathWorks
nodes.synopsis: MathWorks offers commercial MATLAB/Simulink, Offroad Autonomy Library and RoadRunner products with annual or perpetual per-product licensing; the latest release found was R2026b, the second 2026 release [f15877, f8963, f16239]. Its off-road evidence includes shipped excavator, backhoe and haul-truck examples and a Volvo CE human-in-the-loop excavator simulator, with dynamics, controller and sensor models available across the stack [f8285, f15879, f8599, f8960]. On 14 April 2026, IDIADA and MathWorks demonstrated closed-loop frontal AEB virtual-to-physical correlation for on-road cars using proving-ground tests and ISO 18571 metrics, but this did not establish a vehicle rating, and capability-building time was not found [f1761, f1762, f1271, f1763]. For heavy off-road braking, important gaps remain: high-fidelity soil deformation and sensor degradation require other models or custom work, RoadRunner needs custom work-site semantics, and independent validation of the complete automatic-braking stack was not found [f8394, f8607, f8395]. Pricing requires a quote; an unofficial January 2024 list gives indicative annual/perpetual prices of 980/3,920 for MATLAB, 1,480/5,920 for Simulink, 4,680/9,360 for RoadRunner and 3,400/13,600 for RoadRunner Scenario, all presumed US dollars rather than confirmed current prices [f8962, f16142, f16143, f16144, f16145].

nodes.label: ISO 18571
nodes.synopsis: ISO 18571 objectively rates agreement between two time signals, combining corridor, phase, magnitude and slope sub-scores into a single “ISO score”; an example comparison is measured versus simulated deceleration for the same run [f14744, f15331, f15332]. An IDIADA and MathWorks demonstration recorded on 14 April 2026 used ISO 18571 to correlate a closed-loop virtual AEB setup—virtual sensors, vehicle dynamics and controller—against production-vehicle proving-ground tests [f1269, f1762]. The glossary identifies this as the kind of correlation metric needed when simulation is presented in the Euro NCAP manner [f15341]. The cited application is on-road, and the supplied facts report neither achieved scores nor acceptance thresholds or heavy off-road validation results [f1269, f15331]. CORA is described as an older, structurally similar crash-safety rating method, but only as background rather than a method mentioned in the booklet [f14747].

nodes.label: UNECE WP.29
nodes.text: UNECE WP.29
nodes.synopsis: UNECE WP.29 is the World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations, which adopts UNECE vehicle regulations; GRVA is its working party on automated, autonomous and connected vehicles [f15391, f15389]. According to dSPACE, WP.29 added virtual testing to UN R171 at the end of 2024, while independent accounts report that its 2025 supplements to UN R152 permit virtual testing instead of some physical tests for car and van AEBS [f1276, f7546, f7682]. The adopted UN R152 text dated 28 August 2025 requires physical confirmatory tests but leaves their number to agreement between the manufacturer and authority [f7684, f7549, f15401]. A claimed 30% physical-test share in a UTAC CERAM working document and vendor commentary cannot be reconciled with that adopted text; the adopted text governs [f8188]. An AVL presentation also describes WP.29's NATM credibility assessment, but the supplied precedents and requirements concern on-road regulation and do not establish an off-road approval route [f8951, f15389, f1276, f7684].

nodes.label: UNECE GRVA
nodes.text: UNECE GRVA
nodes.synopsis: UNECE GRVA’s January 2024 document GRVA-18-55 found that the proposal to add virtual testing to UN Regulation 152 for AEB did not address every identified aspect of credible virtual-testing capability [f1279, f7144]. The corpus treats this as independent regulatory-working-group evidence that credibility requirements remained unresolved at that point, even for on-road AEB [f1280, f7145]. A draft UN Global Technical Regulation on automated driving systems, discussed at GRVA workshops in March and June 2025, builds a harmonised credibility framework covering toolchain management, requirements, verification and validation; the supplied facts do not establish that it resolves the earlier R152 gaps [f10598, f1279]. For planning, the corpus contrasts vendor claims of replacing substantial physical testing with formal sources—including GRVA—that frame simulation as complementary and require qualified models [f1971].

nodes.label: GRVA-18-55
nodes.text: GRVA-18-55
nodes.synopsis: GRVA-18-55 is a January 2024 UNECE informal document submitted by the United Kingdom, arguing that the proposal to add virtual testing to UN Regulation No. 152 for AEB did not address all aspects of credible virtual-testing capability [f1279, f7689]. Its specific concern was that the proposal appeared to require physical testing only for the final toolchain, whereas physical testing should be used and evidenced for every component [f7690]. The planning chapter describes the document as validating the toolchain against physical tests and then using it within the assessed envelope [f9746]. These accounts distinguish a general validation approach from the unresolved question of whether its component-level evidence is sufficient; the corpus also reports a November 2025 Russian Federation call for mandatory physical verification of the virtual model [f7690, f9746, f8187].

nodes.label: VMAD
nodes.text: VMAD
nodes.synopsis: VMAD stands for Validation Method for Automated Driving and is an informal group under GRVA [f15392]. It developed UNECE’s New Assessment/Test Method (NATM) framework, a finding repeated in Chapter 2 and the glossary [f1281, f15392]. The glossary places VMAD within the on-road UN vehicle-regulation structure, distinguishing WP.29 as the forum, GRVA as the working party, VMAD as the expert group and NATM as the method [f15389]. These facts establish VMAD’s role in an on-road assessment precedent, but provide no dates, implementation timelines or explicit applicability to heavy off-road machines [f1281, f15389, f15392].

nodes.label: New Assessment/Test Method (NATM)
nodes.text: New Assessment/Test Method (NATM)
nodes.synopsis: UNECE’s New Assessment/Test Method (NATM) was developed by VMAD, an informal group under GRVA [f1281, f15392]. NATM combines five evidence pillars— audit and assessment, virtual testing, track testing, real-world testing and in-service monitoring—rather than treating simulation as standalone evidence [f1282, f15407]. Chapter 6 describes its credibility assessment framework as introduced for virtual testing under UN R152, requiring evidence of accuracy, robustness, documentation, verification and validation, calibration and sensitivity analysis [f4829, f4830]. The glossary additionally identifies toolchain management, analysis and uncertainty, and requires the credibility assessment’s outcome to define the envelope in which a virtual tool may be used [f15408, f15409]. EU Implementing Regulation 2022/1426 includes an annex related to NATM and states that simulation shall not substitute for physical tests; the supplied facts concern on-road applications and do not establish applicability to heavy off-road machines [f15410, f1282, f4829].

nodes.label: TÜV SÜD
nodes.text: TÜV SÜD
nodes.synopsis: TÜV SÜD frames simulation as a complementary evidence pillar: models must be qualified, and European automated-driving regulation and ISO 34502 require the virtual platform itself to be shown fit for purpose [f1971, f1283, f1717]. It offers independent simulation and model validation, including VIVALDI-style credibility assessment; the cited work is road-regulatory but is presented as relevant to a defensible validation process [f8831, f8832, f16111]. BMW reported on 6 February 2026 that KBA recognized virtual crash tests after a TÜV SÜD audit, but did not specify a percentage reduction in physical testing [f7566, f7857]. TÜV SÜD also supplied physical-test and ground-truth engineering in PEGASUS, illustrating its role in linking simulation to physical evidence [f1583, f16112]. Separately, its September 2024 announcement that it had become the first notified body under Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 establishes that this notified-body route exists, but these facts do not establish acceptance of virtual-only validation for heavy off-road braking [f11214, f15108].

nodes.label: Europe
nodes.text: Europe
nodes.synopsis: The corpus distinguishes European machinery standards from on-road automated-driving and consumer-testing references: EN 474:2022 is a published type-C safety standard series for earth-moving machinery in Europe and Great Britain [f2717]. ISO and IEC texts provide an international baseline, whereas EN texts can carry legal weight in Europe [f15031]. TÜV SÜD summarizes current European automated-driving regulation and ISO 34502 as requiring the virtual platform itself to be demonstrated fit for purpose [f1283]. Euro NCAP’s 2026–2028 protocols and Virtual Testing v1.00 cover on-road crash avoidance, robustness and virtual testing, but are not applicable to off-road machines [f2843]. As a separate European approval precedent, new-train approval normally includes real-track measurements of stability, rail forces and ride; these facts do not establish an equivalent virtual-approval route for off-road machinery [f14673, f1283, f2843].

nodes.label: Zhao
nodes.text: Zhao
nodes.synopsis: The corpus associates Zhao with on-road research on accelerated simulation and statistical assessment of autonomous-vehicle testing [f1295, f6847, f6900]. In 2016, University of Michigan researchers Zhao, Peng and colleagues used importance sampling to make rare crash and conflict events more frequent in simulation, then statistically reweighted the results [f1295]. A 2017 IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems publication by Zhao, Huang, Peng and colleagues reported very large acceleration for lane-change conflict estimation, although no numerical acceleration factor is supplied here [f6847]. Separately, an ISSRE 2019 conservative Bayesian analysis by Zhao, Robu, Flynn, Salako and Strigini found road-testing assessments highly sensitive to the prior; the supplied facts do not establish whether this finding directly qualifies the accelerated-evaluation results [f6900, f6847].

nodes.synopsis: Foretellix spans on-road validation and off-road offerings: the vendor sells a Level-4 Mining V-Suite, and its March 2021 Volvo Autonomous Solutions partnership aimed to adapt verification for confined areas such as mines and quarries [f8626, f8625, f8692]. Its data platforms ingest logs, derive scenarios and manage regression testing, but compatibility with the eventual sensors’ raw data must be checked [f8658, f8659]. In an anonymous on-road Level 4 developer case, Foretellix reports six months of process change, scenario coverage rising from 12% to 87%, and projected development falling from about 4.5 years to under two years [f1302, f1303]. These are vendor-authored, independently unverified claims with undisclosed staffing, validation duration after capability became available, and remaining physical testing; acceptance was internal or customer-level rather than external safety acceptance [f1304, f1559, f1789, f1309, f1790]. Foretellix appears in the highest-cost example commercial tool chain for coverage-driven scenario management, and its Series C closed at USD 85 million in December 2023 [f9303, f8623].

nodes.label: Simulink
nodes.text: Simulink
nodes.synopsis: The corpus presents MATLAB/Simulink with the Offroad Autonomy Library and RoadRunner as a complete or near-complete commercial simulation platform; an on-road precedent dated 29 July 2025 used Simulink algorithms with virtual vehicles, sensors and metric-driven tests [f8346, f8373, f1335]. Off-road evidence includes shipped R2026b examples of an autonomous excavator, backhoe truck-loading and open-pit haul truck, alongside an undated Volvo Construction Equipment user story describing a real-time human-in-the-loop excavator simulator built with Simulink and Simscape [f15878, f8391]. The stack provides closed-loop articulated-steering dynamics and controller models in R2026b, explicitly supported coupling to Mevea through FMI or TCP/IP and to Unreal through the Offroad Autonomy Library, plus tightly coupled real-time targets through Speedgoat and Simulink Real-Time [f8599, f8699, f8700, f8645]. A proposed middle-cost chain combines these tools with Mevea or AGX Dynamics for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants, but RoadRunner itself does not require MATLAB or Simulink [f16162, f8385]. Licensing is annual or perpetual per product and public pricing is quote-only; the unofficial January 2024 Simulink figures of 1,480 annually and 5,920 perpetually are presumed US dollars and indicative only, not a firm budget basis [f15877, f15880, f16143].

nodes.label: University of Pretoria Vehicle Dynamics Group
nodes.text: University of Pretoria Vehicle Dynamics Group
nodes.synopsis: The University of Pretoria Vehicle Dynamics Group acts as the independent verifier for the South African mining industry's MOSH regime and has worked with mining organizations and an ISO working group [f15795, f1357, f15799]. Its methodology, described in 2020, progresses from controlled laboratory tests to interaction tests in a representative mine, using high-precision GPS as surface ground truth and combinations of lidar, cameras and automotive radar underground; it opened an underground test facility in December 2020 [f1355, f15796, f1356, f1358, f15798]. Across 189 tests, it reported pass rates of 62 percent for detection devices, 42 percent for machine-side systems and 83 percent for third-party interfaces, alongside a testing rate of 1.6 tests per week and an 18-week lead time [f15800, f15801]. The corpus identifies these as the only published independent results for automatic slow-down and stop in mining, limiting the available independent evidence base [f15802]. Its 2024 research found that conservative collision-avoidance systems suffer false-positive interventions causing production losses, increased wear and resistance to adoption, and investigated adding steering rate to collision prediction using modeled South African mining scenarios [f15803, f15804].

nodes.synopsis: Government Gazette No. 47790, Notice 2908 brought South African Mine Health and Safety sub-regulations 8.10.1.2(b) and 8.10.2.1(b) into effect on 21 December 2022, consistently reported across Chapters 2 and 3 and the glossary [f1363, f2078, f15555, f2273, f2791]. Chapter 2 and the glossary distinguish their publication or promulgation on 27 February 2015 from their later commencement, with no transitional period [f1363, f15555]. The provisions cover underground trackless mobile machine-to-pedestrian risk and machine-to-machine risk, with Chapter 3 specifying significant collision risk for the latter [f15555, f2273]. The supplied facts agree on the commencement date and instrument; they do not describe detailed compliance or acceptance requirements [f1363, f2078, f15555, f2273, f2791].

nodes.label: Minerals Council South Africa
nodes.text: Minerals Council South Africa
nodes.synopsis: The Minerals Council South Africa, through its MOSH learning hub, supplied engineering requirements and independent verification methods for Regulation 8.10, which specified what must be done but not how [f15636, f15638, f10458, f10856]. The Council funded a multi-million-rand project whose common requirements were published in January 2022; its compliance approach includes TRL4 and TRL7 verification gates and a fail-to-safe addendum rather than treating Gazette wording as a complete engineering specification [f10857, f2590, f2593]. Specific requirements include a minimum 200 m detection range, a Deutsch DT 12-pin connector with ISO/TS 21815-2 negotiation, and intervention logging at 10 Hz retained for seven days onboard and three months on a server [f2113, f2591, f2592]. DMRE data reported via the Council record 49 mining deaths in 2022, including 17 in the transport and mining category versus 16 in 2021; the narrower trade-press claim of only one TMM collision-related death in 2022 could not be verified in a primary source [f3199, f3200, f3142, f3145]. Trade press also attributes operator over-reliance concerns to a Council study on unintended consequences, but that study was not found, leaving the underlying evidence unavailable [f3445, f3446].

nodes.label: MSHA Safety Program for Surface Mobile Equipment
nodes.text: MSHA Safety Program for Surface Mobile Equipment
nodes.synopsis: MSHA’s Safety Program for Surface Mobile Equipment rule was finalized on 20 December 2023, became effective on 19 January 2024, and required compliance from 17 July 2024 [f2242, f11229]. It requires mine-specific written safety programs identifying hazards and controls, evaluation of currently available and newly emerging feasible safety technologies, and updates at least annually [f2243, f2244, f9806, f15515]. It does not mandate collision avoidance, prescribes no testing requirements, and does not mention simulation, so the corpus does not establish a regulatory requirement for simulation-based collision-avoidance validation [f2245, f2779, f9807]. The rule cites 113 surface-mobile-equipment fatalities over ten years as safety context [f3059]. The reported enforcement total is 863 citations from July 2024 through April 2026, although some passages label this figure Independent and others Expert opinion [f2088, f2246, f5844, f15517]. Chapter 13 says the rule’s status after 2024 was not verified, leaving a verification gap in tension with the reported enforcement through April 2026 [f11231, f5844].

nodes.label: Western Australia
nodes.text: Western Australia
nodes.synopsis: Two autonomous-haulage collisions in Western Australia in 2019 are presented as evidence of communications and traction failures rather than perception failures [f1371]. At Fortescue’s Christmas Creek mine, an autonomous truck reversed into a stationary truck on 11 February 2019; at BHP’s Jimblebar mine, the regulator attributed a collision to an unloaded truck losing traction in bad weather and sliding into a loaded truck’s path [f1372, f1375]. A Western Australian incident report also documents mode misunderstanding and desensitization around autonomous haul trucks, adding a human-factors concern [f10445]. The mines regulator, DMIRS, now DEMIRS, followed up the Fortescue and BHP collisions, while evidence acceptance for the Komatsu FrontRunner case is attributed to the mine operator [f15546, f1830]. The glossary says Australian state mining regulators, including Western Australia’s, do not mandate automatic braking, but explicitly notes that the booklet did not verify DMIRS/DEMIRS codes, limiting confidence in that regulatory conclusion [f15525, f15547].

nodes.label: Fortescue
nodes.text: Fortescue
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 2 reports that an autonomous truck reversed into a stationary truck at Fortescue’s Christmas Creek mine in Western Australia on 11 February 2019, placing the incident within a full-autonomy mining precedent [f1372, f1826]. Press reports suggested a possible Wi-Fi coverage dropout, and a broader summary attributed the Fortescue and BHP incidents to communications and traction failures; Fortescue’s chief executive nevertheless denied that the Christmas Creek collision resulted from failure of the autonomous system [f1373, f1532, f1374]. WA DMIRS, now DEMIRS, followed up the Fortescue and BHP collisions, including interim controls [f1378, f1533, f15546]. Despite these accounts, Chapter 13 classifies the Fortescue, Rio Tinto and BHP incidents as unverified research leads to check before the real review, creating a verification gap across chapters [f11205, f11273]. Published requirement documents from Fortescue and seven other named miners were not found, leaving a separate gap in miner-specific acceptance requirements [f2599].

nodes.label: Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC
nodes.text: Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC
nodes.synopsis: The Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC covers machinery essential requirements, with conformity assessment and harmonised standards listed as its testing and conformity provisions [f2745, f2746]. It applies to machinery placed on the market until 19 January 2027; Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 replaces it from 20 January 2027 [f2199, f2744, f15460, f15063]. The heavy off-road automatic-braking prototype therefore arrives under the new Regulation rather than the Directive [f7754]. The EN adoption of ISO 18497-2 includes an Annex ZA linking to the Directive, while in 2026 the Commission was still preparing the new Regulation’s harmonised-standards list and intended to carry over most Directive-cited standards; that intention does not establish completed carry-over [f1397, f2208].

nodes.label: ISO 34503
nodes.synopsis: ISO 34503:2023 specifies how to describe an operational design domain (ODD), using a hierarchical structure; domain definition sets testing boundaries and therefore determines what coverage means [f15315, f6706, f6782]. Its normative scope is automated road vehicles, with lanes and junctions dominating default attributes, so the booklet transfers its architecture and process to off-road validation rather than treating its content as off-road compliance evidence [f6709, f7182, f15320]. The booklet uses ISO 3450x layering and ODD taxonomy to organize off-road scenarios, but warns that off-road taxonomies remain immature; its proposed taxonomy combines ISO 34503/OpenODD with ODD-UM and EMESRT and is explicitly expert opinion [f15327, f6714]. A November 2025 agricultural ODD proposal also borrows ISO 34503 concepts, providing another example of adaptation rather than demonstrated off-road validity [f1399, f7696]. For planning, the scenario standards require coverage to reflect the ODD but focus on coverage rather than model credibility: they do not address validation against physical data or risk scaling, and establish no physical-to-virtual testing ratio [f8121, f8120, f8119, f7694].

nodes.label: arXiv
nodes.text: arXiv
nodes.synopsis: The corpus uses arXiv research across operational-domain definition, braking logic, synthetic data and simulation credibility, but publication status and applicability limit its authority: the November 2025 agricultural ODD framework is academic work rather than a standard, the 2025 crash-reconstruction braking study was not peer-reviewed, and the 2020 validation review has unclear peer-review status [f1399, f1400, f6347, f7666]. The agricultural framework borrows ISO 34503 concepts from road vehicles and reviews EMESRT PR-5A as an off-road ODD approach [f1399, f6713]. On-road braking examples include a 2023 staged warning/partial/full-braking study assuming 2.5 seconds of driver reaction time and a 2025 time-to-brake approach with activation gates intended to suppress false positives [f6186, f6187]. For simulation inputs, the corpus cites a vendor-co-authored lidar dust model compared against experiments in 2021 and LiDARDustX, covering mines and quarries, published on 28 May 2025; Duc et al.'s May 2025 on-road study found measurable real–synthetic point-cloud gaps and useful performance with a 50/50 mixture, explicitly not a transferable optimum [f6380, f7064, f7073, f7074, f7075]. The 2020 review describes CSAU and EMDAP as emphasizing scaling to address missing data while criticizing their implicit treatment of subjective evidence as a transparency weakness [f7666, f7667].

nodes.synopsis: Toyota’s SEnS+ (August 2021) uses a rear stereo camera to distinguish people from objects and slows the forklift by cutting power, rather than using the brake to decelerate and automatically stop [f15785, f1407, f15786]. This distinction limits its relevance as a precedent for automatic braking: the reported intervention is power reduction, not brake-based stopping [f1407, f15786]. In the on-road regulatory context, Toyota joined the Alliance for Automotive Innovation and Volkswagen in petitioning for reconsideration of FMVSS 127, raising false-positive risk among other concerns [f1517]. Separately, the planning chapter cites Toyota cases and modelling as evidence supporting set-based design and parallel paths, although the supplied fact does not specify those cases or modelling results [f10087].

An Army report summarizing Bekker and Wong terramechanics links tractive and braking force to soil, contact area, load and slip, and states that tracks retain more shear force than tires in soft soil [f6006, f6007]. Project Chrono lists Army organizations among its users and is presented as having off-road evidence, including deformable terrain; these user references do not fill the separately identified AEB validation-case gap [f8497, f9023, f9122, f1426]. The Army also appears as a source of planning methods: RAND developed assumption-based planning for its Force XXI work, documented in 1993 and a 2002 book, while the glossary turns this into an assumption log with vulnerable assumptions, failure signposts and hedges [f9557, f16345]. The U.S. Army Red Team Handbook is cited as documenting red-teaming practice alongside the UK Ministry of Defence handbook, whose third edition dates to 2021 [f9955, f12438, f16359].

nodes.label: TCAS
nodes.text: TCAS
nodes.synopsis: TCAS warns airline pilots of possible mid-air collisions and advises climbing or descending; it has flown on airliners for decades [f15744, f15745]. ACAS X is its replacement or successor, validated largely through simulation using statistical encounter models of near-collisions [f1428, f15744]. Both systems leave the pilot responsible for flying the maneuver, so their relevance to heavy-machine collision mitigation is as precedents for warning logic rather than automatic braking [f15748]. March 2022 RTCA SC-147 minutes recorded European results suggesting ACAS Xa induced more near mid-air collisions than TCAS, while MIT Lincoln Laboratory did not see the same disparity [f1436, f15754]. This disagreement raises questions about encounter or scenario model representativeness, with sensor noise still unassessed, and warns against relying on a single simulation toolchain [f1968, f1969].

nodes.label: NASA
nodes.text: NASA
nodes.synopsis: NASA provides both a long-horizon precedent and an assurance framework: Auto-GCAS research with AFRL and Lockheed Martin began in the early 1980s, and a 2007 NASA release reported 98 percent effectiveness [f1439, f1442]. For simulation-based decisions, NASA requires validation against the real application, uncertainty characterization, and program-defined acceptance criteria approved by technical authority; calibration alone is not validation [f11005, f7791, f12169, f14535]. Credibility is multidimensional and decision-specific, with factors rated separately on a 0–4 scale rather than added into a total; secondary descriptions of an overall lowest-factor score introduce a reporting ambiguity planners should preserve rather than silently resolve [f8018, f14580, f8193, f14587]. The booklet recommends NASA-derived lifecycle structure, credibility maps and evidence ledgers, while retaining virtual testing's hybrid role in defect discovery, scenario exploration and physical-test selection even if it cannot replace most final physical evidence by mid-2027 [f9976, f10908, f10210, f10987]. Evidence for effectiveness remains limited: NASA reports from 2015 and 2017 found assurance-case efficacy evidence mainly in case studies, while this research found no direct experimental evidence that a NASA-style lifecycle outperforms lighter industrial-machinery alternatives, no evidence of Joint Confidence Level effects on outcomes, and no verified NASA defect-cost escalation evidence [f9718, f9543, f9631, f10744].

By that integration milestone, the company credited Auto-GCAS with saving eight F-16 pilots’ lives [f1444]. nodes.synopsis: The Pretoria process is the University of Pretoria’s step-by-step method for independently verifying mining collision-avoidance systems [f15794]. The Vehicle Dynamics Group’s methodology, described in 2020, progresses from controlled laboratory tests to interaction tests in a representative mine, matching the Chapter 2 account of its progression into a mine [f15796, f1467]. It uses high-precision satellite positioning as surface ground truth and combinations of lidar, cameras and automotive radar underground [f15797]. The booklet concludes that this process leaves off-road validation far more physical than the automotive state of the art, while long queues at independent validation gates directly affect a four-month schedule; the supplied facts do not quantify those queues [f15809].

nodes.label: Honda Accord
nodes.text: Honda Accord
nodes.synopsis: NHTSA opened Preliminary Evaluation PE22-003 on 21 February 2022 after 278 complaints alleging inadvertent Honda Collision Mitigation Braking System activation, including 107 Accord and 171 CR-V complaints [f1483, f15760]. Six complaints alleged a collision, and some reported large speed changes despite nothing obstructing the vehicle’s path [f15760]. In April 2024, NHTSA upgraded the case to Engineering Analysis EA24-002, investigating false automatic braking across 2,997,604 vehicles, covering 2018–2022 Accord and Accord Hybrid and 2017–2022 CR-V and CR-V Hybrid [f1485, f10422, f15761]. nodes.label: PE22-002
nodes.synopsis: NHTSA opened Tesla PE22-002 on 16 February 2022 following 354 unexpected-braking complaints involving about 416,000 vehicles; the case concerned 2021–2022 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles [f11169, f1497]. Complainants described random, sometimes repeated highway-speed deceleration of 10–20 mph over one to three seconds, often in sunny conditions with road shadows [f1498]. By closure on 29 June 2026, the investigation covered 695,000 vehicles and about 25,900 incident reports, but identified no crashes, injuries or fatalities and ended without a defect finding or defect action [f1501, f11170, f11171, f1810]. NHTSA concluded that the events neither changed lateral lane positioning nor significantly reduced distance to following vehicles enough to cause a collision, supporting the booklet's conclusion that complaint volume alone does not establish a safety defect [f1503, f1504]. Firmware updates occurred in February and March 2022, and subsequent reports fell to 45 in 2024, 19 in 2025 and three by early 2026; the booklet presents this as evidence that software updates can quickly change the field picture [f1502, f1505]. Its usefulness as a virtual-validation planning precedent is limited: what was validated was not published, and capability-building time, validation time and remaining physical testing were not found [f1807, f1809].

nodes.label: NTSB
nodes.text: NTSB
nodes.synopsis: The corpus uses the NTSB’s 2019 investigation of the 18 March 2018 Uber crash in Tempe as an on-road precedent: pedestrian detection occurred, but classification and path prediction were not correct in time [f10694]. Chapter 2 records that factory forward collision warning and AEB were disabled; Chapter 13 adds that shared radar frequencies were one reason for disabling factory AEB, according to a secondary summary [f1528, f11255]. The investigation also identified a design that precluded emergency braking in the relevant condition and relied on operator intervention; accounts describe a one-second action suppression, with emergency recognition 1.2 seconds before impact and braking beginning only 0.2 seconds before impact [f10695, f10697, f10698, f10871, f10872]. The lessons extend beyond algorithm performance to deficient safety risk management, oversight and safety culture, but the report was an automated-vehicle investigation, not a product-liability judgment [f10696, f11270, f10699]. Source attribution varies: some details are explicitly conveyed through secondary accounts, while parallel statements present the suppression and timing directly as NTSB findings [f10697, f10698, f10871, f10872, f11255].

nodes.label: Volvo
nodes.text: Volvo
nodes.synopsis: Volvo is a precedent for a restricted first release: its published low-speed range is 3–15 km/h, and the cited vendor precedents emphasize constrained rear/reverse interactions rather than coverage of more than 100 site configurations [f1598, f1695, f10469, f10897]. Expert judgment recommends reverse-only, low-speed operation with a brief brake pulse and exclusions for stockpiles, trailer loading and slopes, but this is not a published schedule; Volvo’s 2–3-second braking explicitly alerts the operator to intervene [f1597, f10980]. Volvo’s loader remembers the last slope to avoid braking when reversing down a stockpile, illustrating both a task-specific fix and the false-stop problems created by ordinary work practices [f11520, f11872, f10728]. Its separately fitted Radar Detect system creates a commissioning dependency, and a product liability lawyer expects comparison against Volvo and other competitors as part of a state-of-the-art assessment [f10807, f11133]. An SAE paper dated 27 September 2016 provides an on-road simulation precedent using an instrumented Volvo tractor-trailer with Bendix radar and AEB [f10603]. In the 2018 Uber ATG case, Volvo’s factory collision warning and AEB were disabled; a secondary summary from 2019 attributes this partly to shared radar frequencies, raising analogous but unresolved coexistence questions for multi-OEM sites [f1528, f11255, f11256].

nodes.label: Volvo Autonomous Solutions
nodes.text: Volvo Autonomous Solutions
nodes.synopsis: Volvo Autonomous Solutions participated with Blekinge Institute of Technology in VaViM, a six-month program running from February to August 2022, funded through Vinnova and Drive Sweden to study validation of virtual models for autonomous vehicle systems in fenced areas [f1550, f1721, f15705]. nodes.synopsis: IPG Automotive's commercial CarMaker, TruckMaker and off-highway stack target construction, agriculture and mining, providing closed-loop vehicle, driver, environment and sensor simulation across MIL, SIL, HIL and vehicle-in-the-loop testing [f8436, f8437, f9239]. Cross-chapter precedents include PEGASUS using IPG simulation and a 19 May 2021 publication reporting a typical minimum simulated range of about 20–30 m for digital radar simulators; a 2024 CarMaker ultrasonic-model validation is labeled Independent on-road evidence in one passage but explicitly described as not vendor-independent because of author affiliations in another [f1578, f5306, f4575, f4576]. Independent heavy-machine automatic-braking validation, independent severe-dust/snow/glare evidence, and a same-machine public stopping-distance benchmark were not found, leaving important application-specific validation gaps [f8289, f8444, f6561]. CarMaker reached version 15.0 in 2025, but public prices and a TruckMaker-specific latest release date were not found; IPG also offers consulting and appears in the highest-cost example integration-and-correlation chain [f8441, f8442, f8806, f9308].

nodes.text: Regulation 8.10
nodes.synopsis: South Africa's Regulation 8.10 was promulgated in 2015 and is described as the strongest explicit off-road automatic-braking mandate found in the research, but an expert account says it was also suspended in 2015 because the technology was unavailable; the supplied facts do not resolve its subsequent status [f2272, f2277, f10855]. Its wording covers diesel-powered trackless mobile machines at mines where a risk assessment identifies the stipulated significant collision risk, while coverage of battery-electric machines remains unclear [f2279, f2280]. The regulation publishes no detection percentage, metres-to-object threshold, false-alarm limit or fixed stopping-distance test, consistent with a case-study account that it specified what must be done but not how [f2281, f10856]. Mines check validation and site-acceptance evidence against Regulation 8.10 and MOSH requirements, which include independent verification at two readiness gates [f1614, f12289, f15094]. The research recommends treating South African mine compliance as a design input even when South Africa is not the launch market [f2278].

nodes.label: Komatsu KomVision
nodes.text: Komatsu KomVision
nodes.synopsis: Komatsu KomVision is a human-detection and collision-mitigation product for hydraulic excavators, used in the booklet as a market precedent rather than a simulation tool; it launched on the PC200-11 in Japan in December 2019, followed by the PC200i-12 in December 2024 [f16089, f1641, f1640]. It detects people using cameras and machine learning, while radar on the -12 supports detection of people and objects; false and missed detections depend on weather and surrounding conditions [f1644, f1645]. Its emergency stop operates via the lock lever at travel or swing start, not during an ongoing swing, and the skeptic's review describes operation only at slow travel speeds or motion start [f1642, f11426, f10439]. The travel condition is described as “Low-speed travel,” but numerical speeds and detection ranges were not found, leaving its quantified operating envelope unclear [f1643]. KomVision must be switched off during trailer loading because a rapid stop can destabilize the machine, and Komatsu offered a software update to retrofit existing KomVision machines [f1646, f11427, f10983].

nodes.label: Komatsu PC200-11
nodes.text: Komatsu PC200-11
nodes.synopsis: Komatsu’s KomVision Human Detection and Collision Mitigation system began on the PC200-11 excavator in Japan, going on sale in December 2019 [f1640, f10633]. Chapter 13 distinguishes that sales date from the announcement on 30 March 2020 [f10633]. The PC200-11 provides a restricted, low-speed automatic-braking precedent, rather than evidence of unrestricted braking capability [f10974]. Chapter 2 extends the timeline to the PC200i-12, which followed in December 2024 [f1640].

nodes.label: Japan
nodes.text: Japan
nodes.synopsis: Komatsu’s KomVision Human Detection and Collision Mitigation system went on sale on the PC200-11 excavator in Japan in December 2019, was announced on 30 March 2020, and was followed by the PC200i-12 in December 2024 [f1640, f10633]. The research found no dedicated Japanese off-road automatic-braking rule or identified coverage and testing requirements, but unverified rules leave regulatory status uncertain rather than proving absence [f2308, f15593, f2813, f2871]. General construction-machinery safety provisions apply, but neither an automatic-braking mandate nor the absence of relevant AI legislation should be inferred from the research gaps [f2309, f2394]. A Japanese simulator study published in 2020 found that drivers trusting other vehicles’ AEB braked later; this suggests a possible parallel for ground crew around automatically braking machines, but remains on-road comparison evidence, not evidence about mining operators [f3423, f3462, f3463, f3457]. NIED and JARI in Japan are named alongside French and German facilities as principal ground-truth sources for weather models [f16122].

nodes.label: ISO/TC 127
nodes.text: ISO/TC 127
nodes.synopsis: ISO/TC 127 is the ISO technical committee for earth-moving machinery [f15033]. Nearly every off-road standard covered by the booklet originates from this committee, including standards for collision systems, object detection, brakes, functional safety, autonomous machines and machine definitions [f15034]. Its ISO 21815 collision-system standard covers earth-moving machines defined in ISO 6165, underground mining machines per ISO 19296, and road-construction machines [f15140]. Despite this broad standards role, the booklet found no ISO/TC 127 study applying road-vehicle simulation methods to off-road machines; Chapter 2 specifically identifies OpenSCENARIO, ISO 34502 and the UNECE New Assessment/Test Method in this evidence gap [f15035, f1698].

nodes.label: CEN/TC 151
nodes.text: CEN/TC 151

nodes.label: GMG
nodes.text: GMG
nodes.synopsis: The corpus provides no verified GMG-specific basis for planning virtual validation of off-road collision mitigation or automatic braking systems [f1698, f2602, f7748]. The precedents review found no GMG study on applying OpenSCENARIO, ISO 34502 or the UNECE New Assessment/Test Method to off-road machines; this is a search gap, not proof that such studies do not exist [f1698]. The rules and acceptance-criteria chapter reports that GMG guidelines were not verified [f2602]. The simulation-trust chapter likewise leaves GMG specifics unverified, so the supplied facts establish neither GMG acceptance criteria nor GMG conditions for trusting simulation [f2602, f7748].

nodes.label: UNECE New Assessment/Test Method
nodes.text: UNECE New Assessment/Test Method
nodes.synopsis: For road vehicles, the UNECE New Assessment/Test Method (NATM), documented in WP.29/2022/58 with guidelines WP.29/2023/44, places simulation within a multi-pillar validation approach alongside a scenario catalogue, track tests, real-world tests, audit and in-service monitoring [f1716, f9743]. The corpus identifies NATM's 2022 and 2023 work as a simulation credibility framework covering management, analysis, verification, validation and uncertainty [f7531, f9744]. The outcome of the credibility assessment defines the envelope in which a virtual tool can be used, rather than granting unrestricted use [f9745]. Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 has an annex related to this virtual-testing credibility framework [f9747]. However, no study by the listed industry and standards bodies was found applying NATM, OpenSCENARIO or ISO 34502 to off-road machines, leaving an off-road application evidence gap [f1698].

nodes.label: Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.1.2(b)
nodes.text: Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.1.2(b)
nodes.synopsis: South African regulation 8.10.1.2(b) covers underground trackless mobile machines against pedestrians; its companion 8.10.2.1(b) covers machine-to-machine collisions where significant collision risk exists, and both commenced on 21 December 2022 through Gazette No. 47790, Notice 2908 [f2273]. The skeptic’s review reports that these provisions had been suspended in 2015 because the technology was unavailable [f10724]. Their requirements combine automatic detection and effective warning with slowing a diesel-powered trackless mobile machine to a safe speed and automatically applying its brakes when no preventive action is taken; the system must also fail to safe without human intervention [f2274, f2275, f2276, f10723]. Together with MOSH performance requirements and verification, these are existing off-road provisions [f1713]. The corpus highlights a difference in emphasis: South Africa legally mandates Level 9 intervention, whereas NSW and NIOSH bowtie work favor Levels 1–6 controls such as segregation and site design, treating Levels 7–9 collision systems as backup [f3624].

nodes.label: Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.2.1(b)
nodes.text: Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.2.1(b)
nodes.synopsis: South African sub-regulation 8.10.2.1(b) covers machine-against-machine collisions where there is significant collision risk; it commenced on 21 December 2022 through Government Gazette No. 47790, Notice 2908 [f2273]. The skeptic's review reports that this provision and companion sub-regulation 8.10.1.2(b) had been suspended in 2015 because the technology was unavailable [f10724]. Together, these provisions require automatic detection and effective warning, followed by means to retard a diesel-powered trackless mobile machine to a safe speed and automatically apply its brakes if no action is taken to prevent a potential collision [f2274, f2275]. The collision-prevention system must also fail to safe without human intervention [f2276, f10723]. The precedents chapter treats these regulations, alongside MOSH performance requirements and its verification regime, as existing off-road provisions, although the supplied facts do not specify numerical acceptance thresholds [f1713].

nodes.label: RoadRunner
nodes.text: RoadRunner
nodes.synopsis: RoadRunner, Scene Builder and Scenario create and reconstruct 3D environments from GIS, maps, point clouds and recorded data, and export to CARLA, dSPACE ASM and IPG CarMaker; however, the base editor remains road-oriented and work-site semantics require custom assets and data structures [f8605, f8606, f8607]. Cross-chapter precedents include on-road UAV orthomosaic imports demonstrated in 2021 and academic South African mining collision-avoidance simulations investigating steering-rate-based collision prediction, not operational validation [f3798, f1729]. The MathWorks stack has shipped off-road examples in R2026b, including an autonomous excavator, backhoe truck loading and an open-pit haul truck, but component integration still requires calibration of material, actor, dynamics and timing semantics [f15878, f8729]. RoadRunner with Automated Driving Toolbox reconstructs and replays camera, lidar, GPS and IMU logs, with fidelity bounded by tracking and map-reconstruction accuracy [f8656, f8657]. Licensing is commercial, annual or perpetual per product, and current pricing requires a quote; an unofficial January 2024 list gives RoadRunner prices of 4,680 annually and 9,360 perpetually, presumed USD and indicative only, while academic licenses do not allow concurrent use [f8958, f9155, f16144, f8905]. RoadRunner itself does not require MATLAB or Simulink, although the proposed middle-cost engineering stack combines them with RoadRunner and other simulation tools [f8385, f9285].

nodes.label: NATM
nodes.text: NATM
nodes.synopsis: NATM is the UNECE road-vehicle assessment method whose 2022 guidelines define simulation credibility assessment across management, data and model validation, and team expertise; its frameworks require adaptation before off-road use [f15389, f7143, f5112]. Its multi-pillar approach combines credibility-assessed simulation with physical testing: virtual testing covers the operational design domain within a validated envelope, while physical tests validate the toolchain, confirm the system and remain necessary for highest-integrity claims [f1767, f7840, f7841, f10330]. NATM also includes post-release monitoring as its fifth pillar, feeding operational evidence back into the model, although the weighting of scenario-based versus mileage- or exposure-based safety arguments remains contested [f8052, f8234, f7438]. The booklet recommends an R171 Annex 5 or NATM-style credibility package and replacing TRL with M&S credibility frameworks for the validation toolchain; these frameworks suit high uncertainty and fixed deadlines but are described as largely declarative [f2648, f10031, f10027, f10029]. For planning, the credibility approach maps onto machine-model variant management, and NATM is among the recommended sources for a 2–6-page evidence, V&V and test-strategy section [f2561, f10162].

nodes.label: accelerated evaluation
nodes.text: accelerated evaluation
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends importance sampling or accelerated evaluation for rare-event evaluation, particularly small-probability estimation, while identifying the independent evidence base as on-road [f10336, f7261, f7268]. Michigan's 2016 research validated a statistical acceleration method for rare crashes and conflicts, reporting acceleration factors of 300–100,000 for car-following and 2,000–20,000 for lane changes; related 2017 published work showed very large lane-change evaluation speed-ups [f1779, f1781, f1782, f6847]. These methods deliberately oversample dangerous conditions and can estimate unbiased naturalistic rates only when likelihood ratios are known and the sampling proposal covers the failure region [f6846, f7262]. Trustworthy rates remain constrained by poorly known naturalistic distributions, high model dependence and potentially huge weight variance; the methods cannot establish high-dimensional robustness or account for unmodelled physics [f7264, f7265, f7266, f7263]. The Michigan precedent reduced simulated exposure but was research rather than a production timeline, did not eliminate model validation or sensor tests, and demonstrated academic—not regulatory acceptance of a production AEB system [f1783, f1784, f1785].

nodes.synopsis: EU acceptance of collision-mitigation systems runs through machinery conformity, and Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027, before the mid-2027 validation campaign [f2009, f10700]. The booklet identifies the EU as the most consequential jurisdiction found for machine-learning safety functions and recommends budgeting for notified-body involvement for EU sales after that date unless legal advice concludes otherwise; it separately reports a 2 August 2028 milestone for AI-specific machinery requirements under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 [f2363, f2370, f12418, f2858]. For EU sales, the booklet recommends checking standards status immediately before the 2027 declaration because the harmonized list was unfinished in 2026; EN 474 harmonization, the status of the public-road non-road-machinery proposal, and the consequences of disabling automatic braking remain unresolved [f15084, f15247, f2950, f2953].

nodes.label: North America
nodes.text: North America
nodes.synopsis: North America was included in the research’s search for collision-warning and automatic-braking standards and regulations for earth-moving, mining and construction machines, covering scope, edition, status, and performance and testing requirements [f2036]. If North America or other non-EU markets are the main targets, the skeptic’s review treats the EU Machinery Regulation and Product Liability Directive analysis as background rather than the primary legal context [f11284]. It instead identifies the MSHA, WorkSafe WA and South African Regulation 8.10 material as the primary legal context for those non-EU target markets collectively, without specifying a North America-only allocation [f11285]. Separately, the glossary states that most countries outside North America approve road vehicles against UNECE regulations; that statement concerns on-road vehicles, not the off-road machines targeted by the research [f15390, f2036].

nodes.label: United Kingdom
nodes.text: United Kingdom
nodes.synopsis: The booklet reports UK designation of the EN 474:2022 earth-moving machinery family in August 2026 as a presumption-of-conformity route, not an automatic-braking performance matrix; however, the cited 8 August notice number 0139/26 was not confirmed on gov.uk [f2718, f2220, f2221, f2222, f2875]. No UK collision-avoidance mandate or dedicated off-road rule requiring an ML-based collision-avoidance function to meet a specified ML validation standard by 2028 was found; the mandate finding is explicitly an expert-opinion planning caution, and the review did not verify the Quarries Regulations 1999 or named industry guidance [f2227, f2393, f2225, f2226]. British guidance attributes nearly a quarter of workplace-transport deaths to reversing and 40% of quarry accidents and 60% of quarry deaths to transport, while the booklet warns that differing machine and site populations explain contrasting forward-versus-reversing accident patterns [f2994, f11493, f3618]. For on-road virtual validation, the UK's January 2024 GRVA-18-55 submission challenged the credibility of proposed R152 provisions and called for physical testing evidenced for every toolchain component, rather than only the final toolchain [f7689, f7690]. The UK CCAV-funded Sim4CAMSens program ran from 2023 to 2025 [f4767]. Other UK-origin planning and assurance references include ALARP's reasonably-practicable risk-reduction duty, Def Stan 00-56 Issue 7 safety cases for UK defence systems, and PRINCE2 seventh edition (2023), organized around stages, roles and a project initiation document [f12141, f9709, f16421].

nodes.label: Australia
nodes.text: Australia
nodes.synopsis: Australia's model WHS Regulation 215 requires collision risks involving pedestrians and other mobile plant to be controlled so far as reasonably practicable, with a warning device where collision is possible; the model regulations bind only where adopted by a state or territory [f15531, f2256]. The research found no prescriptive Australian collision-avoidance mandate, but state-specific requirements were not found or verified, so compliance planning must check destination-state WHS adoption and mine legislation site by site [f2270, f7501, f7748, f15550]. Australia has adopted ISO 16001 as AS ISO 16001:2020 and published the modified AS 21815.1:2023 adoption of ISO 21815-1:2022, although its modifications were not verified; no identified off-road document allows simulation to replace a prescribed physical compliance test [f2179, f2721, f2872, f2103]. Reported collision burdens include 26% of Queensland mine and quarry fatalities during 1998–2016, 48 Queensland open-cut coal collisions and near misses from 1 January to 27 May 2017, and 30 NSW underground-coal LHD and personnel-transport collisions in the 12 months to mid-2025 [f3194, f3195, f3196]. Alarm burden can cause operators to ignore, bypass or switch off systems, while an acceptable false-alarm rate remains an open research question; Australian and South African guidance favors context-aware discrimination rather than universally alarming or aggressively suppressing alarms [f3303, f3019, f3621]. Australian ACARP work found that a schematic proximity display helped haul-truck simulator drivers reduce collision risk, and its test framework separates proving object detection from proving Level 8 or 9 intervention [f11837, f11752].

nodes.label: South America
nodes.text: South America
nodes.synopsis: The research included South America in its search for collision-warning and automatic-braking standards and regulations applicable to earth-moving, mining and construction machines [f2036]. The search sought document scope, current edition, status, and performance and testing requirements [f2036]. Chapter 3 and the glossary agree that South America has no continent-wide machinery regime; Chapter 3 adds that Brazil, Chile and Peru use national workplace and mining regulation [f2285, f15577]. These facts establish a national rather than continent-wide regulatory context, but do not identify specific national documents or acceptance requirements [f2285, f15577, f2036].

nodes.label: ISO 15998
nodes.synopsis: ISO 15998 was the former functional-safety standard for electronic machine-control systems on earth-moving machinery [f15250, f2705]. ISO 15998:2008 and its companion ISO/TS 15998-2:2012 were withdrawn on 14 June 2022 and replaced by the ISO 19014 series [f2344, f15251]. A legacy-reference tension remains: ISO 16001:2017 still cites ISO 15998 for environmental conditions, but explicitly permits ISO 19014-3 as an alternative [f2345, f15252]. Old supplier data sheets may continue citing the withdrawn standard, creating a risk in fast-moving projects; readers should treat such references as dated and request the ISO 19014 equivalent [f15257, f15253].

nodes.label: 30 CFR 77.410
nodes.synopsis: 30 CFR 77.410 is in force for US surface coal operations and requires specified mobile equipment—including loaders, forklifts, tractors, graders and trucks—to have a reverse alarm or discriminating detection [f2766, f2232, f15510]. Permitted detection technologies include infrared, ultrasonic, radar or another effective device; lidar is not named and should not be described as approved, although it could fall under the latter category [f2084, f2235, f15511]. The sensing area must give an endangered person adequate time to escape, but the rule specifies no fixed range in metres or speed [f2233, f2622, f2443]. The corpus also identifies internal audible and visual warnings, external audible warnings, and a requirement that alarms be audible above surrounding noise [f2234, f2445]. Crucially for automatic-braking validation planning, this rule does not require automatic braking [f2236, f2769].

Proposed distances of 3 ft for stopping and 5 ft for warning, proposed in 2011, were not adopted, so the regulation supplies no numeric distance for proximity-detection acceptance criteria [f2241, f2449, f15514]. The accounts are consistent across Chapter 3 and the glossary; the central planning gap is the absence of a prescribed numeric distance, not an absence of a stop-before-contact requirement [f2626, f2775, f15514].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 3 and the glossary identify ISO/IEC TS 22440 Parts 1–3 as committee drafts in 2026, rather than published specifications [f2101, f15300, f2384]. The series covers AI functional safety, with Part 1 addressing requirements, Part 2 guidance, and Part 3 examples of application [f2728, f2384]. The committee drafts were registered on 9 February 2026, and their comment period closed on 11 April 2026 [f2385]. Both locations judge publication much before 2027 or 2028 unlikely because the documents remain committee drafts; this is an uncertain forecast, not a confirmed publication schedule [f2386, f15300]. For validation planning, the corpus specifically identifies the series’ testing provisions as still draft provisions [f2729].

Both Chapter 3 and the glossary judge publication much before 2027 or 2028 unlikely, explicitly linking that uncertainty to committee-draft status [f2386, f15300]. Chapter 3 and the glossary agree that publication much before 2027 or 2028 is unlikely, but this is an uncertain forecast rather than a confirmed publication date [f2386, f15300]. nodes.label: ISO 3450
nodes.text: ISO 3450
nodes.synopsis: ISO 3450:2011, edition 4, confirmed in 2022, specifies minimum service, secondary and parking-brake performance and tests for wheeled earth-moving and rubber-tracked machines with top speeds of at least 20 km/h; purpose-built underground mining machines are outside its scope, although an annex provides modifications [f15190, f2433]. It measures stopping distance from brake-control actuation to standstill, including brake-system response but excluding operator reaction, and tests the most adverse braking configuration, including maximum specified payload for dumpers and certain other machines; controllability also matters, so stopping distance alone is insufficient [f5976, f5967, f5968, f6149]. The proposed four-month validation plan uses ISO 21815-3 CxS calculations for each machine model, supplied with ISO 3450 brake data and declared system delays, but passing ISO 3450 does not validate perception or collision-trigger logic [f2638, f2361]. ISO 3450 brake testing is physical, and the research found no provision allowing simulation to replace prescribed physical performance tests [f10431, f2475]. Its machine-performance tests do not establish statistical model transfer, and no defensible calibration-stop count was found for prediction across 100-plus site types, multiple brake architectures and all stated weather conditions [f6163, f6162]. Edition and source verification remain planning gaps: some chapters did not verify ISO 3450 details or its current edition, vendor-reported stopping formulas require checking against the standard, and the glossary says most core standards, including ISO 3450 in the listed group, are being reissued in late 2026 shortly before design freeze [f7013, f7741, f11197, f2436, f15013].

nodes.label: OSHA
nodes.text: OSHA
nodes.synopsis: OSHA rules are law rather than standards; compliance with standards does not establish compliance with law, or vice versa [f2145, f15010]. For machines with obstructed rear views, OSHA rules 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4) and 1926.602(a)(9)(ii) require a reverse alarm audible above surrounding noise or an observer, but specify neither a numeric range nor an automatic-braking mandate [f15505, f15508]. OSHA interpretation letters conditionally accept cameras that genuinely provide a clear rear view, removing the obstructed-view trigger, and radar or doppler warnings that are adequate and timely [f2229, f2230, f15506, f15507]. The glossary summarizes these as alternatives to reverse alarms, while Chapter 3 distinguishes the camera's removal of the trigger from radar's satisfaction of the warning requirement [f15072, f2229, f2230]. The research found no provision in OSHA or the other listed off-road regulatory and standards frameworks allowing simulation to replace a prescribed physical performance test, leaving virtual validation without an identified substitution route [f2103, f2475].

nodes.label: UNECE NATM
nodes.text: UNECE NATM
nodes.synopsis: UNECE NATM is an automated-driving guideline dated 2022, with a master document dated March 2023 [f8101]. It treats simulation as one pillar alongside track and real-world testing; its five-pillar structure also includes in-service monitoring [f2106, f8105]. Simulation credibility must be demonstrated for the intended scope, with risk scaling and toolchain scrutiny covering assumptions, verification, validation, and data quality [f8102, f8103, f8104]. The corpus identifies this multi-pillar structure as a useful template for off-road automatic braking validation, while emphasizing that NATM itself is on-road only [f8106]. An expert-opinion finding reports agreement among UNECE NATM and other credibility communities that validation is required, but no agreement on the metrics to use [f9357].

nodes.label: UN R131
nodes.text: UN R131
nodes.synopsis: UN R131 governs heavy-road-vehicle AEBS, including categories M2, M3, N2 and N3; it is an on-road reference, not a regulation applicable to off-road machines merely because they have automatic braking [f2516, f2814, f2514]. Its 02 series entered into force on 4 January 2023 and is identified with EU OJ L 2025/1329 [f2517, f2815]. Requirements include warning at least 0.8 seconds before emergency braking, a braking demand of at least 4 m/s², and category- and test-speed-specific impact limits—for example, 0 km/h impact against a stationary target for heavy hydraulic-brake trucks at test speeds up to 70 km/h [f2519, f2520, f2521]. Testing includes an ISO 19206-2 child pedestrian target crossing at 5 km/h, passing between stationary cars 4.5 metres apart at 50 km/h without warning or braking, and no more than 10% failed runs per robustness category; a failure warning is required within 10 seconds [f2522, f2523, f2525, f2524]. Chapter 8 and the glossary also state that conscious driver action can interrupt automatic braking, with Chapter 8 explicitly extending interruption to warnings; these provisions remain road-vehicle references rather than off-road acceptance requirements [f6323, f13962, f2814].

nodes.label: Great Britain
nodes.text: Great Britain
nodes.synopsis: Great Britain remains governed by the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, as amended, imposing general essential health and safety requirements and conformity obligations; SI 2026/867 amendments take effect on 20 January 2027 [f2216, f2218, f2217]. The 8 August 2026 notice designated the EN 474:2022 earth-moving machinery family, giving a presumption of conformity, although the booklet flags uncertainty about the notice number [f15244, f15246]. Designation does not turn EN 474 into an automatic-braking performance matrix, and the survey found no dedicated Great Britain off-road automatic-braking test regime [f15245, f2219]. Planning must account for Britain's parallel declaration path and separate standards-designation calendar, rather than assuming one declaration covers both Great Britain and Northern Ireland, where EU product law applies [f15496, f15494]. HSE's cross-industry 2025/26 figures record 126 worker deaths, including 24 from moving vehicles—the second-largest category behind falls from height at 31—but these are not earthmover-, quarry- or mine-specific figures [f3146, f3147]. Undated quarry guidance attributes 40% of accidents and 60% of deaths to transport, while the 2024/25 sources present a tension between an approximately 16% moving-vehicle fatality share and a vendor-reported 14 of 124 deaths [f3206, f3207, f3149, f3152].

nodes.label: Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008
nodes.text: Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008
nodes.synopsis: Great Britain operates under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, which govern which machines may be sold [f2126, f15489]. The regulations (SI 2008/1597), as amended, retain existing European machinery law and impose general essential health and safety requirements and conformity obligations [f15490]. Chapter 3 records designation of the EN 474:2022 family in August 2026; the glossary specifies a notice dated 8 August 2026 and explains that designation gives a presumption of conformity under the regulations [f2126, f15244]. The glossary distinguishes HSE’s workplace-safety enforcement role from the regulations’ machine-sale role and identifies UKCA as the British conformity mark that replaced CE marking after EU departure [f15489].

nodes.label: EN 474
nodes.text: EN 474
nodes.synopsis: EN 474 is presented as the European counterpart of ISO 20474: a type-C earth-moving machinery safety series whose 2022 family includes EN 474-1 and machine-specific parts [f2717, f15238, f15243]. Great Britain designated that family through a notice dated 8 August 2026, providing a presumption-of-conformity route under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, limited to the standard's scope [f15244, f15080]. Although several facts identify the notice as 0139/26, the booklet explicitly says that number was not confirmed on the gov.uk notices page [f2220, f2760, f2875]. Designation does not supply an automatic-braking test or performance matrix; braking-performance evidence must instead come from ISO 21815, ISO 19014 and the safety case [f2720, f15245, f15248]. Harmonisation of EN 474 or EN ISO 21815 under Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 remained unverified because the European Commission was still preparing the list in 2026 [f2209, f15081].

nodes.label: Australia's model WHS regulation 215 requires collision risk to be controlled so far as reasonably practicable.
nodes.text: Australia's model WHS regulation 215 requires collision risk to be controlled so far as reasonably practicable.

nodes.label: Model WHS Regulations regulation 215
nodes.text: Model WHS Regulations regulation 215
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 3 and the glossary agree that Model WHS Regulations regulation 215 requires powered mobile plant collision risks involving pedestrians and other mobile plant to be controlled so far as reasonably practicable [f2254, f15531]. A warning device is required where collision is possible [f2255, f15531]. The corpus identifies no prescribed automatic braking, test speed or distance, and reports no prescribed testing requirements, leaving these provisions without numerical validation criteria [f2257, f2784, f15532]. The regulations are model law and are in force where adopted by states and territories [f2781]. Chapter 3 identifies the June 2023 edition of “Managing the risks of plant in the workplace” as the official explanatory material for the powered mobile plant requirements [f2258, f2782].

nodes.text: Australia's AS 21815.1:2023 is a modified adoption of ISO 21815-1.

nodes.label: AS 21815.1
nodes.synopsis: AS 21815.1:2023 is described as Standards Australia's published, modified adoption of ISO 21815-1:2022, covering collision warning and avoidance on earth-moving machinery [f2259, f2721, f15027]. It carries testing requirements from ISO 21815-1 with Australian modifications, but those modifications were not found in freely accessible material and were not verified, leaving their content uncertain [f2722, f2260, f2872]. The glossary repeats that the booklet could not read the modifications, while Chapter 3 also reports that a Standards Australia catalogue entry was not located; this is a documentation gap rather than proof that the standard is unpublished [f15156, f2873, f2721]. AS 21815.1:2023 is not law unless incorporated by a regulator or a contract, a qualification also stated for the related communication-interface and object-detection standards [f2263, f15157, f15536].

nodes.text: Australia has regulator guidance from NSW and Queensland.

nodes.label: Queensland
nodes.text: Queensland
nodes.synopsis: Queensland provides mining-regulator guidance, but QGN 33 covers autonomous mobile machinery in coal mines and explicitly is not a Recognised Standard; the glossary also states that Queensland does not mandate automatic braking [f2129, f2788, f2789, f15525]. Collision risk remains prominent: collisions accounted for 26% of mineral mine and quarry fatalities during 1998–2016, 48 mobile-equipment collisions and near misses were recorded at open-cut coal mines from 1 January to 27 May 2017, and mobile plant collisions topped the reported high-potential incident list in 2024 [f3103, f3106, f3006]. These reports do not establish complete incident frequencies, because near misses are under-reported and that under-reporting distorts frequency estimates [f3049, f3650]. Queensland's illustrative two-second combined operator-reaction and mechanical delay represents 22.2 metres at 40 km/h before braking distance is added, not a measured operator reaction time or validated reaction-time percentile [f3220, f3313, f3475]. Its guidance calls for worst-case stopping assumptions, scenario-by-scenario assessment, and confirmed operator communication for approaching authorized pedestrians [f3403, f3603, f3365]. Validation must also address object discrimination, traffic context, poor visibility, electronic interference and deliberate operator interference; idealised detection zones can create false confidence, while regulator material indicates that false alarms remain an unresolved problem [f3362, f3233, f3375, f3376, f5753, f15551].

nodes.label: Brazil has general mining safety rules under NR-22 and NR-12.
nodes.text: Brazil has general mining safety rules under NR-22 and NR-12.
nodes.quote: Brazil (NR-22, NR-12), Chile (DS 132) and Peru (DS 024-2016-EM) have general mining safety rules

nodes.label: Brazil
nodes.text: Brazil
nodes.synopsis: Brazil uses national workplace and mining regulation rather than a continent-wide South American machinery regime; NR-22 and NR-12 provide general mining, machinery, brake and operating requirements [f2285, f2130, f2288, f15579]. NR-22 covers occupational safety and health in mining and was last modified by Portaria MTE 105 on 29 January 2026, while NR-12 addresses machinery safety [f2286, f2287, f15578, f2796]. The reviewed Brazilian NR-22 and NR-12 text yielded no automatic-braking mandate, specifically no ISO 21815-style mandate prescribing target or speed tests [f2799, f2289, f15580]. These regulatory gaps mean “not found,” not “not required,” so the booklet does not establish an exemption from numeric acceptance requirements [f2297, f15586]. It also found no dedicated Brazilian off-road rule requiring an ML-based collision-avoidance function to meet a specified ML validation standard by 2028 [f2393].

nodes.label: NR-22
nodes.text: NR-22
nodes.synopsis: Brazil’s NR-22 covers occupational safety and health in mining, alongside NR-12’s machinery safety role [f15578, f15579, f2797]. NR-22 was last modified on 29 January 2026, with Chapter 3 identifying the modifying instrument as Portaria MTE 105 [f2286, f2796]. Together, NR-22 and NR-12 establish general machine, mining, brake and operating requirements [f15579, f2288, f2798]. However, the reviewed Brazilian texts yielded no automatic-braking mandate, specifically no ISO 21815-style mandate with prescribed target or speed tests; this is a review finding rather than evidence that general brake requirements are absent [f2289, f2799, f2798].

nodes.label: NR-12
nodes.text: NR-12
nodes.synopsis: NR-12 is Brazil’s machinery safety regulation; together with NR-22, it covers general mining and machinery occupational safety [f2287, f2797, f15579]. The two regulations set general machine, mining, brake and operating requirements, a scope repeated in the glossary [f2288, f2798, f15579]. Chapter 3 reports that no automatic-braking mandate was found, specifically no ISO 21815-style mandate prescribing target or speed tests in the reviewed Brazilian text [f2799, f2289]. The corpus therefore identifies general safety and braking requirements, but does not establish a prescribed automatic-braking test regime under these regulations [f2288, f2289].

nodes.label: Peru
nodes.text: Peru
nodes.synopsis: Peru uses national workplace and mining regulation rather than a continent-wide South American machinery regime [f2285]. Its DS 024-2016-EM is in force and provides a general mining occupational safety and mobile-equipment risk framework [f2803, f2132, f2294, f15584]. The reviewed material did not reveal a dedicated collision-braking acceptance regime; this is a finding about the review, not proof that such requirements do not exist [f2295, f15585, f2297, f15586]. Numeric acceptance items are explicitly reported as “not found,” not “not required,” for Peru and the other named South American countries [f2297, f15586]. The booklet also found no dedicated off-road rule in Peru requiring an ML-based collision-avoidance function to meet a specified ML validation standard by 2028 [f2393].

nodes.label: DS 024-2016-EM
nodes.synopsis: Peru's DS 024-2016-EM is a mining occupational safety regulation providing general mining safety rules and a mobile-equipment risk framework [f2132, f2294, f15584]. Chapter 3 reports that no dedicated collision-braking acceptance regime was found in the reviewed material, and the glossary repeats that finding [f2295, f15585]. The corpus therefore identifies a general safety framework but leaves collision-braking acceptance criteria unresolved; the finding is limited to the material reviewed, not proof that no such regime exists [f2294, f2295].

nodes.label: India
nodes.text: India
nodes.synopsis: India’s DGMS circulars use Coal Mines Regulations 2017 regulation 216(2) as their regulatory hook; Circular No. 03 of 2024, dated 21 August 2024, calls for proximity-warning or anti-collision devices on wheeled trackless transportation machinery in opencast coal mines [f2301, f2302, f15587]. A 2025 technical circular calls for fail-safe braking before relevant tippers are deployed, while a 2025 Springer article cites an Indian circular setting a maximum speed of 30 km/h [f2303, f2455, f2304]. These are official guidance and enforcement materials, not evidence of a universal automatic-braking requirement for Indian construction machines; the regional survey found a hard automatic-braking mandate only in South Africa [f2306, f15073]. For planning, DGMS expectations form a site-specific acceptance gate beyond market-access validation and OEM testing, so collision mitigation should be configurable to meet those expectations [f2931, f2594, f15597]. Confidence in the circular details is low because the booklet relied on secondary summaries; it found neither a standardised national mine-interaction test matrix nor a dedicated off-road rule requiring a specified ML validation standard by 2028 [f2307, f2453, f2393].
