nodes.label: China
nodes.text: China
nodes.synopsis: The booklet reports that China's Coal Mine Safety Regulations require underground trackless rubber-tired vehicles moving in the same direction to maintain at least 50 m separation, citing a July 2023 article in Meikuang Anquan rather than a review of the regulatory text [f2298, f2299, f15591]. It identifies this distance as the nearest off-road relative of its on-road headway test distances and recommends configurable collision mitigation that can meet China's following-distance expectation [f13890, f15597]. A dedicated, verified Chinese national automatic-braking acceptance rule was not found, and Chinese GB or GB/T adoptions of ISO 21815, ISO 16001, ISO 17757 and ISO 19014 were not established; these are evidence gaps, not proof that relevant standards do not exist [f2300, f15592]. Likewise, the absence finding for ML-based off-road collision-avoidance rules does not establish an absence of AI legislation in China [f2394]. Separately, China conditionally approved Synopsys's acquisition of Ansys with stipulations on customer contracts [f8879].

nodes.label: Coal Mine Safety Regulations
nodes.text: Coal Mine Safety Regulations
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 3 and the glossary report that China's Coal Mine Safety Regulations require underground trackless rubber-tired vehicles traveling in the same direction to maintain at least 50 m separation [f2298, f15591]. The cited source is a peer-reviewed article in Meikuang Anquan published in July 2023, rather than the regulation text itself [f2298, f2299]. Chapter 3 reports that the regulations are in force and cover underground trackless vehicle operation, but both findings rely on academic reporting without direct review of the regulatory text [f2810, f2811]. The 50 m requirement is consistently repeated across the supplied facts; the key gap is primary-source verification, not a conflicting distance [f2135, f2612, f2812, f15591, f2299].

nodes.label: Korea
nodes.text: Korea
nodes.synopsis: The booklet did not verify Korea’s national off-road automatic-braking rules, a gap stated in Chapter 3 and repeated in the glossary [f2310, f15595]. Its broader regulatory review likewise reports that relevant or dedicated rules for Korea were not found or not verified, and that no coverage or testing requirements were identified [f2136, f2813]. Korea’s regulatory status therefore remains uncertain in this research; these findings do not establish that no rules exist [f2871, f2813].

nodes.label: Indonesia
nodes.text: Indonesia
nodes.synopsis: The research did not verify Indonesia’s national off-road automatic-braking rules, a gap repeated in the glossary [f2310, f15595]. Chapter 3 also reports that dedicated off-road automatic-braking rules were not found or not verified, and that no coverage or testing requirements were identified for Indonesia and five other countries [f2813]. Indonesia’s regulatory status therefore remains uncertain in the booklet; the findings establish a verification gap rather than confirming that no rules exist [f2136, f2871].

nodes.label: Canada
nodes.text: Canada
nodes.synopsis: The booklet describes Canadian mining and workplace requirements as provincial, while the glossary identifies CSA M424 as the relevant national standard [f2251, f15525]. No single Canadian federal collision-avoidance or automatic-braking rule was found; this is a research gap, not confirmation that no applicable requirements exist [f2250, f15526, f2871]. Canadian provincial regulations and CSA M424 were not verified, and the research identified no dedicated off-road automatic-braking coverage or testing requirements for Canada [f2252, f15528, f2813]. Before claiming Canadian compliance, the booklet recommends completing a province-by-province market-release requirements matrix [f2253, f15529].

nodes.label: ISO 6165
nodes.text: ISO 6165
nodes.synopsis: ISO 6165 is a vocabulary and classification standard defining earth-moving machinery, including loaders, excavators, dozers, dumpers and graders; ISO 20474 and EN 474 provide general safety requirements for those machines [f15238, f15239]. For ISO 6165 machines, ISO 16001:2017 addresses object detection and visibility aids rather than braking, while a collision-avoidance function that commands brakes falls within the ISO 19014 functional-safety scope [f2180, f15207, f2312]. ISO 19014 is the sector-specific framework, and ISO 13849 does not itself assign the collision function's required Performance Level [f2196, f15264]. Scope must nevertheless be checked carefully: the glossary presents ISO 6165 inclusion as determining applicability of three standards, but Chapter 3 explicitly extends ISO 21815-1:2022 to underground mining machinery under ISO 19296 and road-construction machinery under ISO 22242 [f15240, f2149]. Projects spanning surface and underground machines should therefore assess applicability machine by machine; outside ISO 6165, ISO 19014 should not be assumed to apply, and ISO 19296 or generic standards may apply by contract or jurisdiction [f15249, f15234, f2353].

nodes.label: ISO 19296
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19296:2018 is a published international standard for underground mobile mining machine safety, providing general safety and foreseeable-misuse requirements [f2712, f2191, f15231]. It is not a stand-alone collision-avoidance performance protocol, so its general safety role should not be confused with collision-avoidance performance acceptance [f2193, f15233]. ISO 21815-1:2022 uses ISO 19296 to identify underground mining machines within its scope, while ISO 21815-3:2023 normatively references it alongside ISO 3450 for brakes [f2149, f15232, f2166]. For mining machines outside ISO 6165, the glossary cautions against assuming ISO 19014 applies and says ISO 19296 and generic standards may apply by contract or jurisdiction; applicability therefore remains machine- and context-dependent [f15234].

nodes.label: ISO 10265
nodes.synopsis: ISO 10265:2008 is identified as the brake-performance and testing standard for crawler machines at 20 km/h or less, distinct from ISO 3450 for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines; it was confirmed in 2025 [f5979, f13728, f15189, f5980]. Stopping performance is measured from brake-control actuation to standstill, including system response but excluding operator reaction, with prescribed payload and adverse test configurations [f6540]. ISO 17757 uses physical braking and steering tests in manual and autonomous modes under ISO 3450 and ISO 10265, and the booklet found no simulation wording in those brake standards [f7734, f15197]. These are machine-performance standards rather than statistical model-transfer standards, and they provide no defensible calibration-stop count guaranteeing braking predictions across 100-plus site types, brake architectures and weather conditions [f6163, f6162, f15198]. There is an unresolved evidence tension: later chapters and the glossary make specific scope and testing claims, while Chapters 3 and 13 say ISO 10265 was not verified in the research [f2197, f11197, f5979, f7734, f15192].

nodes.label: ISO 5006
nodes.text: ISO 5006
nodes.synopsis: ISO 5006 is described as defining how to measure the machine operator’s field of view from the cab and map blind areas, distinct from ISO 16001’s requirements and tests for detection and visibility aids [f11547, f15204, f15219]. Chapter 7 uses ISO 5006 and ISO 16001 visibility-type methods to illustrate geometric computation of machine coverage and blind zones, with expert opinion supporting this approach [f5602, f5604]. The glossary proposes reproducing these methods, alongside UN R159’s small-cylinder method, in a digital twin of each machine to compute coverage and blind zones before hardware arrives [f11549, f15220]. However, Chapter 3 reports that ISO 5006 was not verified and evidence was not found, a gap repeated in the glossary; the proposed use therefore should not be mistaken for verified application of the standard [f2197, f15219, f15220].

nodes.label: EU 2022/1426
nodes.synopsis: EU Implementing Regulation 2022/1426 covers automated-driving-system type approval for fully automated road vehicles, not off-road machines; Chapter 10 nevertheless identifies its credibility framework as functionally relevant to off-road automatic braking [f7672, f2214, f8100]. The regulation is dated 5 August 2022, entered into force on 15 September 2022, and is cited in a consolidated version dated 24 March 2026 [f7671]. Annex III Part 4 requires documented model validation, manufacturer-defined acceptance thresholds, ODD-representative data, criticality assessment, characterized variability, and a defined envelope for using the virtual tool; evidence of team competence is also required [f7673, f7674, f7810, f10594, f10596]. Physical tests validate the toolchain and confirm the system, and Part 3 explicitly states that simulation shall not substitute for physical tests, qualifying Chapter 13's language about simulation replacing physical evidence [f7840, f10597, f10473]. Planning guidance recommends an early, two-page credibility-plan dry run against Annex III Part 4 to expose missing elements [f16536, f10922]. There is a cross-chapter scope tension: Chapter 3 says the regulation's contents were not reviewed, whereas later chapters provide detailed requirements and planning uses [f2214, f7674, f10922].

nodes.synopsis: The UK regulatory review did not verify HSE, CPA, Strategic Forum or MPA guidance, leaving a verification gap despite Chapter 4's use of HSE statistics and guidance [f2226, f3204, f3205, f3206, f3207]. For 2025/26, HSE recorded 126 worker deaths across Great Britain; moving vehicles caused 24 deaths, the second-largest category after falls from height at 31, but these figures are not specific to mines, quarries or construction earthmovers [f3146, f3147]. Historical figures require reconciliation: the 2024/25 HSE release gives moving vehicles about 16% of fatal injuries and a preceding five-year average of around 21 deaths annually, whereas a vendor summary reports 14 of 124 deaths for 2024/25; the 2023/24 figures were 25 of 138 [f3149, f3150, f3152, f3151]. HSE's cross-industry guidance attributes nearly a quarter of workplace-transport deaths to reversing and notes costly damage from many reversing accidents without injuries [f3153, f3154]. Its undated quarry guidance attributes 40% of accidents and 60% of deaths to transport and states that seat belts would prevent 25% of all fatal quarry accidents; the lack of a date limits temporal interpretation [f3155, f3156, f3157].

nodes.label: 30 CFR 56.14132
nodes.synopsis: 30 CFR 56.14132 and 57.14132 are in force for US metal and non-metal mines and cover horns and backup alarms [f2770, f2771]. For self-propelled mobile equipment with an obstructed rear view, they require a reverse-activated alarm, specified alternatives, or an observer; the glossary restates this requirement without the equipment and rear-view qualifications [f2237, f15512]. Reverse alarms must be audible above surrounding noise [f2238, f2772]. These provisions do not require automatic braking, so their alarm requirements should not be treated as an automatic-braking mandate [f2773].

nodes.label: 30 CFR 57.14132
nodes.synopsis: 30 CFR 57.14132, discussed alongside 56.14132, is in force for US metal and non-metal mines and covers horns and backup alarms, including alternatives or an observer [f2770, f2771]. Chapter 3 specifies that self-propelled mobile equipment with an obstructed rear view requires a reverse-activated alarm, specified alternatives, or an observer; the glossary restates this requirement without the equipment and visibility qualifications [f2237, f15512]. Reverse alarms must be audible above surrounding noise [f2238, f2772]. These provisions do not require automatic braking, so the cited rules establish alarm-related requirements rather than an automatic-braking mandate [f2773].

nodes.label: NSW Resources Regulator
nodes.text: NSW Resources Regulator
nodes.synopsis: The NSW Resources Regulator’s guidance addresses vehicle interaction controls in mines in New South Wales, Australia [f2786]. Its materials include a July 2022 compliance priorities report on proximity awareness and collision avoidance in open-cut coal, a September 2023 discussion paper, a draft Technical Reference Guide, and a May 2025 fact sheet on collisions involving remote-controlled equipment [f2266, f2264, f2785, f2267]. However, the guidance prescribes no testing requirements, and the Technical Reference Guide remains a draft, leaving a gap for validation planning [f2787]. The regulator recorded 30 LHD and personnel-transport collisions in NSW underground coal mining in the 12 months to mid-2025 [f3196]. It also reported in 2023 that collision technology was viewed as a “silver bullet,” raising concern about over-reliance rather than establishing that technology alone resolves collision risk [f3417].

nodes.label: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
nodes.text: Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996
nodes.synopsis: South Africa’s Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996 is the governing mining law, administered by the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy, since renamed the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources; its Regulations Chapter 8 covers machinery and Regulation 8.10 covers trackless mobile machinery (TMM) [f15553, f15554]. Regulation 8.10 was promulgated on 27 February 2015, while critical sub-regulations addressing underground machine-to-pedestrian and machine-to-machine risks commenced on 21 December 2022 under Gazette No. 47790, Notice 2908, with no transitional period [f2272, f15555]. These provisions require diesel-powered TMMs to detect and warn automatically and, if a potential collision is not prevented, slow to a safe speed and then brake automatically; the system must also fail to safe without human intervention [f15556, f15557]. The law specifies no detection percentage, detection distance, false-alarm limit or stopping test, so MOSH specifications and independent testing supply numerical requirements; South Africa was the only country the booklet found with such a legal mandate [f15558, f15552]. Whether the regulations’ “diesel powered” wording includes battery-electric mining machines remains unclear [f15559].

nodes.label: Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA)
nodes.text: Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA)
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19014-1 provides Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA) to identify safety-related parts of the control system and determine their required Machine Performance Level, MPLr; the glossary explicitly places this method in earth-moving machinery [f2314, f12036, f11973, f15170]. MPLr is assigned through hazard and risk analysis, and design evaluation must demonstrate an achieved level, MPLa, at least as high as MPLr [f15169]. ISO 19014-5 offers MPLr tables for common machine functions, allowing manufacturers to avoid a full MCSSA for each new model when the tables' use cases and assumptions hold, thereby reducing the per-model assessment burden [f2332, f12040, f15174]. The supplied facts consistently describe this conditional shortcut but do not specify the table assumptions or particular MPLr values [f2332, f12040, f15174].

nodes.label: IEC 61508
nodes.synopsis: IEC 61508 is described as the seven-part parent standard for electrical, electronic and programmable safety systems across industries, defining functional safety through correct responses to inputs and faults [f15268, f11991]. Its Safety Integrity Levels range from SIL 1 to SIL 4; for frequently acting functions, SIL 1 permits a dangerous-failure probability band of one per 100,000 to one per million hours [f12050, f12051]. Chapter 10 presents proven in use as a compliance route for reused elements, requiring identical or highly similar elements and use conditions plus justified service history; the glossary adds sufficiently few failures to support a statistical claim [f7933, f7934, f12351]. IEC 61508 practice reportedly demands higher confidence than the 70% used in the ISO 26262 formula, but proven in use does not validate a simulator, and adding automatic braking changes the item relative to the fielded warning system [f7936, f14926]. For planning, IEC 61508 remains an alternative whose status and fit were not verified, and neither its off-line tool classes T1–T3 nor its proven-in-use provisions were verified in detail [f2354, f12054, f10544, f15271].

nodes.label: ISO 25119
nodes.synopsis: ISO 25119 is presented as the functional-safety standard for control systems on tractors and farm machinery, an agricultural counterpart to ISO 13849 and ISO 19014 that descends from IEC 61508 [f15330, f15339, f15268]. The booklet identifies it as a possible alternative to ISO 19014, but its fit for the heavy off-road program was not verified; applicability through a contract remains only a possibility [f2354, f12054, f15343]. Planning and glossary entries describe its editions as current but not reviewed, while other chapters report that current versions, dates, simulation clauses, and tool-qualification or simulation-evidence acceptance rules were not verified [f9785, f15340, f4335, f5111, f7741, f8942]. Chapter 6 states that ISO 25119 and other off-road standards do not define simulation-credibility acceptance, but that conclusion is in tension with the repeated lack of verification of simulation provisions; those provisions should therefore be checked before reliance [f5110, f7741, f8942, f4335].

nodes.synopsis: The Official Journal serves as the publication venue for EU legislation and for Commission references to harmonized standards developed by CEN and CENELEC [f2372, f15077]. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, was adopted on 8 July 2026, published on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026; Chapter 3 attributes the publication date to law-firm summaries [f9796, f2372]. However, the detailed Digital Omnibus machinery provisions, including the AI Act machinery carve-out and delegated-act mechanism, rely on secondary summaries rather than reviewed Official Journal text [f9801, f10309]. The cited Annex I items of Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 were also not reviewed in the Official Journal, leaving a separate primary-source verification gap for planning [f9795].

nodes.label: ISO 26262-8
nodes.synopsis: The booklet uses ISO 26262-8 as on-road reference material for software-tool confidence and qualification under clause 11 and proven in use under clause 14; simulation-tool confidence is also linked to ISO 19014-4 software verification and validation [f12067, f15296, f8035]. Its evidential footing is limited: the 2018 clauses were confirmed only through tables of contents and secondary sources, and the skeptic’s review says ISO 26262-8 was not verified in the research [f7703, f7704, f11196]. Proven in use is a route for claiming compliance for a reused element, not for validating a simulator, and requires identical or highly similar components and use conditions plus sufficient service history with few enough failures to support a statistical claim [f7933, f7579, f12351]. The glossary reports a 70 percent confidence level and explicitly rejects carrying the warning system’s history over to automatic braking because braking changes the item [f15297, f14926]. Planning guidance recommends a 1–1.5-page credibility and tool-qualification section using ISO 26262-8 alongside 7009B and V&V 40, while vendor descriptions of ISO/PAS 8800:2024 tailoring Part 8 for AI remain restricted to road vehicles [f10164, f2388].

nodes.label: ISO 13766
nodes.synopsis: ISO 13766 is the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) standard for earth-moving machinery [f15250]. Chapter 3 specifies that ISO 16001:2017 requires EMC compliance with ISO 13766, a requirement repeated in the glossary for object detection systems on earth-moving machines [f2414, f13023, f15255, f15215]. The glossary explains this as a two-way requirement: electronics must neither emit radio interference that disturbs other equipment nor be disturbed by external interference [f15254]. nodes.synopsis: South Africa Regulation 8.10 requires automatic detection and warning, followed by retardation to a safe speed if the operator does not act, then automatic braking with fail-to-safe behaviour; its test objects include pedestrians and other diesel trackless mobile machines [f2441, f2439, f11182]. The reviewed passages provide no universal distance or speed threshold, stopping-margin value or deceleration curve, consistent with the glossary's statement that the regulation supplies no numerical requirements [f2440, f2611, f2442, f15637]. The Minerals Council describes the regulation as stating what must be done rather than how, and its MOSH programme developed surface collision-prevention performance requirements, a verification regime and independent test specifications to fill that engineering gap [f10458, f15638]. Expert-opinion commentary reports suspension in 2015 because technology was unavailable, while a separate fact records commencement on 21 December 2022 [f10457, f11183, f11184]. Interoperability with collision systems already deployed at customer sites, including legally mandated systems, remains a stated concern [f10513].

nodes.label: ISO score
nodes.text: ISO score
nodes.synopsis: ISO 18571 combines corridor, phase, magnitude and slope sub-scores into a single number often called the “ISO score” [f15332]. Euro NCAP’s on-road virtual-testing protocol requires manufacturers to qualify simulation in-house against physical tests using the ISO score and defined KPIs calculated with Euro NCAP scripts [f15333, f2496]. This qualification sits within a broader submission process covering model dossiers and color-coded predictions for the whole scenario grid [f15447]. Several ISO-score and KPI tolerances remain bracketed and require confirmation, so they should not be adopted as final thresholds in an off-road acceptance specification [f2502, f2503].

nodes.synopsis: NHTSA’s New Car Assessment Program provides consumer ratings using AEB tests at 40–80 km/h; its test values are consumer-assessment values, not law [f15430, f2541]. It does not regulate a quarry loader, haul truck, excavator or dozer merely because that machine has automatic braking [f2514]. Stationary and moving lead-vehicle tests begin at 40 km/h and increase in 10 km/h steps to 80 km/h while no contact occurs; contact ends the series [f2539]. The lead-vehicle-decelerating test family uses headways of 12–40 m and target decelerations of 0.3–0.5 g [f2540]. The final decision notice was signed in November 2024 and appeared in the Federal Register on 3 December 2024 [f2538].

UN R131 requires a child pedestrian target conforming to ISO 19206-2 and crossing at 5 km/h; the glossary identifies heavy trucks as the application and separately attributes the target requirement to the 02 series [f2522, f15120, f15397]. These facts establish on-road target requirements, but do not establish their applicability to heavy off-road machines [f2522, f2546, f15120, f15397].

nodes.label: ISO 19206
nodes.synopsis: ISO 19206 specifies standardized surrogate targets for road-vehicle crash-avoidance testing, including pedestrian, bicycle and vehicle targets [f13499, f15312]. Euro NCAP’s 2026–2028 protocols and Virtual Testing v1.00 cover ISO 19206 targets; the 2026 protocols contain more than 1,200 scenarios and use these targets [f2846, f15445]. The corpus identifies standardized targets as a precondition for comparable tests, but reports that no off-road equivalent of ISO 19206 exists [f15328, f15329]. Chapter 3 therefore recommends transferring the family’s target-design principle rather than copying its on-road targets; off-road surrogates must represent people in protective clothing, light vehicles under a haul truck’s nose, machines and fixed obstacles [f2554, f15325].

nodes.label: EMESRT PR-5A Vehicle Interaction Systems
nodes.text: EMESRT PR-5A Vehicle Interaction Systems
nodes.synopsis: EMESRT PR-5A addresses vehicle–person collisions and provides the sector-specific scenario list and control vocabulary used by mining customers [f15598, f15609]. Its revision history runs from Rev 1.0 in April 2016 through Rev 2.0 in August 2019 to Rev 3.0 in September 2024; the glossary attributes the latest revision date to a vendor white paper [f2581, f15602]. The nine-layer model places operator awareness at Level 7, warnings at Level 8, and intervention to slow or stop the machine at Level 9, motivating validation that also considers roadway design, segregation, procedures, and advisory controls [f2582, f15604, f15611]. Surface interaction scenarios are presented as storyboards covering road encounters, junctions, congested areas, and light–heavy vehicle interactions; the booklet maps project requirements and scenarios to these storyboards and South African MOSH numbers as concrete acceptance targets [f15606, f15610]. Scenario counts remain unresolved: a search snippet gives 24, while the glossary records 24 in a 2019 trade article versus 17 published surface storyboards in EMESRT's 2024 Activity Report [f2584, f15607]. An agricultural research paper also treats PR-5A as a replicable model for operational design domain definition and validation [f15608].

nodes.label: EU

nodes.synopsis: The EU Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC applies until 19 January 2027, and Machinery Regulation 2023/1230, adopted on 14 June 2023, applies from 20 January 2027 [f2744, f2747]. For products sold in the EU after 20 January 2027 whose safety function is performed by machine learning, expert advice is to plan for notified-body engagement under Annex I Part A unless legal advice concludes otherwise [f2643]. For those products, expert advice also anticipates machinery-specific AI requirements by 2 August 2028 [f2644]. Separately, the glossary warns that simulation traceability and archived safety-case records may be disclosed in court under the new EU product liability rules, making record retention relevant beyond regulatory acceptance [f12201].

nodes.label: 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4)
nodes.synopsis: 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4), together with 1926.602(a)(9)(ii), is in force for US construction [f2762]. Chapter 3 and the glossary agree that an obstructed rear view requires a reverse alarm or an observer, with the alarm audible above surrounding noise [f2763, f2764, f15505]. Chapter 3 additionally reports that interpretations allow camera and radar alternatives [f2763]. These rules prescribe neither a numeric range nor automatic braking, so they do not themselves supply those acceptance criteria for a collision-mitigation system [f2765].

nodes.label: 29 CFR 1926.602(a)(9)(ii)
nodes.synopsis: 29 CFR 1926.602(a)(9)(ii), alongside 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4), is in force for US construction [f2762]. When a machine’s rear view is obstructed, these rules require a reverse signal alarm audible above surrounding noise, or an observer [f15505, f2763, f2764]. Chapter 3 also reports that interpretations allow camera and radar alternatives [f2763]. The rules prescribe neither a numeric range nor automatic braking, leaving those parameters unspecified by these provisions for collision-mitigation validation planning [f2765].

nodes.label: Cyber Resilience Act
nodes.text: Cyber Resilience Act
nodes.synopsis: The skeptic’s review identifies the Cyber Resilience Act as imposing cybersecurity duties, but this is recorded as expert opinion [f10816]. Chapter 3 states that the Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 and IEC 62443 were not reviewed, leaving a substantive coverage gap [f2939]. Chapter 13 and the glossary agree that the Act’s application dates were not verified; Chapter 13 treats those dates as relevant leads rather than established findings [f10817, f11194, f15485]. Planners should therefore verify application dates before relying on the Act; the supplied facts establish no verified application deadline [f10817, f11194, f15485].

nodes.label: New Zealand
nodes.text: New Zealand
nodes.synopsis: Across the booklet, New Zealand incidents show that ordinary production tasks at tip heads and stockpiles can produce heavy-machine collisions, with reversing a recurring task phase [f15691, f3211]. The 2017 examples include dozer–777 truck and truck–dozer contacts, night-shift tip-head contact, and a stockpile-loading incident in which a loader bucket caught a reversing truck body and the loader overturned; reported consequences included tyre, rim and structural damage [f3557, f3229, f3345, f3569, f3264]. For October–December 2019, WorkSafe's vehicle-event breakdown was 46% overturning, 27% unintended movement or brake failure, 11% collision with other plant, 4% berm breach and 12% burst tyre [f3198]. This qualifies the broader finding that machine-to-machine and machine-to-light-vehicle near misses and damage collisions were the most frequently reported events across NSW, Queensland and New Zealand: plant collisions were not the leading category in that particular New Zealand quarter [f3583, f3585]. Frequency estimates remain uncertain because near misses were under-reported and the regulator warned that only a small fraction of quarry and alluvial operations had reported events in the preceding year [f3650, f3050, f11621].

nodes.label: NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672
nodes.text: NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672
nodes.synopsis: NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672 (Ruff, 2007) counted 22 fatalities involving blind areas using MSHA fatality reports from 2000 to mid-2006 [f3060]. Rear blind areas of reversing equipment accounted for 67% of victims; dump trucks had the highest share of fatal blind-area accidents at 38%, followed by front-end loaders at 33% [f3062, f3061]. The described accidents frequently involved large dump trucks driving over smaller vehicles or workers in blind spots [f3063]. The report also identified false alarms caused by a truck’s own tyres and protruding structures, connecting accident prevention to proximity-system reliability [f5435]. A vendor patent family citing the report makes the broader claim that false and nuisance alarms have traditionally been the primary reason deployed proximity systems fail; the supplied independent finding identifies specific alarm causes but does not establish that broader ranking [f10711, f5435].

nodes.label: T. M. Ruff
nodes.text: T. M. Ruff
nodes.synopsis: T. M. Ruff’s NIOSH work spans Report 9652, published in May 2000, a 2006 haul-truck radar study and companion accident paper, and Report 9672 from 2007 [f7983, f5173, f3064, f3060]. The 2007 report counted 22 blind-area fatalities from 2000 to mid-2006, with 67% of victims behind reversing equipment; the 2006 paper reported five blind-area fatalities annually and 12% of all surface-mine and quarry fatalities during 1999–2003 [f3060, f3062, f3064, f3065]. These historical findings establish severe blind-zone and equipment-size hazards, but should not be treated as a 2026 fatality rate; the reported dump-truck shares of 38% and 58% concern different periods and measures [f3069, f3068, f3061, f3066]. The booklet identifies Ruff’s 2006 radar study on a 260 t Caterpillar 793B as its best hard false-alarm figure: over seven days and 618 reversals, 580 alarms comprised 102 false alarms, 243 nuisance alarms and 235 actionable alarms, reported as 41% [f5173, f5174, f5436]. Nuisance alarms were valid detections without urgent danger, berm detections were excluded from that count, and staged target tests would not have exposed the operational proportion of actionable alarms; nevertheless, the Morenci trial reported false alarms insufficiently frequent to cause operators to ignore the system [f3271, f3349, f14242, f7001]. Ruff also found rear-tyre detection gaps with a single radar, improved coverage using two antennas about 1.8 m apart with beams crossed inward about 20 degrees, and one antenna failure after approximately six months of continuous vibration exposure [f7039, f7040, f7465].

nodes.label: CDC
nodes.text: CDC
nodes.synopsis: CDC metadata identifies the February 2022 NIOSH haul-truck fatality conference paper, SME preprint 22-085, as not peer reviewed, qualifying its evidentiary status in the accident discussion [f3071]. In the skeptic’s review, an undated NIOSH CDC page reports that HASARD detection distance at the operator cab’s “risk” threshold fell from about 18 inches to 5 inches as speed increased from 3 to 30 inches per second [f10657]. A separate undated archived CDC page describes NIOSH’s Intelligent Proximity Detection program as explicitly seeking better operator acceptance by reducing frustration from frequent false alarms and full stops [f10710]. Across these chapters, CDC-linked material supplies accident-source metadata, quantitative detection results, and an operator-acceptance objective, but the facts provide neither dates for the two program pages nor evidence that the acceptance objective was achieved [f3071, f10657, f10710].

nodes.label: Resources Safety and Health Queensland
nodes.text: Resources Safety and Health Queensland
nodes.synopsis: Resources Safety and Health Queensland (RSHQ) publishes QGN 27 on collision prevention (2017) and QGN 33 on autonomous mobile machinery [f15541]. QGN 27 reports that collisions accounted for 26% of mineral mine and quarry fatalities between 1998 and 2016, while a separate RSHQ alert recorded 48 mobile-equipment collisions and near misses at open-cut coal mines from 1 January to 27 May 2017 [f3103, f3106]. QGN 27 identifies vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-person and vehicle-to-infrastructure interactions as important high-potential incident classes, including a worked scenario of a loader striking a pedestrian on a roadway [f3104, f3105]. Secondary reporting of RSHQ's July 2024 Quarterly Report indicates that mobile plant collisions remained among the leading high-potential incidents and that the Deputy Chief Inspector was particularly concerned about reliance on “positive communication” as the primary control; these later findings are presented through secondary reporting rather than directly from the report [f3109, f3110].

nodes.label: QGN 27
nodes.text: QGN 27
nodes.synopsis: Resources Safety and Health Queensland publishes QGN 27, its 2017 guidance on collision prevention [f15541]. Chapter 4 and the glossary both report its finding that collisions accounted for 26% of mineral mine and quarry fatalities between 1998 and 2016 [f3103, f15542]. QGN 27 identifies vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-person and vehicle-to-infrastructure interactions as important high-potential incident classes, with a loader striking a pedestrian on a roadway as a worked critical-risk scenario [f3104, f3105]. Its worked stopping example shows a machine travelling 22.2 m at 40 km/h during a 2 s reaction-plus-delay period, while its warning about idealized detection zones cautions against a false sense of protection [f15543, f15544].

nodes.label: New South Wales Resources Regulator
nodes.text: New South Wales Resources Regulator
nodes.synopsis: The regulator’s 2023 vehicle-interaction paper reported no meaningful year-on-year reduction in reported incidents and an unresolved gap in reliably distinguishing hazardous from spurious conditions; Chapter 4 dates the paper to July, while the glossary says September [f3111, f15539, f3112, f15540, f15537]. Its July 2025 bulletin recorded 30 collisions involving LHD units and personnel transports in underground coal mines over the preceding 12 months, often involving LHDs carrying large loads [f3113, f3114]. Investigations and incident summaries describe a fatal reversing-dozer collision in 2019 and a March 2026 night-time wrong-side driving incident in which two trucks stopped about 15 m apart; secondary accounts of July 2026 incidents still require checking against the regulator’s own text [f3116, f3115, f3117, f3118, f3119]. The regulator is developing a draft Technical Reference Guide on vehicle interaction controls, while its undated brake-formula guidance is a proposal rather than an adopted rule and draws on ISO 3450:1996 and AS 2958.1 [f15538, f5988, f5981]. That brake guidance proposes minimum mean safe net decelerations of 0.60/0.30 m/s² for service/secondary brakes in service and 0.75/0.40 m/s² for type testing, assuming traction and no skidding [f5982, f5983, f5987]. Its worked examples give stopping distances of 34.4 m, 30.82 m and 42.25 m for different truck, speed, loading and grade conditions, so these are scenario-specific examples rather than one universal stopping-distance requirement [f5984, f5985, f5986].

nodes.label: WorkSafe New Zealand
nodes.text: WorkSafe New Zealand
nodes.synopsis: WorkSafe New Zealand is the national workplace-safety regulator, with an extractives inspectorate covering mines and quarries; it is distinct from WorkSafe Western Australia, which supplies the booklet’s cited Significant Incident Reports [f15673, f15674, f15681]. Its August 2017 alert followed “numerous” heavy-mobile-plant interactions, particularly involving large surface haul trucks, and illustrated ordinary-production collisions during reversing, night-shift work and stockpile loading [f3122, f3123, f3124, f3125]. For October–December 2019, its extractives vehicle- and plant-related notified events comprised 46% overturning, 27% unintended movement or brake failure, 11% collision with other plant, 4% berm breach and 12% burst tyre [f3198]. These figures describe only one quarter with acknowledged incomplete reporting, so planners should not treat them as a long-term national event distribution [f3131, f15680].

nodes.label: D10 dozer
nodes.text: D10 dozer
nodes.synopsis: WorkSafe New Zealand’s August 2017 alert cited an ordinary-production incident in which a D10 dozer reversed into the wheel assembly of a fully loaded 777 dump truck at a tip head [f3123]. The glossary restates this regulator-described incident, connecting the D10 example to the booklet’s accident discussion [f11434, f3123]. Chapter 4 places it alongside another documented tip-head collision involving a reversing truck clipping a dozer at night; the supplied facts do not identify that second dozer as a D10 [f3357]. These facts document collision circumstances but provide no outcome or evidence of collision-mitigation system performance [f3123, f11434, f3357].

nodes.label: Caterpillar 777
nodes.text: Caterpillar 777
nodes.synopsis: The Caterpillar 777 appears as a loaded dump truck involved in a tip-head collision: a D10 dozer reversed into its wheel assembly [f3123, f11434]. Chapter 4 identifies this as an ordinary-production incident cited in WorkSafe New Zealand’s August 2017 alert [f3123]. The chapter places it alongside another documented tip-head collision in which a reversing truck clipped a dozer at night, and summarizes the New Zealand incidents as dozer-against-777 and truck-against-dozer contacts [f3357, f3557]. The glossary repeats the 777 incident, but the supplied facts provide no injury outcomes or evidence of collision-mitigation performance [f11434, f3123, f3357, f3557].

nodes.synopsis: CSIRO contributes expert observations on visibility and driver response: a researcher described dust hiding a light vehicle in South Africa and cited an average driver reaction time of about one second [f3230, f3311]. The one-second estimate is expert opinion, not a field-measured distribution for heavy-machine operators [f3311]. The brake-timing chapter likewise attributes about one second to CSIRO (2007), within a collection of assumptions ranging from 0.5 to 2.5 seconds and patent margins of 1–3 seconds; this variation cautions against treating one second as a universal assumption [f6228]. CSIRO was not assessed as a tools provider, so its recorded status is “not found,” rather than evidence that it does not offer relevant tools [f8835, f16090, f16120].

nodes.synopsis: The corpus links Griffith University’s haul-truck collision-avoidance research to reaction-time assumptions of 0.5–1 second borrowed from road research, citing Henry-Rogers (1960) [f3310]. A 2005 Griffith thesis combined a 0.5-second reaction time with braking to derive detection ranges of 15 m to the sides for people, 50 m to the rear and 100 m to the front [f6207]. Griffith’s 2005 Doppler-radar work used Monte Carlo simulation and a field demonstration, reporting light-vehicle detection at 75 m [f6368]. For planning, that observed detection distance must be distinguished from a braking trigger: the radar work was a detection study, not a brake-threshold study, while the reaction-time assumptions originated in road research [f6369, f3310].

nodes.synopsis: ACARP C24028 was a University of Queensland haul-truck proximity-advisory interface project conducted in 2017, with follow-on work to 2019, using a modified haul-truck simulator [f3314, f15631]. The study found that richer schematic information reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time, although a later experiment with fewer experienced truck drivers found smaller effects [f3316, f15632, f3317]. The booklet treats this simulator study as its main off-road evidence that operator-in-the-loop testing works [f15635]. Its public abstract reports no warning-to-brake reaction time, and an acceptable false alarm rate remains an open research question, leaving gaps for validation planning [f3318, f15633].

nodes.label: Sensors
nodes.text: Sensors
nodes.synopsis: Sensors publications provide evidence and methods for lidar simulation: a 2022 stationary dataset spans six months of rain, snow, fog and sunlight for stochastic modeling, calibration and validation, while 2025 mining work combines real and simulated dusty environments in a public database [f4736, f4737, f3953]. A 2022 off-road lidar de-dusting filter reported F1 = 97.55%, but the skeptic’s review qualifies this as performance on its own collected dataset [f7830, f10563]. On-road evidence shows vibration-related lidar position and intensity drift, and strong target-dependent weather effects: aluminium and steel targets were not observed at 20–30 m in specified rain and fog conditions, whereas retroreflective targets retained at least 74% of their clear-weather point count [f4707, f6382, f6383]. The corpus also cites an on-road rain-and-fog simulation model and a credibility-level process, while noting that a 2023 study described earlier degradation demonstrations as simulation-based or limited to sites such as climate chambers [f6381, f8949, f10567]. Beyond lidar modeling, Sensors reports include a 17-participant work-zone VR study with mean wearable-warning responses of approximately 337 ms for vibration, 443 ms for visual cues and 597 ms for audio, plus 2026 examples involving mine non-line-of-sight perception and a vineyard-rover training environment [f3323, f3324, f4121, f4143].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 4 cites a 2025 IIHS study by Cox, Reagan and Cicchino finding that on-road drivers keep prevention systems enabled more often than warning-only systems [f3460]. In that study, 93% had AEB enabled, while lane departure systems were enabled less often; the stated scope is on-road drivers, not heavy off-road operators [f3461]. Chapter 12 cites Cox (2008) for mathematical flaws in colour risk matrices, including 5-by-5 heat maps: poor resolution, range compression and ranking errors [f9675, f9895]. Subsequent work is reported to confirm problems with ordinal scoring in risk matrices [f9676]. The supplied facts do not establish whether the Cox cited in these two research areas is the same person [f3460, f9675].

nodes.label: Robot Operating System
nodes.text: Robot Operating System
nodes.synopsis: ROS appears across the corpus as an integration and simulation tool: NIOSH evaluated CARLA and ROS for reproducing mine environments, with a planned progression from extensive simulation through small-scale to physical testing [f3488]. TERA provides an off-road example, combining Unity and AGX with configurable excavators, environments, ROS integration and terrain-machine interaction [f4129]. ROS recordings are bags containing every message with its timestamp; ROS and Autoware offer bag-replay and simulation examples, but that evidence is explicitly on-road [f13013, f5607]. ROS 2 is identified as the current generation and is integrated in CARLA, Isaac Sim, Gazebo and BeamNG [f16240]. MathWorks lists ROS among its platform interfaces, but ROS-linked components still require medium relative integration effort because materials, actors, dynamics and timing semantics need calibration despite existing transport and schemas [f8383, f8961, f8729].

nodes.label: NeRF
nodes.text: NeRF
nodes.synopsis: NeRF learns scene color and density with a neural network to render new viewpoints; the booklet treats it as both a scene-reconstruction method and a learned sensor-model approach [f12925, f3813, f4483]. Reconstruction requires multi-camera logs with accurate poses and GPU compute, optionally using lidar, and offers an alternative to explicit geometry conversion [f4226, f3992]. Log-based neural re-simulation supports closed-loop-like evaluation near the recorded trajectory, but artifacts occur at 1–4 m offsets, height changes degrade results more than sideways shifts, and large viewpoint changes limit testing of new sensor mounting positions [f5722, f5724, f3706, f5723]. Industry preference for 3DGS reflects NeRF’s editing and labeling limitations, yet the cited XLD results found NeRF-based EmerNeRF and UC-NeRF more robust than the 3DGS variant PVG at 4 m offsets [f3878, f4329]. SplatAD at CVPR 2025 claims roughly tenfold faster rendering than NeRF methods; its cited NeRF baselines render 9.7–28.2 megapixels per second after 0.9–2.6 hours of training [f4945, f4946]. For heavy off-road validation, the principal evidence gap is that log-based neural re-simulation has very low off-road maturity and the cited evidence is on-road only [f5725].

nodes.label: 3D Gaussian Splatting
nodes.text: 3D Gaussian Splatting
nodes.synopsis: 3D Gaussian Splatting is presented as a neural reconstruction method that learns a scene from posed multi-view images, optionally with lidar, to reproduce view-dependent appearance better than textured meshes; the cited evidence is on-road [f3813]. Its fidelity degrades sharply away from the recorded path, especially with height changes: Para-Lane (2025) reports PSNR falling from 22.99 dB in the recorded lane to 17.05 dB in the adjacent lane, while MV² (August 2026) reports 29.13 dB at drone height versus 10.36 dB from a car [f3706, f3707, f3709]. Across sensor simulation and system testing, it appears both among data-learned sensor-model approaches and in Cao et al.'s CoRL 2025 pseudo-simulation, which uses pre-generated views to approximate closed-loop evaluation [f4483, f5537]. NVIDIA Isaac Sim also offers neural rendering using NuRec and 3D Gaussian splatting, alongside sensor schemas, synthetic-data annotators and ROS 2 integration [f8479]. These uses establish practical relevance, but the reported viewpoint sensitivity limits confidence in extrapolating reconstructed scenes to novel viewpoints, and the supplied independent evidence does not establish performance for heavy off-road machines [f3706, f3707, f3709, f3813, f5537].

nodes.label: PSNR
nodes.text: PSNR
nodes.synopsis: PSNR measures image or field similarity using pixel-matched pairs; higher scores mean greater image fidelity, but these metrics assess appearance and structure rather than perception or decision-software behavior [f4802, f12930, f14791]. Viewpoint changes substantially reduce reported fidelity: XLD's synthetic CARLA benchmark drops from 30.87 dB at zero lateral shift to 19.17 dB at 4 m, while Para-Lane's real-data results fall from 22.99 dB in the recorded lane to 17.05 and 16.26 dB in adjacent lanes [f4001, f4003]. EUVS (2025) reports average PSNR reductions of 24.6% for translation, 25.6% for rotation and 30.6% for both; MV²'s August 2026 results show drone-trained scenes falling from 29.13 to 10.36 dB when viewed from a car [f4005, f4008]. Method and evaluation choices matter: EmerNeRF reaches 24.80 dB at XLD's 4 m shift, and MV²'s PVG car-to-scooter scores range from 14.72 dB without masks to 24.29 dB with ground-truth dynamic masks [f4002, f3890, f3891, f3892]. Diffusion repair improves Para-Lane two-lane results to 19.47 dB but still trails roughly 23 dB on the recorded path; generative novel-view methods report only 13.19–20.82 dB on Waymo in a 2026 preprint, which the corpus characterizes as low fidelity for safety testing and in tension with validation 'data machine' claims [f4013, f3821, f3822, f4330]. These benchmarks provide on-road or synthetic CARLA evidence, not a demonstrated heavy off-road validation result, and PSNR alone does not establish perception or decision-system validity [f4001, f4003, f4008, f3821, f14791].

nodes.label: ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D
nodes.text: ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D is described as a free, open material standard for environment creation and sensor simulation; version 1.0.0 was released on 3 April 2025 [f9178, f9181, f8360, f3714]. It addresses the insufficiency of geometry alone by letting one asset carry camera-, lidar- and radar-relevant material properties, including refractive index, roughness, permeability, wavelength-dependent lookup tables and per-material licence metadata [f4965, f12945, f3918, f13187]. Its usefulness for off-road objects remains tentative, and weather, lighting and sensor contamination are explicitly outside its scope, while volumetric properties remain under development [f7084, f13188, f9372, f3922]. Version 1.1.0 was planned for October 2026, with improved conductivity modelling and conversion of measured reflectance into BRDF, but the main page accessed that month still listed only 1.0.0 and the latest release found elsewhere was also 1.0.0 [f3923, f3924, f3925, f9182]. A vendor co-simulation demonstration combines OpenMATERIAL 3D with OpenSCENARIO, OSI and a physical lidar model, providing an implementation example rather than resolving the off-road applicability and scope gaps [f3981, f7084, f13188].

nodes.label: CropCraft
nodes.text: CropCraft
nodes.synopsis: CropCraft is an open-source Blender and Python tool for procedurally generating agricultural fields, identified in Chapter 5 as dated November 2025 [f3787, f16006, f16238]. Its reported average simulation-to-real mIoU gap was 9.9%, with gaps of 10.6% on Real Montoldre and 9.2% on Real Steininger [f3731, f4141]. CropCraft also found in 2025 that adding even a few real images to synthetic data improves generalization [f4100]. The corpus includes CropCraft among examples supporting procedural generation’s strong off-road record, but explicitly warns that these agricultural examples do not prove applicability to heavy construction-machine braking [f4194, f4148].

nodes.label: mIoU
nodes.text: mIoU
nodes.synopsis: The corpus reports mIoU in two November 2025 simulation-to-real assessments: CropCraft’s agricultural procedural generation and an on-road real-versus-simulated scan comparison [f3731, f4141, f4816]. CropCraft reported an average mIoU simulation-to-real gap of 9.9%, comprising gaps of 10.6% on Real Montoldre and 9.2% on Real Steininger [f4141]. The on-road comparison by the National Research Council Canada, Western University and Transport Canada reported segmentation mIoU of only 21%, alongside an average density-aware Chamfer distance of 0.63 [f4442, f4816]. These results describe different quantities—a simulation-to-real mIoU gap versus a segmentation mIoU score—so the supplied facts do not establish a direct performance comparison between the agricultural and on-road settings [f4141, f4816].

nodes.label: Boreal3D
nodes.text: Boreal3D
nodes.synopsis: Boreal3D is described as an environment-creation tool providing synthetic forest lidar plots through procedural generation [f16005, f15956, f3732]. It contains 1,000 synthetic plots simulated across four laser-scanning platforms: airborne, unmanned, mobile and terrestrial [f4150, f3840]. Its physics-based lidar provides exact structural ground truth, and the booklet cites its forestry work as off-road evidence for statistically matched digital cousins [f4151, f4277]. The preprint dates to January 2025, followed by publication in Remote Sensing of Environment, volume 341, in August 2026 [f4152, f4153]. The glossary groups Boreal3D with CropCraft and AgriGen as supporting agricultural and forest scenes, while the Boreal3D-specific facts describe forest plots [f16086, f16005, f15956].

nodes.label: Blender
nodes.text: Blender
nodes.synopsis: Blender appears as a procedural scene-generation tool for construction, with a 2023 Automation in Construction example scripting scenes using real lighting captured on two dates; CropCraft, an open-source Blender and Python tool dated November 2025, extends its use to agricultural fields [f3733, f3789, f4133, f3787]. Blender pipelines are also listed among systems that automatically provide labels for procedural and simulated scenes, with both independent and vendor evidence attached to that claim [f3975, f3976]. For construction worker detection, a secondary summary in the 2025 Midjourney paper attributes a 50% reduction in required real images and a 16% detector-performance improvement to Kim et al.’s 2023 Blender-rendered synthetic-worker study [f7049, f7050]. In sensor simulation, SynFog (2024) paired a physical fog chamber with a one-to-one Blender virtual twin and found simulated per-channel trends consistently followed real captures as fog density increased, but this evidence is on-road [f4563]. The listed construction and excavation examples, including procedural Blender datasets, are camera-centric, so these facts do not establish equivalent coverage for other sensor modalities or heavy off-road automatic-braking validation [f4137, f4563].

nodes.label: Unity
nodes.text: Unity
nodes.synopsis: Unity is identified as one of the two best-known game engines and is used in both a 2026 off-road digital-twin simulator and the TERA autonomous-excavator simulator [f13171, f13175, f3790, f4129]. The digital twin includes procedural terrain, multiple cameras, lidar, GPS, IMU, dynamic weather and lighting, and failure annotations; TERA combines Unity with AGX, configurable excavators and environments, ROS integration, and terrain-machine interaction [f3790, f4129]. The tool survey lists supported AGX integration with Unity, a Unity lidar module, and Project Chrono Unity interfaces; the glossary dates an AGX Unity reverse auto-brake example with lidar to April 2025 [f8703, f9108, f9025, f15967]. Procedural datasets and ready-made Unity assets support virtual job-site creation, but a 2026 study found Unity-rendered construction scenes still diverged from real photometric distributions despite extensive domain randomization; that study is identified as a preprint [f3733, f3832, f10584, f10585].

nodes.label: MAVS
nodes.text: MAVS
nodes.synopsis: MAVS is an open-source university off-road simulation library associated with Mississippi State University and, in military/general off-road examples, ERDC [f15935, f3740, f4508, f4159]. It procedurally generates terrain with controllable roughness, ecosystem, haze and moonlight, provides automatic scene labels, and offers ray-traced lidar, camera and radar interacting with rain, dust, fog and snow [f3786, f3975, f4508]. Its tire-soil model is validated for sand and clay; dense-vegetation lidar validation was qualitative in 2018, and a field-measurement-based vegetation-override resistance model was reported at GVSETS 2025 [f3965, f4160, f3967]. Validation remains qualified: the 2020 paper described ongoing validation, and cited open-source simulator authors identified real-sensor validation as future work, despite claims of validated individual MAVS models [f4509, f3741, f3740]. A 2023 MAVS-based ecosystem study found changed segmentation results outside the training distribution, while a 2023 simulated-versus-real RELLIS-3D comparison found large domain-shift effects; MAVS frame rates were not found in the corpus [f4098, f4741, f4957].

nodes.label: Project Chrono
nodes.text: Project Chrono
nodes.synopsis: Project Chrono is a free, BSD-3 open-source dynamics engine for wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles, with rigid terrain and SCM, CRM and DEM deformable-terrain models; release 10.0.0 is dated 27 March 2026 [f15907, f8493, f8494, f8496]. Its off-road research relevance includes military and planetary mobility, NATO mobility benchmarks, and listed users including US Army organizations, NREL and JPL [f8675, f4164, f8497]. SCM authors claim empirical-model speed with fidelity comparable to discrete element methods, whereas higher-fidelity CRM runs 50–200 times slower than real time and requires an NVIDIA GPU, motivating selective use to calibrate lower-order models rather than every regression case [f6097, f8499, f8500, f8584]. Developers warn that Pacejka, TMeasy and Fiala handling tire models do not work on deformable terrain, creating a risk that tool coupling silently breaks the physics [f8498, f8725]. Experimental terrain validation is reported, but documented capabilities do not establish machine-specific emergency stopping-distance accuracy; no common production-machine stopping benchmark was found, and the skeptic chapter did not review Chrono validation literature [f8583, f6016, f6561, f10611]. Chrono is not turnkey test management, qualification-ready coupling to Isaac requires major work, and its 2020 sensor framework left real-sensor validation as future work; low-license-cost integration still carries substantial internal labor, while maintenance funding and security-patch cadence were not examined [f8501, f9280, f4341, f16128, f9392, f9393].

nodes.label: Bekker-Wong terramechanics
nodes.text: Bekker-Wong terramechanics
nodes.synopsis: Bekker-Wong is presented as a semi-empirical terramechanics approach for predicting braking force and sinkage on soft soil [f6096, f6461]. The underlying terramechanics findings say tractive and braking forces depend on soil type, contact area, load and slip, and that tracks retain more shear force than tires in soft soil [f6006, f6007]. Across the virtual-job-site and brake-timing chapters, Project Chrono provides an implementation route: its terrain options include a Soil Contact Model using Bekker-Wong pressure-sinkage and shear parameters, alongside rigid terrain and more expensive granular or deformable approaches [f3739, f6014]. The supplied facts identify modeling options and physical dependencies, but provide no numerical braking results or validation accuracy for these models [f6006, f6014, f6461].

nodes.label: ISO 34504
nodes.synopsis: ISO 34504:2024 formalises scenario categorisation through tags, within the ISO 34502–34505 scenario standards dated 2022–2025 [f6731, f8118]. The family adopts the functional, logical and concrete scenario levels originating in PEGASUS, providing a structure used by the scenario catalog [f13258, f6735]. Across chapters, the standards' process and information structure transfer to off-road validation, but their content addresses road vehicles and Level 3 and higher automated driving; they provide methodological precedent rather than off-road compliance evidence [f6642, f7182, f15320]. Off-road adequacy remains unestablished, including validity for mines, quarries, deformable surfaces, dust, articulation and heavy-machine operating conditions [f6734, f7696]. These standards focus on scenario coverage rather than model credibility: coverage must reflect the operational design domain, but they do not address validation against physical data, risk scaling or a physical-to-virtual testing ratio [f7693, f8121, f8120, f8119, f7694].

nodes.label: ISO 34505
nodes.synopsis: ISO 34505 was published in June 2025 and provides methods for evaluating and prioritizing test cases, including frequency, criticality, complexity, operational-domain coverage and optimization of test sets [f7181, f4069, f4070]. Its required test-case attributes are identifiers, objectives, inputs, steps, test platform and expected results; the scenario catalog uses the functional, logical and concrete levels adopted from PEGASUS into ISO 34501–34505 [f6732, f6735, f13258]. Across chapters, the standards’ process and information structure are considered transferable to off-road validation, but their content addresses road vehicles and Level 3 and higher automated driving, not off-road compliance [f6642, f7182, f15320]. Off-road adequacy remains unestablished, including validity for mines, quarries, deformable surfaces, articulation, dust and heavy-machinery vibration or contamination [f6734, f7696]. Although ISO 34505 includes a simulation-validity clause, the corpus characterizes these scenario standards as addressing coverage rather than model credibility, without validation against physical data, risk scaling or a prescribed physical-to-virtual testing ratio [f4071, f7693, f8120, f8119, f7694]. ISO 34505 test-case evaluation contributes to the rationale for separating discovery, population-success estimation and requirement/regression campaigns by purpose, data and governance, while that standards evidence remains on-road [f6934, f6666, f6667, f6668].

nodes.label: ISO/PAS 34506
nodes.text: ISO/PAS 34506
nodes.synopsis: ISO/PAS 34506 concerns qualification of virtual test environments for road vehicles; it remained a draft in October 2026 and should not be treated as a finished standard [f4334, f7695, f15318]. The glossary also distinguishes its Publicly Available Specification status from a full standard [f15052]. Alongside ISO 34502–34505, it offers methodological precedent for structuring site, weather and behavior combinations for off-road automatic braking, with scenario coverage required to reflect the operational design domain, but provides no off-road compliance evidence [f8123, f8121, f15320]. The corpus identifies no demonstrated validity for mines, quarries, earthworks or challenging heavy-machine conditions, and says these frameworks focus on coverage rather than validation against physical data [f7696, f8120]. They also neither address risk scaling nor establish a physical-to-virtual testing ratio, leaving those evidence-planning questions unresolved [f8119, f8122, f15321].

nodes.label: Unreal Engine 5
nodes.text: Unreal Engine 5
nodes.synopsis: Unreal Engine 5 is available in simulation tooling: CARLA switched from UE4 to UE5, though some APIs are unsupported, and VTD 2025.1 added UE5 rendering [f8892, f8428]. The CARLA release information found includes the 0.10.0 UE5 line dated 19 December 2024 and version 0.9.16 dated 16 September 2025 [f9013]. CARLA on UE5 requires an NVIDIA RTX 3000-series GPU or better, at least 16 GB VRAM and 130 GB disk; the glossary contrasts that VRAM minimum with 48 GB cloud GPUs and 96 GB workstation cards [f8850, f16177, f16195]. ISPRS 2024 reported UE5 3DGS performance of 60 FPS for a single building versus 17 FPS for a 23-million-Gaussian terrain scene, providing scene-dependent performance results relevant to hardware-in-the-loop testing [f3893, f3894, f3764]. Open-source platforms offering UE5 rendering and RTX sensors are reported as free for internal use, but the agriculture examples—including UE5 plant simulation presented at a CVPR 2024 workshop—do not establish applicability to heavy construction-machine braking [f9336, f9337, f4146, f4148].

nodes.label: Mississippi State University
nodes.text: Mississippi State University
nodes.synopsis: Mississippi State University is identified as the source of MAVS, an open off-road simulator described across the virtual-job-site and sensor-simulation chapters [f3786, f4508]. MAVS automatically generates terrain with controllable roughness, ecosystem, haze and moonlight [f3786]. Its ray-traced lidar, camera and radar interact with rain, dust, fog and snow, extending its described capabilities from environment creation to sensor simulation [f4508]. The military and general off-road examples associate MAVS with both Mississippi State University and ERDC, but the supplied facts do not specify their respective organizational roles [f4159].

nodes.label: Python
nodes.text: Python
nodes.synopsis: Python is a recurring interface across the simulation tools: Prescan supports Python and MATLAB APIs alongside OpenSCENARIO, while CARLA exposes a Python API alongside other interfaces [f8458, f9005, f9011, f16237]. Sensor tooling also uses Python: CARLA lists cameras, lidar, radar, GNSS and IMU, while BeamNG.tech lists programmable cameras, lidar, radar, ultrasonic and IMU sensors with a Python API [f8468, f9085, f8504]. Beyond these platforms, Project Chrono lists Python, C# and Unity interfaces, and the glossary identifies Scenic, CropCraft and Demify as Python-driven generators [f9025, f9125, f16238]. The job-site chapter identifies CropCraft as an open-source Blender and Python tool dated November 2025 for generating agricultural fields; the tool listings further connect Scenic to multiple simulators and list Python and CPU/GPU for Demify [f3787, f9211, f9143].

nodes.label: AgriGen
nodes.text: AgriGen
nodes.synopsis: AgriGen generates large agricultural scenes in Isaac Sim and is identified in Chapter 5 as reported in September 2026 [f16007, f3788, f4142]. The glossary places it alongside CropCraft and Boreal3D as supporting agricultural and forest scenes, while Chapter 5 includes it in the strong off-road record for procedural site generation [f16086, f4194]. However, AgriGen (2026) describes simulating fields with thousands of vegetation assets as computationally intractable on consumer-grade hardware, highlighting a scaling constraint [f3895]. The cited agricultural examples, including AgriGen, do not establish applicability to heavy construction-machine braking [f4148].

nodes.label: NVIDIA Isaac Sim
nodes.text: NVIDIA Isaac Sim
nodes.synopsis: NVIDIA Isaac Sim is a general robotics simulator, open source under Apache 2.0 since version 5.0, with version 6.1 reaching general availability on 15 September 2026 [f8477, f8478, f8481]. Its capabilities include RTX lidar and radar, cameras, ROS 2 integration and neural rendering; the asset library lists 25 RTX lidar models but only one radar model [f8478, f8479, f8480]. AgriGen demonstrated large agricultural scene generation in September 2026, but the research did not verify Isaac Sim or find construction/mining validation or validation for off-road collision warning [f3788, f5850, f5851, f8491]. Sensor credibility remains a qualification gap: ultrasonic sensing is a PhysX ray-cast range model rather than an acoustic model, while RTX sensor crashes and severe multi-sensor frame-rate losses motivate workload-specific benchmarking [f8548, f8488, f8875]. The core is free for internal R&D, but separate asset/component terms apply and redistribution with Omniverse Kit requires NVIDIA AI Enterprise at an undiscovered price; staff statements describing free use for teams of up to two leave the scope of free use needing clarification [f8483, f8484, f8485, f8486]. An in-house open-source chain offers low license cost but high internal labor, and validated radar and qualification-ready Chrono-to-Isaac heavy-machine coupling still require major work [f16128, f9275, f9280].

nodes.label: Automation in Construction
nodes.text: Automation in Construction
nodes.synopsis: Automation in Construction supplies examples spanning excavator pose estimation with domain randomisation in volume 134 (2022), procedural construction datasets in 2023, and RGB–lidar fusion for construction point-cloud de-dusting in 2024 [f4135, f3789, f5397]. The 2023 work scripted Blender scenes using real lighting captured on two dates; incorporating date-specific lighting improved realism, but the study reported mixed per-class results [f3789, f4133, f7059, f7060]. The excavation de-dusting model by Parsons, Hanafi Sheikhha, Seo and Lee appeared in volume 168 in December 2024 and scored 65.58 percent in one “far dense dust” case, compared with 94.85–96.73 percent in other cases of the same scenario [f10564]. These findings offer examples of synthetic-scene creation and perception testing, while the mixed class results and dense-dust performance drop caution against assuming uniform performance across conditions [f7059, f7060, f10564].

nodes.label: structure from motion
nodes.text: structure from motion
nodes.synopsis: Structure from motion matches points across photographs taken from different positions and solves for camera positions and three-dimensional point locations [f13145, f13144]. In drone or ground photogrammetry, it works with multi-view stereo to turn overlapping, calibrated images into camera poses and sparse geometry, followed by dense point clouds, textured meshes and surfaces [f3794]. The same combination can reconstruct poses, dense points and a textured mesh from a camera-only log [f3988]. Reconstruction from a working machine's recordings can instead combine camera, lidar, IMU and GNSS logs through structure from motion, lidar-inertial SLAM, point-cloud fusion and surfel or mesh generation [f3806]. The glossary identifies COLMAP as a widely used free structure-from-motion program and distinguishes the method from scene reconstruction, the full process of producing a usable virtual site [f13144].

nodes.label: COLMAP
nodes.text: COLMAP
nodes.synopsis: COLMAP is described as a widely used free, open-source structure-from-motion tool that recovers camera positions and a three-dimensional point cloud from photographs; this is one part of the broader process of producing a usable virtual site [f13144, f13146]. Its reconstruction guidance requires good texture, similar illumination, substantial image overlap, at least three observations of each object, and genuinely different camera positions rather than pure rotation [f3799, f4025, f13147]. Textureless scenes, high dynamic range, glare, shadows and reflective surfaces are identified as reconstruction risks; numerous near-identical video frames cannot substitute for different viewpoints, and video downsampling is suggested [f3800, f4040, f4027, f13149]. An on-road EUVS benchmark required more than 800 hours of COLMAP computation, while the glossary reports more than 300 additional hours of manual selection; these figures are not a direct estimate of job-site digital-twin costs [f3898, f13150]. The booklet also names COLMAP as photogrammetry software and includes quarry drone-survey examples, but the supplied facts provide no quantified quarry reconstruction cost [f16003, f3898].

nodes.label: SplatAD
nodes.text: SplatAD
nodes.synopsis: SplatAD, presented at CVPR 2025, reconstructs scenes from recordings using Gaussian splatting and renders both cameras and lidar; the cited research evidence is on-road [f3814, f15954]. Its lidar simulation models rolling shutter, intensity and ray dropout in real time [f4516]. Reported performance includes about one hour of training per scene on one NVIDIA A100 and rendering about an order of magnitude faster than NeRF methods [f4944, f16200, f4945]. Viewpoint changes remain a limitation: the glossary says SplatAD struggles when sensors move, while the March 2026 LiDAR-EVS preprint claims 48.6% and 47.2% lower lidar Chamfer distances than SplatAD at a 3 m lateral shift, without extracted absolute values [f16004, f4009]. A comparable method, LiHi-GS, explicitly excludes deformable objects and harsh weather, but the supplied facts do not establish those same exclusions for SplatAD or demonstrate its suitability for off-road conditions [f4517, f3814, f4516].

nodes.label: CVPR 2025
nodes.text: CVPR 2025
nodes.synopsis: Across Chapters 5 and 6, CVPR 2025 is associated with SplatAD, a neural reconstruction and Gaussian-splatting approach that renders both lidar and camera outputs; the cited evidence is on-road [f3814, f4516]. Chapter 6 adds that it models rolling shutter, lidar intensity and ray dropout in real time [f4516]. SplatAD reports training in about one hour per scene on one A100 and claims rendering about an order of magnitude faster than NeRF methods [f4944, f4945]. The cited NeRF baselines render 9.7–28.2 megapixels per second after 0.9–2.6 hours of training; these facts do not establish equivalent performance for heavy off-road applications [f4946, f3814, f4516].

nodes.label: LiDAR-EVS
nodes.text: LiDAR-EVS
nodes.synopsis: LiDAR-EVS is a March 2026 neural reconstruction preprint that renders lidar as well as cameras, with cited evidence limited to on-road settings [f3817, f4009]. It claims lidar Chamfer distances 48.6% and 47.2% lower than SplatAD at a 3 m lateral shift, but absolute values were not extracted [f4009]. Across the job-site, sensor-simulation and glossary discussions, moving or extrapolated sensor viewpoints remain a challenge; LiDAR-EVS attributes extrapolation failure to single-traversal training and severe overfitting [f4010, f4023, f4518, f16004]. LiDAR-EVS and VEGS attempt to remedy novel-path reconstruction problems, but the corpus does not establish that those problems have disappeared [f4012]. Reported minimal real-to-sim gaps in NeuroNCAP are therefore in tension with critics’ concerns about weak extrapolation and lack of harsh-weather support in LiHi-GS and LiDAR-EVS; the supplied evidence does not establish off-road applicability [f5076, f3817, f4518].

nodes.label: NVIDIA
nodes.text: NVIDIA
nodes.synopsis: NVIDIA is a significant platform dependency: most graphics cards named in the booklet are NVIDIA models because reviewed simulators rely on its ray-tracing libraries, while Chrono CRM terrain requires an NVIDIA GPU—a community-raised dependency risk, not a recommendation [f16192, f8500, f16193]. For sensor-ready assets, NVIDIA specifies separate non-visual material metadata because material behaviour can vary nonlinearly with wavelength and cannot be inferred from visual materials; its radar schema also models wavelength-dependent responses and indirect paths producing ghost detections [f3835, f3926, f3934, f3935]. Ansys/NVIDIA GTC 2020 vendor figures report 14 workstation CPU hours for a 12-second radar scenario and about 12 ms per frame for a GPU real-time version against a 30 fps target, but the supplied facts do not establish equivalent workloads [f4931, f4932]. Licensing descriptions require component-level care: Isaac Sim is described as Apache 2.0 with NVIDIA asset terms, while staff also described free use for teams of up to two; the relationship between those statements is not resolved here [f9014, f8485, f8903]. NVIDIA NuRec Gaussian splatting is integrated into Isaac Sim and CARLA 0.9.16 under an open-core model, while OpenUSD and Omniverse combine an open standard with NVIDIA components [f8609, f9162, f9167].

nodes.label: digital cousins
nodes.text: digital cousins
nodes.synopsis: Digital cousins are synthetic forestry sites that reproduce real-site statistical structure rather than exact geometry; the glossary presents them as an alternative to relying only on exact digital twins [f3837, f4272, f13107]. The approach sits between exact digital twins and pure procedural generation, requires real-site statistics plus a generator, and was introduced in a January 2025 preprint [f3841, f4269, f3838]. Chapter 5 assigns digital cousins medium per-site effort, medium cost and medium visual realism, while reporting full subsequent editing of terrain and objects and full support for moving people and vehicles [f4270, f4271, f4273, f4274, f4276]. They remain valid from new sensor positions and heights, but represent a distribution rather than a specific site—a distinction planners must retain when choosing validation environments [f4275, f4272]. The chapter cites Boreal3D forestry work from 2025 and 2026 as off-road evidence [f4277].

nodes.label: 3DGS
nodes.text: 3DGS
nodes.synopsis: 3DGS provides a log-trained scene representation as an alternative to explicit geometry conversion; neural reconstruction requires multi-camera logs with accurate poses, optional lidar and GPU compute [f3992, f4226]. Chapter 7 positions neural re-simulation as approximately closed-loop near the recorded trajectory, but limited for large viewpoint shifts and new sensor mounting positions, with very low off-road maturity and on-road-only evidence [f5722, f5723, f5725]. Quantitative results reinforce that limitation: XLD’s June 2024 preprint, with a 2025 v3 using synthetic CARLA data, reported PSNR falling from 30.87 dB at zero lateral shift to 19.17 dB at 4 m, while the August 2026 MV² preprint reported drone-trained 3DGS falling from 29.13 to 10.36 dB when switching to car viewpoints [f4001, f4008]. Industry preference for 3DGS editability therefore does not establish superior viewpoint robustness: XLD found two NeRF-based methods held up better than its 3DGS variant at 4 m offsets [f4329]. ISPRS 2024 reported Unreal Engine 5 performance of 60 FPS for a single building and 17 FPS for a 23-million-Gaussian terrain scene, providing hardware-in-the-loop-relevant performance results rather than resolving the generalisation gap [f3893, f3894, f4010].

nodes.synopsis: ASPRS supplies a formal framework for evaluating geometric acceptance when virtual-scene tests require metric truth [f3912]. The glossary identifies the cited laser-scanning reference as the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing positional accuracy standards from 2024 [f13137]. Chapter 5 describes lidar as the most geometrically accurate of the compared site-creation methods, with directly assessable accuracy, citing ASPRS 2024 and USGS 2025 [f4208]. Photogrammetry can achieve measurable centimetre-level accuracy with control, referencing ASPRS 2024, but performs poorly on occluded surfaces [f4198]. Both photogrammetry and lidar are described as having mature accuracy frameworks; the supplied facts do not specify numerical acceptance thresholds for virtual scenes [f4294, f3912].

nodes.label: ASAM
nodes.text: ASAM
nodes.synopsis: ASAM is a Germany-based nonprofit industry association whose OpenX family supplies many of the scene-description formats discussed; despite its road-vehicle roots, the booklet rates OSI and FMI as domain-neutral and transferable to off-road work [f13222, f13197, f13224]. OpenMATERIAL 3D 1.0.0 was released on 3 April 2025 to standardize material properties for lidar, radar and camera simulation; version 1.1.0 was planned for October 2026, while volumetric properties remained under development [f3917, f8614, f3923, f3922]. Across chapters, ASAM reports no standardized simulation-quality metrics, particularly for sensors; QSQ was still at proposal stage in September 2025, and both QSQ and the separate sensor-fidelity project remained under way in 2026 [f8327, f5218, f4835]. High-fidelity OSI work addresses inadequate representations of phenomena such as camera spectral irradiance and radar raw waveforms and runs through March 2027, creating interface-versioning risk around the program’s planned first-tool-chain integration [f7081, f8618, f8619, f15870]. Although OpenX was described as in maintenance mode in 2026, an off-road concept project was active in October 2026; missing terrain, vegetation, manipulation and sensor-degradation concepts mean extensions or a manufacturer domain model are needed, and the booklet considers an off-road extension unlikely before mid-2027 [f7170, f7171, f7195, f7434, f13212]. TestSpecification was still developing infrastructure rather than a mature universal solution in October 2026, and ASAM standards were not verified in this research [f7119, f7702].
