nodes.synopsis: Synopsys acquired Ansys on 17 July 2025 for roughly USD 35 billion; China’s approval included customer-contract stipulations, and the first combined capabilities were planned for the first half of 2026, without confirmation here of delivery [f8329, f8879, f8535]. nodes.label: Sim2Radar
nodes.text: Sim2Radar
nodes.synopsis: The glossary identifies Sim2Radar, alongside RadSimReal, as a research tool addressing the radar simulation-to-reality gap [f15953]. In February 2026, Sim2Radar mapped materials to ITU-R P.2040-4 values at 77 GHz using a Fresnel ray tracer in Mitsuba 3 across five indoor scenes [f3931]. Simulated radar produced about 12% of real point density—251 versus 2,057 points per frame on average—with the passage attributing the gap to real radar’s diffuse scattering and higher-order multipath [f3932, f4305]. Chapter 5 also cites Sim2Radar as independent evidence for requiring wavelength- and band-specific lidar and radar material properties; the reported evaluation scope is five indoor scenes [f4298, f3931].

nodes.synopsis: Project Chrono and Chrono::Vehicle provide multibody and multiphysics dynamics for wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles [f8493]. Across the job-site and tools chapters, Chrono::Vehicle supports rigid and deformable terrain, including semi-empirical SCM Bekker-Wong, granular discrete-element models and continuum models; the tools chapter identifies the continuum option as CRM continuum SPH [f3961, f8494]. Its documentation says deformable terrain relies on collision and contact, rather than a friction value painted onto a visual surface [f3962]. Project Chrono and Chrono::Vehicle are open-source tools licensed under BSD-3, but are not a turnkey test-management product [f8492, f8501].

Chapters 5 and 8 place SCM within Chrono's terrain capabilities, describing Bekker-Wong pressure-sinkage modelling alongside rigid terrain and more computationally expensive granular or deformable alternatives; Chapter 8 also identifies shear parameters [f3961, f6014]. The SCM authors claim in a peer-reviewed paper that their open-source model runs as fast as empirical models while offering fidelity “comparable” to discrete-element methods [f6097, f6463]. nodes.label: ASAM OpenSCENARIO
nodes.text: ASAM OpenSCENARIO
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OpenSCENARIO describes scenarios, while OpenDRIVE describes roads; OpenSCENARIO has an XML form [f16017, f13010]. The booklet recommends keeping the scenario catalog in a manufacturer-owned, domain-neutral, version-controlled Scenic or in-house YAML representation, then exporting to OpenSCENARIO for tools that require it [f14491, f7204]. Tool support spans VTD, the dSPACE chain, CARLA, RoadRunner, Prescan and MORAI, with native support specifically reported for VTD ScenarioEngine [f16017, f9200]. An open co-simulation demo combines OpenSCENARIO and OSI with OpenMATERIAL 3D and a physical lidar model, illustrating use beyond catalog exchange [f3981]. OpenSCENARIO, OpenDRIVE and OSI are described as open, free and ongoing, but their road heritage is a scope caveat for heavy off-road applications; the supplied facts give no version numbers or release dates [f9214, f9217, f9218, f9215].

nodes.label: ASAM OpenDRIVE
nodes.text: ASAM OpenDRIVE
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OpenDRIVE describes roads and is built around a road-traffic domain model; version 1.9.0 is dated May 2026 [f16017, f6691, f7156]. Across chapters and the glossary, its road-network and lane-geometry assumptions are identified as a poor fit for unstructured off-road sites, with suitability for lane-less haul roads remaining a known gap [f3982, f7157, f8617, f16018]. This is not a blanket rejection: OpenDRIVE can model haul roads and structured site roads, and the recommendation is to use it for structured haul-road elements where useful, while providing additional representations for dig faces, stockpiles and free terrain [f7158, f7202]. OpenDRIVE and OpenSCENARIO have support across VTD, the dSPACE chain, CARLA, RoadRunner, Prescan and MORAI, although that tool support does not resolve the stated off-road representation gap [f8616, f16017, f7157]. OpenDRIVE is listed as an open, free standard with ongoing release status [f9214, f9217, f9218].

nodes.label: XLD
nodes.text: XLD
nodes.synopsis: XLD is an on-road benchmark introduced in a June 2024 preprint, with a 2025 v3 using synthetic CARLA data; Chapter 7 cites it as evidence of a significant neural-reconstruction gap at cross-lane viewpoint offsets of 1–4 m [f4001, f5515]. Reported 3DGS PSNR fell from 30.87 dB at zero lateral shift to 23.26, 22.01 and 19.17 dB at shifts of 1, 2 and 4 m, respectively [f4001]. At 4 m, EmerNeRF achieved the best PSNR, 24.80 dB, and EmerNeRF and UC-NeRF held up better than the 3DGS variant PVG, creating tension with industry preference for 3DGS editability [f4002, f4329]. Three cameras substantially reduced the reported drop compared with one camera, indicating that camera configuration affects the benchmark outcome [f4024]. Across chapters, XLD supports caution about off-trajectory neural re-simulation despite proponents’ enthusiasm; its findings align with other benchmarks on viewpoint-change degradation, but the cited evidence remains on-road or urban rather than off-road [f5785, f4289].

nodes.label: Algoryx AGX Dynamics
nodes.text: Algoryx AGX Dynamics
nodes.synopsis: Algoryx AGX Dynamics is a machinery-physics engine covering terrain, tires, tracks, hydraulics and granular material; the booklet positions such tools as strong in terrain and hydraulics but thin in sensor and scenario tooling [f16204, f15965, f8283]. Independent validation evidence includes a 2024 wheel-loader digging model that required a tire-ground friction coefficient of 2.0 to match measurements, with remaining errors attributed to tire-pressure modeling and a flat-ground assumption, and a peer-reviewed 2025 wheel-loader digital-twin calibration including terrain parameters [f6090, f6091, f8292]. Unity and Unreal integration is supported, TERA demonstrates a Unity/AGX excavator simulator with ROS integration, and an April 2025 Unity example added reverse automatic braking with lidar; the latest release found in the comparison was AGXUnity 5.5.1, dated 20 January 2026 [f8703, f4129, f15967, f9112]. The proposed middle-cost stack couples AGX via FMI for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants, but FMI support was explicitly not verified, leaving that integration assumption unresolved [f9286, f9111]. Licensing is commercial, with yearly per-seat Basic, Custom and Premium subscriptions priced on request and separate runtime, OEM and academic licenses [f8575].

nodes.label: Unreal Engine
nodes.text: Unreal Engine
nodes.synopsis: Unreal Engine appears as an environment-creation platform across Falcon, CARLA and MathWorks; their editors are described as domain-neutral, with differing licenses, prices and latest releases [f8358, f9157, f9158, f9160, f9161]. CARLA 0.10.0 migrated to Unreal Engine 5.5 with Chaos physics on 19 December 2024 and included a mining earth-mover asset, while CARLA 0.9.16 was subsequently released on the Unreal Engine 4 line on 16 September 2025 [f8464, f8297, f8466]. MathWorks supports construction, mining and agriculture applications through Unreal scenes exposing camera, lidar and INS, while AGX Dynamics offers Unreal and Unity plugins [f8374, f8380, f8571]. Chapter 5 reports a 2023 Unreal-based excavator perception pipeline, but identifies all its listed construction and excavation examples as camera-centric, limiting their evidence for broader sensor validation [f4132, f4137]. The recommended middle-cost stack combines Unreal with MATLAB/Simulink and off-road tooling, with Mevea or AGX coupled through FMI for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants; establishing capability also requires dynamics, sensor, automation and safety expertise beyond rendering skills [f9285, f16162, f8773].

nodes.text: MATLAB
nodes.synopsis: The corpus positions MATLAB/Simulink with the Offroad Autonomy Library and RoadRunner as a complete or near-complete commercial simulation platform, licensed annually or perpetually per product [f8346, f8373, f15877]. Shipped R2026b examples cover an autonomous excavator, a backhoe loading a truck and an open-pit haul truck; Volvo CE also built a human-in-the-loop excavator simulator on the MathWorks platform [f15878, f15879]. An expert-proposed middle-cost chain combines MATLAB/Simulink, RoadRunner, Unreal and sensor toolboxes with Mevea or AGX Dynamics through FMI for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants [f16162]. Integration evidence includes MAVS in February 2024 and MATLAB APIs for Prescan; RoadRunner Scenario and replay workflows also list MATLAB interfaces, although RoadRunner itself does not require MATLAB or Simulink [f4163, f8458, f9195, f9252, f8385]. Public platform pricing is quote-only: an unofficial January 2024 list gives MATLAB prices of 980 annually or 3,920 perpetually, presumed US dollars and indicative only, rather than a confirmed platform budget [f15880, f8387, f16142].

nodes.synopsis: RELLIS-3D and ORAD-3D (2025) were used with Ground4D for off-road reconstruction [f4167]. A 2023 comparison of MAVS-simulated and real RELLIS-3D data for segmentation showed large domain-shift effects, highlighting a limitation in transferring simulated results to real off-road data [f4741, f12817]. RELLIS-3D is identified as a machine-mounted off-road dataset, but the research did not verify it or the other listed datasets [f5849, f12815]. No validation for off-road collision warning was found for these datasets or the listed open-source simulators; reconstruction use and segmentation comparisons therefore do not establish collision-warning validation [f4167, f4741, f5851, f12816].

nodes.label: SLAM
nodes.text: SLAM
nodes.synopsis: SLAM is one of three approaches presented for measuring real sites in three dimensions, using a moving machine’s own sensors rather than overlapping photographs or laser distance measurements [f13133]. The booklet treats it as a method in its own right because a large installed fleet can supply recordings for site-model acquisition [f13140]. Machine-log reconstruction using classical SLAM, SfM and meshing requires synchronised cameras, lidar, IMU and GNSS, together with calibration [f4216]. A key limitation is visibility bias in forward-facing route logs: they do not observe stockpile backs or upper surfaces that a taller future sensor could see, leaving gaps in the reconstructed site [f13141].

nodes.label: covering arrays
nodes.text: covering arrays
nodes.synopsis: Covering arrays reduce large discrete configuration spaces while retaining interaction coverage; the proposed use is machine-by-sensor-by-weather-by-scenario configuration testing [f4332, f6818, f7233]. They can establish that every t-tuple of discrete values was tested at least once, but cannot establish coverage of interactions above t, continuous regions, or rates [f7234, f7235]. NIST provides an independent evidence base, but evidence that most bugs involve low-order interactions comes from software, and transfer to perception remains unproven [f7238, f7236]. Safety engineers therefore should not assume low-order combinations are sufficient for off-road collision avoidance [f4332]. Available tooling includes NIST ACTS, PICT and commercial test-design tools [f7237].

nodes.label: ISO 3691-4
nodes.synopsis: ISO 3691-4:2023 covers driverless industrial trucks and their systems; Chapter 12 identifies it as current, with a draft international standard for Edition 3 in progress [f15281, f9783]. The glossary places it alongside neighboring-sector standards, describing its scope as driverless warehouse trucks rather than heavy off-road machines [f15276]. Chapter 12 and the glossary report that no simulation provisions were found, while a separate Chapter 12 finding reports no wording on virtual-only validation; these are review gaps, not evidence of permission for virtual-only validation [f9784, f15282, f9459]. The booklet reports revision activity in 2025–2026 and recommends allowing the validation plan to be re-baselined, while explaining that the published edition remains in force during revision [f10368, f10369, f15054]. There is an unresolved verification gap across chapters: Chapter 5 says the standard was not verified and calls for checking editions, application dates and simulation clauses before reliance, whereas Chapter 12 identifies the current edition and reports review findings [f4335, f9783, f9784].

nodes.label: NASA-STD-7009
nodes.text: NASA-STD-7009
nodes.synopsis: NASA-STD-7009B is presented as the current models-and-simulations standard, approved on 5 March 2024, with its companion handbook finalized on 3 February 2026 [f14606, f7604, f7613]. The booklet recommends its credibility scale for the collision-mitigation toolchain and treats it as an internal-board governance template, not an off-road regulation or certification rule [f9433, f8070, f14612]. Credibility is decision-specific: criticality determines the required effort, factors are rated separately from 0 to 4 with thresholds declared in advance, and overall credibility must not be reduced to one scalar [f7606, f14588, f14609, f8068]. Validation must address the real application rather than internal consistency; validation Level 4 requires all outputs to compare favorably with real-system data across the full operating range in the real environment, but the framework does not prescribe a numerical quantity of physical evidence [f10755, f7608, f8069]. Decision-maker reports must include the best estimate, uncertainty, factor-by-factor credibility, caveats on use beyond model limits, and the risk of accepting the result; the final plan should include a model credibility plan and assessment in Appendix D [f14610, f10185]. Applicability remains qualified: a 2026 proposal adapts the framework for on-road automated-driving simulation, but it is not proven for off-road automatic braking, and Chapter 5's statement that the standard was unverified is in tension with later dated descriptions and recommendations [f4832, f8071, f4336, f7604, f9433].

nodes.label: SET Level
nodes.text: SET Level
nodes.synopsis: SET Level is an on-road automated-driving research programme whose consortium published the Credible Simulation Process in August 2021; Chapter 7 also gives a broader 2021–2024 dating for the prostep ivip and SET Level process [f15692, f14592, f5216]. The process embeds simulation credibility in product development, scales credibility to simulation-task criticality, and addresses physical-data validation and transfer through process-level documentation [f15703, f8126, f8127]. For off-road automatic braking, the booklet treats it only as a process template: it is not proven for that application and does not specify the physical evidence still required [f8129, f8130, f8128, f15704]. Chapter 5 says SET Level was not verified in the research and calls for checks before reliance, while Chapter 11 reports agreement on the need for validation but no agreement on metrics [f4336, f9357]. For planning, the booklet recommends borrowing SET Level and related on-road programmes as a schedule reference class, noting that building validation capability took years in every documented case [f9614, f15717, f15713].

nodes.synopsis: South African regulations under the Mine Health and Safety Act covering trackless mobile machinery (TMM) automatic braking were published in 2015 and entered into force on 21 December 2022, with no transitional period [f11454]. For a diesel-powered TMM heading for a collision, the regulations require slowing to a safe speed and then automatic braking if the operator takes no action [f11455]. The collision prevention system must also fail to safe without human intervention, a requirement repeated in Chapter 5 [f11456, f4338]. Chapter 5's expert opinion identifies this fail-safe requirement as making test evidence commercially material [f4338].

nodes.synopsis: Siemens Simcenter appears in two distinct validation roles: vendor sensor-model validation using XenomatiX lidar BSDF, and full multibody machine modelling [f4342, f6454]. The cited sensor-model validations cover on-road targets, leaving their applicability to off-road targets unestablished by these facts [f4342]. Full multibody models with contact and a detailed plant support machine dynamics, actuator and failure analysis, and real-time co-simulation; Simcenter is among the commercial options listed [f6454]. nodes.label: Mie theory
nodes.text: Mie theory
nodes.synopsis: Mie theory contributes to lidar weather simulation through scattering-derived coefficients, alongside Beer–Lambert attenuation and probabilistic placement of droplets or flakes that produce false or lost returns [f4507]. Haider et al. extended a ray-traced lidar model with Mie-theory rain and fog backscatter in August 2023; this evidence is on-road [f4506]. The model matched weather-chamber measurements well at low rain rates, but mismatch increased with rain rate and depended strongly on the assumed drop-size distribution [f4413, f4414]. Chapter 8 also describes a Mie-theory rain and fog lidar model packaged as an Open Simulation Interface functional mock-up unit in Sensors work published in 2023, again with on-road evidence rather than demonstrated heavy off-road validation [f6381].

nodes.label: ray tracing
nodes.text: ray tracing
nodes.synopsis: Ray tracing follows light, radio or sound rays through virtual scenes and is central to physics-based sensor modelling; ray-traced lidar using the actual scan pattern and signal chain is identified as the best-validated sensor-model type [f12952, f12955, f4502]. For radar, RadaRays, published in 2025, found that one-hit models missed multipath and material behaviour, while ray-traced material models achieved much closer agreement with real images; an on-road study also concluded that the complete signal-processing toolchain and sensor-specific impairments must be included [f4531, f4529]. Full-wave simulation of an entire quarry or mine is impractical, so engineering simulators combine approximations, ray tracing and statistical electronics models [f4536]. The glossary identifies ray tracing as the most promising route to trusted models for untested machines or mounting positions because it responds causally to scene and sensor changes, but this transfer capability depends on known materials and sensor internals [f12957, f12964, f12958]. Important limitations remain: a 77 GHz on-road study had to estimate material parameters because reliable values were lacking, and ray-tracing errors grow in heavy precipitation [f4530, f12959].

nodes.label: Haider et al.
nodes.text: Haider et al.
nodes.synopsis: Haider et al. built a tool-independent, ray-traced lidar model incorporating the scan pattern and full signal-processing chain, packaged as an ASAM OSI/FMI unit [f4504]. Chapter 6 dates validation at both time-domain and point-cloud levels to October 2022, and the rain and fog extension using Mie-theory backscatter to August 2023 [f4505, f4506]. Chapter 10 identifies a peer-reviewed rain and fog model published in Sensors 23(15):6891 in August 2023, also validated at time-domain and point-cloud levels [f7819]. All cited validation evidence is on-road; these facts do not establish validation for heavy off-road machines or clarify whether the October 2022 validation covered the later weather extension [f4505, f4506, f7819].

nodes.label: FMI
nodes.text: FMI
nodes.synopsis: FMI is presented as integration glue for simulation tool chains, alongside other standards, with about 250 supporting tools by mid-2025 [f8335, f8336]. A concrete cross-chapter example is Haider et al.’s tool-independent ray-traced lidar model, incorporating scan patterns and the full signal-processing chain and packaged as an ASAM OSI/FMI unit [f4504]. The vendor survey lists FMI for IPG’s CarMaker, TruckMaker and off-highway offerings, while MathWorks provides FMI through partners such as Mevea; Mevea supports Simulink co-simulation through TCP/IP or FMI [f8992, f8383, f8562]. To mitigate supplier dependence and ownership changes, the corpus recommends requiring FMI and other specified export capabilities, plus ownership-change exit clauses [f8887]. Coverage is not fully verified: FMI support for Algoryx AGX Dynamics remains unconfirmed [f9110].

nodes.label: NVIDIA RTX
nodes.text: NVIDIA RTX
nodes.synopsis: NVIDIA RTX is a consumer and workstation graphics-card line with dedicated ray-tracing cores; vendor RTX sensor-simulation platforms use GPU ray tracing with material interaction [f16194, f4928]. One vendor claims its current RTX lidar implementation accounts for transparent and reflective surfaces, but no neutral benchmark applicable to the collision-mitigation validation program was found [f4510, f4929]. The tools chapter reports vendor claims that open-source platforms combining Unreal Engine 5 rendering and RTX sensors exist and are free for internal use [f9336, f9337]. The lowest-cost example chain uses on-premises RTX GPUs or spot cloud computing, with the glossary additionally describing scenario scripts or Scenic and J1939 emulation to ISO/TS 21815-2 [f9268, f16159]. For this lowest-cost open-source-core chain, the manufacturer must characterize RTX sensor performance issues, leaving validation responsibility with the manufacturer despite the available platforms and vendor capabilities claimed [f9282, f4929, f4510].

nodes.label: RadaRays
nodes.text: RadaRays
nodes.synopsis: RadaRays, published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters in 2025, is a real-time radar ray tracer tested with a Navtech CIR radar on a wheel loader in a hall; the booklet identifies this as its most directly relevant heavy-machine radar evidence [f4531, f4532, f15952]. Material-aware reflection modelling substantially improved synthetic-image agreement over a lidar-like model, but the hall required hand-built geometry and tuned materials, and some real double reflections remained missing [f4531, f4824, f4716, f4717, f4962]. Improved image similarity did not deliver a comparable odometry improvement, and an R-CNN trained on real RADIATE data missed most cars in simulated images, partly because target material properties had to be guessed [f5082, f4747, f4855]. These results support evaluating fidelity against the intended downstream function rather than treating image similarity as sufficient evidence of detection or closed-loop intervention performance [f5083, f5084]. Runtime was 7.8–18.8 ms per polar image on an RTX 2070 Super versus 25.8–78.5 ms on a Ryzen 7 3800X CPU over 80,000–400,000 initial rays, limited to the tested radar, model and scene; automatic mesh reconstruction also introduced scanner-occluding artifacts and meshes too large to clean manually [f4936, f4937, f4963, f4964].

nodes.label: Continental
nodes.text: Continental
nodes.synopsis: Continental appears in the sensor-validation evidence through Schmoll et al. (2024), which compared an ultrasonic model in CarMaker with a real Continental sensor; this was the only ultrasonic simulation validation found in the corpus [f4761, f4575]. The study included IPG Automotive and Continental authors, creating a tension between its “Independent on-road” label and the explicit conclusion that it is a published technical study rather than vendor-independent evidence [f4575, f4576]. Separately, Continental is a documented automotive collaborator for AVxcelerate Sensors, but that collaboration does not establish off-road performance [f8536]. These facts therefore offer on-road technical validation and collaboration evidence, not demonstrated off-road performance or vendor-independent validation [f4575, f4576, f8536].

nodes.label: IPG CarMaker
nodes.text: IPG CarMaker
nodes.synopsis: CarMaker/TruckMaker and IPG’s off-highway stack are commercial, near-complete simulation offerings targeting construction, agriculture and mining, with closed-loop vehicle, driver, environment and sensor simulation for MIL/SIL/HIL/VIL [f8347, f15894, f8436, f8989]. The stack supports camera, radar, lidar and other environment sensors plus actuator and ECU coupling; it fits rigid-vehicle and system dynamics well, but high-fidelity deformable soil and particle interaction are not its main role [f8440, f8443]. Vendor-claimed off-highway applications include Linde lidar accident prevention and tractor vehicle-in-the-loop, but independent evidence for severe dust, snow or glare on heavy machines was not found [f15893, f8444]. The only ultrasonic simulation validation found was Schmoll et al. (2024), comparing a CarMaker model against a real Continental sensor; although labeled independent on-road evidence, it included IPG and Continental authors, and publicly accessible details do not establish performance across the requested heavy-off-road weather and soiling matrix [f4761, f4575, f4577]. Integration routes include AVxcelerate Sensors co-simulation and RoadRunner environment exports, although RoadRunner’s base editor remains road-oriented [f15946, f15999, f8701]. The latest CarMaker release found was version 15.0, dated 2025; IPG offers consulting and engineering, but public prices and CarMaker frame rates were not found [f8994, f8806, f8993, f4957].

nodes.label: CEREMA
nodes.text: CEREMA
nodes.synopsis: CEREMA is one of four named weather-test facilities providing the main ground truth for weather models and, together with proving grounds, sensor-model validation [f5056, f5119]. The glossary specifically identifies fog chambers at CEREMA, CARISSMA, NIED and JARI as sources of ground truth for sensor models [f15594]. Fog is the best-reproduced condition for lidar, with chambers at CEREMA, CARISSMA and JARI providing on-road evidence [f4640]. However, the research did not examine booking lead times, capacity or suitability for heavy off-road machines of the size in scope; these unresolved access questions directly affect model validation before mid-2027 [f5120].

nodes.label: CARISSMA
nodes.text: CARISSMA
nodes.synopsis: CARISSMA in Germany is named alongside CEREMA, NIED and JARI as a main source of ground truth for weather models and, together with proving grounds, for validating sensor models [f16122, f5056, f5119]. The booklet identifies fog chambers at these facilities as sources of sensor-model ground truth; fog is described as the best-reproduced condition for lidar, with CARISSMA, CEREMA and JARI providing on-road evidence [f15594, f4640]. Haider et al. (2023) studied lidar rain and fog at NIED and CARISSMA [f4731]. However, the research did not establish facility booking lead times, capacity or suitability for heavy off-road machines of the relevant size, leaving access questions that directly affect validation before mid-2027 [f16124, f5120].

nodes.label: JARI
nodes.text: JARI
nodes.synopsis: JARI in Japan is named alongside CEREMA, CARISSMA and NIED as a main source of ground truth for weather models; weather chambers at these institutions, together with proving grounds, underpin sensor-model validation [f5056, f16122, f5119]. Fog is the best-reproduced condition for lidar, with JARI, CEREMA and CARISSMA fog chambers providing on-road evidence [f4640]. However, the booklet did not examine facility booking lead times, capacity or suitability for heavy off-road machines of the size in scope, leaving practical access and applicability unresolved [f16124, f5120]. These access questions directly affect model validation before mid-2027 [f5120].

nodes.label: MAPE
nodes.text: MAPE
nodes.synopsis: MAPE is one of several metrics used to assess simulation agreement, specifically for sensor-signal models; other options include safety-quantity errors, time-history errors and distribution comparisons [f7553]. Sensor-model validation can apply MAPE to time-domain amplitude, point count and intensity, alongside separate checks of range accuracy, RCS correlation, attenuation and SNR [f4793]. Chapters 6 and 10 both report a 1.7% lidar signal-amplitude MAPE from independent on-road evidence published in 2022; Chapter 10 identifies the model as clear-weather automotive lidar [f4728, f7824]. Chapter 6 also reports 8.5% MAPE for point count and 9.3% for mean intensity, so the low amplitude error should not be treated as representative of every lidar output [f4728, f4729]. The cited numerical evidence is on-road, and these facts do not establish corresponding MAPE performance for heavy off-road machines or adverse weather [f4728, f4729, f7824].

nodes.label: SSIM
nodes.text: SSIM
nodes.synopsis: SSIM is an image- or field-similarity metric used for sensor-model validation and requires pixel-matched pairs [f4802]. It assesses appearance and structure rather than the behavior of perception and decision software [f14791]. A physics-based radar simulator dramatically improved structural-similarity and mutual-information scores, yet a detector trained only on real radar data failed to detect most cars in the simulated images [f14793]. This result highlights a validation gap: improved similarity scores alone do not establish that simulated sensor data will support successful perception [f14791, f14793].

nodes.label: FID
nodes.text: FID
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 6 presents FID, alongside KID, as a distribution-level image- or field-similarity metric for sensor-model validation [f4803]. The 2024 Instance Performance Difference paper warns that FID does not target any specific perception algorithm, a limitation also recorded in the glossary [f4819, f14796]. Whether FID, Chamfer distance or DCD predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain, so the corpus does not establish FID similarity as evidence of safety-relevant perception performance [f5067].

nodes.label: mutual information
nodes.text: mutual information
nodes.synopsis: Mutual information measures how much knowing one image tells you about another and is useful for radar maps [f14772]. Chapter 6 lists it among distribution-level similarity metrics for sensor-model validation, alongside FID, KID, texture and entropy measures [f4803]. RadaRays’ physics-based radar model dramatically improved mutual-information and structural-similarity scores relative to a lidar-like model [f4824]. However, a detector trained only on real radar data still failed to detect most cars in the simulated images, showing that improved similarity scores did not establish successful detector transfer [f14776, f14793].

nodes.label: dSPACE AURELION
nodes.text: dSPACE AURELION
nodes.synopsis: dSPACE AURELION with SIMPHERA is a commercial simulation platform with on-road-only evidence; the corpus found no public validation of quarry or mining terrain, material or weather fidelity, and terrain physics must come from elsewhere [f8445, f8454, f8455, f15895]. Vendor-described capabilities include real-time camera, ray-traced radar, lidar, infrared and ultrasonic simulation, sensor effects and a material database, available locally or in the cloud for SIL/HIL; however, frame-rate figures were not found [f8446, f4957]. Integration with SCALEXIO, VEOS, ASM and ModelDesk provides a route from SIL to HIL, but sensor injection remains sensor- and ECU-specific rather than a uniform interface task [f8448, f8640, f8641]. The latest AURELION release found was 26.2, dated 15 July 2026; version 25.3 added lidar beam divergence and Hesai models and requires maintenance valid through at least 31 August 2025, while new versions generally require valid maintenance [f9057, f8449, f8450, f16152]. Pricing is quote-only, with no public AURELION/SIMPHERA or full-system price found; the highest-cost example chain combines commercial validation, specialist sensors, external heavy-machine dynamics, benches and cloud execution [f8541, f8453, f8642, f16166, f16167].

nodes.label: ASAM QSQ
nodes.text: ASAM QSQ
nodes.synopsis: ASAM QSQ is a standardization project seeking measurable simulation-quality metrics; it was at proposal stage in September 2025, with a proposal workshop held on 11 September 2025 [f14591, f5218, f14599]. The cited project is dated 2025, and the corpus consistently describes it as emerging, under development and unfinished in 2026 [f8325, f5585, f5073, f14591, f14599]. QSQ identifies a lack of standardized metrics for assessing simulation frameworks and models, particularly sensor simulation; the wider credibility communities agree validation is required but have not agreed on metrics [f8952, f9357]. The booklet includes QSQ among its main simulation-credibility references, but characterizes these frameworks as on-road and pre-standard and explicitly says QSQ is not proven off-road [f8323, f14600].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 7 identifies a Credible Simulation Process associated with prostep ivip and SET Level, dating from 2021 to 2024 [f5216]. It also dates the prostep ivip Simulation Credibility paper to 2024 [f5583]. The glossary corroborates that publication year, identifies the paper as version 8.1, and lists it as related work on the Credible Simulation Process [f14593]. The supplied facts establish this process-and-publication connection but do not describe its application to validating the braking system [f5216, f5583, f14593].

nodes.label: Credible Simulation Process
nodes.text: Credible Simulation Process
nodes.synopsis: SET Level published the Credible Simulation Process in August 2021; related work includes prostep ivip’s Simulation Credibility technical paper, version 8.1, dated 2024 [f14592, f14593]. The method embeds credibility activities throughout product development, including task definition, evidence planning, assumption recording, verification and validation, and credibility information accompanying models [f7697, f14594]. Credibility levels scale with the criticality of the simulation task, and the process is cited in a 2025 Sensors paper on continuous verification and validation of active-perception sensor simulations [f15703, f8949]. Alongside M&S SPICE, it addresses validation against physical data and transfer through credibility documentation, but does not specify what physical evidence remains necessary [f8126, f8127, f8128]. For off-road automatic braking, the booklet therefore treats it as a process template, not a proven method [f8129, f8130, f15704].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 7 cites Li et al. at CVPR 2024 for documenting an open-loop failure mode in systems that act [f5244]. Chapter 8 cites two Li et al. papers from 2016 and a related lateral-stability paper from 2013 for articulated-wheel-loader models using 7 and 8 degrees of freedom, Fiala tire models and active braking, with roll instability treated as the critical mode [f6032]. The loader models were validated against a scaled wheel loader and then applied to a ZL50 machine; active braking was modeled as an influence on wheel-loader roll [f6033, f6290]. The supplied facts establish separate contributions to testing methodology and machine dynamics, but do not establish that the CVPR authors and the loader-model authors are the same people or directly connect their findings [f5244, f6032, f6033, f6290].

nodes.label: CAN bus
nodes.text: CAN bus
nodes.synopsis: CAN or J1939 is a source for recording machine state at adequate rate and precision, covering motion, braking, propulsion, automation, engine state and payload, plus implement positions where relevant [f5634]. Recorded CAN or J1939 traffic can also be used for hardware-in-the-loop data injection alongside camera RAW-data and radar detection-level injection [f5281]. Changes to CAN or J1939 interfaces without impact analysis are identified as early warnings that prototype changes may invalidate the pre-built simulator; one account specifies the second quarter of 2027, while another refers to 2027 generally [f10761, f11028]. The recording requirement does not specify numerical rate or precision thresholds, and the injection method does not establish that recorded traffic alone provides adequate coverage [f5634, f5281].

nodes.synopsis: MOSH verification progresses from laboratory testing to Gerotek proving-ground tests and then to a cordoned mine area [f5350]. Under Verification Regime Rev 1 dated 11 October 2025, the controller test evaluates automatic slowdown and stopping effectiveness using light vehicles in a controlled proving-ground environment; the supplied facts do not establish equivalent testing on heavy machines [f5351, f5352]. Bench requirements include detecting a detection-device–machine disconnection within 500 ms and receiving a machine reply within 50 ms [f13351, f13352]. Warning-zone extension uses an operator reaction time of 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention [f13902]. Specified stop gaps are 1.0–4.0 meters at speeds of 10 km/h or less, and 15 ± 5 meters above 10 km/h [f13907].

nodes.synopsis: UN R159 (2021) concerns on-road moving-off information systems that warn truck drivers about pedestrians and cyclists in front of the truck [f5355, f15403, f15389]. The booklet cites its small-cylinder visibility method and tests with road users moving at 3–5 km/h; however, the reported 50 mm cylinder dimension was not confirmed against the regulation text [f5356, f5357, f15404]. Chapter 7 uses the small-cylinder method as an on-road illustration of geometric coverage and blind-zone assessment, an approach supported by expert opinion [f5603, f5604]. The glossary proposes reproducing this method alongside ISO 5006 and ISO 16001 visibility-type methods in each machine’s digital twin before hardware arrives, while Chapter 7 also lists R159 targets among options for ground-truth testing [f15220, f5385].

nodes.label: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods
nodes.text: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods
nodes.synopsis: For comparing the old and new systems, the NIST statistical handbook ties sample size to the performance difference or confidence precision that must be resolved [f5449]. It also provides exact-binomial and Wilson intervals when normal approximations fail, including small samples and probabilities near 0 or 1 [f5450]. For combination coverage and tuning, the handbook documents fractional factorial, screening, response-surface and D-optimal designs [f6804]. Response-surface designs fit local models and optimise a process after influential factors have been identified, while desirability functions combine several responses [f6967, f6968]. The supplied facts establish methodological options but give no selected sample size or application-specific design [f5449, f6804].

nodes.label: Wilson interval
nodes.text: Wilson interval
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 7 identifies Wilson intervals, alongside exact-binomial intervals, as methods provided by NIST for situations where normal approximations fail, including small samples and probabilities near 0 or 1 [f5450]. Chapter 9 describes Wilson intervals as less conservative than Clopper-Pearson and better behaved at moderate sample sizes [f6893]. The glossary retains Clopper-Pearson as the conservative default when misses occur, while naming Wilson as a less conservative alternative at moderate sample sizes [f14211]. The supplied facts give no numerical sample-size threshold for choosing Wilson over Clopper-Pearson [f5450, f6893, f14211].

nodes.label: Clopper-Pearson interval
nodes.text: Clopper-Pearson interval
nodes.synopsis: For detection trials with misses, the booklet recommends Clopper-Pearson exact binomial intervals or another pre-declared binomial interval, rather than continuing testing until a desirable percentage appears [f5452, f6891, f14196]. Clopper-Pearson is described as exact and conservative, making it the safe default for regulators; Wilson is a less conservative alternative that behaves better at moderate sample sizes [f6892, f6893, f14211]. The detection sample-size table allows one or two failures using what the text calls a Poisson or Clopper-Pearson approximation, leaving a terminology tension with the description of Clopper-Pearson as exact [f6884, f6892]. These are mature, non-automotive-specific statistical techniques, but their direct applicability requires respecting independence, representative sampling and homogeneous-rate assumptions [f7398, f7399].

nodes.label: Homogeneous Poisson process
nodes.text: Homogeneous Poisson process
nodes.synopsis: Chapters 7 and 9 and the glossary agree that, assuming a homogeneous Poisson process, zero false alarms over T hours gives a one-sided upper event-rate bound of −ln(alpha)/T, approximately 3/T at 95% confidence [f5456, f6907, f14243, f6908]. Under that assumption, zero unnecessary automatic brakes in about 300 representative operating hours supports a rate below 1 per 100 hours at 95% confidence; about 3,000 hours supports below 1 per 1,000 hours [f6909, f6910]. If two events occur instead, Chapter 9 gives a 95% upper rate bound of about 6.3/T [f6911]. These assurances are conditional: false alarms can cluster by site, weather, machine, obstacle geometry, contamination, bucket passes or dust clouds, and can be non-stationary, so the homogeneous-Poisson assumption must be checked before relying on the bound [f5459, f6913, f6915].

nodes.label: Kalra
nodes.text: Kalra
nodes.synopsis: Kalra and Paddock’s RAND report Driving to Safety was published in April 2016, with Chapter 7 specifying 12 April; its identifier appears as RR-1478 in Chapter 7 and RR-1478-RC in Chapter 9 [f5464, f6920]. The analysis required 275 million failure-free miles to establish, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% fatality-rate improvement with 80% power [f6662, f6663]. The glossary summarizes the broader burden as hundreds of millions to sometimes hundreds of billions of road miles, taking existing fleets tens or sometimes hundreds of years [f15812, f14264]. Chapter 12 uses this statistical burden to justify virtual testing because driving tests alone cannot demonstrate safety at low failure rates; the cited finding concerns road vehicles, not a demonstrated off-road validation result [f9755].

nodes.label: Paddock
nodes.text: Paddock
nodes.synopsis: Paddock co-authored RAND’s Driving to Safety with Kalra; the corpus dates it to April 2016, with Chapter 7 specifying 12 April 2016 [f5464, f6920]. Its analysis required 275 million failure-free miles to show, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement with 80% power [f6662, f6663]. The glossary summarizes the broader requirements as hundreds of millions and sometimes hundreds of billions of road miles, taking existing fleets tens and sometimes hundreds of years [f15812, f14264]. Chapter 12 uses these on-road findings as the statistical rationale for virtual testing, concluding that driving tests alone cannot demonstrate safety at low failure rates; the supplied facts do not establish equivalent mileage requirements for heavy off-road machines [f9755, f6662, f6663].

nodes.label: McNemar's test
nodes.text: McNemar's test
nodes.synopsis: The booklet uses McNemar's test to compare the old and new warning systems using paired hazard-level hit-or-miss results [f14232, f5481]. Chapter 7 and the glossary require parallel recording on the same machine so both systems encounter the same hazards; separate deployments confound site, operator and weather [f5481, f14233, f14236, f14356]. Only discordant pairs inform the test: hazards caught by both systems or missed by both do not contribute to the comparison [f14234]. The illustrative comparison has 12 hazards caught only by the new system versus 3 caught only by the old, testing whether this imbalance exceeds chance; the supplied facts do not report a test result or significance conclusion [f14235].

nodes.label: RUGD
nodes.text: RUGD
nodes.synopsis: RUGD is identified as a machine-mounted off-road dataset alongside RELLIS-3D [f12815]. Chapter 7 states that RUGD, RELLIS-3D, GOOSE and TartanDrive were not verified in this research [f5849]. Both Chapter 7 and the glossary report that no validation for off-road collision warning was found for these datasets; Chapter 7 extends that finding to CARLA, Gazebo and Isaac Sim [f5851, f12816]. The corpus therefore leaves RUGD’s suitability for off-road collision-warning validation unestablished, rather than demonstrating that it is unsuitable [f5849, f5851, f12816].

nodes.label: GOOSE
nodes.text: GOOSE
nodes.synopsis: GOOSE is listed among the off-road datasets considered in the research, but its status was not verified [f5849, f12815]. Chapter 7 and the glossary both report that no validation for off-road collision warning was found for GOOSE and the other listed datasets [f5851, f12816]. This is a gap in the research evidence, not proof that GOOSE is unsuitable; the glossary also distinguishes the explicitly identified machine-mounted datasets RELLIS-3D and RUGD from the unverified listings GOOSE and TartanDrive [f5849, f12815, f12816].

nodes.label: TartanDrive
nodes.text: TartanDrive
nodes.synopsis: TartanDrive is listed among the machine-mounted off-road datasets considered in Chapter 7, but it was not verified in this research [f5849]. The glossary preserves that qualification, listing TartanDrive and GOOSE without claiming they were verified [f12815]. No validation for off-road collision warning was found for TartanDrive or the other listed datasets; Chapter 7 extends this finding to the listed open-source simulators as well [f12816, f5851]. These are limits of the research findings, not proof that TartanDrive cannot support off-road collision-warning validation [f5849, f5851, f12816].

nodes.label: Gazebo
nodes.text: Gazebo
nodes.synopsis: Gazebo is a free, Apache 2.0 open-source robotics simulator providing physics, rendering, camera, lidar, IMU and plugin-defined sensors, with supported ROS 2 integration [f15915, f8525, f8526, f8708]. Release information lists Jetty LTS from September 2025 with support to 2031, and Gazebo Sim 10.5.0 released on 29 July 2026 [f9051, f8528]. The proposed lowest-cost open-source chain uses Gazebo or alternatives for sensors and environments, Chrono for machine dynamics and SCM terrain, and ROS 2; low license costs come with high internal labor and remaining hardware and cloud costs [f16158, f16128, f8739]. Expert opinion characterizes Gazebo as an integration framework requiring extensions for automotive-grade radar, weather, material modeling and enterprise validation management [f8529]. The research did not verify Gazebo or find off-road collision-warning validation, off-road evidence or heavy-machine automatic-braking proof, so its listed capabilities do not establish suitability for this validation task [f5850, f5851, f9047, f8530]. Despite the stated release-support horizon, project funding, maintenance and security-patch cadence were not examined [f15931, f9392, f9393].

nodes.label: MSHA Table M-1
nodes.text: MSHA Table M-1
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 8 and the glossary describe MSHA Table M-1 as a kinematic stopping-performance rule based on constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s², approximately 2.94 m/s² or 0.3 g [f5890, f13634, f6425]. Its stopping-distance formulation uses d = v²/(2a), and the assumed deceleration is close to the worked example’s 3.0 m/s² level-ground value [f13645, f13650]. Chapter 8 gives system-response allowances of 0.5–2.5 seconds by weight class, plus one second of operator time; the glossary gives a two-second total delay for very heavy equipment, contributing 8.3 metres at 15 km/h, without explaining how that total maps to the weight-class allowances [f6058, f13658]. The corpus also describes prescribed stopping tests as running from brake-control actuation to standstill, including system response but excluding operator reaction, so planners should distinguish that test boundary from the operator-inclusive delay allowance [f6540, f6058].

nodes.label: 30 CFR 56.14101
nodes.synopsis: For US surface metal and nonmetal mines, 30 CFR 56.14101 Table M-1 computes maximum stopping distances using constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s² (about 2.94 m/s²), weight-dependent brake-system response time, and one second of operator response time [f5989, f13947]. Brake-system response allowances rise from 0.5 seconds for equipment up to 36,000 lb to 2.5 seconds above 400,000 lb (about 181 t), with intermediate weight-class steps [f5990]. Equipment up to 36,000 lb must stop within 34 ft (10.4 m) from 10 mph (16 km/h), or 89 ft (27.1 m) from 20 mph (32 km/h) [f5991]. Chapter 8 and the glossary also require brakes to stop and hold loaded equipment on its steepest traveled grade, although Chapter 8 specifies a typical load while the glossary says a loaded machine without that qualification [f5992, f13948].

nodes.label: Simcenter EDEM
nodes.text: Simcenter EDEM
nodes.synopsis: EDEM is described as commercial discrete-element modeling software for bulk materials such as soil, ore and coal, with coupling to vehicle and multibody simulation [f8587, f15985, f9134]. Its strongest relevance is mining, quarrying and earth interaction; Chapter 8 gives a concrete tracked-machine soft-soil workflow using Altair MotionSolve/MotionView coupled to EDEM [f8588, f6388]. It is not a perception or ADAS simulator, and its sensor capabilities are listed as not applicable, so its role in collision-mitigation validation is machine–terrain physics rather than sensor simulation [f8590, f9136, f16074]. DEM is computationally expensive, while public pricing and the latest release date were not found, leaving cost and release currency unresolved [f8589, f8591]. The glossary explicitly flags that Chapter 11 calls the tool Siemens Simcenter EDEM whereas Chapter 8 cites an Altair workflow, leaving a naming/vendor-attribution tension to clarify [f15986, f8587, f6388].

nodes.synopsis: The glossary describes Fiala as a simple physical tire model and groups it with Magic Formula/Pacejka and TMeasy as models that assume a firm surface [f13780, f13782]. Chapter 8 describes rigid full-vehicle multibody models with 3–8 degrees of freedom using Fiala or Magic Formula tires to predict braking-related roll, yaw, jackknife and pitch stability, plus load transfer [f6447]. Its cited articulated-loader studies specifically use 7- and 8-degree-of-freedom models, Fiala tires and active braking, treating roll instability as critical; the references include two Li et al. papers from 2016 and a related lateral-stability paper from 2013 [f6032, f13781]. For tool selection, Project Chrono developers report that Fiala, Pacejka and TMeasy handling tire models do not work with deformable terrain, identifying rigid or FEA tires and tracked vehicles as the supported alternatives [f8498]. Thus, the reported use of Fiala for loader stability does not establish suitability for deformable-terrain validation [f6032, f13782, f8498].

nodes.synopsis: SPH is grouped with DEM and FEM terrain models coupled to a multibody machine: these methods are available in research and commercial ecosystems and can predict granular flow, rutting and localized soil failure [f6101, f6468]. They offer high fidelity but are very slow, require very high effort and high-performance computing, and are considered too costly or unusable for exhaustive scenario sweeps [f6469, f6471, f6103, f6474]. Uncertain soil inputs can overwhelm their fidelity, and evidence that they are required for automatic-braking threshold prediction across production machines was not found [f6104, f6475, f6102, f6470]. Chapter 8 and the glossary therefore recommend restricting their use to selected braking limit cases, with Chapter 8 specifying berms, deep aggregate and severe track-soil interaction [f6472, f13835]. Commercial availability should not be confused with established off-road validation: the stated off-road validation status remains research only [f6101, f6473].

nodes.text: AAA
nodes.synopsis: AAA supplies independent on-road evidence and a practical measurement method: its 2024 protocols monitor brake-pedal force to confirm driver braking, while its nighttime tests exposed performance cliffs missed by standard daytime protocols [f6325, f7974]. In October 2019, none of four vehicles avoided a pedestrian target at night at 25 mph; a study published 16 October 2025 reported improvement from 0% to 60% nighttime impact avoidance, still leaving roughly 40% failures under ideal conditions [f7975, f7977]. The 2025 study tested four named vehicles at 25 mph (40 km/h), with the Toyota Camry avoiding impact in every nighttime run and the Chevrolet Malibu ranking lowest [f7976, f7978, f7979]. High-visibility clothing caused complete detection loss in some systems, and both clothing and nighttime conditions were under-represented in consumer protocols, illustrating why physical or virtual protocol-based evidence can give false confidence outside its tested envelope [f7980, f7981, f7982]. The skeptic's review separately records that AAA ADAS repair studies were not verified, leaving that evidence stream unresolved [f10812].

nodes.label: IPG TruckMaker
nodes.text: IPG TruckMaker
nodes.synopsis: IPG TruckMaker is classified as a road-heritage dynamics tool; the IPG off-highway stack adapts on-road capabilities to construction, agriculture and mining [f15973, f8681, f15894]. Its commercial offerings provide closed-loop vehicle, driver, environment and sensor simulation across MIL, SIL, HIL and vehicle-in-the-loop, with camera, radar, lidar, actuator/ECU coupling and FMI interfaces [f8989, f8436, f8440, f8992]. The corpus judges the stack well suited to rigid-vehicle and system dynamics, rather than high-fidelity deformable soil or particle interaction [f6391, f8443]. Vendor claims cite Linde lidar accident prevention and tractor vehicle-in-the-loop applications, but independent evidence for heavy-machine performance in severe dust, snow or glare was not found [f15893, f8444]. Consulting is available, and TruckMaker appears as a dynamics option in the highest-cost example tool chain; however, neither public pricing nor a TruckMaker-specific release date was found [f8806, f9304, f8442].

nodes.label: MSC/Cadence Adams
nodes.text: MSC/Cadence Adams
nodes.synopsis: MSC/Cadence Adams is a commercial, road-heritage, high-end multibody dynamics tool, rather than an environment or sensor simulator [f9146, f15974, f8597, f9148]. Its stated capabilities include rigid-body contact, flexible bodies and machine-mechanism modeling [f6392, f8596]. Chapter 8 includes Adams among commercial options for full multibody models supporting machine dynamics, actuator and failure analysis, and real-time co-simulation; this describes the modeling approach rather than demonstrating an Adams-specific validation workflow [f6454]. Although Chapter 11 includes Adams among vehicle and machine dynamics, terrain and soil offerings, it reports no off-road evidence or off-road autonomy proof, leaving its suitability for this application unsubstantiated in the supplied facts [f8356, f9147, f8598]. No public price or latest release was found, and the interface listing identifies only the Cadence/MSC ecosystem [f9150, f9151, f9149].

It also lists RecurDyn among commercial options for full multibody models with contact and a detailed plant, an approach supporting full machine dynamics, actuator and failure analysis, and real-time co-simulation [f6454]. The glossary nevertheless states that RecurDyn is not discussed in the booklet, contradicting its explicit inclusion in Chapter 8 [f15977, f6392, f6454].

nodes.label: Simscape
nodes.text: Simscape
nodes.synopsis: Simscape is listed as a vehicle and machine dynamics offering and as an implementation option for lumped brake hydraulics coupled to a point-mass model, predicting latency, pressure build-up and its spread [f8357, f6393, f6437]. The glossary describes Vehicle Dynamics Blockset and Simscape as road-heritage tools with articulated steering since R2025a; Chapter 11 identifies articulated-steering dynamics and controller models operating closed-loop in Simulink R2026b [f15975, f8599]. R2026b is the second 2026 release of the twice-yearly MATLAB and Simulink family [f16239]. An undated MathWorks user story reports Volvo Construction Equipment's real-time human-in-the-loop excavator simulator built using Simulink and Simscape, providing an application example but no dated milestone [f8391, f16050]. Despite their inclusion in the dynamics, terrain and soil category, high-detail soil deformation is explicitly not a primary strength of these MathWorks tools [f8357, f8600].

nodes.label: Modelica
nodes.text: Modelica
nodes.synopsis: Modelica is identified alongside Amesim and Simscape as a tool option for lumped hydraulics modeling [f6393]. In the machine-motion and brake-timing chapter, it is also an implementation option for a point-mass model coupled to lumped brake hydraulics, which predicts latency, pressure build-up and its spread [f6437]. Separately, work related to the SET Level Credible Simulation Process proposes carrying credibility information with Modelica models; this is presented as an expert-opinion recommendation in an on-road context, not as demonstrated validation of the brake model [f7698]. The supplied facts identify a modeling capability and a credibility-management proposal, but provide no numerical performance results or dates [f6393, f6437, f7698].

nodes.label: Functional Mock-up Interface
nodes.text: Functional Mock-up Interface
nodes.synopsis: The booklet treats FMI as a major generic simulation-tool integration mechanism and rates FMI/SSP as domain-neutral and transferable to off-road work [f8712, f7167, f13224]. FMI co-simulation can connect reduced-order in-house models with commercial high-fidelity components; Simulink–Mevea integration over FMI or TCP/IP is explicitly supported [f6395, f8699]. By mid-2025, the Modelica Association reported around 250 FMI-supporting tools, with extensive co-simulation support [f8713, f15863]. Recommendations call for OSI and FMI/SSP interfaces with adapters to simulation, HIL and physical automation, and for simulation-tool RFPs to require open-format export including FMI [f7203, f16487]. Adoption does not eliminate integration work: FMI-linked components are rated medium effort because semantics still require calibration, while Chapter 9 explicitly says the research did not verify FMI/SSP's status [f8729, f7165].

nodes.label: Magic Formula tire model
nodes.text: Magic Formula tire model
nodes.synopsis: Magic Formula, also called Pacejka, is an empirical tire model fitted to test data and widely used for road vehicles [f13780]. Chapter 8 identifies it alongside Fiala for rigid full-vehicle multibody models with 3–8 degrees of freedom that predict braking-related roll, yaw, jackknife and pitch stability, plus load transfer [f6447]. Its terrain scope is limited: the glossary says Magic Formula, Fiala and TMeasy assume a firm surface, while Project Chrono developers report that these handling tire models do not work with deformable terrain [f13782, f8498]. For deformable-terrain simulation in Chrono, the reported compatible options are rigid or FEA tires and tracked vehicles, so the braking-model capability should not be read as establishing suitability for deformable off-road ground [f8498, f6447].

nodes.label: DEM
nodes.text: DEM
nodes.synopsis: DEM, SPH or FEM terrain coupled with a multibody machine can predict granular flow, rutting and localized soil failure, but Chapter 8 describes this approach as high-fidelity, very slow and research-only for off-road validation [f6468, f6469, f6473]. Chapter 8 and the glossary recommend restricting these models to selected braking limit cases, including berms, deep aggregate and severe track-soil interaction; Chapter 11 additionally recommends high-detail simulation to understand stopping-distance sensitivity to soil, slope, payload and tire or track interaction [f6472, f13835, f8602]. This recommendation is constrained by the absence of evidence that such models are required for threshold prediction, their reported unsuitability for scenario sweeps and the risk that uncertain soil inputs overwhelm their fidelity [f6470, f6474, f6475]. Their computational burden calls for high-performance computing, with Chapter 11 identifying GPU acceleration and dedicated GPU or HPC workers as suitable [f6471, f8846]. Available tools include Project Chrono/Chrono::Vehicle with SCM, CRM and DEM terrain support, and Fraunhofer Demify for heavy-machinery soil DEM; Chapter 8 also reports that SCM's authors described SCM as “comparable” to DEM [f8494, f9123, f9141, f6463].

nodes.label: FEM
nodes.text: FEM
nodes.synopsis: The corpus treats FEM alongside DEM and SPH terrain models coupled with a multibody machine: these methods predict granular flow, rutting and localized soil failure with high fidelity, but are very slow [f6468, f6469]. They require very high effort and high-performance computing, are described as unusable for scenario sweeps, and have research-only off-road validation status [f6471, f6474, f6473]. Both Chapter 8 and the glossary recommend restricting their braking-validation use to selected limit cases, with Chapter 8 specifying berms, deep aggregate and severe track-soil interaction [f6472, f13835]. This narrow role reflects two limitations: uncertain soil inputs can overwhelm model fidelity, and evidence that these methods are required for threshold prediction was not found [f6475, f6470].

nodes.label: ISO 34501
nodes.synopsis: ISO 34501:2022 provides vocabulary for scenario-based evaluation within the road-vehicle ISO 3450x scenario standards [f15313, f15312]. Chapter 9 treats ISO 34501–34505 as transferable methodological templates for off-road validation, while stressing that their content addresses Level 3 and higher road automated-driving systems rather than off-road compliance [f6642, f7182, f15320]. The chapter's scenario catalog uses functional, logical and concrete scenarios, a three-level abstraction originating in the German PEGASUS project and adopted into ISO 34501–34505 [f6735, f13258, f15322]. The glossary also states that the ISO 3450x series, ISO/PAS 34506 and ISO/TS 5083 establish no physical-to-virtual testing ratio, leaving that allocation unspecified by these standards [f15321].

nodes.label: ASAM OpenODD
nodes.text: ASAM OpenODD
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OpenODD 1.0.0, released on 3 April 2025, provides a technology-independent operating-domain data model in machine-readable YAML and CSV, with restrictive definitions specifying what is allowed and permissive definitions specifying what is excluded [f6707, f6708, f13246]. Its normative scope is automated road vehicles, with default attributes dominated by lanes and junctions; its structure is transferable to off-road validation, but its content is not directly transferable [f6709, f6642, f13245]. Operating-domain definitions establish testing boundaries and therefore the meaning of coverage, making an appropriate taxonomy foundational to validation [f6782]. OpenODD is assessed as having moderate off-road fit, and the manufacturer or industry must author and govern an off-road taxonomy; the proposed adaptation combines on-road and off-road patterns, but its arrangement remains expert opinion [f7162, f7163, f6714]. The booklet recommends a manufacturer-owned, domain-neutral, version-controlled scenario catalog using Scenic or an in-house YAML schema with an OpenODD-style taxonomy, exporting to OpenSCENARIO where tools require it [f14491, f7198].

nodes.text: stratified random sampling
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 9 and the glossary agree that only a frozen stratified random sample can support a release rate claim [f6648, f6867, f14095]. The proposed campaign implements this through a scenario-catalog-fed estimation stream using a frozen, pre-registered stratified random sample [f7355]. Simple or stratified random sampling is recommended for estimating detection, false-alarm and nuisance-brake rates because it can yield unbiased or known-weight estimates with classical confidence intervals for the declared distribution, backed by established statistics [f7239, f7240, f7246]. However, the operational distribution may be uncertain, and sampling cannot establish validity if the declared distribution is wrong [f7244, f7241]. Rare events require enormous exposure, so these methods cannot legitimately claim efficient discovery of very rare failures; no particular tooling is prescribed [f7243, f7242, f7245].

nodes.label: Driving to Safety
nodes.text: Driving to Safety
nodes.synopsis: RAND’s Driving to Safety, by Kalra and Paddock (report RR-1478-RC), was published in April 2016 and supplies the booklet’s statistical reason for pursuing virtual testing [f6920, f15817]. Chapter 9 and the glossary agree that demonstrating autonomous road-vehicle reliability requires hundreds of millions, and sometimes hundreds of billions, of driven miles—distances that existing fleets would need tens or hundreds of years to accumulate [f6921, f15812, f14264]. Showing a fatality rate no worse than the human benchmark of 1.09 fatalities per 100 million miles requires 275 million failure-free miles at 95% confidence [f6662, f6922, f15813]. Demonstrating a 20% fatality-rate improvement requires about 11 billion miles; Chapter 9 specifies 80% statistical power and, in its fuller statement, 95% confidence, while the glossary omits those statistical qualifiers [f6663, f6923, f15814]. These figures concern autonomous road vehicles; the supplied facts do not quantify corresponding mileage requirements for heavy off-road machines [f6921, f6922, f6923].

nodes.synopsis: The corpus identifies ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 as a neutral standard for test documentation and says it separates test processes, design techniques and documentation [f13537, f6947]. nodes.label: response-surface methodology
nodes.text: response-surface methodology
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends response-surface methodology for fine tuning a handful of smooth, continuous parameters, including warning-distance offsets, persistence times, confidence thresholds and filter constants [f6673, f14425, f6965]. After influential factors have been identified, response-surface designs model curvature in a smaller subspace and provide interpretable main effects, interactions and local optimum regions under model assumptions [f6802, f6966, f7221]. The glossary reinforces its use for tuning thresholds and zones, while Chapter 9 also recommends response-surface and D-optimal DOE for constrained physical design spaces [f14104, f7220]. These methods are poor for discontinuous behaviour and cannot establish global corner-case coverage or operational probabilities [f7223, f7222]. Although response surfaces are mature, non-automotive-specific statistical techniques with an independent evidence base, the booklet reports no off-road evidence or published off-road braking application; applicability remains conditional on the stated assumptions being respected [f7398, f7226, f14429, f7399].

nodes.label: ASAM OpenSCENARIO DSL
nodes.text: ASAM OpenSCENARIO DSL
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OpenSCENARIO DSL 2.2.0 is dated 19 March 2026 [f7152, f14486]. Its first-class support for abstract and logical scenarios, parameter variation and key performance indicators suits scenario families, and the booklet rates its off-road fit as moderate [f14486, f7153, f14487]. That fit is constrained by an on-road domain model, shared with the cited OpenSCENARIO XML and OpenDRIVE standards [f6691, f7154, f14487]. Tool support is limited; the cited 2026 preprint addresses compiling OpenSCENARIO 2.1 for CARLA, rather than establishing support for DSL 2.2.0 [f7155, f7152].

nodes.label: ASAM OpenSCENARIO XML
nodes.text: ASAM OpenSCENARIO XML
nodes.synopsis: ASAM OpenSCENARIO XML 1.4.0 is dated 2026, with a secondary listing reporting June 2026 [f7149]. It describes precise, synchronized maneuvers tied to road networks and shares a road-traffic domain model with OpenSCENARIO DSL and OpenDRIVE [f14485, f7150, f6691]. The booklet rates its fit for off-road work without roads or lanes as poor to moderate; world-coordinate placement is possible, but terrain and slopes must come from external assets [f7150, f7151]. XML and OpenDRIVE nevertheless have broad tool support, including VTD, dSPACE, CARLA, RoadRunner, Prescan and MORAI; that interoperability does not resolve the stated off-road modeling limitations [f8616, f7150, f7151].

nodes.label: Scenic
nodes.text: Scenic
nodes.synopsis: Scenic is an open-source, free probabilistic scenario language with native 3D geometry, lane-independent object placement, and interfaces to Python and multiple simulators [f6693, f16024, f9211, f9212]. The booklet considers its programmable semantics adaptable to job sites and better suited to pits, stockpiles and loading areas than road-oriented languages, but Scenic is not a standard and no mining or construction deployment or off-road evidence was found [f8636, f6694, f8637, f9209]. It recommends Scenic or an in-house YAML schema with an OpenODD-style taxonomy for a manufacturer-owned, domain-neutral, version-controlled scenario catalog, with OpenSCENARIO export where required [f14491, f7198]. Scenic integrates with VerifAI for falsification; on-road work in 2021 reported up to a fivefold speed-up from parallel multi-objective falsification, without establishing off-road performance [f16025, f6839, f9209]. Scenic appears in the lowest-cost example tool chain, but its enterprise test governance is thinner than commercial tools', a trustworthy 2026 release date was not found, and funding, maintenance and security-patch cadence were not examined [f9266, f8638, f9213, f9392, f9393].

nodes.text: ODD-UM
nodes.synopsis: ODD-UM is a 2022 conference paper that developed an operating-domain taxonomy for underground mining by adapting BSI PAS 1883 and ISO 17757:2019 [f6711, f9362, f7185]. Across the corpus, it is grouped with the 2024 unstructured-environment ODD work and the November 2025 agricultural ODD preprint as academic off-road domain work, not standards [f6710, f6785, f7185]. These publications offer useful concepts for off-road work, but their non-standard status remains a limitation for planners [f7186]. Chapter 9 uses ODD-UM and EMESRT as off-road inputs to a proposed taxonomy alongside ISO 34503 and OpenODD on-road patterns; that arrangement is explicitly expert opinion [f6714].

nodes.synopsis: Fractional factorial design reduces experimental run count by testing only a chosen fraction of combinations, but deliberately introduces aliasing that makes some higher-order effects indistinguishable [f6800, f14102]. A finding of no main effect for fog therefore cannot rule out a localized, non-linear failure involving a particular combination of fog density, glare and sensor contamination [f6809, f14108]. The glossary also cautions that DOE cannot find a narrow failure region hidden between design points, limiting what planners can infer from apparently reassuring results [f14108].

nodes.label: D-optimal designs
nodes.text: D-optimal designs
nodes.synopsis: D-optimal designs are useful when constraints make regular factorial test grids impossible, although they sacrifice orthogonality and can produce correlated estimates [f14105, f6803, f7224]. Under model assumptions, response-surface and D-optimal DOE establish local response models, curvature and optimum regions; the booklet recommends them for fine tuning thresholds and zones and exploring constrained physical design spaces [f7221, f7220]. After prototype arrival, modest DOE or D-optimal tests should estimate sensor, latency and braking residuals and initialise common parameters; the glossary places DOE in both the coverage and calibration streams [f7381, f14109]. This coverage role is limited: these methods cannot establish global corner-case coverage or operational probabilities and are poor for discontinuous behaviour [f7222, f7223]. An independent evidence base exists, but no off-road evidence is reported; statistics packages are typical tooling [f7226, f7225].

Chapter 9 says these schemes cover continuous parameters more evenly than naive random draws and recommends them for continuous-space coverage, surrogate training and broad exploration [f6813, f6814, f7227]. nodes.synopsis: Chapter 9 names S-TaLiRo alongside Breach and VerifAI as tools for failure-seeking search and includes them among the program’s falsification methods [f6836, f7247]. The glossary explains their purpose as searching for parameter combinations where a function fails [f16025]. Across Chapter 9 and the glossary, this family also includes Bayesian optimization, surrogate-guided search and evolutionary search; the glossary additionally lists fuzzing, reinforcement-learning adversaries and Adaptive Stress Testing [f7247, f14148]. The glossary explicitly identifies a Scenic–VerifAI integration, but the supplied facts do not establish an integration with S-TaLiRo or report S-TaLiRo-specific performance or validation results [f16025, f6836, f7247, f14148].

Chapter 9 specifically states that Scenic 3 integrates with VerifAI, while the glossary describes the Scenic–VerifAI integration without specifying a version [f7175, f16025]. On-road work from 2021 reported up to a fivefold speed-up for VerifAI with Scenic using parallel multi-objective falsification; the supplied facts do not establish that this gain transfers to heavy off-road validation [f6839, f14149].

nodes.label: cross-entropy methods
nodes.text: cross-entropy methods
nodes.synopsis: The glossary places cross-entropy methods in the booklet’s rare-event methods family; Chapter 9 describes these methods as deliberately oversampling dangerous conditions while estimating naturalistic rates through distribution-ratio reweighting [f14161, f6846]. Chapter 9 recommends cross-entropy, importance sampling and accelerated evaluation for small-probability estimation, with unbiased rates conditional on a known likelihood ratio and proposal coverage of the failure region [f7261, f7262]. Trustworthy rate estimation is not established when the naturalistic distribution is poorly known, and these methods carry high model dependence and potentially huge weight variance [f7264, f7265, f7266]. They cannot establish high-dimensional robustness or account for unmodelled physics; moreover, the independent evidence is marked as on-road, leaving an applicability gap for this heavy off-road program [f7263, f7268]. Typical tooling is in-house or academic [f7267].

nodes.label: subset simulation
nodes.text: subset simulation
nodes.synopsis: The glossary includes subset simulation in the booklet’s rare-event methods family; Chapter 9 describes these methods as deliberately oversampling dangerous conditions while estimating naturalistic rates, provided observations can be reweighted by the real-world-to-accelerated distribution ratio [f14161, f6846]. Subset simulation and multilevel splitting originate in structural reliability or, more broadly, reliability engineering, and are recommended for very small probabilities in structural reliability [f6855, f7272, f7269]. They can provide rate estimates through conditional levels, with academic tools identified as typical tooling [f7270, f7273]. However, both methods are described as weak for discontinuous perception responses, and their independent evidence base does not include any collision-avoidance application found by the booklet [f6856, f7271, f6857, f7274].

nodes.label: multilevel splitting
nodes.text: multilevel splitting
nodes.synopsis: The glossary includes multilevel splitting in the booklet’s rare-event methods family; Chapter 9 describes these methods as oversampling dangerous conditions while estimating naturalistic rates, subject to observation-level reweighting [f14161, f6846]. Multilevel splitting and subset simulation originate in reliability engineering, specifically structural reliability, and can estimate rates through conditional levels [f6855, f7272, f7270]. Chapter 9 recommends them primarily for very small probabilities in structural reliability and identifies academic tools as typical tooling [f7269, f7273]. Although the methods have an independent evidence base, no collision-avoidance application or evidence was found, and discontinuous perception responses are an identified weakness [f7274, f6857, f6856, f7271].

nodes.label: NSGA-II
nodes.text: NSGA-II
nodes.synopsis: NSGA-II (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II), attributed to Deb and colleagues in 2002, handles multiple objectives by evolving a whole Pareto front; the glossary says evolutionary methods can produce this front in one run [f14420, f14413]. Chapter 9 recommends these methods for balancing misses, false alarms, unnecessary braking and stopping margin because they expose trade-offs rather than hiding them in one score [f7317, f6971]. The booklet describes them as robust and easy to parallelise over simulation, but requiring many evaluations [f6970, f14421, f6972]. Producing a Pareto front does not resolve the policy choice of an acceptable point, and trying many configurations increases over-fitting risk [f6973, f7320]. Recommended safeguards are nested validation, final-point selection using pre-declared safety constraints and independent-set confirmation; generic engineering evidence exists, but no specific off-road evidence is identified [f7321, f7322].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 9 and the glossary describe robust or worst-case optimization as targeting the worst stratum or a high percentile rather than average performance, protecting difficult conditions such as dust at night [f6988, f14399]. Chapter 9 specifies min-max optimization over strata and says the approach avoids sacrificing weak-stratum performance while favoring stable operating regions [f7329, f7330]. The trade-off is conservatism and a potentially higher nuisance rate [f7331]. Although the approach is described as having lower over-fitting risk, held-out strata remain necessary, and no off-road evidence for robust or worst-case tuning was found [f7332, f7333].

nodes.synopsis: OSI is the message standard used by sensor models delivered as FMUs, and it is among the open standards that make heterogeneous tool chains practical for road ADAS engineering [f13235, f9331]. Chapter 11 identifies Persival as offering credible sensor-model development and validation, including OSI FMUs and weather benches; its middle-cost example stack includes one externally validated sensor model, potentially an OSI FMU from a specialist [f8812, f9287]. However, ASAM’s 2025 high-fidelity OSI project states that existing abstractions insufficiently represent some physical phenomena, notably camera spectral irradiance and radar raw waveform data [f7081]. That project explicitly considers camera, radar and lidar, with ultrasound only a possibility, so the corpus pairs practical OSI-based integration options with unresolved fidelity limitations [f7082, f7081, f8812, f9287].
