nodes.text: ASAM MDF
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 9 and the glossary identify ASAM MDF 4.3.0, dated September 2025, as a standardized binary format for measured signals, bus traffic and sensor data, including metadata and synchronization; Chapter 9 also explicitly includes calculated signals [f7115, f13011]. MDF is a neutral format option rather than a mandatory architecture choice: other structured or in-house formats can satisfy the same architecture if provenance and long-term readability are controlled [f7116, f13012]. For test management, the glossary assigns MDF to measured data and ASAM ATX to test metadata, specifications and results, while ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 covers test documentation [f13537, f16029, f16254]. The resulting planning choice is conditional on data stewardship, not exclusive adoption of MDF [f7116, f13012].

nodes.synopsis: The UNECE New Assessment/Test Method for Automated Driving (NATM) is identified as ECE/TRANS/WP.29/2022/58, a 2022 guideline with an updated master document, WP.29-189-07, dated March 2023 [f7143, f7676]. Its credibility-assessment framework covers management, data and model validation, and team expertise [f7143]. Chapter 12 describes a multi-pillar validation logic comprising a scenario catalogue, simulation and virtual testing, track tests, real-world tests, audit and in-service monitoring, and also references guidelines WP.29/2023/44 [f9743]. These facts are marked as on-road; they do not establish applicability to heavy off-road machines or explain the relationship between the two cited 2023 documents [f7143, f7676, f9743].

nodes.label: ASAM Open Simulation Interface
nodes.text: ASAM Open Simulation Interface
nodes.synopsis: OSI provides domain-neutral sensor and ground-truth interfaces that the research finds transferable to off-road work, and the glossary lists it among open standards for connecting simulation tools [f7166, f15862]. Chapter 9 recommends OSI and FMI/SSP for sensor and model interfaces, with adapters to simulation, HIL and physical automation; the glossary also recommends requiring OSI export in simulation-tool RFPs [f7203, f16487]. Persival offers a concrete implementation pattern: OSI sensor models packaged as FMUs and correlated against real sensor output, while requesting an OSI-packaged black-box FMU is one of five options when suppliers withhold sensor internals [f15948, f16495]. ASAM's 2025 high-fidelity OSI project extends sensor interfaces and runs until March 2027, coinciding with the program's planned first tool-chain integration [f7169, f15870]. Despite these findings and recommendations, the research explicitly says it did not verify OSI's status, leaving a verification gap relevant to interface planning [f7165].

nodes.label: OpenX
nodes.text: OpenX
nodes.synopsis: ASAM publishes OpenX scene and scenario formats, which help support a mature scenario-based structure for road vehicles, including scenario abstractions, catalogs and parameterised generation [f13223, f7410]. ASAM describes OpenX as in maintenance mode in 2026; the assessment anticipates slower core-format evolution and considers off-road extensions unlikely before mid-2027, though that timing remains uncertain [f7170, f13211, f7172]. ASAM's off-road workshop identified missing concepts for deformable and particle terrain, vegetation, heavy-machine manipulation and sensor degradation [f13213]. These gaps do not make OpenX unusable, but off-road work will require extensions or a manufacturer-owned domain model [f7196, f7434]. OpenX-linked components are assessed as requiring medium relative integration effort: existing transport and schemas help, but material, actor, dynamics and timing semantics still need calibration [f8729].

nodes.synopsis: ASAM's 2023 OpenX off-road workshop was followed by the “OpenX in Off-Road Applications” concept project, which was listed as active when accessed in October 2026 [f7191, f7171]. Its scope spans construction, mining, agriculture, defence and consumer recreation, covering both mobility across challenging terrain and manipulation tasks such as excavation, lifting, loading, transportation and material deposition [f7192, f7193, f7194]. The workshop and project identify missing OpenX concepts for soft and particle terrain, deformable terrain, vegetation, heavy-machinery manipulation and sensor degradation [f7195]. Despite the project's active status, the booklet considers an off-road extension unlikely before mid-2027; this is an uncertain outlook rather than a confirmed delivery date [f13212].

nodes.label: Scenic 3
nodes.text: Scenic 3
nodes.synopsis: Scenic 3 is an open-source probabilistic language with peer-reviewed coverage at CAV 2023 [f14489, f7173]. The booklet rates its off-road fit as good, citing native 3D geometry, occlusion-aware visibility, probabilistic placement without lanes and simulator independence [f7174, f14490]. It integrates with VerifAI for falsification, and demonstrations beyond road vehicles include robotics and a Mars-rover-over-rocks example; the latter evidence is labelled independent and vendor project documentation [f7175, f7176]. However, Scenic 3 is not an ISO or ASAM standard, so adopters must provide mappings to requirements, rigs and exchange formats [f7177, f14490].

nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends a domain-neutral, version-controlled scenario catalog, using either Scenic or an in-house YAML schema with an OpenODD-style taxonomy [f7198, f14491]. The glossary adds that the catalog should be manufacturer-owned and exported to OpenSCENARIO when required by tools [f14491]. YAML, alongside JSON and XML, is suitable for structured settings, configuration files, scenario descriptions and small tables, but not gigabytes of sensor data [f13009]. YAML is therefore presented as a scenario-description option rather than a mandatory format or a bulk sensor-data format [f7198, f14491, f13009].

nodes.label: Full factorial DOE
nodes.text: Full factorial DOE
nodes.synopsis: Full factorial DOE tests every combination of selected factors and levels, allowing main effects and interactions to be established over those tested levels without aliasing [f14101, f7208]. Its run count grows exponentially, so Chapter 9 recommends using it for a small number of important factors and levels and for physical confirmation [f14101, f7210, f7207]. Results cannot establish real-world prevalence unless tested levels are weighted to operational frequency [f7209]. The independent evidence base is NIST methodology; no off-road collision-avoidance study was found, leaving a domain-specific evidence gap [f7212]. Typical tooling includes commercial and open-source statistics packages [f7211].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 12 cites EUR-Lex regulation text and the European Commission’s announcement for the Digital Omnibus adoption date of 8 July 2026 and entry-into-force date of 27 July 2026 [f10311, f10312]. It reports application dates of 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 from those same sources, without specifying which provisions apply on each date [f10313]. In contrast, Chapter 9 relies on August 2026 Eurogip commentary, not verified on EUR-Lex, for the possibility that harmonised AI Act standards may confer a presumption of conformity under the Machinery Regulation until machinery-specific AI delegated acts expected by 2 August 2028 [f7431]. The corpus therefore distinguishes reported legal milestones from an unverified interpretation that should remain qualified in planning [f10311, f10312, f10313, f7431].

nodes.label: ASME V&V 40
nodes.text: ASME V&V 40
nodes.synopsis: ASME V&V 40 (2018) is a medical-device model-credibility standard, paired in the booklet with FDA guidance issued in November 2023; its central principle is to scale credibility evidence to model influence and decision consequence within a defined context of use [f14568, f8072, f8073, f8075]. Credibility goals should be set prospectively: there is no universal acceptance error or minimum amount of remaining physical evidence, and physical testing is retained where model risk is high or validation evidence weakest [f14622, f7790, f8076, f7834, f7835]. The booklet rates this as the most transferable reasoning framework for off-road automatic braking, but it is not proven for that application and no direct earth-moving automatic-braking equivalent was found [f8077, f8078, f7740]. Its applicability is limited to physics-based models, including vehicle dynamics and brakes; machine-learned perception requires separate assurance [f14626, f14627, f8220]. Chapter 12 recommends simulation-credibility frameworks instead of TRL for assessing the validation toolchain, while acknowledging that these frameworks can be largely declarative [f10031, f10029].

nodes.text: FAA AC 20-146A
nodes.synopsis: FAA AC 20-146A, Dynamic Seat Certification by Analysis, is regulator guidance dated 29 June 2018 and the booklet’s clearest published precedent for simulation as compliance evidence through a physical anchor plus virtual variants [f7618, f7619, f14665]. A baseline aircraft seat must pass physical dynamic tests, and its model must be validated against them using criteria agreed in advance; eligible modifications within the same seat family may then be substantiated by simulation [f14655, f14656]. Calibration is not validation, model-to-model agreement is insufficient, and extrapolation is limited to similar conditions; changes affecting load paths, failure mechanisms, materials or interfaces require new physical evidence [f7625, f7626, f14658, f14657]. The guidance uses 10% agreement criteria for several seat quantities and permits other model-specific criteria agreed with the authority, but these tolerances must not be transferred to off-road braking [f7777, f7778, f14668]. Its applicability to off-road automatic braking is unproven, the percentage of physical tests eliminated was not published, and the research did not verify broader FAA/EASA certification-by-analysis policy beyond this circular [f8087, f7853, f7634].

nodes.label: EN 14363
nodes.synopsis: EN 14363:2016+A2:2022 governs acceptance of railway vehicle running behavior, with informative Annex T addressing simulation of on-track tests and Annex U extending acceptance to vehicles of the same basic design [f15362, f14674]. It is the only standard identified in the booklet that formally allows validated simulation to extend acceptance to new conditions and modified vehicles; running tests validate the model, and physical running tests remain required for the reference vehicle [f14672, f14675, f8136]. Validation uses at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons from at least 12 track sections, applying limits to the whole set of deviations; the associated DynoTRAIN study used more than 1,000 comparisons during the 2014–2022 case [f15363, f15364, f7854, f7855]. The booklet identifies this framework as the strongest family-transfer and test-reduction precedent for off-road automatic braking, but qualifies its relevance because rail physics is far more deterministic than perception and the framework has no formal risk scaling [f8137, f8138, f8132]. No percentage of physical tests removed across actual rail certifications was published, and no documented accident in which an EN 14363-validated simulation itself created false confidence was found [f7856, f7990].

nodes.label: UTAC
nodes.text: UTAC
nodes.synopsis: UTAC submitted virtual-testing proposals to the United Nations working group on automatic emergency braking; the detailed evidence supplied here concerns on-road AEBS rather than heavy off-road machines [f16110, f7846]. Its earlier AEBS-12-07 proposal allowed virtual validation within a validity domain and proposed removing 10% of the 10 repeated automotive AEBS runs per scenario [f7860, f7845, f7846]. The later UTAC CERAM document AEBS-16-03 includes a 30% physical-test figure alongside validation using 11 SUT-and-target variables and three metrics: IAPE, Double th, and interval [f7686]. Although one account describes that figure as a minimum, the corpus explicitly says it cannot be reconciled with adopted UN R152 text, which leaves physical confirmatory-test numbers to manufacturer–authority agreement; the adopted text governs [f7547, f8188]. UTAC's curve-comparison approach combines peak time, peak value, curve shape and error, but the supplied facts do not establish its applicability to off-road machines [f7771, f7846].

nodes.label: Sprague-Geers time-history error
nodes.text: Sprague-Geers time-history error
nodes.synopsis: The booklet presents Sprague-Geers time-history error as one of several metrics for assessing simulation agreement; it compares magnitude and phase across a whole time trace [f7553, f7763]. The glossary confirms that the method used for the booklet’s reported comparison figures combines magnitude and phase terms [f14743]. Chapter 10 cites its use in FAA seat certification and gives an example acceptance guideline of 10% [f7764]. In the worked example, measured and simulated load peaks are 1,315 lb and 1,360 lb, respectively; the 3.42% peak error and 7.2% Sprague-Geers error both meet that guideline [f7781, f7782]. The supplied facts establish this threshold for the FAA example, not a general acceptance threshold for heavy off-road machine validation [f7764, f7782].

nodes.synopsis: ERA guidance, together with EN 14363:2016+A2:2022 and DynoTRAIN, provides a standards-and-regulatory framework for rail running-dynamics validation; its WAG TSI application guide (GUI/WAG TSI/2023) accepts physical procedures or simulations with validated models as evidence [f8131, f7710]. Across Chapter 10 and the glossary, the guidance permits extending test conditions and modifying a validated model of a tested vehicle to assess a changed vehicle, including comparison with an approved reference vehicle [f7896, f7895, f7897, f15365, f14676]. The framework uses physical-data comparison sets containing at least 24 comparisons from at least 12 sections, retains physical running tests for the reference vehicle, and has an associated validation study using more than 1,000 simulations [f8133, f8136, f8134]. The corpus identifies this as the strongest family-transfer and test-reduction precedent for off-road automatic braking and the closest formal analogue to delta validation, but notes that the framework has no formal risk scaling [f8137, f7898, f8132].

nodes.label: Crater
nodes.text: Crater
nodes.synopsis: After Columbia's January 2003 foam strike, engineers used Crater, an empirical impact-penetration model, to assess tile damage; Columbia was lost on re-entry on 1 February 2003 [f7950, f15843, f14933]. The strike debris was about 400 times the size represented in Crater's test database, while an early briefing reported 640 times; in August 2003, the investigation board found that the assessment was well outside that database and that the analyst was inexperienced [f7582, f7951, f7952]. Crater had overpredicted penetration in small-impact calibration data, but engineers assumed that conservative bias would persist for the much larger strike and overrode its prediction of penetration deeper than the tile [f7955, f7956, f15845]. Chapter 10 presents this as a canonical false-confidence case illustrating the danger of extrapolation [f7581]. The booklet also records a dissenting interpretation: in a 2011 account, Wayne Hale argued that Crater correctly warned of unsafe damage and that management's override, rather than the model's warning, was the failure [f7960, f15853].

nodes.text: NASA-HDBK-7009
nodes.synopsis: NASA-HDBK-7009 is the implementation handbook for NASA's models-and-simulations standard; the B handbook was final on 3 February 2026, accompanying NASA-STD-7009B dated 5 March 2024 [f14603, f7613, f8064]. Its credibility framework makes adequacy decision-specific: criticality sets the required credibility, consistent with Chapter 12's emphasis on defined use and the consequence of error [f7615, f8065, f8068, f9454]. Although the framework uses a Credibility Assessment Scale from 0 to 4, it cautions against a single total credibility score; Level 4 requires comparison with the real system across its range [f8066, f7614, f8068]. It does not numerically prescribe physical evidence, leaving adequacy to the decision authority, and requires caveats for simulation use outside model limits [f8069, f8067]. For off-road automatic braking, it offers an internal-board governance template rather than a certification rule, and its applicability is not proven; Chapter 12's related NATM evidence is explicitly on-road [f8070, f8071, f9454].

However, Chapter 10 reports that the research did not verify DO-178C with DO-330 tool qualification, and the glossary likewise lists both standards as unverified [f7633, f15369]. nodes.label: DO-330
nodes.synopsis: DO-330 is presented as the DO-178C supplement or companion for qualifying software tools whose output is relied on without further checking [f7636, f14661, f15367]. The booklet places it within aerospace practice governing airborne software and evidence-producing tools, and lists it among standards and guides from several domains [f14653, f8154]. Crucially, tool qualification under DO-330 does not establish whether a physics model is valid [f7637, f14662, f15368]. The research did not verify DO-178C or DO-330, so its descriptions provide background rather than verified findings about those standards [f7633, f14664, f15369].

nodes.label: Evaluation Model Development and Assessment Process (EMDAP)
nodes.text: Evaluation Model Development and Assessment Process (EMDAP)
nodes.synopsis: US NRC Regulatory Guide 1.203, dated December 2005, defines EMDAP as four elements comprising 20 steps; its continued nuclear use is illustrated by a 2024 audit plan and a 2025 safety evaluation involving a TerraPower topical report [f14642, f7652, f7660]. The process establishes requirements and a credible, scrutable PIRT, builds an assessment base, develops the evaluation model, and assesses adequacy, including scalability at Step 19 [f7653, f7654, f7656, f7657]. It distinguishes tests of isolated phenomena from coupled-system tests, permits less emphasis on low-ranked phenomena, and considers scale distortion, experimental uncertainty, code and model uncertainty, and applicability [f7655, f7659, f7658]. Expert opinion recommends adapting this logic to automatic braking by testing constituent mechanisms separately and reserving fewer full-system tests for coupled behavior, rather than attempting thousands of full-machine tests; this is not a nuclear requirement for earth-moving machinery [f7668, f7669, f7670]. A 2020 arXiv review, whose peer-review status is unclear, describes EMDAP as emphasizing scaling to address missing data but criticizes its implicit treatment of subjective evidence as reducing validation transparency [f7666, f7667].

nodes.synopsis: NRC Regulatory Guide 1.203, dated December 2005, defines the nuclear-domain Evaluation Model Development and Assessment Process (EMDAP) as four elements comprising 20 steps [f14642, f8088]. Its continued application to new reactor designs is illustrated by a 2025 safety evaluation of a TerraPower topical report and a related 2024 audit plan [f7660]. Experimental databases remain fundamental: PIRT ranks phenomena, with highly ranked phenomena requiring integral and separate-effects test data and lower-ranked phenomena receiving reduced emphasis [f7662, f7836]. Predictions outside the assessment matrix or physical scale require explicit scaling and applicability justification and uncertainty treatment; scale distortion and test uncertainty must not be hidden in a global correlation [f7661, f7663]. NRC also separates calibration from independent validation: agreement with a calibration test does not demonstrate predictive capability on independent data [f8159].

nodes.label: ASME
nodes.text: ASME
nodes.synopsis: ASME guidance distinguishes verification of implementation against mathematics, validation against the real application, and uncertainty quantification; these activities assess model credibility relative to its context of use [f14531, f10601, f9748]. Calibration against a test does not establish predictive capability on independent data, and the booklet cites ASME alongside NASA as requiring real-world validation rather than internal consistency alone [f8159, f14535, f14952]. The cited portfolio includes V&V 40-2018, V&V 10 (2019), and VVUQ 30.1-2024, with the latter addressing scaling methodologies, applicability justification, and uncertainty treatment [f9748, f7664]. The planning chapter synthesizes ASME and other frameworks into a proposed safety-claim decomposition, while the review chapter recommends a one-page credibility map for all seven reviewers [f9725, f10908]. The booklet emphasizes credibility and uncertainty over simulation counts and infers that, without an auditable evidence chain for one slice before prototype arrival, more scenarios add questionable evidence rather than assurance [f10884, f10796]. Even if virtual testing cannot replace most final physical evidence by mid-2027, the booklet identifies a useful hybrid role in defect discovery, scenario exploration, and selecting informative physical tests [f10987].

nodes.label: M&S SPICE
nodes.text: M&S SPICE
nodes.synopsis: M&S SPICE is a 2023 research-and-industry framework for automotive research, published in peer-reviewed proceedings of the INCOSE International Symposium [f8124, f7699]. It derives the credibility required for a simulation task from that task’s criticality and assesses whether the simulation process can deliver that credibility [f14595, f7699, f7700, f8125]. Alongside SET Level Credible Simulation Process, it addresses validation against physical data at the process level and addresses validity and transfer through credibility documentation [f8126, f8127]. For off-road automatic braking, however, these frameworks offer only a process template: they are not proven for that application and do not specify what physical evidence remains necessary [f8129, f8130, f8128].

nodes.label: DynoTRAIN
nodes.text: DynoTRAIN
nodes.synopsis: DynoTRAIN built the simulation-validation method behind the European rail running-approval standard EN 14363, with project results published in 2014–2015 and a broader EN 14363/DynoTRAIN acceptance-extension case spanning 2014–2022 [f14671, f14677, f7854]. Its research compared several vehicle models and software tools with measurements from multiple vehicles and countries, using more than 1,000 simulations [f7711, f14678]. Because engineering judgment applied to large numbers of plots did not scale, DynoTRAIN developed objective validation metrics; the resulting practice uses at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons per quantity from at least 12 track sections, with limits on comparison-set means and standard deviations [f7712, f14680]. The EN 14363 framework with ERA guidance addresses extended test conditions, modified vehicles and approved-reference-vehicle comparisons, while retaining physical running tests for the reference vehicle [f8135, f8136]. The corpus identifies this as the strongest family-transfer and test-reduction precedent for off-road automatic braking, but reports neither formal risk scaling nor a published percentage of physical tests removed across actual rail certifications [f8137, f8132, f7856].

nodes.label: EN 50126
nodes.synopsis: The glossary identifies EN 50126, alongside EN 50128 and EN 50129, as European railway standards covering reliability and safety management, software and electronic signaling [f15359]. Chapter 10 states that EN 50126 was not verified in this research, a gap repeated in the glossary [f7716, f15361]. The research also did not verify risk scaling, validation against physical data, validity envelopes and transfer rules, or remaining physical evidence for the listed standards, including EN 50126–50129 [f8155]. Consequently, the booklet leaves EN 50126’s relevance to off-road automatic braking unverified rather than establishing it as applicable guidance [f8155].

nodes.label: EN 50128
nodes.synopsis: The glossary places EN 50128 within the European railway standards covering reliability and safety management, software and electronic signaling [f15359]. Chapter 10 identifies EN 50716:2023 as its successor, while the glossary also calls that successor the current railway software standard [f7718, f15360]. However, both locations explicitly list EN 50128 and related railway standards as not verified in this research [f7716, f15361]. For planning off-road automatic braking validation, the booklet therefore leaves their relevance, risk scaling, physical-data validation, validity envelopes, transfer rules and remaining physical-evidence requirements unverified [f8155].

nodes.label: EN 50129
nodes.synopsis: The glossary identifies EN 50129 within a group of European railway standards covering reliability and safety management, software and electronic signaling [f15359]. Chapter 10 states that EN 50129 was not verified in this research, and the glossary repeats that limitation [f7716, f15361]. More specifically, the research did not verify risk scaling, validation against physical data, validity envelopes and transfer rules, or remaining physical evidence for a group that includes EN 50129 [f8155]. Its relevance to off-road automatic braking also remains unverified, so the booklet provides a definition but no verified basis for applying it to this use case [f15359, f8155].

nodes.label: EN 50716
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies EN 50716:2023 as the current railway software development standard and the successor to EN 50128 [f7717, f7718, f15360]. The glossary places EN 50716 among European-only standards, alongside railway standard EN 14363 and earth-moving machinery standard EN 474 [f15021]. Both Chapter 10 and the glossary nevertheless list EN 50716 as not verified in this research [f7716, f15361]. Specifically, its relevance to off-road automatic braking, risk scaling, validation against physical data, validity envelopes and transfer rules, and remaining physical evidence were not verified; its catalogue identification therefore does not establish applicability to the braking system [f8155, f7717, f7718].

nodes.label: Sandia Predictive Capability Maturity Model
nodes.text: Sandia Predictive Capability Maturity Model
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 10 identifies Sandia’s Predictive Capability Maturity Model (PCMM; Oberkampf et al., 2007) as a literature-cited decision model for verification, validation and uncertainty quantification maturity, but says it was not separately verified [f7721, f7722]. Chapter 12 compares PCMM with NASA 7009B, ASME V&V 40 and UNECE NATM, dating their origins to 2007, 2024, 2018 and 2022–2024 respectively [f10025]. For the collision-mitigation virtual-testing toolchain, the planning recommendation is to replace TRLs with a credibility maturity scale, specifically NASA-STD-7009B or Sandia PCMM (SAND2007-5948) [f9536, f10031]. The stated rationale is that these frameworks assess simulation maturity, fit high uncertainty with a fixed deadline, and respond to blind-prediction gaps [f10026, f10027, f10028]. The assessment favors documented practice, while acknowledging that the frameworks are “largely declarative”; this and PCMM’s lack of separate verification qualify the recommendation [f10030, f10029, f7722].

nodes.synopsis: MAPE is used to compare signal amplitude, range and point-cloud quantities in lidar sensor models [f7765]. The booklet reports clear-weather lidar-model errors of 1.7% for signal amplitude and 8.5% for point count [f14781, f14782]. Chapter 10 and the glossary agree that these applications report MAPE rather than use it as a thresholded acceptance criterion, so the reported values do not establish an acceptance threshold [f7766, f14787]. Interpretation also requires caution: MAPE misbehaves near zero measured values and, like MAE and RMSE, hides the shape of simulation-versus-measurement errors [f14783, f14785].

nodes.label: NASA-STD-7009B
nodes.text: NASA-STD-7009B
nodes.synopsis: NASA-STD-7009B was approved on 5 March 2024 and establishes modeling and simulation practice around credibility, verification, validation, sensitivity and uncertainty [f9737, f10599]. It assesses credibility across development and use, ties credibility effort to the consequences of a wrong decision, and, alongside ASME V&V 40, retains physical testing where decision risk is high or validation evidence is weakest [f9739, f9738, f7834, f7835]. Programs must define acceptance criteria, obtain technical-authority approval, and disclose dissenting technical opinions with results [f9539, f10600, f9741]. The planning chapter recommends credibility frameworks such as NASA-STD-7009B instead of TRLs for the collision-mitigation validation toolchain; blind-prediction gaps support this choice, although the frameworks are described as largely declarative [f9536, f10031, f10028, f10029]. An assessor-quality package requires more than simulator results, with recommended plan sections of 2–6 pages for evidence, V&V and test strategy, 1–1.5 pages for credibility and tool qualification, and 1–2 pages for results and review protocol [f8026, f10162, f10164, f10178].

nodes.label: EMDAP
nodes.text: EMDAP
nodes.synopsis: EMDAP is the US nuclear regulator’s 20-step safety-analysis modeling process, documented in NRC RG 1.203 dated December 2005; its four elements cover requirements, an assessment base, model development and adequacy judgment [f14640, f8088, f14643, f14644, f14645]. PIRT ranks physical phenomena by importance and understanding, directing test evidence toward highly ranked phenomena and reducing emphasis on low-ranked ones [f14643, f7836, f14646]. Its assessment base combines separate-effects and integral-effects experiments, while Step 19 uses scaling, similarity and applicability analysis to justify applying test-facility evidence to the full-size plant or beyond the test matrix [f14644, f8090, f7901, f8091]. The booklet rates EMDAP the best model for phenomena ranking, uncertainty and validation-matrix discipline for off-road automatic braking, but explicitly says it is not proven in that application [f8093, f8094]. Accordingly, the booklet retains integral full-system tests after submodel validation and treats an assessor-quality package as substantially broader than simulator results alone [f8197, f8026].

nodes.label: PIRT
nodes.text: PIRT
nodes.synopsis: PIRT ranks the physical phenomena that matter most and provides the graded basis for allocating validation evidence in NRC EMDAP: highly ranked phenomena require test data, while lower-ranked phenomena receive reduced emphasis [f14640, f8089, f7836, f14646]. The assessment base uses separate-effects tests, integral-effects tests and scaling analysis to isolate phenomena, exercise coupled behavior and establish applicability of test-rig data [f14644]. For collision-mitigation validation, the assessor package should rank brake fade, dust attenuation, glare and mount vibration, trace scenarios to hazards and EMESRT/ISO 21815, and use the ranking to determine which physical tests to retain [f8030, f14651]. Within the validated parameter hull, changes not touching ranked phenomena can be documented and evaluated through simulation alone, whereas changes touching them should trigger brake calibration and sensor field-of-view and detection checks at the new mount [f7912, f7913]. Full machine-family re-validation is recommended only for variants outside that hull or introducing a new PIRT phenomenon, such as a new sensor type or articulated steering; this is identified as expert opinion [f7918]. The method's subjectivity remains an explicit concern: a peer-reviewed criticism calls for treating it explicitly, and experts disagree about accepting subjective rankings without that treatment [f14652, f8194].

nodes.label: Goal Structuring Notation
nodes.text: Goal Structuring Notation
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends representing simulation credibility and safety arguments in a structured form such as Goal Structuring Notation (GSN), including a GSN or Claims-Arguments-Evidence (CAE) sketch in the plan’s safety-scope section and a preliminary argument in an appendix [f8021, f14983, f12255]. GSN uses diagram shapes to frame top-level goals with context, decompose them through strategies into sub-claims, and connect them to evidence; the glossary identifies the GSN Community Standard version 3, SCSC-141C (2021), as its current definition and credits Tim Kelly with its development in the 1990s [f12249, f9705, f12251, f12250]. CAE is the main alternative, using the same three ideas with different shapes, while SACM provides a formal data model for storing and exchanging arguments [f9706, f12252, f12249]. The proposed virtual-validation claim decomposition combines GSN with NASA model-credibility practice, ASME VVUQ and integrated test-and-evaluation practice [f9725]. These recommendations are not backed by direct comparative evidence of improved heavy-machinery safety outcomes or controlled studies of readers’ understanding of assurance diagrams, neither of which the booklet found [f9722, f9888, f12257].

nodes.label: Machinery Regulation
nodes.text: Machinery Regulation
nodes.synopsis: The capability plan should explain its fit with the Machinery Regulation from 20 January 2027, including possible notified-body assessment for machine-learning safety components [f10236]. The final plan should identify governing rules, applicability sign-off, whether simulation is accepted, relevant Machinery Regulation, PLD and AI Act dates, and an assessor engagement plan [f10165]. Simulation evidence should trace each claimed output to its supporting requirement or hazard and the final pass/fail argument under the Machinery Regulation and ISO 19014 performance levels [f8029]. The regulatory route remains uncertain until notified-body and counsel pre-consultation tests Annex I Part A applicability and simulation-evidence acceptability; no notified-body pre-consultation by early 2027, or ML perception without an Annex I Part A position, are warning signs [f10960, f10786]. The product liability lawyer expects a notified-body or legal opinion on Machinery Regulation and AI Act applicability, while EU-OSHA is cited only as an information agency summarizing the regulation, not as a regulator [f11134, f15686].

nodes.label: dSPACE SIMPHERA
nodes.text: dSPACE SIMPHERA
nodes.synopsis: SIMPHERA is a commercial tool for scenario generation, test management and orchestration of scenario-based testing at scale; paired with AURELION, it is presented as a complete or near-complete simulation platform [f9203, f8362, f8447, f8348]. The combined offering lists camera, ray-traced radar, lidar, infrared and ultrasonic models, plus integration with dSPACE benches and an OSI-compatible SIL/HIL chain [f15896, f15897, f8999]. The latest releases found were SIMPHERA 26.2 on 9 July 2026 and AURELION 26.2 on 15 July 2026 [f9001, f9207]. Evidence is on-road only: no public evidence validates quarry or mining terrain, material or weather fidelity, and terrain physics must come from elsewhere [f8454, f8455, f8997]. The platform appears among examples for the highest-cost tool chain, but no public price was found, so that positioning is not a published quotation [f9303, f9000, f9206].

nodes.label: Siemens Simcenter Prescan
nodes.text: Siemens Simcenter Prescan
nodes.synopsis: Siemens Simcenter Prescan is a commercial ADAS/AV environment, traffic, scenario and sensor simulation tool, listed among complete or near-complete platforms [f8456, f8348]. Its models cover camera, radar, lidar and ultrasonic sensors, with reflective material properties, lighting, weather and radar phenomena [f8457, f15899]. It supports OpenSCENARIO and OpenDRIVE, plus Python and MATLAB APIs [f8616, f16237]. Evidence in the corpus is on-road only: public off-road heavy-machine validation was not found, and translating its road-centric scene semantics and material libraries to quarries and mines is considered non-trivial [f9003, f8461, f15951, f8462]. The latest release found was Prescan 2606, dated 2026, but its exact release date and public price were not found; sensor-model pricing is quote-only [f8459, f8460, f8541, f9006].

nodes.label: Mevea
nodes.text: Mevea
nodes.synopsis: Mevea is a commercial Lappeenranta University spin-off founded in 2005, positioned for mobile machinery across construction, mining, ports, forestry and tractor research [f8560, f9100, f8667]. Its vendor-described capabilities include real-time multibody dynamics, hydraulics, powertrain, sensors, HIL I/O and dynamic soil interaction with buckets, tracks and tires; however, the booklet assesses heavy-machine physics tools as having thin sensor and scenario tooling and explicitly labels Mevea's sensor capabilities as vendor claims [f8561, f8283, f9102]. Documented applications include Siemens SIMOCRANE crane-automation twins in 2023, an academic tractor digital twin with CAN control in 2026, and mining training simulators; Mevea claims over 100 simulator models supplied to more than 50 customers [f8564, f8565, f8567, f8563]. Simulink co-simulation through FMI or TCP/IP is explicitly supported, and the example middle- and highest-cost chains use Mevea for terrain, hydraulics, machine variants or heavy-machine dynamics [f8562, f8699, f9286, f9304]. Its October 2026 seminar covers verification and validation cases from Prinoth, Oamk and IAAPS, while human-in-the-loop simulators such as Mevea may be needed for warning-then-brake human factors; public pricing and the latest release were not found [f8566, f9379, f9104, f9105].

nodes.label: CM Labs Vortex Studio
nodes.text: CM Labs Vortex Studio
nodes.synopsis: CM Labs Vortex Studio is commercial real-time multibody physics software for heavy equipment, including off-road vehicles, earthmoving, cranes and cables, and is identified among the tools with clear heavy-machinery relevance [f8576, f8672, f8663]. Its documented applications are mainly operator training, including OETIO and CONEXPO showcases; autonomy use remains a vendor claim, with no autonomy-validation customers found [f8579, f8674, f8580, f9116, f16048]. CM Labs markets engineering-grade tracked-vehicle and “sensor-grade” simulation, but the booklet's expert assessment characterizes this class of heavy-machine physics tools as strong in terrain and hydraulics yet thin in sensor and scenario tooling [f8577, f9117, f8283]. Vortex supports HIL with real controls and PLCs, and appears as a heavy-machine dynamics option in the highest-cost example chain alongside specialist sensor simulation, test benches and cloud execution [f8578, f8365, f16167, f9304]. The latest documentation or release entry found was version 2024.3, and public pricing was not published, leaving currency and procurement-cost gaps [f8581, f9120, f9119].

nodes.label: Fraunhofer ITWM Demify
nodes.text: Fraunhofer ITWM Demify
nodes.synopsis: The glossary and tools chapter consistently describe Fraunhofer ITWM Demify as research-and-service software for DEM-oriented soil–tool interaction in heavy machinery, rather than a complete collision-mitigation validation suite [f15987, f8592, f9140, f9141]. It is included among the tools with clear off-road and heavy-machinery relevance, with a focus on machine, terrain and granular-material physics [f16074, f8663, f9334]. Demify supports CPU/GPU execution and Python-oriented workflows, while its ecosystem is described as smaller than general commercial suites [f8592, f9143, f8593]. Sensor capabilities are listed as not applicable, and sensor simulation plus test management must be added; this aligns with the broader assessment that heavy-machine physics tools have thin sensor and scenario tooling [f9142, f8594, f8283]. Commercial licensing, public pricing and a numbered or latest release were not found, leaving procurement and version-planning gaps [f8595, f9144, f9145].

nodes.label: Offroad Autonomy Library
nodes.text: Offroad Autonomy Library
nodes.synopsis: The Offroad Autonomy Library is a commercial MathWorks support package for construction, mining and agriculture using Unreal Engine scenes; MATLAB/Simulink, the library and RoadRunner have per-product annual or perpetual licensing [f8374, f8958, f15877]. Its documented capabilities span an MPPI off-road planner available since R2024b, articulated-steering kinematics since R2025a, a vehicle-library loader since R2026b, and traversability analysis; R2026b is the second release of 2026 [f8375, f8376, f8377, f8378, f16239]. Vendor evidence includes shipped autonomous-excavator, backhoe truck-loading and open-pit haul-truck examples, but independent validation for automatic braking on heavy machines was not found [f15878, f8680, f8289]. The package exposes camera, lidar and INS, while radar and ultrasonic are listed in the wider stack rather than confirmed specifically inside the off-road package [f8380, f8960, f8382]. The proposed middle-cost engineering chain combines the MathWorks tools with Unreal and sensor toolboxes, with Mevea or AGX Dynamics coupled through FMI for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants [f9285, f16162].

nodes.synopsis: Cognata is described as a commercial, large-scale ADAS/AV simulation platform adapted from road applications for construction and mining, with digital twins, scenes, sensors and scenario execution [f8971, f8410, f8685]. Its marketed off-road use case covers slopes, boulders, dust, vegetation, darkness and heavy-machine blind spots; it also advertises camera, radar, lidar and thermal simulation, custom sensors and assets, and machine-learning training compressed to months [f8411, f8413, f8412]. However, the listed construction/mining evidence is only a vendor use-case page: named current customers, independent correlation results and independent heavy-machine automatic-braking validation were not found [f8686, f8414, f8415, f8289]. The corpus includes Cognata among complete or near-complete platforms and highest-cost example tool chains, but public pricing, a numbered or latest release, and verified interfaces and standards remain unavailable or unverified [f8346, f9303, f8975, f8416, f8976, f8974]. Cognata reportedly remained independent as of 2025 and had partnerships with Ansys and Microsoft in January 2025 [f8417].

nodes.label: Apache 2.0 license
nodes.text: Apache 2.0 license
nodes.synopsis: The corpus identifies Apache 2.0 as the permissive open-source license for NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Gazebo; Isaac Sim is described as open source since version 5.0, with its core free for internal R&D [f15924, f8477, f8483, f8525, f15915]. The glossary says Apache 2.0 allows companies to use, modify and redistribute software, including in commercial products, provided the original copyright notice is retained, and does not require publication of their own changes [f15925, f15927]. It also identifies an explicit patent grant as an Apache 2.0 feature [f15926]. However, Isaac Sim's Apache 2.0 status does not cover every asset or distribution configuration: separate asset terms apply, and redistribution with certain components requires a paid enterprise license, qualifying the broader licensing descriptions in Chapter 11 [f15903, f15936, f8299].

nodes.text: Duality AI Falcon
nodes.synopsis: Duality AI Falcon is a commercial Unreal Engine digital-twin simulator, with Falcon Editor and web-accessed FalconCloud, listed among complete or near-complete simulation platforms [f8418, f8346]. Its demonstrated application evidence is military off-road use through DARPA RACER-Sim and NASA JPL, rather than construction or mining; Falcon with the Neya autonomy stack is an explicitly supported RACER-Sim combination [f15889, f8423, f8707]. Its non-commercial education license costs USD 20 per month and launched on 20 November 2024, but commercial pricing was not found [f8424, f8425, f15888]. Sensor capabilities were not verified, and although FalconCloud was the latest release entry found, its release date was unavailable [f8979, f8982]. The glossary places Falcon among off-road-relevant research and military programs, while the underlying Unreal Engine editors are described as domain-neutral; editor generality therefore does not establish demonstrated construction or mining use [f16078, f9158, f15889].

nodes.label: AWS g6e.xlarge
nodes.text: AWS g6e.xlarge
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 11 and the glossary report third-party on-demand pricing of about USD 1.861 per hour for AWS g6e.xlarge with one NVIDIA L40S; Chapter 11 specifies 4 vCPUs, 32 GiB and us-east-1 Linux pricing in 2026 [f8310, f16062, f8855]. At that rate, illustrative compute costs are USD 1,861 for 1,000 GPU-hours, USD 18,610 for 10,000 and USD 186,100 for 100,000 [f8867]. Ten instances running continuously for 122 days cost about USD 54,490 and deliver at most about 29,000 GPU-hours, excluding software licenses, storage, network egress, orchestration and support [f8869, f8868]. A one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan lowers the quoted rate to about USD 1.17 per hour, while spot pricing is uncertain: two trackers quoted USD 0.427 and USD 1.8348 per hour [f8859, f8860]. The glossary additionally quotes about USD 30.131 per hour for eight such processors, without specifying that configuration [f16062].

nodes.label: NVIDIA L40S
nodes.text: NVIDIA L40S
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies AWS G6e with NVIDIA L40S GPUs as a generic pay-per-use cloud execution option, rather than an off-road-specific offering; the glossary specifies 48 GB of memory per L40S [f8370, f9257, f16202]. AWS G6e configurations scale to eight L40S GPUs, with maximum resources of 192 vCPUs, 1.536 TB RAM and 400 Gbps networking [f8854]. Third-party trackers give 2026 us-east-1 Linux on-demand prices of USD 1.861/hour for one GPU, USD 10.493/hour for four and USD 30.131/hour for eight [f8855, f8857, f8858]. The glossary also reports about USD 1.17/hour for a single L40S under a one-year commitment, while interruptible spot prices fluctuate widely [f16063]. A four-month campaign using ten GPUs of the cited AWS or Google types is estimated at roughly USD 54,000, but this is an expert estimate rather than an L40S-only configuration quote [f8312].

nodes.text: UNECE NATM credibility framework
nodes.synopsis: UNECE NATM credibility assessment is identified as a main simulation credibility reference alongside SET Level, IAMTS and several ASAM initiatives; that reference set is characterized as on-road and pre-standard [f8323]. The NATM framework is dated 2022–2024 and, alongside NASA-STD-7009B and ASME V&V 40, ties simulation credibility to a defined use and the consequence of error [f9454]. The planning requirement makes this explicit: credibility must be stated relative to intended use, operating envelope and consequence of error [f10293]. NATM's evidence is explicitly on-road, so these facts do not establish its applicability to heavy off-road machines [f8323, f9454, f10293].

nodes.label: OpenUSD
nodes.text: OpenUSD
nodes.synopsis: OpenUSD is an open, domain-neutral format for complete 3D scenes and assets, including geometry, materials and hierarchy; for this heavy off-road program, it is considered at least as strategically important as OpenDRIVE [f13198, f13199, f9363, f13200]. The recommended division of labor is OpenDRIVE for structured haul roads, OpenUSD and OpenMATERIAL for scenes, and OpenSCENARIO exports where required, within a broader standards-based integration architecture [f13216, f15862]. OpenUSD and Omniverse can represent mines and construction sites, but combine an open standard with NVIDIA components and do not constitute a validation method; sensor-material semantics and simulator portability therefore need governance [f8610, f9167, f9168, f8611]. Procurement should require OpenUSD and other open-format exports, alongside ownership-change exit clauses, to mitigate supplier dependence [f8887, f16487]. CARLA and Isaac Sim offer OpenUSD-related capabilities, while manufacturers starting without virtual-testing capability must build OpenUSD and 3D-asset skills alongside the wider simulation and validation disciplines [f8467, f9011, f8479, f8773, f16522]. The standard is free, but the listed release status is only “ongoing,” rather than a dated release milestone [f9170, f9171].

nodes.label: ROS 2
nodes.text: ROS 2
nodes.synopsis: ROS 2 is the current generation of Robot Operating System, common in robotics software, and part of the open-standard integration glue connecting heterogeneous simulation tools [f16240, f8715, f8335]. The corpus identifies integrations with CARLA, Isaac Sim, Gazebo and BeamNG; CARLA 0.10.0 added native support, whereas BeamNG.tech's Autoware/ROS 2 integration is community-provided and dated 2026 [f16240, f8465, f8506, f9031]. Gazebo with ROS 2 is explicitly supported, and Isaac Sim exposes ROS 2 alongside OpenUSD, including for its RTX sensors [f8708, f9018, f9073]. A lowest-cost example combines CARLA, Isaac Sim or Gazebo with Chrono and ROS 2, but low licensing costs come with the highest internal labor requirement and do not eliminate hardware or cloud costs [f16158, f16128, f8739].

nodes.label: VTDx
nodes.text: VTDx
nodes.synopsis: VTDx is the cloud-oriented variant of Virtual Test Drive (VTD), and both are commercial platforms whose ownership moved from Hexagon to Cadence in February 2026 [f8427, f8983, f15891]. The booklet lists them among complete or near-complete simulation platforms, but the evidence provided is on-road only; vendor-cloud off-road relevance follows the underlying platform, leaving off-road applicability unestablished here [f8347, f8984, f9255]. Listed capabilities include camera, lidar and radar sensors, OpenSCENARIO and OpenDRIVE, and SIL/HIL/DIL interfaces or modes [f8985, f8986]. Release information includes version 2026.1 dated 10 April 2026 and a listing for 2026.2 [f8988]. Public prices were not found for VTD/VTDx or the listed vendor-cloud alternatives; the cloud pricing table cites sources dated 2024–2026 [f8987, f9256, f16060].

nodes.label: BeamNG.tech
nodes.text: BeamNG.tech
nodes.synopsis: BeamNG.tech is described as a complete or near-complete commercial B2B simulation platform with real-time soft-body vehicle physics; public pricing was not found [f8350, f8502, f8503, f8508, f15909]. It provides programmable camera, lidar, radar, ultrasonic and IMU sensors, a Python API, and community-based ROS 2 integration, including a 2026 integration with Autoware [f8504, f8506, f9031]. Off-road driving is feasible, but its automotive-scale vehicle model is not a purpose-built excavator, dozer or haul truck with deformable soil [f8507, f15910]. Heavy-machine use is assessed as feasible rather than demonstrated, and independent heavy-machine correlation evidence was not found [f9029, f8509]. The latest release found was version 0.39, released on 20 August 2026 [f8505, f9033].

nodes.label: MORAI
nodes.text: MORAI
nodes.synopsis: MORAI is a commercial, complete or near-complete digital-twin driving simulation platform with scenario libraries and cloud execution, including large-scale cloud simulation [f8510, f8350, f8369, f9034]. It simulates camera, lidar, radar, GPS and IMU sensors, supports OpenSCENARIO 1.x, and is also listed among tools supporting OpenDRIVE [f8511, f8512, f8616]. Reported projects span automotive, trucking, Seoul digital twins, and unmanned ground and defense work, but the corpus found no off-road or mining/construction use evidence and no deformable-terrain support evidence [f8513, f15912, f8514, f8515]. MORAI requires supplier contact for pricing; neither platform pricing nor public large-scale cloud pricing was found, with the cloud comparison citing sources dated 2024–2026 [f15911, f8517, f9038, f9256]. No numbered or latest release was found, and the booklet cautions that vendor-cloud off-road relevance follows the underlying platform, leaving MORAI's suitability for heavy off-road validation unresolved [f8516, f9039, f9255, f9035].

nodes.label: rFpro
nodes.text: rFpro
nodes.synopsis: rFpro is a commercial high-fidelity driving simulator, classified as a complete or near-complete simulation platform, with a particularly detailed camera pipeline [f8518, f8350, f15914]. Its sensor workflows cover image sensors, optics and image signal processing; material dated 29 April 2026 describes full CMOS and ISP modeling and physical validation work [f8549, f8519]. Its focus is automotive and motorsport, and the reviewed evidence is on-road only: no off-road heavy-machine evidence or public off-road validation was found [f8520, f8550, f8521, f15951]. Camera support is documented, but other sensor capabilities, including ultrasonic support, and interfaces and standards were not verified or found [f9042, f8522, f9043, f9090]. Public pricing and a numbered release were not found, although release-related material exists for 2026; these remain procurement and version-identification gaps [f9044, f9045, f9093].

nodes.synopsis: Synopsys AVxcelerate Sensors, formerly Ansys, is a commercial sensor-simulation tool rather than a complete platform [f15917, f9058]. It provides physics-oriented camera, lidar, radar and thermal simulation for SIL/HIL testing, with documented co-simulation with CarMaker and CARLA [f8531, f8532, f15946]. Chapter 11 identifies 2026 R1 as the current/latest release found and reports quote-only pricing [f8533, f9063, f8537, f9062]. No off-road evidence was found, consistent with the glossary's broader finding that none of the named commercial sensor-simulation tools had public off-road validation [f8538, f9059, f15951]. nodes.label: Chrono::Sensor
nodes.text: Chrono::Sensor
nodes.synopsis: Chrono::Sensor is Project Chrono’s sensor offering, classified as open source under BSD-3 and listed as free; the glossary also includes it among open-source sensor-simulation options [f9124, f9076, f9080, f15949]. It supports camera, lidar, SPAD, GPS and IMU sensors, with OptiX ray tracing and modeled lens distortion, noise and lag reported in the tools chapter [f9078, f8495]. Its listed interface is the Chrono API, and the latest release found was 10.0.0, although the supplied facts give no release date [f9079, f9081]. Independent evidence includes lunar and off-road research, providing relevant application context [f9077]. Both the tools chapter and glossary report that physics-based ultrasonic simulation was not found in Chrono::Sensor or the other listed options; this is a reported evidence gap, not an explicit claim that such capability is impossible [f8547, f15950].

nodes.label: Persival
nodes.text: Persival
nodes.synopsis: Persival provides commercial sensor-model services, development and validation, with listed support for lidar, radar and cameras [f8551, f16104, f9096]. Its models follow ASAM OSI, are packaged as Functional Mock-up Units, and are explicitly supported as OSI FMUs inside any co-simulation host [f15948, f8706]. Its Avelon validation workflow correlates simulated and real sensor output and includes weather test benches; Persival is also described as a driver behind ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D [f8553, f8554]. Despite these capabilities, Chapter 11 found no off-road evidence for Persival, and the glossary reports no public off-road validation for any of the named commercial sensor-simulation tools, including Persival [f8556, f8813, f9095, f15951]. Public pricing was not found, and a latest release is listed as not applicable, leaving cost and off-road suitability unresolved in the corpus [f8555, f9098, f9099, f8556].

nodes.synopsis: Chapter 11 places MathWorks Vehicle Dynamics Blockset and Simscape in the vehicle and machine dynamics, terrain and soil tool category [f8357]. The glossary describes them as road-heritage dynamics tools with articulated steering available since R2025a [f15975]. Chapter 11 further reports that Vehicle Dynamics Blockset, Simscape and off-road kinematics provide dynamics and controller models, including articulated steering, operating closed-loop in Simulink R2026b [f8599]. However, high-detail soil deformation is not a primary strength of this tool combination, qualifying its inclusion in the terrain and soil category [f8600, f8357].

nodes.label: RoadRunner Scene Builder
nodes.text: RoadRunner Scene Builder
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 11 identifies MathWorks RoadRunner, RoadRunner Scene Builder and RoadRunner Scenario as commercial environment-creation tools that build and edit 3D environments, import GIS, HD maps and point clouds, reconstruct recorded scenes and parameterize scenarios [f8358, f8605, f9152]. The glossary reinforces their map and point-cloud import capabilities and exports to CARLA, dSPACE and IPG CarMaker; Chapter 11 specifies dSPACE ASM and lists OpenDRIVE, OpenSCENARIO, USD, FBX and glTF, with gRPC additionally listed among interfaces and standards [f15999, f8606, f9154]. They are adaptable to off-road use, but the base editor remains road-oriented, a limitation repeated in the glossary [f9153, f15999]. Pricing requires a quote, and only an unofficial price list was found; the latest release found was R2026b [f9155, f9156].

nodes.label: NVIDIA NuRec
nodes.text: NVIDIA NuRec
nodes.synopsis: NVIDIA NuRec reconstructs scenes from recordings using Gaussian splatting and is described as supporting domain-neutral reconstruction from logs [f15954, f9163]. It is integrated with Isaac Sim and CARLA 0.9.16; Isaac Sim provides NuRec-based neural rendering, while CARLA 0.9.16 added NuRec support [f8609, f8479, f8467]. The tooling inventory lists an open-core license, free internal use, and a latest release found dated 2025 to 2026 [f9162, f9165, f9166]. The glossary cautions that NuRec and related methods reconstruct appearance from logs but struggle with changes in sensor viewpoint [f16004]. Whether such reconstructions can serve as test evidence rather than training data remains uncertain, and the chapter's on-road assessment says learned reconstruction has not eliminated the need for application-specific credibility evidence [f9355, f9358].

nodes.label: Fraunhofer ITWM VMC Road & Scene-Generator
nodes.text: Fraunhofer ITWM VMC Road & Scene-Generator
nodes.synopsis: The glossary describes Fraunhofer ITWM VMC Road & Scene-Generator as building scenes from fused real measurements; Chapter 11 specifies 3D scenes for camera, lidar and radar simulation using real data sources and the REDAR measurement vehicle [f16000, f8612, f9173]. Chapter 11 lists it among environment creation and reconstruction offerings and identifies its delivery model as research and service [f8359, f9172]. Heavy-machine deployment detail was not found on the reviewed page, so the documented scene-generation capability does not establish suitability for heavy-machine deployment [f8613, f9174]. Interfaces and standards were not verified, and neither a public price nor a latest release was found, leaving integration, cost and release status unresolved [f9175, f9176, f9177].

nodes.label: Foretellix Foretify
nodes.text: Foretellix Foretify
nodes.synopsis: Foretellix Foretify is a commercial tool for coverage-driven scenario generation, constrained random variation and large-scale validation management [f8620, f16019]. It supports an OpenSCENARIO DSL and integrations with external simulators, but is not itself a machine or soil physics engine [f8622, f8627]. A 2021 partnership with Volvo Autonomous Solutions adapted Foretify for mines and quarries, providing independent evidence of off-road applicability [f16020, f9184]. An integration with NVIDIA DRIVE was announced [f8624]. The corpus found neither a public price nor a version date or latest release, leaving cost and release currency unresolved [f8628, f9186, f8629, f9187].

nodes.label: AVL SCENIUS
nodes.text: AVL SCENIUS
nodes.synopsis: AVL SCENIUS is a commercial scenario tool supporting the lifecycle from requirements through creation, planning, execution and reporting within an open scenario-based verification and validation tool chain [f8630, f8631, f16022]. The corpus lists it among scenario-generation and test-management offerings [f8361]. The glossary connects AVL's SCENIUS and scenario-based validation services with explicit work in agriculture, forestry, construction and mining, but Chapter 11 distinguishes AVL's broader off-road work from tool-specific evidence: neither off-road evidence nor a heavy-machine deployment of SCENIUS was found [f16099, f9189, f8632]. Pricing and release information also remain gaps: no public price or latest release was found [f9191, f9192].

nodes.label: RoadRunner Scenario
nodes.text: RoadRunner Scenario
nodes.synopsis: RoadRunner Scenario is identified as a commercial scenario-generation and test-management tool, described as adaptable for off-road use; the latest release found was R2026b [f8361, f9193, f9194, f9197, f16023]. The RoadRunner family, including Scenario, builds and edits 3D environments, imports GIS, HD maps and point clouds, reconstructs recorded scenes, and parameterizes scenarios [f8605]. The family supports exports to CARLA, dSPACE ASM and IPG CarMaker using formats including OpenDRIVE and OpenSCENARIO, while RoadRunner Scenario specifically supports OpenSCENARIO, MATLAB and gRPC interfaces [f8606, f9195]. Both the tools chapter and glossary place it in a middle-cost MATLAB/Simulink stack with off-road, Unreal and sensor components; the glossary adds Mevea or AGX Dynamics coupled through FMI for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants [f9285, f16162]. Pricing is available by quote, whereas an unofficial January 2024 price-list copy gives indicative annual/perpetual figures of 3,400/13,600 in presumed US dollars, rather than a confirmed current price [f9196, f8390, f16145].

nodes.label: dSPACE SCALEXIO
nodes.text: dSPACE SCALEXIO
nodes.synopsis: The glossary identifies SCALEXIO as a real-time HIL system and VEOS as PC-based virtual ECU simulation; Chapter 11 groups SCALEXIO, VEOS and AURELION as commercial replay and HIL tools supporting ECU execution with virtual sensors [f16034, f8363, f9219, f8639]. AURELION and SIMPHERA integrate with the dSPACE ecosystem, and the booklet describes the combined tools as a strong route from software-in-the-loop to hardware-in-the-loop testing [f8448, f8999, f8640]. That route requires sensor- and ECU-specific engineering: camera video, radar targets, Ethernet streams and raw stimulation are materially different injection problems [f8641]. J1939 emulation is reported possible per ISO/TS 21815-2, but the listed evidence for these tools is on-road only, leaving off-road applicability unsubstantiated by that evidence [f9221, f9220]. Both the glossary and Chapter 11 place the dSPACE combination among highest-cost example chains, yet neither a public price nor a full-system price was found [f16166, f9303, f9222, f8642].

nodes.label: dSPACE VEOS
nodes.text: dSPACE VEOS
nodes.synopsis: The glossary identifies VEOS as dSPACE’s PC-based virtual ECU simulation tool, alongside SCALEXIO for real-time HIL; Chapter 11 describes the combined SCALEXIO, VEOS and AURELION offering as a strong route from software-in-the-loop to hardware-in-the-loop testing with virtual sensors [f16034, f8639, f8640]. Vendor findings explicitly support a chain combining ASM, AURELION, VEOS and ModelDesk, and integration of AURELION and SIMPHERA with the broader dSPACE HIL ecosystem [f8704, f8448]. Sensor injection remains sensor- and ECU-specific, with camera video, radar targets, Ethernet streams and raw stimulation posing materially different engineering problems; the listed evidence is on-road only, leaving off-road applicability unestablished by that evidence [f8641, f9220]. J1939 emulation is reported possible per ISO/TS 21815-2 [f9221]. These commercial tools appear in the highest-cost example validation chain, but neither a public price nor a full-system price was found, limiting budget certainty [f9219, f9303, f16166, f9222, f8642].

nodes.label: NI VeriStand
nodes.text: NI VeriStand
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies NI VeriStand with PXI and CompactRIO as commercial data-replay and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) tools [f8363, f9224]. Its listed capabilities include real-time testing, plant models, logging and HIL I/O, with plant models and I/O explicitly named as interfaces [f8643, f9226]. The evidence listed is general HIL evidence, rather than a more specific validation claim [f9225]. A PXIe-8842 controller costs about USD 5,200, but this covers only the controller—not a HIL bench—and a complete NI VeriStand/PXI/CompactRIO system requires a quote [f9227, f16035]. No latest release was found, leaving release currency unresolved in the booklet [f9228].

nodes.label: NI PXI
nodes.text: NI PXI
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 11 identifies NI VeriStand with PXI and CompactRIO as commercial offerings for data replay and hardware-in-the-loop testing [f8363, f9224]. The listed capabilities include real-time testing, plant models, logging and hardware-in-the-loop I/O, with plant models and I/O also explicitly listed as interfaces [f8643, f9226]. The PXIe-8842 controller costs about USD 5,200; the glossary clarifies that this price covers only the controller, not a complete HIL bench, while a NI VeriStand/PXI/CompactRIO system requires a quote [f9227, f16035]. The evidence provided is general hardware-in-the-loop evidence, and no latest release was found, leaving the documented evidence scope and release currency limited [f9225, f9228].

nodes.label: NI CompactRIO
nodes.text: NI CompactRIO
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 11 places NI CompactRIO alongside NI VeriStand and PXI among commercial data-replay and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) offerings [f8363, f9224]. The combined offering supports real-time testing, plant models, logging and HIL I/O, with plant models and I/O listed as interfaces [f8643, f9226]. The booklet characterizes its evidence as general HIL evidence, rather than presenting a more specific validation finding [f9225]. A NI VeriStand/PXI/CompactRIO system requires a quote; the approximately USD 5,200 price repeated in the glossary is for a PXIe-8842 controller only, not a complete HIL bench [f9227, f16035]. No latest release was found for the combined offering, leaving its release currency unresolved in the booklet [f9228].

nodes.label: Speedgoat
nodes.text: Speedgoat
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies Speedgoat with Simulink Real-Time as a commercial HIL hardware/software offering, providing turnkey real-time targets tightly coupled to Simulink [f16036, f9229, f8645, f9231]. Speedgoat engineering services also provides real-time and HIL integration, but the cited evidence is general HIL rather than off-road-specific, leaving application-specific validation unestablished [f8814, f9230, f16103]. The middle-cost example stack places Speedgoat or NI in later HIL testing, alongside an externally validated sensor model packaged as an OSI FMU and cloud GPUs for batch runs [f9288, f16163]. No public price was found, so the corpus does not establish Speedgoat's actual cost within that example stack [f8647, f9232, f9288]. The latest release found for the combined Speedgoat and Simulink Real-Time entry was Pulse, dated 15 May 2025 [f9233].

nodes.label: Simulink Real-Time
nodes.text: Simulink Real-Time
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies Speedgoat with Simulink Real-Time as a hardware-and-software HIL offering, alongside other replay and HIL options [f8364, f16036]. These commercial tools provide turnkey real-time targets tightly coupled to Simulink, which is also their listed interface [f8645, f9229, f9231]. Speedgoat engineering services supports real-time and HIL integration around Simulink Real-Time, but the cited evidence is general HIL rather than off-road-specific [f8814, f9230]. No public price was found, leaving a procurement-cost gap [f8647, f9232]. The latest release found for the combined entry was Pulse, dated 15 May 2025; separately, the glossary places Simulink Real-Time in the twice-yearly MATLAB and Simulink release family and identifies R2026b as its second 2026 release, without establishing an updated release date for the combined entry [f9233, f16239].

nodes.label: OPAL-RT
nodes.text: OPAL-RT
nodes.synopsis: The booklet identifies OPAL-RT as a provider of real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) benches, with 4DV-SIM and OP5707XG2 included among data-replay and HIL offerings [f16101, f8364]. Chapter 11 positions 4DV-SIM and OPAL-RT's real-time HIL offerings for off-highway and autonomous vehicles, and cites named off-highway and defense users as off-road evidence [f8648, f8808, f8809]. OP5707XG2 is identified as a CPU/FPGA real-time system, consistent with the glossary's classification of OPAL-RT CPU and FPGA systems as real-time computing hardware [f8650, f16180]. Pricing for 4DV-SIM and OP5707XG2 is quote only, leaving planners without a stated purchase price in these facts [f8651].

nodes.label: OPAL-RT 4DV-SIM
nodes.text: OPAL-RT 4DV-SIM
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 11 positions OPAL-RT 4DV-SIM as a commercial offering for autonomous and off-highway vehicles, adapted from on-road applications for off-highway and defense use [f9234, f8648, f8697]. The glossary echoes the off-highway and defense user evidence; named users include Safran, Valeo, Michelin and Milrem Robotics, with Milrem’s defense-user evidence explicitly labeled as vendor evidence [f16081, f8649, f8698]. The booklet places 4DV-SIM and OP5707XG2 among data-replay and hardware-in-the-loop offerings and lists CPU/FPGA real-time capability; the glossary specifically identifies OP5707XG2 as combining a CPU and FPGA [f8364, f9236, f16037]. Pricing for both offerings is quote-only, and no latest release was found, leaving procurement cost and release currency unresolved [f8651, f9237, f9238].

The listed 2026 public on-demand price range is USD 1.861–30.131 per hour in us-east-1, based on trackers [f9258]. Although included among cloud execution options, the tools table marks its off-road relevance as not applicable, rather than establishing an off-road-specific role [f8370, f9257].

nodes.synopsis: DARPA announced RACER-SIM in January 2022 with Duality Robotics and Intel-Federal as its two prime contractors; its reported Phase 1 budget was approximately USD 6 million [f8419, f15831, f8420, f15832]. Duality, partnered with Neya Systems, was tasked with building an 80 km² virtual off-road environment measuring 20 km by 4 km on a digital-twin simulation platform [f8421, f15833]. Duality Falcon with the Neya autonomy stack is an explicitly supported RACER-Sim combination, although that compatibility claim is vendor-sourced [f8707]. RACER-Sim and NASA JPL provide independent evidence of Falcon's military off-road use, and JPL contracted the same platform for RACER Phase II in September 2024 [f8690, f8978, f15834]. This establishes military off-road relevance, but the corpus does not establish demonstrated construction or mining use for Falcon [f15889].

nodes.label: CRM
nodes.text: CRM
nodes.synopsis: Project Chrono provides SCM, CRM and DEM terrain models [f9123, f15988]. The glossary describes CRM as Chrono’s version of SPH and related continuum methods, which represent flowing soil with particles [f15984]. Developers report that higher-fidelity CRM terrain runs 50–200 times slower than real time, indicating a substantial simulation-time burden [f8499, f15989]. Chapter 11 identifies an NVIDIA GPU requirement and flags this vendor-specific dependency; the glossary repeats the requirement but leaves the maker unnamed [f8500, f15989].

nodes.label: Fraunhofer ITWM
nodes.text: Fraunhofer ITWM
nodes.synopsis: The tools chapter and glossary identify Fraunhofer ITWM as a research/service option with off-road and heavy-machinery relevance, covering construction-site digital twins, operator-in-the-loop simulation, real-data environments and soil simulation [f8665, f8823, f16113, f9172]. InVerS integrates sensor-data acquisition through operator alerting in simulation, while RODOS provides a human-in-the-loop simulator option [f8819, f8820, f16047]. VMC Road & Scene-Generator creates 3D scenes for camera, lidar and radar simulation from fused real data sources using the REDAR measurement vehicle [f8612]. Demify adds soil DEM capability, and the broader InVerS, RODOS and VMC research portfolio covers construction-site digital twins, commercial vehicles and excavator loads [f8822, f8694]. However, the supporting institute pages are classified as vendor evidence, and heavy-machine deployment detail for VMC was not found on the reviewed page; stated relevance should therefore not be treated as documented deployment evidence [f8694, f8613, f8823].

nodes.label: InVerS
nodes.text: InVerS
nodes.synopsis: The corpus identifies InVerS as a Fraunhofer ITWM research project focused on construction-site digital twins [f8694, f16078]. Chapter 11 describes its simulation scope as integrating “sensor data acquisition to alerting machine operators” [f8819]. The glossary places InVerS among off-road-relevant research and military programs, alongside RODOS, VMC and Duality Falcon associated with DARPA RACER-Sim [f16078]. The supporting institute pages are explicitly classified as vendor evidence; the supplied facts provide no independent validation results, costs or availability dates for InVerS [f8694, f8819, f16078].

nodes.label: RODOS
nodes.text: RODOS
nodes.synopsis: Fraunhofer ITWM offers RODOS as a human-in-the-loop driving simulator, and the glossary identifies it as an operator-in-the-loop simulator option [f8820, f16047]. The booklet places RODOS alongside InVerS and VMC among off-road-relevant research projects, with the institute pages classified as vendor evidence [f8694, f16078]. The glossary also situates RODOS within a broader ITWM capability portfolio that includes construction-site digital twins, real-data scenes and Demify soil simulation [f16113]. Human-in-the-loop simulators such as RODOS may be needed to assess warning-then-brake human factors, but the stated need remains uncertain rather than established [f9379].

nodes.label: VMC
nodes.text: VMC
nodes.synopsis: VMC is identified as a Fraunhofer ITWM research project in Chapter 11 and as an off-road-relevant program in the glossary [f8694, f16078]. Chapter 11 specifically says Fraunhofer ITWM offers VMC real-data environments [f8821]. VMC is grouped with InVerS and RODOS in a portfolio covering construction-site digital twins, commercial vehicles and excavator loads, but the supplied facts do not assign each application to an individual project; the supporting institute pages are labeled as vendor evidence [f8694].

nodes.label: Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU)
nodes.text: Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU)
nodes.synopsis: An FMU packages a model to the open Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI) standard as a single file containing equations or compiled code and an input/output description [f13230, f13232]. FMI standardizes connections between simulation programs running together in step, while SSP records FMU wiring and parameters so the complete arrangement can be shared and reproduced [f13230, f13234]. Sensor models are delivered as FMUs using the Open Simulation Interface (OSI) message standard [f13235]. The tools-and-vendors chapter identifies Persival as offering credible sensor-model development and validation, including OSI FMUs and weather benches, connecting the glossary's packaging approach to a named supplier [f8812, f13235].

nodes.synopsis: FMI is an open standard for connecting separate simulation programs in co-simulation; an FMU packages a model, while SSP describes how FMUs are wired together [f13230, f13232]. Around 250 tools supported FMI by mid-2025 [f13233]. The booklet’s middle-cost example tool chain depends on FMI coupling between machine physics and controls, with Mevea or AGX Dynamics providing terrain, hydraulics and machine variants [f13239, f9286, f13236]. FMI also appears alongside OpenDRIVE, OpenSCENARIO, OSI and ROS 2 as enabling heterogeneous road-ADAS tool chains, although that finding is explicitly on-road rather than heavy off-road evidence [f9331].

nodes.label: Assumption-based planning
nodes.text: Assumption-based planning
nodes.synopsis: Assumption-based planning originated at RAND for the U.S. Army’s Force XXI work, with documentation in 1993 and a book in 2002; it tracks load-bearing and vulnerable assumptions through failure signposts, shaping actions and hedges [f9557, f9558, f16345]. The booklet assesses it as a strong fit for first-time capabilities and high-uncertainty programmes with fixed deadlines, recommending it alongside discovery-driven planning for uncertainty retirement rather than as a standalone planning architecture [f9560, f10049, f9591, f16428]. Its status is documented practice supported by Army applications, but outcome evidence and rigorous comparative studies demonstrating schedule or safety improvements were not found [f9564, f10050, f10051, f9562]. To avoid bloated assumption lists, the practical recommendation is a short register of critical assumptions and signposts, with risks, assumptions, issues and unknowns kept separate [f9563, f10054, f9658]. Hedging supports fallback design despite limited outcome evidence, and the recommended plan presentation allocates 1.5–3 pages to risks, assumptions and fallbacks [f9701, f10174].

nodes.label: Discovery-driven planning
nodes.text: Discovery-driven planning
nodes.synopsis: The booklet recommends discovery-driven planning alongside assumption-based planning to retire uncertainty, within a layered programme architecture whose backbone is systems-engineering verification and validation planning [f9591, f16428]. It uses assumption checkpoints and inexpensive learning milestones, especially in the first months and during preparation, to establish feasibility rather than report coding completion [f9566, f9567, f10061, f16272]. The method is judged a high fit for high-uncertainty programmes with fixed deadlines and is attributed to McGrath and MacMillan in 1995, with a subsequent book in 2009 [f10057, f9565]. Its evidence status is documented practice with adjacent randomized-trial support: the closest research tested a related scientific decision-making approach in start-ups in 2020, followed by four replication trials involving 759 firms in 2024 [f10060, f9568]. That support remains limited to the venture domain, and acceptance evidence is lacking, so the recommendation should not be read as demonstrated acceptance suitability for collision-mitigation validation [f10059, f9591].
