nodes.label: Reference class forecasting
nodes.text: Reference class forecasting
nodes.synopsis: Reference class forecasting uses the actual outcome distribution of comparable past projects rather than internal plan details to counter optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation [f9604, f16313]. Its advantage over Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting depends on genuine reference-class similarity: a 2016 empirical test found benefits in accuracy, stability and timeliness, a 2021 study of 52 projects supported similarity-based construction, and a 2025 review reinforced that condition [f9606, f9607, f9609]. The booklet recommends combining it with schedule-risk analysis, using P50/P80, within a layered planning architecture rather than as a standalone method [f10070, f16428]. For the first-of-a-kind virtual safety-test capability considered here, no similar whole-programme reference class exists; component-level classes built from internal records, with stated uplifts, are recommended but are not a separately validated forecasting method [f10299, f9613, f10300]. Practical value is less contested than the behavioural explanation, which remains disputed [f10318, f16316].

nodes.text: earned-value forecasting
nodes.synopsis: Earned-value forecasting is a comparator in the corpus’s assessment of reference class forecasting, whose advantage over it and Monte Carlo depends on a genuinely similar reference class [f9437, f16315, f9606]. Batselier and Vanhoucke’s 2016 empirical test found that advantage across accuracy, stability and timeliness, but only when reference-class similarity was high [f9606]. The glossary reinforces this condition with a 2025 review concluding that reference class forecasting works only when the right reference classes have been constructed [f16315]. These findings therefore do not establish unconditional superiority over earned-value forecasting [f9437, f16315, f9606].

nodes.label: NIH
nodes.text: NIH
nodes.synopsis: NIH’s review model asks whether work should be done, whether it can be done well, and whether the necessary expertise and resources are in place; the glossary repeats this planning framework [f9833, f16461]. The Simplified Review Framework notice NOT-OD-24-010 was released on 19 October 2023 and applies to due dates on or after 25 January 2025, while reviewer materials updated through September 2026 reinforce structured evaluation rather than enthusiasm [f9829, f9835]. For the heavy off-road collision mitigation validation plan, the corpus recommends the NIH Approach section as a structural template, including potential problems, alternative strategies, benchmarks for success, and attention to establishing feasibility in risky early-stage work [f9978, f9979, f9834]. Structured review does not guarantee reviewer agreement: Pier and colleagues’ 2018 study found no agreement on application quality when 43 reviewers assessed the same 25 NIH applications, with Krippendorff’s alpha values all near zero [f9846, f9471]. NIH is one source for the broader skeptical-review checklist, which is practice-derived expert opinion rather than a ranking; the often-cited 1987 Cuca and McLoughlin study on NIH rejection reasons remains unverified in the corpus [f10212, f9841].

nodes.label: Heilmeier Catechism
nodes.text: Heilmeier Catechism
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 12 and the glossary describe DARPA’s Heilmeier Catechism as the most compact reviewer test; DARPA uses its questions to assess and think through proposed research programmes [f9824, f16460]. It asks for a jargon-free goal, current practice and limitations, novelty and reasons for success, beneficiaries and impact, risks, cost, duration, and mid-term and final tests of success [f9825, f9826, f9827, f16460]. The corpus places it within a convergence of funder questions around importance, feasibility and rigor, team and resources, risk, and observable success; ARPA-E and ARPA-H use variants [f9473, f9828]. For planning documents, Chapter 12 recommends using Heilmeier alongside other templates or sources for both a 1–2-page executive decision brief and a 1–2-page problem and decision context section [f10152, f10154].

nodes.synopsis: Horizon Europe assesses proposals on Excellence, Impact, and Quality and Efficiency of the Implementation; the glossary summarizes these criteria as excellence, impact and quality of implementation [f9838, f16462]. nodes.synopsis: Chapter 12 and the glossary consistently identify ISO 16290:2013 as the standard for technology readiness levels (TRLs) [f9512, f14686]. TRLs measure maturity on a scale from 1 to 9, from a basic idea or basic principles to a system proven in real operation [f14684, f15336]. The glossary adds that the standard defines TRLs for space systems and standardizes their assessment criteria, while the scale originated at NASA [f14684, f14686, f15336]. It distinguishes ISO 16290 from ISO 18571 for curve agreement and ISO 25119 for functional safety on farm-machine control systems; these facts do not explain how the space-system TRL framework is adapted to the off-road braking project [f15330, f14684, f9512].

nodes.synopsis: The U.S. Department of Defense requires a Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) for major programmes, documented in DoD Instruction 5000.89 (November 2020) and TEMP Guidebook version 3.1 (January 2017) [f9546, f16407]. The TEMP is the overarching management document for integrated test and evaluation, and its guidance seeks early identification of design and integration issues [f9547, f9548]. DoD treats modelling-and-simulation V&V as part of that integrated strategy, providing a precedent for avoiding separate simulation and test teams; MIL-STD-3022 supplies a standard for documenting model-and-simulation VV&A [f9551, f14663]. These precedents carry a qualification: GAO-26-108457 reports that GAO has recommended revamping DoD test and evaluation policies since 2022 [f9553]. The booklet’s reusable gate-card recommendation draws on DoD entrance and exit criteria and GAO criterion-based decisions, but is explicitly expert opinion [f10205].

nodes.synopsis: Critical Chain is a schedule-planning method attributed to Goldratt in 1997; it aggregates buffers, which the glossary describes as pooled at the ends of chains [f10092, f10091, f9584, f16304]. Chapter 12 and the glossary consistently characterize it as popular but unproven, with a 2003 critique finding its claims unproven [f10096, f9585, f10143, f16304]. The evidence is mixed: practitioner reports support the method, while the planning-method comparison lists a critique as evidence against it or a limitation [f10094, f10095, f10143]. For high uncertainty combined with a fixed deadline, its assessed fit is low-to-medium, and Chapter 12 does not recommend it as the basis of the collision-mitigation validation plan [f10093, f10097].

nodes.label: Flyvbjerg
nodes.text: Flyvbjerg
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 12 attributes the formalization of reference class forecasting to Flyvbjerg (2006; 2008; with Gardner, 2023): estimating from actual outcomes of comparable past projects rather than the current plan’s internal details, to counter optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation [f9604]. The glossary connects this method to Kahneman and Lovallo’s “outside view” and adds that estimates from comparable projects are then adjusted [f16313]. Chapter 12 also associates reference class forecasting plus schedule-risk analysis with Flyvbjerg 2006 and GAO-16-89G [f10062]. The behavioural explanation of cost overruns remains disputed: Love and Ahiaga-Dagbui challenged it in 2018, while Flyvbjerg and colleagues defended it; the practical value of reference class forecasting is described as less contested than its mechanism [f9610, f10317, f10318]. However, Chapter 13 says this literature was not verified in the research and treats reference class forecasting as a relevant lead rather than a verified basis for planning [f10743, f11199].

nodes.synopsis: Klein’s pre-mortem, published in Harvard Business Review in September 2007, asks a team to imagine its programme has failed and explain why, before the project starts [f9659, f16353]. The glossary applies it to virtual validation by imagining an August 2027 safety review board rejection of virtual-testing results and asking what happened; this is a hypothetical exercise, not a reported rejection [f16353]. The corpus found only one direct test: Veinott, Klein and Wiggins (2010), which assigned 178 students to five conditions and found that pre-mortems reduced confidence in the plan more than the alternatives [f9661, f9662]. That evidence has an independence limitation because the test’s authors are linked to the method’s originator [f9663]. Chapter 12 also associates Klein with Goodenough and Weinstock’s 2015 eliminative argumentation with explicit defeaters, which addresses confidence in a safety argument rather than confidence in a plan [f9714, f9662].

nodes.label: Tim Kelly
nodes.text: Tim Kelly
nodes.synopsis: Tim Kelly developed Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) in the 1990s; Chapter 12 cites Kelly (1998) and the GSN Community Standard version 3 (2021) for a notation that connects contextualized goals, strategies, sub-claims and evidence [f12250, f9705]. Kelly's safety-case management approach appears in documented practice as an instrument for linking a roadmap to evidence, and safety-case-driven planning is associated with Kelly 1998 and UL 4600 [f9814, f10112]. For the heavy off-road collision mitigation validation plan, the corpus recommends Kelly's step-by-step argument review (2007) as a suitable source of structure [f9985]. This endorsement sits within a broader disagreement: Kelly and UL 4600 favor safety cases, whereas Haddon-Cave on Nimrod, Leveson and Graydon criticize them [f10319].

nodes.synopsis: A Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) is an overarching document connecting planned virtual and physical tests to the decisions they inform, along with required data, resources, schedule and pass criteria [f16406]. It also links program decisions to test objectives, metrics, entrance and exit criteria, and reporting [f16408]. Its core device, the Integrated Decision Support Key, connects each decision to an evaluation question and the data needed to answer it, a method also described in Chapter 12 [f16409, f9813]. Chapter 12 classifies TEMP alongside NASA-STD-7009B, NATM and V&V planning as documented practice grounded in institutional standards and guidance, but the glossary reports that outcome studies comparing TEMP with alternatives were not found [f10136, f16411]. For the eleven-month collision-mitigation validation program, the glossary judges a literal defense TEMP excessive, distinguishing the useful planning logic from the suitability of its full implementation [f16412, f16409].

nodes.label: Minto's Pyramid Principle
nodes.text: Minto's Pyramid Principle
nodes.synopsis: Minto’s Pyramid Principle is presented as an executive-communication practice and a consulting counterpart to BLUF, using a situation-complication-question-answer opening [f16446, f9851]. Chapter 12 places it alongside military BLUF, Amazon’s six-page narrative and PR/FAQ, the UK Treasury Five Case Model, and Strategic Decisions Group’s Decision Quality [f9851]. The corpus reports finding no direct controlled evidence that pyramid structures, BLUF or six-page narratives improve technical programme approval or success, so these should be treated as practitioner formats rather than proven performance interventions [f9853, f10141].

nodes.label: Amazon
nodes.text: Amazon
nodes.synopsis: Chapter 12 presents Amazon's six-page narrative and PR/FAQ as practitioner formats for executive communication, alongside other planning and decision frameworks [f9851]. The glossary explains working backwards as writing a product press release before building the product, then adding frequently asked questions with honest answers [f16456]. The narrative memo is a sibling of working backwards, with a documented six-page limit, and is read silently at the start of a meeting instead of using slides [f9989, f16458]. The supplied facts describe these formats but do not establish their effectiveness for the collision-mitigation validation plan [f9851, f16456, f9989, f16458].

nodes.label: UK Treasury Five Case Model
nodes.text: UK Treasury Five Case Model
nodes.synopsis: The UK Treasury Five Case Model structures a business case into strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management cases [f16459]. Chapter 12 includes it among practitioner formats for executive communication and recommends it as a documented template for structuring the heavy off-road collision mitigation validation plan [f9851, f9981]. Specifically, the problem and decision context section should occupy 1–2 pages, drawing on Heilmeier and the Five Case Model, while the sustainment and change policy section should occupy 0.5–1 page, drawing on the Five Case Model [f10154, f10180]. These facts establish its structure and recommended planning uses, but provide no evidence of effectiveness or mapping between the five cases and the proposed plan sections [f16459, f9981, f10154, f10180].

nodes.synopsis: The corpus presents Delphi as a disciplined form of expert review that collects and weighs specialists’ beliefs, using anonymous estimates gathered in rounds with feedback between rounds [f16352, f16366]. Chapter 12 and the glossary agree that Delphi generally outperforms unstructured groups, with Chapter 12 citing Rowe and Wright (1999) and broader evidence from reviews and tournaments [f9948, f10133, f16366]. However, agreement among experts does not establish correctness, so consensus should not be treated as proof that a plan is sound [f9948, f16366]. Chapter 12 also reports that methodological reviews published from 2021 to 2024 note wide variation in Delphi study design and reporting, while identifying no single review, leaving the evidence attribution incomplete [f9949].

nodes.synopsis: The Amazon six-pager is a six-page narrative memo, described as a sibling of Amazon’s working backwards method and read silently at the start of a meeting instead of slides [f16458]. Chapter 12 identifies it as a documented template suitable for structuring the heavy off-road collision mitigation validation plan [f9980]. The chapter also recommends a shorter, 1–2-page executive decision brief drawing on BLUF, six-pager and Heilmeier templates or sources, distinguishing the brief from the full six-page memo [f10152, f16458]. These are recommendations about presentation structure, not demonstrated effectiveness: the corpus found no evidence that six-pagers, BLUF or the Pyramid Principle improve approval or success and classifies them as popular but unproven [f10141].

nodes.label: ISO/TS 5083
nodes.text: ISO/TS 5083
nodes.synopsis: ISO/TS 5083:2025 covers the design, verification and validation of automated driving systems [f15319]. The glossary also groups it with the ISO 3450x series as road-vehicle standards for describing, sorting and choosing automated-driving test scenarios [f15312]. Chapter 12 identifies ISO/TS 5083:2025, alongside SOTIF (ISO 21448:2022), as applicable to the perception-model gap, while explicitly treating them as on-road evidence [f10339]. For off-road planning, the glossary limits ISO/TS 5083 and the related standards to methodological precedent rather than off-road compliance evidence, citing their road-vehicle and limited-access-highway scope [f15320]. These standards establish no physical-to-virtual testing ratio, so they do not supply that planning parameter [f15321].

nodes.synopsis: The skeptic’s review identifies the EU automated-driving type-approval regime as the most simulation-friendly regulator found, while emphasizing that simulation cannot substitute for its physical tests [f10410, f11161]. The glossary adds that each model must have documented validation, and both locations require evidence of the competence of teams validating and using the toolchain [f14951, f10412]. nodes.label: WorkSafe Western Australia
nodes.text: WorkSafe Western Australia
nodes.synopsis: WorkSafe Western Australia is a workplace-safety regulator, distinct from WorkSafe New Zealand, and supplies the Significant Incident Reports cited in the booklet; its material becomes part of the primary legal context when target markets are outside the EU, including Australia [f15673, f15681, f11285]. SIR 226 describes an autonomous haul truck colliding with a manned water cart at night after a route was released in the control system but not marked on the ground, with inadequate change management identified as a contributory cause [f10660, f15684, f10664]. SIR 286 describes operators approaching trucks during recovery without recognizing that they were in exception mode rather than suspended; movement resumed when communications were restored [f10718, f15682]. The reports' web pages carry dates of 11 March 2025 for SIR 226 and 7 March 2025 for SIR 286, but their original issue dates remain uncertain; the research's August 2015 dating of the SIR 226 incident is not stated in the page text [f10666, f10718, f11207, f11208]. WorkSafe's 2025 mobile autonomous mining code warns of additional risks when autonomous and manned operations are integrated and calls for continuing supplier–mine consultation, while the review also cites WorkSafe WA among sources documenting false alarms, rejection, overrides and desensitization [f10720, f10721, f10496].

nodes.synopsis: WorkSafe Western Australia's Significant Incident Report 226 describes an autonomous haul truck colliding with a manned water cart at night [f10660, f15684]. The turnaround loop was released in the control system, but its intersection was not delineated on the ground and the route was not communicated to other operators; WorkSafe identified inadequate change management as a contributory cause [f10661, f10662, f10664]. The truck detected the water cart, but its speed and response time were insufficient to prevent the collision, illustrating that detection and a correct digital route do not guarantee safe outcomes [f10663, f11258]. The research dates the incident to August 2015, although the report's page text does not state an incident date; the web page carries 11 March 2025, and the original report issue date remains uncertain [f10665, f11208, f10666, f11207].

nodes.label: Uber
nodes.text: Uber
nodes.synopsis: The NTSB’s 2019 investigation of Uber’s 18 March 2018 fatal crash in Tempe found that the system detected the pedestrian but failed to classify her or predict her path correctly in time; its design also precluded emergency braking in the relevant condition and relied on operator intervention [f10694, f10695]. The corpus reports emergency recognition 1.2 seconds before impact, a one-second suppression of planned braking, and braking beginning only 0.2 seconds before impact; some chapter accounts explicitly attribute these details to secondary summaries [f15433, f10697, f10698, f10872]. The factory emergency brake was disabled, with a secondary account identifying shared frequencies between Uber’s experimental radar and Volvo’s factory radar as one reason; the booklet raises analogous radio-frequency coexistence questions for multi-OEM sites [f15432, f11255, f11256]. The investigation identified deficient safety risk management, oversight and safety culture, not merely an algorithm error [f10696, f15434, f11270]. The booklet therefore treats intervention timing and organizational oversight as central post-accident evidence, while stressing that the investigation was not a product-liability judgment [f15441, f10699].

The glossary describes its scope as access to machine-generated data for machines sold in Europe from 2027 [f15458]. However, the skeptic’s review and glossary explicitly say that the application dates of the EU Data Act and Cyber Resilience Act were not verified in the research [f10817, f11194, f15485].
